context: It is Lake Vostok -- the largest of Antarctica's roughly 675 known subglacial lakes, about 250 km long by 50 km wide, sealed beneath some 4 km of ice for perhaps 15 million years. On 5 February 2012 Russian scientists finished drilling the longest ice core ever (about 3,768 m) and finally broke through to its surface, water no light had touched in millions of years. Lakes Whillans, Ellsworth, and Concordia are other real subglacial lakes, but far smaller. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Vostok

question: The McMurdo Dry Valleys are a stretch of bare gravel and rock in Antarctica so scoured by wind that snow evaporates before it can settle, and parts may not have seen rainfall in nearly two million years. For decades NASA has trained and tested there because the ground is Earth's closest match to one particular world. Which world?
context: The answer is the surface of Mars. The same katabatic winds that hammer the coast keep the McMurdo Dry Valleys -- about 4,500 sq km, the largest ice-free region in Antarctica -- swept clear of snow, leaving cold, rainless, almost lifeless ground. Since the Viking program, NASA has used the valleys as its closest earthly stand-in for the Martian surface. Taylor Glacier here also feeds 'Blood Falls,' a five-storey outflow stained red by iron-rich brine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMurdo_Dry_Valleys

question: Antarctica has two great ice sheets divided by the Transantarctic Mountains — the East and the West. The larger of the two is so vast that if it alone melted, sea levels around the world would rise by about 60 meters. What is this larger ice sheet called?
context: About 70%. Antarctica's ice sheet -- averaging nearly 1.9 km thick -- holds roughly 90% of all the ice on Earth and close to 70% of the planet's fresh water, all locked frozen on a single continent. Because the vast oceans are salt water, most of the world's drinkable water isn't in lakes and rivers at all; it's stacked as ice at the bottom of the world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica

question: Earth's fresh water is not spread evenly around the globe. If you gathered every bit of ice on the planet into one place, roughly 90% of it would come from a single frozen continent at the very bottom of the world. Locked inside that one ice sheet sits more than 70% of the planet's entire supply of fresh water — more than every river, lake, and glacier elsewhere combined. Which of these is Earth's single greatest store of fresh water?
context: Antarctica holds about 90% of all the ice on Earth and roughly 70% of the planet's fresh water — by far Earth's greatest freshwater store. Greenland's ice sheet is a distant second; Lake Baikal is the largest single body of liquid fresh water but tiny beside the frozen continent. Source: British Antarctic Survey Antarctic factsheet; Wikipedia: Antarctica.

question: Antarctica is buried in ice, so it sounds strange to call it a dry place — but its frozen interior almost never sees new snow. Barely 150 mm of moisture falls across it in an entire year, less than in the scorching Sahara. Geographers count a place as a desert by how little water falls, not by how hot or cold it is, so they count the whole frozen continent as the world's largest of one thing. The world's largest what?
context: A desert is defined by how little precipitation it gets, not by heat. Antarctica's interior receives only about 150 mm (6 in) a year — drier than the Sahara — making the frozen continent the largest desert on Earth. Source: Wikipedia: Antarctica ('a polar desert... about 150 mm of water per year').

question: A home freezer sits at about −18 °C, cold enough to freeze meat solid. On 21 July 1983, a small Soviet research base called Vostok Station, perched high on Antarctica's frozen inland plateau at about 3,488 m of elevation, took its routine daily reading. That reading turned out to be the coldest natural air temperature ever measured anywhere on Earth, and it still stands as the world record today. How cold did the Vostok reading get?
context: Vostok Station's −89.2 °C on 21 July 1983 is the coldest natural temperature ever reliably measured at Earth's surface, confirmed by the World Meteorological Organization. (Satellite readings of about −93 °C over the plateau are a separate, lower figure and are not the same as this ground-station record.) Source: WMO archive; Wikipedia: Vostok Station / Antarctica.

question: Antarctica is the only continent with no native people. No one lives there for good, only scientists who rotate through research stations. In 1959, twelve nations signed a landmark treaty on the continent's future. Under that Antarctic Treaty, who owns Antarctica?
answer: No nation owns it, only science and peace
choices: No nation owns it, only science and peace
The twelve treaty nations, as joint owners
The United Nations, as a neutral trustee
Each nation, in the sector it once claimed
context: The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze every territorial claim and set the whole continent aside for peace and science, banning military bases, mining, and nuclear weapons. No country owns Antarctica; only about 1,000–5,000 scientists live there seasonally, with no permanent residents. Source: Wikipedia: Antarctica (Antarctic Treaty System).

question: The McMurdo Dry Valleys are the largest ice-free area in Antarctica. They are a barren stretch of rock and gravel where liquid water almost never appears and almost nothing grows. Since the 1970s, NASA has trained rovers and drilling gear in the valleys as its closest Earth stand-in for the surface of which world?
context: The Dry Valleys' cold, arid, nearly lifeless terrain is Earth's closest match to the surface of Mars; NASA has tested Mars drilling and rover technology there since the 1970s. At about 4,500 km² they are the largest ice-free region in Antarctica. Source: Wikipedia: McMurdo Dry Valleys.

question: In East Antarctica, from the snout of Taylor Glacier, a slow trickle the deep red of blood seeps out across the pure white ice. When British explorers with Robert Falcon Scott's team first stumbled onto it in 1911, they were unsettled — the crimson stain looked like a wound cut into the glacier. It is not blood at all. Today scientists finally know what colors the water at what they still call 'Blood Falls'. What actually stains it that eerie red?
answer: Iron-rich brine that rusts in the air
choices: Iron-rich brine that rusts in the air
Red algae blooming in the meltwater
Fine red dust blown off the rocks
Pink minerals dissolved from the ice
context: Blood Falls flows from the snout of Taylor Glacier. Iron-rich saltwater, sealed beneath the ice and cut off from air and sunlight for about 1.5–2 million years, oxidizes — literally rusts — the instant it reaches the surface, staining the ice blood-red. Source: Wikipedia: Blood Falls.

question: Antarctica is the frozen continent at the bottom of the world. Under all its snow and glaciers sits ordinary bedrock -- rock like any other continent's -- but you would have to drill through an astonishing depth of ice to reach it. Scientists have measured the ice sheet all across the continent using radar. In Terre Adélie, the French-claimed sector facing the Southern Ocean, the ice reaches its thickest point of all. How deep does it go there?
context: Antarctica's ice averages about 1.9 km thick and reaches its greatest measured thickness of roughly 4,776 m — nearly 3 miles — in Terre Adélie. Source: British Antarctic Survey Antarctic factsheet; Wikipedia: Antarctica.

question: In the 1990s, scientists drilling near Vostok Station confirmed that beneath nearly 4 km of solid ice lies Lake Vostok, a lake of liquid fresh water about the size of Lake Ontario. It has been sealed away entirely from sunlight and air. Roughly how long had this hidden lake been cut off from the outside world?
context: Lake Vostok, about 250 km by 50 km (roughly the area of Lake Ontario), lies under about 4 km of ice near Vostok Station. Scientists estimate it has been sealed from sunlight and the atmosphere for perhaps 15–25 million years, making it a target in the search for hardy microbial life. Source: Wikipedia: Lake Vostok.  (Legend.)

question: On Ross Island in Antarctica, Mount Erebus rises 3,794 m as the southernmost active volcano on Earth. More startling still, its summit crater has held the very same restless feature, ringed by snow and ice, since at least the early 1970s. What does Erebus hold at its summit?
context: Mount Erebus (3,794 m, Ross Island) is the southernmost active volcano on Earth and one of only a handful worldwide with a persistent lava lake, churning in its crater since at least the early 1970s — open fire in the heart of the ice. Its gas plume even carries an estimated ~80 g of gold vapor a day. Source: Wikipedia: Mount Erebus.

question: On Antarctica's high plateau, dense super-chilled air grows heavy and pours down the slopes under its own weight. It funnels through coastal valleys at up to about 300 km/h, among the fiercest sustained winds on Earth. What is the name for these powerful gravity-driven downslope winds?
context: Katabatic winds (from the Greek katabasis, 'descent') form as cold, dense air on the high plateau slides downhill under gravity, reaching about 300 km/h. At Commonwealth Bay, explorer Douglas Mawson (1911–14) endured such ceaseless katabatic gales that he titled his account 'The Home of the Blizzard'; Guinness rates it the windiest place on Earth. Source: Wikipedia: Katabatic wind / Commonwealth Bay.

question: Antarctica's ice sheet weighs trillions of tons, and its immense weight has crushed the continent's bedrock far below sea level. At the Bentley Subglacial Trench the buried rock lies 2,555 m down, the lowest land on Earth that is not under ocean. If all that ice were somehow stripped away, what would happen to the buried bedrock over the thousands of years that followed?
answer: It would slowly rise back upward
choices: It would slowly rise back upward
It would slowly sink even deeper
It would stay fixed at its crushed depth
It would crack apart and drift out to sea
context: The ice's colossal weight has pressed Antarctica's bedrock below sea level in many places — the Bentley Subglacial Trench, 2,555 m down, is the lowest land on Earth not covered by ocean. Freed of the ice, the crust would slowly rebound upward over millennia (in places by roughly 1,500 ft), a balancing of load and buoyancy that geologists call isostasy. Source: Wikipedia: Bentley Subglacial Trench; UAF Geophysical Institute.

question: The extinct Glossopteris tree grew more than 260 million years ago. Its fossils turn up in Antarctica, Africa, South America, India, and Australia. Those matching fossils were the first sign that all these southern lands had once been joined into one huge supercontinent. What was that lost landmass called?
context: Glossopteris fossil forests over 260 million years old show Antarctica was once a green corner of Gondwana, the great southern supercontinent (with today's Africa, South America, India, and Australia). Growing through months-long polar light and dark, the trees slammed from summer growth into winter dormancy in as little as a month. Source: ScienceDaily / National Geographic: Antarctic Gondwana fossil forests (Gulbranson & Isbell).

question: Çatalhöyük was a town in central Turkey almost 9,000 years ago. Its mud-brick houses had no streets between them, and no doors on the sides. The houses were packed together wall-to-wall, like a giant honeycomb pattern. How did a family get inside their own home?
answer: They climbed down a ladder through a hole in the roof.
choices: They climbed down a ladder through a hole in the roof.
They crawled through a low tunnel linking house to house.
They walked in from a shared central courtyard.
They pushed aside a mat over a ground-level door.
context: The flat rooftops were Çatalhöyük's real streets -- its walkways and gathering places -- and every home had a hole in the ceiling with a ladder leading down into one main room. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Çatalhöyük.

question: About 9,000 years ago in south-central Turkey, one of the world's earliest towns rose from the plain. Its name today is Catalhoyuk, and the people there lived crammed together in mud-brick houses so tightly packed there were no streets -- families climbed in and out through holes in the roofs. When someone died, the family folded the body tightly, knees drawn up to the chest, and sometimes wrapped it in a reed mat before burial. Where did they lay their dead to rest?
answer: Under the floors and sleeping platforms of their homes.
choices: Under the floors and sleeping platforms of their homes.
Out in a walled cemetery on the edge of town.
Deep in caves in the hills beyond the fields.
Down in pits dug out in the open fields.
context: So every family slept directly above its own buried ancestors. Years later they sometimes dug a skull back up, plastered it, and painted the face with red ochre to bring back the features of the dead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Çatalhöyük.

question: A wall painting at Çatalhöyük, made about 8,600 years ago, is often called the world's oldest map. It looks like a town seen from above, with a two-peaked volcano erupting behind it. But an archaeologist named Stephanie Meece argued that the shape everyone reads as a volcano is really something ordinary. What did she say it was?
context: Meece's rival reading is a leopard skin above an abstract geometric panel -- not a map at all -- and the debate is still open. Fifty years on, geologists tested pumice from Hasan Dağ and confirmed it really did erupt between about 9,500 and 8,400 years ago, overlapping the painting's age; that revived the 'oldest map' reading without proving it. Source: sci.news/archaeology and pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (Schmitt et al.).  (Legend.)

question: In the ancient Greek city of Athens, a flat-topped limestone rock rises about 70 metres straight out of the streets below, like a natural fortress in the middle of the city. On its summit still stand the marble temples built there roughly 2,500 years ago at the height of classical Greek civilization. Even today, from almost anywhere in modern Athens, you can look up and spot the ancient rock and its ruins. What is this famous rock called?
context: 'Acropolis' means 'high city' (from Greek akron, 'highest point,' + polis, 'city'). This flat-topped limestone rock rises about 70 m above Athens (156 m above the sea) and spans roughly 300 by 150 m on top -- a natural citadel that Athenians crowned with their greatest temples. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acropolis_of_Athens ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Acropolis/

question: The Parthenon is the great marble temple that stands on top of the Acropolis of Athens, built by the Greeks around 440 BC and dedicated to their goddess Athena. Its columns and walls were carved from gleaming white marble. Visitors expect them to shine chalk-white in the strong Greek sunlight, but they are always surprised — tiny traces of iron inside the stone slowly react with air and sun. What does the Parthenon marble do instead?
context: Pentelic marble carries a faint trace of iron; as it weathers, the iron oxidizes and tints the stone a warm honey-gold, so the Parthenon seems to glow in the sun and at dusk. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentelic_marble

question: In ancient Athens, the great marble temple on the rocky hilltop citadel called the Acropolis was built to honor the goddess Athena. That temple, the Parthenon, takes its name from Athena's own title, Athena Parthenos. What does the Greek word parthenos mean?
context: Parthenos means 'maiden' or 'virgin' -- a title of Athena, who in myth never married. Her temple, the Parthenon, is literally the house of the maiden goddess. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_Parthenos ; https://www.worldhistory.org/article/785/athena-parthenos-by-phidias/

question: At the foot of the Acropolis lay the busy public heart of ancient Athens. It was an open square where people came to trade, gossip, and argue. Even the philosopher Socrates would stop passersby here with his endless questions. What was this open square called?
context: 'Agora' means 'gathering place.' The Athenian Agora was the city's civic center -- markets, law courts, and shrines -- and the stage on which its democracy and philosophy played out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Agora_of_Athens

question: On a low hill above the Athenian Agora stands a Doric temple from the 400s BC. Remarkably, it is still almost completely intact, with its roof, columns, and walls all in place, while the ruined Parthenon looms on the rock above. Which temple is this, the best-preserved in all of ancient Greece?
context: The Temple of Hephaestus (the Hephaisteion), god of the forge and metalworkers, was built around 450 BC on the western edge of the Agora. Never destroyed like the Parthenon, it still stands almost whole -- roof and all -- making it the most complete ancient Greek temple in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Agora_of_Athens

question: The Parthenon, the marble temple crowning the Acropolis, looks flawlessly straight and rectangular. Yet its architects, Iktinos and Kallikrates, hid a subtle trick in the marble: hardly a line in the whole temple is actually straight. What did they do to its columns?
answer: they made the columns swell in the middle and lean slightly inward
choices: they made the columns swell in the middle and lean slightly inward
they made the columns taper to a sharp point near the top
they made the columns twist in a slow spiral toward the roof
they made the columns lean slightly outward, over the viewer
context: This is entasis: the columns bulge gently at the middle and tilt inward (their axes would meet more than a kilometer overhead), while the marble floor rises a few centimeters at its center. These deliberate curves trick the eye so the temple LOOKS perfectly straight and alive rather than stiff. Source: https://archeyes.com/the-parthenon-architectural-excellence-of-ancient-greece/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon

question: Building the Parthenon on top of the Athens Acropolis in the 400s BC swallowed some 20,000 tons of pure white marble. Every single block came out of one single mountain and had to be hauled roughly 19 km up onto the sacred rock by ox-cart, sled, and sheer human muscle. Ancient Greek quarrymen even gave the marble itself the name of that mountain. From which mountain did all that gleaming Parthenon marble come?
context: The marble came from Mount Pentelicus (Penteli), source of the fine white 'Pentelic' marble that built the Parthenon. An estimated 20,000-22,000 tons were quarried and dragged some 19 km down to Athens and up onto the Acropolis. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentelic_marble ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon_Frieze

question: On the north side of the Acropolis, a smaller temple called the Erechtheion has a famous 'Porch of the Maidens,' where the marble roof rests not on plain columns but on six calm, graceful stone women, each carrying the weight on her head. What are these sculpted figures called?
context: They are the Caryatids -- six marble maidens on the Erechtheion's Porch of the Maidens (about 421-406 BC). The weathered originals now shelter inside the Acropolis Museum, with copies outdoors; Lord Elgin carried one away to the British Museum in London, where it still stands apart from its sisters. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erechtheion

question: Inside the Parthenon once towered a single image of the goddess Athena, nearly 12 m tall. It was crafted by the sculptor Phidias and dedicated in 438 BC, a treasure so valuable it was later stripped bare and finally lost forever. What two costly materials was this colossal statue made of?
context: This was the Athena Parthenos, made by Phidias of gold and ivory over a wooden frame -- a technique called chryselephantine. About 11.5 m tall, it wore some 40 talents of pure, removable gold and held a small winged Victory in its hand. The statue vanished in antiquity; only small Roman copies survive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_Parthenos ; https://greekreporter.com/2023/09/02/statue-athena-parthenos-acropolis/

question: In the Athenian Agora, once a year, citizens who feared that a single man was growing dangerously powerful could gather and scratch his name onto a broken piece of pottery. If enough of these shards carried the same name, that man was banished from Athens for ten full years. What was this yearly practice of banishment called?
context: This was ostracism. Each year Athenians could vote in the Agora to exile one man for ten years by scratching his name on a potsherd -- an ostrakon -- which is where the word 'ostracism' comes from. Archaeologists have dug thousands of these ballots from the Agora, some bearing the names of Athens' most famous statesmen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Agora_of_Athens

question: For more than 2,000 years the Parthenon stood nearly whole atop the Acropolis. It outlasted empires and served in turn as a Greek temple, a Christian church, and finally a mosque. Its ruin came in 1687 during the Morean War, when a Venetian army besieging the Ottoman garrison on the rock scored a direct mortar hit on the temple. What had the Ottoman soldiers stored inside the Parthenon?
context: On September 26, 1687, a Venetian mortar fired by Francesco Morosini from the nearby Hill of Philopappos struck the gunpowder the Ottomans had stored inside the Parthenon. The explosion blew off the roof, collapsed the temple's center, killed about 300 people, and brought down three-fifths of its carved frieze -- ending more than 2,000 years of near-wholeness in a single instant. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon

question: Scattered across the suburbs of Auckland, New Zealand's biggest city, are about fifty low rounded hills — Mount Eden, One Tree Hill, and dozens more — each rising on its own straight out of the streets and parks. These fifty scattered hills are all the same kind of landform. What are they?
context: Auckland sits on the Auckland Volcanic Field — roughly 53 separate volcanic centres of scoria cones, craters, and lava hills scattered across the city. It is a live basaltic field, still capable of erupting. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_volcanic_field

question: Auckland is the largest city in New Zealand, and it wraps around a huge sheltered natural harbour on the North Island's coast. Its people are famous for owning more boats per person than almost anywhere else on Earth. On a sunny weekend, tens of thousands of small yachts and dinghies can crowd the harbour water at the same time, their white triangles filling the view. What well-earned nickname have people given the city of Auckland?
context: Auckland was officially dubbed the 'City of Sails' in 1985. It has long had more boats per head than almost anywhere on Earth — once about one boat for every three households — with tens of thousands moored around its harbours. Source: ahi.auckland.ac.nz/2021/12/11/whats-in-a-name-calling-auckland-through-time/

question: Just off Auckland, one island volcano is the biggest and youngest of the whole area. It has a near-perfect cone shape and rose straight out of the sea only about 600 years ago. Maori people living nearby actually watched it erupt. What is this young island volcano called?
context: Rangitoto rose from the sea around 1450 CE and is so young its lava makes up about 41% of everything the whole field has ever erupted. Its near-perfect symmetrical shield-cone silhouette is the iconic backdrop to Auckland's harbour. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangitoto_Island

question: When Rangitoto erupted off Auckland, it covered the nearby island of Motutapu in fresh volcanic ash. Later, archaeologists dug between the ash layers. There they found a startling trace of the Maori who had lived beside the volcano. What did they find preserved in the ash?
context: On Motutapu, next to Rangitoto, human footprints were found preserved between layers of Rangitoto's volcanic ash — Maori walking across the fresh ashfall, the clearest evidence that people witnessed the eruption within living memory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangitoto_Island

question: Spread across Auckland are some fifty small volcanoes, and the field follows a strange rule: each eruption builds one brand-new cone at a brand-new place, and once it goes cold that cone never fires again — the next eruption starts over somewhere else entirely. Geologists have a single word for a volcanic field that behaves this way. What is it?
context: A monogenetic field erupts each new volcano at a new vent, then abandons it forever (Rangitoto is the lone repeat, in two phases about 50 years apart). Because of this, geologists expect Auckland's next eruption to break out not from an old crater but at a brand-new, presently unknown location. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_volcanic_field

question: In the far south Pacific lies New Zealand, and Auckland is the country's largest city. It sits on a narrow neck of volcanic land -- an isthmus -- squeezed between two harbours, with dozens of old volcanic cones dotting its skyline. Centuries before European sailors arrived, the Maori already lived on that same isthmus and fought over it because it was such rich ground for kumara gardens, fishing, and trade. In their language they knew the place as Tamaki Makaurau. What does that Maori name translate to?
context: Tamaki Makaurau is usually translated 'Tamaki desired by many' (or 'Tamaki of a hundred lovers'). Its fertile volcanic soils and two harbours made it the most sought-after and fought-over ground in the north. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland

question: Ayutthaya was the old royal capital of Siam. Its kings chose to build the city at the spot where three rivers meet, safely above the reach of the ocean tides. That way, no enemy warship could sail up and attack the capital. What kind of landform did this river-guarded capital stand on?
context: Set on its river island, Ayutthaya was founded in 1350 by King U-Thong (crowned Ramathibodi I) and grew so laced with canals that European traders nicknamed it 'the Venice of the East.' The ring of water was chosen partly because the site sat above the reach of the Gulf of Siam's tides, so enemy seagoing warships could not sail straight up to the walls. Source: UNESCO Historic City of Ayutthaya (whc.unesco.org/en/list/576); Wikipedia, Ayutthaya Kingdom.

question: In the ruins of Wat Mahathat rests the single most photographed sight in all of Ayutthaya, sitting right at ground level. It is something serene and beautifully carved, held tight in the twisting roots of an old fig tree that grew up around it across the centuries. What do the roots cradle?
context: The image is old sandstone. A strangler fig earns its name: it begins as a seed a bird drops high in another tree, then sends aerial roots creeping down the host's trunk that thicken into a lattice and slowly envelop it — here embracing a lost Buddha head. How the head came to rest here is uncertain; by tradition it was simply left among the rubble as the old temple fell into ruin, and the fig did the rest. Thais treat the spot as sacred. Source: Wikipedia, Ayutthaya Historical Park; Britannica, strangler fig; thailand-highlights.com.  (Legend.)

question: At Wat Lokayasutharam in Ayutthaya, a Buddha built of brick and white plaster lies stretched on his side — 42 metres long, longer than a blue whale — his head propped on one hand, calm with eyes half-closed. This great reclining pose marks one exact moment in the Buddha's life. Which moment does it show?
choices: his birth in a grove of trees
the day he gives his first sermon
context: A reclining Buddha traditionally depicts the parinirvana — the Buddha lying on his right side at the end of his earthly life, passing into final Nirvana. This one, of brick and stucco, faces west and is among the largest reclining images in Thailand. Source: thaizer.com; renown-travel.com, Wat Lokaya Sutha.

question: Three tall, bell-shaped stone chedis stand in a perfect line at Wat Phra Si Sanphet, once the grandest royal temple inside Ayutthaya's palace — today the postcard image of the whole ruined city. These towers were all raised for the same solemn purpose. What do they hold?
choices: the crown jewels of old Siam
context: The three chedis are royal reliquaries: they hold the ashes of King Borommatrailokkanat and two of his royal successors. Wat Phra Si Sanphet housed no monks — it was the private royal chapel of the palace. Source: thailandforvisitors.com, Wat Si Sanphet; renown-travel.com.

question: Around 1700, Ayutthaya was one of the largest cities on Earth, with nearly a million people, more than London. Merchant ships arrived from far away. Portuguese, Dutch, Chinese, and Japanese traders all came to do business on the island. How did this river capital house its foreign communities?
answer: each nation had its own riverside quarter
choices: each nation had its own riverside quarter
all foreigners shared one walled compound
foreigners could stay only aboard their ships
traders lived inside the royal palace walls
context: Each foreign community kept its own district strung along the rivers. The Japanese village, Ban Yipun, held about 1,000 people under the mercenary Yamada Nagamasa, whom the king raised to noble rank (Okya Senaphimuk); and a Greek adventurer, Constantine Phaulkon, rose from common sailor to become one of King Narai's most powerful ministers. The near-million population figure (per researcher George Modelski) is an estimate. Source: Wikipedia, Ayutthaya Kingdom; southeastasianarchaeology.com.  (Legend.)

question: Along the brick galleries of Ayutthaya's ruined temples, long rows of stone Buddhas still sit in meditation, but almost every statue is broken in exactly the same way. That is the mark left by Burmese soldiers who overran and looted the capital in 1767. What did the soldiers do to the statues?
context: The invaders decapitated the sacred images and prised the gold from them; the long rows of headless Buddhas are among the ruins' most haunting sights. Source: Wikipedia, Ayutthaya Historical Park; thailand-highlights.com.

question: In 1767 a Burmese army burned Ayutthaya after a long siege, and the ruined island capital was never rebuilt. Instead the Siamese made a striking choice: they moved downstream along the Chao Phraya river and founded a brand-new capital there. Which modern city grew out of that new capital?
context: After a 14-month siege the city fell in April 1767 and its Buddhas were stripped of gold; rather than rebuild on the ruins, the Siamese established a new capital downriver that grew into modern Bangkok. Ayutthaya's roofless temples and toppled towers were left as the ruins that stand today, now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Source: UNESCO Historic City of Ayutthaya (whc.unesco.org/en/list/576); Wikipedia, Ayutthaya Kingdom.

question: At Baalbek in the mountains of Lebanon stand the ruins of the greatest Roman temple ever built, the Temple of Jupiter. Six honey-gold limestone columns still rise there in a row after nearly two thousand years. They are the tallest columns the Romans ever raised on any temple in their whole empire, so tall that a grown adult standing right at the base barely reaches the bottom of a single one. About how tall is one column?
answer: as tall as a six-story building
choices: as tall as a single-story cottage
as tall as a six-story building
as tall as a fifteen-story tower
as tall as a thirty-story skyscraper
context: Each of the six survivors stands about 19.9 m (65 ft) tall and nearly 2.5 m thick -- the largest temple columns anywhere in the Roman world. The Temple of Jupiter once had 54 of them, ten across each end and nineteen down each side; earthquakes and stone-robbers toppled the rest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Jupiter_(Baalbek)

question: The three Trilithon blocks at Baalbek -- each about 800 tonnes and over 19 m long -- sit in the temple's western wall exactly where Roman builders placed them two thousand years ago. One thing about these giant blocks still astonishes visitors today. What is it?
answer: the blocks fit so tightly no knife blade slips between them
choices: the blocks were floated to the site down a river canal
the blocks fit so tightly no knife blade slips between them
the blocks are carved with the names of the men who cut them
the blocks are hollow inside to reduce their great weight
context: A knife blade still won't slide into the joints between the three Trilithon blocks, set in the western podium wall over 4 m up. They rest on a lower course of about two dozen 'smaller' foundation stones -- each of those still weighs around 300 tonnes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Jupiter_(Baalbek)

question: In the quarry just outside Baalbek lies a colossal cut block of about 1,000 tonnes that Roman workers shaped but abandoned -- it was never dragged to the temple. For centuries local people have known this stranded giant by a vivid nickname. What is it called?
answer: the Stone of the Pregnant Woman
choices: the Stone of the Pregnant Woman
context: The 'Stone of the Pregnant Woman' (Hajar al-Hibla) still lies in the quarry, roughly 1,000 tonnes (some estimates up to 1,200). Folk legends say a pregnant woman, or a race of giants, once lifted it -- but in truth it was simply left where Roman quarrymen carved it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baalbek_Stones

question: Archaeologists working at Baalbek in Lebanon long knew that the Romans began the enormous Temple of Jupiter there around 16 BC — but no one could pin down when the huge building was finally finished. The answer, about AD 60 under Emperor Nero, was eventually settled not by any grand imperial inscription but by a small, surprising clue that an ordinary workman had left behind on the stones. What was that clue?
answer: a line of graffiti scratched by a worker
choices: a hoard of coins buried in the foundation
a dedication carved in the emperor's honor
a line of graffiti scratched by a worker
a sundial set into the temple floor
context: The completion date was fixed from a scratch of graffiti a worker left on one of the topmost column drums -- so the temple took roughly 75 years to raise. Everyday marks like this often date ancient buildings more precisely than grand official inscriptions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Jupiter_(Baalbek)

question: Baalbek's builders had already set 800-tonne blocks into the temple wall -- but in 2014 a German Archaeological Institute team found an even greater one at the ancient site: a single limestone block roughly 19.6 m long and about 1,650 tonnes. What record does the Baalbek block hold?
answer: the largest stone block ever cut by human hands
choices: the largest stone block ever cut by human hands
the largest stone block ever polished by human hands
the largest stone block ever moved by human hands
the largest stone block ever raised by human hands
context: A German Archaeological Institute team led by Jeanine Abdul Massih measured the block at about 19.6 m long, 6 m wide, 5.5 m high, and roughly 1,650 tonnes -- the largest stone ever cut by people anywhere on Earth. It was carved but never dragged from the quarry: flawed limestone at one edge meant it might crack if anyone tried to move it, so it still lies exactly where the quarrymen shaped it -- which is why it holds the record for the largest block ever CUT, not moved or raised. Source: heritagedaily.com; smithsonianmag.com; archaeology.org

question: Baalbek's 800-tonne Trilithon stones sit inside a Roman temple that Roman builders raised, so the real puzzle is not WHO moved them but HOW. One engineer calculated that about 512 men could drag a stone of more than 500 tonnes across the ground. In his reconstruction, what did those men rely on?
context: No one has proved exactly how Rome's crews shifted the 800-tonne Trilithon, and that open question is genuine -- but the answer is human, not alien: the megaliths lie beneath a temple Roman builders demonstrably raised. Engineer Jean-Pierre Adam calculated that about 512 men working capstans (rope-winding drums) and pulley blocks could drag a 557-tonne stone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baalbek

question: In the ancient city of Babylon, around 575 BC, King Nebuchadnezzar II raised a huge ceremonial city gate called the Ishtar Gate, named for the Babylonian goddess of love and war. Its whole face glowed a deep, brilliant blue. Thousands of glazed clay bricks had been fired to match the color of the most prized blue gemstone of the ancient world, mined far away in the mountains of Afghanistan. Which precious blue stone did the Ishtar Gate imitate?
context: Facing an entire city gate in the color of lapis lazuli -- one of the ancient world's most treasured stones -- announced Babylon's wealth to everyone who approached. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ishtar_Gate/

question: Babylon, with its towering ziggurats and its dazzling blue Ishtar Gate, was one of the greatest cities of the entire ancient world, ruling the plain of Mesopotamia around 600 BC. Its ruins still lie today in the country of Iraq, about 85 km south of the modern capital Baghdad. The city was built right on the banks of one of Mesopotamia's two great rivers. On which river did ancient Babylon rise?
context: Babylon stood near the modern Iraqi town of Hillah, and the Euphrates ran through the very heart of the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon

question: Rows of golden animals stride across the Ishtar Gate's deep-blue walls: wild bulls, lions, and a stranger scaly beast called the mushhushshu, with a serpent's head and a flicking forked tongue. The lions belonged to the goddess Ishtar. The dragon was the sacred beast of which of Babylon's gods?
context: Marduk was Babylon's supreme god, and the mushhushshu was his guardian creature; the wild bulls on the gate honored the storm-god Adad. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishtar_Gate

question: The mushhushshu, the sacred dragon striding across the Ishtar Gate, is stitched together from several animals. It has a snake's scaly body and forked tongue, a horned and crested head, and powerful front legs taken from a lion. Its two hind feet come from a very different creature. What are the mushhushshu's back feet?
context: This snake-lion-eagle mix made the mushhushshu one of the strangest monsters in all of ancient art; its Sumerian name means roughly 'furious serpent.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mushhushshu

question: The very name of the ancient Mesopotamian city Babylon comes from two Akkadian words, Bab-ilim, spoken by the Babylonians themselves more than three thousand years ago in what is now Iraq. For centuries, both the Babylonians and the later scholars who read their clay tablets took those two little words together to name something grand and holy, something that fit a city full of temples and ziggurats. What was Bab-ilim traditionally taken to mean?
context: Modern scholars think this is a folk etymology laid over an older, forgotten name -- but for the ancients, Babylon was the gate of the gods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon

question: King Nebuchadnezzar II, who raised the Ishtar Gate around 575 BC, left a proud inscription carved on it. He wrote that he had set wild bulls and fierce dragons upon the gate for one reason above all others. By his own words, why did he cover the gate in beasts?
answer: so that people might gaze on them in wonder
choices: so that people might gaze on them in wonder
so that no enemy would dare approach
so that the gods would guard the city
so that his name would never be forgotten
context: His dedication reads that he adorned the gateways 'with luxurious splendor so that people might gaze on them in wonder.' Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ishtar_Gate/

question: Here is the strange twist of the Ishtar Gate: the towering blue gate you can walk through today is not in Iraq at all. Archaeologists dug up its shattered bricks in the early 1900s, carried them thousands of miles away, and rebuilt the whole 14-meter gate indoors inside a world-famous museum. In which museum can you visit the Ishtar Gate today?
context: The archaeologist Robert Koldewey excavated the gate's bricks between 1902 and 1914, and the reconstruction was finished in Berlin in 1930. Even so, only the smaller front gate was rebuilt -- the original was a far larger double gate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishtar_Gate

question: A grand ceremonial road ran straight out through Babylon's blue Ishtar Gate toward the great temple of the Babylonian god Marduk. Its high walls were glazed with rows of striding golden lions that seemed to march along beside every traveler who walked the road. The Babylonians gave this Processional Way a proud, boastful name in their own tongue — 'Aibur-shabu.' What did that Babylonian name actually mean?
choices: The sun shall never set here
The road shall shine with gold
context: The road ran over half a mile out to the Bit Akitu, the New Year festival house; each spring the statue of the god Marduk was carried in procession down it and out through the gate. Source: https://madainproject.com/processional_street

question: The Bible tells of the Tower of Babel, a great tower built to reach the sky. Behind that story most likely stood a real structure in Babylon: a colossal stepped temple-tower, or ziggurat, whose name meant 'the foundation of heaven and earth.' What was this real ziggurat called?
context: Etemenanki was dedicated to Marduk and rebuilt by Babylon's kings. Centuries later Alexander the Great ordered the crumbling tower torn down to be rebuilt grander -- but he died in 323 BC before the work was done. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etemenanki

question: When the archaeologist Robert Koldewey uncovered the Ishtar Gate, its lions and bulls were unmistakably real animals -- which made him wonder about the mushhushshu dragon striding among them. In 1918 he suggested the strange beast might be modeled on a real creature known only from fossils. What did Koldewey compare the mushhushshu to?
context: Koldewey reasoned that if the gate's lions and bulls were real animals, the dragon might be too -- perhaps a dinosaur remembered in legend. Most scholars, though, think the mushhushshu was always a purely mythical guardian. Source: https://new-cryptozoology.fandom.com/wiki/Sirrush

question: Babylon's most famous wonder is one that nobody has ever found. The fabled Hanging Gardens, counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, have left no ruins and no foundation anywhere in Babylon's soil. The Oxford scholar Stephanie Dalley argues the gardens were real but bloomed at a different Mesopotamian city entirely. Which city does she name?
context: Legend said King Nebuchadnezzar II built the gardens for his homesick wife, Queen Amytis, who missed her green mountain homeland -- but the Hanging Gardens are the only one of the Seven Wonders whose site has never been confirmed. Dalley argues the real gardens were built by the Assyrian king Sennacherib at Nineveh. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon

question: About a thousand years ago the kings of the Bagan Empire ruled a stretch of what is now central Myanmar. To gain merit for the next life, they and their nobles kept building brick temples -- one after another -- along the wide Irrawaddy River. At dawn today, hot-air balloons float up over the Bagan plain as the mist clears. Temple spires poke out of the trees in every direction. About how many temples still stand there today?
context: Over 2,200 brick temples and pagodas still stand on the Bagan plain today, scattered along a bend of the Irrawaddy River. The famous dawn balloons -- Balloons Over Bagan has flown the dry-season skies since 1999 -- drift over the whole misty field as the sun comes up. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagan)

question: When Bagan was the capital of the Pagan Kingdom, from 1044 to 1287, its kings covered the plain with brick monuments. The 2,000 that still stand today are only the leftovers. How many temples, pagodas, and monasteries had been built across the plain at the kingdom's peak?
context: At its height, more than 10,000 temples, pagodas, and monasteries rose on the Bagan plain during the Pagan Kingdom (1044-1287). Centuries of neglect, looting, and earthquakes have since thinned them to the roughly 2,200 that survive. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagan)

question: Bagan's most beloved temple is a whitewashed shrine crowned with a golden spire, completed in 1105 under King Kyansittha. Down its dim inner corridors stand four gilded Buddhas, each over 9 metres tall, one facing each point of the compass. By what name is it known?
context: The Ananda Temple, finished in 1105 under King Kyansittha, is Bagan's best-loved shrine. Its four standing gilded Buddhas each rise 9.5 m (31 ft) and face north, south, east, and west; the spires were re-gilded for the temple's 900th anniversary in 1990. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ananda_Temple)

question: Bagan's largest temple, the brooding Dhammayangyi, was raised around 1167 by King Narathu. Legend says he had murdered his own father and brother to seize the throne, and that guilt drove him to demand masonry so flawless that no gap could be found between the great blocks. Any mason whose work fell short was executed. According to the legend, what was Narathu's cruel test for a tight-enough joint?
answer: Whether a needle could pass between two blocks
choices: Whether a needle could pass between two blocks
Whether water could seep through the seam
Whether a hair could be drawn through the gap
Whether daylight showed through the joint
context: Dhammayangyi (built about 1167-1170) is the largest temple on the Bagan plain, and its brickwork really is famously tight. Legend says King Narathu, atoning for murdering his father and brother, had masons executed wherever a needle could be pushed between two bricks -- historians treat this as folklore. Its inner sanctums were later bricked up, for reasons still unknown. (Source: havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/dhammayangyi-temple-bagan-myanmar)

question: Bagan sits in an active earthquake belt, and on 24 August 2016 a magnitude-6.8 quake rippled across the plain in a single day, cracking spires and toppling temple tops among its roughly 3,250 monuments. When the shaking stopped, how many of them had been damaged?
context: A magnitude-6.8 earthquake struck central Myanmar on 24 August 2016, damaging nearly 400 of Bagan's roughly 3,250 monuments in a single day. Bagan sits in an active seismic zone, and repeated quakes over the centuries are one reason so few of the plain's thousands of original temples still stand. (Source: phys.org/news/2016-08-quake-scores-myanmar-heritage-bagan.html)

question: From a dawn balloon, the Bagan plain glows a warm red-brown -- spire after spire the colour of rust stretching to the horizon, quite unlike the pale grey monuments of many other great temple cities. What is almost every one of Bagan's temples built from?
context: Almost every structure at Bagan is brick, not the carved stone of Cambodia's Angkor Wat or Java's Borobudur -- which is why the plain reads as a forest of red-brown spires rather than grey stone towers. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagan)

question: In 762 the caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad on the Tigris and named it Madinat al-Salam, the 'City of Peace.' He placed his palace and the main mosque at the dead center, with four gates opening toward distant cities. Al-Mansur gave the whole capital one bold geometric shape rarely used for a city. What shape was al-Mansur's Baghdad?
context: Al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 and named it Madinat al-Salam, the 'City of Peace.' His perfectly round capital took about 100,000 workers and roughly 18 million gold dinars to build, with four gates named for the roads to Kufa, Basra, Damascus, and Khorasan and the caliph's palace at the exact center. Nothing of the Round City survives today -- its circular walls have left virtually no trace. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_City_of_Baghdad

question: Baghdad rises on the Tigris, one of two great rivers, with the Euphrates, that run down through the land now called Iraq. The ancient Greeks gave the whole region cradled between these rivers one famous name, and there the world's first cities and first writing were born. What did the Greeks name this region?
context: Mesopotamia is Greek for 'the land between the rivers' (mesos, 'middle,' and potamos, 'river'). This region between the Tigris and Euphrates -- now Iraq -- is called the cradle of civilization: the world's first cities, the first writing (cuneiform), and the wheel appeared here, and far older cities like Babylon, Ur, Uruk, and Nineveh rose in the same land. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesopotamia

question: Caliph al-Ma'mun ruled Baghdad in the early 800s. He treasured the scholars at his House of Wisdom, who were translating Aristotle, Euclid, and the Greek doctors into Arabic. Legend says he rewarded every finished translation with one remarkable prize. What is al-Ma'mun said to have paid for a completed book?
context: By legend, al-Ma'mun (ruled 813-833) loved learning so much that he paid a translator the weight of each finished book in gold. Under him Baghdad's House of Wisdom became the greatest repository of books in the world, carrying Greek, Persian, and Indian works -- Aristotle, Plato, Euclid, Hippocrates, Galen, and the Indian astronomer Brahmagupta -- into Arabic. Source: https://www.1001inventions.com/house-of-wisdom/

question: Around 820, a Baghdad mathematician named al-Khwarizmi wrote a founding book on solving equations, and he helped bring a new way to write numbers into the world. Two everyday English words trace back to him -- one from his book's title, one from his own name. Which two words did al-Khwarizmi give us?
context: Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780-850) wrote 'Al-Jabr' around 820; its title word al-jabr ('restoration') became ALGEBRA, and he is called the father of algebra. His own name, Latinized as 'Algoritmi,' became ALGORITHM. He also introduced the Hindu-Arabic numerals and the decimal place-value system -- the digits and the zero we still use -- which reached Europe through 12th-century Latin translations. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khwarizmi

question: In 1258, the Mongols under Hulagu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, stormed Baghdad and destroyed the libraries that had made it the world's capital of learning. A famous chronicler said the Tigris River was stained for days by what the Mongols hurled into it. According to that account, what did the Tigris run with?
answer: black with the ink of books
choices: black with the ink of books
red with the blood of the slain
white with the ash of scrolls
context: Hulagu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, sacked Baghdad in February 1258. So many books were thrown into the Tigris that chroniclers said the river 'ran black with ink' -- a dramatic traditional claim some modern historians dispute. The last Abbasid caliph, al-Musta'sim, was rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses on 20 February 1258, because the Mongols had a taboo against spilling royal blood on the ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad_(1258)  (Legend.)

question: Almost nothing of golden-age Baghdad survives -- al-Mansur's first capital and the House of Wisdom are long gone. But one Abbasid college, founded in 1227, still stands on the bank of the Tigris and was old enough to live through the Mongol sack of 1258; a modern Baghdad university revived its name in 1963. What is this rare survivor, among the oldest universities still standing on Earth?
context: The Mustansiriya Madrasa was founded by Caliph al-Mustansir in 1227 and survived the 1258 Mongol sack, making it among the oldest universities on Earth still standing. Its name was revived by a modern Baghdad university in 1963. With the Round City and the House of Wisdom gone, the Mustansiriya and the Tigris/Mesopotamia setting are among the few pieces of golden-age Baghdad you can still visit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mustansiriya_University

question: On Bali's south coast, the Uluwatu temple clings to a sea-cliff high above the waves. What does the name 'Uluwatu' mean in Balinese?
context: The name joins two Balinese words - 'ulu' (tip, edge, or head) and 'watu' (rock or stone) - so Uluwatu means the very end of the rock, the temple perched where Bali's land drops away into the sea. Source: Wikipedia, 'Uluwatu Temple'.

question: The Indonesian island of Bali is ringed with a chain of Hindu sea-temples, built centuries ago to be seen from the water and to guard the whole coast. One of the most famous, Tanah Lot on Bali's southwestern shore, sits alone on a single great rock right at the shoreline. Its very name in the Balinese language means 'land in the sea.' Twice a day the ocean around it changes dramatically. What actually happens to Tanah Lot when the tide comes in?
answer: the rising sea cuts it off as an island
choices: the rising sea cuts it off as an island
the waves break clean over its shrine roof
its hidden sea-caves boom and throw up spray
a rolling mist rises and hides it from shore
context: Tanah Lot means 'land in the sea'. Perched on a lone rock offshore, it is one of Bali's guardian sea-temples, meant to be seen and worshipped from the water; at high tide the sea closes around it, and it can only be reached on foot once the tide falls again. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tanah Lot'.

question: As the sun sets on the Uluwatu cliff, up to 150 bare-chested men pack into a circle. By firelight they chant 'cak-cak-cak' and act out an ancient story. This famous Balinese fire-dance, the Kecak, is missing something almost every other dance has. What is it?
choices: there is no costume of any kind
there is no leader to cue them
context: The interlocking 'cak' of the chorus does the work of a whole gamelan - no drum, no gong, no strings, just up to 150 voices as the entire orchestra. The Kecak was shaped in the 1930s by Balinese dancer Wayan Limbak with German painter Walter Spies, built around an older trance ritual to retell the Ramayana epic. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kecak'.

question: Below Bali's volcanoes, whole hillsides are carved into glowing green rice terraces. For over a thousand years, water running down from the peaks has been shared among farmers by a network of canals, weirs, and small water-temples. Groups of 50 to 400 growers meet to agree on who gets each drop. The United Nations honored this living system in 2012. What is it called?
context: The Subak dates back to the 9th-11th century; today around 1,559 of them cover Bali, each led by an elected chairman called a 'pekaseh' who makes sure every member farmer gets a fair share of the water. UNESCO named the Subak landscape a World Heritage Site in 2012 (Cultural Landscape of Bali Province, #1194). Sources: Wikipedia, 'Subak (irrigation)'; UNESCO World Heritage List #1194.

question: Bali's famous terraced rice paddies grow in some of the richest volcanic soil on Earth, and the source of that richness towers over the whole Indonesian island — the still-active volcano Mount Agung, Bali's highest peak at 3,031 metres. Every so often the mountain erupts violently and coats the countryside below. What does the volcano give to the fields that makes them so astonishingly fertile?
answer: the ash it showers on the fields
choices: the ash it showers on the fields
the minerals dissolved in its springs
the pumice it scatters down its slopes
the clay left by its old lava flows
context: Volcanic ash weathers into some of the most fertile soil on Earth, which is why farmers cluster around volcanoes worldwide. At 3,031 m, Mount Agung is Bali's highest peak, and the Balinese revere it as a replica of Mount Meru, the cosmic mountain and home of the gods. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mount Agung'.

question: High in Bali's cool northern mountains, Lake Batur -- the island's largest lake and its chief source of water -- fills part of an ancient volcanic basin ringed by highlands. The still-smoking cone of Mount Batur rises from the same basin floor, and the lake-goddess temple Pura Ulun Danu Batur stands on the shore. What do geologists call this kind of large landform?
context: A caldera is the huge bowl left behind when a volcano's summit collapses into the emptied magma chamber below - far larger than an ordinary summit crater. Batur's caldera measures about 10 by 13 kilometres. Cradled inside it, Lake Batur is Bali's largest lake and the chief source of the island's water, and on its shore stands Pura Ulun Danu Batur, dedicated to Dewi Danu, goddess of the lake, honoured as the wellspring that feeds every rice terrace below. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Mount Batur'; 'Pura Ulun Danu Batur'.

question: The Balinese did not scatter their water-temples at random. Across Bali's terraced rice-lands, each small temple stands exactly where a spring first rises or where one channel forks in two - the very points that decide who downstream receives water. This careful placement follows a Balinese philosophy of harmony among three things: people, nature, and the divine. What is that guiding philosophy called?
context: Tri Hita Karana means 'the three causes of well-being' - harmony among people (pawongan), nature (palemahan), and the divine (parhyangan). Because the divine and the land must stay in balance, the water-temples sit precisely at the springs and forks that govern the flow, turning the whole terraced valley into a single machine of faith and farming. Sources: UNESCO World Heritage List #1194; Wikipedia, 'Subak (irrigation)'.

question: Bangkok is the capital of the kingdom of Thailand, in Southeast Asia. Its full ceremonial name — a single unbroken Thai word 168 letters long — is listed by Guinness World Records as the longest place name anywhere on Earth. Ordinary Thais would never say the whole thing in daily speech. Instead they simply call their capital by two short words, Krung Thep. What does the everyday nickname Krung Thep mean?
context: Krung Thep is only the start of Krungthepmahanakhon, the 168-letter name that opens 'City of angels, great city of immortals...' Centuries ago foreign traders found the older village name 'Bangkok' easier to pronounce, so the world kept it while Thais use the grand one. Source: Guinness World Records; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangkok

question: Old Bangkok, the capital of the kingdom of Thailand, was laced with hundreds of narrow canals called khlongs. Vendors paddled between floating markets. Most ordinary people got around by wooden boat, not by road. In the 1800s, charmed Western travellers gave the Thai capital a nickname borrowed from a famous canal-city on the other side of the world in Italy. Which European water-city did they compare Bangkok to?
context: 'The Venice of the East,' Westerners called it. Floating markets still sell fruit and goods from boats on the water, and the Chao Phraya River remains the city's great watery highway. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chao_Phraya_River

question: Thailand's most sacred image, the Emerald Buddha, sits high on a golden altar in the royal chapel inside Bangkok's Grand Palace. For all its fame, the little figure is not carved from emerald at all. From what single block of stone was it truly carved?
context: It is one block of deep-green jade (nephrite); 'emerald' describes only its color. Legend credits the sage Nagasena with making it in 43 BCE, but scholars date the carving to about the 15th century. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_Buddha

question: Across the Chao Phraya River from the Grand Palace rises Wat Arun, the 'Temple of Dawn.' Its steep central spire climbs about 70 metres above the water. Up close the tower glitters, because builders coated it in millions of bits of an unexpected material. What is it?
context: The shards were broken Chinese porcelain that had reached Bangkok as ballast weighting empty trading ships; masons pressed the colorful pieces into the spire's plaster. The temple is named for Aruna, the Hindu god of the dawn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Arun

question: The Emerald Buddha is the most sacred and most fiercely guarded Buddha image in Thailand. It sits high on a soaring golden altar inside Bangkok's Grand Palace. Pilgrims gazing up at that towering shrine expect a figure grand enough to match it. How tall is the Emerald Buddha itself, head to crown?
context: Just 66 cm (26 inches) tall, the Emerald Buddha is dwarfed by the vast golden hall around it — a reminder that in Thailand this image's power lies in its holiness, not its size. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_Buddha

question: A short walk from the Grand Palace, inside Bangkok's Wat Pho, a single gilded Buddha lies stretched on its side, 46 metres head to toe — so vast that visitors must walk its full length to take it all in. The glowing giant looks like solid gold, but that is only a skin of gold leaf. What is the huge statue built from underneath?
context: The Reclining Buddha measures 46 metres long and 15 metres high — brick and plaster covered in gold — among the largest Buddha images in Thailand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Pho

question: The Emerald Buddha owns three glittering golden costumes — one for the hot season, one for the rainy, one for the cool — and at each turn of the seasons it is solemnly re-dressed. By ancient custom, only a single person in all Thailand is permitted to climb up and change its robes. Who?
context: Only the King — or a senior royal standing in for him — may climb up to change the headdress, in a ceremony that marks each change of season. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_Buddha

question: When the Thai king Rama I founded his brand-new royal capital in the year 1782, he laid it out on an island in the Chao Phraya River around a small, modest old village that already stood on the ground, called Bang Makok. That humble village name — the very root of the word 'Bangkok' the whole world still says today — was in ordinary Thai and simply named a fruit tree that grew there. What did Bang Makok mean?
context: 'Makok' is the olive-plum tree, so 'Bang Makok' meant the place where it grew. Rama I ringed the island with canals and named the new royal district Rattanakosin, 'Jewel of Indra,' after the Emerald Buddha it would come to house. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rattanakosin_Kingdom

question: The Reclining Buddha of Wat Pho ends in two colossal flat feet, each sole five metres long and divided into 108 squares. Every square holds a sacred emblem of a Buddha: lotus flowers, white elephants, dancers, and tigers. What shimmering material is used to decorate these 108 panels?
context: Each sole is inlaid with 108 mother-of-pearl panels showing the lakshanas — the auspicious signs by which a Buddha is recognized. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Pho

question: Wat Pho is honored as the birthplace and national school of one traditional Thai art, so treasured that its teachings were carved onto stone tablets and figures around the temple. Its academy has since trained practitioners now working in 145 countries. Which art began here?
context: Wat Pho's stone tablets and figures recording the body's healing lines make it the acknowledged home of Nuad Thai (traditional Thai massage); its school has trained more than 200,000 therapists who now practice in 145 countries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Pho

question: Bangkok has almost no high ground. The whole city spreads across the flat lowland at the end of the Chao Phraya River's 372-kilometre course, where its waters finally reach the Gulf of Thailand — land lying so close to sea level that heavy monsoon rains routinely send water into the streets. Geographers have a specific name for the kind of landform that Bangkok is built on. What is it?
context: A delta is the low, flat, fan-shaped land a river builds by dropping its load of mud and sand where its current slows and meets the sea. The 372-kilometre Chao Phraya's delta is why Bangkok sits barely above sea level and floods so easily, and why the old city was threaded with canals rather than roads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chao_Phraya_River

question: In the Spanish city of Barcelona, the Catalan architect Antoni Gaudi began work on a huge spired Catholic church in the year 1882. Builders were still working on that same church more than 140 years later, and even today it is not yet finished — one of the longest continuous building jobs anywhere in the world. Millions of tourists visit every year to watch it slowly rise higher above the city. What is this famous unfinished church called?
context: The Sagrada Família's first stone was laid on 19 March 1882. For over 140 years it remained a working building site — one of the longest construction projects in human history — as generation after generation of Barcelonans carried on Gaudí's design. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sagrada Família' (corroborated by Grokipedia).

question: The Catalan architect Antoni Gaudi spent the last forty years of his life pouring himself into building the Sagrada Familia church in Barcelona, Spain. He actually lived on the building site itself and turned down every other paying job that came his way. When a passing tram struck him down in the street in 1926, he was buried inside the very church he had begun. What loving nickname did the people of Barcelona give him?
context: Antoni Gaudí (1852–1926) grew so single-mindedly devoted to the Sagrada Família that he became known as 'God's Architect.' He lies buried in a crypt beneath the basilica he never saw finished — at his death, less than a quarter of it had been built. Source: Wikipedia, 'Antoni Gaudí.'

question: In February 2026, workers in Barcelona lifted the last arm of a giant cross onto the Sagrada Familia's central tower. That made it the world's tallest church. The old record had stood since 1890, held by another towering church. Which one did the Sagrada Familia finally pass?
context: The Tower of Jesus Christ tops out at 172.5 m, edging past Germany's Ulm Minster (161.5 m), which had reigned as the world's tallest church since 1890. The tower first overtook Ulm on 30–31 October 2025; the top arm of its cross was set in place on 20 February 2026 — exactly 144 years after building began. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Sagrada Família' and 'List of tallest church buildings'; My Modern Met (2026).

question: Antoni Gaudi was the deeply Catholic Catalan architect of the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona, Spain. When he set the final height for the church's tallest central tower, he laid down a strange and humble rule for himself. The tower had to stand exactly one metre below the top of Montjuic, the tallest natural hill inside Barcelona. Why did Gaudi refuse to let his own tower rise any higher than that hill?
answer: so no work of man would rise above the work of God
choices: so no work of man would rise above the work of God
so the tower would better survive strong sea winds
so it would not overshadow Barcelona's old cathedral
so sailors could still sight Montjuïc from far out at sea
context: Gaudí capped his central tower one metre below the summit of Montjuïc, Barcelona's highest natural hill, because he believed the work of man should never stand taller than the work of God. Even now, as the world's tallest church, the Sagrada Família bows to Barcelona's own hill. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Sagrada Família'; ArchDaily (2026).  (Legend.)

question: Step inside the Sagrada Familia and Gaudi's stone columns lean apart and split as they rise. Each one divides into several thinner shafts high overhead to hold up the roof without heavy outside supports. Gaudi said he had not built a plain hall of pillars at all, but a stone version of one particular kind of natural place. What did Gaudi say his soaring interior was meant to be?
context: Gaudí conceived the nave as a stone forest: the branching, tree-like columns carry the vaults from within, so the Sagrada Família needs none of the external flying buttresses that prop up the walls of a Gothic cathedral. Source: Wikipedia, 'Antoni Gaudí' (corroborated by Grokipedia).

question: The Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí spent decades designing the vast Sagrada Familia basilica in Barcelona. To find the exact curves that would let his heavy stone arches stand without cracking or toppling, he hung little bags of birdshot from a web of cords until they sagged into perfect natural loops. Then, to read his design, he did one surprising thing to the whole sagging model. What did Gaudí do?
answer: he turned the whole model upside down
choices: he turned the whole model upside down
he froze it solid over one winter
he traced its shadow onto a wall
he studied it only in a mirror
context: The shape a chain makes when it hangs freely is called a catenary. Flipped upside down, that same curve lets stone stand in pure compression — no tension, no cracking. Gaudí built these hanging birdshot models for the Colònia Güell church and used the principle throughout the Sagrada Família. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Antoni Gaudí'; Grokipedia, 'Sagrada Família.'

question: The Sagrada Família stands inside the Eixample, the vast grid of streets that engineer Ildefons Cerdà drew across Barcelona in 1859. From above, Cerdà's grid looks unlike an ordinary checkerboard: every single city block has its four corners sliced flat, so each block becomes an octagon. Why did Cerdà cut the corner off every block?
answer: to open up light, air, and sightlines at every crossing
choices: to open up light, air, and sightlines at every crossing
to trace the line of the old city walls
to let rainwater drain straight to the sea
to echo the floor plan of Catalan cathedrals
context: Those cut-off corners are called chamfers. Cerdà's chamfered (octagonal) blocks let in more light and air, opened up sightlines, and — in the horse-and-carriage era — gave vehicles room to turn at each junction. The Eixample's octagon blocks are one of the most recognizable city grids on Earth. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eixample.'

question: On the Indonesian island of Java, a craft called batik has been practiced for many centuries. To make a piece of batik cloth, the artist first draws a design onto plain fabric using hot melted wax dripped from a small copper spouted tool called a canting. Then the whole cloth is soaked in a bath of colored dye. Only after the dye dries is the wax boiled off. Why does the artist lay down the wax first?
answer: It blocks the dye, so the covered areas stay uncolored
choices: It blocks the dye, so the covered areas stay uncolored
It soaks up the dye, so the covered areas turn darkest
It stains the covered areas a brighter shade
It softens the cloth so the dye spreads more evenly
context: This is wax-RESIST dyeing, the heart of batik. The wax is not paint and adds no color of its own — it simply protects the cloth so those lines can't take the dye. When the wax is later removed, the hidden pattern surfaces pale against the colored ground. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batik

question: The finest batik on Java is drawn by hand with a tool called the canting. It is a tiny copper cup of hot wax with a thin spout, held on a handle and trailed over the cloth like a pen. The trouble is that the hot wax keeps hardening and clogging the narrow tip. To clear it and keep drawing, what does the artisan often do?
answer: Blow through the tip to push the wax out
choices: Blow through the tip to push the wax out
Dip the tip in cold water to loosen it
Scrape the tip clean with a knife blade
Tap the cup sharply against the wax pan
context: Hand-drawn batik is 'batik tulis' — written batik — and the canting (say 'chan-ting') is its pen: a copper reservoir (the nyamplung) ending in a spout (the cucuk) on a wooden handle. A quick puff of breath through the spout clears a clog without interrupting the line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canting

question: Drawing every wax line by hand with the canting can take a Javanese artist weeks or months for a single cloth. In the 1800s, workshops found a way to make batik far faster: instead of drawing the wax line by line, they pressed the whole pattern on in one go. What tool made that possible?
context: The stamp is the 'cap' (pronounced 'chop'), and cloth made this way is 'batik cap.' One press lays down a whole repeating block of the pattern, so a workshop can produce in a day what hand-drawing would take weeks to do. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batik

question: On the Indonesian island of Java, artists make patterned cloth called batik by drawing their designs onto the fabric with hot melted wax and then dyeing it. By the very end of the whole batik process the finished cloth actually looks a mess — its beautiful pattern is still buried under a hard crust of dyed wax and is completely invisible to the eye. The very last step, called nglorod, is what finally makes the design appear. What is that last step?
answer: Boiling the cloth so the wax melts away
choices: Boiling the cloth so the wax melts away
Scrubbing the cloth with sand and stones
Peeling the hardened wax off by hand
Freezing the cloth so the wax cracks off
context: In nglorod the cloth is boiled in hot water, often with soda ash (sodium carbonate), to melt off every trace of wax and reveal the once-hidden pattern. Because the wax can be laid on thick, this washing-out can take days. Source: iwarebatik.org/batik-production-process/

question: In the royal courts (keraton) of Yogyakarta and Surakarta on Java, only the sultan and his family could wear the grandest batik designs — like the diagonal parang — and the court could punish any commoner caught in one. A single length of cloth showed at a glance who was royal and who was not. What were these royalty-only patterns called?
context: These reserved patterns were the larangan — literally 'forbidden.' The parang was the classic example, and it came ranked by scale: the grandest, Parang Barong, belonged to the reigning sultan alone, while the smaller, more delicate Parang Klitik was worn by the royal princesses. In 1785 Sri Sultan Hamengku Buwono I of Yogyakarta declared Parang Rusak a larangan motif. Source: sonobudoyo.jogjaprov.go.id; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parang_(batik)

question: A Javanese legend traces the parang pattern to Sultan Agung, the great 17th-century king of Mataram. The story says he designed it while meditating at Parangtritis on Java's southern coast. Watching one thing there for hour after hour, he shaped its endless diagonal chain. What was his inspiration, in the story?
answer: The waves crashing against the cliffs
choices: The waves crashing against the cliffs
A column of soldiers on the march
context: This is a legend, not documented history. The parang is a row of interlocking S-shapes running on a diagonal; the name comes from the Javanese 'pereng' (a slope or cliff), and the unbroken chain is said to symbolize continuity — striving that never stops, like the sea forever chopping at the rocks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parang_(batik)

question: The diagonal parang, born in the royal courts of Java, carries a fierce, warlike energy: its unbroken chain of S-shapes reads like a blade chopping without pause — the pattern of kings and warriors. For that reason, Javanese tradition warns guests never to wear parang to one particular celebration. Which one?
context: By tradition the parang's battle-energy — its endless 'chopping' — is believed to foreshadow conflict, so wearing it to a wedding is thought to risk strife between the newly married couple. This is folk belief, not fact: the very S-chain that symbolizes a king's unceasing struggle is what makes it feel wrong at a celebration of union. Source: seasia.co/2025/10/07/the-paradox-of-parang-why-a-noble-batik-is-taboo-at-weddings  (Legend.)

question: At the center of Beijing stands the largest palace complex on Earth. It covers 72 hectares and holds about 8,700 rooms and 980 halls, wrapped in a moat 52 metres wide. For five centuries, emperors ruled from inside, and ordinary people were kept out. What is this vast walled palace called?
context: Begun in 1406 and finished in 1420 under the Ming Yongle Emperor, the Forbidden City housed 24 emperors until 1924. It sprawls across 72 hectares with about 980 surviving buildings and roughly 8,700 rooms -- the largest and best-preserved palace complex in the world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City

question: In old Beijing, the walled capital of China's emperors for more than five hundred years, you could pick out which grand buildings belonged to the emperor himself just by looking down at the color of the glazed roof tiles from a high perch. One single shade was reserved by law for the throne alone — any ordinary person caught using that color on their own roof faced a harsh imperial punishment. Which color glowed on the imperial royal roofs of old Beijing?
context: Golden-yellow was the emperor's exclusive color, so the Forbidden City's roofs shine gold while common Beijing roofs stayed grey. One grand exception: the Temple of Heaven's Hall of Prayer wears deep-blue tiles to echo the sky. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City

question: In the heart of Beijing stands the Forbidden City, the vast palace where China's emperors lived and ruled for nearly 500 years. A famous legend says its builders counted out exactly 9,999 and a half rooms -- half a room short of a full ten thousand on purpose. In old China, ten thousand was a sacred number. According to the tale, why would no emperor allow his own palace to reach a full 10,000 rooms?
answer: ten thousand rooms belonged to Heaven's palace alone
choices: ten thousand rooms belonged to Heaven's palace alone
ten thousand was a number that invited bad luck
the workers ran out of timber before finishing
imperial law forbade counting rooms past 9,999
context: In the tale, the full 10,000 rooms belonged to the Jade Emperor's palace in Heaven, so an earthly ruler stopped at 9,999 1/2 rather than match the gods. A 1973 on-site survey actually counted about 8,707 rooms (980 buildings, 8,886 bays) -- the 9,999 figure is folklore, not fact. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City; chinahighlights.com/beijing/forbidden-city/  (Legend.)

question: The Forbidden City's grand south gate rises about 38 metres from a red U-shaped wall, crowned with five watchtower pavilions. Only the emperor himself was allowed to walk through the tall central archway at its base. What is this great front gate called?
context: The Meridian Gate (Wumen), nicknamed the Five-Phoenix Tower for its five pavilions, is the tallest and grandest of the Forbidden City's gates. Only the emperor could use the central archway; officials and princes filed through the smaller side passages. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian_Gate

question: The Temple of Heaven's Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests is a round tower of wood, 38 metres tall beneath three stacked roofs, first raised in 1420. Carpenters and engineers still travel to study one astonishing feature of how it was built. What is that feature?
answer: it stands without a single nail
choices: it stands without a single nail
it is the tallest timber tower in China
it is the oldest surviving hall in Beijing
it was raised in a single year
