context: A massive earthquake in 1303 loosened the Great Pyramid's smooth white Tura-limestone casing, and medieval Cairenes carted it away to build the city -- into structures such as Sultan al-Hasan's mosque (1356) and, later, Muhammad Ali's Alabaster Mosque -- leaving the stepped stone core we see today. Source: thevintagenews.com; scienceinsights.org

question: When the Fatimid general Jawhar founded a brand-new royal capital in Egypt in 969 AD, he named it after a planet that was rising in the sky at that very moment -- a planet the Arabs called al-Najm al-Qahir, 'the Conquering Star.' From that name comes Cairo's Arabic name, al-Qahira, 'the Victorious.' After which planet was Cairo named?
context: Cairo's Arabic name, al-Qahira ('the Victorious' or 'the Vanquisher'), comes from al-Najm al-Qahir, 'the Conquering Star' -- the planet Mars -- which was rising in the sky as the Fatimid general Jawhar founded the city in 969 AD. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo  (Legend.)

question: The ancient Egyptians called their country Kemet, 'the Black Land,' after the dark, rich soil that fed their whole civilization -- set against the barren 'Red Land' desert stretching away on either side. What natural event laid down this fertile black soil, year after year?
answer: the Nile's yearly flood, dropping fresh silt
choices: the Nile's yearly flood, dropping fresh silt
ash blown in from distant volcanoes
rotting reeds from the river marshes
fine dust carried on the desert winds
context: The Nile's yearly flood spread a fresh layer of black silt across the valley, making Egypt astonishingly fertile; Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'the Black Land,' set against Deshret, 'the Red Land' of the surrounding desert. Source: historycollection.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deshret

question: Table Mountain rises straight up behind Cape Town, its summit a broad, level plateau rather than a peak. On many days a low white cloud forms along the top and pours slowly over the mountain's front edge, hanging there for hours before it burns off in the sun. Capetonians long ago gave this recurring cloud an affectionate nickname. What do they call it?
context: That draping cloud is Cape Town's beloved 'tablecloth,' formed when moist sea air is forced up the slope and cools into cloud right at the rim, then spills over and vanishes in the warmer air below. Locals say the mountain has 'laid its tablecloth.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain; hiketablemountain.co.za.

question: Cape Town has a playful old legend to explain Table Mountain's cloud. Long ago, they say, an old Dutch pirate named Jan van Hunks sat smoking his pipe on the mountain. A stranger showed up and dared him to a smoking contest. For days they puffed away, and their smoke piled higher into a huge white cloud. Too late, van Hunks saw who his rival really was. In the legend, who had he been smoking against?
context: In the folktale the stranger was the Devil, and a lightning bolt ended their duel; when the 'tablecloth' pours over Table Mountain, Capetonians joke that Jan van Hunks and the Devil are at it again. It is legend, not history. Source: awoltours.co.za; the-legends.fandom.com/wiki/Jan_van_Hunks.

question: Above the city of Cape Town in South Africa rises the huge flat-topped peak called Table Mountain. Ride the cable car to the top and climb over the warm sun-baked rocks. You will almost surely meet its most common little mammal -- round and plump, with no tail, about the size of a big guinea pig. It naps in the sun. What do locals call it?
context: The dassie, or rock hyrax, is a plump, tail-less little mammal that lives in colonies among the warm summit rocks and is the animal visitors spot most often on top of Table Mountain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain; awoltours.co.za.

question: Most people reach the top of Table Mountain by cable car. The cars first opened in 1929. They glide up the cliff in under five minutes and can hold 65 people at a time. They are one of only a few of their kind in the world, thanks to one strange thing they do on every trip. What is unusual about Table Mountain's cable cars?
answer: the floor rotates a full turn
choices: the floor rotates a full turn
the two cars pass midway up
the roof opens for the view
the cabin is walled in glass
context: Since 1997 the cableway's 'Rotair' cars have a floor that spins a full 360 degrees during the climb, so all 65 passengers see the whole panorama without moving — one of only a handful of rotating cableways on Earth. The cableway first opened on 4 October 1929. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain_Aerial_Cableway.

question: The cableway sets visitors down near one end of Table Mountain's flat top, but that spot is not quite the mountain's highest. The true summit lies a little higher, out across the broad plateau, and reaching it means a walk of a few kilometres over the level rock. By what name is this true high point of Table Mountain known?
context: Maclear's Beacon, a stone cairn about 1,086 m (3,563 ft) high, is the true summit of Table Mountain — a little higher than the upper cableway station. Sir Thomas Maclear built it in 1865 as a trigonometrical survey station. Devil's Peak, Lion's Head and Signal Hill are the neighbouring heights around the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain.

question: In South Africa, right above the city of Cape Town, rises Table Mountain -- a huge flat-topped sandstone plateau visible from ships far out at sea. Its slopes are not covered in tall forest. Instead, low tough bushes and bright wildflowers grow all over the rocky ground, blooming in a hundred shapes and colors. The Dutch-descended settlers who came to the Cape gave this special shrubland its own Afrikaans name. What is it called?
context: Fynbos — Afrikaans for 'fine bush' — is the fine-leaved, flower-rich shrubland that makes up about 80% of the Cape Floral Kingdom and cloaks most of Table Mountain. Chaparral, maquis and matorral are its cousins in California, the Mediterranean and Chile. Source: wwf.panda.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fynbos.

question: Table Mountain rises straight above Cape Town in South Africa. Its flat top is only a few square miles wide -- tiny compared to a whole country -- yet botanists have counted about 2,200 different kinds of wild flowering plants growing on it. The island nation of Britain, hundreds of times larger in area, has its own well-known list of native flora. How does Table Mountain's plant count stack up against Britain's?
answer: it beats the whole of Britain's flora
choices: it beats the whole of Britain's flora
it holds about half of Britain's flora
it holds about a tenth of Britain's flora
it matches one English county's flora
context: Table Mountain National Park holds over 2,200 flowering-plant species — more than the roughly 1,490 native species of all Great Britain — with about 90 of them found nowhere else on Earth. Source: nature-reserve.co.za; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain_National_Park.

question: Botanists divide all the plant life on Earth into just six great 'floral kingdoms.' One of the six is the Cape Floral Kingdom, the fynbos realm of the Cape of Good Hope. Among the six, this Cape kingdom holds one record all its own. Which record is it?
context: The Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of Earth's six floral kingdoms (with the Antarctic, Australasian, Boreal, Neotropic and Palaeotropic), yet the richest for its size; the wider Cape Floristic Region became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. Source: wwf.panda.org; southafricatourism.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Floristic_Region.

question: Table Mountain's flat crown is armoured with a pale, extremely hard sandstone. Geologists date this rock to a time so ancient — very roughly half a billion years ago — that when its sand was first settling on an old sea floor, one whole great branch of life had not yet made its home on dry land anywhere on Earth. Which group of living things had not yet moved onto the land when Table Mountain's sandstone was forming?
context: Table Mountain Sandstone is hard quartzitic rock laid down in the Ordovician period, roughly 450-510 million years ago. Land plants were only just beginning to green the continents; the first animals would not crawl ashore for tens of millions of years yet. Hundreds of millions of years of erosion then planed the summit dead flat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain.

question: Look north from Table Mountain's top and you'll see a low, flat island in the bay. For most of the 1900s, South Africa's apartheid government used it as a prison. Nelson Mandela was held there for 18 of his 27 years in jail before he walked free in 1990. What is this prison island off Cape Town called?
context: Robben Island — Dutch for 'seal island' — sits in Table Bay within sight of the summit. The apartheid government imprisoned Nelson Mandela there for about 18 of his 27 years, forcing him to labour in a glaring limestone quarry that damaged his eyes; he walked free in 1990 and became South Africa's first democratically elected president. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robben_Island; history.com.

question: In the volcanic region of Cappadocia in central Turkey, thousands of skinny stone cones called fairy chimneys still stand tall against the sky. Their pale rock is soft, and wind and rain should have worn the cones flat long ago. Yet each cone wears a dark cap. What sits on top of each cone and keeps it from wearing down?
choices: a knot of thick tree roots
context: Each fairy chimney is capped by a chunk of harder rock. Wind and rain wear the soft rock (volcanic tuff) around it far faster, but the hard cap shields the column directly beneath -- so the pillar survives as a tall cone wearing a stone 'hat.' Turkish speakers call them peri bacalari, 'fairy chimneys.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy_chimney; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia

question: In the volcanic region of Cappadocia in central Turkey, an entire underground city called Derinkuyu had been sealed off and forgotten for so long that nobody knew it was there. In 1963, a local Turkish villager broke through into an unknown dark space right inside his own home, and stumbled into the lost city. What was he doing when he found it?
answer: knocking down a wall in his basement
choices: knocking down a wall in his basement
digging out a deeper water well
chasing a stray goat into a crack
context: In 1963 a resident of Derinkuyu, renovating his home, knocked through a basement wall and found a passage leading into a vast underground network no one had used for centuries. The site opened to visitors in 1969. Source: interestingengineering.com/culture/derinkuyu-underground-city-turkey

question: Cappadocia's pale 'tuff' -- rock made from the ash of ancient volcanoes -- is soft enough that people carved whole homes and churches into it with simple hand tools. Stranger still is what the freshly cut rock does once air reaches the newly exposed surface. What happens to tuff then?
choices: it crumbles back into loose ash
it swells up and seals its own cracks
context: Freshly cut tuff is soft enough to carve with hand tools, but exposure to the air hardens its surface into durable stone -- ideal for rooms meant to last. Cappadocia's tuff came from three ancient volcanoes, Mount Erciyes, Mount Hasan, and Golludag, which buried the region in ash millions of years ago. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia

question: In the Cappadocia region of central Turkey, farmers digging a wall behind their house in 1963 broke through into a huge hidden chamber. It turned out to be one entrance to Derinkuyu, an ancient underground city carved out long ago as a refuge from raiders. You might picture an underground hideout as a cellar just a few steps down. But Derinkuyu plunges level beneath level into the soft volcanic rock, with stables, kitchens, chapels, and wells on each floor. Roughly how far down does its lowest floor reach?
context: Derinkuyu descends about 85 meters -- as deep as an 18-story building is tall, but going downward. Its carved levels could shelter as many as 20,000 people at once, along with their livestock and stores of food. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city

question: Most of Derinkuyu's tunnels stay within Derinkuyu itself, linking level to level and room to room. But one passage, chipped through solid volcanic rock for some eight kilometers, runs far past its outer edge. What lies at the far end of that hand-cut tunnel?
context: The tunnel leads to Kaymakli, a second underground city -- so Derinkuyu was never alone. Roughly 8 to 9 kilometers of hand-cut passages join the two, letting people travel from one buried city to the other without ever surfacing. Kaymakli holds its own marvels, including a single block of hard andesite drilled with 57 holes, used to cold-work copper ore deep underground. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaymakli_Underground_City

question: Derinkuyu is a vast underground city carved into the soft volcanic rock beneath Cappadocia in central Turkey, dug centuries ago as a hiding place from invaders. Deep inside, its defenders needed to seal off a narrow passage in seconds when raiders broke in -- a barrier they could shut from within, but that no attacker could shove open from the far side. What kind of door did they devise for this?
answer: a huge round stone rolled across the passage
choices: a huge round stone rolled across the passage
a thick oak slab banded with iron bars
a heavy portcullis of iron-tipped stakes
a hinged gate cast from solid bronze
context: Each level of Derinkuyu could be blocked by a great disc of stone, like a millstone -- up to about 1.5 meters across and weighing around half a ton -- rolled across the tunnel from the inside, so raiders could not pull it open. A small hole cut through the center let defenders jab spears out at anyone trying to force through. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city; loveexploring.com; thetravelbunny.com

question: Derinkuyu, the ancient underground city carved into the soft volcanic rock beneath Cappadocia in central Turkey, plunged eight storeys or more into the earth. Thousands of people and their animals could crowd into its deepest levels and stay hidden for weeks at a time -- yet so far below ground, the air should have grown stale and deadly. What kept fresh air flowing all the way down to the lowest floors?
answer: a hidden network of shafts running up to the surface
choices: a hidden network of shafts running up to the surface
great fires kept burning to draw out the stale air
gangs of workers pumping air down with huge bellows
cloth fans waved all day long by the children
context: More than 50 narrow ventilation shafts pulled fresh air down to Derinkuyu's lowest floors. One shaft, about 55 meters deep, doubled as a well -- and it could be sealed off from below, so an enemy laying siege from above could not reach or poison the defenders' water. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city; interestingengineering.com/culture/derinkuyu-underground-city-turkey

question: In the Cappadocia region of central Turkey, whole valleys are full of pale stone cones taller than houses. Long ago, ash from ancient volcanoes hardened into soft rock, and wind and rain wore it down unevenly, leaving these cones behind. Many still wear a single dark boulder on top like a hat, protecting the softer rock underneath from the weather. What do the locals of Cappadocia call these cones?
context: Their Turkish name is peri bacalari, 'fairy chimneys.' Some rise as tall as about 40 m (130 ft). Source: Smithsonian, 'Turkey's Fairy Chimneys' (smithsonianmag.com/travel/fairy-chimneys-turkey-180956654/).

question: In the volcanic region of Cappadocia in central Turkey, families have lived inside the pale rocky cliffs and stone cones for centuries. Kitchens, bedrooms, stables, and even whole hidden churches are all cool cave rooms cut into the stone. Today some are turned into cave hotels for travelers. How did people first make these rooms?
answer: by carving the rooms into solid rock by hand
choices: by walling off the mouths of natural caves
by carving the rooms into solid rock by hand
by tunneling into old collapsed lava tubes
by digging pits and roofing them with slabs
context: Cappadocia's soft rock let people hollow homes and churches straight out of the cliffs by hand; many of those rock rooms are now cave hotels. Source: Much Better Adventures, 'How Cappadocia's Fairy Chimneys Formed' (muchbetteradventures.com/magazine/cappadocia-fairy-chimneys/).

question: In central Turkey there is a region called Cappadocia, famous for its strange stone cones and its underground cities. The name Cappadocia is very old -- older than the Romans, older than the Greeks who wrote it down -- and its real meaning is not certain. But one folk story is loved by many. It says the name comes from an old Persian phrase meaning the land of what?
context: The beloved folk etymology reads 'Cappadocia' as 'land of beautiful (or good) horses,' but modern scholars doubt it and favor a meaning closer to 'place below' -- the low country. Legend. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cappadocia' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia).

question: Millions of years ago, two nearby volcanoes -- Mount Erciyes and Mount Hasan -- buried the region of Cappadocia in central Turkey under deep layers of ash. Over long ages the ash hardened into a pale stone. It is soft enough that a person with a hand tool can carve a room out of it, yet firm enough to hold up a 40-metre fairy-chimney cone for many centuries. What do geologists call this hardened ash rock?
context: The rock is tuff -- compacted volcanic ash. Mount Erciyes, central Anatolia's tallest peak at 3,916 m, was one of its sources. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cappadocia' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia).

question: One of the most famous travel sights in the world happens over the region of Cappadocia in central Turkey at dawn. Dozens of them lift off the valley floor at once -- great colored bulbs of fabric filled with hot air heated by roaring burners -- and float above the pale stone cones called fairy chimneys. Riders standing in wicker baskets watch the cone-covered land glow at sunrise. What fills the dawn sky here?
context: Cappadocia is one of the world's top spots for hot-air ballooning, letting visitors see the same soft-rock cones from above. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cappadocia' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia).

question: Left bare, Cappadocia's soft tuff washes away quickly in the rain -- so why do thousands of cones still stand tall, each with a hard boulder balanced on its tip? The hard cap shelters the column directly beneath it while the rock all around is stripped lower and lower. Geologists have one name for this process. What is it?
context: This is differential erosion. The cones were NOT 'blown' into shape by wind; each hard basalt cap simply protects the soft tuff beneath it from rain while surrounding rock wears down. Source: Much Better Adventures (muchbetteradventures.com/magazine/cappadocia-fairy-chimneys/).

question: In 1963, a man in the Cappadocian town of Derinkuyu was renovating his house when he broke through a wall and found a mysterious hidden room behind it. That accident led to something staggering that had lain forgotten beneath the whole town for centuries. What was down there?
answer: a whole city carved deep underground
choices: a flooded cavern lake and hot springs
a whole city carved deep underground
a buried Roman arena and its stone seats
a royal tomb stuffed full of gold
context: Derinkuyu is an underground city carved about 18 levels deep, roughly 85 m (280 ft) down. Since the 1963 rediscovery, 600+ tunnel entrances have been found in the area. Source: Wikipedia, 'Derinkuyu' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city).

question: Among Goreme's rock-cut chapels, one is nicknamed the 'Dark Church' for its single tiny window. That gloom once seemed a defect, but it proved a gift: the church's 11th-century Byzantine frescoes are the best-preserved in all Cappadocia, still glowing in blue, red and gold. Why did being so dark protect them?
answer: sunlight never reached the pigments to fade them
choices: sunlight never reached the pigments to fade them
raiders could not find the chapel in the gloom
cool dark air kept mould from ever taking hold
lamp smoke sealed the paint under a hard glaze
context: The Dark Church (Karanlik Kilise) in the Goreme Open-Air Museum: its lack of windows kept out the sunlight that fades pigment, so its mid-11th-century frescoes stayed vivid. Source: Peter Sommer Travels, 'Goreme' (petersommer.com/blog/archaeology-history/goreme).

question: Derinkuyu, the ancient underground city carved into the soft volcanic rock beneath Cappadocia in central Turkey, was more than a cellar. It was a full city cut down into the stone, with stables, wells, chapels, storerooms, and rooms for pressing wine and oil. When invading armies swept through Cappadocia, roughly how many people could climb down and live in Derinkuyu with their animals?
context: Derinkuyu could shelter around 20,000 people plus their animals and food, with stables, wells, wine and oil presses, cellars, chapels, and a barrel-vaulted room used as a religious school. Source: Wikipedia, 'Derinkuyu' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city).

question: When invaders found the entrances to Derinkuyu, its people could still shut them out level by level. Each floor was sealed with a special door: a huge round slab of stone, like a half-tonne millstone with a hole bored through its middle, rolled across the passage. What was the crucial trick about these doors?
answer: they could only be rolled shut from the inside
choices: they rang a warning bell when an enemy pushed them
they could only be rolled shut from the inside
they were so smooth that attackers slid off them
they swung wide at the touch of a hidden lever
context: The round stone doors weighed up to 500 kg and had a hole through the center; they sealed each level from the INSIDE, so defenders could lock invaders out floor by floor. Source: Wikipedia, 'Derinkuyu' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city).

question: Sheltering 85 metres down, at the foot of Derinkuyu's roughly 18 levels, should have meant stale, deadly air -- yet thousands could hide there for long stretches. The builders had threaded a hidden system through the entire warren of tunnels to fix that. What kept even the deepest levels breathable?
answer: a network of shafts bored up to the open surface
choices: giant leather bellows pumped by teams of workers
a network of shafts bored up to the open surface
fires kept burning to draw fresh air downward
hollow reed pipes running out to the hillsides
context: More than 50 ventilation shafts -- plus a well plunging about 55 m -- kept the lowest levels of Derinkuyu breathable and watered, so thousands could live underground for long stretches. Source: Wikipedia, 'Derinkuyu' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city).

question: In Peru's dry Supe Valley stand six great pyramids of packed earth. The town around them, called Caral, was built about 2600 BC — the same years Egyptian workers were stacking the Great Pyramid of Giza clear across the world. Among all the ancient towns of North and South America, what is Caral known as?
answer: the oldest city in the Americas
choices: the oldest city in the Americas
the largest city in the Americas
the highest city in the Americas
the driest city in the Americas
context: Radiocarbon dating of the reeds and the woven 'shicra' carrying-bags used to haul stone puts Caral's building at about 2627 BC — as old as, or older than, Egypt's Step Pyramid of Saqqara — yet the two civilizations rose with no contact between them. Caral lies about 182 km north of Lima and only 23 km from the Pacific, and was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009. Source: Wikipedia, 'Caral'.

question: About 2600 BC, in Peru's dry Supe Valley, a few thousand people built the town of Caral around six great pyramids of packed earth. It is the oldest city known in the Americas. But diggers there keep coming up empty on one thing found in almost every other city its size. Which of these has never been found at Caral?
context: Archaeologists have found no defensive walls, no weapons, and no mutilated bodies at Caral — no signs of war. Important: this is an absence of EVIDENCE, not proof that Caral was ever perfectly peaceful; it means these particular signs simply have not turned up. Source: Wikipedia, 'Caral'.  (Legend.)

question: About 5,000 years ago, along the dry Pacific coast of what is now Peru, people built the city of Caral -- one of the oldest cities in all of the Americas, older even than Egypt's Great Pyramid. It had pyramids, plazas, and sunken circular courts. One big surprise from Caral's ruins was a stash of 32 small objects, each one carefully carved from the wing and leg bones of condors and pelicans. They date to about 2170 BC. What were they?
context: The 32 bone flutes were accompanied by 37 cornetts (a kind of horn) carved from deer and llama bone. They are among the oldest wind instruments ever found in the Americas, and mark Caral as a deeply musical, ceremonial city. Source: Wikipedia, 'Caral'.

question: Caral, in Peru's Supe Valley, is the oldest city known in the Americas — built around 2600 BC, at the same time as Egypt's Great Pyramid. Its two most famous spots sit right in front of its biggest earthen pyramids. Each is a wide ring dug into the ground with a low wall around it, big enough for the whole town to gather inside for a ceremony. What is this signature Caral space called?
context: Caral has two of these sunken circular plazas — round courts dug below ground level: one at the foot of the Great Pyramid's staircase, and a second fronting the Pyramid of the Amphitheatre. Ringed by low walls, they let crowds gather for ritual below the towering earthen mounds. Source: Popular Archaeology, 'Caral: America's Oldest City'.

question: The mighty Inca ran their whole empire without an alphabet. They tracked their people, taxes and records on a special counting device. At Caral, a city 4,000 years older than the Inca, diggers found what may be the oldest known example of that device. What is it called?
context: A quipu (also spelled khipu) is a set of knotted cotton or wool cords, where the position and type of each knot recorded numbers and information. Remarkably, Caral had no pottery at all — a 'preceramic' city that left almost no art — yet its people knotted cords to keep records. Archaeologist Ruth Shady said the find points to a knotted 'writing' tradition in the Andes lasting some 4,500 years. Sources: gogeometry.com; Wikipedia, 'Norte Chico civilization'.  (Legend.)

question: Caral, in Peru's Supe Valley, is the oldest city known in the Americas, built about 2600 BC. It stood on a dry desert shelf only 23 km from the Pacific. Its people traded with the coast, hauling dried anchovies and sardines back up the valley. Above every other, one crop was the backbone of Caral's trade. Which was it?
context: Caral's economy ran on cotton — but not for eating. The people grew it to make fishing nets and textiles, then traded the cotton (alongside crops like squash and beans) down to Pacific fishers for their catch of anchovies and sardines. Unlike most later American civilizations, Caral was not built on maize. Source: Wikipedia, 'Norte Chico civilization'.

question: About 6,000 years ago, near the village of Carnac on the coast of Brittany in northwest France, Stone Age farmers cut more than 3,000 tall pillars of local granite and dragged them across the fields to set them upright. It is the biggest field of standing stones on Earth. How do they stand?
context: Near the little town of Carnac in Brittany, more than 3,000 menhirs — a menhir is a single upright standing stone — march across the fields in long parallel rows, not in a ring like Stonehenge. It is the largest field of standing stones anywhere on Earth, hewn from local granite by Neolithic farmers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnac_stones

question: On the coast of Brittany in northwestern France stand the stones of Carnac -- more than 3,000 huge upright rocks arranged in long straight rows across the countryside. Early Neolithic farmers dragged them into place, one generation after the next, starting even before they had metal tools. Now line Carnac up against the world's other famous old sites. Where does it fall in time?
answer: raised long before Egypt's pyramids and Stonehenge
choices: raised long before Egypt's pyramids and Stonehenge
built in the same age as the pyramids and the Sphinx
raised a few centuries after Britain's Stonehenge
younger than Rome's Colosseum and aqueducts
context: The Carnac stones were raised during the Neolithic, roughly 4500-3300 BC, by some of Europe's earliest farming people — centuries before Stonehenge's great circle and before the Egyptian pyramids. Standing among them, you are looking at monuments older than almost any other famous wonder on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnac_stones

question: Near the village of Carnac on the Brittany coast of France stand more than 3,000 tall granite pillars, set up in long rows about 6,000 years ago by Stone Age farmers. In the 1900s a Scottish engineer named Alexander Thom studied those rows for years. He came away with one bold idea about why the ancient people set them up. Other scholars still argue over it. What did Thom think Carnac was built to be?
answer: an observatory for the sun and moon
choices: an observatory for the sun and moon
a great market for trading tribes
context: Scottish engineer Alexander Thom spent years surveying Carnac and argued that its rows form a giant ancient observatory, with stones aligned to key sunrises and moonrises at the solstices. It is the most famous theory about the site — but it is disputed and has never been proven. In truth no one knows why Neolithic people raised thousands of menhirs in rows: an astronomical calendar, ceremonial processions, territory markers, and honoring the ancestors have all been proposed, and the purpose remains genuinely unsolved. Source: https://cparici.com/en/carnac-alignments-guide/; https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/antiquity/article/abs/lunar-observatory-hypothesis-at-carnac-a-reconsideration/

question: A short way from Carnac, at Locmariaquer, Neolithic people raised the Grand Menhir — at nearly 21 metres tall and around 330 tons, the largest single standing stone any prehistoric people ever set upright. Yet a visitor today never sees it looming over the fields. Why not?
answer: it lies toppled, broken into four huge pieces
choices: it lies toppled, broken into four huge pieces
it slowly sank deep into the coastal marsh
later builders carried it off for their stone
an earthquake toppled it into the open sea
context: At Locmariaquer, a short way from Carnac, Neolithic people around 4700 BC raised the Grand Menhir Brise — about 20.6 m (68 ft) tall and roughly 330 tons, the largest single standing stone any prehistoric people ever set upright. Its name means 'the Great Broken Menhir': a few centuries later it fell and shattered into four huge pieces, and today it lies toppled on the ground. Whether it was deliberately pulled down or thrown by an earthquake is still argued. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locmariaquer_megaliths; https://www.worldhistory.org/Locmariaquer/

question: The village of Carnac sits on the Brittany coast of France, ringed by more than 3,000 tall standing stones set up by Stone Age farmers. In the great burial mounds nearby, raised more than 6,000 years ago, archaeologists found polished ceremonial axe-heads of beautiful green jade laid beside the region's most powerful dead. Where had the green stone for those axes come from?
answer: from the Alps of central Europe
choices: from the Alps of central Europe
from the beaches of Carnac itself
from Egyptian traders across the sea
context: Beside Carnac rises the Saint-Michel tumulus, the largest burial mound in continental Europe. Inside its chambers the high-status dead were buried with treasures carried from far away: polished axe-heads of jade from the Alps, and beads and pendants of green callais (variscite) from Iberia. Moving such prized stone hundreds of miles shows these were powerful, hierarchical peoples more than 6,000 years ago. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Michel_tumulus; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnac_stones

question: Carnac's thousands of menhirs so mystified people that once only magic seemed to explain them. Breton legend supplies a vivid answer, starring Saint Cornelius, a holy man with one miracle left to work. According to the old story, what are these standing stones?
answer: a pagan army turned to stone as it marched
choices: a pagan army turned to stone as it marched
a forest of trees turned to stone long ago
a company of giants turned to stone at dawn
a wedding party turned to stone mid-dance
context: This is folklore, not history. A Breton Christian legend says Saint Cornelius (Saint Cornely), fleeing a whole pagan Roman army, reached the shore and turned the soldiers to stone — which is why the menhirs stand in ranks like marching men. A local variant credits the wizard Merlin with petrifying a Roman legion. Both are folk tales invented to explain the strangely orderly rows, not real accounts of how the stones were raised. Source: https://www.solosophie.com/carnac-stones/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnac_stones

question: Cartagena sits on the Caribbean coast of Colombia in South America. Beginning in the 1500s, the Spanish ringed the old town with 11 km of thick stone wall to keep out pirates raiding from the sea. The tops of those walls are so wide that Cartagenans use them as part of daily life. What do the tops serve as today?
context: Las Murallas took shape in stages from 1614 to 1796, and the ramparts are so thick that their tops became public space to walk and gather on. Cartagena's walled old town and forts were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Colombia

question: Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast of Colombia, was the most walled city in Spain's American empire in the 1500s and 1600s. Stone rings and a fort guarded every side. All those walls guarded one thing every Caribbean pirate craved. Waiting in the harbor for the yearly fleet home to Spain was what?
choices: gold from the West African coast
context: Cartagena was Spain's treasure vault on the Caribbean: American silver was gathered here for the yearly fleet home, which is exactly why the crown walled and fortified the city so heavily — the treasure drew the pirates. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Colombia

question: Above Cartagena stands Castillo San Felipe, often called the greatest fort the Spanish ever built in the New World. Its walls rise about 41 meters tall. To build it, the Spanish used a stone found right around Cartagena, not shipped from Europe. What is San Felipe mostly built of?
context: Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, on the Hill of San Lazaro, rises about 41 m (135 ft) and is widely called the greatest fortress the Spanish built in the New World. Much of it was raised from coral mined out of the region's reefs, its walls wide at the base and narrowing to the parapet. Source: https://www.frommers.com/destinations/cartagena/attractions/el-castillo-de-san-felipe-de-borajas/

question: Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast of Colombia, was the most walled Spanish city in the Americas. The great hilltop fort of San Felipe, built by the Spanish in the 1600s to guard the town from pirates, is full of narrow tunnels cut through its heart. The Spanish shaped those tunnels so well that the guards had one strange edge over any attacker. What could the defenders do because of the tunnels?
answer: hear approaching enemies through the stone
choices: hear approaching enemies through the stone
keep the powder magazine cool and dry
hide troops to spring a counterattack
context: San Felipe is riddled with galleries built so that sound carried along them; by tradition, defenders could hear an enemy's footsteps coming. Some chambers were even mined so they could be blown up to bury attackers who broke inside. Source: https://www.frommers.com/destinations/cartagena/attractions/el-castillo-de-san-felipe-de-borajas/  (Legend.)

question: Cartagena's harbor had two sea gates: a wide one and a narrow one called Bocachica. In 1741, the Spanish captain Blas de Lezo faced a huge British fleet of nearly 200 ships. He funneled them into the narrow gate under his guns. To block the channel, what did Blas de Lezo do?
answer: sank his own ships across it
choices: sank his own ships across it
threw a bridge of boats across it
packed it with rafts of burning tar
context: The Spanish sealed the wide Bocagrande and forced attackers through the narrow Bocachica, straight under the 49 guns of Fort San Luis. In the channel Blas de Lezo scuttled ships and strung a chain boom across it to obstruct the passage. His garrison of roughly 3,000 held off Admiral Edward Vernon's fleet of nearly 200 ships and some 25,000 men, who withdrew to Jamaica with heavy losses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cartagena_de_Indias

question: Cartagena's walls guarded Spain's silver, but also a much darker trade. Spain let only a few ports in the Americas sell enslaved Africans, and Cartagena was one. Over a million captive Africans were landed at its docks. In which of Cartagena's squares, now a pleasant tourist plaza, did the buying and selling take place?
answer: the triangular Plaza de los Coches
choices: the triangular Plaza de los Coches
the broad Plaza de la Aduana
the church-side Plaza de Santo Domingo
context: The Spanish crown authorized only a few American ports to sell enslaved Africans, and Cartagena was one of them; well over a million captives were landed at its docks over the city's history. The market centered on the triangular Plaza de los Coches, now a tourist square; nearby, the Jesuit Pedro Claver met the arriving ships to minister to the captives. Source: https://www.mirandakaufmann.com/bbchistorymagcartagena.html

question: Mexico's Yucatan has almost no rivers or lakes on top. Rain sinks straight down through the soft rock into hidden groundwater below. To reach fresh water, the ancient Maya climbed down into round, cliff-walled pools. What are these pools called?
context: With almost no surface rivers, the Yucatan's estimated 10,000 cenotes were the region's only reliable source of drinkable water, so the Maya built cities like Chichen Itza right beside them. The word 'cenote' comes from the Yucatec Maya ts'ono'ot, meaning a well or water-cavern. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: A cenote — a natural round water pool in the ground — is not dug by hand. It forms on its own. Over ages, rain slowly eats away at soft limestone rock and hollows out long caves full of groundwater. Then, all at once, one cave is thrown open to the sky. What happens?
context: This is classic 'karst' collapse: slightly acidic rainwater dissolves the limestone into caverns, and when a cave roof finally falls in, the cool groundwater below is exposed as a natural open well. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: To the Maya, a cenote was far more than a well. Peering into its still, dark water, with the sky mirrored on the black surface, they believed they were gazing at the threshold of another world — the realm of the rain god Chaac. In Maya belief, where did a cenote's deep water lead?
answer: down to Xibalba, the land of the dead
choices: down to Xibalba, the land of the dead
up to the Flower Mountain of the sun
back to the roots of the world tree
context: The Maya held that a cenote's deep water was a doorway to Xibalba, the watery underworld, and a home of Chaac, the rain god — the pools were thresholds to the afterlife, not merely wells. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote  (Legend.)

question: The Sacred Cenote at Chichen Itza is a round pool ringed by cliffs too steep to climb down for water. In dry years, the Maya cast offerings into it to beg the god Chaac for rain. When Edward Thompson dredged the pool after 1904, what did he pull up from the mud below?
context: Edward Herbert Thompson, the American who owned the Chichen Itza site, began dredging the Sacred Cenote in 1904 and brought up jade, gold, and human skeletons — offerings the Maya had cast into the roughly 60 m-wide, cliff-ringed pool to petition Chaac for rain. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: Near Tulum on Mexico's Yucatan coast, two round, deep-blue cenotes — natural water-filled sinkholes — sit side by side, joined below ground by a flooded tunnel about 400 metres long that divers love to swim through. Someone gave the pair the Spanish name 'Dos Ojos.' What does that name mean?
context: 'Dos Ojos' is Spanish for 'Two Eyes' — two round neighboring sinkholes near Tulum that sit side by side like a pair of eyes, linked by an underwater corridor about 400 m long. Source: https://cenotesworld.com (Cenote Dos Ojos)

question: Mexico's Yucatan peninsula is dotted with thousands of round water-filled sinkholes called cenotes. From the air they look scattered at random. But along one huge arc about 180 km wide, they crowd into a perfect curving line. This Ring of Cenotes sits right above a huge buried structure. What lies beneath the ring?
answer: the crater of the dinosaur-killing asteroid
choices: the crater of the dinosaur-killing asteroid
the caldera of an ancient supervolcano
the basin of a vanished inland sea
the fault of a drowned mountain range
context: That curving Ring of Cenotes traces the buried rim of the Chicxulub crater — the roughly 66-million-year-old scar of the asteroid impact tied to the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs. The cenotes cluster where the impact left the rock fractured and weak. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_crater

question: Geologists estimate that the asteroid which blasted out the Chicxulub crater was about 10 kilometres wide — not a boulder but a rock the size of a mountain. Imagine standing it upright next to Mount Everest, the highest mountain on Earth. What would you see?
answer: the asteroid towering over the summit
choices: the asteroid towering over the summit
the asteroid reaching only halfway up
the asteroid level with the base camp
the asteroid barely clearing the foothills
context: The Chicxulub crater is about 180-200 km wide, and the impactor was roughly 10 km (6 mi) across — so large that, set on end at sea level, it would have risen higher than Mount Everest (about 8.8 km). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_crater

question: Near Tulum, cave divers spent years mapping two flooded cave systems, Sistema Sac Actun and Sistema Dos Ojos. In 2018, they announced a discovery that made headlines among cave explorers around the world. What had the divers found deep in the drowned passages?
answer: a flooded tunnel joining the two systems
choices: a flooded tunnel joining the two systems
a sunken chamber piled with Maya gold
an unknown kind of blind white cave-fish
a lost stone staircase built by the Maya
context: In 2018 divers confirmed a flooded connection between Sistema Sac Actun and Sistema Dos Ojos near Tulum, merging them into a single system of over 370 km of passage — one of the longest underwater caves on Earth. (The current record-holder is nearby Sistema Ox Bel Ha, surveyed to about 541 km.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistema_Sac_Actun

question: Deep inside the flooded Sac Actun cave, divers descended into a pitch-black pit they named Hoyo Negro, the 'Black Hole,' and their lights fell on a human skull resting on the bottom. The teenage girl, later nicknamed 'Naia,' seemed at first like a recent lost swimmer — until scientists dated her bones. How long ago had Naia actually lived?
context: In the deep pit called Hoyo Negro, divers found 'Naia,' the skeleton of a teenage girl about 13,000 years old, resting at 43 m depth beside the bones of an Ice Age mastodon at 60 m — among the oldest human remains ever found in the Americas. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistema_Sac_Actun

question: Far from the Yucatan, in the Mexican state of Tamaulipas, a flooded pit called El Zacaton drops more than 300 metres straight down — one of the deepest water-filled sinkholes on Earth. Its odd name comes from something strange that covers its surface and shifts about in the wind. What is it?
context: El Zacaton, in Tamaulipas, is one of the deepest known water-filled sinkholes on Earth — about 339 m (1,112 ft) deep — and is named for the free-floating islands of 'zacate' grass that drift across its surface in the wind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zacaton

question: El Zacaton is a deep, dark flooded shaft that is very hard to reach. In 2007, NASA lowered an autonomous swimming robot into it, not mainly to study the sinkhole, but to rehearse for a much stranger future mission. What did the robot's designers want it to explore one day?
answer: the ocean under the ice of Jupiter's moon Europa
choices: the ocean under the ice of Jupiter's moon Europa
the sea under the ice of Saturn's moon Enceladus
the methane lakes on Saturn's moon Titan
the deep trenches of Earth's own oceans
context: In 2007 NASA sent an autonomous diving robot called DEPTHX (Deep Phreatic Thermal Explorer) into El Zacaton as a testbed for exploring the ocean beneath the ice of Jupiter's moon Europa; it mapped the flooded pit and discovered new kinds of bacteria. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zacaton

question: In a dry canyon in what is now New Mexico, the Ancestral Puebloans raised huge stone houses. The largest held about 650 rooms, rose four stories tall, and covered nearly two acres. Until the 1800s, it was the biggest building in North America. What is this greatest of the Chaco great houses called?
context: Pueblo Bonito ('beautiful village' in Spanish) is the largest and most famous great house at Chaco; at its height it held roughly 650 rooms in a great D-shaped sweep four storeys tall, and its scale rivaled the Roman Colosseum. Chetro Ketl is a neighboring Chaco great house; Casa Rinconada is Chaco's great kiva (a huge circular ceremonial room); Cliff Palace is the famous cliff dwelling at Mesa Verde. The builders were the Ancestral Puebloans (an older name, 'Anasazi,' is now avoided; today's Pueblo peoples are their descendants), who lived at Chaco from about 850 to 1150 CE. Source: Wikipedia, Chaco Culture National Historical Park; WebSearch (Pueblo Bonito).

question: Raising the great houses of Chaco used up about 200,000 pine and fir trees. But the canyon and its surroundings held almost no big timber, so the heavy roof beams had to come from mountain forests up to 70 miles away. How did the Ancestral Puebloans move those beams across that distance to Chaco?
choices: dragged them along the ground on ropes
context: There were no wheels and no horses, oxen, or other heavy draft animals anywhere in the pre-Columbian Americas, and no navigable river reaches Chaco, so human porters shouldered the beams the entire way. Archaeologists note the timbers show almost no drag marks, evidence they were carried rather than dragged or rolled. Some 200,000 trees' worth of straight pine, fir, and spruce beams were cut, cured, and hauled roughly 110 km (70 miles) by hand from ranges such as the Chuska Mountains. Source: Wikipedia, Chaco Culture National Historical Park.

question: Chaco Canyon was more than a place to live. It was a busy workshop and trading center. Diggers there have recovered about 200,000 worked pieces of one prized stone, shaped by skilled craft workers into beads and jewels. Traders carried them for hundreds of miles across the Southwest. Which stone was Chaco famous for cutting?
context: That stone is turquoise, and Chaco was the great turquoise-working center of the ancient Southwest: roughly 200,000 worked pieces have come out of the ruins, cut and polished in specialized workshops and traded across a network reaching hundreds of miles. Rough turquoise was carried in from distant mines, shaped at Chaco into beads and mosaics, and sent out again as finished ornaments. Source: Wikipedia, Chaco Culture National Historical Park.

question: The Ancestral Puebloans built wide, well-made roads, some about 30 feet across. Their routes reached tens of kilometers out from Chaco Canyon and linked it with roughly 30 far-off villages. Researchers still cannot fully explain why the builders chose the paths they did. What was special about the routes the Chaco roads took?
context: The Chaco roads hold astonishingly straight bearings, driving across mesas, ridges, and canyons rather than bending around them. The 'Great North Road' runs about 35 miles almost due north. Because a dead-straight line is rarely the easiest route, many researchers think the roads were laid out for ceremonial or symbolic reasons more than for easy travel; over 400 miles of these engineered roads have been mapped across the wider Chacoan world. Source: Wikipedia, Chaco Culture National Historical Park; WebSearch (Chaco Research Archive; SAH Archipedia).

question: For about three hundred years, Chaco Canyon was the beating heart of the Ancestral Puebloan world. Then, around 1130 CE, the building suddenly stopped and the people drifted away. Tree rings from the region's old timbers reveal why: a drought had struck, and not an ordinary dry spell but the single worst one in the whole thousand-year record. About how long did this megadrought grind on?
context: Tree-ring dating shows great-house building at Chaco stopped around 1130 CE, right as a punishing megadrought — lasting roughly 50 years, from about 1130 to 1180 — settled over the Southwest; it was the most intense drought in the North American record for that thousand-year span. In this high desert, where farming always hung on scarce, unreliable rain, a dry spell half a century long was ruinous, and the Ancestral Puebloans migrated away to resettle across the wider Southwest, their descendants becoming today's Pueblo peoples. Chaco had flourished from about 850 to 1150 CE. Source: WebSearch (worldhistory.org; Crow Canyon 'A.D. 1130-1180 Megadrought'; SERC Carleton tree-ring lab).

question: High on Fajada Butte, a rocky tower rising from the floor of Chaco Canyon, an ancient spiral is pecked into the cliff behind three tall leaning slabs of stone. On just one day each year, at midday, sunlight slipping between the slabs forms a thin blade of light that slices straight down through the exact center of the spiral. On which day does this 'Sun Dagger' pierce the spiral's heart?
context: Artist Anna Sofaer first noticed the Sun Dagger in 1977 while recording rock art on Fajada Butte, and the next year founded the Solstice Project to study it. At the summer solstice a single dagger of light bisects the spiral through its center; at the equinoxes two daggers appear; and at the winter solstice two daggers bracket the spiral like bookends, so the marker tracks the whole solar year. Accuracy note: by 1989 erosion (largely from modern foot traffic loosening the soil) had shifted one slab, so the dagger no longer crosses the exact center at solstice; the site was stabilized and closed to visitors in 1990. This describes the alignment as documented in the 1970s. Source: WebSearch (Solstice Project / Anna Sofaer; PlanetQuest; Ancient Origins).

question: The Ancestral Puebloans aligned Chaco's great houses and its great kiva, Casa Rinconada, with the compass directions and with the rising and setting sun. But researchers studying the buildings found they also line up with a far slower rhythm of the sky, one that takes 18.6 years to complete a full cycle, far longer than the sun's yearly round. Which slow celestial cycle did the Chacoans build their walls to track?
choices: the path of the planet Venus
context: This 18.6-year rhythm is the lunar standstill, the slow swing in how far north and south along the horizon the moon rises and sets. Researchers with the Solstice Project found that Chaco's great houses and the great kiva of Casa Rinconada align not only to the cardinal directions and the sun but to the extremes of this lunar cycle. It is a rhythm so slow that no one could watch a full cycle in the prime of life, so the builders had to hand their sky-knowledge down across generations. Scholars still debate how deliberate every alignment was, but the precision at Chaco is striking. Source: WebSearch (worldhistory.org; Solstice Project; Casa Rinconada).  (Legend.)

question: The Chimu built Chan Chan on Peru's dry northern coast, near modern Trujillo. Its walls, plazas, and royal courts covered about 20 square kilometers. That made it the largest city in ancient South America. The whole desert city, even its towering walls, was built from just one thing. What was it?
context: Chan Chan sprawled over roughly 20 sq km near modern Trujillo -- the largest city of pre-Columbian South America and the largest earthen (adobe) city ever built in the Americas. Its ten-metre walls were shaped from millions of hand-made mud bricks, and they survived only because it almost never rains on this desert coast. Source: whc.unesco.org/en/list/366 ; worldhistory.org/Chan_Chan ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan_Chan

question: In the 1400s, on the dry desert coast of northern Peru, the Chimu people built their capital city, Chan Chan — the largest city of mud brick ever built anywhere in the world. Walk the ruins today and its towering walls run on for kilometers, every surface carved with the same reliefs repeated over and over. What did the Chimu sculpt again and again across the walls of their desert capital?
context: The Chimu were an ocean people who lived off the Pacific's rich fisheries, and they carved the sea across their city: friezes of fish, waves, and seabirds such as pelicans cover the walls, with endless cross-hatching thought to picture a fisherman's net. Source: worldhistory.org/Chan_Chan ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan_Chan

question: By the 1400s Chan Chan was a crowded desert capital of tens of thousands. Around 1470 a rising empire swept down the coast, seized the city, took its last king prisoner for life, and marched Chan Chan's celebrated goldsmiths off to work its own treasuries. Which empire absorbed the Chimu?
context: Around 1470 CE the Inca conquered Chan Chan and absorbed the Chimu into their empire, keeping the last Chimu king, Minchancaman, a lifelong prisoner in the Inca capital Cuzco and carrying off the city's renowned goldsmiths. Source: worldhistory.org/Chan_Chan ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan_Chan

question: In 1861, to fit new sewers under swampy Chicago, 500 workers set 1,000 screw-jacks under the six-story Tremont House hotel. They turned all the jacks together and raised the whole building about six feet. The most astonishing part was who never moved out during the lift. Who?
answer: the paying guests, still in their rooms
choices: the paying guests, still in their rooms
the digging crews, down in the trench
the city mayor, there on a dare
context: The Tremont House was raised while fully open for business. One guest is said to have watched the view from his window climb several feet without ever realizing the hotel was moving. In the 1850s-60s Chicago jacked up hundreds of buildings this way to slip sewers beneath them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_of_Chicago  (Legend.)

question: In the 1850s and 1860s, the American city of Chicago was so low and muddy that the whole downtown had to be jacked up several feet on giant screws to drain the streets. Some wooden buildings stood right in the way of the work. Rather than knock them down, crews handled them in a way a visiting Scot said he saw happening almost daily. What did they do with these houses?
answer: rolled them down the streets to new lots
choices: rolled them down the streets to new lots
buried them under the new roadbed
context: The visiting Scot, David Macrae, wrote that scarcely a day passed that he 'did not meet one or more houses shifting their quarters.' Whole wooden buildings were rolled through the streets on logs to new lots instead of being demolished. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_of_Chicago

question: After the Great Fire of 1871 leveled wooden Chicago, the rebuilt city climbed upward. In 1885, William Le Baron Jenney finished a ten-story tower that weighed only a third as much as a stone building its size. Its outer walls held up nothing, hanging like a curtain. What carried the whole weight instead?
choices: a hidden core of poured concrete
a lattice of heavy oak timbers
deep stone piers under each floor
context: Jenney's Home Insurance Building is widely credited as the world's first skyscraper, though the claim is genuinely debated. Its iron-and-steel frame carried the load, so a building's height was no longer limited by the thickness of its walls. It rose 10 stories (later 12) and was demolished in 1931. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Insurance_Building  (Legend.)

question: Chicago's elevated trains, or 'the L,' run downtown on a rectangle of tracks that was finished in 1897. That rectangle of rails circles the whole business district. The circling tracks gave the neighborhood its one-word nickname. What is downtown Chicago called?
context: The 'L' is short for 'elevated.' The downtown ring of elevated track, the Union Loop, was completed in 1897 and financed by transit magnate Charles Tyson Yerkes; the loop of rails literally names the neighborhood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22

question: Chicago drank from Lake Michigan, but the Chicago River carried the city's sewage straight into that same lake. In 1900, after digging the Sanitary and Ship Canal, engineers broke the last dam at dawn on January 2. The river then did something no major river had done before. What happened to the Chicago River?
choices: it vanished into a covered tunnel
it stilled into a wide lagoon
context: Reversing the river sent Chicago's sewage down toward the Mississippi watershed instead of into its own drinking-water lake. Workers broke the final dam at dawn on January 2, 1900, and the full reversal was complete by January 17; the American Society of Civil Engineers later called it a 'Monument of the Millennium.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Sanitary_and_Ship_Canal

question: For nearly a hundred years starting in 1865, the Union Stock Yards on Chicago's South Side were the world's biggest meatpacking district. Their slaughterhouses dumped waste into one dead-end branch of the Chicago River for decades, until it became a stagnant, reeking industrial sewer. That fouled branch earned a nickname that Chicagoans still use. What is it?
context: The branch is the South Fork of the Chicago River, nicknamed 'Bubbly Creek' because so much rotting stockyard waste sank into it that decomposition gases bubbled up through the surface. It was one of the horrors that pushed Chicago toward its great sanitation projects. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_River

question: In most big cities the finest waterfront fills with private high-rises. Chicago is the great exception. Furious at schemes to build on the shore, mail-order tycoon Aaron Montgomery Ward won four Illinois Supreme Court cases, starting in 1890, to keep the Lake Michigan lakefront open to the public. What fills that protected shore today?
answer: a long chain of public parks
choices: a long chain of public parks
a public boat harbor and docks
context: An 1836 canal-commissioners' map had marked the ground 'A Common to Remain Forever Open, Clear and Free of Any Buildings.' Aaron Montgomery Ward, the 'watchdog of the lakefront,' won four Illinois Supreme Court cases to enforce it, and Daniel Burnham's 1909 Plan of Chicago made it doctrine, declaring the lakefront by right belongs to the people. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Montgomery_Ward

question: When Chicago's Sears Tower (now the Willis Tower) topped out in 1973 at 1,451 feet, it was the world's tallest building — a title it held about 25 years. Engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan built its frame not as one solid block but as nine separate square 'tubes.' How did he arrange those nine tubes?
choices: stacked one on top of another
context: The 108-story tower's nine bundled square tubes stop at different heights, giving its stepped silhouette and bracing one another against Chicago's wind. Its glass Skydeck 'Ledge' boxes jut out over the street about 1,350 feet up. It remained the world's tallest building until 1998. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willis_Tower

question: Chicago is startlingly flat — you can see for miles with barely a rise. That flatness is the smooth, level floor of something vast that filled this basin at the end of the last Ice Age, then drained away about 13,000 years ago. What is the city built on the bed of?
context: The vanished water was Glacial Lake Chicago, the meltwater ancestor of Lake Michigan, which formed as the glaciers retreated about 13,000 years ago. The city's flatness is its fossil lakebed, and sandy ridges like Ridge Road trace its ancient beaches. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Chicago

question: Chicago sits at a low, swampy gap early settlers called 'Mud Lake' — a six-mile portage where, in high water, a canoe could slip across from one great water system to another. In 1673 Louis Jolliet and Jacques Marquette crossed it, and Jolliet saw its huge value: a short canal here would join two watersheds. Which two water systems does the Chicago Portage link?
answer: the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River
choices: the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River
the Missouri and the Ohio rivers
the St. Lawrence and the Atlantic coast
context: The Chicago Portage is a low gap in the subcontinental divide between the Great Lakes and Mississippi watersheds; settlers called its marshy middle 'Mud Lake.' Jolliet's idea for a canal there became the Illinois & Michigan Canal (opened 1848), which made Chicago the hub of the Midwest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Portage

question: Begun in 1975 and still unfinished, one of Earth's largest engineering projects hides beneath Chicago. Giant bores driven hundreds of feet underground, up to 33 feet across, feed reservoirs holding more than 17 billion gallons of storm water and sewage that would otherwise foul Lake Michigan. Chicagoans know this buried megaproject by a blunt two-word nickname. What is it?
context: The system is the Tunnel and Reservoir Plan (TARP), or 'Deep Tunnel': about 109 miles of tunnels as much as 350 feet underground and up to 33 feet across, feeding reservoirs like Thornton (7.9 billion gallons). With over 17 billion gallons of capacity and decades and billions of dollars invested, it is among the largest civil-engineering works ever built. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunnel_and_Reservoir_Plan

question: El Castillo is the step-pyramid at the heart of Chichen Itza. Count every stair on all four sides, plus the last step onto the temple platform, and you have counted 365 in all. The Maya built the pyramid as a calendar in stone, matched to one great cycle. Which cycle?
answer: the days of the solar year
choices: the days of the solar year
the days of the ritual round
the days of the Venus cycle
the days of the lunar year
context: 91 steps on each of the four staircases make 364, and the step onto the top platform makes 365 — the length of the Haab', the Maya solar year, a calendar carved in stone. The other options are real cycles the Maya counted separately: the 260-day Tzolk'in ritual round and the 584-day Venus cycle. This is the widely accepted reading; because some steps are eroded, the total is counted 'including the top platform.' Source: Wikipedia, 'El Castillo, Chichen Itza' (91x4 + top platform = 365, matching the Haab').  (Legend.)

question: Twice a year, on the spring and autumn equinox, the late afternoon sun hits the stepped edge of El Castillo's north staircase. Seven triangular shadows link into one long, rippling body. For about half an hour, a great serpent seems to slither down the stairs to the carved stone snake head at the base. Which god do the Maya show coming down the pyramid?
context: The effect is real and deliberately engineered by the builders: broken by the pyramid's stepped northwest edge, the equinox sun casts seven triangles of light down the north balustrade (alfarda), so a body of light and shadow ripples down to the great carved serpent-head at the base — the descent of Kukulkan, the Feathered Serpent. (Quetzalcoatl is the related Aztec god; Chaac is the rain god; Itzamna a creator.) It shows for roughly half an hour, about 4:30-5:10 pm. Sources: mayan.org Chichen Itza guide; Wikipedia, 'El Castillo'; yucatanmagazine.com.

question: High on the walls of Chichen Itza's Great Ball Court hang two heavy stone rings, carved with twined feathered serpents, set about 26 feet above the ground. Teams kept a solid rubber ball moving using only their hips, knees, and elbows. To score, what did a team have to make the ball do at one of these rings?
answer: send it up through the ring
choices: send it up through the ring
knock the ring off the wall
circle the ball around the rim
bounce it off the ring's face
context: Driving a heavy rubber ball up through a vertical stone ring 8 m (26 ft) overhead — with no hands or feet — was so hard that a single goal could end the game. The rings are carved with intertwined feathered serpents. At about 168 m by 70 m, with walls 8 m high and 36 m apart, this is the largest ancient ball court in all the Americas. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Chichen Itza'; World History Encyclopedia.

question: Carved stone panels run the length of Chichen Itza's Great Ball Court, spelling out the game's deadly stakes. On one, a defeated ball-player kneels — beheaded. From his severed neck the Maya sculptor sent not plain blood but seven shapes bursting upward, one of them blossoming into a plant, as if blood were becoming life. What did the carver shape those streams into?
context: The relief ties the ballgame to sacrifice and fertility: from the decapitated captain's neck spring seven streams carved as serpents, one of them turning into a plant — blood becoming new life. Several such panels line the Great Ball Court. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Chichen Itza'; World History Encyclopedia (Great Ball Court reliefs).

question: Behind a plaza bristling with carved stone pillars rises Chichen Itza's Temple of the Warriors. At its summit lies a stone man leaning back on his elbows, knees drawn up, head turned sharply aside, with a shallow dish resting on his belly to hold offerings. Maya and Toltec builders set this same reclining figure atop temples across old Mexico. What is it called?
context: A Chac Mool is a reclining stone figure — head turned 90 degrees, a bowl or disk on its belly to receive offerings — found at Toltec and Maya sites across central Mexico and the Yucatan. This one crowns the Temple of the Warriors, fronted by the Group of a Thousand Columns. (An atlante is a pillar carved as a standing warrior; a stela a carved standing slab; a zoomorph a boulder carved as a creature.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Chichen Itza.'

question: At the northern edge of Chichen Itza the ground simply opens: a sheer-walled natural pit about 60 m across, its cliffs dropping some 27 m to still green water. In times of drought the Maya threw gold discs, carved jade, balls of copal incense — and human offerings — into this pool to plead with the hook-nosed god who ruled the rains. Which god did they beg?
context: This is the Sacred Cenote (Cenote Sagrado), about 60 m across with cliffs dropping ~27 m to green water. Into it the Maya cast gold, jade, copal incense and human offerings to petition Chaac, the hook-nosed Maya rain god. (Tlaloc is the Aztecs' rain god; Kukulkan the feathered serpent; Itzamna a creator.) Between 1904 and 1910 the American consul Edward Herbert Thompson dredged and dived the pool, raising gold, jade, pottery, incense and human bones — many of children and young adults offered in droughts. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chichen Itza' (Cenote Sagrado; Thompson 1904-1910).  (Legend.)

question: El Castillo hides a secret: it was raised right over an older, smaller pyramid, sealed whole inside it. In April 1935, archaeologists tunneling into the buried temple came upon a stone throne shaped like a crouching beast. It was painted brilliant red, with two spheres of jade for its eyes and white shell for its fangs. What animal was this hidden throne carved as?
context: Sealed inside El Castillo is an older pyramid; tunneling in during April 1935, archaeologists found the inner temple's throne carved as a jaguar — the Maya emblem of kingship — painted bright red (the 'Red Jaguar Throne'), its spots inlaid jade discs, its eyes jade spheres, its fangs white shell. A reclining Chac Mool with mother-of-pearl eyes guarded it. Source: Wikipedia, 'El Castillo, Chichen Itza' and 'Red Jaguar Throne.'

question: Chichen Itza's Great Ball Court — the largest in the ancient Americas, a stone avenue 168 m long between two high parallel walls — hides a marvel of sound: speak a quiet word at the temple on one end, and a friend at the temple on the far wall, more than 135 m (450 ft) off across open stone, hears it plainly. A few cathedral domes are famous for the same trick. What is this kind of acoustic space called?
context: The Great Ball Court is a natural whispering gallery: a soft word at one end temple carries clearly to the far temple over 135 m (about 450 ft) away, and a single handclap in the court sets off a booming flutter echo between the parallel walls. Popular guides exaggerate the effect (claiming it works 'in any wind'), but the long-distance whisper transmission is real and measured. Sources: Acoustical Society of America, 'Acoustics of the Great Ball Court at Chichen Itza' (JASA); ResearchGate, 'Whispering gallery at Chichen Itza's Great Ballcourt.'  (Legend.)

question: Across the whole Yucatan Peninsula there is scarcely a river or lake on the surface, yet the great Maya cities all cluster around deep, water-filled sinkholes. The reason lies in the bedrock: the peninsula is a vast slab of soft limestone, and rain does something to it that leaves the surface bone-dry. What happens to the rain?
answer: it soaks straight down into the rock
choices: it soaks straight down into the rock
it evaporates in the tropical heat
it is drunk up by jungle roots
it runs off quickly to the coast
context: The Yucatan is a flat slab of porous limestone (a karst landscape): rain sinks straight through it, so there are almost no surface rivers or lakes. Groundwater gathers below, and where the limestone roof collapses it exposes the water table as a sinkhole — a cenote (Maya ts'ono'ot, 'water deposit'). Cenotes were the region's only reliable fresh water, which is exactly why the Maya built their cities beside them. Sources: Britannica, 'cenote'; Monroy-Rios (Northwestern), Yucatan karst speleogenesis; chichenitza.com.

question: Beside the pyramids at Chichen Itza stands El Caracol, a round tower on a broad platform, named 'the snail' for the spiral stair coiling up inside. Its narrow windows and the sight lines across its corners are no accident. They point to the horizon spots where one sky-body rises and sets at the ends of its 8-year cycle, the one the Maya watched to time planting and war. Which sky-body did El Caracol track?
context: El Caracol ('the snail,' for its inner spiral stair) is an observatory: about 20 of its 29 identified sightlines — through narrow windows and along wall corners — point to the horizon extremes where Venus rises and sets across its 8-year cycle (five Venus cycles are close to eight years). The Maya tracked Venus closely to time planting and warfare. Source: Aveni et al., 'The Caracol Tower at Chichen Itza,' Science 188:977 (1975); Wikipedia, 'El Caracol.'

question: Clap your hands once at the foot of El Castillo's great staircase and the steps answer with a strange downward chirp — a rapid, ringing note that slides from high to low. Acoustic engineer David Lubman, who first measured the effect in 1998, found the echo uncannily mimics the piping call of one bird the Maya held sacred. Which bird does the pyramid seem to echo?
context: The chirp is a real, measurable effect, not magic: the evenly spaced stone steps act like a diffraction grating — a 'picket fence' that reflects a clap back as a rapid run of tones sliding high to low, close to the piping call of the quetzal, the bird the Maya held sacred. California acoustic engineer David Lubman first documented it in 1998; Declercq and colleagues explained the physics in 2004. Sources: Nature News 2004, 'Mystery of chirping pyramid decoded'; Declercq et al., JASA 116(6):3328 (2004); Lubman, Acoustical Society of America.

question: On a plain in central Bohol in the Philippines, rounded cone-shaped hills rise on every side. Each hill is so alike in shape and size that the whole field looks laid out to one plan. You might expect a dozen odd mounds, but the plain is crowded with them. About how many of these near-matching cones stand there?
context: The cones -- about 1,268 counted -- spread across more than 50 square kilometers around the towns of Carmen, Batuan and Sagbayan, and rise mostly 30 to 120 meters, the tallest as high as a 30-story building. A local legend even claims two feuding giants made them, hurling sand and boulders at each other for days until they tired, made peace, and left the mounds scattered behind. Sources: UNESCO Bohol Island Global Geopark; Wikipedia 'Chocolate Hills'; GeologyScience 'Chocolate Hills Philippines'.

question: Every dry season, Bohol's Chocolate Hills turn a deep chocolate-brown across the whole plain. Yet crack open a hill and you find no brown rock at all: the stone inside is pale gray limestone. So what actually dries out and browns, painting the hills their famous color?
answer: A blanket of coarse cogon grass
choices: A blanket of coarse cogon grass
A carpet of moss and lichen
context: The color is the grass, not the rock: the hills are pale grey limestone, and only the coarse cogon grass (Imperata cylindrica) blanketing them dries brown in the dry months -- so when the rains return, the same hills green up again. That seasonal brown coat is exactly what earned them the name 'Chocolate Hills.' Sources: GeologyScience 'Chocolate Hills Philippines'; Wikipedia 'Chocolate Hills'.

question: On the Philippine island of Bohol, more than a thousand pale grey cones — the famous Chocolate Hills — rise across a broad inland plain. In the wet season they are green; in the dry season they turn chocolate brown. Split one of the cones open, though, and its limestone is crowded with tiny fossils. What kind of fossils are they?
context: The pale limestone still holds proof it was underwater: fossil shells of foraminifera, coral, mollusks and algae from a sea that covered Bohol in Pliocene-to-Pleistocene times. The cone shape has its own label -- 'cone karst' or 'cockpit karst.' The hills became a National Geological Monument in 1988, and in 2023 Bohol was named the Philippines' first UNESCO Global Geopark. Sources: GeologyScience 'Chocolate Hills Philippines'; UNESCO Bohol Island Global Geopark; Wikipedia 'Chocolate Hills'.

question: A bare, stony limestone plateau rises in southwest Slovenia, above the sea near Trieste. It is pocked with sinkholes and with streams that drop into the ground. Geographers took this plateau's own name and now use it worldwide for every place where water drains like this. What is that term?
context: The plateau is the Kras (German 'Karst'); English borrowed the word in the late 1800s, and its pre-Indo-European root simply means bare, stony rock — the land literally named after being rock without soil. From this one tableland above Trieste, 'karst' spread worldwide to name any limestone country where water drains underground. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karst)

question: Rainwater looks harmless. Yet on Slovenia's Kras plateau it is slowly eating the rock. As each drop falls through the air, it takes in a gas and becomes a mild acid, strong enough over ages to hollow out caves in solid limestone. Which acid does plain rain turn into?
context: The gas is carbon dioxide: raindrops dissolve it to form weak carbonic acid, which slowly eats the limestone and tunnels downward. That is why karst has so few surface streams or lakes — its drainage runs underground. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karst)

question: In southwest Slovenia, the Reka River rolls along like any ordinary river, wide enough to swim. Then, near one village, the whole flow pours off the land and into the rock. It is never seen at the surface again. Into what does the Reka disappear?
context: The Reka starts as an ordinary surface stream ('Big Creek') on Mount Snežnik, then at the village of Škocjan plunges off the surface into the Škocjan Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reka_(river))

question: After it sinks at Škocjan, the Reka thunders through Hanke's Channel, a rock-walled void so vast its ceiling is lost in the dark far overhead. In fair weather the river is a modest ribbon on the cavern floor, but downstream the passage pinches to a narrow gap that can plug like a bottleneck. After a heavy storm, the backed-up flood climbs the cavern walls with nowhere to escape. How high up the rock can the trapped water rise?
context: Hanke's Channel is a giant rock-walled canyon inside the Škocjan Caves — about 3.5 km long, 10–60 m wide, and over 140 m from the black water up to the ceiling. In heavy rain the trapped water can rise more than 100 m when a downstream siphon cannot drain the flood fast enough, nearly filling the void. It ranks among the largest underground river canyons known. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Škocjan_Caves)

question: The Reka River vanished underground at Škocjan, but it was never destroyed. It races unseen through the limestone for about 34 kilometers, then bursts back into the daylight near the Adriatic coast by Trieste. It rises from the ground as a cluster of springs under a brand-new name. As what river does the Reka come back to the sea?
context: After some 34 km underground, the Reka resurges as the Timavo springs near San Giovanni di Duino, flowing only about 2 km in the open before reaching the Gulf of Trieste. Roughly a third of the Timavo's water is the sunken Reka; the rest is rain soaked straight into the plateau. Virgil's Aeneid described the river bursting from the mountain in many mouths. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Škocjan_Caves)

question: Lake Cerknica in Slovenia is the country's largest lake — but only for part of the year. Each wet season water floods its broad basin; then every summer it drains away completely down holes in its own floor, leaving a bed that dries green and where farmers cut hay. Geographers have a special word for this kind of flat basin, where a whole lake fills and vanishes with the seasons. What is such a basin called?
context: A polje is a flat-floored karst plain.
