He recorded that before Christianity 'the Slavs did not have their own letters, but read and communicated by means of strokes and incisions' -- tallies and rough sketches. He credited Saint Constantine (Cyril) with later composing 'thirty-eight letters ... suitable to express Slavic sounds.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernorizets_Hrabar  (Legend.)

question: In Great Moravia, Cyril and Methodius saw that no Greek or Latin letter could spell many Slavic sounds. So around 863 they built a new alphabet of loops, circles, and crosses. They named it 'Glagolitic,' from the Old Church Slavonic word 'glagol.' What does 'glagol' mean?
context: 'Glagol' means 'word' or 'utterance,' so the alphabet's name means, roughly, 'speech itself.' Glagolitic -- around 41 letters of loops, circles, crosses, and triangles -- was the first alphabet ever used for Slavic manuscripts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glagolitic_script

question: The alphabet is named Cyrillic after Saint Cyril of Thessaloniki. Yet Cyril never made it. He and Methodius had made Glagolitic, and Cyril died in Rome in 869. The neater script we now call Cyrillic was put together a bit later. His followers built it at the Preslav school. In which realm did those scholars work?
context: Constantine took the monastic name 'Cyril' only weeks before he died in Rome on 14 February 869 -- so the alphabet honors a name he held only at the very end of his life, and one he never made. His disciples, taken in by Tsar Boris I of Bulgaria, adapted it at the Preslav Literary School (founded 886, later moved to Veliki Preslav under Tsar Simeon I the Great). The oldest dated Cyrillic inscription (921) was found near Krepcha, Bulgaria. As one summary puts it, the name Cyrillic 'denotes homage rather than authorship.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script

question: Open a Russian newspaper and the letters look almost Greek -- because the scholars who built Cyrillic took most of its shapes straight from Greek formal book-script. But Greek had no signs for certain Slavic sounds like 'sh', 'zh', and 'ch'. Where did they find letters for those missing sounds?
context: The Preslav scholars adapted Greek uncial (formal book-script) for most letters, but borrowed shapes from the brothers' earlier Glagolitic for sounds Greek lacked: Zh, Sh, Shch, Ts, Ch, and Yu. So Glagolitic quietly survives inside every page of modern Cyrillic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script

question: Across the Slavic world, the newer Cyrillic quickly pushed the older Glagolitic aside. But in one country, priests and clerks kept writing the swirling loops of Glagolitic in daily papers. They kept it up as late as the early 1800s, nearly a thousand years after it was born. Where did this last stronghold of Glagolitic survive?
context: The surprise is the direction: Glagolitic clung on longest not in the Slavic east but in Croatia and Dalmatia, where priests and notaries on Adriatic islands like Krk kept writing the old script into the early 1800s -- alongside Latin and Cyrillic. Its swirl of loops, circles, and triangles had first been shaped in Great Moravia nearly a thousand years before. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glagolitic_script

question: In Ethiopia sits a place called Dallol. Its top steams with pools that glow neon green, yellow, and orange over a crust of twisted salt. It looks so much like another world that scientists visit it to train for space trips. Which planet does Dallol stand in for?
context: Dallol's alien, acidic, sulphur-and-iron landscape is studied as a stand-in for Mars -- a 'planetary field analog' scientists use to practice how they'd hunt for life on other worlds. The Danakil around it is also the hottest place on Earth by year-round average temperature (near 35 C), and its floor lies about 120 m below sea level. (Grokipedia 'Dallol (hydrothermal system)'; PMC 'The Dallol Geothermal Area ... Planetary Field Analog'; Wikipedia 'Danakil Depression'.)

question: In the scorching Danakil Depression of northern Ethiopia lies Dallol, one of the strangest spots on Earth. No painter could ever invent its colors -- the crust glows in bright bands of neon green, gold, and fiery orange. From deep below, super-hot salty brine wells up through the ground and dries on the surface in the sun. As it dries, what actually paints these bizarre colors?
context: As the hot brine cools and evaporates, dissolved iron, copper and sulphur crystallize out and crust the salt in greens, yellows, oranges and whites -- the ground is literally painted by minerals, not by living things. (Grokipedia 'Dallol (hydrothermal system)'; Wikipedia 'Dallol (hydrothermal system)'.)

question: For hundreds of years, Afar miners have cut the salt of the Danakil into flat slabs called amole. They load them onto camel trains, about forty slabs a camel. Then they carry them deep into the Ethiopian highlands. For a long time, Ethiopians used these salt slabs as what?
context: The slabs are called amole, and for centuries they served as actual currency across Ethiopia -- 'white gold.' Afar miners still cut the flats of Lake Karum (Lake Asale, about 120 m below sea level) by hand and load roughly forty blocks per camel. (Great Ethiopian Tours 'Lake Asale Salt Flats & Camel Caravans'; IBTimes UK 'white gold'.)

question: Dallol, in the blazing Danakil Depression of northern Ethiopia, sits above a shallow chamber of red-hot magma. Rainwater sinks down into the cracked crater, and the magma only a few kilometers below heats it near boiling. The scalding water then wells back up as a brine full of dissolved iron and sulphur. That leaves the little pools of Dallol about as acidic as which common household liquid?
context: One of the most fiercely acidic natural waters ever measured: the pools are hydrothermal -- groundwater heated by shallow magma and so saturated with sulphur that their pH plunges near 0, measured as low as about -1.7, roughly the acidity of battery acid. That is far beyond the ordinary sour bite of lemon juice or vinegar. (Grokipedia 'Dallol (hydrothermal system)'; ACS Earth & Space Chemistry, 'A Polyextreme Hydrothermal System Controlled by Iron', pH 0.1 to -1.7.)

question: Under the Danakil sit thick layers of salt, up to two kilometers deep in places. The salt did not fall from the sky. It piled up over ages. An arm of one sea kept flooding the sinking basin, then drying up in the desert sun. Which sea kept pouring in and drying away?
context: An arm of the Red Sea repeatedly flooded the sinking basin and then dried out, each cycle leaving salt behind. The evaporite deposits run over 500 m thick and reach as much as 2 km (some estimates ~2,500 m). (Wikipedia 'Danakil Depression'; Grokipedia 'Danakil Depression'.)

question: The Danakil sits over the Afar Triple Junction. There, three great plates of Earth's crust are pulling apart: the African, Arabian, and Somali. They split the land open a centimeter or two each year. Geologists think that if this keeps up for millions of years, the whole basin will grow into what?
context: This is the Afar Triple Junction, where the Nubian (African), Arabian and Somali plates pull apart at roughly 1-2 cm a year -- the continent is being torn open, and geologists expect the sea to eventually flood in and form new oceanic crust here. Framed as a far-future prediction. (Grokipedia 'Danakil Depression'; Wikipedia 'Danakil Depression'.)  (Legend.)

question: A short trek from Dallol stands the volcano Erta Ale. It holds a lake of lava whose churning surface has not fully hardened since at least 1906, the longest-lived on Earth. Our planet has over a thousand active volcanoes. Yet open lava lakes are so rare that in 2019 the whole world had only about how many at once?
context: Erta Ale means 'smoking mountain' in the Afar language, and locals call its southernmost pit 'the gateway to hell.' Its lava lake has been present since at least 1906, the longest-lived on Earth; in 2019 only about eight volcanoes worldwide had a lava lake at all. (Wikipedia 'Erta Ale'; Grokipedia 'Erta Ale'.)

question: In the busy Syrian city of Damascus, blades sold in the market were prized far and wide for a strange beauty. Across the bright, polished steel ran a rippling pattern of wavy dark bands, almost like flowing water. No ordinary sword had this look. How did the Damascus smiths give the blades this pattern?
answer: It was forged into the steel itself.
choices: It was forged into the steel itself.
It was painted on with dark dye.
It was etched in with acid later.
It was inlaid with silver wire.
context: The watered look came from the steel's own structure — microscopic bands of hard carbide crystals locked into the metal during forging, not paint or acid brushed on afterward. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus_steel.

question: Everyone called them Damascus blades, and smiths in Damascus, Syria, really did forge and sell them — yet Syria made no such steel of its own. The metal arrived as small cakes called 'wootz,' carried thousands of miles from where it was truly made. Where did the steel come from?
context: The wootz ingots were made in southern India and Sri Lanka and traded across the Middle East; smiths in Damascus forged them into the finished swords, which is how the blades got their city name. It was essentially branding — Syria never mined the metal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wootz_steel; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus_steel.

question: The famous curved blades known as Damascus steel carry the name of Damascus, the great Syrian city where medieval traders bought and sold them across the Arab world. But the Arabic word 'damas' behind that city name had a second, everyday meaning that fit the rippling look of the blades perfectly. What else did 'damas' mean in Arabic?
context: 'Damas' means 'watered' in Arabic — a perfect match for the water-like ripples running down the blade, which is why the patterned metal is still called 'watered' or 'damask' steel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus_steel.

question: The steel that became Damascus blades was made far to the east, on the island of Sri Lanka. Smiths sealed iron and carbon in clay pots and fired them white-hot. Instead of long human labor, they used a free natural force the island gave them. What powered the furnaces of Sri Lanka?
context: The word 'wootz' comes from the Tamil 'urukku,' meaning 'to melt.' Sri Lankan smiths packed iron with carbon-rich bamboo and leaves in sealed clay crucibles and used the monsoon winds to drive their furnaces hot enough to melt it into ultra-high-carbon steel — about 1.5% carbon, versus under 1% in ordinary steel. That extreme carbon is what let the watered bands form. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wootz_steel.

question: For hundreds of years in the Middle Ages, Middle Eastern smiths in Damascus, Syria and elsewhere forged sword blades with strange rippling water-like patterns in the steel. These 'Damascus blades' cut so well that wild legends grew around them -- stories retold for centuries but never once proven true. According to the most famous of these tales, what could a real Damascus blade do?
answer: Slice a wisp of silk falling onto its edge.
choices: Slice a wisp of silk falling onto its edge.
Cleave a lesser sword in two with one blow.
Cut through an iron bar without dulling its edge.
Bend into a full circle and spring back straight.
context: These are unverified LEGENDS, retold for centuries but never documented. The best-known claimed a Damascus blade so keen it could slice a wisp of silk drifting down onto its edge — cut clean in mid-air, with nothing behind it. Other tales said such a blade could cleave a lesser sword in two, or cut through an iron bar, without ever dulling its edge. The real swords were superb, but these feats were only retold, never proven. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus_steel.

question: Real Damascus steel begins as a small cake of high-carbon iron called wootz, smelted long ago in southern India and Sri Lanka. For centuries, smiths in Damascus, Syria and other Middle Eastern cities imported wootz cakes and forged them into sword blades with rippling water-patterned steel. Then, slowly, the wootz supply dried up and the tradition faded. By around 1900, what had become of the art of making real Damascus steel?
answer: The know-how had died out and was forgotten.
choices: The know-how had died out and was forgotten.
Ottoman rulers had banned it and burned the forges.
Cheap factory steel had quietly driven it out.
The last smiths had carried the secret to Europe.
context: A whole technology humans simply forgot how to do. Production faded until, by about 1900, no living smith could make true wootz Damascus; the last account of the old process was recorded in 1903 in Sri Lanka by the scholar Ananda Coomaraswamy. In the 1990s, metallurgists John Verhoeven and Alfred Pendray reproduced the watered pattern and found that a trace of vanadium in the old Indian ore — something no ancient smith knew was there — was a hidden key to the bands. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus_steel; sciencenotes.org.

question: In 2006, a German team led by Peter Paufler in Dresden slid a real Damascus sabre from the 1600s under a strong microscope. They reported something amazing hidden in the old steel, perhaps the secret of its edge. Other scientists still argue about the claim today. What did they say they found inside the blade?
context: DISPUTED. Paufler's Dresden team (Nature, 2006) reported carbon nanotubes and cementite nanowires inside a 17th-century sabre, but other scientists — including John Verhoeven — argued the 'nanotubes' were really just cementite rods, so the finding is still contested. Long before, in 1819–1820, Michael Faraday himself tried to crack the secret with the cutler James Stodart and guessed wrong, blaming a noble-metal alloy rather than the steel's carbon. Source: nature.com/articles/444286a; cen.acs.org.

question: The Syrian city of Damascus was already a busy town before 2000 BC -- older even than the Trojan War of Homer's tales. Ever since, it has been ruled by one power after another, from the Aramean kings of the Bible to the Ottoman sultans of Istanbul. Of all the cities on Earth, which special crown does Damascus claim best?
answer: the world's oldest continuously inhabited city
choices: the world's oldest continuously inhabited city
the world's oldest planned royal capital
context: Jericho was founded far earlier -- perhaps 11,000 years ago -- but its people abandoned it again and again; Damascus's glory is that it was NEVER emptied, with large-scale settlement reaching back before 2000 BC. Its chief rivals for the 'oldest continuously inhabited' crown are nearby Aleppo and Byblos. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus

question: At the heart of old Damascus stands a grand mosque. It sits on ground that had been holy for over three thousand years. First it held a temple to the storm-god Hadad, then a Roman temple of Jupiter, then a Christian church. Since 706 AD a mosque has stood there in its first form. What is this old mosque called?
context: The caliph al-Walid I commissioned the Umayyad (Great) Mosque in 706 AD; it was finished around 711-715. Roughly 12,000 laborers from Egypt, Persia, India, Greece and North Africa built it, and about 4,000 square metres of its walls were sheathed in gold mosaics picturing a green, watery Paradise. The spot had been sacred for millennia: a temple to Hadad, then a Roman temple of Jupiter, then the Christian Cathedral of St John the Baptist (converted to a church under Emperor Theodosius I in 391 AD). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Mosque

question: Inside the great mosque of old Damascus sits a small domed shrine. Christian and Muslim pilgrims pray there side by side. It is one of very few holy spots shared by both faiths. Both hold that it keeps the head of a prophet each honors. Whose head do they think rests below that dome?
answer: the head of John the Baptist
choices: the head of John the Baptist
context: The shrine is the Maqam Nabi Yahya -- Yahya ibn Zakariya is John the Baptist's name in Islam, where he is honored as a prophet just as in Christianity. The historian Ibn Asakir wrote that workers found the relic in a cave beneath a planned pillar during construction; al-Walid had it reburied and the column above marked. It is one of the few shared Muslim-Christian pilgrimage sites -- though at least six places, including cathedrals in Amiens and Rome and a museum in Munich, also claim the Baptist's head. This is tradition, not proven fact. Source: https://www.catholicworldreport.com/2025/08/29/how-john-the-baptist-became-linked-to-the-umayyad-mosque-in-damascus/  (Legend.)

question: In old Damascus you can still walk a 1,500-meter Roman avenue. It was once the grand main street lined with tall columns. The Bible sends a newly blinded Saul of Tarsus to a house along it in the story of his conversion. What is this old Roman avenue called?
context: The Street Called Straight is the Via Recta, the Roman city's decumanus maximus, running about 1,500 metres across the old city. It appears in Acts 9:11, where the Lord tells Ananias to 'go into the street which is called Straight' to find the newly blinded Saul of Tarsus -- soon to become the apostle Paul. Its eastern end reaches the Bab Sharqi, a surviving Roman triumphal gate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_Street

question: The Barada River pours down from the snows of the Anti-Lebanon Mountains. It spreads across the desert plain around Damascus. That water feeds a wide ring of orchards and gardens that has fed the city for thousands of years. It marks Damascus as a true oasis. What is this green belt called?
context: The Barada rises in the Anti-Lebanon Mountains and spills toward Damascus, which sits about 680 metres high and some 80 km inland from the Mediterranean. Its waters fan out into the Ghouta, the ring of irrigated orchards and cropland that let a great city flourish on the desert's edge for thousands of years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus

question: Damascus gave its name to the most prized steel of the medieval world -- sword blades rippled with wavy, watery patterns, forged and traded through the city, though the raw wootz ingots were shipped in from far-off India and Sri Lanka. Production faded and stopped by about 1900. What happened to the way these blades were made?
answer: it was lost and never recovered
choices: it was lost and never recovered
it was banned by the Ottoman sultans
it was carried off to forges in Toledo
it was locked inside the Umayyad Mosque
context: 'Damascus' steel takes its name from the city that forged and traded the blades (the Arabic root 'damas' means 'watered,' for the ripples) -- but the raw wootz ingots came from southern India and Sri Lanka. Production ceased by about 1900, and the exact crucible-and-heat technique that produced the patterns is still debated, not settled. Tall tales grew up around the blades -- that one could slice a silk scarf drifting onto its edge, or cut through iron bars without dulling -- but those are unproven legends, not established feats. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus_steel

question: On July 10, 1913, a thermometer at Furnace Creek in Death Valley, California, climbed to a stunning 134 degrees Fahrenheit. Some modern experts think the old reading may have run a bit too high. Even so, the World Meteorological Organization still lists that Death Valley number as the hottest what, ever measured anywhere on Earth?
context: The 56.7 C reading at Greenland Ranch (now Furnace Creek) on July 10, 1913 remains the WMO-recognized record for the hottest AIR temperature ever measured on Earth. Beware the classic trap: the hottest GROUND-surface temperature belongs elsewhere -- satellites clocked Iran's Lut Desert near 70.7 C in 2005, and Death Valley's own sun-baked ground once hit 93.9 C in 1972. Official records use air readings taken in shade in a standard shelter. Weather historian Christopher Burt argues the 1913 figure runs about 2-3 C too high; the most reliable modern readings -- 54.4 C on Aug 16, 2020 and July 9, 2021 -- are still under WMO review. Sources: Wikipedia 'Highest temperature recorded on Earth'; Grokipedia 'Death Valley National Park'; nps.gov/deva weather page.

question: In 1849, pioneer families took a Gold Rush shortcut. They got stuck for weeks in a blazing California basin. Two young men, William Manly and John Rogers, hiked out on foot and came back with food and water. As the party finally climbed free, one looked back and, so the story goes, said 'Goodbye, Death Valley.' The grim name stuck. Yet of the whole stranded party, how many had actually died?
context: The ominous name came from the Lost '49ers. At Christmas 1849 the Bennett-Arcane families, chasing a Gold Rush shortcut, got stranded near Furnace Creek. William Manly and John Rogers walked out on foot and returned with supplies to lead the survivors to safety; as they climbed out, one reportedly looked back and said 'Goodbye, Death Valley,' and the name stuck. For all the dread, only one of the party had died. (The farewell line is traditional lore, not a documented quote.) Sources: dvnha.org 'Lost 49ers'; Wikipedia 'Bennett-Arcane Long Camp'.  (Legend.)

question: Badwater Basin sits deep in California's Death Valley. Its cracked white salt flat is the lowest dry land in all of North America, 282 feet below sea level, and in summer it bakes in temperatures over 120 degrees Fahrenheit. Yet only 15 miles from that hot, salty floor stands a huge desert surprise. What sits so close to the lowest, hottest place on the continent?
choices: a canyon deeper than the Grand Canyon
a lake of bright turquoise water
a forest of giant cactus trees
context: That peak is Telescope Peak in the Panamint Range, 11,049 feet high and often snow-capped in winter -- more than 11,300 feet of vertical relief in only about 15 horizontal miles. The lowest point in North America stares straight up at an 11,000-foot summit. Badwater itself sits 86 m (282 ft) below sea level; a 'SEA LEVEL' sign painted high on the Black Mountains cliff marks how far down the boardwalk really is. Sources: Grokipedia 'Death Valley National Park'; nps.gov Badwater Basin.

question: In Death Valley, the floor of Badwater Basin is almost 200 square miles of bright white salt. Salty water seeps up and dries in the heat, so the crust cracks into a repeating pattern that covers the flat to the horizon. What shape do these salt cells form?
context: Badwater's salt pan -- nearly 200 square miles of sodium chloride, plus calcite, gypsum and borax -- dries into repeating hexagonal cells as briny groundwater wells up, evaporates, and the shrinking crust cracks (the same shrinkage geometry that makes cooling basalt form hexagonal columns). The whole flat is the ghost of Ice Age Lake Manly, which once filled the valley up to 600 feet deep before it evaporated and left the minerals behind. Sources: nps.gov Badwater Basin; Grokipedia 'Death Valley National Park'.

question: On Racetrack Playa, a flat, cracked lakebed in northern Death Valley, heavy rocks -- some over 600 pounds -- sit at the end of long trails scraped across the mud, as if they had wandered off on their own. In 2014, scientists finally caught the rocks in the act of moving. What actually slides these 'sailing stones' across the flat?
answer: thin winter ice sheets nudged by a light wind
choices: thin winter ice sheets nudged by a light wind
sudden whirlwinds strong enough to shove them
brief floods that lift and float them along
the slow heaving and buckling of the mud
context: The 'sailing stones' were a mystery from 1948 until 2014, when Richard and James Norris and Ralph Lorenz planted GPS-tracked rocks and a time-lapse camera and finally filmed the motion (published in PLOS ONE). On rare cold nights a shallow pond freezes into millimetre-thin ice; morning sun melts it into floating panels that a light 3-5 m/s breeze shoves along, dragging the embedded rocks up to about 5 metres a minute across a playa so flat its ends differ by only 1.5 inches. Not magnets, not aliens -- ice and wind. Sources: Wikipedia 'Racetrack Playa'; Grokipedia 'Death Valley National Park'.

question: Death Valley in California is the driest place in North America -- it gets less than two inches of rain in an average year. Yet big storms really do blow off the Pacific Ocean and sweep east across California toward the valley. Something happens to those storms on the way. Why does almost none of their rain ever reach the valley floor?
answer: a wall of mountain ranges wrings the storms dry first
choices: a wall of mountain ranges wrings the storms dry first
a permanent dome of high pressure blocks the clouds
a cold ocean current offshore chills the rain away
the desert's own heat evaporates the rain in midair
context: Death Valley is a rain-shadow desert. The National Park Service counts four major mountain ranges between the valley and the Pacific; as storms are forced up each range, they drop their rain and snow on the western slopes, so the air arriving over the valley floor has been wrung dry -- under two inches of rain a year, the driest place in North America. Source: nps.gov/deva weather and climate page.

question: Death Valley was not carved out by a river. The entire region is being stretched apart, part of the Basin and Range extension that continues to widen the American West, and fresh fault cracks still split the ground near Badwater after major earthquakes. Because that stretching has never stopped, what is Death Valley still doing today?
answer: sinking a little deeper every year
choices: sinking a little deeper every year
filling in with blown sand every year
drying out and shrinking every year
pushing upward a few inches every year
context: Death Valley is a 'pull-apart' basin: the crust is being stretched by Basin and Range extension, with right-lateral shear along the Walker Lane, so the floor keeps dropping roughly 5-10 mm a year while fresh fault scarps appear near Badwater. It isn't a finished landform but an active one -- the valley is quite literally still getting deeper. Source: Grokipedia 'Death Valley National Park'.

question: For most of the year Death Valley's floor is bare gravel and salt. But after a rare soaking winter, the barren valley suddenly blazes with sheets of yellow Desert Gold flowers stretching to the mountains -- a 'superbloom' that draws crowds in big years like 1998, 2005, and 2016. Where had all these flowers been hiding through the long dry years in between?
answer: as seeds lying dormant in the dry soil
choices: as seeds lying dormant in the dry soil
as bulbs tucked beside the mountain springs
as roots surviving beneath the salt flats
as spores carried in on the desert wind
context: After a rare wet winter, Desert Gold and other wildflowers burst from seeds that had lain dormant for years in the soil, then bloom and re-seed before the killing heat returns -- a 'superbloom,' roughly once a decade, with famous years in 1998, 2005 and 2016. The dormant-seed-bank strategy lets desert annuals wait out drought as seeds underground rather than as bulbs or roots. Even the endemic Death Valley pupfish clings on in salty Salt Creek -- life persisting in the hottest, lowest, driest corner of the continent. Sources: earthsky.org Death Valley superbloom; Grokipedia 'Death Valley National Park'.

question: Above the ruins of old Delhi, a slim tower of red and grey sandstone rises 72 metres into the sky. It has rings of balconies and gets thinner as it climbs. Started in 1199, it is still the tallest brick tower of its kind. What is this famous Delhi tower called?
context: Begun in 1199 by Qutb ud-Din Aibak, the Qutb Minar climbs 72.5 m (238 ft) in bands of red and grey sandstone, its upper storey later rebuilt in white marble — the tallest brick minaret on earth and the crown of a whole ruined city. Delhi itself has been built and rebuilt roughly seven times across the Yamuna plain, which is why it is nicknamed the 'city of seven cities.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutb_Minar

question: In the 1600s, the great Mughal emperor of India, Shah Jahan, moved his capital to the ancient city of Delhi in northern India. Beside the Yamuna river he built a huge walled palace-fortress. Its outer ramparts ran about 2.4 kilometers around vast halls, marble courtyards, and gardens. From it, Mughal emperors ruled for nearly 200 years. What is this famous Delhi fortress called?
context: Shah Jahan's Lal Qila — 'Red Fort,' for its red sandstone walls — was begun in 1638 and finished in 1648, its ramparts running about 2.4 km and rising 18–33 m. Its architect, Ustad Ahmad Lahori, also designed the Taj Mahal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Fort

question: In the courtyard beside the Qutb Minar stands a slim, dark iron column, 7 metres tall, forged in the Gupta age about 1,600 years ago. For sixteen centuries it has stood in Delhi's open air and monsoon rains. Engineers still travel there to marvel at how well it has held up. What has this ancient pillar famously resisted?
context: The Delhi iron pillar is about 7.2 m tall and weighs over 6 tonnes, forged around the 5th century CE in the Gupta age. Ordinary iron left in the open for 1,600 years would have rusted to flakes long ago; this one has not — a puzzle that has drawn metallurgists for generations. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_pillar_of_Delhi

question: In Delhi, India, beside the great victory tower called the Qutb Minar, stands an even older wonder -- a single iron pillar about 24 feet tall, forged around 1,600 years ago. What makes it famous is that after all those centuries out in the open air, it has barely rusted. For hundreds of years, visitors performed the same hopeful ritual at its base, certain it would grant them a wish. What did they do?
answer: reached both arms around it from behind till their fingertips met
choices: reached both arms around it from behind till their fingertips met
walked around it seven times before the morning sun rose
pressed a copper coin into a crack and left it to stick
poured river water at its foot and drank from cupped hands
context: The belief was that if you stood with your back to the pillar and stretched your arms around it until your fingers met, your wish would come true. So many sweaty hands rubbed the base that the ancient surface began to suffer, and in 1997 the Archaeological Survey of India ringed the pillar with a fence to protect it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_pillar_of_Delhi  (Legend.)

question: The Qutb Minar has stood through more than eight centuries of Delhi's history, and more than once it has been battered and repaired. In 1369 its top storey was shattered, and Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt it, splitting the fourth storey into two. What had wrecked the tower's crown?
context: Qutb ud-Din Aibak finished only the first storey; his son-in-law Iltutmish added three more by about 1220. After lightning struck in 1369, Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the shattered top and split the fourth storey into two, giving the tower its present five storeys. The whole Qutb complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutb_Minar

question: The Quwwat-ul-Islam — 'Might of Islam' — beside the Qutb Minar was the first mosque built in Delhi, begun in 1193 by Qutb ud-Din Aibak. Its courtyard is ringed with richly carved stone columns, no two alike, whose lotus-blossoms, bells, and looping chains look nothing like a mosque's usual decoration. A Persian inscription over the gate records plainly where that stone came from. What does it say?
answer: taken from 27 Hindu and Jain temples torn down to build it
choices: taken from 27 Hindu and Jain temples torn down to build it
carved by Hindu stonemasons the sultan hired for the work
carried by camel from the old temples of distant Mathura
cut fresh, then decorated in the style of the conquered land
context: A Persian inscription over the eastern gate states outright that the Quwwat-ul-Islam — the first mosque in Delhi and the oldest surviving Ghurid building in India — was raised from the materials of 27 demolished Hindu and Jain temples. The reused columns still carry their original bell-and-chain and lotus carvings, plainly visible in the stone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quwwat-ul-Islam_Mosque

question: Humayun's Tomb in Delhi is more than one man's grave. Within its red sandstone chambers and across its garden lie more than a hundred Mughal emperors, princes, and nobles, buried over the centuries. What nickname did this crowd of royal graves earn the great mausoleum?
choices: the Tomb of a Hundred Kings
the Garden of the Mughal Dead
context: Humayun's Tomb (built 1565–1572) was the first great garden-tomb on the Indian subcontinent. More than a hundred Mughals lie buried across the complex, earning it the nickname 'the Dormitory of the Mughals.' UNESCO listed it in 1993. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humayun%27s_Tomb

question: The 1,600-year-old iron pillar beside the Qutb Minar has scarcely rusted, though ordinary iron left in the open would have crumbled to flakes long ago. In the 2000s, metallurgist R. Balasubramaniam finally worked out its secret. What keeps Delhi's iron pillar from rusting?
answer: its iron is rich in phosphorus, which grows a thin, self-healing protective film
choices: its iron is rich in phosphorus, which grows a thin, self-healing protective film
a hidden layer of chromium was mixed in, as in modern stainless steel
a baked coat of clay and linseed oil once sealed the whole surface
the iron is so exceptionally pure that nothing in it can corrode
context: The iron holds unusually high phosphorus — about 0.25%, versus under 0.05% in modern iron — which grows a thin, self-healing film (misawite giving way to a crystalline iron-hydrogen-phosphate skin) only about one-twentieth of a millimetre thick after 1,600 years. It is the impurity, not purity, that protects it. Metallurgist R. Balasubramaniam of IIT Kanpur worked out the chemistry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_pillar_of_Delhi

question: Humayun's Tomb rises at the heart of a vast walled garden in Delhi, divided into four equal quarters by raised stone walkways and channels of running water. The design is meant as an earthly picture of the four rivers of paradise. What is this classic four-fold garden design called?
context: Char bagh means 'four gardens' in Persian: a paradise garden quartered by walkways and water channels standing for the four rivers of paradise, here subdivided into 32 smaller plots. Humayun's Tomb, funded by his widow Empress Bega Begum, set the pattern for the Mughal garden-tombs to come. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humayun%27s_Tomb

question: Golden Persian letters run along the marble arches of the Diwan-i-Khas, the Hall of Private Audience in Delhi's Red Fort, boasting that no place on earth is lovelier. Repeated three times over for emphasis, the famous couplet begins: 'If there is a paradise on earth...' — how does it go on?
answer: '...it is this, it is this, it is this.'
choices: '...it is this, it is this, it is this.'
'...it is here, it is here, it is here.'
'...it is ours, it is ours, it is ours.'
'...it is now, it is now, it is now.'
context: The couplet reads, 'Agar firdaus bar ru-ye zamin ast, hamin ast-o hamin ast-o hamin ast' — 'If there is a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this.' It is traditionally credited to the poet Amir Khusrow, though modern scholars doubt that attribution. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diwan-i-Khas_(Red_Fort)

question: Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, with its soaring white double dome on a red-sandstone base, was modelled on Timur's mausoleum, the Gur-e-Amir, in Samarkand. Its design was carried forward, grander still, into one final tomb that perfected the form — completing a lineage of great domes running from Samarkand, to Delhi, to one last monument. Which one completes it?
context: Humayun's Tomb was modelled on Timur's Gur-e-Amir mausoleum in Samarkand and became the prototype that led, decades later, to the Taj Mahal at Agra — a dome lineage running Samarkand → Delhi → Agra. It was designed by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas in red sandstone with a white double dome. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humayun%27s_Tomb

question: For nearly a century the Red Fort in Delhi held the most dazzling seat on earth — a solid-gold throne that took seven years to make, blazing with some 26,733 gems, among them the Koh-i-Noor diamond and the great Timur Ruby. By what name is this lost treasure of the Red Fort remembered?
context: The Peacock Throne — Takht-e-Taus — took about seven years to build and was studded with some 26,733 gems, including the Koh-i-Noor diamond and the great Timur Ruby, and was said to have cost twice as much as the Taj Mahal. It was later carried away from Delhi and eventually broken up, its jewels scattered into crowns and treasuries around the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacock_Throne  (Legend.)

question: High in the mountains of central Greece, the ancient Greeks believed Delphi sat at the exact center of the earth. They set a carved, dome-shaped stone there to mark the spot. Borrowing their word for a part of the human body, what did the Greeks call this center of the world?
context: The Greek word was omphalos, meaning 'navel' -- the belly-button of the earth. A carved, dome-shaped omphalos stone marked the spot; the one in the Delphi museum today is a Roman-era copy. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omphalos_of_Delphi

question: Delphi was not built on flat ground. Its temples and treasuries climb a steep hillside in central Greece in terraces, looking down toward the blue waters of the Gulf of Corinth far below. On the slopes of which mountain was the sanctuary of Delphi built?
context: Delphi clings to the southern slopes of Mount Parnassus in central Greece, ringed by tall cliffs; the dramatic setting high above the Gulf of Corinth was part of why the Greeks felt the place was holy. https://www.worldhistory.org/delphi/

question: Kings, generals, and ordinary Greeks travelled for days to Delphi to ask about the future before any great undertaking. The prophecies did not come from a priest or a council of elders. The oracle's voice belonged to a single woman who sat in Apollo's temple. What was this priestess of Delphi called?
context: The Pythia was among the most powerful women of the ancient world, consulted before wars, voyages, and the founding of new cities. The oracle could be asked its prophecies on only one day each month. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythia

question: Why should Delphi, of all the places on earth, be its exact center? Greek myth gave a vivid answer: the god Zeus set two creatures loose from the opposite edges of the world, flying toward each other at matching speed, and where they met he dropped the omphalos stone. What pair of creatures did Zeus release to find the center of the world?
context: The two eagles met directly above Delphi, fixing it as the middle of everything, and the Roman-era omphalos stone was once topped by two gilded eagles echoing Zeus's birds. This is myth, not history. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omphalos_of_Delphi  (Legend.)

question: Before it was ever called Delphi, the sanctuary carried the older name Pytho. Greek legend tied that name to a monster: the god Apollo, arriving to claim the site, killed a huge creature that guarded the spring. The priestess who later prophesied there, the Pythia, was named after it. What creature did Apollo kill at Delphi?
context: The slain serpent was named Python; from it came the sanctuary's older name, Pytho, and the priestess's title, Pythia. Apollo claimed the site and became the god of its prophecies. This is myth. https://www.worldhistory.org/delphi/  (Legend.)

question: King Croesus of Lydia, one of the richest men alive, sent to Delphi to ask whether he dared attack the mighty Persian Empire. The oracle promised that if he marched, 'a great empire would be destroyed.' Encouraged, Croesus attacked. Which empire was destroyed in the war that followed?
context: Croesus lost the war, and his kingdom of Lydia fell to Cyrus the Great of Persia. The tale, told by the historian Herodotus, became the ancient world's most famous warning about the oracle's double-edged riddles. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croesus  (Legend.)

question: The Pythia gave her prophecies seated on a tripod above a crack in the floor of Apollo's temple, where the ancients said strange fumes rose to cloud her mind. Long dismissed as legend, the story got fresh support in the 1980s when geologists found two fault lines crossing beneath the temple. They proposed that quakes heated the rock and released a specific gas through the fissures. Which gas did they name as the likely cause?
context: Geologist Jelle de Boer and archaeologist John Hale proposed that fault movements heated underground bitumen and freed ethylene, a gas once used as an anaesthetic. A 2001 sample from a spring near Delphi showed about 0.3 parts per million of ethylene. It remains a real but DEBATED theory, not proven fact. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythia

question: Delphi was not only a place of prophecy but also a place of wisdom. Carved at the entrance to Apollo's temple stood short sayings credited to Greece's legendary Seven Sages, read by every visitor who came to consult the oracle. Which of these maxims was carved at the temple of Delphi?
context: The Greek was gnothi seauton, 'know thyself'; beside it stood meden agan, 'nothing in excess.' Because prophecy and philosophy met at its temple, Delphi shaped Greek thinkers for centuries. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphic_maxims

question: Denali is the tallest mountain in North America, rising over 20,000 feet above the wide taiga forests of Alaska. Long before mapmakers or European explorers ever came, the Koyukon people were already living in the valleys around it. For countless generations they had used a name of their own for the mountain at the heart of their home: 'Denali.' In the Koyukon language, what does 'Denali' mean?
context: In Koyukon, 'Denali' means 'the High One' (or 'the Tall One') -- a name the Koyukon have used for the mountain for centuries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali.

question: Denali, the tallest peak in North America, rises out of the Alaska wilderness. Its height on official U.S. maps had read 20,320 feet ever since a 1952 survey done with older ground-based instruments. Then in 2015 the U.S. Geological Survey published a new official figure -- 20,310 feet -- ten feet lower than the number generations of Americans had grown up with. What produced the new, slightly lower number?
answer: A modern GPS remeasurement of the peak
choices: A modern GPS remeasurement of the peak
A recount using the older survey math
A switch to a metric baseline height
A correction for the summit's snow depth
context: The 2015 USGS GPS survey put Denali at 20,310 ft (6,190 m), ten feet under the 1952 figure of 20,320 ft -- the mountain hadn't shrunk; the measurement simply got sharper. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali (USGS 2015).

question: The Seven Summits are the highest peak on each of Earth's seven continents. In North America that peak is Denali, in the state of Alaska. In Asia it is Mount Everest, which climbs higher above sea level than any other mountain on the planet. Denali is not the tallest of the Seven Summits, but it does stand out from the other six in one special way. Which one?
answer: The most northerly of the seven
choices: The most northerly of the seven
The most equatorial of the seven
The only volcano among the seven
The most difficult of the seven
context: Denali (~63 degN, just below the Arctic Circle) is the coldest and most northerly of the Seven Summits -- which is why it demands cold-weather mountaineering skill far out of proportion to its 6,190 m height. Source: rei.com; atlasandboots.com.

question: Denali, the tallest peak in North America, rises from the flat Alaskan lowland at its foot all the way to its icy summit -- a climb of about 18,000 vertical feet. That is one of the biggest base-to-summit rises of any mountain on land. Mount Everest's peak in Asia reaches higher above sea level than Denali. So how can Denali's actual rise from its base to its top still be bigger than Everest's?
answer: Everest's climb begins on an already-high plateau
choices: Everest's climb begins on an already-high plateau
Everest is measured only during the dry season
Everest's true base lies hidden beneath the sea
Everest's summit has never been fully surveyed
context: Denali's base-to-summit relief is about 18,000 ft (5,500 m) -- among the greatest on land -- because it springs from a near-sea-level plain. Everest tops out higher above the sea but climbs only ~12,000-15,000 ft above its own high base. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali (relief); Britannica.

question: In December 2003, a weather station high on Denali -- the giant peak in Alaska -- logged a reading so far outside normal that it still stands as a North American record more than twenty years later. Denali's summit, at 20,310 feet, is famous for how murderous its winter cold can get. Which weather record did Denali set that December?
answer: The lowest wind chill ever recorded
choices: The lowest wind chill ever recorded
The strongest surface gust ever recorded
The heaviest single snowfall ever recorded
The lowest barometric pressure ever recorded
context: On Dec 1, 2003, a summit station recorded a wind chill of -118.1 degF (-83.4 degC) -- a North American record; the air temperature that month hit -75.5 degF (-59.7 degC). Denali's far-north latitude plus great height make it one of the coldest mountains on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali (climate); BBC Science Focus.

question: Imagine two climbers standing at exactly the same height above the sea -- 6,190 meters up -- one on Denali in the far Alaskan north, the other on a mountain near the equator. Both are breathing thin air, but the climber on Denali struggles far more for every breath than the equatorial climber. Why is the very same altitude harder to breathe up near the pole?
answer: The atmosphere is squashed thinner over the poles
choices: The atmosphere is squashed thinner over the poles
Cold air holds much less oxygen than warm air
Falling snow scrubs oxygen out of the summit air
Fierce winds blow the breathable air off the peak
context: Earth's atmosphere is thinner over the poles than the equator, so Denali's 6,190 m summit air is as thin as roughly 7,000 m in the tropics -- it feels physiologically some 800 m higher. NOVA notes Everest, if it stood at Denali's latitude, would feel about 3,000 ft higher. Source: pbs.org/wgbh/nova/denali/extremes/pressure.html.

question: Unlike most old mountains, Denali in Alaska is still slowly growing -- over the ages it inches taller instead of wearing down. Running 1,250 miles beside it lies the great Denali Fault, one of the largest cracks in North America's crust. Deep below that fault, two of Earth's giant tectonic plates are pushing against each other. Which plate movement is driving the whole Alaska Range upward?
answer: The Pacific plate grinding beneath North America
choices: The Pacific plate grinding beneath North America
The Atlantic seafloor spreading apart far offshore
A rising mantle hotspot melting through the crust
The Indian plate crashing northward into the range
context: The Denali Fault arcs more than 1,250 miles across southern Alaska; there the Pacific plate grinds beneath (subducts under) the North American plate, uplifting the Alaska Range. The fault slips about 7 mm a year, and the ongoing squeeze may lift Denali roughly another kilometer over the next ~2 million years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali_Fault; nps.gov.

question: Devils Tower became famous when Steven Spielberg used it in his 1977 film 'Close Encounters of the Third Kind.' It is the spot where humans finally meet the aliens. In the most famous scene, one man is so haunted by the shape of the tower that he sculpts it at the dinner table. What does he sculpt it from?
context: In 'Close Encounters of the Third Kind' (1977), the obsessed everyman Roy Neary (played by Richard Dreyfuss) can't stop molding a shape he doesn't understand — including out of his mashed potatoes at the dinner table. That shape is Devils Tower, the Wyoming landmark where the film's alien mothership finally lands, a scene that made the tower's outline one of the most recognizable in the world. Source: Intermountain Histories 'Close Encounters of the Third Kind and Devils Tower'; Cowboy State Daily '50 Years Later, Sci-Fi Fans Still Find Their Close Encounters At Devils Tower.'

question: In 1906, the United States made a new law. It let a president protect a natural or historic wonder on public land right away. That September, President Theodore Roosevelt used the law on Devils Tower. It was the first place in the country to get this kind of protection. What was Devils Tower the first of?
context: The 1906 Antiquities Act let a president quickly protect 'objects of historic or scientific interest' on federal land. On September 24, 1906, Theodore Roosevelt used this brand-new power to make Devils Tower the very first national monument in United States history. Source: National Park Foundation 'Devils Tower National Monument'; NPS 'DETO 110th Anniversary.'

question: On the coast of Northern Ireland, the Giant's Causeway is a mass of neat stone columns packed edge to edge — and Devils Tower is ribbed with the very same kind of columns, only supersized, up to 600 feet tall. Both are hard igneous rock, and both got their columns the same way. What splits such rock into tidy, many-sided columns?
answer: cooling shrinks and cracks it apart
choices: cooling shrinks and cracks it apart
surf pounds it into stacked blocks
wind-blown sand scours grooves in it
creeping glaciers grind it into ribs
context: As a thick body of molten rock cools, it shrinks, and the shrinking pulls it apart into a honeycomb of cracks that grow downward into long, four- to seven-sided columns — a process called columnar jointing. The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland is the world's most famous example; Devils Tower is the same thing supersized, its columns of gray-green phonolite reaching up to about 600 feet tall and 20 feet wide. Source: NPS 'Devils Tower Geologic Formations'; Wikipedia 'Devils Tower'; EarthDate 'Devils Tower.'

question: Devils Tower's rock — hard igneous phonolite — first hardened deep underground, tens of millions of years ago, hidden inside the layered rock of the plains. Yet today it stands as a bare tower in the open air. Which process took that buried rock and turned it into the free-standing tower we see?
answer: erosion stripped away the rock that once covered it
choices: erosion stripped away the rock that once covered it
an earthquake split the ground and pushed it up
a glacier bulldozed the surrounding land away
underground pressure slowly squeezed it upward
context: Devils Tower's phonolite cooled from magma underground about 40 million years ago, wrapped in much softer sedimentary rock. Over the last several million years, rivers and weather wore that soft rock away, exhuming the tough core that now stands 867 feet tall. Geologists say the tower was uncovered, not built up — a landform revealed by erosion rather than piled up by lava or plates. Source: EarthDate 'Devils Tower'; Wikipedia 'Devils Tower'; NPS 'Devils Tower Geologic Formations.'

question: The Lakota and Kiowa call Devils Tower 'Bear Lodge,' and their stories explain its shape. In the Kiowa version, seven girls playing on the plains were chased by a giant bear; they climbed onto a low rock and prayed, and the rock rose higher and higher beyond the bear's reach — while the bear's claws raked long grooves down its sides. Carried up with the rising rock, what did the seven girls finally become?
answer: the seven stars of the Pleiades
choices: the seven stars of the Pleiades
the seven stars of the Big Dipper
the seven peaks of the Black Hills
the seven colors of the rainbow
context: To more than 20 tribes this rock is Bear Lodge — Mato Thipila in Lakota. In the Kiowa legend the seven girls became the Pleiades, the little star cluster also called the Seven Sisters; in Lakota tellings the bear's claws scratching the rising rock explain the tower's vertical columns. The name 'Devils Tower' came from an 1875 U.S. expedition under Colonel Richard Irving Dodge, whose interpreter reportedly mistranslated Mato Thipila as 'Bad God's Tower.' Many tribes today ask that the older name, Bear Lodge, be restored. Source: ICT 'The Legend of Devils Tower'; Travel Wyoming 'Bear Lodge: The Sacred Legend of Devils Tower'; NPS 'Devils Tower or Bear Lodge?'

question: Devils Tower looks so much like the neck of an old volcano that a volcano was long the favorite explanation for it. But geologists are now certain no volcano ever erupted here, and their conclusion rests on one telltale clue. Which clue convinced them there was never an eruption?
answer: the total absence of volcanic ash
choices: the total absence of volcanic ash
the great height of the columns
the gray-green color of the rock
context: Devils Tower is made of igneous rock that cooled from magma, so a volcano was the obvious guess. But an erupting volcano blankets the land in ash, and the sedimentary rocks around Devils Tower contain none — so no eruption ever happened here. Geologists still debate exactly what the tower is: a laccolith (a blister of magma that domed up the layers), a volcanic neck, or another kind of intrusion. What they all agree on is that the magma cooled underground and erosion later exposed it. Source: EarthDate 'Devils Tower'; Wikipedia 'Devils Tower.'

question: The Continental Divide of the Americas runs along the very top of the Rocky Mountains, all the way from Alaska to the tip of South America, like a giant tilted roof laid across two continents. Rain that lands on the divide's western slope runs downhill toward the west coast of North and South America. Which ocean does that western water finally reach?
context: The Continental Divide rides the crest of the Rockies (and, farther south, the Andes), sorting every raindrop by the slope it lands on: west to the Pacific, east — by way of the Gulf of Mexico — to the Atlantic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Divide_of_the_Americas

question: The Mississippi River gathers rain and snowmelt from 31 U.S. states — almost half the country — and funnels every drop down to the Gulf of Mexico. Geographers have a single term for all the land whose water drains into one river system like this. What is that term?
context: That whole water-gathering territory is a drainage basin (also called a watershed or catchment); the ridge-line separating one basin from the next is a drainage divide. The Mississippi's basin covers roughly 41% of the contiguous United States. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin

question: Triple Divide Peak in Montana is a rare spot where meltwater from a single summit runs off to three different seas. One creek runs to the Pacific. Another reaches the Atlantic by way of the Gulf of Mexico. The third creek flows north across Canada and drains into a bay along the country's northern edge. Which body of water does that third creek finally reach?
context: Triple Divide Peak (8,025 ft) is called the 'hydrological apex' of North America: one summit feeding the Pacific, the Atlantic/Gulf of Mexico, and — via the Nelson River — Hudson Bay toward the Arctic. Some geographers argue Snow Dome in Alberta is the truer apex if Hudson Bay is counted as part of the Atlantic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_Divide_Peak_(Montana)

question: High in the Teton Wilderness of Wyoming lies a lonely mountain creek that flows up out of the forest and climbs to the very crest of the Continental Divide -- the huge ridge along the Rockies that separates east-flowing water from west-flowing water. Right at the crest, that creek does something almost no other stream on Earth does. What happens to the creek right there?
answer: It splits in two, its halves bound for opposite oceans
choices: It splits in two, its halves bound for opposite oceans
It sinks into a cave and flows onward underground
It spreads into a marsh and evaporates in the sun
It tumbles off a cliff as a tall waterfall
context: The site is the 'Parting of the Waters' at Two Ocean Pass, a National Natural Landmark since 1965. North Two Ocean Creek forks: Atlantic Creek travels 3,488 miles to the Gulf of Mexico, Pacific Creek 1,353 miles to the Pacific. It is said a fish could swim clear across the Continental Divide here. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parting_of_the_Waters

question: One river's drainage basin covers roughly 7 million square kilometres, about 40 percent of an entire continent. Its network of rivers reaches into nine different countries. No river on Earth drains a wider stretch of land. Which river commands this record-breaking basin?
context: The Amazon's basin covers about 7,000,000 km² — some 35–40% of South America — spread across nine countries and territories, the largest drainage basin on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_basin

question: The Continental Divide does not only creep along low ridges. Where it crosses Colorado, it climbs the high spine of the Rocky Mountains. Its highest point in North America sits above 14,000 feet. Which Colorado peak is the highest point the divide crosses?
context: Grays Peak, Colorado (14,278 ft / 4,352 m) is the highest point on the Continental Divide in North America. Colorado's tallest mountain overall, Mount Elbert, stands higher still but sits off the divide. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Divide_of_the_Americas

question: The Congo River winds back and forth across the equator through the middle of Africa. Along the way it gathers the runoff of the world's second-largest rainforest, and its full flow is one of the mightiest of any river anywhere. After a long journey of some 4,700 kilometers through jungle and rapids, into which ocean does the Congo finally empty its brown water?
context: The Congo drains the world's second-largest river basin (~3.7 million km²) and Africa's largest rainforest, emptying into the Atlantic at the Gulf of Guinea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_Basin

question: In southern Wyoming, the Continental Divide does something peculiar. Instead of running as one clean line, it splits and loops around a wide sagebrush desert called the Great Divide Basin. Rain and snow that fall inside the loop can never reach the Pacific, the Atlantic, or any ocean at all, so the water just pools and evaporates. Geographers have a special name for a basin like this, sealed off from every sea. What is it called?
context: An endorheic basin has no outlet to the sea. Wyoming's Great Divide Basin is a rare gap where the Continental Divide splits and wraps around it, so its water pools and evaporates internally rather than reaching any ocean. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Divide_of_the_Americas

question: Deep in southern Venezuela runs the Casiquiare. It is a natural channel that does what rivers almost never do. It breaks away from one great river and carries its water off into a completely different river system, quietly joining two river worlds that maps usually draw as separate. Which two river basins does it link?
choices: the Amazon and the São Francisco
context: A river that splits and feeds two different systems is a bifurcation. The Casiquiare branches off the upper Orinoco and flows ~320 km into the Rio Negro (an Amazon tributary) — the world's largest natural link between two major river basins. Alexander von Humboldt confirmed the connection in 1800. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casiquiare_canal

question: In 2016, Canada's shrinking Kaskawulsh Glacier stopped feeding the north-flowing Slims River and diverted its meltwater into a neighboring river bound for the Gulf of Alaska — within a single season, the Slims' old channel ran dry. It was the first event of its kind ever witnessed by scientists as it happened. Geologists have a vivid name for this sudden rerouting. What is it called?
context: This is river capture (also called stream piracy). The 2016 Kaskawulsh event was the first river capture ever observed by scientists in real time. Geologists think the Casiquiare is slowly capturing the upper Orinoco the same way — eventually pirating it into the Amazon basin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_capture

question: In Boston, the Freedom Trail climbs Breed's Hill, where colonial militia fought the Battle of Bunker Hill in 1775. It is one of more than a hundred smooth, egg-shaped hills scattered across the city. A passing ice sheet shaped each one from the rubble it dragged along under itself. What do geologists call this kind of whale-backed hill that moving ice shapes from its own debris?
context: Both Breed's Hill and Bunker Hill are drumlins — whale-backed hills a glacier moulds from its own glacial till (ground-up rock). The word comes from the Irish 'droimin,' a 'little ridge' (first written down in 1833). When drumlins crowd together, the bumpy country is nicknamed a 'basket of eggs'; Boston sits on more than 100 of them, and many of the Boston Harbor Islands are drowned drumlins. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drumlin; https://www.nps.gov/places/bunker-hill.htm

question: Clew Bay in County Mayo, on Ireland's west coast, is packed with a scatter of little rounded green islands — the drowned tops of a drumlin field that the sea flooded after the last ice age. A well-known local saying brags that the bay holds exactly one island for every ___ of the year. Every what?
context: Clew Bay is a drowned drumlin field: about 12,000 years ago the ice-moulded hills stood on dry land, then the post-glacial sea rose and flooded the low ground between them, leaving each rounded summit as an island. Surveyors actually count roughly 141 named islands and islets, not 365 — the 'one for every day of the year' line is a local saying, not a survey count. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clew_Bay  (Legend.)

question: Between Rochester and Syracuse, New York, roughly 10,000 drumlins crowd the countryside — each a smooth hill of glacial debris that the moving ice sheet moulded as it ground slowly past. Geologists prize a drumlin field because its shape preserves one lost fact about the Laurentide glacier, gone now for 18,000 years. What can they read from the shape of the drumlins?
answer: the direction the ice was flowing
choices: the direction the ice was flowing
the thickness of the ice sheet
the number of winters the ice lasted
the temperature of the vanished glacier
context: A drumlin is a frozen compass. Its steep, blunt end faces UP-ice — back toward where the glacier came from (geologists call it the 'stoss' end) — and it tapers into a long, gentle tail pointing the way the ice flowed. So a whole field of drumlins, all streamlined the same way, records the vanished glacier's direction of travel. The Rochester–Syracuse field, moulded under the Laurentide Ice Sheet about 18,000 years ago, is one of the largest on Earth: roughly 10,000 drumlins over about 12,000 square km. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drumlin; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0037073806002466

question: In the Swedish city of Uppsala, a long, winding natural ridge runs for miles right through the middle of town. It is so straight and uniform that it looks like a man-made railway embankment. It is really the fossil bed of a river that once flowed in a tunnel underneath a glacier, left standing high and dry when the ice melted away. What is this kind of glacial ridge called?
context: An esker is water's signature under the ice: it is built of well-sorted sand and gravel, proof that a flowing meltwater river — not the ice itself — laid it down (a moraine, by contrast, is the unsorted rubble a glacier dumps straight off its melting edge). Because the river ran in a tunnel at the glacier's base, its gravel bed was left standing above the surrounding land once the ice vanished. Uppsala's esker, the Uppsalasasen, runs for roughly 250 km, straight through the heart of the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esker

question: Across the boggy heart of Ireland runs the Eiscir Riada, a chain of eskers whose gravel stands dry above the surrounding bog. For centuries it carried the Sli Mhor, the 'Great Way' between Dublin and Galway. But old tradition gives the ridge a grander role. After the battle of Magh Lena, around the 2nd century AD, legend says the Eiscir Riada was used to do what important thing?
answer: divide Ireland in two between two rival kings
choices: divide Ireland in two between two rival kings
carry the war dead to burial by the western sea
wall the great monasteries off from raiders
guide pilgrims to a holy well at its end
context: Old Irish tradition made the Eiscir Riada the line that split the island in two after the battle of Magh Léna: the northern half, Leath Cuinn ('Conn's Half'), went to Conn Céadchathach — Conn of the Hundred Battles — and the southern half, Leath Mogha ('Mug's Half'), to Mug Nuadat. It is a legend, not recorded history, placed around the 2nd century AD. In everyday life the ridge earned its fame as a road: the name joins Old Irish 'escir' (ridge) with 'riad' (the riding of horses — a road), and because an esker stands raised and dry above otherwise impassable bog, the Eiscir Riada carried the Sli Mhor, the main east–west route linking the monasteries of Clonard, Durrow, and Clonmacnoise on the Shannon. Source: https://www.encyclopedia.com/international/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/eiscir-riata; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esker_Riada

question: In eastern Finland, the Punkaharju ridge is a knife-thin esker — a glacier's old gravel riverbed — that snakes for 7 km between two lakes, in places barely 10 metres wide, carrying both a road and a railway right along its crest. Tsar Alexander I was so struck by the ridge when he visited in 1802 that in 1843 the state acted on his wish. What did Finland do to Punkaharju?
answer: it was set aside as one of the world's earliest protected areas
choices: it was set aside as one of the world's earliest protected areas
it was sliced in two by a shipping canal
it was crowned with an imperial summer palace
it was chosen as Finland's new capital
context: Punkaharju threads between two lakes of the vast Saimaa system — Puruvesi and Pihlajavesi — along a ridge in places only about 10 metres wide, yet it carries both a road and a railway on the glacier's old riverbed. Tsar Alexander I of Russia (Finland was then a Russian grand duchy) visited in 1802 and asked that the ridge be preserved; it was formally protected in 1843, one of the earliest such protections anywhere in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punkaharju_Ridge

question: Rising straight out of the desert coast of Dubai, a spire of steel and glass climbs 828 metres into the sky. Since the day it opened, it has been the tallest building on Earth, taller than any tower raised before it. What is this record-breaking skyscraper called?
context: The Burj Khalifa opened on 4 January 2010 and rises 828 m (2,716 ft) with 163 floors — the most of any building on Earth. It broke eight world records at once, unseating Taipei 101 as the world's tallest, and has held the title ever since. Architect Adrian Smith of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it; originally to be named 'Burj Dubai,' it was renamed for Sheikh Khalifa of Abu Dhabi after he lent Dubai a $10 billion bail-out to finish it. Source: Guinness World Records (guinnessworldrecords.com/records/hall-of-fame/burj-khalifa-tallest-building-in-the-world).

question: Off the coast of Dubai, engineers spent years pulling sand and rock up from the seabed to build a vast artificial island. It is so enormous that astronauts can trace its shape from orbit. Its winding edges added hundreds of kilometres of new beach to the city. What shape did the builders give this island?
context: The island is Palm Jumeirah, built entirely from dredged sand and rock — land reclamation begun in June 2001, with no steel frame, just stacked stone and sand. Its palm design has a central 'trunk,' sixteen leaf-like 'fronds,' and a curving outer 'crescent' breakwater ring, and its long shoreline added hundreds of kilometres of beachfront to Dubai's coast. (Dubai's other famous project, 'The World,' really is shaped like a map of the world.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palm_Jumeirah.

question: Long before its skyscrapers appeared, Dubai was a modest coastal port. Its divers held a single breath and plunged forty feet into the warm Persian Gulf. They did this thirty to fifty times each day, staying underwater for nearly two minutes. What treasure were the divers hunting along the seabed?
context: Old Dubai's breath-hold pearl divers were called ghawas. Before oil, pearling was the coast's lifeblood — most men in the towns worked in diving or seafaring — until the 1930s, when the Great Depression and Japan's new cultured pearls (perfected by Kokichi Mikimoto) collapsed the natural-pearl market almost overnight. Source: gulfnews.com — 'Step into the UAE's pearl diving history.'

question: Dubai looks out over the Persian Gulf, a shallow, hot arm of the Indian Ocean that averages only about 36 metres deep. Ringed by desert under a relentless sun, its water grows far saltier than the open ocean it connects to. Which natural process chiefly makes this warm, shallow sea so salty?
context: The Persian Gulf is a shallow, hot, very salty arm of the Indian Ocean, only about 36 m deep on average. Ringed by desert with little fresh water flowing in, it loses water to strong evaporation faster than rain or rivers can replace it, so salt concentrates and its water turns saltier than the open ocean it connects to. Those same warm, shallow waters and their oyster beds made Dubai's coast rich long before oil — until Dubai struck oil in 1966 at the offshore Fateh field, and its ruler Sheikh Rashid, knowing the oil would run out, poured the money into trade, turning a creek-side pearling port into a modern megacity. Source: britannica.com/place/Persian-Gulf.

question: Dubrovnik is a beautiful walled coastal city in Croatia. Above its historic Old Town runs a raised stone path about 1,940 metres long. From one side you gaze down at terracotta rooftops. From the other you overlook the open Adriatic sea. What are you walking along the top of?
context: Dubrovnik's complete, unbroken ring of city walls — about 1,940 m around — is the world's most famous city-wall walk, running high above the terracotta roofs and the sea. A modern aside: those walls stood in for King's Landing in HBO's Game of Thrones. Source: Wikipedia 'Walls of Dubrovnik'; wallsofdubrovnik.com.

question: Dubrovnik's landward wall rises 25 metres high and stretches up to six metres thick. From 9th century Saracen raiders to bombs in 1991, army after army tried to break it. Through every century of these terrible sieges, what does the city proudly boast about these walls?
answer: they were never breached by a hostile army
choices: they were never breached by a hostile army
they were the tallest city walls in Europe
they were the thickest walls in the Mediterranean
they were rebuilt higher after every siege
context: In all its centuries the wall was never breached by a hostile army, holding off everything from 9th-century Saracen raids to the 1991-92 bombardment. It is up to ~25 m high and up to ~6 m thick on the exposed land side, and thinner (~1.5-3 m) toward the sea. Source: wallsofdubrovnik.com ('never successfully breached'); Wikipedia 'Walls of Dubrovnik'.

question: In the walled seaside city of Dubrovnik on Croatia's Adriatic coast, one long, straight street called the Stradun runs 300 meters right through the heart of the Old Town, from one great gate to the other. For hundreds of years, countless footsteps have polished its pavement until today it shines like a mirror in the sunlight. What pale stone is the Stradun paved with, end to end?
context: The Stradun (also called Placa) is a ~300 m ribbon of white limestone buffed mirror-smooth by centuries of feet. After the great 1667 earthquake shattered the city, the street was rebuilt in matching baroque — which is why its houses line up so harmoniously today. Source: Wikipedia 'Stradun (street)'; Wikipedia 'Dubrovnik'.

question: On the eastern Adriatic coast, in what is now Croatia, the walled city of Dubrovnik became one of Europe's greatest little sea-trading powers. From 1358 to 1808, its merchant fleet sailed the Mediterranean and traded with rivals like Venice. It never fought a big war — it kept its freedom by clever diplomacy and by paying tribute to any empire, Ottoman or Habsburg, that might threaten it. What was this little sea-trading republic called?
context: The city we call Dubrovnik was for ~450 years the Republic of Ragusa, staying free between the Ottomans and Venice by diplomacy and tribute rather than armies. Its merchant fleet was so famous that the English word 'argosy' — a great merchant ship — comes from 'Ragusa.' Source: Wikipedia 'Republic of Ragusa'.

question: Above the gate of Fort Lovrijenac, which guards the seaward approach to Dubrovnik, the little republic carved a single Latin word. It was the same word displayed on its banner and its whole reason for existence. Which single Latin word was this republic's proud creed?
context: Ragusa's whole creed was one word — Libertas ('Liberty') — flown on its flag and carved over the Lovrijenac fortress gate: 'Non bene pro toto libertas venditur auro' — 'Freedom is not sold for all the gold in the world.' Source: Wikipedia 'Republic of Ragusa'; Wikipedia 'Fort Lovrijenac'.

question: All along the coast around Dubrovnik, whole rivers pour into holes in the ground and vanish, flowing on through hidden caves before bursting back out near the sea miles away. Geologists borrowed the name of a plateau on this very Adriatic coast for land shaped this way, and now use it for such terrain worldwide. What is that term?
context: 'Karst' — the caves, sinkholes and gleaming cliffs left where water dissolves limestone — takes its name from the Kras (Dinaric) plateau on this same north-Adriatic coast, and geologists now use it worldwide. That blazing white karst stone against the blue sea earned Dubrovnik its nickname 'the Pearl of the Adriatic,' credited to the poet Lord Byron. Source: Wikipedia 'Karst'; Wikipedia 'Dubrovnik'.

question: Easter Island is one of the loneliest inhabited islands on Earth. Across it stand about 900 giant carved figures with heavy brows and long torsos. Most face inland, with their backs turned to the sea, watching over the old village sites. What are these famous stone statues called?
context: The Rapanui carved about 900 of these giant figures, most standing on the coast with their backs to the sea, gazing inland over their villages. The moai are the island's signature wonder. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Moai; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moai.

question: On Easter Island the great statues do not stand loose on bare ground. Along the coast, islanders built long stone platforms of fitted stone. The statues were raised onto these platforms in rows facing their villages. What did the islanders call one of these stone platforms?
context: Each moai was raised onto a long stone ceremonial platform built along the shore, called an ahu. The largest ahu carried a whole row of moai. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Moai; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahu_Tongariki.

question: Almost every one of the island's hundreds of moai was cut from the soft volcanic rock of a single crater. On its inner and outer slopes, hundreds of half-finished giants still lie or stand where the carvers left them, some never even freed from the bedrock. Which crater is this great moai quarry?
context: Rano Raraku's soft, compressed volcanic ash (tuff) carves easily with stone tools; about 95% of all known moai came from this one quarry. Hundreds of unfinished statues remain frozen mid-work on its slopes. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Moai; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rano_Raraku.

question: Rapa Nui sits alone in the southeast Pacific Ocean. The nearest mainland coast, Chile, lies about 3,500 kilometres east. Even its closest neighboring island is roughly 2,000 kilometres away. Which tiny island is Rapa Nui's nearest inhabited neighbor?
context: Tiny Pitcairn Island lies about 2,075 km from Rapa Nui; the Chilean mainland is roughly 3,500 km off. The whole island is only about 164 sq km — one of the most isolated inhabited places on Earth. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Easter_Island; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Island.

question: For years, Rapa Nui was famous for its 'Easter Island heads.' Rows of giant stone faces poked from a grassy quarry slope, seeming to be nothing but enormous heads. Then archaeologists cleared away the soil around several of them and overturned that whole picture. What did they uncover?
answer: statues with full torsos and arms buried in the soil
choices: statues with full torsos and arms buried in the soil
unfinished statues still joined to the bedrock
rock carvings and petroglyphs cut into the slope
the stone picks the carvers left behind
context: The famous 'heads' are really whole statues: excavation showed full torsos and arms below the surface, the bodies swallowed over centuries by quarry rubble and washed-down soil. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rano_Raraku; grokipedia.com/page/Moai.

question: Along Rapa Nui's coast the moai were raised in rows on great stone platforms. The most famous line of all stands shoulder to shoulder on the island's largest platform: fifteen restored giants gazing inland in a single unbroken row. By what name is this celebrated platform of fifteen moai known?
context: Ahu Tongariki is the island's largest platform, carrying fifteen moai. Clan wars had toppled them, and in 1960 a tsunami from the great Chilean earthquake swept the fallen giants far inland; a 1990s project led by Claudio Cristino and Patricia Vargas re-raised the fifteen, using a crane donated by the Japanese firm Tadano. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahu_Tongariki; grokipedia.com/page/Easter_Island.

question: For centuries the standing moai were pictured with blank, empty eye sockets. Then in 1979, at Anakena beach, Sergio Rapu Haoa's team pieced together a fragment that solved the mystery. Once a statue was standing upright, its sockets had once been fitted with brilliant colored inlaid eyes. What were the whites of those eyes made from?
context: The whites were white coral, the pupils a disc of black obsidian or red scoria. The eyes were added only after the moai stood on its ahu, 'switching on' the statue's gaze — a secret uncovered only in 1979, when Sergio Rapu Haoa's team reconstructed a coral eye found at Anakena beach. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Moai; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moai.

question: The Rapanui somehow moved hundreds of moai — each weighing 10 tonnes or more — clear across their island with no wheels, no metal, and no draught animals. In 2012 archaeologists Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo showed one way a small crew could do it: with just 18 people, three ropes, and a 4.35-tonne replica, they moved the giant 100 metres in 40 minutes.
