context: The mound is Cheonmachong, the 'Heavenly Horse Tomb,' opened in 1973. The painted birch-bark mudguard shows the Cheonma, a mythical white 'sky horse' -- one of the very few Silla paintings that survive. Inside lay about 11,500 objects: a gold crown, gold bracelets and rings, and a 98 cm sword. The mound itself is 47 m across and 12.7 m high. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheonmachong  (Legend.)

question: In a Gyeongju field rises Cheomseongdae, a curved bottle-shaped tower of pale granite raised in the 630s under Queen Seondeok. From it, Silla astronomers watched and recorded the stars, sun and moon -- which makes it an observatory. Cheomseongdae holds a record that no other observatory in East Asia can claim. What is it?
choices: the tallest one in all of Asia
the most accurate one of its age
context: Cheomseongdae, built in the 630s under Queen Seondeok, is the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia. It is also a calendar in stone: about 362 blocks (near the days of the lunar year) stacked in 27 layers -- Seondeok was Silla's 27th ruler -- standing 9.17 m tall, with a small window that has 12 layers of stone above and 12 below, for the 12 months. Source: worldhistory.org/Cheomseongdae/

question: High on Mount Toham above Gyeongju, a stone dome shelters the Seokguram Grotto: a serene granite Buddha, 3.5 m tall, carved in the 8th century by the minister Kim Daeseong. The builders aimed the whole shrine with great care so that the Buddha looks out at one exact thing. What does the Buddha face?
answer: the first light of sunrise over the sea
choices: the first light of sunrise over the sea
the summit of the sacred mountain behind
the roofs of the royal tombs below
the gate of the temple down the slope
context: The Seokguram Grotto (begun 751) was aimed east so the Buddha catches the first light of sunrise over the East Sea, about 750 m above the water. Its builders used no mortar at all -- the domed roof is locked together with carved stone rivets, and its proportions follow careful geometry, the golden rectangle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seokguram

question: Below Seokguram stands Bulguksa temple, finished in 774, where two stone pagodas face each other across the courtyard -- one plain, one richly carved. In 1966 workers opened the plain pagoda, Seokgatap, and found a Buddhist scroll that had lain sealed inside for over 1,200 years. Why did that scroll astonish the world?
answer: it is among the oldest printed texts ever found
choices: it is among the oldest printed texts ever found
it is the first text printed with movable metal type
it is the oldest printed text with a known date
it is the oldest text ever written by hand
context: The scroll is the Great Dharani Sutra, printed from carved wooden blocks around 704-751 CE -- among the world's oldest surviving printed texts, though scholars still debate the exact date. (Movable metal type came far later, with Korea's Jikji of 1377; the oldest printed text bearing its own date is the Diamond Sutra of 868 CE.) Bulguksa (finished 774) is famous for its twin pagodas: plain Seokgatap, which hid the scroll, and ornate Dabotap, so beloved it is engraved on South Korea's 10-won coin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulguksa

question: For nearly a thousand years -- from 57 BCE to 935 CE -- Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom. Its rulers left so many monuments behind -- surveys still count more than 600 ancient burial mounds alone, along with old stone pagodas, temple terraces and Buddha carvings -- that Gyeongju has earned a single famous nickname. What is Gyeongju called?
choices: the city of a thousand kings
the gate to the eastern sea
context: Gyeongju was the Silla capital for nearly a thousand years, from 57 BCE to 935 CE. So many tombs, pagodas, temples and Buddhist carvings still stand across the open valley that the city is nicknamed 'the museum without walls.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeongju

question: Off the coast of northern Vietnam, an emerald-green sea is crowded with steep limestone towers that rise straight out of the water. Sailing through them feels like threading a forest made of stone. Roughly how many of these islands and islets fill Ha Long Bay?
context: More than 1,600 limestone islands and islets rise from Ha Long Bay, scattered across about 1,500 square kilometers of emerald-green sea off northern Vietnam — a drowned forest of stone. Source: NASA Earth Observatory, 'The Emerald Isles of Ha Long Bay' (science.nasa.gov).

question: The name Ha Long means 'descending dragon.' A Vietnamese legend tells how the Jade Emperor sent a Mother Dragon and her children swooping down from the sky to defend the coast from northern invaders. In the legend, how did the dragons raise the islands that walled the enemy fleet out of the bay?
answer: They spat jewels of jade and emerald that sank and turned to stone
choices: They spat jewels of jade and emerald that sank and turned to stone
They lashed the water with their tails until the waves froze into rock
They breathed fire that hardened the sea into blackened peaks
They dove beneath the waves and their scales sank and turned to stone
context: The bay's name, 'descending dragon,' comes from this legend: the Jade Emperor sent a Mother Dragon and her children to defend Vietnam, and the jewels of jade and emerald they spat into the sea turned to stone and became the islands that walled out the invaders. Source: SciTechDaily, 'Bai Tu Long Bay and the Legend of the Mother Dragon'; Grokipedia, 'Ha Long Bay'.

question: Rain is faintly acidic. Over millions of years, it slowly dissolved a thick slab of limestone in northern Vietnam into a maze of steep stone pinnacles -- a landscape geologists call tower karst. Today those same pinnacles stand as islands in the open sea. What turned the karst hills of Ha Long into a bay full of islands?
answer: Rising seas after the Ice Age drowned the valleys between them
choices: Rising seas after the Ice Age drowned the valleys between them
A powerful earthquake dropped the whole plain below the sea
Ancient rivers carved deep channels that the tide slowly filled
Old volcanoes blasted craters that later filled with seawater
context: Ha Long's islands are 'tower karst': faintly acidic rain dissolved a thick slab of limestone into steep pinnacles, then after the last Ice Age rising seas drowned the valleys between them, leaving only the tops above water. The tallest towers rise up to about 400 meters straight out of the sea. Source: UNESCO/IUCN evaluation via Grokipedia, 'Ha Long Bay'; NASA Earth Observatory, 'The Emerald Isles of Ha Long Bay'.

question: Among Ha Long Bay's thousands of stone towers, one slender pillar is called Dinh Huong, or the 'Incense Burner.' It is a much-loved symbol of the bay. The Vietnamese government put its picture on an everyday object where millions of citizens see it each day. On what everyday object does Dinh Huong appear?
context: Dinh Huong — the 'Incense Burner' islet — is so iconic it appears on Vietnam's 200,000-dong banknote. A nearby twin-rock called Trong Mai, the 'Fighting Cocks,' is a national symbol of Vietnamese tourism. Source: Vietnam.travel, 'Ha Long Bay's most mesmerizing islets'; thenewway.vn, 'Dinh Huong Islet'.

question: In Ha Long Bay's Bo Hon cluster, a narrow crack in a limestone tower leads inward before opening into a hall the size of a cathedral. It is about 500 meters long and 30 meters high, and its ceiling is hung with giant stalactites. When French explorers first mapped this hidden chamber in 1901, what did they name it?
choices: The Cave of the Dragon King
The Grotto of a Thousand Lamps
context: French explorers mapped this cave in 1901 and named it 'Grotte des Surprises' — the Cave of Surprises — for the way its narrow entrance opens into a vast inner hall. In Vietnamese it is Sung Sot, 'Surprise Cave'; it runs about 500 meters long and up to 30 meters high, hung with giant stalactites. Source: Oxalis Adventure, 'Explore Sung Sot Cave'; Vietnam Discovery, 'Surprise Cave'.

question: Some of Ha Long Bay's islands hide a secret in their very center: a perfectly still lake sits deep inside the island, ringed on every side by sheer limestone walls, with the open sea nowhere in sight. There is only one way to reach such a hidden lake. What is it?
answer: By paddling a small boat through a low sea-cave tunnel
choices: By paddling a small boat through a low sea-cave tunnel
By climbing over the cliff walls with ropes and ladders
By a stone staircase carved down through the rock
By a hidden footpath winding up and over the ridge
context: These sealed lakes are drowned sinkholes — dolines — trapped inside the rock. Ba Ham Lake, inside Dau Be island, is a chain of three ringed by cliffs; the tunnel in runs about 152 meters with a ceiling only 1.5-2.8 meters high, passable only at low tide. Dau Be island alone hides six such enclosed lakes. Source: HalongBayLux Cruises, 'Ho Ba Ham Islet'; UNESCO/IUCN evaluation via Grokipedia, 'Ha Long Bay'.

question: For a long time, writing in Korean meant learning thousands of Chinese characters. Only rich nobles had time for that. Then King Sejong made a new alphabet called Hangul. It swept the old system aside. How many letters are in the basic Hangul set?
context: Modern Hangul has just 24 basic letters — 14 consonants and 10 vowels; the original 1446 system had 28 (17 consonants, 11 vowels). Those few simple letters replaced the thousands of Chinese characters (Hanja) scholars once had to memorize. Hangul was created in 1443 and formally published in 1446. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hangul; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunminjeongeum.

question: King Sejong of Korea could already read Chinese, like every nobleman at his court. Yet in the 1440s he spent years designing a brand-new alphabet called Hangul. His own scholars fought him on it. Why did Sejong say he created it?
answer: so ordinary people could finally read and write
choices: so ordinary people could finally read and write
so the army could send its orders in secret code
so Buddhist monks could copy their sutras faster
so merchants could keep neater trade accounts
context: Sejong introduced Hangul to his court in 1443 (published 1446) precisely so commoners and women — over 99% of whom could not read the borrowed Chinese characters — could finally read and write for themselves. Unlike most alphabets, which grew slowly over centuries, Hangul was a single, deliberate royal invention. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hangul; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul.

question: In 1446 King Sejong of Korea published a brand-new alphabet called Hangul, made so ordinary people could finally read and write. The scholar Jeong Inji was amazed at how easy the new letters were to learn. He wrote that a wise man could master the whole Hangul script in a single morning. And even the slowest, dullest learner would need only how long?
context: The line comes from Jeong Inji's postface to the Hunminjeongeum Haerye (1446): a wise man could learn the script in one morning, 'even a stupid man' in ten days. It is often misattributed to King Sejong himself, but the boast was Jeong Inji's. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunminjeongeum_Haerye; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul.  (Legend.)

question: No other major alphabet in the world was designed the way Hangul's consonants were. King Sejong's scholars drew each consonant letter as a tiny diagram, and every one pictures the very same kind of thing. The square 'm', the angular 'k', and the letter for 'n' are each a little picture of what?
answer: your mouth and tongue in the act of making that sound
choices: your mouth and tongue in the act of making that sound
an object from nature whose name opens with that sound
a stroke borrowed from the matching Chinese character
a musical note marking the sound's pitch
context: Hangul is the only major 'featural' alphabet — its consonant shapes diagram the speech organs. ㅁ (m) is a closed square like sealed lips, ㄴ (n) shows the tongue tip at the ridge behind the teeth, ㅅ (s) pictures a pointed tooth, ㅇ the round open throat, and ㄱ (k) the tongue root blocking the back of the mouth. Linguist James McCawley called Hangul 'the most ingeniously devised writing system that exists.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul; grokipedia.com/page/Hangul.  (Legend.)

question: Hangul's vowels hide a tiny model of the universe. Every Korean vowel is built from just three simple marks, each representing one part of an ancient Korean cosmology: a round dot for the heavens, a flat horizontal line for the earth, and a single vertical stroke. What does that last mark represent?
context: The three vowel marks encode a tiny cosmology from the Hunminjeongeum Haerye: a round dot ㆍ for heaven, a flat line ㅡ for earth, and an upright line ㅣ for the standing human — combined to build every Korean vowel. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hangul; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul.  (Legend.)

question: Not everyone in Korea welcomed the new alphabet. In 1444, the year after Hangul appeared, Choe Manri — a senior scholar in King Sejong's own Hall of Worthies — sent the king a blistering petition demanding he scrap it and keep the classical Chinese characters. What did Choe warn that a homegrown Korean script would do?
answer: drag the kingdom down to the level of the northern barbarians
choices: drag the kingdom down to the level of the northern barbarians
empty the treasury that paid the royal scribes
anger the spirits who guarded the old characters
let commoners forge the king's own decrees
context: In his 1444 petition Choe Manri (Ch'oe Malli), a deputy in the Hall of Worthies, argued that only barbarians — the Mongols, Jurchens, Tanguts, Japanese and Tibetans — invent their own scripts, so a Korean script would make Joseon 'alike to the barbarians.' Elite yangban scholars long sneered at Hangul as eonmun ('vulgar script'), keeping Chinese characters for themselves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choe_Manri; grokipedia.com/page/Hangul.  (Legend.)

question: Scholars often call Hangul one of the most scientific writing systems ever invented — and in 2009 that reputation produced a remarkable first. A small people who had never had an alphabet of their own chose to write their language in Korea's Hangul: the first time any non-Korean language ever adopted the script. Which people made that choice?
answer: the Cia-Cia of Buton Island, Indonesia
choices: the Cia-Cia of Buton Island, Indonesia
the Hmong of the Vietnamese highlands
the Chamorro of the island of Guam
context: In 2009 the Cia-Cia people (about 40,000 speakers) of Buton Island, Indonesia officially adopted a modified Hangul to write their previously unwritten language — the first non-Korean language to use Hangul as its primary script, a real-world test of the design scholars praise as one of the most scientific ever made. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hangul.

question: In the heart of Hanoi, the Old Quarter tangles into a maze nicknamed the '36 Streets'. Lanes like Hàng Bạc, Hàng Thiếc, and Hàng Mã have worn the same old names for centuries. Read one of these names and it tells you exactly what?
answer: The goods once sold along the lane
choices: The family that first settled the lane
The temple standing at the lane's end
The goods once sold along the lane
The emperor who first paved the lane
context: The word 'Hàng' means 'merchandise', so each 'Hàng + product' name is a fossil of the guild that clustered there after the 11th century: Hàng Bạc = Silver Street, Hàng Thiếc = Tin Street, Hàng Mã = Paper-Offerings Street, Hàng Gai = Silk Street. Roughly 76 lanes survive today, many still wearing the name of a vanished trade. Source: lasiestahotels.com/mamay/hanoi-old-quarter-streets-name.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanoi

question: At the edge of Hanoi's Old Quarter, a vermillion-red wooden footbridge arches in a bright curve across Hoàn Kiếm Lake to a temple on a small island. The Vietnamese gave this bridge, Cầu Thê Húc, a poetic name. What does 'Thê Húc' mean?
context: The Húc Bridge (Cầu Thê Húc), 'Perch of the Morning Sunlight', leads to Jade Island and Ngọc Sơn Temple — the Temple of the Jade Mountain — which honors the 13th-century general Trần Hưng Đạo. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoàn_Kiếm_Lake

question: The lake at the Old Quarter's edge is called Hoàn Kiếm, the 'Lake of the Returned Sword'. According to legend, Emperor Lê Lợi had wielded a magic sword to drive the Ming Chinese army out of Vietnam. One day, as he boated across the lake, a great animal broke the surface and demanded the blade back for its true owner, the Dragon King. What creature rose to reclaim the sword?
context: In the legend the golden turtle god Kim Quy reclaimed the sword the Dragon King had lent Lê Lợi to expel the Ming; the grateful king renamed the lake Hoàn Kiếm, 'Returned Sword'. A crumbling islet still holds Tháp Rùa, Turtle Tower, and giant softshell turtles really did live in the lake — the last famous one died in 2016. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoàn_Kiếm_Lake

question: Hanoi is one of Asia's oldest capitals. In the year 1010, Emperor Lý Thái Tổ moved his royal seat to the banks of the Red River delta and gave the new city a grand, auspicious name it would carry for centuries. What was that original name?
answer: Thăng Long, 'City of the Ascending Dragon'
choices: Thăng Long, 'City of the Ascending Dragon'
Đại La, 'City of the Great Rampart'
context: By tradition Lý Thái Tổ saw a golden dragon rise over the Red River as he arrived, and named his capital Thăng Long, 'City of the Ascending Dragon' — the 1010 founding and the name are settled history, while the dragon vision is the founding legend. Đại La, Đông Đô, and Cổ Loa are all real early names of the Hanoi area. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanoi

question: In Hanoi's Old Quarter, old shop-houses are called 'tube houses.' They are just 2 to 4 metres wide at the street, but run 20 to 60 metres straight back. Why did families build them so thin at the front and so long behind?
answer: Tax was charged by a house's width along the street
choices: The lanes were too cramped to build any wider
Guild law capped how wide each shopfront could be
Tax was charged by a house's width along the street
Yearly floods pushed homes onto narrow dry ridges
context: Because the tax on a house was set by how wide it stood along the street, families built 'tube houses' (nhà ống) just a few metres wide but 20-60 metres deep — rarely up to 100 m. The narrow front was the shop; the family lived down the long tail and upper floors, with tiny interior courtyards pulling in light and air. Source: academia.edu (Tube houses in Hanoi Old Quarter); lasiestahotels.com/mamay/hanoi-old-quarter-streets-name.html

question: The oldest temple in Hanoi's Old Quarter honors the city's guardian spirit, Long Đỗ. Legend says that in 1010, when Emperor Lý Thái Tổ tried to raise the walls of his new citadel, they kept crumbling no matter how he laid the stone. He prayed at this temple, and an animal appeared and traced a great loop around the site; when the king built his ramparts along that trail, the walls at last held firm. What animal's path did the king follow?
context: The temple is named Bạch Mã — 'White Horse' — after this very legend; it is the oldest in the Old Quarter and honors the city-god Long Đỗ. By legend the white horse galloped the very loop the king's citadel walls then traced. Source: vinpearl.com/en/bach-ma-temple; authentiktravel.com (Bạch Mã Temple)

question: Hanoi grew up along the Red River where it spreads across its broad delta toward the sea. In 1831 the emperor Minh Mạng renamed the city Hà Nội, a name that pins exactly where it lies. What does 'Hà Nội' literally mean?
context: 'Hà Nội' means 'inside the river' — the city is cupped in a curve of the Red River (Sông Hồng). A delta is the fan of fertile land a river builds from dropped silt as it nears the sea; a dike is a raised earth wall that holds water back — the low, flood-prone city is ringed with them. Minh Mạng adopted the name in 1831, replacing the old Thăng Long. ('Land of Nine Dragons', Cửu Long, is the name of the far-southern Mekong delta.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanoi; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_Delta

question: Harar is an old walled town in Ethiopia. Inside a stone wall with just five gates, 368 twisting alleys pack into barely one square kilometre. The place is such a maze that people just call it that. But its walled old town has one ancient name. What is it called?
context: The single stone ring wall that wraps Harar's old town gives it the name the Jugol — about 3.5 km around and 4-5 metres high, pierced by just five historic gates, it squeezes the entire fortified town into barely one square kilometre. Inside, 368 narrow, twisting alleyways make the old town so dense it is often simply called a maze behind the wall; UNESCO lists the site as Harar Jugol, the Fortified Historic Town. Source: UNESCO WHC list/1189; nationalparks-worldwide.com/eaf/ethiopia/cities/harar/harar.html.

question: Many Muslims call the small Ethiopian town of Harar the fourth-holiest city of Islam. Inside its walls stand 82 mosques and over a hundred shrines, earning it the name 'City of Saints.' Harar ranks just behind Islam's three holiest cities. Which three are they?
context: Mecca (the Kaaba) and Medina (the Prophet's city) are Islam's two holiest sites, with Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa third; the fourth-holiest claim for Harar is widely held rather than a universal ranking. Inside Harar's one square kilometre stand 82 mosques — three of them from the 10th century — and 102 saints' shrines; its Arabic name Madinat al-Awliya means 'City of Saints.' Source: UNESCO WHC list/1189; ovpm.org/city/harar-jugol-ethiopia/.

question: Harar is famous for a startling ritual that unfolds just outside its stone wall every night. After dark, a lone man settles in the blackness beyond the town gate and does something almost no one else on Earth would dare. What is his nightly practice?
answer: Feeding wild spotted hyenas raw meat by hand
choices: Feeding wild spotted hyenas raw meat by hand
Juggling lit torches for passing caravans
Wrestling a leopard to the ground for crowds
Walking barefoot across a bed of hot coals
context: Every night outside Harar's wall, a 'hyena man' hand-feeds strips of raw meat to wild spotted hyenas that slip into town through gaps called 'hyena doors' — sometimes offering the meat off a stick held in his own mouth. Yusuf Mume Saleh began the nightly feeding around the 1950s-60s, reportedly to stop the hyenas raiding his goats, and his son Abbas Yusuf carries it on. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotted_hyenas_in_Harar; nationalgeographic.com/photography/article/this-man-lives-with-hyenas.

question: Harar is an ancient walled Muslim city in eastern Ethiopia, famous for its narrow lanes and old Islamic scholars. Step into one of Harar's tall old 'gey gar' houses and the walls glow bright red. There is a raised sitting platform and little display niches set into the walls. Filling those niches is one craft the townsfolk are famous for. What decorates a Harari home's walls?
context: Harar's 'gey gar' (city houses) have brightly painted interiors built around a raised platform called a nadaba, with wall niches (taqet) that display hung Harari basketry — a colourful woven craft that gives the homes an interior style unlike the usual layouts of Muslim countries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harar; UNESCO WHC list/1189.

question: For centuries Harar shut out all outsiders. Its people believed the town would fall the day a Christian passed the gates. In January 1855 the English explorer Richard Burton got inside anyway, the first European known to enter. How did Burton get through the gates?
choices: Under a sultan's letter of safe-conduct
By bribing a gatekeeper with coffee
Over the wall through a hyena hole
context: Richard Burton slipped into Harar in disguise in January 1855, the first European known to enter, and told the story in 'First Footsteps in East Africa' (1856); he had earlier used disguise to reach Mecca as well. The old belief that a Christian's entry would doom the city was local legend — Harar did not fall. Source: Richard F. Burton, 'First Footsteps in East Africa' (1856), burtoniana.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harar.

question: One of France's most dazzling young poets stunned the literary world by abandoning poetry for good in his early twenties. Arthur Rimbaud sailed to Africa and spent his last years, from 1880 to 1891, living inside the walls of Harar as a highland caravan trader on the old route down to the coast. In that famous market town, what goods did Rimbaud deal in?
context: Arthur Rimbaud, who wrote his revolutionary poetry as a teenager and abandoned it by about 21, spent 1880-1891 as a merchant in Harar dealing in coffee, hides, and musk along the great caravan route to the coast; a grand house in the town is now kept as the Rimbaud museum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harar.

question: Harris Tweed is a fine wool cloth from Scotland's Outer Hebrides. Top fashion brands around the world sell it. By law, every real length must be woven in just one place on the islands. Where is real Harris Tweed woven?
context: By law, every genuine length of Harris Tweed is handwoven by the islanders in their own homes on foot-powered treadle looms — never in a factory, and with no electricity. It is famous as a world-class cloth still made this cottage way, on the windswept Outer Hebrides of Lewis, Harris, the Uists, Benbecula and Barra. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed

question: Harris Tweed is a heavy wool cloth hand-woven in the Outer Hebrides, the windswept islands off Scotland's west coast. By the early 1900s, cheap machine-made cloth from mainland mills was being sold as 'Harris Tweed.' So in 1909 the Hebridean islanders won a trademark to guard the real thing. A stamp is still pressed on every real length. What is this famous mark called?
context: The mark is the Orb — a globe topped with a cross, registered in 1909 after islanders fought back against machine-made knock-offs. It is the oldest British certification mark still in use, stamped on the cloth only once inspectors confirm each length was handwoven in the Outer Hebrides. Source: wipo.int/web/wipo-magazine/articles/from-the-croft-to-the-catwalk-the-harris-tweed-certification-mark-38379; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed

question: Off the wild west coast of Scotland lie the Outer Hebrides, a chain of storm-lashed islands. For centuries, Gaelic-speaking crofters and weavers there wove a thick, hard-wearing wool cloth from the fleece of their own island sheep. Outsiders now know it around the world as Harris Tweed and prize it for winter coats. Long before that fame, the island weavers had their own Gaelic name for their prized fabric — 'clò-mòr'. In Scottish Gaelic, what does 'clò-mòr' mean?
context: 'Clò-mòr' means 'the big cloth' — the weavers' own name for it in Scottish Gaelic, used on Lewis and Harris for centuries before merchants and fashion houses ever called it 'Harris Tweed'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed; craftatlas.co/crafts/harris-tweed

question: Harris Tweed, the famous hand-woven wool cloth from Scotland's Outer Hebrides, has a rarer legal shield than a normal trademark. Passed in 1993, this British law says the cloth must be pure new wool, dyed and spun in the Outer Hebrides, and hand-woven by the islanders themselves in their own homes. What kind of shield is this?
choices: a royal warrant from the Crown
a worldwide patent on the weave
context: The protection is the Harris Tweed Act 1993 — a UK Act of Parliament passed for this one cloth. It defines Harris Tweed in law as fabric handwoven by the islanders at their homes in the Outer Hebrides, finished there, and made from pure virgin wool dyed and spun in the Outer Hebrides. Source: legislation.gov.uk/ukla/1993/11/enacted; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed

question: On the Scottish islands of Lewis and Harris, in the Outer Hebrides, home weavers still make the famous Harris Tweed cloth. By law it must be woven in the weaver's own house or shed, never in a factory. Each weaver works a small single-width loom that runs only on foot power — the weaver's own two feet on the pedals, with no motor and no electricity. This English-built loom has been the standard on the islands for about a hundred years. What is this old island loom called?
context: The loom is the Hattersley — the single-width treadle loom that traditional, independent island weavers still use in their own homes on Lewis and Harris. The Outer Hebrides mills use a newer, double-width loom, the Bonas-Griffith rapier loom, but by law both kinds must be pedal-powered in a weaver's home for the cloth to earn its Orb mark. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed; annstweed.com/pages/the-process-of-weaving-tweed-on-a-hattersley-loom

question: The old Harris Tweed came in deep, muted reds and purple-browns with a faintly earthy scent — colours the islanders drew from a natural dye called 'crottle', gathered by hand across the Outer Hebrides. What kind of living thing is crottle?
context: Crottle is a lichen (Parmelia saxatilis) that islanders scraped from the rocks of Lewis and Harris. Boiled with the wool, it dyed Harris Tweed its deep reddish purple-brown and left the cloth with a distinctive earthy scent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed

question: Along the shore of Havana, the capital of Cuba, runs an 8 km stone sea-wall and wide walkway. On calm summer evenings, Cuban families stroll and fish there under the palm trees. But when winter storms blow in off the sea, giant waves burst clean over the wall and flood the whole road behind it. What is this famous Havana seafront walk called?
context: The Malecón, begun in 1901, runs 8 km from the mouth of Havana Harbor in Old Havana, past Centro Habana and Vedado, to the mouth of the Almendares River. Built to hold back the sea, it turns into a wall of thundering spray during the winter frentes fríos (cold fronts), sending waves clear over the road. Source: Wikipedia, 'Malecón, Havana.'

question: Pirates raided and burned Havana again and again in the 1500s. So Spain sent an Italian builder, Battista Antonelli, to raise a huge stone castle at the harbor mouth. Work began in 1589 to guard the narrow gap. What is this fortress called?
context: El Morro — Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro — was designed by Battista Antonelli and begun in 1589. With its sister fort La Punta directly across the channel, it helped make Havana one of the safest ports in the Americas; a lighthouse, the Faro del Morro, was added in 1846 and still marks the entrance. Source: Wikipedia, 'Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro'; Encyclopedia.com, 'El Morro (Havana).'

question: Havana's harbor squeezes into a gap barely wider than one ship. The Spanish wanted no pirate slipping in at night. So every night they dragged a barrier across the water, from one fort to the other, until dawn. What did they pull across each night?
context: The 'boom defence' — a heavy chain strung each night from El Morro across to the fort of La Punta on the far side — could be raised to snag and damage any ship that tried to force the entrance. Together with the forts it closed Havana's port from dusk to dawn, and helped make the bay one of the safest anchorages in the New World. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'El Morro (Havana)'; Wikipedia, 'Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro.'

question: The great stone fortress of La Cabaña stands guard high above the mouth of Havana's harbor in Cuba. For over three centuries, at exactly nine o'clock each night, the same signal has been given from La Cabaña. Long ago it warned Havana's citizens that the city gates were about to close for the night. What marks nine o'clock in Havana?
context: El cañonazo de las nueve — the nine o'clock cannon — has boomed nightly since colonial times, when it signaled the closing of the city gates; a matching gun was fired at six each morning to announce their opening. Today the shot rings out from the Fortaleza de San Carlos de la Cabaña, the fortress beside El Morro on the same side of the harbor mouth. Source: TheCubanHistory.com; Wikipedia, 'Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro.'

question: Silver mined across the Americas was shipped to one Caribbean port: Havana. Two convoys met there and waited. Then they crossed the Atlantic to Spain together, under armed guard. What was this yearly convoy called?
context: Spain built its convoy-and-fortress system after French privateers sacked Havana in the 1550s–60s. Twice a year the flota gathered the wealth of the empire in Havana's bay, then sailed for Spain in one heavily armed body — which is exactly why the Crown ringed this single harbor with stone forts. Source: Wikipedia, 'Spanish treasure fleet'; Wikipedia, 'Havana.'

question: Whoever held Havana's harbor held the sea-road between the Americas and Europe. In 1592 the Spanish Crown gave the city a grand official title to match its importance — a name it still carries on its coat of arms four centuries later. What did the Crown call Havana?
answer: the Key to the New World
choices: the Key to the New World
context: In 1592 the Spanish Crown officially styled Havana 'Key to the New World and Rampart of the West Indies' (Llave del Nuevo Mundo y Antemural de las Indias Occidentales). A golden key still appears on the city's coat of arms — a reminder that whoever locked or unlocked this harbor commanded the whole route to Spain's Atlantic empire. Source: Wikipedia, 'Havana.'

question: One night in August 1973, a Bronx DJ named Kool Herc set up two turntables in the rec room of his own building. It was his sister Cindy's summer party. That party is now called the birth of hip-hop. What was the address?
context: The party is usually dated August 11, 1973. Herc's sister Cindy Campbell had rented the rec room to raise money, and the night ran until 4 a.m. Importantly, 1520 Sedgwick is the most-credited birthplace but not the only one — historians note hip-hop 'developed slowly in several places' in the 1970s Bronx, so this is best remembered as THE famous origin party, not the sole birthplace. In 2021 the U.S. Congress passed a resolution recognizing the building as hip-hop's birthplace, and Herc called it 'the Bethlehem of hip-hop culture.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1520_Sedgwick_Avenue  (Legend.)

question: The 1973 rec-room party in the West Bronx that launched hip-hop wasn't put on by a record label or a club — it was thrown by DJ Kool Herc's teenage sister, Cindy Campbell. She rented the room for $25 and charged a small fee at the door. Why did Cindy throw the party?
answer: to raise money for back-to-school clothes
choices: to raise money for back-to-school clothes
to raise money for a new sound system
to welcome new neighbors to the building
context: Cindy Campbell charged 25 cents for girls and 50 cents for boys; the party ran from 9 p.m. to 4 a.m., and the Campbells' parents supplied the refreshments. She was saving for new back-to-school clothes — and ended up helping bankroll the birth of a global culture. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1520_Sedgwick_Avenue

question: DJ Kool Herc watched the dancers at his Bronx parties and spotted a pattern: the crowd went wild not during the chorus, but during one short, pounding stretch of each song. To give the dancers more of it, Herc put two copies of the same record on two turntables and looped that stretch endlessly. What is that stretch of a song called?
context: Herc called his two-turntable looping trick the 'Merry-Go-Round': he cued the break on one copy while the other played, then switched back and forth 'with no slack.' His favorite break records were conga-heavy tracks like 'Apache' and 'Bongo Rock' by the Incredible Bongo Band — 'Apache' became known as hip-hop's national anthem. Looping the break was the foundation the whole music grew from. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DJ_Kool_Herc  (Legend.)

question: In the 1970s South Bronx, a new sound was catching on: hip-hop, born at neighborhood parties where DJs spun records into a big pounding sound system. Soon those Bronx DJs took the parties out into public parks and schoolyards for free summer block parties. But a park has no outlet for a huge sound system. So the DJs tapped city power right off the street, for free. What did they open up and plug into?
context: With no promoters and no outlets, DJs would pop open the base of a street lamppost and wire their sound systems into it for free power — a signature image of early Bronx hip-hop. Herc's own rig, the 'Herculords,' ran two turntables into a booming Shure 'Vocal Master' PA with tall speaker columns, so loud that people came just to stand and watch. Early park home bases included '63 Park and Boston Road. Source: https://www.nycgovparks.org/about/history/hip-hop  (Legend.)

question: At DJ Kool Herc's early-1970s Bronx block parties, Herc worked the turntables while his friend Coke La Rock took up the microphone, hyping the dancers with playful shout-outs and chants over the beat. Coke La Rock is remembered as the first person ever to work a mic this way at a hip-hop party. What vocal art — now the voice of hip-hop worldwide — was he the first to perform?
context: Coke La Rock (born April 24, 1955, in the Bronx) rapped alongside DJ Kool Herc and is widely credited as hip-hop's first MC — 'MC' stands for Master of Ceremonies. He had no stage name and often performed out of the crowd's sight, so at first no one knew who was doing the rhyming. His shout-outs to friends in the room were the seed of what became rapping. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coke_La_Rock

question: When DJ Kool Herc looped the beat at his Bronx park jams, certain dancers dropped low and attacked the floor — spinning, flipping, and freezing in sharp poses to outdo their rivals. Whole crews battled each other move for move on the concrete. What is this Bronx-born dance called?
context: DJ Kool Herc named the dancers 'b-boys' and 'b-girls,' the 'b' usually said to stand for 'break' — they saved their wildest moves for the looped break. Breaking has four move families: toprock (standing steps), downrock or footwork (hands on the floor), power moves (spins like the windmill, backspin, and headspin), and freezes (holding a pose off the ground). Herc even gave a second story for the word: 'this man broke... he went to the breaking point,' dancing himself into a frenzy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakdancing  (Legend.)

question: In the 1970s Bronx, DJ Kool Herc could loop a break by ear, but the beat often slipped as he did it. A younger Bronx DJ, Grandmaster Flash, treated the turntable like a science: working the record with his fingertips and the crossfader, he learned to cut, repeat, and stretch a tiny slice of a song dead on the beat, over and over. What did Flash name this precise cutting method?
context: Grandmaster Flash — Joseph Saddler, born January 1, 1958, in Barbados and raised in the Bronx — turned DJing into a precise science with his 'Quick Mix Theory,' using a fingertip on the vinyl and the crossfader to cut, repeat, and extend a tiny piece of a record exactly on the beat. To make it possible he also invented the DJ slipmat — a felt-and-waxed-paper pad that let a record spin or stop freely under his hand — and used 'punch phrasing,' jabbing short horn hits over a running beat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash

question: Around 1975, a 12-year-old Bronx DJ named Grand Wizzard Theodore was spinning records at home. His mother yelled at him to turn it down. As he pressed his hand on the record to quiet it, he made a new sound no DJ had used on purpose. He loved it so much he built a whole move around it. What did Theodore invent that day?
context: Grand Wizzard Theodore (Theodore Livingston) is credited with inventing the scratch — now one of the most recognizable sounds in music — around 1975, when he was about 12. Holding the record still under his hand, he rubbed it back and forth against the needle and fell in love with the rhythmic sound it made. The legend is that he discovered it while his mother stood in the doorway telling him to turn the music down. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Wizzard_Theodore

question: In the 1970s Bronx, Lance Taylor had been a feared 'warlord' of the Black Spades, one of the borough's biggest street gangs. Taking the name Afrika Bambaataa, he redirected that same organizing power away from gang violence and into a peaceful cultural movement that would spread hip-hop around the world. What did Bambaataa found?
context: Afrika Bambaataa (Lance Taylor, born April 17, 1957, in the Bronx) founded the Universal Zulu Nation, turning gang energy into a cultural movement. He took his name from the Zulu chief Bhambatha, who led an armed rebellion in South Africa in the early 1900s; Bambaataa said the name meant 'affectionate leader.' His 1982 track 'Planet Rock' fused drum machines and synths into a new sound called electro-funk. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrika_Bambaataa  (Legend.)

question: From his home turf in the 1970s Bronx, Afrika Bambaataa insisted hip-hop was never just music — it was a whole culture. He named its four core 'elements,' the creative pillars people still use to describe it: DJing on the turntables, MCing on the mic, dancing on the floor, and one more. What is hip-hop's fourth element?
context: Afrika Bambaataa is credited with naming hip-hop's 'four elements' — DJing, MCing, breaking, and graffiti — the framework people still use to describe the culture. His Universal Zulu Nation later added a fifth element: knowledge. Bambaataa also helped popularize the very word 'hip hop'; a January 1982 magazine interview with him is often cited as the first time the term named the culture. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Afrika_Bambaataa  (Legend.)

question: The acrobatic floor dance that Bronx teenagers invented at their 1970s park jams spread across the whole world over the next fifty years. In 2024 it earned an honor no other dance born on a city street had ever received. What happened to this Bronx-born dance in 2024?
answer: it became an official Olympic sport
choices: it became an official Olympic sport
it became a UNESCO heritage tradition
it became a Broadway dance musical
it became a professional world league
context: Breaking — the dance the Bronx b-boys and b-girls created — became an official Olympic sport at the 2024 Paris Summer Olympics. Japan's Ami Yuasa won the first-ever women's gold and Canada's Philip Kim won the men's title. A dance once powered by electricity tapped from Bronx lampposts had reached the Olympic Games. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakdancing

question: In the heart of Hiroshima stands one broken ruin. It is kept just as it was on the morning of 6 August 1945: a hollow brick shell topped by a bare metal frame. It was the only building near the blast that kept its shape. What does the city call it?
context: Genbaku Dome means 'Atomic Bomb Dome' in Japanese. Of all the structures near the center of the blast, this one alone kept its shape while everything around it was flattened, and its skeletal shell still stands at the heart of the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial.

question: The Hiroshima bomb flattened wood and brick alike for miles around. Yet one building just 160 meters from the center kept its walls and dome frame up. Why did this one place survive when all around it fell?
answer: the blast burst high overhead, pressing its walls down from almost straight above
choices: the blast burst high overhead, pressing its walls down from almost straight above
its brick-and-concrete walls were built far sturdier than the wooden shops nearby
the wide river beside it soaked up much of the blast's outward energy
taller buildings clustered around it took the first force of the shockwave
context: The bomb detonated about 600 meters up and almost directly above the building, so the shockwave bore down through its vertical brick-and-concrete columns instead of striking them from the side -- which is why its shape held while the city flattened for kilometers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial.

question: In Hiroshima's Peace Park, one monument is nearly buried under paper cranes sent by kids around the world. It honors Sadako Sasaki. She was two when the bomb fell. Later she got leukemia and folded crane after crane. She trusted a legend that a thousand cranes grant a wish. She died at twelve. One bronze figure crowns the monument. What does it show?
answer: a girl lifting a folded crane high overhead
choices: a girl lifting a folded crane high overhead
a girl kneeling to fold a crane in her lap
a boy cupping a paper crane in both hands
a mother shielding a small child from the flames
context: Unveiled on 5 May 1958, the Children's Peace Monument is topped by a bronze girl holding a folded crane above her head. Its inscription reads, 'This is our cry, this is our prayer: for building peace in the world.' Children from around the world still send origami cranes by the thousand, gathered in glass cases around its base. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children%27s_Peace_Monument + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadako_Sasaki.  (Legend.)

question: Long before it was a ruin, the domed building in Hiroshima was no monument. It opened in 1915. Its copper dome and European lines stood out over the low wooden shops. A visiting Bohemian architect, Jan Letzel, drew the plans. What was the building first built to be?
context: It opened in 1915 as the Hiroshima Prefectural Commercial Exhibition Hall -- about 25 meters tall, its brick reinforced with concrete and crowned with an oval copper dome. Its Czech designer, Jan Letzel (1880-1925), left Japan for Prague in 1923 and died there in 1925, twenty years before his cheerful exhibition hall became the world's most famous ruin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Letzel.

question: For decades the shell of the Atomic Bomb Dome has stood untouched in Hiroshima. It is braced up but never patched or rebuilt, a warning kept for the world. In late 1996, after long debate, the shattered dome got a famous title. What did the ruin become?
choices: one of the New Seven Wonders
context: The Atomic Bomb Dome was nearly demolished in the years after the war, but Hiroshima resolved to keep it, and in December 1996 UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site -- listed as a stark reminder of the destructive force humankind can unleash, and a symbol of hope for lasting peace. Mayor Shinzo Hamai had championed saving the shell; a permanent-preservation resolution passed the city council in 1966, and the dome stands guarded from collapse but never repaired. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial.

question: Hiroshima's people expected their flattened city to lie dead for years. Yet only three days after the bomb -- on 9 August 1945 -- one part of the city's transport was already moving again, its riders too stunned and penniless to pay, waved aboard for free. What had started running again so soon after the blast?
context: On 9 August 1945 a Hiroden streetcar ran again between Koi and Tenma-cho, astonishing survivors who had thought the city finished. Two of the cars damaged that day, numbered 651 and 652, still carry passengers through Hiroshima today. Source: Japan Tourism Agency (mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/en) + gethiroshima.com.

question: After the blast, experts warned that Hiroshima's poisoned ground would stay barren for decades -- at the very center, at first, not even grass would grow. Yet in the spring of 1946, trees that had stood within a kilometer of the explosion did something the survivors had thought impossible that soon. What did these scorched trees do?
answer: put out fresh green buds and new leaves
choices: put out fresh green buds and new leaves
bloomed out of season, months too early
shed their scorched bark in long black strips
leaned and slowly toppled as the soil shifted
context: These A-bombed survivors are called hibaku jumoku, 'survivor trees.' Fresh leaves the next spring became living proof the city would recover; by 2011 about 170 trees that had lived through the bombing still grew in Hiroshima, roughly a dozen within 1,000 meters of the blast. Because it flowered so fiercely in the ruins, the oleander was chosen as Hiroshima's official flower. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibakujumoku.

question: Hoi An's most famous landmark is a roofed wooden footbridge more than 400 years old, with a carved dog guarding one end and a carved monkey the other. Right at the center of the span, the Japanese Covered Bridge carries something you would never expect a bridge to hold. What is built into its middle?
context: The Japanese Covered Bridge (Chua Cau) has spanned Hoi An for over four centuries with a tiny temple built right into its middle. By legend the mismatched guardians -- a dog at one end, a monkey at the other -- mark the zodiac years the work began (Year of the Monkey) and finished two years later (Year of the Dog). Source: Vietnam Discovery, Japanese Covered Bridge; corroborated by Atlas Obscura.

question: Once a month, Hoi An's old town switches off its electric lights and glows only with hundreds of colored silk lanterns, while paper lanterns drift down the Thu Bon River carrying people's wishes. The town never fixes a calendar date for this -- it waits on the moon. On which phase of the moon does the lantern night fall?
context: Hoi An holds its lantern night on the 14th day of every lunar month -- the eve of the full moon -- then darkens its streets anyway, so the lanterns become the only glow on the brightest night of the month. Families hang silk lanterns and float paper ones down the Thu Bon carrying wishes. Source: Hoi An Guidebook, Lantern Festival guide; corroborated by Klook Hoi An lanterns guide.

question: For 400 years Hoi An was one of Southeast Asia's busiest trading ports, crowded with ships from China, Japan, India and Europe. Then the big ships stopped coming, the trade moved about 30 km north to Da Nang, and the town sat almost untouched for centuries. The cause wasn't war or politics -- it was the Thu Bon River. What did the river do to Hoi An's harbor?
answer: silted up until big ships couldn't dock
choices: silted up until big ships couldn't dock
swung its course away from the town
swept the old docks out to sea
dropped too low for ships to enter
context: Mud carried by the Thu Bon slowly filled Hoi An's port with silt, so ocean-going ships shifted to the deeper harbor at Da Nang and the merchant town was left behind. That very decline preserved it: UNESCO listed Hoi An in 1999 as an exceptionally well-kept small-scale trading port (Western traders once knew it as 'Faifo'). Sources: UNESCO World Heritage #948; La Siesta Hoi An history.

question: At Prayagraj in India, the pale, silty Ganges pours into the clearer blue-green Yamuna. For a stretch you can watch the two colors slide side by side in a sharp line before they mix. A place where two rivers meet and join like this is called a ___?
context: At the Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj (Allahabad), the silt-laden Ganges and the clearer Yamuna meet, and their different colors stay visibly separate in a line before mixing — the classic picture of a river confluence. A delta or estuary instead forms where a river meets the sea; a tributary is a stream that feeds a larger river. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triveni_Sangam

question: The sacred confluence at Prayagraj is called the Triveni Sangam — the 'meeting of three rivers.' Yet a visitor on the bank sees only two, the Ganges and the Yamuna. Hindu tradition holds that a third river joins them here unseen, flowing in secretly from underground. Which river is this invisible third one?
context: 'Triveni Sangam' means 'confluence of three rivers,' but only the Ganges and Yamuna are real. Hindu tradition says the Sarasvati — a lost, mythical river — flows underground and joins them invisibly from below, which is why the site is counted as three. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triveni_Sangam  (Legend.)

question: In 2025 the Maha Kumbh at Prayagraj drew about 660 million Hindu pilgrims to bathe at the Sangam. It was the largest peaceful gathering ever. Legend says gods once churned the sea. Drops of a mystery liquid spilled from a pitcher onto four spots on earth. Pilgrims have flocked there ever since. What was the liquid said to be?
choices: the poison of the churned sea
the waters of the sacred Ganges
context: Legend says the four Kumbh Mela sites — Prayagraj, Haridwar, Nashik, and Ujjain — were sanctified when drops of amrita, the divine nectar of immortality, fell there during the mythological churning of the ocean. The 2025 Maha Kumbh drew about 660 million pilgrims to bathe at the Sangam, nearly triple the roughly 240 million of 2019 — the largest peaceful gathering on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumbh_Mela

question: The Jordan River is oddly short, only about 250 km from its snow springs on Mount Hermon. From its start it runs downhill into a long trench that sinks far below sea level. What slow force carved out this deep valley?
choices: a glacier grinding out a valley
context: The Jordan runs down the Jordan Rift Valley, part of the Great Rift system, where the Arabian and African plates slowly pull apart. Because the trench floor keeps dropping below sea level, this one short river passes the lowest freshwater lake and ends at the lowest dry land on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_River

question: In the Middle East, the Jordan River flows south down a long crack in the Earth called the Jordan Rift Valley. Along its course, the river widens into a broad blue lake fished for thousands of years and known also as Lake Tiberias or the Kinneret. Among all the freshwater lakes on Earth, what record does this one, the Sea of Galilee, hold?
context: The Sea of Galilee — also called Lake Tiberias or the Kinneret — sits about 210 m below sea level, the lowest freshwater lake on the planet (its level drifts between roughly 209 and 215 m). The Jordan flows in from the north and out to the south toward the Dead Sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Galilee

question: The Jordan finally pours into the Dead Sea, whose shore is the lowest dry land anywhere on Earth — about 430 m below sea level. Its water carries so much salt — roughly a third of it is salt, nearly ten times as much as the ocean — that it behaves unlike any swimming hole a child has known. What happens to a person who wades in and leans back?
answer: they float so easily they cannot sink
choices: they float so easily they cannot sink
they sink quickly to the bottom
they must swim hard to stay afloat
they are dragged along by a current
context: The Dead Sea's surface is about 430 m below sea level — the lowest dry land on Earth — and still dropping about a meter a year. Its water is roughly 34% salt (near 1.24 kg per liter), so dense that bathers float and cannot sink; it is too salty for fish or plants, and only bacteria and microbial fungi live there. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea

question: Hong Kong has almost no flat land, so its buildings climb straight up the steep hillsides -- 669 of them at least 150 m tall, packed one behind another into a wall of glass and steel. That crowded skyline earns the city a Guinness World Record. For what?
choices: the most crowded streets on Earth
context: As of 30 January 2025, Guinness World Records counted 669 buildings at least 150 m tall in Hong Kong -- more than any other city on Earth. Shenzhen is second (626), New York third (434), and Dubai fourth (424). With mountains and sea leaving almost no flat land, Hong Kong had nowhere to build but up. Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/505189-city-with-the-most-buildings-150-m-or-taller

question: Victoria Peak (locals just call it 'The Peak') rises 552 m over Hong Kong Island. Climbing its steep face on foot was once rough. So in 1888 the Peak Tram opened, hauling people up by cable on a slope reaching 48 percent. What claim did the Peak Tram make when it opened?
answer: the first funicular railway in Asia
choices: the first funicular railway in Asia
the steepest cable railway in the world
the oldest mountain railway in China
the highest hillside railway in Asia
context: A funicular is a cable railway on a steep slope where two cars are joined by a cable over a wheel at the top, so each car counterweights the other as one climbs and the other descends. The Peak Tram opened on 30 May 1888 as the first funicular in Asia, climbing nearly 400 m up a grade reaching 48% in about five minutes. Victoria Peak, 552 m, is the highest point on Hong Kong Island. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_Tram ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Peak

question: Every night at eight, about 40 skyscrapers on both sides of Victoria Harbour light up together. Colored beams, lasers, and searchlights flash in time with music. The ten-minute show is called 'A Symphony of Lights.' Guinness World Records lists it with one global title. Which one?
answer: the world's largest permanent light-and-sound show
choices: the world's largest permanent light-and-sound show
the world's first laser light-and-sound show
the world's brightest nightly light-and-sound show
context: 'A Symphony of Lights' began on 17 January 2004 and runs nightly at 8:00 PM for about ten minutes, involving roughly 40 buildings on both sides of Victoria Harbour. Guinness World Records recognises it as the world's largest permanent light-and-sound show. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Symphony_of_Lights

question: The name 'Hong Kong' -- heung gong in Cantonese -- sounds mysterious to visitors who step off the boat into diesel and sea-salt air. Yet it means 'Fragrant Harbour,' a name earned honestly: through the Ming and Qing dynasties, boats loaded one sweet-smelling cargo at the Aberdeen shore and shipped it out across the region, scenting the whole port. What was that cargo?
context: 'Hong Kong' (heung gong) means 'Fragrant Harbour.' During the Ming and Qing dynasties, agarwood and other fragrant incense woods were shipped out of the Aberdeen-area harbour, so the boat people called the port the 'fragrant harbour.' Source: https://www.lungfushannaturalist.hku.hk/post/the-origin-of-the-name-hong-kong

question: For decades Kowloon Walled City was the most crowded place on Earth -- some 33,000 people jammed into a single block of leaning towers, its lower alleys never touched by sunlight. Hong Kong finally condemned it and pulled it down between 1993 and 1994. On the cleared block the government then opened something new. What?
context: By 1987 about 33,000 people lived in Kowloon Walled City, packed into 2.6 hectares -- a density near 1.2 million people per square kilometre, for a time one of the densest places humans have ever lived. It was demolished between March 1993 and April 1994, and Kowloon Walled City Park, a quiet classical Chinese garden, opened on the site in December 1995. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kowloon_Walled_City

question: Ride the Peak Tram up Victoria Peak after dark and something eerie seizes the view. As the car climbs the steep slope, the glittering skyscrapers outside seem to do something impossible -- an illusion a 2013 University of Hong Kong study traced to a mismatch between the tram's seats and its straight window frames, which trick the brain. What do the towers appear to do?
answer: lean far over, as if toppling
choices: lean far over, as if toppling
context: University of Hong Kong researcher Chia-huei Tseng documented the illusion in a 2013 study: the tram's tilted seats and its straight window frames trick the brain about which way is 'up,' so the passing skyscrapers appear to lean and even topple. The effect is strongest at night and weakens if you stand up. Source: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/06/130620162848.htm

question: Kowloon Walled City packed 33,000 people into roughly 350 towers. Bridges, shared stairs, and roofed alleys laced them all together. People made a famous boast about crossing it. From one end of the block to the other, they said, you could travel the whole way without once doing what?
context: Kowloon Walled City was so densely interconnected by staircases and passageways that a person could reportedly travel from the north end to the south end of the whole block without ever touching solid ground. Its roughly 350 buildings, mostly 10-14 stories, were fed by only about 8 water pipes and built with no architects and no building codes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kowloon_Walled_City  (Legend.)

question: Victoria Harbour is so deep and sheltered that the largest ocean ships can anchor right beside the skyscrapers -- the very reason Hong Kong grew into one of the world's great natural ports. The harbour formed long ago, after the last Ice Age, when rising seas swept inland and flooded the mouths of old rivers that once wound down between Hong Kong's hills. Geographers have a special name for a coast drowned like this. What is it?
context: A ria is a river valley drowned by a rising sea -- here, the post-glacial Holocene sea-level rise flooded the low ground between ranges of hills. (A fjord is the same idea carved by a glacier instead of a river.) The result is deep, sheltered water, which is exactly why Hong Kong became one of the world's great natural ports; Victoria Harbour covers about 41.88 km2 and sees on the order of 220,000 ship visits a year. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ria ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Harbour

question: Deep under Hawaii, a plume of hot rock stays fixed. The Pacific plate creeps slowly northwest over it. Each old island drifts away as a new one is born. The drift is only 5 to 10 cm a year. This speed is often compared to what slow, everyday thing?
choices: grass growing in a spring lawn
context: Geologists really do clock the Pacific plate at roughly the speed your fingernails grow -- about 5 to 10 centimeters a year. Slow as that sounds, over millions of years that steady creep is exactly what drags each Hawaiian island off the hotspot and lines the whole chain up by age. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_hotspot

question: Hawaii's Big Island sits right over the hot spot today. One of its volcanoes is among the most active on Earth and is still erupting. Its lava ran for 35 straight years, from 1983 to 2018. That was one of the longest lava flows ever. Name this restless volcano.
context: Kilauea, on the Big Island's southeastern flank, is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth and still erupts today; its 1983-2018 flow ran about 35 years, one of the longest eruptions ever documented. The volcano itself is young -- only about 210,000 to 280,000 years old -- because it sits almost directly over the hotspot, while the older islands to the northwest have long gone cold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%ABlauea

question: At the far northwest end of Hawaii's main islands lies an island whose volcanoes died long ago. Over 5 million years, rain has carved its slopes into deep green canyons and knife-edge ridges. Which Hawaiian island is this ancient, deeply eroded one?
context: Kauai, at about 5 million years old (roughly 5.1-5.5 million), is the oldest of Hawaii's main islands. The plume that built it moved on long ago, leaving it extinct while rain carved its deep canyons and knife-edge ridges. The younger islands lie to the southeast, closer to the still-burning hotspot. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_hotspot

question: The Hawaiian hotspot has built at least 129 volcanoes over about 85 million years. Yet only a handful still stand above the waves as islands today. What became of the other 120 or so once the plate carried them away from the hotspot?
answer: they sank into drowned seamounts and atolls
choices: they sank into drowned seamounts and atolls
they fused into one enormous island
they blew apart and vanished completely
they drifted back over the hotspot
context: As the plate hauls each volcano off the hotspot it cools, stops erupting, and slowly sinks -- worn down until it drowns as a flat-topped seamount or a ring-shaped coral atoll. Over its ~85-million-year history the Hawaiian hotspot has built at least 129 volcanoes; more than 123 are now extinct. The whole chain is a graveyard of islands the plate carried away. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_hotspot

question: Follow the Hawaiian islands northwest and they do not simply stop. Beneath the sea they run on as a chain of more than 80 dead undersea volcanoes, stretching 6,200 km almost to Russia. To geologists, this immense undersea trail is a fossil record of what?
answer: the path the Pacific plate has drifted
choices: the path the Pacific plate has drifted
the boundary where two plates collide
the rim of a vast sunken crater
the shoreline of a lost continent
context: Because the hotspot stays put while the Pacific plate slides over it, the plate prints a volcano, then carries it away -- so the whole Hawaiian-Emperor chain, read backward from Hawaii, traces exactly where the plate has traveled. It runs about 6,200 km (3,900 mi) and holds more than 80 dead undersea volcanoes: a fossil record of the plate's entire path. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian%E2%80%93Emperor_seamount_chain

question: About 35 km off the Big Island's southeast coast, an underwater volcano is already erupting. Its summit still sits about 975 m beneath the waves. In another 10,000 to 100,000 years of eruptions, what will it finally do?
answer: rise above the sea as Hawaii's next island
choices: rise above the sea as Hawaii's next island
collapse into a deep undersea trench
drift away and go extinct like the older islands
merge quietly with the Big Island's coast
context: Kamaehuakanaloa -- renamed from Loihi in 2021 -- sits over the leading edge of the Hawaiian hotspot, about 35 km off the Big Island's southeast coast, its summit still ~975 m (3,200 ft) underwater. Its last known eruption was in 1996, during a swarm of about 4,070 earthquakes. In another 10,000 to 100,000 years it is expected to break the surface as Hawaii's newest island. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C5%8D%CA%BBihi_Seamount

question: The Galapagos ride their own hotspot, but here the age pattern runs east to west. The eastern islands are the oldest and going quiet, while one young western island under 700,000 years old sits right over the plume and is the whole chain's most active volcano. Which fiery western island is this?
context: The Galapagos hotspot lies to the west, so Fernandina (under 700,000 years old) is the youngest and most volcanically active island, erupting often. The older eastern islands -- San Cristobal (~4 million years) and Espanola (~3.2 million) -- have drifted off the plume and gone quiet. It is the same conveyor as Hawaii, just read the other direction. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernandina_Island

question: Trace the Hawaiian-Emperor chain far enough and it takes an abrupt, sharp turn -- the volcanoes stop trending northwest and swing almost precisely due north. Together they form a distinct elbow in the seafloor approximately 47 to 50 million years old. What does this famous kink in the chain most likely record?
answer: a change in the direction of the plate's motion
choices: a change in the direction of the plate's motion
the collision of two ancient continents
the impact site of a giant meteorite
the boundary of a drowned ice sheet
context: The elbow -- dated to about 47-50 million years ago, where the northwest-trending Hawaiian ridge kinks to the north-trending Emperor seamounts -- was long read as the moment the Pacific plate swung course by roughly 60 degrees. It is one of the most striking features on the entire ocean floor, though whether the plate alone changed direction is now debated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian%E2%80%93Emperor_seamount_chain

question: At the far end of the Emperor seamounts, the oldest surviving link in the whole hotspot chain -- Meiji Seamount, about 82 million years old -- has nearly finished its long ride. It now sits at the edge of the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench off Russia. What is happening to this ancient seamount there?
answer: it is being pulled down into the earth and destroyed
choices: it is being pulled down into the earth and destroyed
it is rising once more into a brand-new island
it is drifting slowly back toward Hawaii's hotspot
it is tearing open along a mid-ocean ridge
context: Meiji Seamount, at about 82 million years the oldest surviving link in the Hawaiian-Emperor chain (nearby Detroit Seamount is confirmed at ~81 Myr), has ridden the Pacific plate all the way to the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench. There the plate dives beneath Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula in a process called subduction, dragging the ancient seamount down to be destroyed -- the conveyor delivering its cargo to its end. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_Seamount

question: Deep inside the Earth, hot plumes of rising rock can burn upward through the crust — and not only under ocean floor. One such plume has been burning through solid continent for millions of years. As North America crept slowly southwest over the top of it, the plume scorched a 500-mile trail of dead volcanic calderas across Idaho's flat Snake River Plain before parking beneath its present home. Under which famous US national park does that hotspot now sit?
context: Yellowstone's plume is the classic continental hotspot. As North America drifted southwest, the plume 'burned' a line of dead calderas eastward across Idaho's Snake River Plain -- from the McDermitt field on the Nevada-Oregon border (~16 million years ago) through Bruneau-Jarbidge and Heise -- until it reached the Yellowstone Caldera in Wyoming (~640,000 years ago). The same conveyor as Hawaii, printed on a continent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_hotspot

question: For decades the great 47-to-50-million-year-old elbow in the Hawaiian-Emperor chain was explained one way: the Pacific plate simply changed direction. But newer research challenged that neat story, arguing the seafloor evidence fits better if something else was moving too across those millions of years. What does this modern view propose was also drifting?
answer: the hotspot plume itself was drifting south
choices: the hotspot plume itself was drifting south
the mid-ocean ridge was creeping northward
the Earth's spin axis had wandered
a nearby plate boundary was jumping
context: The classic explanation credited a ~60-degree change in Pacific-plate motion for the bend. But newer research argues the plume beneath Hawaii itself drifted south by hundreds of kilometers before about 47 million years ago. Today many scientists think the bend records a MIX of both -- a moving plate and a moving plume -- not a single settled cause. A good reminder that even textbook geology still has open questions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian%E2%80%93Emperor_seamount_chain

question: About 66 million years ago the Indian plate drifted over the same kind of deep plume -- the Reunion hotspot -- and the ground tore open. Floods of runny basalt poured out again and again, burying much of western India under layers more than 2 kilometers thick, covering an area the size of a country. This vast staircase of ancient lava is known as what?
context: The Deccan Traps buried much of India in basalt -- over 500,000 sq km, a volume near 1 million cubic km, with layers more than 2 km thick -- erupting right at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary (~66 million years ago), the same moment the dinosaurs died out. That timing has tempted scientists to blame the eruptions, but most now credit the Chicxulub asteroid impact as the main killer, with the Deccan volcanism a debated accomplice. The same Reunion plume that flooded India still builds the volcanic island of Reunion today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deccan_Traps  (Legend.)

question: In central Vietnam, the wide river that curves past the old imperial city of Hue is called the Song Huong — in English, the Perfume River. The name is no exaggeration. Each autumn the water truly turns fragrant, so much that people can smell it as they cross the bridges. Something drifting down on the current gives the river its sweet scent. What is it?
answer: Orchard blossoms drifting down from upstream hills
choices: Orchard blossoms drifting down from upstream hills
Incense drifting down from riverside pagodas
Perfume workshops that once crowded its banks
Lotus flowers carpeting the river's surface
context: The Perfume River (Sông Hương) runs about 30 km from where its two source branches, the Ta Trach and Huu Trach, meet at the Bang Lang fork in the Annamite Range. Each autumn, blossoms from fruit orchards far upstream fall into the current and drift down, scenting the whole river - the real origin of its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfume_River

question: In 1804, after years of civil war, Emperor Gia Long finally reunified Vietnam under one throne. He chose the town of Hue in the center of the country as his new capital and began raising a great walled citadel there beside the Perfume River. For his imperial palace inside — with its yellow-tiled roofs, moats, and inner forbidden compound — he consciously modeled the whole plan on one grand foreign palace-city. Which one did he copy?
context: Gia Long, founder of the Nguyen dynasty, laid out Hue in 1804; his son Minh Mang finished the core in the 1830s. The plan copied Beijing's Forbidden City but was adapted to Vietnamese feng shui - its back to Ngu Binh Mountain, its face to the Perfume River. The Nguyen ruled from here until the last emperor, Bao Dai, abdicated in 1945. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Imperial_City_of_Hu%E1%BA%BF

question: Nested at the heart of the Hue citadel, behind a wall of its own, lay the Forbidden Purple City. This was the emperor's private household. Besides the emperor and his own family, only one kind of servant could live and work within these inner walls. Who?
context: The Forbidden Purple City took its name from Beijing's Forbidden City, whose Chinese name means 'Purple Forbidden City' - the 'purple' evoking the pole-star enclosure of heaven, home of the celestial emperor. Only the emperor, his family, and his castrated eunuch servants could pass within; the eunuchs alone were trusted to serve so close to the imperial women. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Imperial_City_of_Hu%E1%BA%BF

question: The Nine Holy Cannons guarding the Hue citadel are the largest bronze cannons Vietnam ever cast. Although Emperor Gia Long meant them to guard the imperial throne forever, they were never once actually fired. When he had them founded in 1803, what bronze did he melt down to make them?
answer: The weapons of the defeated Tay Son dynasty
choices: The weapons of the defeated Tay Son dynasty
Temple bells collected from across the kingdom
Old bronze coins withdrawn from circulation
Cannon captured from foreign trading ships
context: Gia Long had the Cuu Vi Than Cong cast in 1803-1804 from the melted-down bronze weapons of the Tay Son dynasty he had just overthrown - four cannons named for the seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter) and five for the elements (metal, wood, water, fire, earth). Meant as the throne's eternal guardians, they were never once fired. Source: https://www.vietnam.vn/en/cuu-vi-than-cong-tuyet-tac-nghe-thuat-duc-dong-cua-trieu-nguyen

question: In the pine hills around Hue, each Nguyen emperor raised himself a grand garden-tomb of pavilions, lotus ponds and stone stelae. The strangest belongs to Emperor Tu Duc, who finished his in 1867 - then did what no one expects of a tomb's owner. What did Tu Duc do with his own tomb?
answer: He moved in and lived there for years before dying
choices: He moved in and lived there for years before dying
He sealed it and never set foot there again
He handed it over to shelter Buddhist monks
He had it demolished and rebuilt twice over
context: Tu Duc built his tomb in 1864-1867 and used it as a pleasure-retreat while still alive - boating on Luu Khiem lake, reclining in the Xung Khiem Pavilion to compose poetry among his concubines. He had 104 wives and concubines but, left sterile by smallpox, never fathered a son, and he wrote his own tomb epitaph, an act traditionally thought a bad omen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_T%E1%BB%B1_%C4%90%E1%BB%A9c

question: Emperor Tu Duc's lavish garden-tomb at Hue draws crowds today, yet it hides a startling secret: his body was never actually buried inside it. By tradition his real grave was dug elsewhere in Hue and kept hidden forever by one grim measure. What became of the roughly 200 servants who buried him?
answer: They were all beheaded on their return
choices: They were all beheaded on their return
They were exiled from the kingdom for life
They were sworn to lifelong silence
They were buried alive beside him
context: This is legend, not documented fact: by the traditional account the roughly 200 servants who carried out Tu Duc's secret burial were all beheaded on their return, so none could ever reveal the true grave - which has never been found. Tu Duc's grand tomb thus honours an emperor who is not actually buried in it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_T%E1%BB%B1_%C4%90%E1%BB%A9c

question: In Miami on the U.S. Gulf coast, TV forecasters warn Florida that a hurricane is on the way. That same week in the Philippines, weather offices track a giant storm they call a typhoon. And off the coast of India, fishermen brace for what they call a cyclone. But if scientists watched all three storms from a satellite in space, they would see the very same shape — a huge spinning wheel of clouds with a calm eye at its center. How are these three kinds of storm really related?
answer: They are one and the same storm, just named by region.
choices: They are one and the same storm, just named by region.
They are three separate storms, ranked by wind speed.
They are three separate storms, one for each ocean.
They are the same storm seen at three life stages.
context: One storm, three names. The spinning tropical cyclone is called a hurricane over the Atlantic and northeastern Pacific (around the Caribbean), a typhoon over the northwestern Pacific (around the Philippines), and a cyclone over the Indian Ocean and South Pacific (around India and Australia). Same beast, three regional names. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone

question: Hurricane Hunter pilots fly right into an Atlantic hurricane. First they batter through a ring of the fiercest winds and heaviest rain. Then they suddenly burst into a strange calm at the center -- a circle of still air with blue sky above. What is this quiet core of the storm called?
context: The eye is a calm, often cloud-free circle of sinking air, typically 30-65 km across, ringed by the eyewall -- where the winds are strongest, the air rises fastest, and the rain is heaviest. Observed eyes have ranged from just 3 km wide to a giant 370 km. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone

question: Along low-lying coasts like the U.S. Gulf Coast, most people fear a hurricane's shrieking wind. Yet the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) finds water, not wind, causes nearly 90% of tropical-cyclone deaths.
