context: Europe called the porcelain secret the 'Arcanum.' d'Entrecolles mailed the first detailed Western account of Jingdezhen's methods in 1712 (a second letter followed in 1722), spreading the recipe and later helping found France's Sevres works. Germany's Meissen had in fact already achieved hard-paste porcelain around 1708-10 using local kaolin, so the letters did not give Europe its first porcelain -- they revealed the recipe to the wider West. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francois_Xavier_d'Entrecolles; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain.

question: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain on earth, but climbers fear K2 more. K2 is the second-tallest peak. It sits on the China-Pakistan border, and it kills climbers far more often than Everest does. What chilling nickname have mountaineers given K2?
context: American climber George Bell coined the 'Savage Mountain' nickname after the 1953 expedition, saying, 'It's a savage mountain that tries to kill you.' At 8,611 m (28,251 ft), K2 stands second only to Everest's 8,849 m, rising in the Karakoram range on the China–Pakistan border. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: Everest, Annapurna, and Nanga Parbat wear ancient local names passed down for centuries. K2 is the odd one out. It is not a word in any language, and it means nothing in the tongues of the people who live nearest it. This lonely peak on the China-Pakistan border was simply too remote to have earned a common local name. Where, then, does the strange label 'K2' come from?
context: In 1856 the British surveyor Thomas Montgomerie, working on the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, labelled the Karakoram peaks K1, K2, K3 and so on — the 'K' standing for Karakoram. K1 later reverted to its local Balti name, Masherbrum, but K2 sat so deep in the range that no common local name reached the mapmakers, so the survey code stuck. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: Everest, though far taller than K2, is climbed by hundreds each year, and fewer than one in fifty climbers die on it. K2 is a different beast, and its dark reputation used to rest on a single grim number. Of the climbers who reached the summit of K2, roughly what share never made it back down alive?
context: K2's fatality rate has historically run above 20% — roughly one death for every four climbers who reached the top — which is why the peak, not taller Everest, earns its dread. By comparison, Annapurna is usually ranked the single deadliest 8,000er by death-to-summit ratio, historically closer to one in three. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: Near the very top of K2 lies the most feared stretch in all of mountaineering: a short but brutally steep gully of snow and ice that every summit climber must cross. Worse, it sits right below a wall of hanging ice cliffs, called seracs, that can break loose without warning. What is this dreaded passage on K2 called?
context: The Bottleneck, a couloir around 8,200 m, funnels climbers directly under a band of hanging seracs. On 1–2 August 2008, a serac collapse there sheared the fixed ropes and eleven climbers died — K2's worst single disaster. Lower on the mountain lie other named cruxes like House's Chimney and the Black Pyramid. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: K2 threw back climber after climber until 31 July 1954, when an Italian team led by the geologist Ardito Desio finally put two men on the summit. The route they cut that day proved so reliable that most climbers have followed the same line up K2 ever since. What is this classic route called?
context: Italians Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli reached the summit on 31 July 1954 via the Abruzzi Spur, on the expedition led by geologist Ardito Desio. The ascent stayed controversial because support climber Walter Bonatti and porter Amir Mehdi were forced to bivouac in the open above 8,000 m. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: During a fierce storm high on K2 in 1953, an American team was struggling to lower a desperately sick teammate when six roped-together climbers slipped at once and began sliding toward a deadly plunge. In a heartbeat, one of them, Pete Schoening, stopped the whole falling chain with a single move that mountaineers still speak of simply as 'The Belay.' How did Schoening save all six?
answer: wedged his ice axe behind a rock
choices: looped the rope around his shoulders
wedged his ice axe behind a rock
caught the rope with his bare hands
anchored them with a tent stake
context: Pete Schoening braced a single ice axe behind a boulder and held all six of his roped teammates during the 1953 American expedition's storm-battered retreat — a save mountaineers still simply call 'The Belay.' The sick climber they were lowering, Art Gilkey, was later swept away and died. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2  (Legend.)

question: By 2021, thirteen of the world's fourteen 8,000-metre peaks had been climbed in the dead of winter. Only K2 held out, having thrown back every winter attempt for decades in cold near minus 40 and hurricane winds. Then on 16 January 2021, ten climbers finally stood together on the frozen summit, completing what many call the last great first in high-altitude mountaineering. Whose team pulled off this historic first winter ascent of K2?
context: The ten Nepali climbers deliberately regrouped about ten metres below the top so that no one would be first, then stepped onto the summit together while singing Nepal's national anthem. The team was led by Nirmal 'Nimsdai' Purja and Mingma Gyalje Sherpa; of the ten, only Purja climbed without supplemental oxygen. Sources: https://www.planetmountain.com/en/news/alpinism/k2-nepalese-mountaineers-claim-historic-first-winter-ascent.html ; https://www.ukclimbing.com/news/2021/01/first_winter_ascent_of_k2_made_by_all-nepali_team-72688

question: Kabuki is Japan's dazzling theatre of painted faces and frozen poses. It did not start in a grand hall but out in the open air. Around 1603, a former shrine dancer named Izumo no Okuni led an all-female troupe in a wild new dance-drama. They performed on the dry, pebbled bed of a river running through Kyoto. On which river's dry bed did kabuki first take shape?
context: The river is the Kamo (Kamo-gawa), and the exact spot — its wide, dry, pebbled bed in central Kyoto — is remembered as the Shijogawara. There, around 1603, Izumo no Okuni, a former miko (shrine maiden) by tradition linked to the great Izumo Taisha shrine, drew crowds with a flashy, avant-garde dance-drama that grew into kabuki. In a famous irony, the theatre a woman founded on this riverbed would ban women within a generation and become entirely male. The other choices are real rivers of the Kyoto region: the Kamo, Katsura, and Uji all feed the Yodo River system. Source: Grokipedia 'Kabuki'; Wikipedia 'Kabuki'.

question: Kabuki takes its name from the kabukimono. These were flashy young rebels on the streets of Kyoto and Edo in the early 1600s. They wore mismatched clothes and swaggered against every custom. Their nickname came from the old Japanese verb kabuku. What did kabuku first mean?
context: The verb kabuku literally meant to tilt or lean off-center, and from it came kabukimono — roughly 'the tilted, crooked ones' — a nickname for the outrageously dressed show-offs of the early 1600s who flouted every rule of proper dress. Only later were the three kanji 歌 (song), 舞 (dance), 伎 (skill) chosen to write 'kabuki' — a clever phonetic fit that also happens to describe the art. Source: Grokipedia 'Kabuki'; Wikipedia 'Kabuki'.

question: At the most thrilling moment of a kabuki play in Edo, or old Tokyo, the hero suddenly slams to a halt, with every muscle locked, one foot stamped down, and both eyes crossed hard toward the nose. He holds the statue-still pose while a fan in the crowd bellows out his stage-name. What is this frozen, cross-eyed climax pose called?
context: The frozen pose is the mie; the crossed-eye glare freezes a moment of peak emotion (and, by tradition, wards off evil). As the actor holds it, a devoted fan shouts his stage-name — a cry called kakegoe. The mie and the bold makeup style were pioneered by the great actor Ichikawa Danjuro I (1660–1704). keren are spectacular stage tricks and chunori is 'flying' on wires above the crowd; aragoto is Edo's bombastic superhuman-hero style. Source: Grokipedia 'Kabuki'; Wikipedia 'Kabuki'.

question: Osaka's kabuki theatres were temples of spectacle, each outdoing the last with new stage machinery. Around 1758 the Osaka playwright Namiki Shozo built a bold new device into the theatre. It was an innovation Western stages would not copy for over a century. Playhouses worldwide still use it today. What did Namiki Shozo add to the Osaka stage?
answer: the mawari-butai, a giant revolving turntable
choices: the mawari-butai, a giant revolving turntable
the hanamichi, a raised walkway into the crowd
the seri, a set of trapdoor stage elevators
the chunori, a rig for flying actors on wires
context: The device is the mawari-butai (revolving stage), a giant turntable set into the stage floor and credited to the Osaka playwright Namiki Shozo around 1758 — the world's oldest revolving stage, predating similar machinery in Western theatres by well over a century, and still standard in playhouses today. Kabuki loved such spectacle: seri trapdoors lifted actors and whole sets up through the floor, chunori ('riding in the sky') hoisted an actor over the audience on wires, and the hanamichi was a raised walkway that carried actors dramatically through the crowd. But the spinning stage was Osaka's own. Source: Wikipedia 'Namiki Shozo I' & 'Revolving stage'; Playbill 'History of the Theatrical Turntable'; KABUKI WEB.

question: Kano is one of the oldest cities of West Africa. It guarded its trans-Saharan trade behind walls that ran about 11 miles around the town and rose up to 30 feet high. Building began around 1100 under Sarki Gijimasu, and later kings made them taller. What were Kano's mighty walls built from?
context: The walls, called the Ganuwa in Hausa, were begun by Sarki (King) Gijimasu around 1095-1134 and extended by his successors over the following centuries. By 1851 the explorer Heinrich Barth recorded them as roughly 10-11 miles around and up to 30 feet high; after the British conquest in 1903, General Frederick Lugard said he had 'never seen anything like it in Africa.' Sources: Wikipedia, 'Ancient Kano City Walls' & 'Kano (city).'

question: In one corner of Kano, deep clay pits brim with near-black indigo, and cotton cloth has been dipped and re-dipped there by hand since around 1498 - the oldest indigo-dyeing pits still worked anywhere in Africa. These pits sit beside one of Kano's old city gates and take its name. Which gate is it?
context: The Kofar Mata dye pits are the oldest indigo-dyeing pits still in use in Africa: cloth has been coloured in the same clay pits for more than five centuries. (Wikipedia says 'more than 500 years'; the specific date of about 1498 comes from Kohan Textile Journal and other textile-trade sources.) The dye uses just three natural ingredients - indigo-plant leaves, wood ash, and potash - left to ferment in the pits for weeks. In its prime Kano had some 270 pits; only a few dozen still work today. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Kofar Mata Dye Pits'; Kohan Textile Journal.

question: Kano sat on the southern edge of the Sahara. King Muhammad Rumfa opened its Kurmi Market in the 1400s. Camels then carried Kano's goods across the desert to Timbuktu and beyond. What was Kano most prized for across the desert?
context: By 1851 Kano was exporting on the order of 10 million pairs of leather sandals and 5 million tanned hides a year, and its indigo cloth and leather reached as far as Timbuktu, Tripoli, Lake Chad, Morocco, and Europe. The Kurmi Market itself was established by the reforming king Muhammad Rumfa (reigned about 1463-1499). Source: Wikipedia, 'Kano (city).'

question: On the east bank of the Nile in southern Egypt lay the ancient city of Thebes, capital of the pharaohs. For 2,000 years, one pharaoh after another kept adding halls, columns, and stone gateways to a single vast temple honoring the sun-god Amun. Today we call this huge temple complex Karnak. Its own ancient Egyptian builders called it 'Ipet-isut'. What did that name mean to them?
choices: the House of a Million Years
the Horizon of the Two Lands
the Throne of the Rising Sun
context: 'Ipet-isut' means 'the Most Select of Places' — the ancient Egyptians' own boast that Karnak was the finest, holiest ground in all of Egypt. It stood at Thebes (modern Luxor) on the Nile's east bank, dedicated above all to Amun-Re, king of the gods. Source: discoveringegypt.com/karnak-temple; Britannica /place/Karnak.

question: Karnak, on the Nile at Luxor, grew for two thousand years into the largest religious complex ever built. Egyptologists are so struck by its scale that they don't call it a temple at all — they give the whole sprawl a grander nickname. What is Karnak often called?
context: Karnak is the largest religious complex ever built — a whole 'city of temples' that grew for two thousand years until it sprawled across more than 2 square kilometres. It is not one building but a walled expanse of temples, chapels, pylons, courts, and its own sacred lake, so vast that the single word 'temple' no longer fits it. Guinness World Records lists Karnak as the largest ancient Egyptian temple site. Source: guinnessworldrecords.com; discoveringegypt.com/karnak-temple; britannica.com/place/Karnak.

question: Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall is a forest of 134 stone columns. Down its central aisle stand twelve giants, each rising as high as a six-storey building — about 21 metres — their tops flaring open like blossoms. These pillars were all carved to imitate a single plant that grew along the Nile. Which plant?
context: The twelve central columns of Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall stand about 21 m (69 ft) tall — a six- to seven-storey building — carved as papyrus stalks crowned with open-blossom tops. Papyrus was Egypt's own plant: it grew thick along the Nile, and its stalks were pressed into sheets to write on. The 122 shorter outer columns (roughly 10–15 m) wear closed papyrus-bud tops. At about 5,000 sq m, the hall is the largest room of any religious building in the ancient world. Source: memphis.edu/hypostyle; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnak.

question: Karnak was not built to one plan. Over nearly two thousand years its courts, pylons, and halls piled up in clashing styles, their walls out of line, each generation of builders adding onto the last. Who were the builders who kept enlarging Karnak across twenty centuries?
answer: a long line of Egypt's pharaohs
choices: a long line of Egypt's pharaohs
the temple's guild of master masons
context: About thirty different pharaohs added to Karnak between roughly 2000 BCE (the Middle Kingdom) and 204 BCE (the Ptolemies) — nearly two thousand years. No king ever declared it finished; each simply built onto, or right over, the work of the one before. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnak; discoveringegypt.com/karnak-temple.

question: For the great festivals, priests carried the god Amun's statue out of Karnak in a slow procession, down a broad avenue guarded on both sides by more than a thousand stone sphinxes with the heads of rams. Where did this Avenue of Sphinxes lead?
context: The Avenue of Sphinxes — the 'Rams' Road' — ran about 2.7 km from Karnak south to Luxor Temple, lined by over 1,000 sphinxes; the ram-headed ones honoured Amun, whose sacred animal was the ram. Buried for centuries, it was re-excavated and reopened on 25 November 2021 with a torch-lit pharaonic parade through Luxor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_of_Sphinxes; timesofisrael.com.

question: Beside the temples at Karnak lies a great rectangular stone-lined lake, about 120 metres long, its water rising from the Nile's own water table. Each day, before performing the god's rituals, the temple's priests walked down its steps. What did they do there?
answer: bathed to purify themselves for ritual
choices: bathed to purify themselves for ritual
launched boats bearing the god's statue
drew the drinking water for the city
washed the temple's fine linen robes
context: Karnak's Sacred Lake — about 120 m by 77 m and 4 m deep, the largest at any Egyptian temple — was dug on the orders of the warrior-pharaoh Thutmose III. Priests bathed in its water to purify themselves before serving the god. The fallen half of Hatshepsut's broken obelisk now lies on the ground nearby. Source: madainproject.com/karnak_sacred_lake; discoveringegypt.com/karnak-temple/karnak-temple-sacred-lake.

question: The tallest ancient obelisk still standing in Egypt rises almost 30 metres at Karnak. Queen Hatshepsut had it hauled 200 km down the Nile from the pink granite pits at Aswan. From how much stone was this 300-tonne pink needle cut?
answer: a single unbroken block of granite
choices: a single unbroken block of granite
a granite shell over a brick core
context: Hatshepsut's obelisk at Karnak — about 29–30 m tall and over 300 tonnes — was cut from ONE block of pink Aswan granite, floated downriver, and raised upright: the tallest ancient obelisk still standing in Egypt. Its twin broke and now lies on its side near the Sacred Lake. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precinct_of_Amun-Re; exploreluxor.org/hatshepsut-obelisk.

question: Karnak's grandest gateway — the First Pylon, a pair of sloping stone towers 113 metres wide — was never finished. Against its inner wall the ancient builders left behind the very thing they had used to lift massive stone blocks dozens of metres into the air. What still stands there today?
answer: a long ramp of mud brick
choices: a long ramp of mud brick
a crane of rope and timber
a spiral of carved stone steps
context: Karnak's First Pylon — about 113 m wide and 43 m high, the largest pylon in Egypt — was never completed. Against its inner face the builders' great mud-brick construction ramp still stands: workers dragged the huge stones up such earthen ramps to build ever higher, then removed them when the job was done. Here, the work unfinished, the ramp was simply left behind. Source: madainproject.com/first_pylon_karnak_temple; digitalkarnak.ucsc.edu/1st-pylon.

question: The columns of Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall are carved as giant papyrus stalks, and the twelve tallest flare open at the top like blossoming flowers. To the priests, the whole shadowy hall stood for one watery place out of Egyptian myth. Which one?
answer: the marsh where the creator-god first rose from the water
choices: the marsh where the creator-god first rose from the water
the field of reeds where the blessed dead lived forever
the papyrus swamp where the infant Horus hid from Seth
the underworld river the sun-god sailed each night
context: The papyrus columns — the twelve central ones opening like blossoms — turned the hall into a stone image of the primeval marsh: the watery chaos of Nun from which the creator-god Atum first rose on the mound of creation at the beginning of the world. Colossal 70-tonne stone architraves once roofed it over, keeping it in permanent twilight, like a real marsh at dusk. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hypostyle_Hall.

question: In 1903, workers digging in one of Karnak's courtyards broke through into a deep hidden pit. Inside lay a staggering hoard that the temple's own priests had buried there in ancient times, then sealed away and forgotten. What had they hidden underground?
answer: a mass of stone and bronze statues
choices: a mass of stone and bronze statues
a chest of gold and silver
a tomb of the high priests' mummies
context: Karnak's 'Cachette' — a pit in the Cachette Court opened in 1903 — held roughly 900 stone statues and many thousands of bronze figures. Over the centuries the temple filled with donated statues; rather than throw sacred images away, the priests reverently buried the old ones in this pit. It remains one of the greatest single finds of Egyptian sculpture ever made. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precinct_of_Amun-Re.

question: In Ghana, weavers use wooden looms to make kente cloth. They weave bright strips only four inches wide. Then they sew the strips together into one wide cloth. Which town is the famous home of kente weaving?
context: Bonwire, in Ghana's Ashanti Region, has been the heart of kente weaving for centuries and is still one of West Africa's most important weaving centers. Each cloth is built from narrow strips, only about four inches wide, sewn edge to edge into one wide piece. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth)

question: Ashanti legend says the first kente weavers, deep in the forest, watched one small creature build with great care. They copied its work with silk and cotton. Which creature does the tale say taught people to weave?
context: The trickster spider of Ashanti folklore is Anansi (Ananse), and tradition credits him with teaching people to weave. In the fuller tale, hunters watched a spider spin its web in the forest around 1720 and reproduced it at home. Because the story is passed down orally, the weavers' names change between tellings — it is remembered as legend, not fixed history. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth)

question: In Ghana, kente's older name was nwentoma, or 'woven cloth.' The word 'kente' is thought to come from the Akan word kenten. That was the name of a common home item with a tight, woven look like the cloth. What is it?
context: 'Kente' is thought to come from the Akan word kenten, 'basket,' because the cloth's tight, interlaced weave looks basket-like. The Asante's own older name for it, nwentoma, means simply 'woven cloth.' (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth)

question: Among the Ashanti kingdom of Ghana in West Africa, master weavers make kente — a bright cloth woven in narrow strips and stitched together into royal robes for kings and queens. In kente every color carries a meaning: gold stands for wealth, blue for peace, green for growth. A band of black is not a sign of mourning as it might be elsewhere in the world. Among the Ashanti, what does black cloth stand for?
context: In kente's language of color, every shade carries meaning: gold for royalty and wealth, blue for peace and harmony, green for growth and renewal, red for the blood of the ancestors, and black for maturity and the ancestral spirits. A cloth can be 'read' as much as worn. (Source: explorekumasi.com/history-and-symbolism-of-kente)

question: For generations the finest kente belonged to the Ashanti court at Kumasi in Ghana: only kings and chiefs could wear the richest cloths, and a great chief wore his in one customary way. How was a chief's kente traditionally worn?
answer: Over one shoulder, like a toga
choices: Over one shoulder, like a toga
Wound around the head as a turban
Tied at the waist as a skirt
Draped over the head as a veil
context: Kente was long reserved for royalty. In the 1700s the Asantehene Opoku Ware I set up a weaving workshop to develop the craft, and only kings and chiefs could wear the richest cloths — draped over one shoulder, toga-style. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth)

question: In the weaving workshops of Ghana's Ashanti Region, the most intricate kente of all is called Adweneasa. It needs extra heddles on the loom, commands the very highest price, and a master weaver dares to name a cloth this only once in a great while. Translated from the Akan, what proud boast does the name Adweneasa make?
context: Adweneasa means roughly 'I have exhausted my skill' — the name a master weaver gives a cloth only when he has poured every technique he knows into it. The most decorated of all kente patterns, it needs extra heddles on the loom and commands the highest price. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth)

question: When Ghana won its independence in 1957, its first leader, Kwame Nkrumah — though not himself an Ashanti — chose the royal Ashanti cloth, kente, to stand for the whole new nation. In 1960 he presented a kente cloth to hang inside one of the world's most famous buildings, where a version still hangs today. Which building received it?
context: Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana's first leader after independence in 1957, was not himself Asante, but he chose kente to represent the whole new nation. In 1960 he gave a kente cloth to hang at the United Nations in New York (a replacement still hangs there), helping make kente a worldwide symbol of African heritage and pride. (Source: npr.org/sections/goatsandsoda/2020/06/11)

question: In the far north of the United States, right up against the Canadian border, lies the state of Minnesota. It calls itself the Land of 10,000 Lakes, though the real count is 11,842. Most are small round ponds, no more than 10 meters deep. About 12,000 years ago a huge ice sheet melted back from North America and left them dotted across the plains. They all share one odd trait most lakes on Earth don't. What is it?
answer: It has no river flowing in or out.
choices: It has no river flowing in or out.
It fills the crater of an extinct volcano.
It is saltier than the open sea.
It is a thin ribbon in a mountain valley.
context: Minnesota's slogan says '10,000,' but the counted tally of lakes at least 10 acres in size is 11,842 — hollows the retreating Wisconsin ice sheet, in places over a kilometer thick, left as it pulled back roughly 12,000 years ago. The tell of these ice-born ponds is that no river feeds them and none drains them; they fill with rain and groundwater alone. Source: Geography of Minnesota; Kettle (landform), Wikipedia.

question: In the far north U.S. state of Minnesota, thousands of small ponds are round, riverless, and no more than 10 meters deep, fed only by rain and the water table underground. About 12,000 years ago, the last ice age was ending, and a giant continental glacier was slowly melting back across the whole region. As it retreated, it left these ponds behind. Which of these describes how such a pond forms?
answer: A block of buried glacier ice melts and the ground over it caves in.
choices: A block of buried glacier ice melts and the ground over it caves in.
A looping river bend gets cut off and stranded as a curved pond.
Groundwater dissolves the limestone below until the surface sinks in.
A meteor slams down and punches a round crater into the plain.
context: This collapse pit is called a KETTLE — literally the footprint of a melted ice block. As the glacier that dimpled Minnesota pulled back, meltwater streams buried a stranded block of 'dead ice' under sand and gravel; when it finally thawed, the ground heaped on top slumped into a rounded, riverless basin. The other three make real lakes too — an oxbow from a cut-off river bend, a sinkhole pond in dissolving limestone, a crater from a meteor — but none is born from buried ice. Source: Kettle (landform), Wikipedia.

question: In 1845 Henry David Thoreau built his cabin on the north shore of Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts. It is a small, steep-sided pond that plunges over 100 feet deep, yet no stream flows into it and none flows out - its water so clear that Thoreau imagined a hidden spring feeding it from the bottom. What kind of lake is Walden Pond?
context: Walden Pond covers about 64.5 acres yet plunges to roughly 102 feet - a small, steep-sided kettle that a buried glacier block left about 10,000 to 12,000 years ago. With no inlet or outlet, Thoreau guessed a hidden bottom spring fed its famously clear water. Source: Walden Pond, Wikipedia.

question: Wisconsin's Kettle Moraine is named for the pits - kettles - that dot it, each a hollow left where a buried block of glacier ice melted out. But the same vanished ice also heaped the opposite landform right beside those pits: rounded hills of sand and gravel that pile up, some standing 300 feet above the lakes. What are these glacial mounds called?
context: The Kettle Moraine formed where two great tongues of the Laurentide Ice Sheet met - the Green Bay Lobe on the west and the Lake Michigan Lobe on the east - dumping sediment between them. Its kettles hold water from 3 to 200 feet deep, while kames of piled gravel rise as much as 300 feet above them: pits and mounds from the very same ice. Source: Kettle Moraine, Wikipedia.

question: From the Dakotas up into Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba lies a huge belt of shallow, round, rain-filled ponds. More than half of North America's ducks and geese hatch there. That makes it the top waterfowl nursery on the continent. What are these ponds called?
context: This belt of glacial kettle wetlands - the Prairie Pothole Region - spreads across roughly 800,000 square kilometers of the northern Great Plains. Though it holds only about a tenth of the continent's waterfowl breeding habitat by area, more than half of North America's migratory waterfowl hatch among its potholes, earning it the nickname 'the duck factory.' Source: Prairie Pothole Region, Wikipedia.

question: Time and war have taken down the walls of most old Silk Road trading cities. But in Uzbekistan, high in Central Asia, the town of Khiva still keeps its ancient heart. It is called the Itchan Kala, an inner town wrapped inside thick mud-brick walls ten metres high. What record does Khiva's walled old town hold in Central Asia today?
answer: the largest walled town in Central Asia
choices: the largest walled town in Central Asia
the oldest walled town in Central Asia
the tallest-walled town in Central Asia
the most-fought-over walled town in Central Asia
context: Itchan Kala, Khiva's inner walled town, is the largest surviving walled town in Central Asia: a rectangle roughly 650 x 400 m ringed by crenellated mud-brick walls about 8-10 m high and 5-6 m thick, with an inner-wall circuit of about 2,200 m. Bukhara, Samarkand and Merv were once walled too, but only Khiva keeps its full circuit intact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itchan_Kala

question: In Central Asia, in what is now the country of Uzbekistan, the old oasis city of Khiva rose from the sands ringed by tall mud walls. On the Silk Road caravan trail, Khiva was the very last watering place — the last spot where a merchant could top up his water skins and feed his camels. Beyond Khiva's western gate lay a brutal 400-km slog across shifting sand dunes toward Persia. Which Central Asian desert did the Silk Road traders have to cross?
context: Khiva was the final fortified stop before the Karakum ('black sand') desert crossing to Persia (Iran) on the Silk Road. The Kyzylkum lies the other way, toward Bukhara; the Taklamakan and Gobi are far to the east, in China and Mongolia. Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/543/

question: Khiva's Kalta Minor is a wide tower covered in blue and green tiles. Yet 'Kalta' means 'short.' Its builder, Muhammad Amin Khan, wanted the tallest minaret in the Muslim world. Instead it stops at just 29 m. Why did the tower never rise to its planned height?
choices: an earthquake sheared off its top
the soft ground could bear no more
the royal treasury ran out of money
context: Muhammad Amin Khan began the Kalta Minor in 1851, intending a minaret of 70-80 m (legend says 110 m); when he was killed in 1855, the work simply stopped and was never resumed. 'Kalta' means 'short,' and its turquoise majolica is said to be 'still as bright as in 1855.' Khiva's tallest FINISHED tower is the later Islam Khodja minaret (1908-10), about 57 m — nearly double the stubby Kalta Minor. Sources: https://www.advantour.com/uzbekistan/khiva/kalta-minor.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaltaminor

question: Most great Central Asian mosques soar into tiled domes and towering arches. Khiva's Djuma (Friday) Mosque does the exact opposite: a low, dim, flat-roofed hall lit only by a few shafts of daylight. What astonishing feature fills the whole interior and holds up its flat roof?
answer: a forest of carved wooden columns
choices: a forest of carved wooden columns
a grid of ancient granite piers
a cage of riveted iron beams
a rank of glazed brick pillars
context: The Djuma Mosque's flat roof rests on a forest of about 212 carved wooden columns set in 17 rows, each cut from karagach (black elm). Roughly 25 are ancient (10th-16th centuries) and four date to the 10th-11th century — over a thousand years old. The mosque was founded in the 10th century and rebuilt in 1788-89. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juma_Mosque,_Khiva ; https://www.orexca.com/uzbekistan/khiva/juma_mosque.htm

question: In 1990 a United Nations group gave Khiva's walled Itchan Kala a big global honor. They picked the small desert town over the grand domes of Samarkand and Bukhara. It was the first place in all of Central Asia to earn this honor. Which honor did Khiva claim first for the region?
choices: a Creative City of Craft listing
context: UNESCO inscribed Itchan Kala in December 1990 (14th session; reference #543; criteria iii, iv, v) — the first World Heritage Site in Uzbekistan and in all of Central Asia, ahead of Samarkand and Bukhara. UNESCO calls it 'a coherent and well-preserved example of the Muslim architecture of Central Asia.' (The queue's 1991 date is corrected here: every source gives 1990.) Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/543/

question: Most old towns have one great church or palace people line up to see. Khiva's Itchan Kala is just 650 by 400 metres across. That is smaller than many modern shopping malls. But inside its walls, mosques, madrasas, minarets, palaces, and tombs stand shoulder to shoulder. About how many old monuments are packed into this one small walled town?
context: Within its walls Itchan Kala packs over 50 historic monuments — about 20 mosques, 20 madrasas and 6 minarets, plus palaces and mausoleums — alongside some 250 old houses (mostly 18th-19th century), so complete that the whole town looks frozen in time. UNESCO calls it 'a coherent and well-preserved example of the Muslim architecture of Central Asia.' Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/543/

question: In the far northeast of Tanzania in East Africa, right near the Kenyan border, a huge snowcapped volcano lifts its head above the flat plains — Kilimanjaro. It stands almost 6,000 m tall. Climbers come from all over the world to spend a week trekking up its slopes to reach the summit, Uhuru Peak, the 'Roof of Africa'. Of all the mountains on Earth, what record does Kilimanjaro hold?
choices: the tallest peak in the tropics
context: Kilimanjaro isn't the highest mountain on Earth (Everest wins that), but because it stands alone and rises about 4,600 m straight from the plains, it's the tallest free-standing mountain in the world -- one giant, not a peak in a crowded range. Source: andbeyond.com/destinations/africa/tanzania/kilimanjaro; climbing-kilimanjaro.com/interesting-kilimanjaro-facts.

question: Mount Kilimanjaro is Africa's tallest mountain, rising alone out of the plains of northeast Tanzania with a snowy peak so high it can be seen far across the border in southern Kenya. There is one Kenyan wildlife park where safari-goers regularly snap photos of elephants and zebras with Kilimanjaro's floating white peak filling the sky behind them. Which park is it?
context: Amboseli National Park in southern Kenya is famous for exactly this view: flat, dusty plains with snow-topped Kilimanjaro -- actually across the border in Tanzania -- floating on the horizon. Source: amboseli.ke/mount-kilimanjaro-the-majestic-backdrop-of-amboseli-national-park; earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/2720/mount-kilimanjaro-tanzania.

question: Kilimanjaro is a huge extinct volcano in northeast Tanzania in East Africa, standing almost right on the equator. On the dry plains below, thorny acacia trees dot the savanna where lions and elephants roam, and the heat bakes the ground all year long. Yet climbers who take the week-long trek up its slopes to reach the top, Uhuru Peak, find the summit always covered by what?
context: Kilimanjaro's summit sits only about 3 degrees south of the equator, yet Uhuru Peak wears permanent glaciers and snow -- ice in the tropics, high enough that it never fully melts. Source: education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/kilimanjaro; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kilimanjaro.

question: Mount Kilimanjaro in northeast Tanzania is really a giant volcano built of three ancient cones. Two of the cones have worn down over time, but the tallest and youngest one still rises to 5,895 metres. It holds the summit called Uhuru Peak, where climbers stand on what East Africans call the Roof of Africa. What is the name of this tallest cone of Kilimanjaro?
context: Kibo is the youngest, tallest cone and holds Uhuru Peak; jagged Mawenzi (5,149 m) is extinct and, unlike Kibo's walk-up, a technical rock climb; old Shira collapsed long ago into a flat plateau. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kilimanjaro; climbmountkilimanjaro.com/about-the-mountain/location-geology-appearance.

question: In 1889, German geographer Hans Meyer was the first to climb Kilimanjaro. He gave its highest point a grand German name. When Tanganyika won its freedom in 1961, the peak was renamed Uhuru, Swahili for 'freedom.' What had Meyer named the Roof of Africa first?
context: After his 1889 ascent, Hans Meyer named the summit 'Kaiser Wilhelm Peak' for the German emperor. When Tanganyika (now Tanzania) won independence in 1961, Lt. Alexander Nyirenda climbed up and lit the Uhuru ('freedom') Torch on the roof of Africa, and the peak became Uhuru Peak. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uhuru_Torch; ultimatekilimanjaro.com/the-true-meaning-of-uhuru-peak.

question: In 1926 a missionary pastor named Richard Reusch climbed near the frozen summit of Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania and found the body of a leopard that had somehow wandered that high up. Even after years lying near the top, the leopard had not rotted away. Ernest Hemingway later wove the strange find into a famous short story. Up in the harsh, freezing, thin summit air, what had happened to the leopard's body?
answer: it had freeze-dried into a mummy
choices: it had frozen inside a glacier
it had freeze-dried into a mummy
context: Pastor Richard Reusch found the freeze-dried leopard at about 5,600 m on Kibo's rim; no one knows why it climbed so high (he guessed it chased a goat). Ernest Hemingway made it famous in 'The Snows of Kilimanjaro' (1936), and the spot is now called Leopard Point. Source: earthtouchnews.com/discoveries/discoveries/the-amazing-story-of-the-frozen-leopard-atop-mount-kilimanjaro; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Snows_of_Kilimanjaro_(short_story).  (Legend.)

question: Kilimanjaro's summit ice cores show the mountain survived a brutal global drought about 4,200 years ago — the same dry catastrophe that helped topple the Akkadian Empire in Mesopotamia. Climatologists have a formal name for this event. What is it called?
context: About 85% of the ice present in 1912 is gone. An ice core shows melting on this scale hasn't happened in roughly 11,700 years -- even that 300-year drought left the ice intact. Scientists project the cap could vanish around 2050, though the exact timing is debated. Source: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0906029106 (Thompson et al.); ultimatekilimanjaro.com/mount-kilimanjaros-glaciers-estimated-to-be-gone-by-2050.

question: Kilimanjaro's summit looks dead and frozen, but its highest cone, Kibo, is only dormant, not extinct. When scientists pushed a probe just 30 cm beneath the floor of Kibo's inner crater -- expecting frozen rock so near the icy 5,895 m summit -- the reading stunned them. What temperature did the probe find?
context: Nested inside Kibo's summit crater is the inner Reusch Crater, whose ash pit still steams with sulphurous fumaroles. A probe pushed just 30 cm under the crater floor read 78.5 C (173 F) -- scalding rock a stone's throw from the equator's highest ice. Kibo is not dead, only sleeping. Source: ultimatekilimanjaro.com/reusch-crater-the-ash-pit-on-kilimanjaro; markhorrell.com/blog/2017/a-brief-introduction-to-kilimanjaros-volcanic-crater.

question: Climb Kilimanjaro and in a single week you rise through five climate zones, from tropical foothills at its base to an arctic summit far above. One belt partway up is unmistakable: it is studded with giant groundsels and giant lobelias, oversized plants that tower over the trail. Which of the mountain's five zones is this?
context: This is Kilimanjaro's heath and moorland zone, the belt famous for its giant groundsels and giant lobelias. It is one of five zones a climber crosses in a few days -- cultivated farmland (bananas, coffee, maize), tropical rainforest, heath and moorland, stark alpine desert, and the arctic summit -- so a single week's walk feels like traveling from the equator to the pole. Source: kilimanjaropark.org/climate-ecological-zones; climbing-kilimanjaro.com/mount-kilimanjaro-climate-zones.

question: Kilimanjaro is so vast it makes its own weather. Damp trade winds sweep in off the Indian Ocean and meet the mountain's broad southern flank, which drinks in 2,000-3,000 mm of rain a year and grows a dense rainforest belt -- even as the far higher summit stays a near-desert. What is this kind of rainfall called?
context: This is orographic rainfall: a mountain forces moist air upward until it cools and drops its water on the windward slope. Kilimanjaro's southern rainforest belt collects 2,000-3,000 mm a year, while the far higher summit -- in the mountain's own rain shadow -- gets barely 100 mm, mostly as snow. Source: altezzatravel.com/articles/kilimanjaro-climate-zones; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5569136.

question: Off the coast of Tanzania sits a small island you can only reach by boat. In the Middle Ages it was no fishing village. It was one of the richest cities of the Indian Ocean. Over ten thousand people lived there and traded African gold for Chinese porcelain. Which Swahili-coast island city was it?
context: Kilwa Kisiwani — the name means 'Kilwa on the island' in Swahili — sat on the southern Swahili coast of what is now Tanzania. From the 1100s to the 1400s it was the leading trading city of the East African coast, home to an estimated 10,000-plus people dealing in gold, ivory, and luxuries carried across the Indian Ocean. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kilwa Kisiwani'; Grokipedia (Kilwa Kisiwani).

question: Kilwa's Great Mosque and its cliff-top palace rise in neat grey stone blocks. The whole Swahili coast used one signature stone for building, from Kilwa to Zanzibar to Lamu. It was cut into blocks like any rock from a quarry. What stone were Kilwa's walls built from?
context: Swahili cities built in 'coral rag' — blocks of coral limestone cut straight from the living reef offshore and squared into masonry, often finished with a fine coral-lime plaster. Kilwa, Zanzibar's Stone Town, and Lamu all share this pale coral stonework, the signature material of the East African coast. Source: Wikipedia, 'Great Mosque of Kilwa' and 'Kilwa Kisiwani'.

question: The Great Mosque of Kilwa is the oldest still standing on the East African coast. It broke with the usual plan and had no open courtyard. Sultan al-Hasan later added a new feature to it. It was the first of its kind on the coast, and the biggest anywhere on the coast until the 1800s. What did the sultan raise over the mosque?
context: The oldest sections of the Great Mosque date to the 11th-12th century; Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman added its great dome in the early 1300s. It was the first true dome raised on the East African coast and remained the largest dome on the coast until the 19th century — the traveller Ibn Battuta remarked on it after his 1331 visit. Source: Google Arts & Culture / archnet.org; Wikipedia, 'Great Mosque of Kilwa'.

question: Kilwa had no gold mines of its own, yet it grew fabulously rich on gold. The secret was control of a single coastal harbour, the one place where all the gold carried out of the deep African interior reached the sea. Kilwa seized that harbour and taxed every shipment bound for Arabia and India. Which port made Kilwa the gatekeeper of African gold?
context: Sofala, on the coast of what is now Mozambique, was the outlet for gold mined in the far interior of southern Africa. Kilwa controlled Sofala and taxed the gold, ivory, and goods flowing through it toward Arabia and India — growing rich as the middleman without ever mining an ounce of gold itself. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kilwa Sultanate'.

question: Dig in the ruins of Kilwa and you find its own money. Small copper coins were struck at its mint from the 1100s onward. Each was stamped with the ruling sultan's name and one odd extra flourish. What did Kilwa's coins carry, besides the sultan's name, that almost no other coins of the age did?
answer: a line of Arabic rhyming verse
choices: a line of Arabic rhyming verse
the name of the mint town
context: Kilwa began minting its own coins in the 1100s under Sultan Ali bin al-Hasan — mostly copper, with occasional silver and gold — each inscribed with the ruling sultan's name and a short Arabic rhyming couplet. Very few sub-Saharan African cities struck their own coinage; Kilwa's mint marks how sophisticated and independent the city-state had become. Source: EBSCO Research Starters; CNG Coins; Numista Kilwa catalogue.

question: On a high sandstone cliff above the Indian Ocean, Sultan al-Hasan built Husuni Kubwa. It had over a hundred rooms set around sunken courtyards. It was the largest stone building in all of sub-Saharan Africa before modern times. One of its luxuries still amazes visitors today. What did the sultan build into his cliff-top palace?
context: Husuni Kubwa ('the big fort/palace') was raised by Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman around 1310-1333 on a sandstone cliff over the sea. Its 100-plus rooms, sunken courtyards, and octagonal bathing pool made it the largest building in sub-Saharan Africa before the modern era — and part of it doubled as a warehouse, with terraces and a staging area for loading goods onto trading ships. Source: WebSearch (archnet.org, worldhistory.org); Wikipedia, 'Kilwa Kisiwani'.

question: By Swahili legend, a Persian prince named Ali ibn al-Hassan of Shiraz bought the site of Kilwa from its local king for as much colored cloth as would stretch all the way around it. When the king had second thoughts and came back to reclaim his land, he found he could not reach it: overnight the newcomers had done one thing that put Kilwa forever beyond him. What had they done?
answer: dug away the land bridge to the mainland
choices: dug away the land bridge to the mainland
burned every boat drawn up on the shore
walled off the whole neck of land
flooded the low approaches with seawater
context: The Kilwa Chronicle tells that Ali ibn al-Hassan of Shiraz bought the island for enough cloth to ring it, then — when the local king tried to take it back — the settlers had already dug away the land bridge, so Kilwa was now a true island beyond his reach. It is a founding legend, not documented history, but it captures how Kilwa's island setting protected its wealth. Source (legend): Wikipedia, 'Ali ibn al-Hassan Shirazi'; the Kilwa Chronicle.

question: Kilwa's copper coins were struck for a busy island port on the Indian Ocean — yet they did not all stay by the sea. Archaeologists digging in the ruins of a great kingdom deep in the African interior, hundreds of miles from any coast, pulled two of Kilwa's own coins from the soil, hard proof of how far the little island's trade reached across the continent. In whose ruins were the buried Kilwa coins found?
context: Two copper coins minted at Kilwa were excavated at Great Zimbabwe, the dry-stone-walled kingdom of the southern African interior whose gold flowed down to the Swahili coast. The coins are physical proof of a trade web binding a tiny Indian Ocean island to a kingdom hundreds of miles inland — gold flowing out to the coast, and Kilwa's own coins carried back in. Source: WebSearch (EBSCO Research Starters; numismatic records); coins of Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman, r. 1310-1333.

question: In Japan, when a treasured pottery tea bowl breaks, it can be repaired with an old craft called kintsugi. The mender first glues the broken pieces back together with tree-sap lacquer. Then he traces every crack with sparkling metal dust, so the old breaks shine as bright lines across the bowl — the repair itself turned into beauty. Which metal is traditionally dusted into the cracks in the classic kintsugi fix?
context: Kintsugi means 'golden joinery' — kin, 'gold,' plus tsugi, 'joinery.' The shards are bonded with urushi, a lacquer tapped from a Japanese tree, and the seams are dusted or mixed with powdered gold so the repair is meant to be seen, not hidden — usually becoming the most striking feature of the whole piece. Gold isn't the only choice: silver dust makes a variant called gintsugi, and platinum is used too. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kintsugi

question: In old Japan, when a favorite tea bowl broke, a craftsman could mend it with a special repair called kintsugi — piecing the shards back together with tree-sap lacquer mixed with pure gold dust. The healed bowl came out crisscrossed with shining gold seams along every old crack. Some tea-bowl collectors fell so hard for these glowing cracks that a strange rumor spread about them. What were these tea fans said to do to their own perfect pots?
answer: smash them deliberately, shattering the perfect glaze
choices: smash them deliberately, shattering the perfect glaze
boil them fast so the sudden heat crazed the glaze
chill them in ice water until the glaze cracked through
bury them for a year so the damp soil crazed the glaze
context: This one is a LEGEND, not settled fact: some tea collectors were said to love gold-mended pottery so much that they deliberately smashed prized pieces just to have them repaired with glittering seams. It fits the Japanese ideas behind kintsugi — wabi-sabi, the beauty found in imperfect and impermanent things, and mottainai, a hatred of waste — where a bowl's break becomes part of its story and makes it more treasured, not less. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kintsugi

question: One old story traces the birth of Japan's kintsugi craft to Ashikaga Yoshimasa, a shogun who ruled Japan in the 1400s. His favorite Chinese tea bowl had cracked, and he sent it back to China hoping the craftsmen there could return it as beautiful as before. The bowl came home mended, but the fix was so ugly it disappointed him — and pushed Japan to invent a lovelier way. In the story, how had the Chinese repaired the bowl?
answer: clamped back together with metal staples
choices: filled in with a plug of coarse gray clay
clamped back together with metal staples
sealed under a thick, mismatched glaze
bound along the crack with waxed cord
context: This origin tale is a LEGEND, not documented history. As the story goes, in the late 1400s the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa sent a cracked tea bowl to China for a fix, and it returned merely clamped with ugly metal staples — so Japanese craftsmen sought a lovelier mend, and gold-lacquer kintsugi grew from that. A real bowl sits behind the legend: the 13th-century 'Bakohan' celadon tea bowl, sent to China for a replacement, came home fastened with big metal staples said to look like a locust — and it was prized more for them. It still wears those staples today in the Tokyo National Museum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kintsugi

question: On the island of Crete rose Knossos, the grandest palace of Bronze-Age Europe. It was first built around 1900 BC. Tens of thousands of people lived there. Later Greeks wove the whole palace into their most famous legend. What did they remember Knossos as?
context: Knossos was the largest building of Minoan Crete, first built around 1900 BC and home to tens of thousands of people. Its floor plan of some 1,300 interconnecting rooms across as many as five floors so bewildered later Greeks that they reworked the palace itself into the legend of the Labyrinth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knossos.

question: On the Greek island of Crete stand the stone ruins of Knossos, once the palace of the ancient king Minos more than 3,000 years ago. In Greek legend, King Minos kept a fearsome beast caged deep in a twisting maze under his palace — a Labyrinth so tangled that anyone who was sent in never found the way back out again. Which monster did the story say lurked there?
context: The Minotaur -- a monster with a bull's head on a man's body -- was said to be caged in the labyrinth King Minos had his architect Daedalus build beneath the palace. Source: knossos-palace.gr/2023/08/24/the-myth-of-theseus-and-the-minotaur/.  (Legend.)

question: In the legend, the hero Theseus sailed from Athens to Crete. He agreed to go down into the winding depths under Knossos to kill the Minotaur. But no one sent in had ever found the way back out. Princess Ariadne, the king's daughter, gave Theseus one thing so he could trace his path and escape. What did she give him?
context: Theseus unspooled 'Ariadne's thread' as he went in, slew the Minotaur, then followed the thread back out to safety -- the thread that saved the hero. Source: knossos-palace.gr/2023/08/24/the-myth-of-theseus-and-the-minotaur/.  (Legend.)

question: In the old Cretan legend of the palace of Knossos, the sea god Poseidon punished King Minos by cursing his queen. Queen Pasiphae, wife of Minos, was driven by the gods into a wild, unnatural love for one particular animal that Poseidon had sent up out of the sea. From that union the man-eating Minotaur was born, half human and half beast. What animal did Pasiphae fall in love with?
context: In the myth, Queen Pasiphae's unnatural love for a white bull produced the Minotaur -- a monster with a bull's head and a man's body. To feed it, King Minos forced conquered Athens to send seven youths and seven maidens to Crete as tribute, until the hero Theseus killed the beast and ended the toll. Source: greekmyths-greekmythology.com (myth of Theseus and the Minotaur).  (Legend.)

question: On the Greek island of Crete, at the ruined palace of Knossos, archaeologists found a wall painting made by Minoan artists around 1450 BC — about 3,500 years ago. The bright fresco froze three young athletes mid-motion in a real and risky sport with a live, charging bull. Museums today call the painting 'Bull-Leaping'. What were the athletes doing in the scene?
choices: wrestling the bull to the ground
sacrificing the bull at an altar
context: Minoan painters used a strict color code -- men shown dark reddish-brown, women pale white -- so in this Bull-Leaping (Taureador) Fresco the two pale figures gripping the bull's horns and tail are women, and the dark figure vaulting its back is a youth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bull-Leaping_Fresco.

question: Knossos was the great palace of Bronze Age Crete, the seat of the Minoan people about 3,500 years ago. In the queen's rooms of that palace, one of the loveliest surviving Minoan wall paintings still colors the plaster. The bright blue fresco shows sleek sea animals curving through the water, surrounded by darting little fish. Which sea animals star in this famous Knossos fresco?
context: The Dolphin Fresco decorated the Queen's Megaron (the royal apartments) -- leaping dolphins and small fish across the wall, one of the most charming images in all Minoan art. Source: odysseyadventures.ca (Knossos, Royal Apartments).

question: In ancient times on the Greek island of Crete, the Minoan kings built a huge palace called Knossos. Its winding halls were so confusing that later Greeks told stories of a Labyrinth here that trapped the Minotaur. Deep in the ruins, archaeologists found the same shape carved into the stone walls again and again. Many scholars now think the very word 'Labyrinth' grew from the old Minoan name for this one symbol. Which symbol covers the walls?
context: The double axe was called 'labrys,' and 'Labyrinth' probably meant 'House of the Double Axe' -- so the palace's very name may come from the axe-marks carved on its stones. Source: worldhistory.org/Minoan_Civilization/.

question: The Minoans piped fresh water through Knossos in clay pipes nearly 3,700 years ago. The pipes ran clear and never clogged. Europe would not match this feat for thousands of years. They did it with one odd design choice. How was each clay pipe shaped where it joined the next?
choices: sealed with lead at each joint
pierced with holes at each joint
context: The narrowing sped the water up -- like a thumb over a hose -- and the faster flow scoured out sediment so the pipes never clogged. Source: toilet-guru.com/minoan/; goworldtravel.com/crete-palace-of-knossos/.

question: In the queen's rooms at Knossos, diggers found what may be Europe's oldest example of a fixture we still use at home today. It was built into the palace about 3,700 years ago, more than a thousand years before Rome. It even had its own drain to the palace sewer. What was this fixture?
context: The seat sat over a drain to the sewer and was flushed by pouring in a jug of water -- what may be Europe's oldest flushing toilet, engineered roughly 3,700 years ago, over a millennium before Rome's aqueducts. Source: goworldtravel.com/crete-palace-of-knossos/.

question: Deep within Knossos survives the Throne Room, where a single carved gypsum seat still stands against the wall where the Minoans set it more than 3,000 years ago -- the oldest stone throne in all of Europe. Painted on the plaster to either side, a pair of guardian beasts sit facing it, watching over whoever once took the seat. Which creatures flank the throne of Knossos?
context: The gypsum throne is flanked by painted griffins -- mythical beasts with a lion's body and an eagle's head -- and is the oldest stone throne in Europe. Sir Arthur Evans called it King Minos's throne, but most archaeologists now think the room was sacred, used in 'epiphany' rituals in which a High Priestess appeared in the role of the goddess. Source: greekreporter.com (the mystery of the oldest throne in Europe at Knossos).

question: Sir Arthur Evans did not simply uncover Knossos -- between 1905 and 1930 he rebuilt whole sections of the palace and repainted its fallen columns in vivid reds and blues. Critics say he partly invented what visitors see today, sneering that he had turned the ancient site into 'a museum of a museum.' Which material did Evans choose to raise his new walls?
context: The reinforced concrete let Evans permanently 'reconstitute' the palace, but froze his own guesswork into the ruins -- leaving what Mary Beard called 'a museum of a museum.' It was also Evans who coined the name 'Minoan,' after the legendary King Minos. Source: thearchaeologist.org (Palace of Minos: restoration vs preservation); lrb.co.uk (Mary Beard, 'Builder of Ruins').

question: Around 1250 CE, on India's east coast by the Bay of Bengal, builders raised a grand temple to Surya, the Hindu sun god. Rather than build the usual boxy shrine, they shaped the whole structure — walls, base, and terraces — to look like one sacred form. What is the Konark Sun Temple carved to look like?
context: The whole temple is Surya's cosmic war-chariot rendered in stone, the sun god shown forever riding it across the heavens. It was built around 1250 CE on the Odisha coast beside the Bay of Bengal and is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Konark_Sun_Temple

question: A grand temple might show a carved wheel or two as decoration. The Konark Sun Temple's stone platform carries a whole fleet of them -- a long row of huge wheels down each side -- with a team of straining stone horses carved heaving the building forward. How many wheels and how many horses did the sculptors carve in all?
context: The chariot rides on 24 wheels and is pulled by seven horses, and the numbers carry meaning: the seven horses are read as the seven days of the week, and the 24 wheels as the fortnights of the year, making the whole temple a giant 'wheel of time.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konark_Sun_Temple

question: Each of Konark's giant stone wheels has a raised hub, wide spokes, and a fine rim of beads. People long thought this was just decoration. In truth, every wheel is laid out as a real science tool that visitors can still read today. What kind of tool does a Konark wheel work as?
context: Every wheel is a working sundial. The shadow a spoke throws onto the beaded rim tells the hour, the eight broad spokes split the day into eight three-hour 'prahars,' and the fine beads between them let a careful reader tell the time down to a few minutes. Source: worldhistory.org/Konarak_Sun_Temple

question: Konark, on India's eastern coast in the state of Odisha, is a huge 13th-century Hindu temple carved to look like the chariot of Surya, the sun god. Its tall main spire once rose over 200 feet, but that great tower collapsed into rubble centuries ago. Only one huge, richly carved section still stands almost whole — the part visitors line up to photograph today. Which section of the Konark Sun Temple survives?
context: The fallen tower was the deul, the main spire above the sanctum; what survives is the jagamohana, the great audience hall, about 39 m high. The original spire's height is debated: traditional accounts say roughly 68-70 m (over 200 ft), while some scholars estimate closer to 45 m. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konark_Sun_Temple

question: For centuries, European sailors crossing the Bay of Bengal fixed their position by the towering Konark temple looming over the Odisha shore -- a seamark so dependable it was marked on their charts. To these foreign crews the Hindu temple went by a blunt, two-word English nickname that stuck for generations. What did the sailors call Konark?
context: Sailors paired it with the 'White Pagoda,' the bright Jagannath temple up the coast at Puri, using the two as landmarks in the Bay of Bengal. Konark's stone had weathered to a dark hue, which earned it the name 'Black Pagoda.' Source: grokipedia.com/page/Konark_Sun_Temple

question: History and legend clash over why Konark's great spire fell. Scholars point to poor-quality stone, a sinking foundation, or a lightning strike. But the old sailors' legend blames a single powerful object once fixed at the temple's summit -- the very thing said to have lured passing ships toward this coast to their doom, and whose removal, the tale goes, brought the whole tower crashing down. According to the legend, what once stood atop Konark?
context: This is legend, not history, and no record of the magnet survives. The story claims the summit lodestone threw ships' compasses into chaos and even held the temple's iron idol floating in mid-air, and that removing it doomed the tower. Scholars instead blame the poor khondalite stone, subsidence, or lightning. Source: orissapost.com

question: Krakatoa was a small volcanic island sitting in the narrow sea between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra. In August of 1883 the whole mountain blew itself apart in an eruption so violent that it produced the loudest sound ever recorded on Earth, heard nearly 3,000 miles away. What is the name of that narrow sea between Java and Sumatra?
context: Krakatoa sat on the Sunda volcanic arc — the chain of fire-mountains where the Indo-Australian plate dives beneath Southeast Asia — right in the Sunda Strait dividing Java from Sumatra. The 1883 eruption was heard across roughly a quarter of the planet. Source: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'.

question: On the morning of 27 August 1883, Krakatoa's final blast at 10:02 a.m. was one of the most violent explosions the Earth has ever produced. When the smoke and steam finally cleared over the Sunda Strait, sailors were stunned by what they found where the volcano's peak had towered. What had happened to the island of Krakatoa itself?
answer: Almost the whole island had vanished into the sea
choices: Almost the whole island had vanished into the sea
It had doubled in height from fresh lava
It had split into a ring of tall new peaks
A glowing lava lake had filled its crater
context: The climactic explosion destroyed most of the island, leaving a submarine caldera — a great crater below the sea — where the mountain had stood. Source: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'.

question: When Krakatoa blew up on 27 August 1883, the boom rolled 3,000 miles across the ocean. It reached Rodrigues Island, near Mauritius, about four hours later. It is the farthest a sound has ever been heard on Earth. The islanders were baffled by a far-off booming from the east. What did the police chief and colonists think they were hearing?
answer: Distant naval guns firing out at sea
choices: Distant naval guns firing out at sea
Dynamite blasting at a faraway mine
The first tremors of a great earthquake
A violent thunderstorm over the horizon
context: On Rodrigues the police chief logged 'the roar of heavy guns' from the east; colonists nearly 5,000 km away truly thought warships were firing. The blast was also heard 3,110 km away in Perth, Australia — audible across about a thirteenth of the globe. Sources: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'; Live Science, 'Krakatoa Volcano'.  (Legend.)

question: The Royal Mail Ship (RMS) Norham Castle was sailing about 64 km (40 mi) from Krakatoa when the explosion's shockwave slammed into the ship. Afterward her captain wrote a now-famous line in the log: the blast had done the very same thing to more than half the men aboard. What had it done to half the crew?
context: The blast reached roughly 180 decibels at the source. The captain of the Norham Castle, about 64 km away, recorded that the explosion had ruptured the eardrums of more than half his crew. Source: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'.

question: Krakatoa's official death toll of 36,417 makes it one of the deadliest eruptions in history — yet hardly any of those people were burned by the volcano at all. Something else did almost all the killing, erasing whole coastal towns in minutes. What was it?
choices: A vast slide of hot mud
context: The collapsing volcano launched tsunamis up to 42 m (138 ft) high onto Java and Sumatra. Of the 36,417 official dead, more than 34,000 — about nine in ten — drowned. Sources: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'; NOAA/NCEI, 'On This Day: Historic Krakatau Eruption of 1883'.

question: When Krakatoa's sea-surge struck the coasts, it left one unforgettable calling card. A Dutch steam gunboat named the Berouw had been anchored in the Sunda Strait; the water seized her and left her somewhere no ship should ever be. Where did the Berouw end up?
answer: Carried far inland, stranded up a river valley
choices: Carried far inland, stranded up a river valley
Smashed to splinters on the outer reef
Dragged far out into the open sea
Flipped upside down at her mooring
context: The Berouw was swept about 2.5 km (over 1.5 mi) up a river valley and left stranded roughly 9 m above sea level; all 28 of her crew died. On nearby Sebesi island, every one of the ~3,000 inhabitants was killed. Sources: Live Science, 'Krakatoa Volcano'; VolcanoDB, 'Krakatoa Eruption'.

question: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, a volcanic island in Indonesia, released about 200 megatons of energy — enough to hurl volcanic ash 50 miles up into the sky. Compare that to the largest nuclear weapon humans have ever set off: the Soviet Union's Tsar Bomba, detonated in 1961 above the Arctic. How did the single Krakatoa blast compare in raw power to Tsar Bomba?
context: The eruption's energy — roughly 200 megatons of TNT — was about four times the yield of the largest nuclear weapon ever detonated. Sources: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'; VolcanoDB, 'Krakatoa Eruption'.

question: Krakatoa's blast punched a pulse of pressure into the atmosphere that spread outward like a ripple across the whole sky. Barographs at weather stations all over the world kept detecting it for five straight days as it swept past them. How many times did that single pressure wave circle the entire planet?
answer: About three and a half times
choices: About three and a half times
context: Barographs recorded the wave seven separate times over five days — four times heading away from Krakatoa and three times bouncing back — meaning it circled the Earth about three and a half times. Sources: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'; VolcanoDB, 'Krakatoa Eruption'.

question: Krakatoa had blown itself off the map, leaving only open sea above its sunken crater. But volcanoes on the Sunda arc do not stay dead. In late 1927 a brand-new island pushed up out of the waves at the very same spot, and Indonesians gave it a name that captured exactly what it was. What did they call it?
context: Anak Krakatau — Indonesian for 'Child of Krakatoa' — first broke the surface from the drowned crater in late December 1927 and became a permanent, ever-growing island by 1930. Sources: VolcanoDB, 'Krakatoa Eruption'; Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'.

question: For months after Krakatoa's 1883 eruption, ash and sulphur high in the atmosphere turned sunsets blood-red around the world. One evening in New York, Poughkeepsie, and New Haven, the glow so alarmed residents that they did something startling. What did they do?
answer: Called out the fire brigades to fight the red sky itself
choices: Called out the fire brigades to fight the red sky itself
Crowded into the churches, fearing the world had ended
Fled inland, sure a great wildfire was sweeping in
Read the blood-red glow as an omen of coming war
context: The dust veil turned skies blood-red worldwide for months; fire brigades in New York, Poughkeepsie, and New Haven were called out to 'fires' that were only the red evening sky. The same veil cooled the Northern Hemisphere's summer by about 0.4°C the next year. Source: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'.  (Legend.)

question: The story did not end in 1883. From Krakatoa's drowned crater, a young volcano called Anak Krakatau had spent decades quietly rebuilding in the Sunda Strait. Then, in December 2018, with no warning at all, disaster returned to the strait. What did Anak Krakatau do that December night?
answer: Its flank slid into the sea, raising a sudden tsunami
choices: Its flank slid into the sea, raising a sudden tsunami
It buried the coast under a metre of scalding ash
It split open and drained the strait into itself
It flung molten rock all the way to Java
context: In December 2018 the flank of Anak Krakatau collapsed into the sea, triggering a sudden, warning-free tsunami along the Sunda Strait that killed 437 people, injured more than 14,000, and displaced tens of thousands — the child echoing its parent 135 years later. Source: VolcanoDB, 'Krakatoa Eruption'.

question: At the mouth of a limestone cave beneath Krakow's Wawel Hill, in southern Poland, sits a large bronze dragon. The Polish sculptor Bronislaw Chromy set it there in 1972 to honor the old Wawel Dragon legend of the city. Tourists crowd around and wait for the show, because every few minutes the bronze beast does something that makes them all jump. What does this Krakow dragon do?
answer: shoots a jet of real flame
choices: shoots a jet of real flame
puffs a cloud of cold mist
context: The bronze dragon was sculpted by Bronislaw Chromy and set at the cave mouth in 1972. A hidden gas nozzle lets it shoot a jet of real flame every few minutes, delighting the crowds below Wawel Castle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wawel_Dragon_(statue)

question: The bronze Wawel Dragon statue that guards a cave beneath Krakow's royal castle in Poland puffs out a real jet of flame all on its own every few minutes. But visitors who do not feel like waiting can trigger the fire themselves in one strange, modern way that would have astonished the sculptor when he made it in 1972. How can you make the Krakow dragon breathe fire on command?
choices: toss a coin in a slot
context: It's true -- a hidden system lets visitors send a text message (SMS) to a special number and make the dragon spit fire on command, on top of the automatic burst it gives every few minutes. Source: https://www.thevintagenews.com/2018/03/09/wawel-dragon/

question: The Dragon's Den under Krakow's Wawel Hill in southern Poland is not a dug-out tunnel. It is a real natural cave, a chain of underground rooms with about 80 metres of passage open to visitors beneath the royal castle. The hill above it is made of soft limestone. What slow natural process hollows out a cave like this in a hill of soft limestone?
choices: lava draining from a volcanic tube
a glacier grinding through the hillside
sea waves cutting into a cliff
context: Slightly acidic rainwater seeps into cracks and slowly dissolves soluble limestone, carving out caves, sinkholes and towers over thousands of years -- a landscape geographers call KARST. Wawel Hill is limestone, so the Dragon's Den (Smocza Jama) is a genuine karst cave; the whole thing runs about 270 m, with roughly 80 m open to visitors through three chambers. Legend put a fire-breathing dragon in it, but the cave itself is pure earth science. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smocza_Jama

question: Krakow's Rynek Glowny was laid out as the main market square of the Polish city in 1257, back when Krakow was the royal capital of Poland. Today the Renaissance Cloth Hall, the twin-towered St Mary's Basilica, and long rows of cafes still frame the same paved plaza. Among all the town squares of medieval Europe, what makes Krakow's Rynek Glowny stand out?
context: Rynek Glowny was laid out in 1257 under Magdeburg law, each side running more than 200 m (about 3.8 hectares) -- the largest medieval town square in Europe. Krakow's Old Town, square and all, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978, among the very first sites ever listed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Square,_Krak%C3%B3w

question: Long ago in Krakow, a city on Poland's Vistula River, a terrible dragon lived in a cave beneath Wawel Hill and ate the town's sheep and daughters. Knights in armor charged in with swords and lances, and none came back. Then a humble shoemaker's helper named Skuba stepped forward with a strange, quiet idea instead of a sword. What clever trap did Skuba set to kill the dragon?
choices: a pit lined with sharp stakes
a mirror to turn it to stone
context: In the popular version, Skuba stuffed a sheep with sulfur and left it outside the lair. The dragon gulped it down, and the burning sulfur gave it such a raging thirst that it drank from the Vistula River until it swelled up and burst. It's Krakow's best-loved legend -- the dragon is a story, but the Dragon's Den cave below Wawel is real. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wawel_Dragon

question: Chained above a doorway of Wawel Cathedral in Krakow hang three huge pale bones. They have hung there since at least the 1500s. People long called them the bones of the slain Wawel Dragon and said they kept the city safe. In 1937 a scholar from Jagiellonian University studied them. What did these 'dragon bones' turn out to be?
answer: a whale bone, a mammoth bone, a rhino bone
choices: a whale bone, a mammoth bone, a rhino bone
a whale bone, a walrus bone, a seal bone
a mammoth bone and two aurochs bones
context: A Jagiellonian University scholar identified the chained bones in 1937 as a whale bone, a mammoth bone and a rhinoceros bone -- Ice-Age and ocean giants, not a dragon. They have hung by the cathedral door since at least the 1500s, long believed to protect Krakow; one legend even warns that when the bones finally drop from their chain, the world will end. Source: https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/the-bones-of-the-wawel-dragon-krakow-poland

question: Every hour, high in the taller tower of St Mary's Basilica above Krakow's market square, a live trumpeter leans out over the city and plays a short bugle call known as the 'hejnal.' For centuries the tune has ended the same strange way -- the very thing that makes Poles find it unforgettable. How does the hejnal always end?
answer: it breaks off abruptly in mid-note
choices: it breaks off abruptly in mid-note
it fades into a slow drumbeat
it rises to a triumphant blast
context: The live hejnal stops abruptly in mid-phrase every hour. Oral tradition says it marks a medieval watchman shot in the throat by an arrow as he trumpeted a warning -- a legend, not documented history. The trumpeter plays it four times, once toward each compass direction, and Polish national radio has broadcast the noon call live every single day since 1927. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mary%27s_Trumpet_Call

question: When World War II ended, Warsaw and most Polish cities lay in bombed-out ruins, yet Krakow still stood with its great market square, its Cloth Hall and its Gothic churches almost untouched. One grim reason it was spared lay in what the German occupiers chose to make of the city. What did the Nazis use Krakow as?
answer: the capital of their occupation government
choices: the capital of their occupation government
a supply depot behind the front
a hospital city for the wounded
a prison camp for captured officers
context: The Nazis made Krakow the capital of the General Government, their occupation regime, and Governor-General Hans Frank ruled Poland from Wawel Castle itself. Because they meant to 'Germanize' the city rather than raze it, Krakow's medieval Old Town escaped the destruction that flattened Warsaw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krak%C3%B3w

question: Krakow's hourly trumpet call, the hejnal, famously breaks off mid-note, and nearly every guidebook says it honors a medieval watchman whose throat an arrow pierced as he blew his warning. Yet historians say this dramatic 'arrow' tale is no ancient memory at all, but the work of one modern writer. Where did the popular arrow legend actually come from?
context: The broken tune is genuinely old, but the arrow-in-the-throat backstory was popularized by American author Eric P. Kelly in his 1928 children's novel 'The Trumpeter of Krakow,' which won the Newbery Medal -- Kelly admitted he spoke little Polish. A romantic tale, not a medieval record. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mary%27s_Trumpet_Call  (Legend.)

question: In the north of Kyoto, Japan, a three-story wooden hall stands at the edge of a still pond in a quiet temple garden. Its two upper floors are wrapped in real gold leaf that glows in the afternoon sun. On a calm day, the whole gold building shows up again, upside down, mirrored perfectly in the water below. What is this famous golden Kyoto hall called?
context: This is Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion. The pond is called Kyoko-chi, 'Mirror Pond,' named for exactly this flawless reflection. Its sister temple, Ginkaku-ji, is the 'Silver Pavilion.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinkaku-ji

question: The Golden Pavilion that visitors photograph beside its pond in Kyoto, Japan today is actually a 1955 reconstruction. The original Kinkaku-ji hall had stood in the same spot since about 1397, but on one night in the summer of 1950 it was destroyed and reduced to ash. The event so shocked Japan that the novelist Yukio Mishima later wrote a famous book about it. How was the original Kinkaku-ji lost?
answer: A troubled young monk deliberately set it ablaze
choices: A troubled young monk deliberately set it ablaze
A lantern left burning caught the old timber
A summer lightning strike ignited its roof
A fire spread to it from the burning city
