context: The arsonist was Hayashi Yoken, a 22-year-old novice monk, who set the fire at 2:30 a.m. on 2 July 1950 and then tried to take his own life on the hill behind the temple; he died of tuberculosis in 1956. The shock ran so deep that the novelist Yukio Mishima built his 1956 novel, 'The Temple of the Golden Pavilion,' around him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinkaku-ji

question: Kyoto's Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion of Japan, looks from across its pond like one single shining hall. But its three stacked floors are each built in a completely different Japanese architectural style. The ground floor is styled as a Heian-era noble's palace. The middle floor is a samurai warrior's residence. The gold-covered top floor copies the style of what kind of building?
context: The three styles are shinden-zukuri (Heian aristocrat) on the bottom, buke-zukuri (samurai) in the middle, and a Chinese Zen hall on top, gilded gold both inside and out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinkaku-ji

question: At Fushimi Inari, the great Shinto shrine that climbs the wooded south hills of Kyoto, Japan, hundreds of stone animals stand guard among thousands of bright orange gates. They are the messengers of Inari, the Japanese god of rice and grain harvests. Many of these stone guardians are carved with a rice-store key held in their mouths. What animal are these Fushimi Inari statues?
context: The foxes are called kitsune, believed to carry Inari's messages; the key in their mouths opens the rice granary, since Inari is the god of rice and prosperity. Fushimi Inari, founded in 711 CE by the Hata clan, is the head of some 32,000 Inari shrines across Japan. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fushimi_Inari-taisha

question: About 10,000 vermilion torii gates tunnel up Fushimi Inari's sacred Mount Inari, and the rows keep lengthening year after year. Each gate was paid for by a single business or person, whose name is painted right down its back. Why did each of these donors put up their gate?
answer: In thanks for a wish the god had granted
choices: In thanks for a wish the god had granted
In hope of good fortune in the year ahead
In prayer for a bountiful rice harvest
In memory of a family member who had died
context: Every torii on Mount Inari was paid for by a business or a person as thanks for a wish the god had granted, with the donor's name painted down the back; the vermilion color is believed to ward off evil and promise a bountiful harvest, so the tunnels keep growing as new gates are donated. About 10,000 gates now climb the mountain, and the densest stretch, the Senbon Torii ('thousand torii'), holds roughly 800 by itself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fushimi_Inari-taisha ; gov-online.go.jp

question: At the foot of the Arashiyama hills west of Kyoto, a long wooden bridge has crossed the river on the same spot since the year 836. It carries the name Togetsukyo -- given, by tradition, after a retired emperor watched something one night. What did he see?
answer: The moon seemed to walk across it
choices: The moon seemed to walk across it
The sun set exactly beneath its arch
Cherry petals covered it like snow
Its lanterns doubled in the water
context: Togetsukyo means 'Moon-Crossing Bridge.' By tradition the name comes from a retired emperor who said the moon looked as though it were walking from one end to the other. A bridge has stood at this spot below Arashiyama since 836. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arashiyama

question: Kiyomizu-dera's wide porch juts thirteen meters — about four stories — out over a wooded hill. It rests on tall wood pillars, built without a single nail. 'To jump off the stage at Kiyomizu' became a Japanese saying for taking the plunge. In the Edo era, people really did leap from it. What did the records show about those who jumped?
choices: Only about 15 percent survived the fall
Fewer than half survived the fall
context: Records from the Edo period show that about 85 percent of those who leaped from the stage survived; the government banned the practice in 1872. The entire stage rests on its tall pillars without a single nail. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiyomizu-dera

question: In Kyoto's preserved Gion district in Japan, wooden teahouses line the lantern-lit Hanamikoji street, and at dusk geisha still slip between them in silk kimono. Kyoto has kept its own local words for these women: in Kyoto tradition a fully trained geisha is called a geiko, not a geisha. What is a young apprentice geisha called by that same Kyoto tradition?
context: In Kyoto a full geisha is a geiko and an apprentice is a maiko. Both entertain guests in the exclusive teahouses, called ochaya, along Gion's Hanamikoji street. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gion

question: A quiet two-kilometer stone path winds along a cherry-lined canal through east Kyoto. It is called Tetsugaku-no-michi, 'the Path of Philosophy.' It honors Nishida Kitaro, a famous modern Japanese thinker. He walked its full length in deep thought every morning on the way to work. Where was he headed?
context: Nishida Kitaro, one of Japan's most famous modern philosophers, was said to meditate along this canal on his daily walk to Kyoto University; the path took its name, Tetsugaku-no-michi, 'the Path of Philosophy,' from his habit. It runs from Ginkaku-ji, the Silver Pavilion, to Nanzen-ji temple. Source: japan-guide.com/e/e3906.html

question: In the Arashiyama grove west of Kyoto, timber bamboo grows so tall and dense that walking the paths feels like passing through a green cathedral. In 1996 Japan's Ministry of the Environment added the grove to a national list of 100 treasures worth preserving -- chosen not for a sight, but for something you can only hear. What did the list protect?
answer: The creak and hiss of wind through the bamboo
choices: The creak and hiss of wind through the bamboo
The birdsong echoing off the tall stalks
The temple bells drifting up the valley
The rush of the river below the grove
context: The 'Soundscapes of Japan,' one hundred sounds chosen by the Ministry of the Environment in 1996, are noises the nation judged worth protecting. Arashiyama earned its place for the eerie creaking and hissing of wind moving through its giant timber bamboo. Source: arashiyamabamboogrove.org

question: Kyoto, the old imperial capital of Japan, holds an astonishing number of historic treasures — roughly 1,600 Buddhist temples and 400 Shinto shrines packed inside the city and its wooded hills. In 1994 the United Nations cultural body UNESCO honored Kyoto by adding it to its World Heritage list. But UNESCO made an unusual choice about exactly what part of Kyoto to protect. What did it do?
answer: Grouped seventeen scattered sites into one listing
choices: Grouped seventeen scattered sites into one listing
Named the whole old city one protected zone
Chose its three greatest temples to represent all
Listed the imperial palace and its gardens alone
context: The listing, added in 1994, is called the 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto,' and it groups seventeen separate sites in and around the city into one World Heritage Site. Kyoto -- founded in 794 by Emperor Kanmu and Japan's capital until 1868 -- still holds roughly 1,600 Buddhist temples and about 400 Shinto shrines. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto

question: Kyoto came through World War II almost untouched, which is why its ancient temples still stand while cities like Tokyo and Osaka were rebuilt from ash. Yet in early 1945 Kyoto sat near the very top of the United States' list of atomic-bomb targets. Why did the city survive?
answer: A US official struck it from the target list to save its treasures
choices: A US official struck it from the target list to save its treasures
The US war secretary had once honeymooned there and loved it
Thick mountain fog hid the city from the bombers for months
Japan surrendered before Kyoto's turn ever came up
context: The US Secretary of War, Henry Stimson, personally had Kyoto removed from the atomic-target list, arguing the ancient capital was a treasure-house of Japanese art and religion; Nagasaki was added in its place. A popular story claims Stimson spared Kyoto because he had honeymooned there, but this is a legend: historian Alex Wellerstein has shown Stimson honeymooned in Canada in 1893 and first visited Kyoto only in the 1920s, as a government official. The real, documented reason was the city's cultural significance. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto ; blog.nuclearsecrecy.com

question: La Paz sits deep in an Andes canyon, while its twin city El Alto spreads across the plateau rim about 400 m higher. For years a single switchback road was the only link between them. In 2014 the city opened a transit line that cut the 90-minute climb to about 11 minutes. What kind of transit connects the canyon floor to the rim above?
context: The answer is Mi Teleférico ('My Cable Car'), opened in 2014 and now the backbone of La Paz-El Alto transit: gondola cabins gliding over the rooftops in place of the old switchback crawl, with a new cabin departing about every 12 seconds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mi_Teleférico; theworld.org (PRX), 2025.

question: Riding Mi Teleférico over La Paz feels like reading a big-city subway map. But the map hangs in the sky, and you switch between cable-car lines instead of trains. Its ten routes are labeled the same way many subway systems label theirs. How are Mi Teleférico's ten lines named?
context: Each line carries a color: Red, Yellow, Green, Blue, Orange, White, Sky Blue, Purple, Brown, and Silver -- a cable-car metro map painted across the Andean sky. The Silver Line (Línea Plateada), opening 9 March 2019, completed what Guinness World Records certified as the world's largest public-transit cable-car network. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mi_Teleférico; Guinness World Records.

question: In most cities the rich pay for the high ground and its wide views. Poorer families crowd the low streets. La Paz flips that map. The grandest homes sit down in the Zona Sur. Low-income families build higher up the canyon walls. What makes the low ground the prized place to live in La Paz?
answer: the air is warmer and richer in oxygen there
choices: the air is warmer and richer in oxygen there
the ocean is visible from the lower streets
the oldest colonial palaces stand down there
the river keeps the low ground green and cool
context: In La Paz, altitude -- not the skyline view -- is the luxury. The affluent Zona Sur lies around 3,250 m in warmer, more breathable air, while lower-income neighborhoods climb past 4,000 m up the canyon walls, the reverse of the usual class map. When Mi Teleférico's gondolas linked these long-separated districts, an anthropologist noted they connected neighborhoods the road network had effectively kept apart. (Bolivia is landlocked, so no ocean is anywhere in sight.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz; theworld.org (PRX), 2025.

question: Bolivia is the country geographers use to catch you out. Name its capital and you may be told you are wrong. High in an Andes canyon, La Paz is the city most travelers think is the capital. But quiz-masters say the honest answer is trickier. Why is Bolivia's capital so hard to pin to one city?
answer: its capital is split between two separate cities
choices: its capital is split between two separate cities
its capital was never fixed in the constitution
its capital changes with each new government
its capital rotates among several cities
context: Bolivia keeps two capitals. La Paz became the de-facto (administrative) capital in 1898 and holds the president and congress, the highest seat of government on Earth, while the constitutional capital remains Sucre, the lower colonial city that still houses the supreme court and the rest of the judiciary. Both cities are 'the capital,' each answering a different question -- a favorite geography footnote worth getting precisely right. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz.

question: El Alto Airport serves La Paz from a flat plain about 4,058 meters up. It is the highest major airport on Earth. The thin air holds so few oxygen bits that a jet's wings and engines have much less to grip as it speeds up. What does that thin air force every airliner leaving El Alto to do?
answer: roll much farther before lifting off
choices: roll much farther before lifting off
burn much less fuel on the way up
lift off at a much steeper angle
context: Thin air means less lift and less engine thrust, so jets need long takeoff rolls and often fly with reduced loads out of El Alto. The airport sits above El Alto itself, which at roughly 4,000-4,150 m and about 885,000 people (2024 census) ranks among the highest big cities in the world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Alto.

question: One snow-capped giant fills nearly every view in La Paz. Its three peaks glow 6,438 meters above the canyon. It is the emblem of the city, seen from streets all across town. This is Illimani, the tallest peak of the Cordillera Real. In the Andean tradition of the region, how is Illimani honored?
answer: as an apu, a mountain guardian spirit
choices: as an apu, a mountain guardian spirit
as a volcano that once buried the valley
as the source of the canyon's river
as the tomb of an ancient Inca ruler
context: In Andean belief an apu is the protective spirit of a sacred mountain, and Illimani is revered as the guardian watching over La Paz. Its first recorded ascent was in 1898 by the British climber William Martin Conway with Italian guides. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illimani.

question: About 10 km south of La Paz stands the Valle de la Luna, or 'Moon Valley.' It is a bone-white forest of clay spires so lunar-looking that local tales credit Neil Armstrong with naming it after his 1969 Moon landing. Geographers place it in the same landform family found across the Dakotas and the dry American West. Which landform is it?
context: Badlands form where soft, poorly cemented rock -- here clay and sandstone -- erodes fast into a labyrinth of spires and gullies (karst instead needs soluble limestone). The Neil Armstrong naming story is a popular local tradition, not documented fact. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valle_de_la_Luna_(Bolivia).

question: The thin air over La Paz and El Alto shapes everything: who lives high and who lives low, how hard a jet labors to climb out, and how fast newcomers fall ill with soroche -- the headaches and nausea of altitude sickness. Yet the drop in oxygen is not as extreme as the misery suggests. At about 3,600 m, roughly what share of sea-level oxygen does each breath still deliver?
context: At La Paz's altitude the air carries only about two-thirds of the oxygen available at sea level -- enough of a drop that unacclimatized visitors get soroche within 6-24 hours, yet high enough that millions live and work here for life. This single fact underlies the city's long takeoff rolls and its upside-down class map. Source: biologyinsights.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz.

question: In 1472, Portuguese sailors reached the coast of West Africa and found a settlement spread across low islands and creeks — not solid ground, but a watery maze where the ocean crept inland through shallows and pools. They gave the place a Portuguese name that stuck, and today it is the biggest city in Nigeria. What does 'Lagos' mean in Portuguese?
context: The explorer Rui de Sequeira reached the area in 1472 and called it 'Lago de Curamo' — and 'lagos' is simply Portuguese for lakes or lagoons. The city grew up on islands and sandbars threaded through a huge coastal lagoon, so the watery name fit perfectly. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lagos' and 'Ruy de Sequeira.'

question: An entire neighborhood of wooden houses stands on tall stilts above the Lagos Lagoon, with no dry land beneath them. Residents paddle canoes from door to door, and visitors nickname it 'the Venice of Africa.' What is this famous stilt district of Lagos called?
context: The stilt district is Makoko, sometimes called 'the Venice of Africa.' It is really six villages — four floating on the lagoon and two on land — home largely to the Egun people, who came from Badagry and neighbouring Benin, and who live mainly by fishing the lagoon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Makoko.'

question: The Yoruba are one of the largest peoples in Nigeria. Long before Portuguese sailors arrived in 1472 and gave the coastal city its new name — Lagos, meaning 'lakes and lagoons' — the Yoruba already had their own name for the place. In Yoruba homes and markets today, that older name is still the everyday word for the city. What do Yoruba speakers call Lagos?
context: Yoruba speakers call the city Èkó, a name older than the Portuguese 'Lagos.' Its exact meaning is debated — some say a farmstead or hamlet, others a Benin war-camp — but Èkó is still the everyday Yoruba name for Lagos today. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lagos'; Pulse.

question: An 11.8-kilometre bridge strides clear across the Lagos Lagoon on tall concrete piers, one of several great spans that thread sprawling Lagos together over its waters. When it opened in 1990 it was the longest bridge in all of Africa. What is this record-setting Lagos bridge called?
context: The Third Mainland Bridge runs 11.8 km (7.3 mi) across the Lagos Lagoon. When it opened in 1990 it was the longest bridge in Africa, holding that title until Cairo's 6th of October Bridge overtook it in 1996. Source: Wikipedia, 'Third Mainland Bridge'; Institution of Civil Engineers.

question: In 1991 Nigeria took the title of capital away from crowded, coastal Lagos and gave it instead to Abuja. What kind of city is Abuja?
answer: a planned capital, built from scratch in the country's centre
choices: a planned capital, built from scratch in the country's centre
an old walled emirate city, ruled for centuries by an emir
a colonial seaport, founded by British traders on the coast
an ancient Yoruba kingdom's royal capital in the southwest
context: Abuja is a planned city, built from scratch in Nigeria's centre, and the seat of government moved there on 12 December 1991. Yet Lagos kept the crown that matters most to daily life — it still generates roughly 30–35% of Nigeria's GDP and handles the large majority of the country's port trade. Source: Wikipedia, 'Abuja' and 'Lagos.'

question: Off the shore of Lagos, engineers are raising an entire new district on land reclaimed from the ocean, shielded by a colossal 8.5-km sea barrier nicknamed 'the Great Wall of Lagos.' While the lagoon's poorest families live out in stilt houses standing in the water, this gleaming district is being walled off from the sea instead. What is this new city-on-reclaimed-land called?
context: The reclaimed-land district is Eko Atlantic, rising off Victoria Island behind a sea wall of about 8.5 km nicknamed 'the Great Wall of Lagos.' The contrast is stark: while Makoko's families live out in the lagoon water, this luxury city is being walled off from the same sea. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eko Atlantic'; ekoatlantic.com.

question: In the old Pakistani city of Lahore, across a wide plaza from the Mughal Fort, the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb ordered a great mosque built out of deep red sandstone. It was raised in just two years and finished in 1673. For the next three hundred years, no larger mosque stood anywhere on Earth. What is this famous Lahore landmark called?
context: The Badshahi ('Imperial') Mosque was commissioned by the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb and built in just two years, 1671–1673. Its four octagonal corner minarets each rise 60 metres (196 feet), and worshippers climb 22 steps just to reach its main gate. It remained the largest mosque on Earth for over three centuries, until the late 20th century, and its construction was overseen by Aurangzeb's foster brother Fidai Khan Koka, then governor of Lahore. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badshahi_Mosque

question: Inside Lahore's Fort, emperor Shah Jahan built a small marble pavilion around 1631. Its walls and ceiling hold thousands of tiny mirrored tiles. Light one candle in the dark, and its flame breaks into countless points across the ceiling, like a private galaxy of stars. What is this dazzling hall called?
context: The Sheesh Mahal ('Palace of Mirrors', about 1631–32) was built for the emperor Shah Jahan. Its mirror-work is a craft called ainakari, in which thousands of tiny convex mirror-tiles multiply a single flame into countless points of light. A semi-octagonal marble pavilion, it is also inlaid with pietra dura — precious stones set into the white marble — and pierced screens called jali, and is often called 'the jewel in the crown' of Lahore Fort. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheesh_Mahal_(Lahore_Fort)

question: The main entrance to the Mughal Fort in Lahore, Pakistan is a towering gateway added by the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb in 1674. On either side of its high arch, two huge round brick towers rise up like giant fluted drums, guarding the way into the royal fort. What is this famous grand entrance called?
context: The Alamgiri Gate, the main entrance to Lahore Fort, was built by the emperor Aurangzeb in 1674 and is flanked by two huge semi-circular fluted bastions — one of the fort's most iconic faces. The fort as a whole holds 21 notable monuments spread across more than 20 hectares. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore_Fort

question: In Lahore, emperor Shah Jahan laid out a royal pleasure-garden that steps down the land in three great terraces, each about four to five metres above the next. He gave them poetic names meaning 'Bestower of Pleasure,' 'Bestower of Goodness,' and 'Bestower of Life.' What is this famous Lahore garden called?
context: Shah Jahan's Shalimar Gardens step down in three descending terraces — Farah Baksh (upper), Faiz Baksh (middle) and Hayat Baksh (lower) — completed in 1642 after only about 17 months of work, and threaded with some 410 fountains that spray into wide marble pools. They are laid out as a charbagh, a Persian 'four-part paradise garden' quartered by water channels to picture an earthly Eden. The Lahore Fort and the Shalimar Gardens were jointly inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shalimar_Gardens,_Lahore

question: After the Mughal empire crumbled, Lahore fell under Sikh rule in the early 1800s, and the vast marble courtyard of the Badshahi Mosque lost its sacred use. Its new masters put that enormous walled space to a rough, worldly purpose. What did the Sikh forces turn the great courtyard into?
context: After the Mughal empire declined, Lahore came under Sikh rule, and the vast courtyard of the Badshahi Mosque was used as a military stable while the surrounding cells (hujras) served as soldiers' quarters — a stark fall for what had been the largest mosque on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badshahi_Mosque

question: The hundreds of fountains and pools of Lahore's Shalimar Gardens demanded a constant flood of water, yet the garden sits on the dry Punjab plain far from any river. The Mughal noble Ali Mardan Khan solved it with one vast public work that carried water down from the distant foothills of Kashmir. What did he build to feed the gardens?
context: To feed the hundreds of fountains of the Shalimar Gardens, the Mughal noble Ali Mardan Khan had a canal dug roughly 100 miles (about 160 km) to bring water from the foothills of Kashmir down to the dry Lahore plain — an enormous public work built just to keep a paradise garden flowing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shalimar_Gardens,_Lahore

question: The outer face of Lahore's Fort — a wall about 440 metres long — is covered edge to edge in a glittering mosaic of glazed tile and painted fresco. It shows elephant fights, galloping camels, polo matches and painted angels. Among these real scenes, the fort's famous Picture Wall also shows a creature from Persian myth. Which mythical creature is worked in among the real animals?
context: The outer 'Picture Wall' of Lahore Fort runs about 440 metres (1,450 feet) long and up to 15 metres high, and is often called the largest mural in the world. Begun under the emperor Jahangir and decorated through the 1620s in glazed kashi-kari tile and fresco, it shows elephant fights, camels, horses, polo games and angels — and among them coil winged Persian dragons, a picture-book of Mughal court life laid across the fort's face. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore_Fort

question: In old Lahore stands what many call the most richly decorated mosque of the entire Mughal age — nearly every surface, inside and out, sheathed in glazed tile of cobalt, green, and gold. Remarkably, it was paid for not by an emperor but by a physician from Chiniot who rose to become the royal doctor and then governor of Punjab. What is this famously tiled mosque called?
context: The Wazir Khan Mosque (built 1634–1641) was paid for by Hakim Ilam-ud-din Ansari, a physician from Chiniot who rose to become the royal doctor and then governor of Punjab under the title 'Wazir Khan.' Nearly every surface, inside and out, is sheathed in kashi-kari faience tilework — cobalt blue, cerulean, white, green, orange, yellow, purple and red — with true-fresco painting; widely called 'the jewel of Lahore,' it is considered the most ornately decorated mosque of the entire Mughal era, its four minarets each rising about 107 feet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wazir_Khan_Mosque

question: In southern Siberia, in the far east of Russia, Lake Baikal curves for over 600 kilometres through an ancient split in the Earth's crust. It plunges more than a mile straight down at its middle — the deepest lake anywhere in the world. Because that trench is so long and so deep, Baikal holds far more water than anyone might guess from its size on a map. Among all the freshwater lakes on the planet, which record does this one lake hold?
answer: the largest freshwater lake by volume
choices: the largest freshwater lake by volume
the largest freshwater lake by area
the highest freshwater lake on Earth
the longest freshwater lake on Earth
context: By sheer volume Lake Baikal holds about 23,615 cubic kilometres of water — more than any other freshwater lake on Earth, and roughly a fifth of all the planet's unfrozen surface fresh water. Several lakes (Superior, the Caspian) spread across more surface area, but none matches Baikal's staggering depth-fed volume. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal.

question: Most lakes are only fleeting features of the landscape. They slowly fill up with mud and river silt and vanish within ten or twenty thousand years of forming. But Lake Baikal, a long crescent-shaped lake in southern Siberia, in Russia, has defied that fate on a scale that stuns geologists — outliving the vanishing of countless other lakes. Roughly how long has Lake Baikal held its water?
context: At an estimated 25 to 30 million years old, Baikal is by far the oldest lake in the world — most lakes fill with sediment and disappear within 10,000 to 20,000 years. Baikal has existed since long before modern humans, or even our ape ancestors, walked the Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal.

question: Drop a weighted line over the side of a boat on Lake Baikal in southern Siberia, Russia, and it just keeps going down. It plunges past the floor of every other lake on Earth into a deep rift valley in the crust that cuts far below the level of the sea. Roughly how deep does Baikal's deepest point actually lie?
context: Baikal's deepest point reaches 1,642 metres (5,387 feet) below the surface — the deepest lake on Earth, and deeper than four Eiffel Towers stacked end to end. Its floor lies well below sea level, cradled in one of the deepest continental rifts on the planet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal.

question: As many as 330 rivers and streams pour their water into Siberia's Lake Baikal, tumbling down from the surrounding mountains. Yet only a single river ever carries water back out of the lake, off toward the distant Arctic Ocean. Which river is that lone outlet?
context: As many as 330 rivers and streams flow into Baikal, but the Angara alone flows out, carrying the lake's water toward the Yenisei River and eventually the Arctic Ocean. In Buryat legend the Angara is Baikal's runaway daughter, fleeing to marry the Yenisei. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal.

question: Lake Baikal teems with life: some 2,600 kinds of animals crowd its waters, from freshwater sponges that grow in branching forests to snails and pale, deep-swimming fish. Biologists who study these creatures are struck by one astonishing fact about them. What is it?
answer: most of them live nowhere else on Earth
choices: most of them live nowhere else on Earth
most of them also live in the Arctic Ocean
most of them were carried in by human settlers
most of them die if the water ever freezes
context: About 80% of Baikal's roughly 2,600 known animal species live nowhere else on Earth — biologists call such one-place-only species 'endemic'. That staggering biodiversity, together with the lake's record age, depth and volume, earned Lake Baikal a place on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1996, where it is celebrated as the world's oldest and most voluminous freshwater lake. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal; yichuans.me/datasheet/output/site/lake-baikal (inscribed 1996).

question: Olkhon, the great island near the heart of Lake Baikal, is the spiritual centre of the Buryat people. At its Cape Burkhan, twin marble peaks drop straight into the water at a spot so sacred that shamans held their rites there and the Buryat long forbade ordinary people even to set foot. In Buryat belief, what is this rock?
answer: the home of the lake's guardian spirit
choices: the home of the lake's guardian spirit
the tomb of the first Buryat ruler
the gateway to the land of the dead
the anchor that steadies the island
context: Cape Burkhan, also called Shaman Rock, on Olkhon Island is among the holiest sites in Buryat shamanism, long held to be the dwelling of the lake's guardian spirit. Told here as belief, not settled fact. Source: msabelli.wordpress.com; pomexplores.com.  (Legend.)

question: Lake Baikal sits deep in southern Siberia, more than 1,700 kilometres from any sea. It is the world's oldest and deepest lake, and the animals inside it have been cut off from the ocean for millions of years. That long isolation gave Baikal a single, unlikely resident found in no other lake on Earth. What is it?
answer: it is the only lake with its own resident seal
choices: it is the only lake with its own resident seal
it is the only lake ringed by active volcanoes
it is the only lake with ocean-like tides
it is the only lake that drains into two seas
context: The nerpa (Pusa sibirica) is the world's only seal that lives entirely in fresh water, stranded some 1,700+ kilometres from the nearest ocean — probably cut off when Ice-Age meltwater rivers that once linked Baikal to the Arctic dried up. That makes Baikal the only lake on Earth with its own resident seal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikal_seal; biologyinsights.com.

question: In most very deep lakes, the water far below the surface is a dead, lifeless zone where almost nothing survives. Lake Baikal defies this rule — living creatures flourish more than a kilometre beneath its surface. What unusual property of Baikal's water makes such deep life possible?
answer: it stays rich in oxygen down to the very bottom
choices: it stays rich in oxygen down to the very bottom
it stays warm down to the very bottom
it carries no trace of salt at any depth
it is fed by warm underground springs
context: In most very deep lakes the bottom water is starved of oxygen and nearly lifeless, but Baikal stays rich in oxygen all the way down, so creatures thrive more than a kilometre below the surface. Scientists credit powerful seasonal mixing that carries oxygen into the depths. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal.

question: Lake Baikal rests in a slowly widening gap where the Eurasian and Amur plates pull apart. The basin gets about two centimetres wider each year. Geologists say that if this pulling continues for tens of millions of years, it could tear the continent in two. What do they predict Baikal itself will eventually become?
context: Baikal is a rift lake: it sits where the Eurasian and Amur plates are pulling apart, widening the basin by up to about two centimetres a year. Geologists say that if the spreading continues, the rift could one day split the continent and fill with sea — turning Baikal into a new ocean. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikal_Rift_Zone.

question: Every winter, Lake Baikal in Siberia freezes over into a solid sheet of clear ice. Starting in the 1990s, satellites began to spot strange dark circles several kilometres across appearing on that frozen surface — perfectly round rings that puzzled scientists for decades. Researchers finally traced the rings to something moving in the water far below. What forms these giant 'ice rings'?
answer: warm water eddies spinning beneath the ice
choices: warm water eddies spinning beneath the ice
cold currents sinking from the surface
hot springs venting from the lakebed
context: These dark 'ice rings', several kilometres across, form when warm eddies of water swirl beneath the frozen surface and thin the ice from below. First spotted from space, they baffled scientists for years before the hidden underwater eddies were identified. Source: livescience.com/ice-rings-lake-baikal.html.

question: When a fierce Siberian winter locks Lake Baikal in ice, the wind-driven waves freeze mid-surge and shatter into jagged, glass-clear shards that jut as high as twelve metres, heaped along the shore like a field of broken glass. These transparent ice shards are famous for glowing what colour?
context: In a hard freeze, wind-driven waves lock into jagged, transparent 'hummocks' that can rear several metres high — the tallest to around twelve — and glow an unearthly turquoise where light passes through the clear ice. Source: mymodernmet.com/lake-baikal-russia-ice-hummocks.

question: On Lake Baikal's deep bed, plants rot and give off a gas that streams upward toward the surface. When the rising bubbles meet the underside of the winter ice, they freeze in place as stacks of pearly white discs, hanging in the crystal-clear ice like frozen strings of pearls. What gas is trapped in these frozen columns?
context: Methane released by plants rotting on the deep lakebed rises in bubbles that freeze against the underside of the ice, stacking into pearly white discs you can look straight down into. Source: apod.nasa.gov/apod/ap181218.html (Methane Bubbles Frozen in Lake Baikal).

question: Lake Natron is a shallow 'soda lake' on the floor of the East African Rift in northern Tanzania, where the water is so hot and caustic that almost nothing can live in it. Yet the whole lake glows a deep red and orange — bright enough that astronauts have picked it out from orbit. What gives this scalding, harsh lake its striking blood-red color?
answer: Salt-loving microbes whose red pigment dyes the water
choices: Iron-rich minerals dissolved out of the red desert rock
Salt-loving microbes whose red pigment dyes the water
Fine red dust blown in off the surrounding desert
Red soda crystals that crust the shallow lakebed
context: The red is alive, not a mineral: halophilic (salt-loving) cyanobacteria pack the scalding brine, and their red photosynthetic pigment dyes the whole lake. A 'soda lake' is one saturated with dissolved sodium carbonate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Natron ('The red accessory photosynthesizing pigment in the cyanobacteria produces the deep reds').

question: The salt caked thick along the shores of Lake Natron in Tanzania is called natron — mostly sodium carbonate, a chalky white salt that dries out anything it touches. Thousands of years ago and thousands of kilometres to the north, the ancient Egyptians harvested this exact same salt from lakes in their desert for one famous purpose. What did they use natron for?
answer: To dry out and preserve the dead as mummies
choices: To flavour and preserve their stored food
To make the blue glaze on temple tiles
To dry out and preserve the dead as mummies
To tan animal hides into leather
context: Natron -- sodium carbonate -- is the very salt ancient Egyptians packed around bodies to dry them out for mummification; Lake Natron is essentially a whole lake of embalming salt. Source: Smithsonian, 'Flamingos Find Life Among Death' ('a chemical once used in Egyptian mummification'); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natron.

question: Wade into most lakes and nothing happens. Wade into Lake Natron and the scalding water can burn your skin and eyes -- it is packed with dissolved soda and heats to around 60 C. Chemically, Natron's water is a natural version of which harsh household substance?
answer: Lye, the caustic cleaner that unclogs drains
choices: Lye, the caustic cleaner that unclogs drains
Bleach, the cleaner that whitens laundry
Ammonia, the cleaner that washes windows
Baking soda, the powder that raises cakes
context: Natron's water is a natural lye, loaded with sodium carbonate and trona; its pH sits near 10.5 and can spike above 12 in the dry season, while temperatures reach about 40 C and can approach 60 C -- caustic enough to burn skin and eyes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Natron (pH 'can reach greater than 12'; highs near 60 C).

question: Photographer Nick Brandt's haunting images show birds and bats from Lake Natron looking like blackened stone statues. Those pictures fed a viral story that the lake instantly turns animals to stone on contact. What is actually happening to these creatures?
answer: The soda slowly coats creatures that had already died
choices: The caustic water petrifies them the instant they touch it
Minerals seep in and replace their bones with rock
The fierce heat bakes them into hardened clay shells
The soda slowly coats creatures that had already died
context: The 'turns animals to stone' story is sensationalized: the soda does not petrify the living on contact -- it slowly encrusts animals that have ALREADY died, sealing them in a hard soda-salt crust like natural mummies. Nick Brandt found and posed calcified birds and bats for his book 'Across the Ravaged Land.' Source: Smithsonian; NBC News, 'Lake That Turns Animals to Stone? Not Quite.'  (Legend.)

question: Lake Natron is the single most important nursery on Earth for the lesser flamingo -- up to 2.5 million of them, most of the world's population, hatch on low soda-crust islands far out in the lake. Foxes and jackals prowl the shore but almost never reach the nests. What keeps the predators away?
answer: A moat of scalding, caustic soda-water they will not cross
choices: Massed adult flamingos forming a wall around the chicks
A moat of scalding, caustic soda-water they will not cross
Tall mud nest-mounds too steep for a predator to climb
Parent birds carrying the chicks to safety each night
context: Natron hosts about 2.5 million lesser flamingos -- some 75% of the world population -- the most important breeding site on Earth for the species. The caustic water and the ring of scalding soda around the seasonal evaporite islands form a moat no fox or jackal will cross, so the nests are almost untouchable: the lake defends its own nursery. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Natron ('Its caustic environment is a barrier against predators'); Smithsonian.

question: South of Lake Natron rises Ol Doinyo Lengai, the Maasai 'Mountain of God' and the only volcano on Earth that erupts carbonatite lava -- so cool, at barely 500 C, that it flows out jet black instead of glowing red. Stranger still is what becomes of that black lava within hours of hardening on the slopes. What happens to it?
answer: It weathers to white powder that feeds the lake below
choices: It shatters into black glass all across the slopes
It slowly reheats from within and glows dull red
It weathers to white powder that feeds the lake below
It hardens into rock that never wears away
context: Ol Doinyo Lengai (Maasai for 'Mountain of God'), about 15 km south of the lake and 2,962 m tall, is the only active volcano erupting carbonatite (natrocarbonatite) lava. Because it is only about 500-600 C -- roughly half the heat of ordinary lava -- it pours out jet black, then within hours absorbs moisture from the air and weathers to white soda powder that rain washes downhill to feed Lake Natron its strange chemistry. Source: volcanosatlas.com/volcano/lengai-ol-doinyo; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natrocarbonatite.

question: On the night of 21 August 1986, everyone in the valleys below Lake Nyos -- a quiet crater lake in the volcanic highlands of Cameroon -- lay down to sleep and never woke. In a single night 1,746 people and thousands of cattle died, yet on the bodies there was no wound, no flood, and no fire. Something had welled silently up out of the lake and settled over the villages while they slept. What invisible thing came up out of the lake?
context: The killer was ordinary carbon dioxide (CO2) -- not a poison-gas attack, just invisible CO2 in a deadly amount. Because CO2 is about 50% denser than air, the cloud hugged the ground, rolled downhill, and pooled in the valleys, smothering every breathing thing within about 25 km (16 miles) of the lake. One survivor, Joseph Nkwain, woke unable to move or speak to find his family had died in the night. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nyos_disaster; Britannica 'Lake Nyos disaster.'

question: For decades, volcanic gas seeps up from the magma far beneath Lake Nyos and dissolves into the cold, pressurized water at the very bottom, where the lake's layers never mix. The trapped gas builds and builds until, one night, a disturbance lets it all rush out at once -- like popping the cap on a shaken soda bottle. Geologists have a special name for this rare event, a lake bursting with its own pent-up gas. What is it called?
context: A limnic eruption -- from limne, Greek for lake. Volcanic CO2 dissolves into the deep water under pressure and, because the lake never fully overturns, it builds up for years until a disturbance tips the water past its limit and the gas fizzes out all at once. Scientists still aren't sure what set Nyos off -- the leading guesses are an underwater landslide or a spell of cold rain that suddenly mixed the layers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nyos_disaster; Britannica 'Lake Nyos disaster.'

question: After the Lake Nyos disaster, engineers had to make the lake safe before the deadly gas could build up again. Their fix, first installed in 2001, is a long pipe sunk straight down into the deep water. Once someone gives it a start, the pipe shoots a tall fountain of water high into the air -- and then keeps fountaining for years, all on its own, with no pump. What keeps that fountain rising by itself?
answer: the carbon dioxide bubbling out of the rising water
choices: the carbon dioxide bubbling out of the rising water
the heat of magma boiling the water from below
the inflow of mountain rivers feeding the lake
the wind funneling down the crater walls
context: As the deep water rises, the drop in pressure lets its dissolved gas fizz out of solution; the bubbles make the column lighter than the water around it, so it accelerates upward -- a self-powered 'gas lift,' exactly like a shaken soda bottle erupting the moment you open it. The first degassing pipe went in in 2001, with two more added in 2011. Only three lakes on Earth are known to be able to erupt this way -- Nyos and Monoun in Cameroon, and giant Lake Kivu on the Rwanda-Congo border, where about two million people live around the shores. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nyos_disaster; eos.org/science-updates/cameroons-lake-nyos-gas-burst-30-years-later.

question: Lake Superior sits at the top of North America's five Great Lakes, along the wild border where the northern United States meets Canada. It is so vast that standing on one shore you cannot see across to the other side. Of all the freshwater lakes on Earth, what world record does Superior hold?
choices: the largest by total volume of water
context: Lake Superior covers about 82,100 km2 (31,700 sq mi) along the US-Canada border -- more surface than any other freshwater lake on Earth. It is largest by AREA; by sheer volume of water it ranks only third in the world, behind Siberia's Lake Baikal and Africa's Lake Tanganyika. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Superior; lakesuperior.com.

question: The five Great Lakes — Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario — lie between the United States and Canada. Together they form the biggest system of freshwater lakes on Earth. If you scooped up every drop of fresh water sitting on the planet's surface — every lake, river, and pond — the Great Lakes alone would hold a huge share of it. About how much of Earth's surface fresh water do these five lakes hold together?
context: The five Great Lakes -- Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario -- together hold roughly 21%, about one-fifth, of all the fresh water on Earth's surface (some six quadrillion gallons). Source: css.umich.edu Great Lakes factsheet; US EPA / NOAA.

question: Lake Superior is the largest of the Great Lakes by surface area. Yet one lake on the far side of the world holds even more water than Superior, and it plunges more than 1,600 metres down to its floor, deeper than any other lake on Earth. Which lake out-holds even mighty Superior?
context: The lake is Siberia's Lake Baikal -- the deepest lake on Earth at about 1,642 m (5,387 ft) and the largest of all by volume, holding more liquid fresh water than any other lake. Superior is the largest freshwater lake by surface AREA but only third by volume, behind Baikal and Lake Tanganyika. Africa's Tanganyika is the world's longest freshwater lake (~410 miles), and Lake Victoria is the largest tropical lake. Source: worldatlas.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Superior.

question: Lake Superior, the largest of North America's Great Lakes, has swallowed hundreds of ships in storms over the centuries. Sailors have long said that Superior 'never gives up its dead' — the drowned from its wrecks are almost never found floating back to the surface. What property of Superior's deep water best explains this eerie fact?
answer: it stays near-freezing, about 4 C, the year round
choices: it stays near-freezing, about 4 C, the year round
it is far deeper than a body could ever rise from
its currents drag the drowned out toward the middle
it is unusually heavy with dissolved minerals
context: Below about 200 m (110 fathoms), Superior stays a constant ~4 C (39 F) all year. That cold slows decay and the buildup of gases that would normally refloat a drowned body, so shipwreck victims tend to stay on the bottom -- the origin of the sailors' saying that Superior 'never gives up its dead.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Superior.  (Legend.)

question: Lake Superior is famous for the 'Gales of November' -- ferocious autumn storms that sink ships. In November 1913, one such storm battered the Great Lakes for days with 90-mph winds and 35-foot waves, sinking a dozen ships and killing up to 250 people. What sets off these sudden November monsters?
answer: cold Canadian air crashing into warm, moist Gulf air
choices: cold Canadian air crashing into warm, moist Gulf air
the warm lake itself feeding the storm like an ocean
leftover tropical hurricanes tracking up from the Gulf
a jet stream buckling far south out of the Arctic
context: The fierce autumn 'Gales of November' form when cold Canadian air slams into warm, moist air drawn up from the Gulf. The Great Storm of 1913 -- the 'Big Blow' or 'Freshwater Fury' -- battered the lakes for days with ~90 mph gusts and 35-foot waves, sinking 12 ships and killing up to about 250 people. Source: canr.msu.edu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_Storm_of_1913.

question: The five Great Lakes of North America — Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario — look ancient and eternal on a map. Yet as lakes they are astonishingly young: their basins only took their present shape about 10,000 years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age. What carved these enormous hollows out of solid North American bedrock?
context: During the last Ice Age, ice sheets more than a mile thick crept south across North America, scraping and gouging the bedrock -- a process geologists call GLACIAL SCOURING -- to carve the five Great Lakes' basins. Meltwater filled them to roughly their present form only about 10,000 years ago, making these giant lakes geological newborns. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Superior; USGS Great Lakes.

question: Around Lake Superior, the land itself is still slowly rising -- because for tens of thousands of years, ice more than a mile thick pressed the crust down, and only recently melted away. The land rises unevenly, its north shore lifting faster than the south and gently tilting the lake's water southward. What do geologists call this slow rise of crust freed from a great weight of ice?
context: Freed of the mile-thick ice that once pressed it down, the crust is slowly springing back up -- a process called glacial isostatic adjustment, or ISOSTATIC REBOUND. Around Superior the north rises faster than the south (Michipicoten Island rises about 35 cm per century faster than Marquette, Michigan), slowly tilting the lake's water toward its southern shore. Source: ijc.org; medium.com/the-environment.

question: Along Lake Superior's north shore and its wild Isle Royale, the rock is dark basalt about 1.1 billion years old. It formed when North America itself began to tear apart along a 3,000-km crack, flooding the gash with lava -- until the tearing mysteriously stopped and the continent stayed whole. What is this ancient failed split beneath Lake Superior called?
context: Superior's north shore and Isle Royale rest on 1.1-billion-year-old flood basalt of the MIDCONTINENT RIFT -- a roughly 3,000-km buried scar where the North American continent began to tear apart, then stopped. Lava filled the crack, and its copper-rich veins later made Michigan's Keweenaw Peninsula a legendary copper-mining district. Source: livescience.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midcontinent_Rift_System.

question: Lake Tanganyika threads down eastern Africa as a thin blue ribbon of water, forming a shared border between four countries — Tanzania, Burundi, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Zambia. It runs about 673 kilometres from tip to tip, yet is never more than 70 kilometres across. Among all the world's freshwater lakes, what record does its long, narrow shape earn it?
choices: the world's largest freshwater lake by area
context: Lake Tanganyika is the world's longest freshwater lake -- 673 km (418 miles) end to end but only 16-72 km wide, a thin ribbon threaded down the East African Rift Valley. Baikal (636 km) is deeper and older, and Superior is larger by area, but for sheer length Tanganyika wins. Source: guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/497936-longest-lake.

question: Most of Earth's fresh water is frozen in ice caps or buried deep underground. Only a thin slice is liquid and within reach at the surface. Astonishingly, one single African lake — Tanganyika — holds a huge chunk of all that reachable fresh water. About how much of the world's liquid surface fresh water sits in this one lake?
context: This single African lake holds about 16% -- roughly one-sixth -- of all the world's available (liquid, surface) fresh water. Because most of Earth's fresh water is frozen in ice caps or locked underground, the reachable share is small, so a sixth of it sitting in one lake is astonishing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika.

question: The floor of Lake Tanganyika in East Africa plunges to roughly 1,470 metres below the surface — a freshwater abyss so deep the cold, black bottom sits well below the level of the distant Indian Ocean. On all of Earth, only one lake sinks deeper than Tanganyika. Which lake is it?
context: Tanganyika's floor lies about 1,470 m (~4,800 ft) down, making it the world's second-deepest lake. Only Lake Baikal in Siberia goes deeper -- past 1,600 m. Malawi, Superior, and Victoria are all far shallower. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika; guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/497936-longest-lake.

question: A lake is usually a fleeting feature on Earth's map. A glacier gouges out a hollow or a river shifts its course, and within a few thousand years silt and reeds choke the basin. Lake Tanganyika, along the East African Rift, has utterly defied that fate. About how long has this remarkable lake's basin held water?
context: Lake Tanganyika is one of the oldest lakes on Earth -- its central basin began forming roughly 9-12 million years ago, when most of today's lakes did not yet exist. Ordinary lakes silt up and vanish within a few thousand years, but Tanganyika has endured for millions. Only a handful of lakes, such as Siberia's Lake Baikal, are older still. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika.

question: Lake Tanganyika lies along the East African Rift. This is a huge crack in the crust where the continent is slowly pulling apart, a few millimetres wider every year. Studying this ever-widening crack, geologists make a bold prediction about the deep future of the lake. What do they expect will eventually become of it?
answer: it will flood and grow into a whole new ocean
choices: it will flood and grow into a whole new ocean
it will erupt into a long chain of volcanoes
it will crack apart into many smaller lakes
it will sink into the deepest dry basin on land
context: Tanganyika sits in the Albertine Rift, the western branch of the East African Rift, where the continent splits a few millimeters a year -- so it is a 'rift lake' (like Baikal). Geologists expect the rift to keep widening until the sea floods in and a new ocean is born, cleaving off the eastern 'Somali' piece of Africa, much as the Red Sea once opened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika.

question: Near its sunlit surface Lake Tanganyika teems with life -- more than 250 kinds of colorful cichlid fish found nowhere else on Earth. Yet most of the lake by volume, everything below about 100 m, is a black realm where almost nothing lives at all. What makes the vast deep of Tanganyika a lifeless zone?
answer: the deep water holds no oxygen at all
choices: the deep water holds no oxygen at all
the deep water stays frozen the year round
the deep water is far too salty for life
the deep water is boiling hot near the bed
context: Tanganyika is 'meromictic': its layers almost never turn over (flushing time up to ~7,000 years). Below about 100 m the water holds no oxygen and is rich in toxic hydrogen sulfide, so life -- including its 250+ endemic cichlid species -- crowds the thin sunlit top while the huge, still deep lies dark and dead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika; lakepedia.com/lake/tanganyika.html.

question: High in the Andes mountains of South America, on the border between Peru and Bolivia, sits Lake Titicaca. Its shore rests about 3,812 metres above sea level — high enough to stand level with many mountain peaks in other parts of the world. Yet even here, thin air and all, working steamboats and ferries still cross its waters carrying passengers and goods between Peruvian and Bolivian ports. Among all the world's lakes, what is Titicaca's claim to fame?
choices: the world's highest lake of any kind
context: Higher lakes and even ponds dot the Andes and Himalaya, but no full-size boats sail them -- so geographers use the careful phrase 'highest navigable.' Titicaca's steamers and cargo boats work a lake set higher than many mountain peaks. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Titicaca; britannica.com/place/Lake-Titicaca.

question: Out on the open water of Lake Titicaca, the Uros people build the very ground they stand on: some 60 islands, home to about 1,200 people, that actually float on the lake. When the bottom layer rots, they lay fresh material on top. They can even pole a whole island to a new location. What do the Uros weave the islands, their houses, and their boats all from?
context: Totora is a tall reed that grows thick in Titicaca's shallows. From this one plant the roughly 1,200 Uros make the island underfoot, the thatched house, and the curved boat with its animal-head prow -- ground, home, and craft from a single reed. Sources: smithsonianmag.com/travel/people-peru-live-manmade-islands-constructed-plants-180956218/; britannica.com/plant/totora.

question: Bolivia has no seacoast at all, yet it keeps thousands of sailors and a fleet of boats, based high in the Andes on Lake Titicaca. The country has drilled this navy for more than a hundred years. What does Bolivia dream its mountain-lake navy will someday accomplish?
answer: reach the open ocean from a coastline won back
choices: reach the open ocean from a coastline won back
carry an expedition down the Amazon to the Atlantic
patrol the lake frontier it shares with Peru
join a combined South American fleet at sea
context: Bolivia lost its Pacific coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879) and has been landlocked ever since. Its navy trains on Titicaca and the country still marks a yearly 'Day of the Sea,' keeping alive the hope of one day sailing from its own shore. Sources: observers.france24.com/en/20091126-Bolivia-landlocked-sea-navy-Chile-war-Pacific-ocean; britannica.com/place/Lake-Titicaca.

question: Lake Titicaca holds a huge amount of water, yet almost none of it ever reaches the ocean. A single slow river, the Desaguadero, trickles south into small Lake Poopo. It carries off barely a tenth of the lake's water. So where does the other ninety percent of Titicaca's water go?
answer: it evaporates into the thin, sun-blasted mountain air
choices: it evaporates into the thin, sun-blasted mountain air
it seeps down into deep underground caverns
it freezes into glaciers along the frozen shore
it soaks away into the surrounding Altiplano marshes
context: A lake with no real outlet is called endorheic, or closed-basin. Titicaca's only drain, the Desaguadero River, carries off about 10% of its water to small Lake Poopo; the other ~90% evaporates under the fierce high-altitude sun and wind. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Titicaca.

question: Divers exploring the bed of Lake Titicaca have brought up sealed stone boxes that were lowered into the water as offerings to the gods some five centuries ago. Cracking one open, archaeologists found its gift perfectly preserved. What lay sealed inside these sacred stone boxes?
answer: a tiny llama figurine carved from spiny-oyster shell
choices: a tiny llama figurine carved from spiny-oyster shell
a clay tablet inscribed with an unknown script
the bones of a condor wrapped in fine cloth
a string of knotted cords that recorded tribute
context: Underwater archaeologists have raised more than a dozen sealed stone boxes from Titicaca's bed. One recovered intact held a tiny llama carved from Spondylus (spiny-oyster) shell -- hauled some 2,000 km from Ecuador -- beside a rolled sheet of gold, sunk about 500 years ago as a gift to the gods. Sources: sciencealert.com/an-ancient-llama-encased-in-stone-and-sunk-underwater-was-likely-a-gift-to-inca-gods; livescience.com/65126-lake-titicaca-offerings.html.

question: To the Inca, Lake Titicaca was the most sacred water in the world -- the place where creation began. In their accounts, the creator god Viracocha rose from the lake and called forth the sun, and from these same waters came Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo. According to Inca belief, who were Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo?
answer: the first Inca, sent to found their people
choices: the first Inca, sent to found their people
two mountain spirits who guard the lake's depths
the twin children of the moon and morning star
the priests who first built temples on the shore
context: In Inca belief, the creator Viracocha rose from Titicaca and made the sun, and the first Inca -- Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo -- emerged from its waters to found their people at Cusco. It is told as sacred origin, not history. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isla_del_Sol; chacanacenter.com/post/lake-titicaca-isla-del-sol.  (Legend.)

question: At 3,812 m, the Altiplano around Lake Titicaca is so cold that little grows on the open plateau -- yet farmers raise potatoes, quinoa, and llamas in a mild belt right along the lakeshore. How does the presence of the huge lake let crops thrive on its shore where the bare plateau cannot?
answer: it soaks up the day's heat and releases it at night
choices: it soaks up the day's heat and releases it at night
it shelters the shore fields from the cutting plateau wind
it floods the shore each year with fertile mountain silt
it wraps the shore in mist that blocks night frost
context: The huge lake is a thermal buffer: it soaks up the day's intense sun and slowly releases that heat at night, warming a narrow shore belt enough to grow potatoes and quinoa and graze llamas where the frost-bitten Altiplano cannot. (The thin air here also holds about a third less oxygen than at sea level.) Sources: swallowsnotes.com/blog/lake-titicaca-and-high-altitude-geography; internationalparks.org/peru/Titicaca.

question: In East Africa, Lake Victoria stretches across the shared borders of Tanzania, Uganda, and Kenya. It is a freshwater sea nearly as big as the whole island of Ireland — about 60,000 square kilometres of open water dotted with fishing villages. It also happens to sit almost exactly on the equator, so it never leaves the tropics. Among all the world's lakes, what record does Lake Victoria truly hold?
answer: the largest tropical lake in the world
choices: the largest tropical lake in the world
the largest freshwater lake in the world
the deepest lake in the world
the oldest lake in the world
context: Lake Victoria covers about 59,947 km2 -- the largest lake in Africa and the largest tropical lake on Earth. But by surface area it is only the world's SECOND-largest freshwater lake; North America's Lake Superior is bigger. So 'largest tropical' and 'largest in Africa' are true, while 'largest freshwater' belongs to Superior. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria

question: Baikal drops more than 1,600 metres down, and Tanganyika nearly 1,470. The world's great lakes are famous for their depths. Lake Victoria covers an area the size of Ireland, yet breaks that pattern. Across most of that huge expanse, how deep is Victoria on average?
context: Victoria averages only about 40 m deep, with a maximum around 80-84 m -- astonishingly shallow for a lake the size of Ireland. Rift lakes like Tanganyika (~1,470 m) and Baikal (~1,600 m) sit in deep tectonic cracks; Victoria instead spreads thin across a broad, gently dished basin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria

question: The Nile, the longest river on Earth, does not simply appear in the Egyptian desert. It is born far to the south, where Lake Victoria spills over a cataract and rushes north on its roughly 6,600 km journey to the Mediterranean. At which lakeside town does the Nile begin its journey?
context: The White Nile spills out of Lake Victoria at Jinja, Uganda -- historically at Ripon Falls, now drowned beneath the Nalubaale Dam -- and flows some 6,650 km to the Mediterranean, the longest river on Earth. Its other great branch, the Blue Nile, begins far away at Lake Tana in Ethiopia. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria

question: Victoria's deep neighbours, Lakes Tanganyika and Malawi, lie inside the Great Rift Valley, in giant cracks where the African continent is slowly splitting apart. But Lake Victoria sits on stable old rock BETWEEN the rift's two arms. How did its broad, saucer-shaped basin form?
answer: the land slowly warped and tilted, ponding rivers backward
choices: the land slowly warped and tilted, ponding rivers backward
a giant meteorite blasted the hollow out on impact
a huge volcano collapsed into a circular crater
an ice-age glacier scooped the basin out
context: Victoria sits on the stable ancient (Precambrian) shelf BETWEEN the Eastern and Western arms of the Great Rift Valley. As the plateau slowly tilted and back-warped, west-flowing rivers were ponded backward into a broad, shallow hollow -- a down-warped basin, not a rift crack. That is why it is so wide yet so shallow. Source: wldb.ilec.or.jp/Display/html/3586

question: Drilling deep into the floor of Lake Victoria, geologists read the layered sediments. They concluded that at least three times in its past, this enormous lake has done something almost unimaginable for so vast a body of water. The most recent was about 15,000 years ago. What had actually happened?
answer: it dried up completely, its bed becoming dry land
choices: it dried up completely, its bed becoming dry land
it froze solid all the way to the bottom
it split apart into several separate lakes
it turned as salty as the ocean
context: Sediment cores suggest Lake Victoria has dried out completely at least three times, most recently drying up around 17,300 years ago and refilling about 14,700 years ago -- so the lake on today's bed is only a few thousand years old. Being so shallow makes it easy to lose in a long drought. (Framed as geologists' reconstruction; confidence is moderate.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria  (Legend.)

question: Lake Victoria is one of the most lightning-struck places on Earth, and the Red Cross estimates that 3,000 to 5,000 fishermen drown on it every year. Its storms keep an eerie daily schedule: thunderheads pile up over the surrounding land by afternoon, then unleash their full fury out over the open water in the dead of night. What flips the storms out onto the lake after dark?
answer: the cooling land and still-warm lake pull the night winds together over the water
choices: the cooling land and still-warm lake pull the night winds together over the water
cold winds pour down off the surrounding highlands onto the lake at night
the moon's night-time pull drags the lake's humid air upward into storms
the lake vents warm gases after dark that spark the towering thunderheads
context: By day, thunderstorms build over the warm land around Victoria. At night the land cools but the lake holds its heat, so converging night winds drive the storms out over the water -- making Victoria one of the most thunderstorm- and lightning-active places on Earth, with the northern lake seeing storms 200-plus days a year. The Red Cross estimates 3,000-5,000 fishermen die here annually in the sudden waves. Source: science.nasa.gov (NASA Earth Observatory); nature.com/articles/ncomms12786

question: In June 1783, southern Iceland did not grow a new mountain -- the ground simply split. Along a 25-kilometre crack called Lakagigar, red lava fountained up from more than 130 separate vents at once, all in a line. Geologists have a special name for an eruption like Laki's. What is it?
context: Laki's fissure -- Lakagigar, 'the craters of Laki' -- is a 25-km line of more than 130 vents that opened on 8 June 1783. A fissure eruption feeds lava up through a long crack in the crust instead of a single central cone, and Laki poured out one of the greatest lava floods in recorded history, roughly 14 cubic kilometres of basalt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki

question: Most eruptions people picture are quick and violent: a mountain blows its top and falls quiet within days. Laki, the great crack that tore open across southern Iceland in 1783, was different. It welled up quietly and simply kept flowing. Roughly how long did Laki pour out lava before it finally stopped?
context: Laki opened on 8 June 1783 and did not stop until 7 February 1784 -- about eight months of near-continuous lava. Icelanders call the disaster the Skaftareldar, the 'Skafta Fires,' after the river valley the lava buried. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki

question: Laki's lava burned only a handful of farms, yet within two years about four out of every five sheep in Iceland were dead. The animals were not killed by the fire itself, but by something the eruption spread across the pastures where they grazed. What killed the sheep?
answer: fluorine gas that settled on the grass
choices: fluorine gas that settled on the grass
volcanic ash that buried the grass
glacier floodwater that drowned the grass
freezing frost that killed the grass
context: About 8 million tonnes of fluorine drifted down onto Iceland's grass. Sheep that grazed it died of fluorosis -- brittle bones and swollen joints -- and roughly 80% of the island's sheep (about 190,000 animals) perished, along with about half its cattle and half its horses. The killer was the gas, not the lava. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki

question: With most of Iceland's sheep, cattle, and horses dead, the people had almost nothing left to eat. The famine that followed Laki -- remembered as the Modhuhardindin, the 'Mist Hardships' -- swept the whole island. Roughly what share of Iceland's entire population did it kill?
choices: about one person in a hundred
context: The Modhuhardindin, the 'Mist Hardships,' killed roughly a fifth of everyone in Iceland -- about 20% of the population -- by 1785. Through poison gas and famine, a crack in the ground had come close to starving an entire nation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki

question: The summer of 1783 turned strange across much of the world. A pale bluish haze -- a 'dry fog' -- hung over Europe and part of North America, so thick it dimmed the sun. The American statesman Benjamin Franklin puzzled over it, writing that the sun's rays were so weak 'they would scarce kindle brown paper.' Where had this vast fog actually come from?
answer: sulfur gas carried south from Iceland
choices: sulfur gas carried south from Iceland
smoke from vast wildfires in Russia
dust blown from the Sahara desert
ash from an eruption of Italy's Vesuvius
context: Laki released about 120 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide -- roughly six times the amount from the huge 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption -- and winds carried it across Europe as a choking 'dry fog.' The English naturalist Gilbert White wrote that the sun 'looked as blank as a clouded moon, and shed a rust-coloured ferruginous light.' Franklin's guess at a distant volcanic cause was among the first times anyone tied a faraway eruption to Europe's weather. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki ; Benjamin Franklin, 'Meteorological Imaginations and Conjectures' (1784).

question: In July 1783, lava from the Laki volcano crept toward a small church at Kirkjubaejarklaustur. The pastor, Jon Steingrimsson, gathered his people inside and preached his famous 'Fire Sermon.' By the time the service ended, the lava had stopped at the edge of the town. Icelanders named that spot for the day it was saved. What do they call it?
context: The lava halted at the settlement's edge, and the spot has been called Eldmessutangi -- 'Fire Mass Point' -- ever since; eldmessa is Icelandic for the 'Fire Sermon' Reverend Jon Steingrimsson preached there on 20 July 1783. Whether the sermon truly stopped the flow or the lava simply reached a natural barrier, Icelanders have told the tale for more than two centuries, and Steingrimsson also kept a careful eyewitness diary of the whole disaster. Told as a legend. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki ; https://www.forbes.com/sites/robinandrews/2018/04/24/the-legend-of-the-icelandic-pastor-who-appeared-to-stop-a-lava-flow/

question: Laki's haze ruined harvest after harvest across France in 1783, and six years later, in 1789, that same hungry, angry France exploded into revolution. The neat gap between the two events has tempted some writers to name the Icelandic volcano a hidden spark of the Bastille's fall. Historians urge caution: that leap risks one classic reasoning trap. Which trap is it?
answer: mistaking a striking coincidence in time for a proven cause
choices: mistaking a striking coincidence in time for a proven cause
mistaking one vivid example for proof of a general rule
mistaking a claim's popularity for evidence that it is true
mistaking the lack of any disproof for solid proof
context: The link is genuinely debated -- some serious historians argue Laki's ruined harvests deepened France's hunger and unrest, while others doubt it mattered much. The trap is treating the mere fact that the eruption came first as proof that it caused the Revolution; logicians call this 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' -- 'after this, therefore because of this.' A striking coincidence in time is a reason to investigate, never a finished proof. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki ; https://news.climate.columbia.edu/2011/04/05/maybe-ben-franklin-was-wrong

question: In the highlands of northern Ethiopia, around the 12th century, a Christian king named Lalibela set his people to a huge task. They took solid rock — not stone blocks stacked up, but the bedrock still joined to the ground — and shaped it into eleven complete churches, all still standing today in the town that now bears the king's name. All they had were hammers and chisels. How did the workers shape each church out of the living rock?
answer: They chiselled down from the surface, cutting the rock away all around each church.
choices: They chiselled down from the surface, cutting the rock away all around each church.
They carved deep caves into a cliff face and smoothed the fronts into grand facades.
They hollowed long halls back into a hillside, roofed by the natural slope above.
They dug soft rock into a warren of hidden underground rooms and chapels.
context: The whole wonder of Lalibela is that these churches were EXCAVATED, not built: with hammers and chisels the workers cut straight down into one mass of volcanic rock, chipping away everything around each church until it stood as a single unbroken piece of the mountain -- no bricks, no mortar, and no foundation, because nothing was ever stacked up. Four of the eleven were freed on every side; the other seven still share one wall with the cliff. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela' (all 11 carved top-down from scoriaceous basalt with only hammers and chisels); Met Museum essay.

question: In the highlands of Ethiopia, about 800 years ago, King Lalibela ordered eleven Christian churches to be carved down into solid volcanic rock. Their roofs sit level with the ground and their halls are hollowed out beneath. The town now bears the king's name. Who fills them now, day after day?
answer: White-robed Ethiopian Orthodox priests and pilgrims, gathered to worship.
choices: White-robed Ethiopian Orthodox priests and pilgrims, gathered to worship.
Archaeologists, sifting the floors for the buried treasure of the Zagwe kings.
Curators and ticketed tourists, filing past altars roped off behind glass.
A caretaker or two, guarding stone halls that emptied long ago.
context: These are still LIVING churches. Eight hundred years on, white-robed Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo priests hold daily worship, and thousands of pilgrims -- many wrapped in white cotton shawls called netela -- fill the site for festivals like Genna (Ethiopian Christmas) and Timkat/Timket (Epiphany). Lalibela was never abandoned to become a ruin. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela' (active Ethiopian Orthodox churches in daily use).

question: You cannot see Bete Giyorgis, Lalibela's Church of St George, as you cross the plain toward it. You reach it down a narrow canyon that spirals lower and turns into a tunnel -- and only at the rim of its deep pit do you finally meet it, by looking straight DOWN onto its roof. What shape does that roof reveal?
answer: A Greek cross, with four equal arms.
choices: A Greek cross, with four equal arms.
A long rectangle, like a great hall.
A perfect circle, ringed by pillars.
context: Bete Giyorgis, the Church of St George, is carved from red volcanic tuff and stands roughly 15 m tall (some sources say ~12 m) inside a quarried pit whose trench measures about 25 m by 25 m. You approach unseen down a spiralling man-made canyon that becomes a tunnel, with sheer drops on every side, and first meet the church by looking down onto its Greek-cross roof. It was the last of the eleven built and is the best-preserved -- often called the 'Eighth Wonder of the World'; its three-tiered plinth is traditionally said to represent Noah's Ark. Source: Wikipedia, 'Church of Saint George, Lalibela.'

question: In 1187 the Muslim general Saladin captured Jerusalem, the Holy City, from the Christian crusaders who had held it. The long pilgrimage from Ethiopia to the shrines of Palestine grew hard and deadly for Ethiopian Christians. King Lalibela of the Zagwe kings, ruling from the highlands of northern Ethiopia, answered by carving eleven churches down into the living rock at his capital. What did he want them to be?
answer: A new Jerusalem, a holy land his people could reach at home.
choices: A new Jerusalem, a holy land his people could reach at home.
A war-shrine, a blessing on the army sent to retake the city.
A monk's refuge, a haven for those fleeing the Holy Land.
A relic-treasury, a vault for what the faithful saved before the fall.
context: King Gebre Meskel Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty (reigned about 1181-1221) built his New Jerusalem after Saladin captured Jerusalem in 1187 and cut off the Ethiopian pilgrimage route to the Holy Land -- so he brought the Holy Land home in stone. Source: Met Museum essay, 'The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela'; Wikipedia.

question: At Lalibela in the mountains of northern Ethiopia, medieval Ethiopian Christians carved eleven whole churches straight out of the bedrock around the 12th century. The grandest of them is Bete Medhane Alem — its name means 'Savior of the World.' It stands inside its own huge quarried pit, its columns and long halls all hewn from a single piece of rock, open to the Ethiopian sky above. Among all the churches on Earth, what record does Bete Medhane Alem hold?
answer: It is the largest monolithic church in the world.
choices: It is the largest monolithic church in the world.
It is the oldest surviving church in all of Africa.
It is the only church ever cut in the shape of a star.
It is the highest church standing anywhere on Earth.
context: Bete Medhane Alem ('House of the Savior of the World') measures about 33.5 m by 23.5 m and is believed to be the largest monolithic (single-rock) church in the world -- an entire cathedral-sized building hollowed out of one mass of stone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela.'

question: King Lalibela's carvers did not stop at the churches -- they reshaped the very ground between them to echo the geography of the Holy Land. A channel cut through the rock divides the northern churches from the southern ones, and they gave that trench a sacred name. What did they call it?
context: The channel named the River Jordan divides the churches into a northern group of five and a southern group of five, with Bete Giyorgis standing on its own -- mirroring the Holy Land and symbolizing an earthly and a heavenly Jerusalem on either bank. The real Jordan is the river where Christians believe Christ was baptized. The churches are all linked by a maze of tunnels and trenches cut through the rock. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela.'

question: Every church at Lalibela in northern Ethiopia was carved downward — not built up from the ground, but cut into a pit hollowed out of solid rock, so each church sits at the bottom of an open stone well.
