The Ethiopian highlands are pounded by heavy summer rains that would fill those pits like buckets. To keep the sunken churches from flooding, what did the medieval carvers shape into the surrounding rock?
answer: Sloping roofs and drainage trenches, angled to run the water off.
choices: Sloping roofs and drainage trenches, angled to run the water off.
Sump pits gouged into each church floor to swallow the runoff.
Stepped terraces quarried above the pits to turn the rain aside.
A rock moat and carved spouts cut around each church.
context: Because the churches sit in pits below ground, the medieval carvers cut drainage channels and trenches to carry the highland rains away, and angled the free-standing roofs to shed rainwater -- everything shaped from the rock itself, nothing added on. Some of these original channels are now clogged with centuries of sediment, which is why water damage threatens the site today. Source: Met Museum essay, 'The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela.'

question: The churches of Lalibela were so vast, and rose so fast, that medieval Ethiopians told a wondrous story to explain the speed. By day, the workmen chiselled the rock; by night, the tradition holds, the carving went on without them, and each day's work was doubled. According to this legend, who worked the night shift?
answer: Angels, carving through the night to double each day's work.
choices: Angels, carving through the night to double each day's work.
The king himself, who could not rest until it was finished.
Pilgrims, who arrived in the dark from every corner of the land.
The spirits of the mountain the churches were cut from.
context: This is a devotional LEGEND, not history. King Lalibela's own medieval hagiography claims he completed all eleven churches in twenty-four years with the help of angels; some versions say angels finished an entire church in a single night while the men slept, doubling each day's work. The story is told as a sign of holiness -- and the churches' astonishing scale is the real wonder that inspired it. Source: hagiographic tradition, per africanarguments.org and ancient-origins.net.

question: Earth has more than 1,500 active volcanoes. Almost none of them hold a churning lake of molten lava that never freezes over. Only a rare few, like Hawaii's Kilauea and Ethiopia's Erta Ale, do. Out of all Earth's volcanoes, about how many hold a lava lake at any one time?
context: At any given time only about eight volcanoes on Earth hold a permanent, churning lava lake -- a truly exclusive club. The known set has included Nyiragongo (DR Congo), Erta Ale (Ethiopia), Kilauea (Hawaii), Erebus (Antarctica), Masaya (Nicaragua), Ambrym (Vanuatu), Mount Michael, and Villarrica (Chile). A lava lake is rare because the volcano must stay open and hot enough to keep the rock molten without erupting it all away or sealing over. Source: Wikipedia, 'Erta Ale' (only about eight lava lakes worldwide as of 2019).

question: Mount Nyiragongo rises 3,470 m over the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. A lake of molten lava churns and glows red in its wide crater. Just 12 km downhill sits a crowded city of about a million people, sleeping every night in its glow. Which city lives in the shadow of Nyiragongo's fire?
context: Goma, home to about a million people on the shore of Lake Kivu, sits barely 12 km from Nyiragongo's summit crater and one of the largest lava lakes ever known. Living in the volcano's nightly red glow makes Goma one of the most dangerous city sites on Earth -- which is why Nyiragongo was named a 'Decade Volcano' in 1991, singled out for urgent study because it is both very active and close to a huge population. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mount Nyiragongo.'

question: Most lava creeps so slowly you could walk away from it. But on 10 January 1977, the crater wall of Mount Nyiragongo split open. Its whole lava lake drained out in under an hour, and the flood tore downhill at about 60 km/h — faster than most people can run. Why was Nyiragongo's lava so freakishly fast when most lava barely crawls?
answer: Its lava is unusually thin -- very low in silica
choices: Its lava is unusually thin -- very low in silica
Its lava is unusually hot -- far hotter than most lava
Its lava is unusually gassy -- frothing with bubbles
Its lava is unusually acidic -- rich in sulfur
context: Nyiragongo's lava is unusually low in silica (alkali-rich, almost feldspar-free rock), which makes it extraordinarily thin and fluid -- thick, silica-rich lava barely creeps. So when the crater wall cracked on 10 January 1977, the lake drained in under an hour and raced downhill at up to about 60 km/h, the fastest lava flow ever recorded, killing at least 50 people. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mount Nyiragongo.'

question: On a continent buried under ice, one mountain keeps a lake of fire churning in its crater all year long. It rises over frozen Ross Island and is the southernmost active volcano on Earth. Its red glow flickers against the glaciers around it. Which volcano is this pool of fire on the ice?
context: Mount Erebus, on Ross Island, is the southernmost active volcano on Earth (3,792 m) and holds one of the world's few permanent lava lakes -- a pool of fire ringed by Antarctic ice, and the only volcano now erupting rare phonolite lava. Explorer James Clark Ross named it in 1841 after his ship HMS Erebus, itself named for Erebus, the Greek personification of underworld darkness -- so a volcano of fire on the ice carries the name of the dark realm of Hades. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mount Erebus.'

question: Mount Erebus, the volcano that keeps a lava lake burning amid Antarctica's ice, does something almost magical as it breathes out its volcanic gases. Mixed into that plume is a fine mist of something precious -- about 80 grams of it every single day. Tiny crystals of it ride the wind and settle in the snow up to 1,000 km from the crater. What treasure does Erebus exhale into the polar air?
context: Scientists estimate Mount Erebus releases roughly 80 grams of gold vapour a day, condensing out of its hot volcanic gases, and tiny gold crystals blown from it have been found in the snow up to 1,000 km away -- a volcano quietly gilding the Antarctic snow. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mount Erebus.'

question: In Tanzania, Ol Doinyo Lengai erupts the strangest lava on Earth. It is so cool -- barely 500-600 C -- that it hardly glows in daylight, and so runny that it pours out jet black, like motor oil rather than fire. Then, over just hours or a few days, out in the open air, this black lava does something no other lava in the world does. What becomes of it?
answer: It turns chalky white, like snow
choices: It turns chalky white, like snow
It hardens into black glass, like obsidian
It rusts to a deep blood red
It crumbles into soft grey ash
context: Ol Doinyo Lengai is the only volcano on Earth erupting 'natrocarbonatite' lava -- barely 540-593 C, the coolest and most fluid lava known, so it pours out black like motor oil and hardly glows except at night. Within hours to days the sodium-rich black rock reacts with the air and turns chalky white, as if the crater had been dusted with snow. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ol Doinyo Lengai.'

question: In northern Tanzania, the Maasai and Sonjo peoples have lived for centuries in the shadow of Ol Doinyo Lengai, the fire-mountain that erupts the world's strangest lava. Long ago they gave it the name everyone still uses today. What does the name Ol Doinyo Lengai mean in the Maasai language?
context: In the Maasai language Ol Doinyo Lengai means 'the Mountain of God' -- to the Maasai and Sonjo peoples it is the earthly home of their creator deity, Engai, and they hold the fire-mountain sacred rather than fearful (their religious tradition, presented as they hold it). Source: Wikipedia, 'Ol Doinyo Lengai.'  (Legend.)

question: In 713 CE, a Buddhist monk named Hai Tong began carving a huge Buddha into a cliff at Leshan, China. The cliff stood high above the spot where three strong rivers crash together into one wild channel. What did Hai Tong hope his giant Buddha would do?
answer: calm the deadly rapids that wrecked passing boats
choices: calm the deadly rapids that wrecked passing boats
hold back the river's destructive summer floods
drive off the water demons haunting the junction
win the region years of plentiful harvests
context: Hai Tong began the Leshan Giant Buddha around 713 CE, hoping the enormous holy figure gazing over the water would settle the deadly rapids that kept wrecking boats where the rivers met. Source: travelchinaguide.com (Hai Tong initiated the project around 713 CE, motivated by boat accidents at the confluence of three rivers).

question: The Leshan Giant Buddha was carved in the 8th century out of a red sandstone cliff in Sichuan, southwestern China. He sits about 71 metres tall — as high as a 20-storey building — with his hands resting on his knees. A grown adult standing at his base barely reaches the top of one stone toe. What is just one of the Buddha's feet wide enough to hold?
answer: a crowd of over a hundred people
choices: a crowd of over a hundred people
a single row of parked market carts
a small grove of newly planted trees
a mere handful of people at a time
context: The Leshan Giant Buddha stands about 71 metres tall — the largest pre-modern stone Buddha ever carved — and it is built to a scale that shrinks any visitor: its instep runs roughly 8.5 metres across, broad enough for more than a hundred people to crowd onto a single foot, while each ear stretches some 7 metres long. Source: advantour.com (71 metres / 233 feet tall; largest stone Buddha in the world; foot platform ~8.5 metres across, holds over a hundred people; ears 7 metres long).

question: The Leshan Giant Buddha in Sichuan, China was carved facing one of old China's most feared river crossings — the churning point where three separate rivers slam together into a single, roiling flow that regularly capsized passing boats. A monk named Haitong began the Buddha in 713 CE, hoping the giant's calm presence would soothe the waters. Which three rivers meet right at the Buddha's feet?
answer: the Min, the Dadu, and the Qingyi
choices: the Min, the Dadu, and the Qingyi
the Yangtze, the Yellow, and the Wei
the Mekong, the Salween, and the Yalong
the Han, the Xiang, and the Gan
context: The Buddha sits exactly at the confluence of the Min, Dadu, and Qingyi rivers, and gazes across the water toward sacred Mount Emei — inspiring the local saying, 'The mountain is a Buddha and the Buddha is a mountain.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leshan_Giant_Buddha (confluence of the Min, Dadu, and Qingyi rivers; faces Mount Emei).

question: For more than 1,200 years, the Leshan Giant Buddha has stood open to Sichuan's heavy monsoon rains. Yet its soft red sandstone has barely worn away — amazing for a statue carved right into a cliff. Which hidden bit of engineering, built into the Buddha by its Tang-dynasty makers, has quietly kept the rain off it all this time?
answer: a concealed system of drainage channels
choices: a concealed system of drainage channels
a concealed lining of waterproof lacquer
a concealed layer of lime-and-straw plaster
a concealed reservoir that stores the rainwater
context: The Tang builders cut concealed gutters and channels through the Buddha's coiled hair, its collar, its chest, and behind its ears; these quietly carry rainwater away from the soft sandstone, and the system has kept the statue from crumbling for over 1,200 years. Source: advantour.com (hidden drainage channels within the hair, collar, chest, and behind the ears to divert rainwater).

question: While the Leshan Giant Buddha was being carved, greedy local officials tried to seize the donation money the monk Hai Tong had gathered for the work. According to legend, Hai Tong stopped them with a single shocking act that shamed them into leaving the funds alone. What did he do?
answer: he gouged out one of his own eyes
choices: he gouged out one of his own eyes
he chained himself to the cliff face
he swore to fast until work resumed
he knelt in the rapids and prayed
context: The story goes that Hai Tong gouged out one of his own eyes to prove his sincerity, and the ashamed officials backed off. It is a legend rather than documented fact, but it captures the fierce devotion of the monk who began a Buddha he would never live to see finished. Source: advantour.com ('After he proved it by gouging out one of his own eyes, the officials felt ashamed').

question: Carving the Leshan Giant Buddha meant hacking a staggering amount of stone off the cliff face — and all that rubble had to go somewhere: straight down into the three rivers below. Over the long decades of work, all that fallen rock ended up doing something to the very water the monks feared. What did the dumped stone do to the river?
answer: it reshaped the churning currents of the junction
choices: it reshaped the churning currents of the junction
it piled up a broad beach where boats could moor
it raised the riverbed and threw up new rapids
it split the flow around a new midstream island
context: Whether or not it soothed the river in the way its builders prayed for, the carving genuinely tamed the water: the enormous volume of rock hacked off the cliff and dumped below reshaped the currents where the three rivers met and made the crossing safer for boats — an accidental piece of river engineering. Source: advantour.com ('the enormous volume of stone was removed from the cliff and deposited into the river below... unintentionally altered the currents and made the waters genuinely safer for navigation').

question: On a hill called Marpo Ri, above the city of Lhasa high on the Tibetan plateau, white and red walls climb thirteen storeys into the sky. Behind those walls stack more than a thousand rooms, chapels and halls. For centuries this vast fortress-monastery was the winter home of the Dalai Lamas, the spiritual leaders of Tibetan Buddhism. What is this huge landmark called?
context: The Potala Palace rises thirteen storeys on the Red Hill (Marpo Ri) above Lhasa, holding more than a thousand rooms. It was the Dalai Lamas' winter residence for centuries and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potala_Palace

question: The Potala Palace is a giant even among palaces. It has over a thousand rooms and some 200,000 statues. Its stone walls are up to five metres thick. The fortress is 400 metres wide, and it stands 3,700 metres above the sea on the Red Hill above Lhasa. Which record does the Potala hold among world palaces?
context: Though the Potala sprawls 400 m wide with more than a thousand rooms and some 200,000 statues, its true world record is altitude: standing about 3,700 m up on the Red Hill above Lhasa, it is widely called the highest palace on Earth, where the thin plateau air holds roughly a third less oxygen than air at sea level. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potala_Palace

question: High in the Himalayan region of Central Asia, Lhasa is the ancient capital of Tibet. It sits about 3,650 metres up on the Tibetan Plateau, making it one of the highest cities on Earth. For over a thousand years it has been the sacred heart of Tibetan Buddhism, home to great temples and monasteries visited by pilgrims from all over the region. The city's own name joins two Tibetan words, lha and sa. What does the name 'Lhasa' mean?
context: In Tibetan, lha means 'god' and sa means 'place' — so Lhasa is the 'Place of the Gods,' a fitting name for the sacred heart of Tibetan Buddhism high on the plateau. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lhasa

question: Above the Tibetan capital of Lhasa rises the Potala Palace — a white-and-crimson fortress climbing thirteen stories up the Red Hill. Work on it began in 1645, and it became the winter home of the Dalai Lama, the Buddhist ruler of Tibet. One particular Dalai Lama ordered its building to unite his country under his rule and stand as the seat of Tibetan power. Which Dalai Lama built the Potala Palace?
context: The Great Fifth began the present Potala in 1645. Its outer shell rose in only about three years, but the painted and gilded interior took forty-five more years to finish — long after his own death. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potala_Palace

question: The Potala Palace in Lhasa, Tibet is really two palaces joined into one massive complex on the hill of Marpo Ri. The outer White Palace held Tibet's government offices and the Dalai Lama's own living rooms. The inner Red Palace, finished around 1694, was built strictly for sacred purposes. What does the Red Palace hold at its heart?
answer: the golden tombs of past Dalai Lamas
choices: the golden tombs of past Dalai Lamas
a vast library of Buddhist scriptures
the great assembly hall of monks
a shrine of a thousand buddhas
context: The Potala's halves are named for their colours: the White Palace (Potrang Karpo, 1649) for government and living quarters, the Red Palace (Potrang Marpo, 1690–1694) for chapels and the jewelled golden funerary stupas of past Dalai Lamas. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potala_Palace

question: About a kilometre east of the Potala, in the heart of old Lhasa, stands the site that Tibetan Buddhists revere above every other. Pilgrims who have travelled for months drop to the ground and stretch full-length toward its doors, again and again. Which sacred place is this?
context: The Jokhang, founded by King Songtsen Gampo around 640 CE, is the holiest shrine in Tibetan Buddhism. It enshrines the Jowo Shakyamuni, a gilded Buddha said to portray him at age twelve, brought to Lhasa by the Tang princess Wencheng — Tibet's single most revered statue. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jokhang

question: The very name 'Potala' — the Tibetan palace of the Dalai Lamas in Lhasa — was borrowed from a mountain in Buddhist myth. Mount Potalaka was said to be the paradise-home of a great bodhisattva, an enlightened being who chooses to stay in the world to help others. Tibetan Buddhists believe each Dalai Lama is a living embodiment of that same being. Which figure of Buddhist devotion is this?
choices: Maitreya, the buddha of the future
Amitabha, the buddha of pure light
context: 'Potala' comes from Mount Potalaka, the mythical mountain-paradise of Avalokiteshvara — Chenrezig in Tibetan — the bodhisattva of compassion whom the Dalai Lamas are believed to embody. The palace was thus imagined as his paradise made earthly on the Red Hill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Potalaka  (Legend.)

question: The 5th Dalai Lama died in 1682, while the Red Palace of the Potala was still years from finished. His regent, Desi Sangye Gyatso, feared the great work would halt if the news spread — so for more than a decade he kept an astonishing secret. What did the regent do?
answer: hid the death, saying the ruler was in long retreat
choices: hid the death, saying the ruler was in long retreat
had the ruler's seal forged onto new orders
dressed a look-alike monk to sit in his place
announced the ruler had begun a lifelong silent vow
context: When the Great Fifth died in 1682 with the Red Palace unfinished, his regent Desi Sangye Gyatso concealed the death for some fifteen years, telling Tibet the ruler had withdrawn into a long meditation retreat, so that work on the Potala would not stop. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Potala_Palace

question: Around the Jokhang temple at the heart of Lhasa runs a stone-paved pilgrim path about a kilometre long. From dawn, an unbroken river of pilgrims shuffles along it spinning handheld prayer wheels, every one of them keeping the temple on their right as they circle it clockwise. What is this famous pilgrim circuit called?
context: The Barkhor is the middle of Lhasa's three sacred circuits (the inner Nangkhor, the middle Barkhor, and the outer Lingkhor). Pilgrims always walk it clockwise, keeping the holy Jokhang on their right, turning prayer wheels as they go. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barkhor

question: At Niagara Falls, on the border between the United States and Canada, the great river plunges over a cliff and throws up a huge cloud of spray. On a sunny day, a bright rainbow suddenly glows in that drifting mist — even though not a single drop of rain is falling from the sky. Millions of tiny water droplets hang in the air where the spray floats out from the falls. What is really making those colors appear in the mist?
answer: Each raindrop bending the sunlight like a tiny glass prism
choices: Each raindrop bending the sunlight like a tiny glass prism
Sunlight bouncing off the flat river surface below
The droplets glowing with their own faint color
Sunlight scattering through colored dust in the air
context: Every clear, round droplet works like a miniature prism: sunlight refracts (bends) as it enters, reflects off the drop's back wall, then refracts again on the way out — fanning white light into its colors. Millions of drops doing this at once paint the arc you see. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

question: At Niagara Falls on the US-Canada border, spray from the great cascade drifts across the viewing platforms all day long. A photographer working there teaches visitors one simple rule about the rainbow that flashes in the mist. The bow will only appear when the sun, the falling water droplets, and your own eyes line up in exactly the right order. As you stand facing the drifting mist, where does the sun need to be for the rainbow to show?
context: A rainbow always centers on the antisolar point — the spot directly opposite the sun — so the sun sits at your back and the bow appears ahead of you. The bright arc rides about 42 degrees out from that center point. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

question: At Niagara Falls, where the river thunders over a cliff on the US-Canada border, spray hangs in the air and a rainbow bends across the mist whenever the sun shines. Whether at Niagara or anywhere else in the world, the colors of every rainbow always stack in exactly the same order — from the outer edge of the arc to the inner edge, one hue after another. Which color rides along the outer rim of the bow?
context: Red rides the outer edge and violet the inner, in every rainbow. Red light refracts (bends) the least as it passes through each drop, so it lands farthest out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

question: After a storm clears at Niagara, a second, fainter rainbow sometimes appears just outside the bright one — a 'double rainbow.' In that outer bow the light has bounced twice inside each drop instead of once. What has that done to its band of colors compared with the main bow?
answer: The color order reverses, with violet outside and red inside
choices: The color order reverses, with violet outside and red inside
The colors hold their usual order but the bow looks fainter
The colors blur together into one pale, whitish band
The bow keeps red outside but loses its blues and greens
context: The extra internal bounce flips the sequence: the secondary bow shows violet on the outside and red on the inside, a mirror of the primary. It looks fainter because light escapes at each reflection. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

question: When a double rainbow hangs over Niagara Falls, the ribbon of sky trapped between the bright inner bow and the faint outer bow looks noticeably darker than the sky on either side. This dark strip between the two bows has its own name. What is it called?
context: It is Alexander's band, after Alexander of Aphrodisias, the Greek philosopher who first described it around 200 AD. It looks dark because the raindrops send almost no light back to your eye from that in-between angle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

question: On the Zambezi River in southern Africa, on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe, water crashes over a cliff more than a mile wide into a narrow gorge below. The local Kololo people called this place Mosi-oa-Tunya — 'the Smoke that Thunders.' The Scottish explorer David Livingstone reached it in 1855 and renamed it Victoria Falls after his queen. Its spray plume climbs 400 metres into the sky and can be seen 50 kilometres away. Among all the world's waterfalls, what record does Victoria Falls hold?
answer: the largest single sheet of falling water
choices: the largest single sheet of falling water
the tallest single drop of falling water
the widest spread of separate cascades
the greatest volume of falling water
context: Victoria Falls holds the record for the largest single sheet of falling water — about 1,708 m (5,604 ft) wide and 108 m (354 ft) high, a curtain more than a mile across. Angel Falls in Venezuela plunges far higher (979 m) and Iguazu spreads into some 275 separate falls, but neither pours in one unbroken sheet like this. The mist climbs 400 m and, on full-moon nights, can raise a moonbow. The Lozi people called the falls Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the Smoke that Thunders'; David Livingstone renamed it for Queen Victoria in 1855. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Falls; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls

question: A hiker who catches a moonbow in the spray of Victoria Falls is often startled: to the naked eye the arc looks ghostly and almost colorless — a pale bow in the dark — yet a camera left open on a tripod records it in full rainbow color. Why does the eye see only white?
answer: Moonlight is far too dim to fire the eye's color-sensing cone cells
choices: Moonlight is far too dim to fire the eye's color-sensing cone cells
The eye's color cones cluster near the center, missing the wide arc
The eye adapts slowly to the dark, and color is the last sense to return
At such distance the eye can no longer separate one color from another
context: Color vision comes from cone cells, which need fairly bright light to respond. Moonlight is sunlight reflected off the moon and dimmed hundreds of thousands of times — below the cones' threshold — so only the rod cells (which see in gray) fire, and the moonbow reads as white. A camera's long exposure gathers enough light to record the real colors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonbow

question: Moonbows need a bright, low moon and spray thick enough that the wind can't scatter it — a rare pairing. In the entire Western Hemisphere, one waterfall is famous as the only place where moonbows appear on a dependable schedule, its steep gorge walls trapping the mist. Which waterfall is it?
choices: Iguazu Falls, on the Brazil–Argentina border
Niagara Falls, on the US–Canada border
context: It's Cumberland Falls in Kentucky, nicknamed the 'Niagara of the South' (about 68 ft high, 125 ft wide). Its narrow gorge traps the spray so the wind can't disperse it, making its moonbows uniquely reliable. Niagara once showed moonbows regularly too, but modern light pollution has drowned them out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_Falls

question: Lima sits in one of the driest deserts on Earth. It gets less than an inch of rain a year. Even so, a damp gray sea fog rolls in for half the year. It coats the streets in the morning and burns off by noon. That fog earns Lima the nickname 'the gray city.' What do locals call it?
context: The garúa is Lima's damp gray sea-fog. The city gets under 25 mm of rain a year -- one of the driest capitals on Earth -- yet humidity averages 84%, and from roughly May to November the low cloud-ceiling gives Lima its nickname 'the gray city.' The moisture usually burns off by afternoon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima (climate); geodiode.com/lima.

question: In the middle of Lima's fancy Miraflores district, glass towers and busy traffic surround a strange mound. It rises 22 metres high and is built from millions of hand-made mud bricks. A coastal people raised this adobe pyramid around 500 AD, long before the Inca ever reached this coast. What is this ancient pyramid called?
context: Huaca Pucllana in Miraflores is a seven-platform adobe pyramid about 22 m tall, raised by the pre-Inca Lima culture (~200-700 AD), roughly a thousand years before the Inca reached the coast. Archaeologists found benches and pits where its people made offerings of fish and sea creatures to their water gods. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huaca_Pucllana; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima_culture.

question: In Lima, the builders of a great adobe pyramid stood their mud bricks upright and spaced them apart like books on a shelf -- a technique nicknamed the 'bookshelf' method. This coast is one of the most earthquake-shaken on Earth. When the ground heaves, what does this design let the pyramid do?
answer: flex and settle back into place
choices: flex and settle back into place
crack apart and spread along its base
context: The builders stood the adobe bricks on end and spaced them apart -- the 'librero' or bookshelf method. The air-gaps let the whole pyramid flex and settle rather than crack, which is how a mud-brick structure has ridden out about 1,500 years of earthquakes on one of the world's most seismic coasts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huaca_Pucllana (construction).

question: Under the Basilica of San Francisco in old Lima runs a maze of catacombs. They served as the city's graveyard until 1810. As many as 70,000 of the colonial dead were buried down there, then forgotten. Workers reopened the tunnels in 1951. How did they find the bones laid out?
answer: sorted by type into neat geometric wells ringed with skulls
choices: sorted by type into neat geometric wells ringed with skulls
heaped in a jumbled pile where the tunnels once flooded
sealed one by one in small name-carved marble niches
burned to ash and kept in long rows of clay urns
context: The catacombs under the Basilica of San Francisco served as Lima's cemetery until 1810; an estimated 70,000 colonial dead lie there. Rediscovered in 1951, the bones are sorted and stacked in geometric designs, with skulls and femurs ringing circular wells. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_and_Convent_of_San_Francisco,_Lima.

question: The cold current running up the coast off Lima does more than kill the rain. As it flows, it drives deep, nutrient-loaded water up to the sunlit surface, and that feeds a burst of life so vast that this one thin strip of cold sea off Peru pulls in a giant share of every fish humanity hauls from all the world's oceans combined. About how large is that share?
answer: close to one-fifth of the entire world's catch
choices: close to one-fifth of the entire world's catch
about one hundredth of the world's catch
roughly half of the entire world's catch
around one in a thousand of the world's catch
context: The Humboldt Current's upwelling drags nutrients from the deep and feeds the richest fishery on Earth -- close to a fifth of the entire world's marine catch, more than any other current system. Its tiny anchoveta yielded over 12 million tons in 1970 alone, before an El Nino crashed the stock in 1972. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current (fishery).

question: The palace of Knossos on Crete was one huge building. It had hundreds of rooms, staircases, and light-wells wound so tightly around a central court that a stranger could get lost for hours. Greek legend turned this real maze into the prison of a monster. Young Athenians were sent as tribute for it to eat, until a hero killed it. Name that legendary monster of Knossos.
context: The Minotaur — a monster half-man and half-bull — was said to prowl the Labyrinth, a maze the craftsman Daedalus built beneath the palace; the hero Theseus killed it and escaped by following a thread. Knossos's genuinely baffling floor plan is widely thought to have inspired the whole legend. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knossos)

question: Knossos's Linear B tablets were never built to last — soft, sun-dried scrap that scribes wiped clean and reused within the year. Yet archaeologists dug them from the ground 3,000 years later, perfectly legible. They owe that survival to the very catastrophe that ended the palace. What destroyed the palace of Knossos?
context: The Linear B tablets were unbaked jottings meant to be wiped and reused within the year — but when the palace burned, the blaze fired the wet clay like a kiln, turning throwaway notes into near-indestructible bricks. The same palace fires preserved Linear B tablets at Pylos and Mycenae on the mainland. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B)

question: For fifty years after Sir Arthur Evans dug them up at Knossos, no one could read the Linear B tablets. Scholars dreamed they might hold lost poems or secret prayers of a forgotten faith. When the script was finally cracked in 1952, the truth was far more ordinary. What was really written on the tablets?
context: Linear B tablets are almost all palace accounts — inventories of sheep, wheat, olive oil, chariot wheels, spears and swords. A precious few record offerings to gods whose names we still know: Zeus, Poseidon and Athena, worshipped in the Aegean more than 3,000 years ago. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B)

question: Sir Arthur Evans had pulled a whole lost people out of the ground at Knossos. They had grand palaces and their own writing. But history had left him no name for them. So Evans reached into Greek myth and borrowed the name of the Labyrinth's legendary king, said to have ruled on Crete and demanded tribute from Athens. By what name do we know this lost people today?
context: Evans coined 'Minoan' after King Minos, the mythical Cretan king of the Labyrinth story. He also named the two scripts he dug up: Linear A (the older, the Minoans' own) and Linear B (the younger). (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans)  (Legend.)

question: Everyone thought the tablets from Knossos held some lost, strange tongue — the private speech of a vanished people. Then in 1952, Michael Ventris sounded out the signs. The words that came back were ones scholars knew at once from far later writings. What language did Linear B turn out to be?
context: Ventris proved Linear B was an early form of Greek — the language of the Mycenaeans, the mainland Greeks who ruled Crete — pushing written Greek back some 500 years before Homer. He announced it on BBC radio on 1 July 1952; the broadcast drew the classicist John Chadwick in to help him. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B)

question: Michael Ventris attacked Linear B like a wartime codebreaker, sorting its signs into a grid long before he knew what a single one meant. His way in was a gamble on a handful of words that recur across the Knossos tablets: guess correctly what they stood for, and their sound-values would crack open the whole grid. Ventris bet — rightly — that these key words were what?
context: Ventris reasoned that words found only on the Crete tablets must be Cretan place-names — and three of them, Knossos, Amnisos and Tulissos, became his 'wedge' into the grid, fixing real sound-values at last. He built on Alice Kober, an American scholar whose study of repeating word-endings (her 'triplets') proved the language changed word-forms like Greek or Latin; she died in 1950, before the solution. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decipherment_of_Linear_B)

question: The clinching proof that Michael Ventris had read Linear B correctly came from a single tablet dug up at Pylos, on the southern mainland, by the archaeologist Carl Blegen. Beside a small drawing, Ventris's sound-values spelled out the word ti-ri-po-de — and the picture showed exactly the object that word names. What was drawn on the tablet beside ti-ri-po-de?
context: The 'tripod tablet' (PY Ta 641) was Ventris's clincher: ti-ri-po-de (Greek tripode, 'tripod') sat beside a three-legged pot, and a word he read as 'four-handled' sat beside a pot with four handles. Carl Blegen wrote that it fit so perfectly it seemed too good to be true. Our own word 'tripod' descends straight from that ancient one. (classics.cam.ac.uk; linearbknossosmycenae.wordpress.com)

question: Michael Ventris had made Linear B speak Greek again — yet the older script buried beneath it at Knossos, Linear A, still defeats every scholar who tries it. Oddly, the sounds are no obstacle: because Linear B borrowed its signs, scholars can read Linear A's syllables aloud with ease. One thing, never yet found, is what would finally crack it. What is that missing key?
context: Linear A records the Minoans' own, still-unknown language. Because Linear B borrowed its signs, scholars can even pronounce Linear A aloud — but sounding out words in a language nobody knows yields nothing but noise. Cracking it would take a bilingual inscription tying it to a language we already understand (the way the Rosetta Stone's Greek text unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs) — yet no such bilingual, no surviving relative language, and no other key has ever turned up. So the Minoans keep their silence. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_A)

question: Lisbon, the capital of Portugal, spreads along the wide River Tagus where it meets the Atlantic Ocean. From the Belem docks on the western edge of the city, in the summer of 1497, the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama set sail with four small ships on a voyage that made Lisbon a launch point of the Age of Discovery. What did da Gama's fleet open for Europe?
choices: the first crossing to the Americas
the first voyage around the world
context: Vasco da Gama's fleet rounded Africa and reached India in 1498, opening the sea route that made small Portugal a maritime power and Lisbon a gateway of the Age of Discovery. The Belém Tower still guards the shore where the ships set out. (Source: Wikipedia, Belém Tower / Vasco da Gama 1497.)

question: On the morning of 1 November 1755, a strong earthquake flattened much of Lisbon in minutes. About forty minutes later, a wall of water rushed in from the Atlantic. It surged up the Tagus and drowned the crowds who had run from the rubble to the open waterfront. What is this kind of deadly sea wave called?
context: A tsunami is a wave, or train of waves, set off when an undersea quake shoves the ocean floor. The 1755 wave reached the harbor about 40 minutes after the shaking; fires from toppled church candles then burned for days — three disasters in a single morning. (Source: Wikipedia, 1755 Lisbon earthquake.)

question: On All Saints' Day, 1 November 1755, an enormous earthquake struck Lisbon, the capital of Portugal. Buildings collapsed all across the city and fires broke out in the ruins. Sailors along the docks of the Tagus River had survived the shaking — but they had only minutes before a giant tsunami wave came roaring up the river mouth. In those minutes, they watched the Tagus itself do something strange, and any old salt on the wharves knew at once it was a terrible warning. What did the water do?
answer: it pulled back and bared the muddy seabed
choices: it pulled back and bared the muddy seabed
it rose slowly and swallowed the quays
it spun into a whirlpool off the river mouth
it turned glassy and eerily still
context: The retreating sea is the classic tsunami warning — the trough of the wave arrives before the crest, sucking the water out. Survivors described a plain of mud strewn with old shipwrecks and lost cargo, exposed for minutes before the water roared back in. (Source: Wikipedia, 1755 Lisbon earthquake.)

question: In the heart of Lisbon stands the medieval Carmo Convent, whose great stone vault crashed down on the congregation hearing Mass that morning. When Lisbon rebuilt, it chose to treat this one ruin differently from every other. What did the city do with the Carmo Convent?
answer: left it roofless and open to the sky, as a memorial
choices: left it roofless and open to the sky, as a memorial
rebuilt it grander than before, crowned with a dome
cleared the ruins to open a new public square
hauled its stones away to build elsewhere
context: Lisbon never re-roofed the Convento do Carmo. Its skeletal Gothic arches still stand open to the sky in the city center as a memorial to 1 November 1755, and the shell now houses an archaeological museum. (Source: golisbon.com, Carmo Church; corroborated Grokipedia, Carmo Convent.)

question: On All Saints' Day, the Lisbon quake killed thousands of worshippers as they knelt at Mass. The most devout were struck down in the act of prayer, inside their own churches. Across Europe, the horror pushed thinkers like Voltaire to reopen one old, painful debate. Which debate did the Lisbon disaster thrust back to the center of European thought?
context: That so many faithful died at church on a holy day forced Europe to confront the 'problem of evil.' Voltaire pressed the question in his Poème sur le désastre de Lisbonne (1756) and mocked easy optimism through Dr. Pangloss in Candide (1759); Rousseau replied by blaming crowded cities. (Source: Wikipedia, Poème sur le désastre de Lisbonne; 1755 Lisbon earthquake.)

question: As Lisbon still smoldered, the king's chief minister, the Marquis of Pombal, did something no ruler had done after such a disaster. He sent every parish priest a list of questions. How long did the ground shake? Which way did the buildings fall? Did the sea rise or drop first? The priests' answers earned Pombal a founding place in one science. Which science did his parish survey help start?
context: Pombal's questionnaire asked how long the shaking lasted, which way walls fell, and whether the sea rose or fell first and how high. Archived at the Torre do Tombo, the priests' replies form the first large-scale objective survey of an earthquake — a founding document of modern seismology, the science of earthquakes. (Source: Wikipedia, 1755 Lisbon earthquake.)

question: After the great 1755 earthquake destroyed downtown Lisbon, the Marquis of Pombal rebuilt the district on a clean grid. He was determined the new buildings would survive the next major tremor. Inside the thick masonry walls he installed a hidden wooden frame that let the buildings sway and absorb the tremor's shocks instead of shattering. Soldiers reportedly marched around scale models to test the design. What was hidden inside those Pombaline walls?
answer: a cage of interlocking wooden beams
choices: a cage of interlocking wooden beams
a core of poured Roman concrete
a lattice of forged iron rods
a filling of packed sand and cork
context: The gaiola pombalina — a hidden three-dimensional timber cage inside the masonry — lets a Pombaline building flex and dissipate a quake's energy, one of the world's first deliberately earthquake-resistant systems. The story that troops marched around mock-ups to shake them is traditional and not firmly documented. (Source: Wikipedia, Gaiola (construction); Pombaline cage study, repositorio.ucp.pt.)

question: Across north-central China, the Loess Plateau heaps soft, pale-yellow earth up to 200 to 300 metres deep — enough to bury whole hills — across 640,000 square kilometres. The grains are silt-fine, and the layers built up slowly through the ice ages. How did all this yellow ground get here?
answer: Blown in as dust on the wind
choices: Blown in as dust on the wind
Washed down and dropped by rivers
Ground up and dumped by glaciers
context: Loess is silt-sized dust that the wind carries and drops grain by grain. China's Loess Plateau — about 640,000 square kilometres, up to 200–300 m thick near the Liupan Mountains — is the largest such deposit on Earth, piled up over the ice ages from glacial 'rock flour' and fine dust off the cold Central Asian deserts (the Gobi region), not laid down by glaciers or rivers directly. Wind-dropped loess blankets roughly a tenth of all the land on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loess_Plateau; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loess; grokipedia.com/page/Loess_Plateau.

question: In northern China, the Huang He winds nearly 5,500 kilometres from the mountains of Tibet all the way to the Yellow Sea. It runs so thick with pale, muddy sediment that people simply call it the Yellow River. Along one stretch, the river passes through a region blanketed in fine, wind-blown yellow soil hundreds of metres deep. There the current tears at the soft banks and carries the loose earth downstream. Where does more than 90% of the Yellow River's yellow silt come from?
answer: silt stripped from the Loess Plateau
choices: silt stripped from the Loess Plateau
ash washed down from volcanic highlands
sand carried in from the Gobi Desert
clay eroded off the Tibetan Plateau
context: As the Huang He crosses the Loess Plateau it tears loose the soft yellow silt — more than 90% of everything the river carries — which is exactly why it is named the Yellow River. It is the most sediment-laden major river on Earth: about 34 kilograms of silt per cubic metre of water (versus 10 for the Colorado and just 1 for the Nile), roughly 1.6 billion tons of loess a year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loess_Plateau; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_River.

question: The Loess Hills of western Iowa are pale yellow hills built from wind-blown silt, more than 90 feet deep and stretching nearly 200 miles along the Missouri River. Along with China's Loess Plateau, they are one of only two places on Earth where wind-dropped silt piles into free-standing hills. Before the wind ever carried the silt here, where did all that fine yellow dust originally come from?
answer: rock that ice-age glaciers ground to flour
choices: rock that ice-age glaciers ground to flour
ash that ancient volcanoes threw skyward
sand that far-off deserts sent drifting
clay that an ancient inland sea left behind
context: Iowa's loess began as glacial 'flour': as ice-age glaciers ground across North America they crushed bedrock into a dust-fine powder, meltwater flooded that silt down the Missouri River Valley, and wind then lifted and heaped it into the Loess Hills — not desert dust, but the leftover grindings of the ice. The hills run about 200 miles along the Missouri River in western Iowa, the wind-piled silt often more than 90 feet deep and cresting over 350 feet above the floodplain at Murray Hill. The only comparable loess on Earth is in Shaanxi, China — the Loess Plateau — and in a few spots Iowa's crests narrow to blade-thin 'razor ridges' under ten feet wide that fall away at near-ninety-degree angles. That same deep, wind-laid silt is a big reason the Corn Belt's soil runs so thick, dark, and rich. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loess_Hills; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loess.

question: At the Tower of London — the ancient stone fortress on the north bank of the River Thames — official keepers watch over at least six large black ravens day and night. They feed and count the birds, and take it very seriously indeed if even one goes missing. What does the old English legend say will happen if the ravens ever leave the Tower for good?
answer: the Tower will crumble and the kingdom will fall
choices: the Tower will crumble and the kingdom will fall
the crown jewels will crumble to dust
the Tower's great clock will stop forever
England will lose its next great war
context: This is a LEGEND, not history. The Tower's own historians think the raven story was invented in Victorian times, and the first written record of ravens at the Tower is only from 1883. Real ravens are still kept there today, with names like Huginn, Muninn, Edgar, and Poppy. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tower_of_London ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravens_of_the_Tower_of_London

question: In September 1666, a fire broke out at the shop of the king's own baker in London. A dry east wind fanned the flames, and within days the disaster was devouring much of the city, becoming known ever after as the Great Fire. On which narrow London street did that famous bakery stand?
context: The baker was Thomas Farriner, the king's baker, and the Great Fire burned for about four days. Pudding Lane took its name not from cakes but from the 'puddings' (animal offal) carted down it toward the river. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Great_Fire_of_London ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London

question: On 10 January 1863, the city of London opened a new kind of railway. Instead of running across open fields on iron tracks, this line ran through brick-lined tunnels dug beneath the crowded streets, with steam locomotives huffing and hissing along inside the tubes. About 38,000 curious Londoners squeezed into its gas-lit wooden cars on the very first day, coughing on smoke and grinning at the novelty. The company was called the Metropolitan Railway. What world record did the Metropolitan Railway set?
context: It ran through brick tunnels dug just below the streets by a method called 'cut-and-cover.' Because electric trains did not exist yet, the steam locomotives carried special 'condensing' gear to swallow their own smoke inside the tunnels. The first line ran 3.75 miles from Paddington to Farringdon. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Metropolitan_Railway ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Railway

question: The Tower of London, the medieval royal fortress on the River Thames, keeps a small flock of ravens on its grounds — free to walk about, but expected never to leave. Every few weeks the appointed Ravenmaster performs one small, deliberate task on each bird that quietly keeps the whole group grounded. What does he do?
answer: trims the lifting feathers on just one of its wings
choices: trims the lifting feathers on just one of its wings
clips a light metal ring around one of its legs
ties a thin leather cord to one of its feet
feeds it a heavy grain so it stays too plump
context: Trimming the flight feathers on only one wing leaves a raven able to hop and glide but too unbalanced to fly far, and comfortable food and shelter do the rest. It is done about once every three weeks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravens_of_the_Tower_of_London

question: For 600 years the Tower of London kept a Royal Menagerie of exotic animals given to English kings: lions, an elephant, and stranger creatures still. One beast, a gift to King Henry III from the King of Norway, was led down to the River Thames on a long rope each day so it could wade in and catch its own fish. What animal was this royal fisher?
context: The white bear arrived around 1252. The Royal Menagerie lasted from 1235 to 1835, when its animals were finally moved out, helping to found London Zoo. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tower_of_London

question: The Great Fire of 1666 raged across London for four days, swallowing about 13,200 houses, 87 churches, and the old St Paul's Cathedral, and leaving perhaps 100,000 people homeless. With an entire city ablaze, you might expect a huge death toll. How many deaths were officially recorded?
context: Only a handful of deaths were ever verified, often given as around eight, though some historians suspect poorer victims went uncounted. The destruction was enormous, but the fire spread slowly enough that most people could flee. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Great_Fire_of_London

question: Wander through the glass towers of London's financial district — the square mile still called the 'City of London' — and you keep meeting chunks of a thick, weathered stone wall. It once ringed the whole town beside the River Thames, and its line still roughly traces the boundary of that first walled city. Which ancient people founded London and built that wall?
context: The Romans founded Londinium about AD 47 to 50, soon after invading Britain, and around AD 200 they ringed it with the great London Wall. Its stones still surface between the modern City's glass towers and roughly trace the old walled boundary. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Londinium ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Tower_of_London

question: In the City of London rises the Monument, a tall stone column that Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke built close to where the Great Fire of 1666 first broke out. The column stands exactly 202 feet tall, and that number was chosen on purpose. What else does 202 feet measure?
answer: the distance from the column to the spot where the fire began
choices: the distance from the column to the spot where the fire began
the length of the burning street from one end to the other
the height that the flames were said to have reached
the width of the widest gap the fire leapt across
context: So the Monument's height equals its distance from the fire's starting point on Pudding Lane, a hidden piece of geometry by Wren and Hooke, who also used the hollow column for astronomy experiments. A spiral stair of 311 steps climbs to the top. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Great_Fire_of_London

question: High inside the dome of St Paul's Cathedral (the great church Christopher Wren built after the Great Fire) is a narrow walkway 259 steps up. Murmur a few words at one spot, and a friend standing more than 100 feet away on the far side hears them clearly. How does the whisper travel so far?
answer: the whisper clings to the curved wall and creeps around it
choices: the whisper clings to the curved wall and creeps around it
the whisper echoes straight across the open dome
the whisper rises up and the dome funnels it back down
the whisper travels through hidden speaking-tubes in the wall
context: This is the Whispering Gallery. The sound does not cross the open space; it hugs the smooth, curved inner wall of the dome and travels along it, so a whisper can run right around and be heard clearly on the opposite side. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul%27s_Cathedral

question: Only about ten years after Londinium was founded, the rebel queen Boudica of the Iceni swept down on the young town around AD 60 and razed it utterly to the ground. Dig beneath the modern City of London today and you can still meet that day face to face: a single unmistakable band running through the soil. What is that band?
answer: a layer of bright red burnt ash
choices: a layer of bright red burnt ash
a layer of shattered grey pottery
a band of pale river clay
a seam of rusted iron nails
context: Boudica's army burned Londinium so fiercely that the heat baked the earth red. Archaeologists call this scorched stratum the 'Boudican destruction horizon,' and it turns up wherever they dig deep enough beneath the old City. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Londinium

question: Because London sits on a tidal river, a storm surge charging down the North Sea can be squeezed higher and higher as it funnels up the narrowing Thames Estuary, enough to drown the low heart of the city, as a killer flood in 1953 warned. To stop it, ten huge steel gates now lie hidden along the riverbed at Woolwich, letting ships sail over them until a surge threatens. How do these gates rise to wall off the sea?
answer: they rotate upward on pivots to stand upright across the river
choices: they rotate upward on pivots to stand upright across the river
they inflate with air and swell up to the water's surface
they are winched straight up out of slots in the riverbed
they telescope upward, stacking section on section
context: This is the Thames Barrier, working since 1982. Its four big central gates each stand 20.1 m (66 ft) high and weigh about 3,700 tonnes; normally they rest curved-side-down on the riverbed, then rotate up to block the tide. It has been closed against dangerous surges more than 200 times. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Barrier

question: In northern Laos, the old town of Luang Prabang sits on a narrow finger of land. There the muddy-brown Mekong meets the blue-green Nam Khan. At the tip of the point you can watch the two rivers flow side by side in different colors before they finally blend. What do we call the meeting-place of two rivers?
context: A confluence is where two rivers join. At Luang Prabang the sediment-heavy Mekong runs brown while the Nam Khan sweeps in clearer and blue-green at about a 45-degree angle, so for a stretch below the junction the two colors flow side by side before mixing; in the dry season sandbars surface where they meet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luang_Prabang; thehungrytravellers.blog.

question: At dawn in Luang Prabang, hundreds of barefoot monks in orange robes walk silently through the streets in one long line, holding out their bowls. Townspeople kneel and place a handful of sticky rice into every bowl. They do this every morning of the year. What is this daily alms-giving called?
context: Tak Bat (also called Sai Bat) is a living daily practice, not a display for tourists. The rice is soaked overnight and cooked before dawn; the monks eat only what they collect, sharing it for breakfast and a single midday meal, then take no more food for the rest of the day. Source: tourismluangprabang.org; rainforestcruises.com.

question: In the mountains of northern Laos, where the Mekong River meets the smaller Nam Khan, sits an old royal town that was once the capital of a Buddhist kingdom. Over the centuries it wore three different names — first Muang Sua, then Xieng Thong, and at last Luang Prabang, the name it still carries today. The final name was given for a sacred golden statue of the Buddha kept in the royal palace. What does the name 'Luang Prabang' mean?
context: 'Luang' means royal or great; 'Prabang' (Phra Bang) is the sacred gold Buddha image the town guards. That statue was given in 1359 by a Khmer king to Fa Ngum, founder of the Lan Xang ('Million Elephants') kingdom, and the town — once Muang Sua, then Xieng Thong — renamed itself in its honor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luang_Prabang.

question: In the very center of Luang Prabang rises a forested hill about 100 meters high. Pilgrims climb its long stone staircase of more than 300 steps, passing shrines, to a gilded stupa at the summit — and from the top the two rivers curl around the town's temple roofs at sunset. What is this hill in the middle of town called?
context: Mount Phousi (about 100 m) is the sacred hill at the heart of the peninsula; the main route climbs roughly 328 steps to That Chomsi, the gilded stupa on top, the classic place to watch sunset over the Mekong–Nam Khan confluence. The distractors are other famous stair-climbed sacred peaks: Mount Popa (Myanmar), Doi Suthep (Thailand), and Adam's Peak (Sri Lanka). Source: bestpricetravel.com; thecommonwanderer.com.

question: Wat Xieng Thong, the golden royal temple King Setthathirath raised in Luang Prabang in 1559, still stands with its famous low, sweeping roofs. When Black Flag raiders stormed and burned much of the town in 1887, this one temple was left untouched on purpose. Why did the raiders spare Wat Xieng Thong?
answer: one of their leaders had studied there as a monk
choices: one of their leaders had studied there as a monk
the townspeople had walled up its entrance
the raiders feared the temple was cursed
it sat too far out on the river point to reach
context: Wat Xieng Thong (built 1559–1560) is the masterpiece of the 'Luang Prabang style,' its tiered roofs sweeping almost to the ground. Tradition holds that when Haw 'Black Flag' fighters raided the town in 1887, one of their commanders had trained there as a young monk and ordered it left alone — which is why the 16th-century temple survives today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Xieng_Thong.

question: On the red-painted rear wall of Wat Xieng Thong, Luang Prabang's magnificent golden royal temple, thousands of tiny glass tiles form one of the most beloved images in all of Laos. They shimmer against the deep crimson background. What does this famous glass mosaic depict?
context: The back wall of Wat Xieng Thong's main hall carries a 'Tree of Life' rendered in colored mirror-glass mosaic against a deep red ground — one of the most photographed images in Laos. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Xieng_Thong.

question: About 30 km south of Luang Prabang, Kuang Si Falls pours down pale rock terraces into a staircase of pools that glow an unreal aquamarine — yet no dye or algae colors them. The blue-green comes straight from the bedrock the stream runs over. What in that bedrock tints Kuang Si's pools that color?
context: Kuang Si's color is a real earth process, not dye. Flowing water dissolves calcium carbonate out of the limestone bedrock; the fine mineral particles it carries scatter blue light, tinting the pools aquamarine. The same dissolved mineral re-hardens along the rims as travertine, slowly building the terraces higher — which is why Kuang Si is called a travertine waterfall. Source: geologyscience.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuang_Si_Falls.

question: The most famous photo of Machu Picchu shows the ruins with a steep, sugarloaf peak rising right behind them. Brave visitors climb it by a scary stair-cut trail. Many think this peak is the mountain the city is named for. But that name really belongs to a different summit. Which peak stands behind the ruins?
context: That sugarloaf is Huayna Picchu, the sharp sister summit; Machu Picchu's ruins sit on the saddle between it and the peak the city is named for. Climbers reach its top by a near-vertical stair carved into the granite, nicknamed the 'Stairs of Death.' The whole site lies at 2,430 m (7,970 ft), so often lost in cloud it's called the 'cloud city.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: High in the Andes mountains of Peru, the Inca built a city of grey stone on a narrow ridge between two green peaks around the 1400s. Today tourists know the ruins as Machu Picchu and imagine the name hides some mysterious Inca secret. In fact, the Inca were just naming the taller of the two mountains that rise behind the ruins — plainly, in their own language, Quechua. What does 'Machu Picchu' mean?
context: 'Machu' means old and 'pikchu' means peak, so Machu Picchu is simply 'old peak' (or 'old mountain'). Its sharp neighbor Huayna Picchu is the 'young peak.' There was nothing mystical about the label; it was everyday Inca geography. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: Machu Picchu is a lost Inca city high in the Peruvian Andes, perched on a narrow saddle of stone with sheer cliffs plunging about 450 metres on three sides. Far below the ruins, a single river winds in a tight hairpin bend that almost circles the entire ridge — a natural moat wrapped around the sacred city. Which river makes that great loop?
context: The Urubamba River swings around the ridge on three sides in a tight hairpin, roughly 450 m of vertical cliff below the citadel, so that nature very nearly moats the whole site. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: For years, romantic stories imagined Machu Picchu as an ancient city built by a lost race. The real story turns out to be simpler. It was purpose-built around 1450 and used for only about 80 years before being abandoned. What was Machu Picchu actually built to be?
context: Machu Picchu was a royal estate, a country retreat built around 1450 for the Inca emperor Pachacuti and lived in for only about 80 years (c. 1420-1530), not the work of any vanished ancient race. When the Inca left, the cloud forest simply grew over it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: In 1911, American explorer Hiram Bingham was guided up to Machu Picchu by a local farmer. He then told the world he had found a 'lost city' hidden by the jungle. But his own team's notes gave the celebrated 'find' away. What did Bingham actually find at the ruins?
choices: fresh offerings laid at a mountain shrine
context: Machu Picchu was never 'lost' to the people of the valley. When Melchor Arteaga guided Bingham up on 24 July 1911, the Richarte and Alvarez families were already farming the old terraces, and Richarte's young son led Bingham the final stretch to the ruins. A local, Agustin Lizarraga, had even carved his name at the site in 1902, nine years before Bingham arrived. Bingham's label 'the Lost City of the Incas' made the ruins world-famous, and quietly erased the families already living there. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu'; salkantaytrekking.com.

question: When the Spanish conquistadors overran the Inca empire, they looted Cusco's temples and tore Inca stonework apart to raise churches on the ruins. Almost every great Inca site met that fate, yet Machu Picchu's walls still stand nearly whole today. Why did this one site come through intact?
choices: the Inca defended it to the last
its granite was too hard to break
an Inca treaty placed it off-limits
context: Machu Picchu sits hidden on a remote cloud-forest ridge, and the Spanish conquistadors simply never located it, so unlike Cusco it was never sacked, never quarried for a cathedral, never burned. That is the real reason its dry-stone walls survived almost untouched for four centuries. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: Hikers on the ancient Inca Trail don't scramble up to Machu Picchu from the valley floor; they arrive the way the Inca did, cresting a high point on the old royal road where the whole city suddenly bursts into view, framed between its two peaks. Inca Trail walkers know this spot by its Quechua name. What is it called?
context: It's the Inti Punku, the 'Sun Gate,' a stone doorway on the Qhapaq Nan, the great Inca road that once knit the empire together. It was the main Inca approach to the estate, and Inca Trail hikers still crest it to catch that first framed view of Machu Picchu cradled between its peaks. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: The wide green terraces cascading down Machu Picchu's slopes look like nothing but farmland. They are flat shelves for growing maize and potatoes on a mountainside. But engineers studying the site found the terraces quietly do a second job just as vital as feeding the estate. What is that hidden second job?
choices: collecting water for the dry months
hiding the city from the valley below
context: Machu Picchu's roughly 5 hectares of terraces (andenes) grew the estate's food, but their deeper genius is structural: packed layers of stone, gravel, and soil behind stout retaining walls turn each terrace into a buttress, anchoring the steep, rain-soaked slope against landslides. The city farms its own mountain into staying put. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu'; waterhistory.org.

question: Machu Picchu was built on ground that shakes, so the Inca engineered even its doorways to ride out earthquakes without cracking apart. Every door, window, and wall-niche at the site is cut to the same distinctive, quake-resistant shape rather than a plain upright opening. What shape are they?
context: Every opening at Machu Picchu is a trapezoid, noticeably wider at the base than the top and tilted slightly inward. That shape lowers the wall's center of gravity so the opening flexes instead of cracking, which is why the doorways still stand square after five centuries of Andean tremors. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: At the highest ceremonial point of Machu Picchu, the Inca carved a single squat pillar straight out of the living granite bedrock. Its angled faces align with the sun's yearly path, and Inca priests believed the stone could 'tie' the sun in place at the solstice so it would never wander off. What is this carved solar pillar called?
context: It's the Intihuatana, Quechua for the 'hitching post of the sun' (inti = sun). Carved from a single piece of bedrock, its faces track the solstices, and Inca priests held that it tethered the sun to its yearly course. Similar stones elsewhere in the empire were later destroyed, making Machu Picchu's a rare survivor. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu'; salkantaytrekking.com.  (Legend.)

question: The finest walls at Machu Picchu were laid with no mortar, no cement, nothing between the stones at all; each granite block was ground to match its neighbors so exactly that even today you cannot slide a knife blade into the seams. Strangely, this snug but mortar-free fit is the very thing that lets the walls outlast the region's frequent earthquakes. How do these mortarless walls behave when the ground shakes?
answer: the blocks jostle, then resettle in place
choices: the blocks jostle, then resettle in place
the stones lock tighter under the load
hidden timber frames absorb the shock
the whole wall rocks on a stone base
context: With no mortar to crack, the individually shaped ashlar blocks can shift a little when the earth heaves, and then gravity drops them back into their exact places once the shaking stops; Andean guides say the stones 'dance.' A mortared wall would simply crack, but Machu Picchu's flexes and survives, its joints still so tight a knife blade won't enter. Source: machupicchu.org.

question: Visitors to Machu Picchu marvel at the stone temples, plazas, and terraces on the surface. But civil engineer Kenneth Wright calculated that the visible city is only a fraction of the actual work. Well over half of the entire building effort went into structures no tourist ever sees. Where did the majority of the Inca's labor actually go?
choices: into a hidden network of tunnels
context: Kenneth Wright found that roughly 60% of the building effort at Machu Picchu lies underground: deep stone foundations and a hidden bed of crushed rock that drains the region's torrential rain straight through the site instead of letting it wash the terraces off the ridge. As Wright put it, 'Without good drainage, there would be no Machu Picchu existing today.' The most impressive thing about the wonder is the part you cannot see. Sources: Kenneth Wright engineering studies (machupicchu.org; PBS NOVA).

question: On a dirt road near Morondava on Madagascar's west coast, a row of huge trees nearly 30 meters tall rises straight out of flat, bare fields. It is one of the most photographed sights on the whole island. Which trees give this famous 'Avenue' its name?
context: These are Grandidier's baobabs (Adansonia grandidieri), the biggest and tallest of Madagascar's baobabs. Six of the world's nine baobab species grow only on Madagascar, making the island the true home of the baobab. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_of_the_Baobabs

question: A Grandidier's baobab lives through Madagascar's long dry season by soaking up the rains and storing water in its soft, spongy wood. Because of this hidden tank, one thing about the tree slowly grows and shrinks between the wet and dry seasons. Which one?
context: A Grandidier's baobab trunk can be up to about 3 m across, and it visibly fattens after the rains and shrinks through the drought as the stored water is used up. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adansonia_grandidieri

question: On the island of Madagascar, off the east coast of Africa, a dirt road near the western town of Morondava is lined with about twenty huge baobab trees — vast bottle-shaped giants up to 30 metres tall. They stand completely alone in flat, open farmland, with no other tall trees anywhere near them, and were never planted there in a neat row on purpose. So why do these lonely giants stand by themselves in bare fields?
answer: They are the last survivors of a forest that was cleared around them
choices: They are the last survivors of a forest that was cleared around them
They poisoned the soil so no other tree could grow beside them
They were carried there as seedlings by an ancient flood
They only sprout where lightning has burned the older trees
context: The Avenue was once dense tropical forest. As people cleared the land for rice and pasture, they left the massive baobabs standing. Malagasy tradition calls the baobab 'renala' -- 'mother of the forest.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_of_the_Baobabs

question: More than nine of every ten plants and animals in Madagascar live naturally nowhere else on Earth. Biologists call a species found in only one place 'endemic,' and few lands are as endemic as this island. What long-ago event set the stage for so much unique life to develop only here?
answer: The island broke away and drifted alone for tens of millions of years
choices: The island broke away and drifted alone for tens of millions of years
A ring of active volcanoes walled the island off from the mainland
Repeated ice ages killed off every species that could not adapt
A great desert down the middle trapped species along the coasts
context: Cut off by open ocean, Madagascar's plants and animals evolved on their own for millions of years, producing whole groups of living things unique to the island. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar

question: In western Madagascar rises a forest made not of trees but of stone: thousands of gray limestone blades, packed side by side and sharp enough to slice through boots and skin. The Malagasy name for it warns that this is a place 'where one cannot walk barefoot.' What is this needle-sharp stone forest called?
context: The Tsingy de Bemaraha, above the Manambolo River gorge, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1990. Its razor peaks are so dangerous that almost no one crosses them on foot. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsingy_de_Bemaraha_Strict_Nature_Reserve

question: Madagascar's western 'stone forest' is a field of blade-sharp gray limestone pinnacles, but it was not chiseled or blasted from the ground. Over millions of years, one patient natural force worked its way into every crack of a flat limestone plateau. It eroded the rock from within, leaving only thin needle-walls of stone standing. What carved this stone forest?
context: Rainwater is faintly acidic and slowly dissolves limestone. This process -- which also carves caves and sinkholes -- creates the landscape geographers call karst. The Tsingy de Bemaraha is one of the most extreme karst formations on Earth. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsingy_de_Bemaraha_Strict_Nature_Reserve

question: In Madagascar's parched southern region grows a strange 'spiny forest' of tall, leafless, thorn-studded, water-storing stems — the plant family Didiereaceae. They look so exactly like the cacti of the American deserts that a gardener can graft a piece of one directly onto a living cactus. The two plants will fuse together and continue to grow as a single organism. What does the fact that this graft succeeds tell us about the two plants?
answer: They are true cousins of the American cacti
choices: They are true cousins of the American cacti
They just evolved to look alike, but are unrelated
They were carried from America by early sailors
They interbred with American cacti long ago
context: This is the surprise: the Didiereaceae are not unrelated cactus look-alikes but genuine relatives of the New World cacti -- close kin, close enough that a piece of one will graft onto a cactus and fuse into a single growing plant, even though the two families live an ocean apart on different continents. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didiereaceae

question: Madagascar did not tear loose from the rest of the world all at once. Geologists find the island broke free in TWO separate steps, tens of millions of years apart, as the ancient southern supercontinent Gondwana split into pieces. From which two landmasses did Madagascar break away -- first one, then the other?
answer: First from Africa, then from India
choices: First from Africa, then from India
First from Africa, then from Australia
First from Africa, then from Antarctica
First from Africa, then from Arabia
context: Madagascar rifted from Africa in the Early Jurassic, about 180 million years ago, and only later split from the Indian subcontinent about 88-90 million years ago. Adrift ever since, it carried an ancient cargo of life. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar

question: Madagascar broke away so early and drifted alone so long that it evolved entire families of plants -- and whole groups of living things -- that live on no other land in the world. Because its wildlife is so unlike anywhere else, scientists gave the island a grand nickname that treats it as a world unto itself. What do they call Madagascar?
context: Ecologists nickname Madagascar the 'eighth continent' because, like a continent, it holds entire plant families (such as Sarcolaenaceae and Sphaerosepalaceae) found nowhere else; over 80% of its plant species are endemic. https://vanilla.symrise.com/the-eighth-continent

question: Astronauts on the International Space Station can recognize Madagascar by an alarming sight: its rivers empty into the sea in enormous plumes the color of blood, spreading red stains far out across the blue water. One astronaut said the island looks as if it is 'bleeding to death.' What turns the rivers of Madagascar blood-red?
answer: Iron-rich red soil washing off the stripped land
choices: Iron-rich red soil washing off the stripped land
A vast bloom of blood-red coastal algae
Red ash drifting from inland volcanoes
Red dust blown in from the African mainland
context: Farmers clearing land by slash-and-burn, along with overgrazing and fires, have stripped much of Madagascar's forest since the 1950s. Bare highland soil -- heavy with red iron oxide -- erodes into the rivers (up to 400 tons per hectare a year) and pours out to sea; the Betsiboka River's red plume is famously visible from orbit. https://www.amusingplanet.com/2018/12/betsiboka-madagascars-red-river.html

question: Off Norway's Lofoten Islands spins the Moskstraumen — the real whirlpool Edgar Allan Poe's 1841 story first carried into English as the word 'maelstrom,' the one Jules Verne made the doom of Captain Nemo's submarine. The word is Dutch. What does 'maelstrom' literally mean?
context: 'Maelstrom' is Dutch — malen ('to grind') + stroom ('stream') — a 'grinding stream.' Poe carried the word into English in his 1841 tale 'A Descent into the Maelström'; Herman Melville dropped it into Moby-Dick a decade later, and Jules Verne made it the climax of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea. The real Moskstraumen off the Lofoten Islands is powerful but bounded — the ship-swallowing vortex is literary exaggeration. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moskstraumen

question: Near Bodo in Norway, a sea-strait barely 150 metres wide swallows the tide every six hours. Up to 400 million cubic metres of water blast through the gap and tear into whirlpools 10 metres across. Which strait is this, often ranked among the strongest tidal currents on Earth?
context: Saltstraumen, about 10 km from the town of Bodø, is often called one of the strongest tidal currents in the world: every six hours up to 400 million cubic metres of seawater force through a strait only 150 m wide, spinning whirlpools up to 10 m across and 5 m deep. ('Strongest' is debated — sources say 'one of,' not 'the.') The other three are real rivals elsewhere: Norway's own Moskstraumen, off the Lofoten Islands, is the original 'maelstrom' that named them all; Japan's Naruto Strait, between Shikoku and Awaji Island, spins whirlpools up to 20 m across; and Scotland's Gulf of Corryvreckan, between Jura and Scarba, is called the third-largest whirlpool in the world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltstraumen

question: Between the Scottish islands of Jura and Scarba, the Gulf of Corryvreckan roars so loudly it is heard miles off — the third-largest whirlpool in the world. In August 1947 a small boat's engine died here; its passengers were swept toward the vortex and stranded on a bare rock until lobstermen rescued them. One of them was a writer racing to finish a novel that became one of the century's most famous. Which book was he writing?
context: The writer was George Orwell, then living on the Scottish island of Jura to finish Nineteen Eighty-Four. In August 1947 his boat's engine failed in the Gulf of Corryvreckan — between Jura and Scarba, caused by the flood tide racing over a basalt pinnacle — and lobstermen rescued his stranded party. He finished his first draft about three months later. (Animal Farm was already published, in 1945.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Corryvreckan
