context: UNESCO made Nan Madol a World Heritage Site in 2016 — the first in the Federated States of Micronesia — billing it as the only ancient city ever built atop a coral reef. Source: smithsonianmag.com; whc.unesco.org (2016 inscription).

question: On the reef beside the Pacific island of Pohnpei stands Nan Madol, a ruined stone city built centuries ago right on the water. Its walls are stacked from what look like giant 'logs' of dark rock, but they are really natural basalt columns. They cooled long ago from lava into tall prisms with strikingly regular sides. What cross-section shape do these natural basalt columns most often show?
context: Nan Madol's basalt 'logs' are natural columnar basalt — thick lava cooling and cracking into mostly six-sided prisms, the same process that built Ireland's Giant's Causeway — stacked crisscross with coral rubble packed into the gaps. Source: thearchaeologist.org; heritagedaily.com (2020).

question: Off the tropical reef of the tiny Pacific island of Pohnpei, in Micronesia, an ancient people built an entire stone city on the water — nearly a hundred artificial islets laced together by narrow canals. They spoke Pohnpeian, and the name they left for their reef-city carries a quietly poetic meaning. What does the name Nan Madol mean?
context: 'Nan Madol' means the space between — a nod to the tidal canals weaving among its islets; its older traditional name was Soun Nan-leng, 'Reef of Heaven.' Source: Ancient Origins; Khan Academy/Smarthistory; Gene Ashby, 'Pohnpei, An Island Argosy.'

question: On the reef beside the Pacific island of Pohnpei in Micronesia stands Nan Madol — a ruined city of stacked basalt built by the Saudeleur lords roughly 800 years ago. Its grandest islet, Nandauwas, is ringed by double-tiered basalt walls rising some 25 feet high — dry-stacked with no mortar at all, and still standing today. What did these great walls guard at their heart?
answer: the tomb of the first Saudeleur king
choices: the tomb of the first Saudeleur king
a shrine to the thunder god Nahn Sapwe
the dynasty's hoard of sacred treasure
the great feasting hall of the priests
context: Nandauwas, the grandest islet, is the royal tomb compound in the sacred sector; its double-tiered, dry-stacked basalt walls rise up to about 7.6 m (25 ft), guarding the tomb of the first Saudeleur ruler. Source: labrujulaverde.com; thearchaeologist.org ('over 25 feet high').

question: Nan Madol, the ancient reef-city built on the tropical Pacific island of Pohnpei in Micronesia, is made entirely of enormous dark basalt columns. Every column came from one single volcanic plug on the island of Pohnpei itself, then was somehow moved out to the reef and stacked into walls. Where on Pohnpei did the ancient builders cut all that stone?
choices: on the same shore as the reef city
in a river valley just inland
context: The columnar basalt came from a volcanic plug on the far side of Pohnpei (some accounts place it near Sokehs, roughly 25 miles away) and was moved clear across the island and out over the water to the reef. Source: heritagedaily.com (2020); clickpetroleoegas summary.

question: Add up every basalt column and every basket of coral fill stacked onto the reef at Nan Madol. Scholars have estimated the total weight the builders shifted by hand, remarkable given they had no wheels, no pulleys, and no metal tools at all. Roughly how much stone did they haul out into the sea?
context: Scholars estimate roughly 750,000 tonnes of basalt and coral were stacked here (a scholarly estimate, not a measured figure) — averaging about 1,850 tonnes a year across four centuries of building, all with no metal, wheels, or pulleys. Source: clickpetroleoegas floating-city article; WebSearch corroboration on the 750,000-tonne estimate.

question: No one has ever proved how the builders of Nan Madol moved basalt columns weighing 5 tonnes — some as much as 50 — from the quarry out to the reef, with no wheels and no draft animals. Archaeologists have one leading hypothesis, still unproven. What is their best guess?
answer: they floated the columns on log rafts at high tide
choices: they floated the columns on log rafts at high tide
they rolled the columns overland on palm-trunk rollers
they dragged the columns across the reef on ropes
they ferried the columns inside large sailing canoes
context: How the multi-tonne columns were moved is still unsolved; the leading idea is that they were floated around the coast on palm- or bamboo-log rafts riding the tides — but there is no definitive proof, and dragging or a mix of methods remain possible. Source: clickpetroleoegas summary; vocal.media/history (Nan Madol basalt transport).

question: Around the year 1200, on a reef beside the Pacific island of Pohnpei, the Saudeleur lords began raising Nan Madol — a city of nearly a hundred small artificial islets built up out of stacked basalt logs. The Saudeleurs are remembered for a first as remarkable as their stonework. It was an accomplishment no earlier chief on Pohnpei had ever managed. What was that great achievement?
answer: uniting all of Pohnpei under one rule
choices: uniting all of Pohnpei under one rule
inventing a written script for the island
sailing on to settle distant Hawaii
carving the Pacific's first stone money
context: The Saudeleur were priest-kings — the first dynasty to unite Pohnpei's roughly 25,000 people under a single rule — and they governed from Nan Madol's islets until about 1628, when oral tradition says the warrior Isokelekel overthrew the last Saudeleur. Source: heritagedaily.com (2020); Grokipedia/Wikipedia (Nan Madol).

question: Nan Madol, the stone city built by the Saudeleur lords on the reef of Pohnpei in Micronesia, is made up of roughly 92 artificial islets. They were deliberately sorted into two named precincts — Madol Powe and Madol Pah — each set aside for a different half of Saudeleur life. Along what line was the reef city divided in two?
answer: one half for the sacred dead, the other for the living rulers
choices: one half for the sacred dead, the other for the living rulers
one half for the noble-born, the other for the commoners
one half for the farmers, the other for the fishing clans
one half for the warriors, the other for the merchants
context: Nan Madol split in two: Madol Powe, the sacred upper sector (about 58 islets) where priests lived and the dead were entombed, and Madol Pah, the lower royal-administrative sector for the living. Source: Grokipedia/Wikipedia (Nan Madol); smarthistory.org/nan-madol.

question: In AD 79 a young Roman, Pliny the Younger, watched Mount Vesuvius erupt across the Bay of Naples. He wrote the only eyewitness account that survives. To capture the shape of the towering ash cloud, he compared it to a single kind of tree that grows all over Italy. Which tree did Pliny say the cloud looked like?
context: Pliny wrote that the cloud rose on a long trunk that then 'spread out into a number of branches' -- the exact silhouette of the Italian stone pine, or umbrella pine, whose flat, spreading canopy still crowns Italian hillsides. His letters to the historian Tacitus are why we can still picture that day. Source: cmuntz.hosted.uark.edu (Pliny the Younger, letters); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Younger.

question: Pompeii was buried so fast that many things left empty pockets in the hard ash. The originals inside rotted away long ago. In 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli pumped plaster into these pockets, let it set, then chipped away the ash. His most famous casts showed the shapes of what?
context: The bodies had decayed to nothing, leaving cavities in the rock-hard ash; Fiorelli's plaster technique turned those hollows into exact figures -- you can see faces, folds of clothing, even a chained dog twisting on its back. He effectively 'un-froze' Pompeii, restoring its people to their final moments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeii.

question: Mount Vesuvius is no relic of the past. It erupted again in March 1944, in the middle of World War II, with Allied forces camped all around the Bay of Naples. Falling ash and hot cinders rained down on a nearby base and wrecked about 80 war machines parked there. What did the 1944 eruption destroy?
context: The eruption buried the village of San Sebastiano and destroyed or badly damaged roughly 80 American B-25 Mitchell bombers parked at a nearby airfield -- a volcano stealing planes out from under an air force. It was Vesuvius's last eruption to date; the mountain has been ominously quiet ever since. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Vesuvius.

question: West of Naples lies the Campi Flegrei, the 'burning fields', where the ground itself runs hot and gases hiss up through cracks. At its Solfatara crater, visitors can walk right up and stand beside more than 150 of one bubbling, blistering feature. What bubbles away at Solfatara?
context: Solfatara is a shallow crater inside the Campi Flegrei that has steamed for thousands of years -- the Romans imagined it an entrance to the underworld. Its fumaroles hiss out sulphur gases, and more than 150 mud pools plop and bubble at boiling heat: a small, safe window onto the giant volcanic system sleeping below. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campi_Flegrei.

question: The AD 79 eruption of Vesuvius blasted a column of ash and pumice about 33 km straight up before flattening into a huge canopy near the top of the sky. Scientists sort eruptions into named styles by their behavior. They reserve one name for this most violent, tall-column type. What do they call this style of eruption?
context: The name honours Pliny the Younger, whose AD 79 letters described exactly this kind of column so precisely that scientists adopted his account as the model. So the most violent class of eruption on Earth is named after a teenage boy who simply watched carefully and wrote it down. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Younger.

question: West of Naples lies the Campi Flegrei, a true supervolcano. Its eruptions can dwarf anything Vesuvius has ever done. About 39,000 years ago it unleashed the Campanian Ignimbrite. It hurled out roughly 200 cubic kilometers of magma. Its grey ash layer, which geologists still dig up today, settled far from the volcano. How far from Naples did the ash carry?
context: The Campanian Ignimbrite spread its ash as far as Eastern Europe -- one of the biggest eruptions the Mediterranean has ever seen, and far larger than the AD 79 blast that buried Pompeii. It is a reminder that the gentle holiday coast of the Bay of Naples sits directly atop one of the most powerful volcanic systems on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campi_Flegrei.

question: In 1538, inside the restless Campi Flegrei near Pozzuoli, the ground split open and erupted for eight days straight. When it finally stopped, the terrified locals found the landscape permanently changed -- a new feature had appeared where there had been none a week earlier. What did the eight-day eruption create?
context: The new hill was named Monte Nuovo -- 'New Mountain' -- and at nearly 500 years old it is still one of the youngest mountains in Europe, built in a single week by the Campi Flegrei. It is a vivid reminder that this sleeping supervolcano can reshape the map almost overnight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campi_Flegrei.

question: In the town of Pozzuoli, built inside the Campi Flegrei, the ground does something eerie: over months and years it slowly swells upward by metres and then sinks again, lifting harbours out of the water and later dropping them back -- all without a violent earthquake. Geologists gave this slow rising and falling of the land its own name. What is this phenomenon called?
context: The word comes from Greek for 'slow earthquake': bradyseism. Heat and pressure from magma and gases deep under the Campi Flegrei push the ground up, then let it settle, moving whole neighbourhoods vertically by metres over years. In the 1980s Pozzuoli rose so much that its harbour became unusable and part of the old town had to be evacuated. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macellum_of_Pozzuoli.

question: The three marble columns still standing in the ruined Roman market at Pozzuoli each carry a neat band of small round holes, several metres up the shaft -- always in the same narrow band, never higher or lower. What made those holes in the hard marble?
context: The holes were drilled by Lithophaga, marine 'date mussels' that bore into rock -- and they can only have done so while the columns stood underwater in the sea. Because the columns never fell, that band of borings, up to about 5.8 m (19 ft) high, proves the whole market slowly sank beneath the waves and later rose back up. The geologist Charles Lyell put these columns on the frontispiece of his 'Principles of Geology' (1830). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macellum_of_Pozzuoli.

question: Beneath the streets of Naples runs a vast labyrinth cut into soft volcanic tuff. The Greeks first dug it 2,500 years ago for building stone; the Romans turned the shafts into aqueducts and water cisterns. Then, in the 1940s, as World War II reached Naples, the people of the city put the ancient caverns to a dramatic new use. What did Neapolitans use the old tunnels for during the war?
context: The caverns were enlarged with stairways and packed with tens of thousands of people sheltering from Allied bombing raids -- all cut into the same soft tuff the local volcanoes had laid down, quarried by Greeks, plumbed by Romans, and finally hiding Neapolitans from the bombs. Tuff is easy to carve yet hardens in air, which is why a single rock made Naples both buildable above and hollow below. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naples_underground_geothermal_zone.

question: In the old capital city of Nara in central Japan, more than a thousand wild sika deer roam the parks and stroll along the streets. Visitors buy small brown biscuits called shika senbei — deer crackers — and the deer swarm around anyone holding one. Over the centuries, many of the deer of Nara have learned one funny little trick to beg for a treat. What is it?
answer: Dip their heads in a bow
choices: Dip their heads in a bow
Nudge bags open with their noses
context: Nara's roughly 1,200 free-roaming sika deer are a designated natural treasure, and their head-dip 'bow' -- a learned trick used to beg for shika senbei rice crackers -- is the city's signature sight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nara_Park; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nara,_Nara.

question: For more than a thousand years, the wild deer of Nara — an old capital in central Japan — have walked the city freely and safely, mixing with people in the streets. For most of that time, killing one of the deer was punished by death. The very last person executed for it died in the year 1637. What made these deer so fiercely protected?
answer: They were revered as sacred messengers of a Shinto god
choices: They were revered as sacred messengers of a Shinto god
They were believed to carry the souls of the dead
They were royal game reserved for the emperor's hunts
They were kept as living charms to ward off fire
context: The deer of Nara were revered as sacred messengers of the god of Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Shrine). By legend the tie began when the thunder god Takemikazuchi rode to Nara's Mount Mikasa on a white deer to guard the new capital. Harming a deer stayed a capital offense until 1637, the last recorded execution for it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nara_Park; worldhistory.org/Kasuga_Taisha.

question: In the Japanese city of Nara, an ancient wooden temple hall houses the Daibutsu — a giant bronze Great Buddha cast more than 1,200 years ago. Inside that hall stands one huge wooden pillar. A hole is cut through its base, said to be the exact size of one of the giant statue's nostrils. A fun temple story tells what happens to a kid who can squeeze all the way through. What?
answer: They are granted good fortune or enlightenment
choices: They are granted good fortune or enlightenment
They must leave an offering at the altar
They may ring the temple's great bell once
They earn a blessing written by the monks
context: The pillar hole in Todai-ji's Great Buddha Hall (Daibutsuden) is said to match the size of the Daibutsu's nostril; crawling through it is a popular custom said to bring good luck or enlightenment, and a queue forms for it. The hole and the tradition are real; the reward is folklore. Source: travel/reference accounts incl. muza-chan.net 'Sightseeing Nara, the Hole in the Pillar.'  (Legend.)

question: Nara's deer are the only deer in Japan that bow -- the same trick is never seen at other deer parks like Miyajima. Researchers at Nara Women's University argued the bow is a learned habit, not an instinct, and one unusual stretch of time proved them right when the deer suddenly bowed far less. What had changed?
answer: The COVID lockdown had emptied the park of tourists
choices: The COVID lockdown had emptied the park of tourists
A harsh winter had thinned the herd's numbers
The temple had banned the sale of deer-crackers
The oldest, tamest deer had died off that year
context: Nara Women's University found the deer bow specifically to beg shika senbei from people -- and when COVID-19 travel limits emptied the park, bows fell from about 10.2 to 6.4 per session, evidence the bow is learned from tourists, not instinct. Deer at Miyajima never learned it. Source: sj.jst.go.jp/stories/2023/s0712-01p.html.

question: In 752, Nara's giant bronze Buddha was finished. To bless it, 10,000 monks and 4,000 dancers held a huge ceremony. A priest from India named Bodhisena led the last and most important act. What did he do to finish the statue?
choices: Lit a flame in its open palm
Rang a bronze bell nine times
context: The 752 'eye-opening' (kaigen) ceremony marked the Daibutsu's completion at Todai-ji. The Indian monk Bodhisena painted in the pupils before 10,000 monks and 4,000 dancers -- a sign of how far Buddhism's networks reached, carrying a priest from India to eighth-century Japan. The seated bronze Vairocana stands about 15 m tall. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Ddai-ji.

question: The Daibutsuden, the vast hall in Nara that shelters the Great Buddha, held one remarkable world record for centuries -- right up until 1998. Here is the twist: the hall standing today, rebuilt in 1709, is only about two-thirds as wide as the original, shrunk from 11 bays to 7 because the temple ran out of money. What record did even this smaller hall long hold?
answer: The largest wooden building on Earth
choices: The largest wooden building on Earth
The widest stone hall in the world
The heaviest tiled roof ever raised
The tallest timber hall ever built
context: Todai-ji's Daibutsuden was the world's largest wooden building until 1998. Completed in 1709 (about 57 m long, 50 m wide, 49 m high), it is roughly 30% smaller than its predecessor, cut from 11 bays wide to 7 for lack of funds -- so even the shrunken version held the record. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Ddai-ji.

question: Before the year 710, Japan did something strange each time an emperor died: it moved the whole capital city to a new site. Empress Genmei ended the costly habit by setting up a fixed capital at Nara. Why had the capital been moved every time an emperor died?
answer: A place where someone had died was believed spiritually polluted
choices: A place where someone had died was believed spiritually polluted
Each dead emperor's ghost was believed to haunt his old palace
The gods were believed to abandon a city once its ruler died
Priests declared a used palace unlucky for the coming harvest
context: Heijo-kyo, founded in 710 under Empress Genmei, was Japan's first permanent capital. Earlier the capital had moved after nearly every emperor's death, because a place of death was believed spiritually polluted; the Taiho Code of 701 helped centralize the state and end the practice. Nara was laid out on a vast grid modeled on Chang'an, the Tang capital of China (today's Xi'an). Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Nara_period; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heij%C5%8D-ky%C5%8D.

question: In a desert in Peru, the old Nazca people scraped huge pictures into the ground. Some lines run for miles. Up close, each one just looks like a scratch in the dirt. The big shapes only come into view from one place. Where must you look from?
context: Most Nazca figures reveal themselves best from about 500 m up, which is why the giant shapes went almost unnoticed for so long. A huge design drawn on the ground like this — by the Nazca here, or in the chalk-cut horses of England — is called a geoglyph. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines (best seen ~500 m up; 'geoglyph'); worldhistory.org/article/665/nazca-lines.

question: The Nazca desert floor is covered in dark reddish pebbles, stained by rust. The Nazca used no paint and dug no deep ditches. So how did they make their pale lines and giant animal shapes stand out on the dark ground?
answer: they scraped away the dark pebbles to bare the pale ground
choices: they scraped away the dark pebbles to bare the pale ground
they poured pale river clay along each outline
they scorched the surface stones white with rows of fire
they laid down long lines of bleached seashells
context: Each line is a shallow trough only 10-15 cm deep. The Nazca simply lifted away the dark, iron-oxide-coated pebbles that carpet the surface, baring the paler subsoil beneath — a faint colour contrast that reads clearly from above. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines (reddish iron-oxide surface pebbles removed to reveal pale subsoil; lines 10-15 cm deep).

question: On a flat plain in southern Peru, ancient people scraped away the dark stones on the surface to reveal the pale ground beneath. Their designs — long straight lines and huge animal shapes — are called the Nazca lines. Each scratch is only 10 to 15 cm deep in loose desert dirt. Wind should have wiped them out in a few lifetimes. Yet they have lasted about 2,000 years. What feature of the land explains why the shallow marks are still there?
answer: it lies in one of the driest deserts on Earth
choices: it lies in one of the driest deserts on Earth
it is sealed under a hard crust of salt
it stays buried under drifting sand
it is floored with the hardest rock on Earth
context: The Nazca pampa, on Peru's bone-dry southern coast, is one of the driest places on Earth. With almost no rain to wash them away, the shallow lines have barely eroded in some 2,000 years — the very aridity of this coastal desert is what made the drawings, and their survival, possible. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines (one of the driest places on Earth; near-total lack of rain preserves the lines).

question: On a dry plain in southern Peru, ancient Nazca artists scratched more than 70 huge animal shapes into the desert floor about 2,000 years ago. One of them has become the symbol of the whole site. It is the most common picture on Peruvian postcards and stamps, and most tourists book a small plane just to fly over it and see the whole shape from the air. About 93 m across, which animal is it?
context: The Nazca hummingbird, about 93 m long with a needle beak and outstretched wings, is the best known of the figures. The pampa holds more than 70 animals in all, among them a monkey with a tightly spiralled tail, a condor stretching some 134 m, and a spider about 47 m across. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines (hummingbird ~93 m; >70 zoomorphic figures; condor ~134 m, spider ~47 m); machutravelperu.com/blog/nazca-lines-hummingbird.

question: In 2020, on a dusty hillside above the Nazca plains of southern Peru, workers building a new tourist lookout spotted a faded shape carved into the ground. It shows a lazy, long-tailed animal about 37 m across, drawn by scraping away the dark surface stones. It dates from about 200 BCE, older than the other famous Nazca drawings. Which animal is it?
context: The 'Nazca cat,' about 37 m across, dates to roughly 200-100 BCE (the Late Paracas period) — older than the hummingbird and the other classic figures, and one of the oldest geoglyphs on the pampa. Fading and nearly lost to erosion, it was spotted only in 2020 during work on a hillside viewpoint. Source: Peru Ministry of Culture, Oct 2020, via smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/2000-year-old-cat-etching-found-peru; cnn.com/style/article/nazca-lines-peru-cat.

question: High on a Nazca hillside stands a ~35 m figure with one hand raised, so strange-looking that an early pilot nicknamed it 'the Astronaut.' In the 1960s, writers claiming the desert lines were runways for alien spacecraft pointed to it as a visiting spaceman. Archaeologists, giving the Nazca full credit for their own art, read the figure not as an alien but as a figure from Nazca belief. What do they think it actually depicts?
context: The 'ancient astronaut' idea came from Swiss writer Erich von Daniken, whose 1968 bestseller Chariots of the Gods? branded the desert's long trapezoids alien runways and this hillside figure a spaceman. Investigator Joe Nickell later laid out a giant Nazca figure using only wooden stakes and cord, showing a small team needed no help from the stars. Archaeologists read the round-headed figure as an owl-man or shaman. Source: allthatsinteresting.com/nazca-lines; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines (von Daniken 1968; Nickell's period-tool recreation).

question: For decades, new Nazca figures turned up only slowly, one at a time, as researchers combed the desert on foot. Then in 2024 the known count suddenly almost DOUBLED in a single six-month stretch — more than 300 new figures at once. What made this sudden burst of discovery possible?
answer: an AI trained to spot faint figures in old aerial photos
choices: an AI trained to spot faint figures in old aerial photos
a rare rainstorm that darkened the pale lines
a swarm of tourists' camera drones, by chance
a rediscovered box of century-old survey maps
context: In 2024 a survey by Japan's Yamagata University with IBM used AI to comb aerial imagery and turned up 303 new figurative geoglyphs in just six months — nearly doubling the known total and speeding discovery roughly 16-fold. Many are small 'relief-type' figures of people and llamas set beside ancient walking trails. Source: yamagata-u.ac.jp/en/information/info/20240924; france24.com/en/live-news/20240924-ai-research-uncovers-300-ancient-etchings.

question: For 40 years, German mathematician Maria Reiche lived next to the Nazca desert. She measured every line and swept the sand off them with a broom. Locals half-joked she was a witch. She became famous for one big idea about what the whole desert of lines really was. Their real purpose is still debated today, but which idea did she spend her life defending?
answer: a giant calendar of the sun and stars
choices: a giant calendar of the sun and stars
a giant map of the Nazca homeland
a giant plan for irrigation canals
context: Maria Reiche (1903-1998) mapped the lines for four decades and championed the idea that they formed a giant astronomical calendar marking solstices and star-risings. The theory traces to 22 June 1941, when historian Paul Kosok watched the midwinter sun set exactly along one line and called the desert 'the largest astronomy book in the world.' Today many scholars lean instead toward water and fertility ritual — and, because each animal is one unbroken line, toward ceremonial paths meant to be walked — so the calendar remains just one contested theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Reiche; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kosok; worldhistory.org/article/665/nazca-lines.  (Legend.)

question: In New Orleans, earthen levees taller than a house hold the Mississippi back. Stand atop one out in Lakeview, a neighborhood built on drained swamp that lies below sea level, look out at the passing river, then turn and look back at the town behind you. What do you see?
answer: The river runs higher than the streets.
choices: The river runs higher than the streets.
The river flows straight through the streets.
The river drops over a waterfall downtown.
The river splits the town into islands.
context: New Orleans really does sit lower than the river beside it. About 65% of the city lies at or below mean sea level, while the Mississippi at its yearly high-water mark rises to roughly 14 feet above sea level, so behind the levees the river runs higher than the streets, and only those earthen walls and the pumps hold it out. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Orleans.'

question: In 2005, Hurricane Katrina hit New Orleans. Whole new neighborhoods went under water. But the French Quarter, the oldest part of town, stayed mostly dry. It goes back to where the first settlers built in 1718. On land this flat, where was the highest, safest ground?
answer: Right along the river, on its natural high banks.
choices: Right along the river, on its natural high banks.
On the shore of Lake Pontchartrain, to the north.
Far out on a sandy island in midstream.
Up on a low hill set a mile inland.
context: In a flat delta the highest ground is the strip of land right beside the river. Every flood, the Mississippi dropped its heaviest silt first at its own edge, building a 'natural levee' ridge 10-20 feet above sea level. Bienville's settlers laid the French Quarter (the Vieux Carre) on that ridge in 1718, which is why it stayed mostly dry in Hurricane Katrina while lower, drained-swamp neighborhoods flooded. Sources: Wikipedia, 'New Orleans'; SERC/Carleton coastlines module.

question: People in New Orleans, a city in southern Louisiana built on soggy ground below sea level, say a hard rain used to lift buried coffins right out of the ground. They would float down the street. That story, plus an old French and Spanish habit brought by the city's early settlers, led New Orleans to bury its dead in one very unusual way. What way is it?
answer: Above-ground stone tombs, in rows like little streets.
choices: Above-ground stone tombs, in rows like little streets.
Deep graves sealed under heavy concrete slabs.
Graveyards set far off on high, dry ridges.
Cremation, the ashes kept inside the cathedral.
context: New Orleans buries much of its dead above ground in stone tombs, whole 'Cities of the Dead' laid out like little streets. St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, opened in 1789 on Basin Street, is the oldest: a single square block holding thousands, including the voodoo priestess Marie Laveau, believed to lie in the Glapion family crypt. The high-water-table 'floating coffins' story is the reason locals give; the French-Spanish Catholic custom of wall vaults also shaped the tradition. Sources: experienceneworleans.com; Wikipedia, 'St. Louis Cemetery.'  (Legend.)

question: The old French Quarter of New Orleans, the Vieux Carre, was settled right on the bank of the Mississippi in 1718. As the great river reaches the old city, it does one dramatic thing plain to see from the levee. What does the Mississippi do as it passes the Vieux Carre?
answer: It curls around the old city in a great bend.
choices: It curls around the old city in a great bend.
It splits into two channels around a midstream island.
It tumbles over a line of rapids downtown.
It runs dead straight for miles past the docks.
context: The Mississippi curls around the old French Quarter in a huge sweeping bend, and it is from that great crescent-shaped curve that New Orleans takes its nickname, 'the Crescent City.' Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville founded the city in 1718 for the French Mississippi Company, naming it La Nouvelle-Orleans for Philippe II, Duke of Orleans. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Orleans.'

question: At Congo Square in New Orleans, a French colonial law of 1724 gave enslaved Africans their Sundays free. By the hundreds they gathered there to drum and to dance the Bamboula and the Calinda, keeping the rhythms of their African homelands alive. Over the next century those Sunday rhythms grew into a wholly new American music, born in this city. What music was it?
context: The Code Noir of 1724 gave enslaved Africans their Sundays free, and at Congo Square they gathered by the hundreds; the architect Benjamin Latrobe, visiting in 1819, counted 500 to 600 people dancing in tribal groups. The African rhythms they kept alive there fused, over generations, into jazz. The square is now inside Louis Armstrong Park in the Treme, and you can still hear those rhythms in New Orleans jazz funerals, second-line parades, and Mardi Gras Indian processions; the name 'Congo Square' was officially restored in 2011. Source: Wikipedia, 'Congo Square.'

question: In 1913 the New Orleans engineer A. Baldwin Wood built the most powerful water pumps on Earth, giant spinning screws that sucked the swamp dry and let the city drain its marshes and raise whole new neighborhoods like Lakeview on the reclaimed land. But that triumph hid a curse: draining the swamp is the very reason New Orleans keeps sinking today. How does pulling the water out drop the land itself?
answer: The drained soil dries, rots, and packs down.
choices: The drained soil dries, rots, and packs down.
The pumps crack the bedrock, which slumps down.
Lake water seeps in and hollows the earth.
The weight of new buildings presses the mud down.
context: Wood's 1913 screw pump was 12 feet across, the largest and most powerful in the world; his 1927 version could move a million gallons every five minutes, and some 1913 pumps still ran through Hurricane Katrina. But draining the swamp let the spongy organic soil dry out, decay, and compact, so the ground itself dropped: more than half the city is now below sea level. Geographer Richard Campanella said of the pump builders, 'Their intentions were good... Instead, they created a new and bigger one.' Wood's drainage designs were copied worldwide, even helping drain the Netherlands' Zuiderzee. Source: Historic New Orleans Collection, 'The Pumps That Built (and Sank) the City.'

question: For thousands of years the Mississippi has wandered across its delta, switching course again and again, and today it is straining to do so once more, to forsake its long, sluggish channel past Baton Rouge and New Orleans for a shorter, steeper run to the Gulf. Since 1963 a single giant floodgate complex, the Old River Control Structure, has fought to hold it in place. Where is the river trying to go instead?
context: The Old River Control Structure, completed in 1963, holds roughly a 70/30 split, letting about 30% of the flow go to the Atchafalaya while the rest stays in the channel past Baton Rouge and New Orleans. In the great flood of 1973 the river nearly tore the structure out and almost captured the Atchafalaya for good, which would have left both cities stranded on a stagnant backwater while the Mississippi built a whole new delta near Morgan City. The close call forced the Army Corps of Engineers to add an auxiliary structure. Source: Wikipedia, 'Old River Control Structure.'

question: Coastal Louisiana is drowning. Since the 1930s the marshy shoreline at the mouth of the Mississippi River has lost nearly 1,900 square miles of wetland, an area the size of Delaware, slipping into the Gulf of Mexico at times as fast as a football field of marsh every hour. The land is sinking because the mud that once built it and fed the roots of the marsh grass no longer arrives from upriver. What main cause do scientists point to for the missing mud?
answer: Levees and dams upstream trap the river's mud.
choices: Levees and dams upstream trap the river's mud.
Salt water from the Gulf poisons the marsh grass.
Hurricanes have torn the wetlands away for good.
Drainage pumps have sucked the coastal marshes dry.
context: Because upstream levees and dams keep the Mississippi from spilling over and laying down fresh sediment, the delta marshes are no longer being rebuilt, and they are sinking and washing away. Coastal Louisiana has lost nearly 1,900 square miles of land since the 1930s, an area about the size of Delaware, at times vanishing as fast as a football field of wetland every hour, leaving New Orleans ever more exposed to storms. Sources: USGS via nola.com; mississippiriverdelta.org.

question: When the Statue of Liberty was set up on her small island in New York Harbor in 1886, her outer skin was a shiny reddish-brown metal, the colour of a new penny. She stayed that colour for years. Then, slowly, over the decades, she turned the pale mint-green you see today. What actually turned her green?
choices: Workers repainted her a protective green
Her bronze surface tarnished like an old coin
Salt spray bleached the dark metal pale
context: The statue's skin is copper only about 2.4 mm thick -- roughly two pennies stacked. Air, water, and pollution weathered it to a green layer of verdigris (copper patina) that now actually protects the metal underneath; the green is corrosion, not paint or bronze. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Liberty

question: In the middle of Manhattan in New York City stretches Central Park, a huge green rectangle covering 843 acres. Its rolling meadows, quiet lakes, and rocky woods look like a piece of wilderness the city just happened to grow up around. But the truth about that natural-looking scenery is surprising. What is it?
answer: Almost every hill, pond, and tree was placed on purpose
choices: Almost every hill, pond, and tree was placed on purpose
It is the last untouched wilderness left on the island
It was once a royal hunting forest from colonial days
It formed in a glacier-carved valley long ago
context: Central Park only looks natural. Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux's winning 'Greensward Plan' (chosen April 1858) landscaped the whole park from scratch in the 1850s-60s -- the 'natural' park is the most man-made thing in the city. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park

question: Several great suspension bridges hang over the rivers around New York City. Only one of them was the longest bridge in the whole world on the day it opened in 1883. Its main span stretched almost 1,600 feet across the East River, joining the island of Manhattan to Brooklyn for the very first time. Which bridge was it?
context: The Brooklyn Bridge opened May 24, 1883; its 1,595.5-foot main span made it the world's longest suspension bridge, and it was among the first strung from bundled steel wire -- each of its four main cables holds 5,282 galvanized steel wires. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge

question: Grand Central is New York City's grand train station. High over its main hall a huge blue-green vaulted ceiling shows the gold stars of the zodiac, painted like a great map of the night sky. Two months after the station opened in 1913, a sharp-eyed commuter looked up on his way to work and told the newspapers something was wrong with the star map. What was the mistake?
answer: The whole sky is reversed, east swapped with west
choices: The whole sky is reversed, east swapped with west
Two of the twelve zodiac signs are missing
The stars glow in the wrong seasonal colors
A thirteenth constellation was invented and added
context: A commuter spotted the reversed zodiac within two months of the 1913 opening. Officials floated a 'God's-eye view from outside the heavens' explanation; astronomer Harold Jacoby's leading theory is that the painter laid the flat sky-chart on the floor and projected it upward, flipping the image. https://www.untappedcities.com/the-hidden-history-of-grand-central-terminals-celestial-ceiling/

question: Grand Central Terminal is the great train station in the heart of New York City. Its main concourse is roofed by a huge painted ceiling showing the zodiac in gold stars on a turquoise sky. In the 1990s, workers scrubbed away decades of grime and made the whole ceiling glow again — except near the star sign Cancer, where they left one small square dirty on purpose. Why keep that one grimy patch?
answer: To show how much indoor tobacco smoke had blackened it
choices: To show how much indoor tobacco smoke had blackened it
To hide an old water stain they could not remove
To preserve the original artist's faded signature
To mark the center point of the painted sky
context: During the 1990s restoration, one dark rectangle near Cancer was deliberately left uncleaned -- a preserved patch showing how much tar and nicotine from decades of indoor tobacco smoking had blackened the whole ceiling. https://www.untappedcities.com/the-hidden-history-of-grand-central-terminals-celestial-ceiling/

question: Central Park is the giant green rectangle in the middle of Manhattan in New York City. Its peaceful meadows and duck ponds give no hint of the violence that built them. To clear the rocky ridges and swampy hollows on the site in the 1850s, workers set off enormous blasting charges of gunpowder day after day. Just how much gunpowder did leveling the whole site take?
answer: More than was fired at the Battle of Gettysburg
choices: More than was fired at the Battle of Gettysburg
More than was fired at the Battle of Bunker Hill
More than was fired at the Battle of Yorktown
More than was fired at the siege of the Alamo
context: Building Central Park meant hauling out about 5 million cubic feet of soil and rock and trucking in over 18,500 cubic yards of topsoil from Long Island and New Jersey -- and blasting the rocky site used more gunpowder than was fired at the Battle of Gettysburg. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park

question: To sink the Brooklyn Bridge's huge stone towers into the riverbed, workers dug inside giant air-pressurized underwater chambers called caissons. Many came up wracked with pain -- some paralyzed, some killed -- by an illness the doctors of the 1870s could not explain. What do we now call it?
context: Surfacing too fast from the pressurized caissons caused decompression sickness -- 'caisson disease,' the bends. Chief engineer John A. Roebling died of tetanus before construction began; his son Washington was left paralyzed by it and directed the work by telescope from his bedroom while Emily Warren Roebling ran the site for years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge

question: Manhattan's streets form a strict grid of squares. One older road breaks the pattern by slanting across the whole island. Where it crosses the square blocks, it opens a famous triangle plaza: Times Square, Herald Square, Madison Square. Which road is it?
context: Broadway is the one great diagonal breaking Manhattan's grid -- an older route following the island's natural lay of the land. It slices across the right-angle streets and carves out the triangular 'squares.' The rigid grid itself was set by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioners%27_Plan_of_1811

question: The Hudson River flows past Manhattan. Twice a day its current stops and runs backward as salty ocean water pushes 150 miles upstream to Troy. The Lenape called it 'the river that flows both ways.' Because of this, the lower Hudson is not really a river, but what?
context: The Hudson beside Manhattan is a tidal estuary -- an arm of the sea whose current reverses with the ocean tides all the way up to Troy, about 150 miles inland. The Lenape/Mahican name Muhheakantuck means 'the river that flows both ways.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River

question: New York's tallest skyscrapers cluster in two spots: Midtown and the Financial District. That is no accident. Such huge towers must sit on very hard, ancient bedrock, which happens to lie near the surface in just those two places. What is this tough base rock called?
context: Manhattan's skyscrapers stand on hard metamorphic bedrock -- chiefly Manhattan schist -- well suited to carrying enormous towers. Where that rock lies near the surface, in Midtown and the Financial District, is where the tallest clusters rise. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan

question: When the Empire State Building opened in New York City in 1931, it was the tallest tower on Earth, its 102 stories soaring above Manhattan. The slender metal spire crowning the very top was not mere decoration — it was built for a strange, futuristic job that never once worked in practice. What was the spire originally meant to do?
answer: Let zeppelins dock and drop off passengers
choices: Let zeppelins dock and drop off passengers
Broadcast the world's first television signal
Serve as a giant lightning rod for the city
Hold a rotating searchlight for ships at sea
context: The Empire State Building's spire was designed as a mooring mast where zeppelins would dock and let passengers off -- but the plan was abandoned once it was clear the high winds swirling around the tower made airship docking impossible. Built in about 410 days during the Great Depression, the tower stayed the world's tallest for roughly 40 years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Building

question: New York City drinks over a billion gallons of water every single day. All of it is carried through long tunnels from mountain reservoirs deep in the Catskill Mountains of upstate New York, more than 100 miles to the north of the city. What is the astonishing thing about how nearly all of that water reaches the city's taps?
answer: It runs the whole way downhill by gravity, with no pumps
choices: It runs the whole way downhill by gravity, with no pumps
It is filtered clean through the bedrock as it travels
It is pulled from the Atlantic and then desalinated
It is chilled inside mountain tunnels to stay fresh
context: About 95% of New York City's drinking water -- over a billion gallons a day -- arrives by gravity alone, no pumps, flowing downhill through aqueducts from Catskill and Delaware watershed reservoirs up to about 125 miles north. Part of it runs through the Delaware Aqueduct, at about 85 miles the world's longest continuous tunnel, carrying roughly half the city's water beneath the Hudson River without a single pump. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_water_supply_system

question: New Zealand's two main islands look alone in the South Pacific. But maps of the sea floor show they are just the high peaks of one huge slab of land. Most of it is under the ocean, hidden from every world map. What did scientists name this sunken continent?
context: About 94% of Zealandia lies underwater; only New Zealand, New Caledonia and a few smaller islands rise above the sea. Because it is genuine, continuous continental crust -- not scattered ocean islands -- geologists formally argued in 2017 that it counts as a true continent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealandia

question: New Zealand is one of only two lands that poke above the waves from a huge sunken continent in the southwest Pacific Ocean called Zealandia. Nearly all of Zealandia — about 94% of it — lies drowned under the sea. New Zealand's only partner still above water is a chain of tropical islands far to the north. Which land is that partner?
context: New Caledonia and New Zealand are the only large pieces of the continent Zealandia to break the surface -- New Caledonia near its northern end, New Zealand toward the south. Everything between is drowned continental shelf. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealandia

question: The whole continent under New Zealand — called Zealandia — is almost entirely sunk beneath the Pacific Ocean. Yet the highest point of dry land still poking above it rises 3,724 m into the clouds. It stands as a snow-and-ice peak in the Southern Alps of New Zealand's South Island. Which mountain is that highest point?
context: Officially Aoraki / Mount Cook, keeping its Maori name Aoraki. At 3,724 m it is the highest point not only of New Zealand but of the whole continent of Zealandia -- nearly all of which lies drowned beneath the Pacific. Source: geosociety.org/gsa-today/march-april-2017/zealandia-earths-hidden-continent

question: About 80 million years ago, New Zealand broke away from the other continents. It drifted alone so long that one whole group of land animals never got there. Only two tiny kinds ever crossed the open sea to settle. Birds filled in the empty space. With nothing on the ground to hunt them, some birds gave up flight for good. Which group of land animal is New Zealand almost entirely missing?
context: New Zealand's only native land mammals are two tiny bat species. With no cats, rats, deer or monkeys to hunt them or compete with them, birds and insects evolved to fill the empty roles -- several birds even lost the power of flight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna_of_New_Zealand

question: Trace your finger straight down New Zealand's South Island and you follow one of Earth's great cracks in the crust -- a nearly ruler-straight boundary, about 600 km long, where the Pacific and Australian plates grind past each other. Along it a young mountain range is still being shoved skyward. What is this plate-boundary fault called?
context: The Alpine Fault runs about 600 km up the spine of the South Island, where the Pacific and Australian plates slide past each other and heave up the Southern Alps. It ruptures in huge earthquakes roughly every few centuries; the last great one struck around 1717 AD. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_Fault

question: In the wild southwest of New Zealand's South Island, Ice Age glaciers cut a maze of steep valleys. The sea later filled them, forming long dark arms walled by cliffs. The most famous is Milford Sound, where Mitre Peak jumps 1,692 m out of the water and over 6 metres of rain fall each year. Rudyard Kipling called it the 'eighth Wonder of the World.' What is this whole drowned-valley region called?
context: The region is named for its fiords -- sea-drowned glacier valleys such as Milford Sound. Though early sailors called them 'sounds' (a word for river-carved inlets), they are technically fiords, gouged by ice and later flooded by the sea. Milford is one of the wettest inhabited places on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Sound

question: Lake Taupo, in the middle of New Zealand's North Island, looks like a calm holiday lake. But its broad round basin is really a huge scar in the Earth. About 25,600 years ago, this spot blew up with such power that it threw out 1,170 cubic km of rock and ash, then sank into the giant crater the lake now fills. Blasts this size are called supervolcanoes, and only a few are known on Earth. Out of every super-eruption in history, what is the Taupo blast?
context: The Oruanui eruption about 25,600 years ago was Earth's most recent VEI-8 event -- the very top of the volcanic explosivity scale, and no volcano anywhere has erupted on that scale since. Lake Taupo sits in the Taupo Volcanic Zone, fed by the Pacific plate diving beneath the North Island, the same engine behind Rotorua's geysers and boiling mud. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taup%C5%8D_Volcanic_Zone

question: In the green farmland of Ireland's Boyne Valley stands Newgrange, a huge grass-topped stone mound covering an ancient burial chamber. Farmers of the Neolithic age built it around 3200 BC — long before writing, long before metal tools. That makes this Irish tomb about 500 years older than two of the most famous ancient landmarks on Earth. Which two?
answer: Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza
choices: Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza
Petra and the Great Wall of China
context: Newgrange went up around 3200 BC -- roughly five centuries before either Stonehenge's great stone circle or Egypt's Great Pyramid of Giza. Its Neolithic builders had no metal tools and no writing. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newgrange ; https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: Newgrange is a huge grass-topped burial mound in eastern Ireland, built more than 5,000 years ago. The front of it shines with a curved wall of bright white stone, studded with dark round rocks like pebbles. Its Stone Age builders hauled that white rock about 80 km from the Wicklow Mountains, working with no wheels and no metal tools. What is that white stone?
context: The bright facade is white quartz carried from the Wicklow Mountains, set with dark granite cobbles from the Mourne Mountains to the north -- stone moved dozens of kilometres by people with no carts. (The gleaming wall is a modern reconstruction from quartz found scattered at the mound's foot.) Source: https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: Newgrange is a massive grass-topped stone dome in eastern Ireland, about 85 metres across. Its Stone Age builders, working around 3200 BC with no metal tools and no wheels, gathered every rock and basketful of earth by hand and stacked it all up by muscle alone. Roughly how much stone and earth did they pile up to build it?
context: The mound is about 85 metres wide, 12-13 metres high, and covers roughly an acre -- an estimated 200,000 tonnes of stone and earth, all gathered and stacked by hand in the Stone Age. Source: https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: The builders of Newgrange aimed their whole tomb at a single sunrise each year. Above the doorway they left a small stone opening, so that at dawn on that one morning a blade of sunlight shoots 19 metres straight down the passage and floods the pitch-dark inner chamber -- even with the great stone door shut. Which sunrise did they build it to catch?
context: For a few mornings around the winter solstice -- the shortest days of the year -- the rising sun threads the passage and lights the inner chamber for about 17 minutes before fading, a light show engineered over 5,000 years ago. Sources: https://www.newgrange.com/winter-solstice-newgrange.htm ; https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: At the door of Newgrange sits a huge 5-tonne slab. It is carved with Ireland's most famous ancient symbol: a bold pattern of coils winding in and out of each other. It was cut 5,000 years ago with only flint, since Ireland then had no metal at all. What is this coiled symbol called?
context: The great entrance stone (Kerbstone K1) carries a bold triple spiral -- a 'triskele' -- about 3 metres long, cut with nothing but stone and flint tools. Another famous triskele hides deep inside the chamber. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newgrange ; https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: Newgrange's inner chamber is roofed by corbelling -- flat stones stacked so each juts a little further inward than the one below, with no mortar anywhere, meeting in a dome nearly 6 metres up. Astonishingly, after more than 5,000 years that chamber is still bone-dry. What clever trick did the builders use on the roof-stones to keep the rain out?
answer: they cut grooves in the stones to run rainwater off
choices: they cut grooves in the stones to run rainwater off
they sealed the joints with sticky river clay
they smeared the stones with black pine tar
they dug hidden drains beneath the chamber floor
context: The mortar-free corbelled vault has kept the chamber watertight for over 5,000 years -- partly because the builders cut grooves into the roof-stones to channel rainwater outward, away from the room below. Source: https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: At dawn on a December morning in 1967, archaeologist Michael J. O'Kelly stood alone in the black inner chamber of Newgrange and became the first person in modern times to watch the ancient sunbeam creep down the long passage and light up the tomb. Studying the small stone slot above the entrance that let the beam in, O'Kelly gave it the plain English name it still carries today. What did he call it?
context: On 21 December 1967, Michael J. O'Kelly watched the solstice beam creep in, 'lighting up everything as it came' -- the first recorded modern witness -- and coined the term 'roof-box' for the opening that channels the light. Source: https://www.rte.ie/brainstorm/2025/1220/1549633-newgrange-winter-solstice-light-show-sunrise-discovery-michael-j-okelly/

question: Newgrange does not stand alone. It rises in Bru na Boinne, a sacred bend of Ireland's River Boyne where Stone Age people raised a whole ritual landscape of tombs, built long before the age of the Egyptian pharaohs. Two other giant passage-tombs share this ground with Newgrange, each a grass-topped mound with its own carved stones and dark inner chamber. What are the names of these two great sister-tombs?
context: Newgrange, Knowth, and Dowth are the three great passage-tombs of Bru na Boinne -- a Neolithic ritual landscape of at least 90 monuments in a loop of the River Boyne, older than the pharaohs and named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993. Knowth alone holds more than a third of all the megalithic art in Western Europe. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%BA_na_B%C3%B3inne ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowth

question: Niagara Falls sits on the border between New York and the Canadian province of Ontario. It is really three waterfalls sitting side by side. The big curved Horseshoe Falls tumbles over on the Canadian side. Two smaller falls — American Falls and Bridal Veil Falls — pour across the U.S. side. How much of the river's water pours over the Horseshoe alone?
context: Niagara is really three waterfalls side by side: the giant Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side, the wide American Falls, and the slender Bridal Veil Falls beside it. The Horseshoe crest curves about 670 m (2,200 ft) across, and its water drops an average of 57 m (188 ft) into a plunge pool roughly 35 m deep. Almost the whole river — close to nine-tenths of the flow — thunders over the Horseshoe alone, leaving only about a tenth for the American and Bridal Veil falls combined. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls

question: Niagara Falls thunders over a cliff on the border between the United States and Canada, where the Niagara River tumbles into a deep rocky gorge. Right at the brink of the drop, a big wooded island called Goat Island stands midstream, planted exactly where the river tips over the edge. What does Goat Island do to the great waterfall?
answer: Splits it into two separate falls
choices: Splits it into two separate falls
Splits it into three separate falls
Separates the small Bridal Veil Falls off
Bends the flow into the Horseshoe's curve
context: Goat Island parts the river into the Canadian Horseshoe Falls and the American Falls. A second, much smaller scrap of rock — Luna Island — then splits the slender Bridal Veil Falls off from the American Falls, which is how Niagara ends up as three falls in all. Both big falls were already there when Europeans first described the site before 1678. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls

question: Stand at Niagara and you'd swear the falls were fixed in place forever — but geologists have proved they are not. Over the roughly 12,000 years since the Ice Age, the falls have shifted about 11 km from the cliff near Queenston where they first began to thunder. What are the falls slowly doing?
choices: Sinking down into a deepening pit
Growing taller as fallen rock piles up
Drifting sideways toward the Canadian shore
context: A waterfall that walks: Niagara gnaws its way upstream, toward Lake Erie, leaving the long gorge behind it as its trail. It once retreated fast — up to about a metre a year — but since engineers diverted much of the flow, today's regulated erosion has slowed to roughly 0.3 m a year or less (some estimates near 0.1 m). Source: ijc.org/en/niagara-falls-moving

question: Niagara's cliff is built in two layers: a hard cap of Lockport dolostone resting on a bed of Rochester shale. This layering is the very reason the falls keep crumbling their way upstream. What is the plunging river actually doing to the cliff to make it retreat?
answer: Scooping out the shale bed from under the cap
choices: Scooping out the shale bed from under the cap
Grinding the dolostone cap thinner from above
Freezing in the shale and cracking it apart
Dissolving the dolostone cap in the river water
context: The river can't easily attack the tough Lockport dolostone cap, so instead it hollows out the weak Rochester shale underneath until the overhanging ledge, left unsupported, snaps off. Geologists call a waterfall that eats its way upstream like this a 'knickpoint.' Source: serc.carleton.edu/vignettes/collection/25474.html

question: In late March 1848, the water over Niagara's crest slowed to a bare trickle. The great riverbed lay bare and drying in the sun. Curious townsfolk climbed down onto the naked rock. By many accounts, what long-buried objects did they pry out of the mud?
answer: Old muskets, bayonets and iron tomahawks
choices: Old muskets, bayonets and iron tomahawks
Spanish gold coins and jeweled crosses
Dinosaur bones and ancient fossil shells
Ship timbers and heavy iron anchors
context: With the falls stilled, people reportedly walked far out on the dry bed — some all the way to Goat Island, a few even driving buggies — and a cavalry troop is said to have paraded on the exposed rock. Treasure-hunters dug up weapons from the War of 1812, which had been fought along this very river. These colourful accounts are widely retold but not all independently verified. Source: smithsonianmag.com/travel/when-niagara-falls-ran-dry-180972198  (Legend.)

question: On the morning of March 29, 1848, people living near Niagara Falls on the U.S.–Canada border woke to an eerie silence. The great falls that usually thundered day and night had all but stopped. The riverbed below was drying to mud, and children walked out on rocks nobody had ever seen. Something upstream, out on Lake Erie, had choked off almost the entire flow of the Niagara River. What had blocked it?
answer: A huge jam of lake ice had dammed it
choices: A huge jam of lake ice had dammed it
A sudden earthquake had shifted its channel
A landslide had buried the gorge in rock
A long drought had emptied Lake Erie
context: A warm spell cracked the winter ice on Lake Erie; then easterly winds shoved the floes into the mouth of the Niagara River, where they piled into a natural ice dam between Buffalo and Fort Erie. For roughly 30 to 40 hours barely a trickle went over the crest — the only near-total stoppage ever recorded. When the dam gave way, the river roared back to life. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls

question: A few kilometres below the falls, the Niagara gorge makes a sharp right-angle turn. The whole river erupts into a huge, deep basin of spinning water called the Niagara Whirlpool. About 5,500 years ago, the falls eroded backward and broke into something hidden underground. What did the retreating falls cut into?
answer: An old river gorge, long buried under debris
choices: An old river gorge, long buried under debris
A soft pocket of ash from an old volcano
A deep cavern carved by underground streams
A crack left open by a long-ago earthquake
context: The falls sliced into the St. David's Gorge, an ancient valley that an earlier river had carved and glaciers had then packed with loose debris, lying crosswise to Niagara's path. The whirlpool basin is about 518 m long, 365 m wide and up to 38 m deep, and it can even run backward — at full flow the water spins counter-clockwise, but the churning sometimes reverses and forces incoming water to dive beneath itself to reach the outlet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Whirlpool

question: In June 1969, engineers did something astonishing: they switched the American Falls off. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers dumped tens of thousands of tons of rock across the river, building a dam that shoved the entire flow over to the Horseshoe Falls and left the American Falls bone dry for months. Why did they deliberately shut the falls down?
answer: To let geologists examine the crumbling rock face
choices: To let geologists examine the crumbling rock face
To hunt the dry riverbed for sunken treasure
To film a blockbuster movie on the bare cliff
To lay the footings for a new stone bridge
context: Starting June 9, 1969, the Army Corps built a 600-foot cofferdam out of more than 28,000 tons of rock, steering the river toward the Horseshoe Falls and leaving the American Falls dry for about five months so scientists could study its unstable, crumbling face. Source: history.com/articles/niagara-falls-dewatering-1969

question: In 1969, engineers at Niagara Falls built a temporary dam upstream and shut off the American Falls entirely so they could study its crumbling cliff face up close. When the water stopped, they found a huge heap of fallen sandstone boulders piled at the foot of the dry cliff, dumped there by past rockfalls. Everyone assumed the pile ought to be hauled away to make the falls look grand again. The study turned up a surprise. What were those boulders actually doing?
answer: Bracing the cliff and holding it up
choices: Bracing the cliff and holding it up
Cementing into a solid new stone ledge
Making the cliff collapse even faster
Washing slowly downstream in the current
context: The talus — rubble from rockfalls in 1931 and 1954 — was actually propping up the fragile cliff. Clearing it away would only trigger MORE collapse, so in 1975 the International Joint Commission decided to leave the boulders in place and simply pin the rock face with bolts and cement. Source: history.com/articles/niagara-falls-dewatering-1969

question: Niagara Falls is astonishingly young — it simply did not exist 13,000 years ago. At the close of the last Ice Age, the glaciers that had buried Southern Ontario under 2–3 km of ice finally melted back. What did that great melt do to give birth to the falls?
answer: It filled the Great Lakes, which spilled over a long ridge
choices: It filled the Great Lakes, which spilled over a long ridge
It cracked open a fault that split the land apart
It let the sea rush inland and flood a deep valley
It uncovered a volcano that blasted out a gorge
context: As the ice sheets melted about 12,500 years ago, the newly filled Great Lakes had to drain toward the sea — and their overflow began pouring over the edge of a long cliff-like ridge called the Niagara Escarpment, near Queenston. That first plunge was the birth of the falls, which have been marching upstream ever since. Source: niagaraparks.com/visit-niagara-parks/plan-your-visit/niagara-falls-geology-facts-figures

question: In Viking-age Scandinavia, someone who wanted to record a name or a boast owned no paper, no pen, and no ink -- none of it had reached the frozen North. Their whole alphabet was built from short, straight lines. So how did a Viking actually make these letters?
answer: Cut them into wood or stone with a knife
choices: Cut them into wood or stone with a knife
Pressed them into wet clay with a reed
Brushed them onto bark with berry dye
Wove them into cloth with coloured thread
context: Runes are an alphabet made to be knifed into wood and stone -- no paper or ink required. Being cut by hand is why they are all short, sharp strokes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runes

question: Our word 'alphabet' is stitched from the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta. The Norse of Scandinavia named their own row of runes with the very same trick -- by running its first six letters together into one word. What did the Vikings call their set of runes?
context: The runic alphabet is the FUTHARK, named f-u-th-a-r-k after its first six runes -- the same naming trick behind 'alphabet' (alpha + beta). The 'aett' was a group of eight runes within it; ogham and Cyrillic are entirely separate scripts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runes

question: At Jelling in Denmark stands a great royal runestone, raised around 965 CE by King Harald Bluetooth. Its runes spell out a boast: that Harald had 'won for himself all Denmark and Norway' -- and then done one more thing that changed his people forever. What else does the stone boast that Harald did?
context: The inscription calls him 'the Harald who won for himself all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian.' Because it records the kingdom's conversion, the stone is nicknamed 'Denmark's baptismal certificate' -- though remember it is a king's own boast in stone, not neutral history. Source: en.natmus.dk/historical-knowledge/denmark/prehistoric-period-until-1050-ad/the-viking-age/the-monuments-at-jelling/the-jelling-stone/  (Legend.)

question: One face of the great Jelling stone in Denmark shows Christ with his arms flung wide -- but he isn't nailed to a wooden cross. Instead his body is wrapped and tangled in ribbon-like branches, as though held fast in a living tree. This carving, made around 965 CE, holds a famous record. What record is it?
answer: The oldest image of Christ in Scandinavia
choices: The oldest image of Christ in Scandinavia
The oldest human figure carved in the North
The only image of Christ on any runestone
The first Christian carving in Scandinavia
context: It is the oldest known image of Christ found in Scandinavia. Scholars think the carver posed Christ 'hanging in a tree' on purpose, to echo Odin, who in Norse myth hung nine nights on the world-tree Yggdrasil -- the old gods giving way to the new faith, frozen in stone. Source: en.natmus.dk/historical-knowledge/denmark/prehistoric-period-until-1050-ad/the-viking-age/the-monuments-at-jelling/the-jelling-stone/

question: Visitors to Jelling in Denmark today see the great runestone as bare grey granite -- rough, weathered, and plain. But researchers studied tiny traces caught deep in the carved grooves. They realised the stone looked utterly different the day King Harald first raised it. How did the Jelling stone look at first?
context: The bare grey stone was once painted in vivid colour. Denmark's National Museum used surviving specks of pigment to reconstruct the original hues -- a reminder that Viking monuments, like ancient Greek temples, once blazed with colour rather than standing plain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelling_stones

question: Every phone, headset, and speaker that pairs wirelessly carries a small blue 'Bluetooth' symbol. Engineers picked that name in 1997 after King Harald Bluetooth of Denmark, who had once united quarrelling Danish tribes -- just as the technology unites gadgets. And the story goes that the little symbol hides a secret about the king himself. What is the Bluetooth logo said to be?
answer: His two initials, joined into one rune
choices: His two initials, joined into one rune
A tiny map of his united kingdom
The shape of his blackened tooth
context: The Bluetooth NAME really was inspired by Harald Bluetooth -- proposed by Intel's Jim Kardach in 1997 because Harald united Denmark as the tech unites devices. The logo being his bind-rune (the runes Hagall/H and Bjarkan/B merged) is the popular, widely-repeated story rather than a documented fact. His own nickname likely came from a dark, dead tooth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluetooth  (Legend.)

question: Denmark's Jelling stones are famous, but the most remarkable runestone of all stands in Sweden. Around 800 CE a father named Varinn raised the tall grey Rok stone in memory of his dead son Vamod. Among the many thousands of runestones known across Scandinavia, the Rok stone holds one celebrated record. What record does it hold?
answer: The longest runic inscription ever found
choices: The longest runic inscription ever found
The tallest runestone in all Sweden
context: The Rok stone carries about 760 runes -- the longest known runic inscription -- carved across all five faces of the slab. It is also a puzzle-box of cipher runes and riddles, and it even name-drops the Gothic king Theodoric the Great on his horse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%B6k_runestone

question: Runes from Viking Scandinavia look sharp and angular -- built from diagonal and upright strokes, but almost never a flat horizontal line running across a letter. This was no style choice at all; it came straight from the physical way every rune was made. Why did rune-carvers avoid horizontal strokes?
answer: It runs along the grain and splits the plank
choices: It runs along the grain and splits the plank
It was the hardest stroke to cut cleanly
It took twice as long to carve
It needed a much longer knife to cut
context: Runes are angular on purpose. Cut by knife into wood, a horizontal stroke runs along the grain -- blurring the letter and threatening to split the plank -- so carvers used clean diagonal and upright cuts. Curves were dropped for the same reason: they are hard to slice cleanly. Runes also had no fixed direction, running left-to-right, right-to-left, or alternating line by line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runes

question: Wind and the spinning Earth bend the ocean's surface currents into five huge, slow whirlpools. Two turn in the Pacific, two in the Atlantic, and one in the Indian Ocean. Each one covers a whole ocean basin. What are these five ocean whirlpools called?
context: Each of the five subtropical gyres turns clockwise north of the equator and counterclockwise to the south. Eddies are much smaller swirls, a maelstrom is one violent whirlpool, and vortices can be any size — only 'gyre' names an ocean-wide loop. Source: oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/gyre.html

question: Each of the five ocean gyres gathers drifting plastic into a patch of garbage in its calm center. One of these patches covers an area about twice the size of Texas, and it was the first one ever found — a yacht captain sailed into it by accident in 1997. Which ocean garbage patch is it?
context: It drifts in the calm heart of the North Pacific Gyre, halfway between California and Hawaii. Yacht captain Charles Moore sailed into it by accident in 1997, and oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer coined the name 'garbage patch.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pacific_garbage_patch

question: One ocean whirlpool is the biggest on Earth. Four mighty currents ring it. It covers about 20 million square kilometers of turning sea. A single drop of water takes about four and a half years to ride around it. Which of the five gyres is this giant?
context: The North Pacific Gyre spans roughly 20 million square kilometers, walled by the North Equatorial, Kuroshio, North Pacific, and California currents. A drop of water takes about 54 months to finish one loop. Source: grokipedia.com/page/North_Pacific_Gyre

question: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is a vast swirl of floating plastic trash in the North Pacific Ocean, drifting roughly halfway between Hawaii and California. It spreads across a huge stretch of open water — bigger than the state of Texas. But no satellite has ever taken its picture from space. No camera in orbit can see it at all. Why is something that enormous invisible from orbit?
answer: It's really a thin haze of fingernail-size microplastics, not a solid raft
choices: It's really a thin haze of fingernail-size microplastics, not a solid raft
It sinks far too deep below the ocean surface for any camera to spot
It stays hidden beneath a permanent, thick bank of ocean storm clouds
It drifts far too fast for any orbiting satellite to lock onto it
context: About 94% of the patch's estimated 1.8 trillion pieces are microplastics smaller than a fingernail — so diffuse the 'patch' is more a peppery soup than an island you could ever walk on. Source: nature.com/articles/s41598-018-22939-w

question: The Ocean Cleanup is a non-profit group that scoops trash out of the sea. In recent years its ships hauled up and weighed the plastic drifting in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, the giant plastic swirl in the North Pacific between Hawaii and California. One kind of debris outweighed every other, nearly half (about 46%) of the total mass. Which kind of debris makes up almost half the patch's weight?
context: The 2018 Ocean Cleanup study put the patch's plastic near 79,000 tonnes, and roughly 46% of that mass was discarded or lost fishing gear — 'ghost' nets that keep snaring sea life for years. Source: nature.com/articles/s41598-018-22939-w

question: Out in the middle of the North Atlantic Ocean drifts the Sargasso Sea, a warm patch of water choked with rafts of golden floating seaweed. Sailors have known it for centuries and eels are born in its depths. In one striking way it is unlike every other named sea on planet Earth. What is it that makes the Sargasso Sea one of a kind?
answer: It is the only sea with no land coastline at all
choices: It is the only sea with no land coastline at all
It is the only sea that never freezes over in winter
It is the only sea lying entirely below global sea level
It is the only sea where no fish are able to live
context: The Sargasso has no land borders whatsoever — it is walled instead by four ocean currents: the Gulf Stream, the North Atlantic, the Canary, and the North Equatorial. It is the only sea on Earth defined by moving water alone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea

question: In 1492, Christopher Columbus's ships pushed west into the Sargasso Sea and found the water matted with mile after mile of thick golden weed. His sailors grew frightened — not of storms or monsters, but of the seaweed itself. What did Columbus's crew fear the Sargassum would do?
answer: snag the ships and hold them trapped forever
choices: snag the ships and hold them trapped forever
clog the hulls until the timbers rotted away
hide sea serpents coiled within the weed
grow thick enough to walk across to land
context: Columbus's 1492 crossing left the first written account of the Sargasso Sea. His crew's dread of being caught fast in the weed seeded centuries of legends about ships trapped forever in the Sargassum — though the weed never actually stops a vessel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea

question: The Sargasso Sea is a calm patch of the North Atlantic Ocean east of the Caribbean. It is one of the strangest seas on Earth: it has no coast at all, and is ringed only by ocean currents. It gets its name from its golden Sargassum weed, which drifts in great rafts across the surface. Biologists give this seaweed a rare label — 'holopelagic' — for the remarkable way it lives out its entire life. What is true of Sargassum weed across its whole life cycle?
answer: It drifts on the open sea and even breeds there, never touching bottom
choices: It drifts on the open sea and even breeds there, never touching bottom
It dies back each winter, then regrows from spores when spring returns
It anchors to a reef to release its spores, then tears loose and floats off
It sinks to the seabed each night and rises to the surface each day
context: 'Holopelagic' means Sargassum completes its whole life — growing, drifting, and breeding — without ever attaching to the bottom. The Sargasso's water is so clear that divers can see down as far as 60 meters. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea

question: Around 30° north, the belt of ocean surrounding the Sargasso Sea can go so windless that old sailing ships sat becalmed for weeks, their sails hanging dead, unable to move. Spanish crews gave this dead-calm zone a grim nickname: the 'horse latitudes.' Where did that strange name come from?
answer: Crews threw dying horses overboard to save their drinking water
choices: Crews threw dying horses overboard to save their drinking water
The glassy calm water mirrored the shape of a horse's head
Wild horses once swam across these waters between continents
The first ship to chart the zone was named the Sea Horse
context: Becalmed for weeks with drinking water running low, crews reportedly threw dead and dying horses overboard to save what water remained — the grim story behind the name 'horse latitudes.' Source: oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/horse-latitudes.html  (Legend.)

question: Here is one of the ocean's oldest riddles. From Aristotle's day until 1920, no one could solve it. Every freshwater eel in Europe and North America is born in one small patch of open ocean.
