They drift and swim thousands of miles to rivers far apart. They return only once, to breed where they began. In which sea are all of these eels born?
context: Danish biologist Johannes Schmidt cracked it in 1920 by chasing ever-smaller eel larvae across the Atlantic until the tiniest led him to the Sargasso Sea — a nursery with no shore where every Atlantic eel begins life. Source: science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.1501694  (Legend.)

question: In the walled Old City of Sanaa, the capital of Yemen high in the mountains of the Arabian Peninsula, more than 6,000 slim houses stand packed close together like early skyscrapers. Many are five to nine stories tall, richly patterned in white trim like frosted gingerbread, and older than a thousand years. What are these ancient towers mostly built from?
context: Sanaa's tower houses are built of packed (rammed) earth and burnt mud brick, with only the lowest floor in stone -- yet they climb five to nine stories and have stood for centuries, earning old Sanaa its nickname as a city of ancient skyscrapers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a; UNESCO WHS 'Old City of Sana'a' (whc.unesco.org/en/list/385/).

question: Sanaa is so old that people have lived there without a break for more than 2,500 years. An old Islamic tradition pushes its start even further back, to the family of Noah after the Great Flood. Legend says the city was first laid out at the foot of Mount Nuqum. By whom?
context: In Islamic and biblical tradition, Shem (Sam) is a son of Noah, and Yemeni legend credits him with founding Sanaa below Jabal Nuqum, the mountain that overlooks the old city. Historians cannot confirm any founder, but the unbroken 2,500-year habitation is well established. This is legend, not verified history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a.

question: Climb to the top rooms of a Sanaa tower house. The afternoon sun pours in through half-round fans of red, blue, and green glass. They sit above each window in lacy carved white gypsum, washing the walls in colored light. What are these stained-glass fanlights of Sanaa called?
context: These are QAMARIYA windows -- the name comes from qamar, Arabic for 'moon,' for their crescent-fan shape. Panes of colored glass are set into fretted gypsum plaster. By contrast, a mashrabiya is a projecting latticed wooden window-screen, not a stained-glass fanlight. Qamariya windows are a hallmark of old Sanaa's tower houses. Source: whc.unesco.org/en/list/385/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a.

question: From a distance, Sanaa's brown mud towers look iced like gingerbread -- every floor outlined and swirled with bright white patterns. But the builders didn't paint those white gypsum friezes only to look beautiful. On a house made of mud brick, what practical job does the white gypsum coating do?
answer: it sheds rain that would wash the mud away
choices: it sheds rain that would wash the mud away
it reflects the sun to keep the rooms cool
it seals cracks against burrowing insects
it lets the family mark out their own house
context: Old Sanaa gets real rain, and unprotected mud brick would erode. The white gypsum (juss) friezes and copings act like a waterproof skin, channeling rainwater off the vulnerable earthen walls -- so Sanaa's famous 'gingerbread' decoration is also its raincoat. Source: whc.unesco.org/en/list/385/.

question: For more than a thousand years, anyone entering the walled Old City of Sanaa — the ancient mountain capital of Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula — has had to pass under a single tall fortified gate cut through the city's high clay walls. Traders leading camels, pilgrims and travelers still crowd through it today. What is this great gate called?
context: This is BAB AL-YEMEN, the 'Gate of the Yemen' -- the grand gate of old Sanaa, over a thousand years old and still the main way in through the city's high walls of packed clay. The other choices are famous gates of other Islamic cities: Bab al-Nasr and Bab Zuweila in Cairo, Bab Boujeloud in Fez. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bab_al_Yemen; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a.

question: In 1972, workers repairing the attic of the Great Mosque of Sanaa -- among the oldest mosques on earth -- pulled a cache of ancient parchments from sacks hidden in the roof. Under ultraviolet light, one page revealed a faint second layer of writing beneath the visible text: long ago, someone had scraped the page clean and written over it. What did scholars find in that hidden, erased under-layer?
answer: an even older copy of the Quran
choices: an even older copy of the Quran
a merchant's tally of spice prices
a map of the caravan roads to Mecca
a Christian gospel in old Syriac
context: This is the SANAA PALIMPSEST (part of the 'Sanaa manuscript'). A palimpsest is a page whose original writing was scraped off and overwritten; here, ultraviolet imaging recovered a lower Quranic text older than the upper one. Radiocarbon dating placed the parchment at roughly 578-669 CE, ranking it among the very oldest Qur'anic manuscripts known -- a rare window into how the earliest copies were written. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a_manuscript.

question: Palenque is an ancient Maya city on a jungle-covered cliff in Chiapas, in southern Mexico. Its grandest building is a steep stepped pyramid with a small temple perched on top. Inside the pyramid, a hidden stairway drops deep into its heart to the tomb of a Maya king. What is this famous pyramid-temple called today?
choices: the Temple of the Foliated Cross
context: The pyramid takes its name from three stone tablets in its summit temple carved with 617 Maya glyphs, one of the longest hieroglyphic texts in the ancient Americas, recording the life of the king buried within. In 1948 the archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier spotted the trapdoor-like floor slab that hid the stairway. Source: Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: In 1948 the digger Alberto Ruz Lhuillier spotted two rows of stone-plugged holes in a floor slab of Palenque's summit temple. The slab looked made to be lifted. Under it lay a stairway packed with rubble. His crew dug down for four seasons. In June 1952, about 25 metres inside the pyramid, they broke through a sealed wall. What lay in the room beyond?
context: It was the first tomb ever found inside a Maya pyramid, overturning the old belief that these pyramids were only solid platforms for temples. In the anteroom lay the skeletons of six young attendants, apparently sacrificed to accompany their king. The king within was K'inich Janaab' Pakal. Source: mayan.org, Pakal's Tomb; Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: Inside the tomb of the Maya king Pakal at Palenque, the royal skeleton lay wearing a mask built from some 200 small fitted pieces of a single precious stone, its eyes made of shell and gleaming obsidian. The Maya prized this green stone above gold itself. Of what stone was Pakal's death mask made?
context: Jade, carved and polished and set in mosaics, was the most treasured material of the Maya world, a symbol of breath, water, and life. Pakal's mosaic mask, about 200 pieces of jadeite with eyes of shell and obsidian, now rests in the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City. Source: mayan.org, Pakal's Tomb; Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: Deep inside Palenque's great pyramid, King Pakal's coffin lid is a single carved limestone slab. It weighs about five tons and is a masterwork of old American art. The relief shows the king tipping back at the moment of death. In his 1968 book Chariots of the Gods?, Erich von Daniken said the carving showed Pakal at the controls of a rocket. Maya scholars flatly reject this. The sacred image Pakal falls along stands at the very center of the Maya universe. What is Pakal really shown falling along?
context: That sacred image is the Maya World Tree, a great cross-shaped ceiba whose roots reach the underworld and whose branches hold up the sky; von Daniken mistook its branching, cruciform form for a rocket. Pakal is carved at the instant of death, falling down the trunk into the underworld, as the scholar Linda Schele put it, 'down the Milky Way.' The ancient-astronaut reading ignores the Maya writing and symbols carved all around the figure, which name the scene plainly. Source: Wikipedia, K'inich Janaab' Pakal.  (Legend.)

question: When Alberto Ruz cleared the hidden stairway inside Palenque's Temple of the Inscriptions, he found a hollow, serpent-shaped stone tube built along the steps, running from Pakal's sealed tomb far below all the way up to the temple floor 25 metres above. Archaeologists puzzled over why the Maya would run this narrow duct out of a sealed tomb. What did they build it to carry?
context: Alberto Ruz Lhuillier named this hollow stone tube the 'psychoduct.' Shaped like a serpent, it runs from Pakal's sarcophagus up the hidden stairway to the temple floor above, and the Maya are thought to have built it as a road for the dead king's soul to pass between his tomb and the living world. It is one of the eeriest features of any Maya pyramid. Source: Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: Rising from the middle of Palenque's rambling royal palace is a structure found at no other Maya city in the world. From its upper rooms, whose walls carry carved glyphs of the planet Venus, Maya priests seem to have watched the jungle horizon and tracked the movements of the sky. What is this famous Palenque structure?
context: Palenque's four-storey palace tower is unique in the Maya world, its inner walls carved with glyphs of Venus, whose cycles the Maya followed closely. One striking claim: at sunset on the winter solstice, seen from the tower, the sun appears to drop straight into the Temple of the Inscriptions, the pyramid holding Pakal's tomb. Source: World History Encyclopedia; Wikipedia, Palenque.

question: Beneath the plaza of Palenque, the Maya vaulted the Otulum stream inside a stone channel running nearly 300 metres. In one stretch, known as the Piedras Bolas aqueduct, they engineered a first for the entire ancient Americas, a feat of water control no other New World people is known to have managed. What did Palenque's builders achieve here?
context: By vaulting the stream and then sharply narrowing part of the channel, Palenque's engineers forced the water under pressure, able to spurt upward, perhaps to feed a fountain or basin. Penn State researchers call the Piedras Bolas aqueduct the earliest known pressurized water feature in the New World, centuries before the Spanish arrived. Source: Penn State News, 'Maya plumbing'; Wikipedia, Palenque.

question: Cross the empty Syrian desert and you reach Palmyra: a whole ancient Roman-era city of pale golden stone still standing amid the sand. Two thousand years ago it was a rich caravan stop between Rome and Persia. One grand paved street runs down the heart of the ruins for more than a kilometre, once lined with hundreds of tall stone pillars. What is Palmyra's famous main street called?
context: The Great Colonnade is Palmyra's spine -- a ceremonial street about 1.1 km long lined with columns roughly 9.5 m high, mostly raised in the 2nd century AD, and you can still walk between the standing pillars today. Palmyra's beauty earned it the nickname the 'Bride of the Desert.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Palmyra should not exist. It sits deep in the empty Syrian desert, far from any river -- yet a thriving city grew there, ringed by twenty kinds of date palm. The reason was one natural source of fresh water, the only reliable water for days in any direction. What is this famous desert water source called?
context: The Efqa spring was Palmyra's whole reason for being -- an oasis in a sea of sand, the one dependable water on the desert crossing, so every caravan crossing the wilderness HAD to stop there. That is exactly why a great city could rise in such an unlikely spot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Palmyra grew into one of the richest cities of the Roman East, even out in the middle of nowhere. Its spot was everything: every caravan hauling silk and spices between the Mediterranean and Persia was funnelled through this one desert city. How did Palmyra turn all those caravans into a fortune?
answer: charged a toll on their goods
choices: charged a toll on their goods
context: Palmyra worked like a desert toll-booth on the Silk Road. It even carved its customs law onto a great stone slab -- the Palmyrene Tariff -- spelling out the tax on every kind of good passing through, and those profits paid for the city's grand monuments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Outside Palmyra, in a bleak desert gully now called the Valley of the Tombs, more than fifty grand monuments to the dead still stand. Some held whole families across a hundred years or more. Palmyra's grandest tombs took a shape rarely seen anywhere else in the old world. What shape did these family tombs take?
context: Palmyra's tower tombs rose as high as four storeys -- stone apartment blocks for the dead, with family members sealed in shelf-niches floor above floor. The most recent one dates to about AD 128. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Queen Zenobia was the rebel ruler of Palmyra, the desert caravan city. She broke away from Rome and built a short-lived desert empire. Around AD 272 the emperor Aurelian marched on Palmyra, crushed the revolt, and captured her. By many accounts, what fate did his captive queen then meet?
answer: paraded through Rome in golden chains
choices: paraded through Rome in golden chains
beheaded on the spot in the desert
ransomed back to the Persian court
died of fever on the road to Rome
context: By many accounts Aurelian spared his royal captive. After leading Zenobia through Rome in golden chains in his triumph of AD 274, he is said to have let her live out her days in a comfortable villa at Tibur (modern Tivoli). The ancient sources disagree about her end, so Zenobia's final fate is really legend as much as settled history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenobia

question: In 2015 the militants of ISIS (the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria) blew up Palmyra's greatest old monuments on purpose. They dynamited the Temple of Bel and the Arch of Triumph in a campaign of cultural destruction. Yet archaeologists are sure these ruins can be rebuilt, stone by stone. What made that possible?
choices: carved fragments buried in the sand
context: Detailed 3-D scans and photographs had been made before the war, so the 'New Palmyra' project (2015) -- built on work by the Syrian coder Bassel Khartabil -- created digital models to guide the rebuilding, and reconstruction of the Arch of Triumph began in October 2022. The scans mattered all the more because of what ISIS had done in August 2015: days before it began dynamiting the city's ancient temples, it publicly beheaded Palmyra's 83-year-old antiquities chief, Khaled al-Asaad, who had guarded the ruins for about half a century, for refusing to reveal where the city's treasures were hidden. He had said, 'I am from Palmyra, and I will stay here even if they kill me.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khaled_al-Asaad

question: In southwestern Turkey a whole hillside gleams brilliant white, as if a waterfall of snow had frozen mid-tumble into hundreds of shallow terraced pools. The pools are made of a soft chalky rock left behind by hot mineral springs bubbling out of the ground. Locals named the place 'Pamukkale.' What do those two Turkish words mean?
context: The soft, piled-up look of the white rock reminded people of mounds of cotton: pamuk means 'cotton' and kale means 'castle.' Pamukkale sits in Denizli Province in southwestern Turkey, in the valley of the Menderes -- the river the ancient Greeks called the Meander. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamukkale

question: Up close, Pamukkale's blinding-white cliff isn't snow and isn't salt -- it is solid rock, built up in smooth ledges as scalding, mineral-rich spring water spills down the slope and hardens in the sun. Geologists have a special name for this pale, hot-spring stone. What is it?
context: As the hot spring water cools at the surface, the dissolved lime (calcium carbonate) it carries hardens out and lays down another paper-thin layer -- the very same mineral recipe that grows a cave stalactite, except here it builds terraces in open sunlight instead of dripstone in the dark. Tufa is the softer cousin left by cool water; Pamukkale's dense, banded, hot-spring stone is travertine. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamukkale

question: In southwestern Turkey stands Pamukkale, a huge white cliff carved into hundreds of stepped hot-spring pools. Mineral-rich water bubbles up from underground and spills down its terraces. The cliff is not a dead, finished fossil left from long ago. As long as those hot springs keep flowing over the ledges, something is still happening to the stone itself, year after year. What is happening to the stone?
choices: the old stone is dissolving away
the terraces are turning to marble
the whole cliff is sliding downhill
context: The terraces are alive: as long as the seventeen hot springs flow, fresh travertine is laid down and the whole white formation -- already about 2,700 m long and 160 m high -- keeps growing. When pools grey with algae and grime, keepers rotate and re-flood clean water across them to keep the white bright; a hotel-driven greying in the late 20th century was reversed by closing the terraces to bathers and traffic. Source: https://www.naturalworldheritagesites.org/sites/hierapolis-pamukkale/

question: Pamukkale in southwestern Turkey is a vast white cliff of stepped stone pools filled with hot spring water. The shimmering white terraces alone would be a marvel. But climb to the very top of that cliff, and you find something amazing perched right up there — the healing springs drew visitors from across the ancient world, and they built here for real. Its marble ruins still crown the white stone today. What was built on the top?
context: The city is Hierapolis, the 'holy city' -- a Greco-Roman spa resort with a theatre seating around 15,000, colonnaded streets, temples, and one of the ancient world's largest necropolises (a sprawling city of tombs) for pilgrims who came to 'take the waters.' In 1988 UNESCO listed Hierapolis-Pamukkale as a single World Heritage Site, honoured for BOTH its natural white terraces and its ancient ruins. Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/485

question: Hierapolis was a Roman spa city built atop Pamukkale's white cliffs in what is now southwestern Turkey. When an earthquake shook it down long ago, the marble columns of a temple tumbled straight into a hot-spring pool below. That pool, nicknamed for the Egyptian queen Cleopatra, stays a swimmable 36 degrees Celsius year-round. It draws bathers from across the world for a startling reason found almost nowhere else on Earth. What can bathers do here?
answer: swim in among the sunken ancient columns
choices: swim in among the sunken ancient columns
drink the spring said to cure blindness
walk a glass floor above the ruins
float over a mosaic of the sea-god
context: The bath is nicknamed Cleopatra's Pool (the Antique Pool); legend even says Cleopatra herself once swam here -- a charming story, not history. Long ago an earthquake toppled the pool's marble portico straight into the thermal spring, and its fluted columns and carved blocks still rest across the bottom -- so bathers float in the roughly 36 degrees C mineral water directly above the fallen ancient stone. Source: https://visitingturkey.com/destinations/pamukkale/cleopatra-pool

question: At Hierapolis the priests would lead bulls and birds up to the mouth of one particular cave -- and within moments the animals would collapse dead, while the priests standing right beside them walked away unharmed. Having no science to explain it, the Greeks and Romans gave the killing cave a dreadful name and built a shrine over it. By what name did they know it?
context: They called it the Ploutonion -- 'Pluto's Gate' -- a doorway to the underworld of Pluto, god of the dead. The geographer Strabo wrote of it: 'I threw in sparrows and they immediately breathed their last and fell.' Long dismissed as a myth, the walled-up cave was rediscovered in 2013 by archaeologist Francesco D'Andria, together with an inscription to Pluto and Kore and a statue tied to Hades and the three-headed dog Cerberus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ploutonion_at_Hierapolis  (Legend.)

question: For centuries the eunuch Galli priests at Hierapolis seemed to carry divine protection: they could stride right up to the deadly Pluto's Gate -- where any animal dropped dead -- and stroll back out alive, every single time. Yet there was nothing miraculous about it at all. What was the simple, natural reason the priests survived?
answer: the deadly gas lay in a low invisible layer
choices: the deadly gas lay in a low invisible layer
the priests had slowly grown immune to it
the priests quietly held their breath inside
the gas only turned deadly after nightfall
context: The carbon dioxide seeping from the cave is heavier than air, so it collects in an invisible 'lake' along the ground -- lethal to a low animal (or one held down into it) but harmless to a tall priest whose head stayed up in the breathable air above. It looked like a miracle; it was simple physics. A 2018 study led by biologist Hardy Pfanz measured CO2 up to 91% deep in the grotto, with the gas layer about 40 cm deep and deadliest at dawn after building up overnight -- and researchers still found freshly killed birds, mice, and dozens of beetles at the site. Source: https://www.science.org/content/article/roman-gate-hell-killed-its-victims-cloud-deadly-carbon-dioxide

question: The continents ride on huge slabs of rock called tectonic plates, and those plates slowly drift. North America and Europe sit on plates that are pulling apart, widening the Atlantic Ocean between them. We do not have to work out this drift only from old rocks. Since the space age, one modern tool has clocked the split in real time — down to the millimeter, year after year. Which tool?
context: GPS was built to tell you where your car is, but it is precise enough to watch continents move -- fixed ground stations on either side of the Atlantic creep apart on the readouts by roughly 2.5 cm a year. It turned Wegener's century-old idea into something we now measure directly. Source: https://earthhow.com/continental-drift-plate-tectonics/.

question: Spread a world map flat. Across one ocean, two facing coasts look like torn halves of a single shape. The outward bulge of one slides right into the inward curve of the other. The mapmaker Abraham Ortelius pointed out the match back in 1596, long before anyone could explain it. Which two coastlines fit together like puzzle pieces?
answer: West Africa and eastern South America
choices: West Africa and eastern South America
eastern North America and northwest Europe
context: The resemblance is striking enough that people noticed it for centuries -- Abraham Ortelius pointed it out in 1596 -- yet it took until the 1900s and Alfred Wegener to argue the coasts really had been torn apart, not just coincidentally shaped alike. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_drift.

question: The Appalachian Mountains run up the east side of North America, worn down to green ridges. Their rock belt doesn't simply stop at the coast. It was once part of a mountain chain now stranded on the far shore of the Atlantic, torn away when the ocean opened between them. Which range across the water is the Appalachians' severed other half?
context: Wegener pointed to matching mountain belts like this as evidence the continents had once been joined: the Appalachians of North America line up with the Scottish Highlands, and South Africa's Karroo rock beds match Brazil's Santa Catarina beds across the ocean. Tellingly, the man pressing these clues was no geologist -- Alfred Wegener was a meteorologist and polar explorer, an outsider whose profession his critics held against him. Sources: https://www.discovermagazine.com/planet-earth/continental-drift-a-revolutionary-theory-that-was-once-considered ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Wegener.

question: Matching coastlines could just be a coincidence. The real jolt came when geologists dug up the same fossil animal on both shores of the South Atlantic. This small reptile, called Mesosaurus, showed up in rocks in Brazil and in South Africa. It was a freshwater creature and could never have swum across a salt ocean. Which idea did the fossil evidence support?
answer: the two coasts were once a single joined land
choices: the two coasts were once a single joined land
an ancient land bridge later sank beneath the sea
the same species arose on each coast separately
river floods rafted the fossils across the ocean
context: Wegener stacked up more of these twin-continent clues: the Glossopteris fern turns up across South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica -- one flora scattered over five now-separate lands. The tidiest explanation was that the lands had once been joined. Yet geologists still resisted for decades, because Wegener could not name a force strong enough to move a continent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_drift (Glossopteris: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Wegener).

question: In 1970 the drilling ship Glomar Challenger hauled up long cores of rock from deep beneath the floor of the Mediterranean Sea. Scientists Kenneth Hsu and William Ryan studied the layers, which recorded conditions about 5.5 million years ago, and reached a startling conclusion about the entire Mediterranean. What had once happened to it?
answer: it had dried up into vast salt flats
choices: it had dried up into vast salt flats
it had frozen over into a thick ice shelf
it had drained away through the seafloor
it had boiled off in a volcanic upheaval
context: Cut off from the Atlantic when the Strait of Gibraltar sealed, the Mediterranean -- itself the shrinking remnant of the ancient Tethys Ocean -- evaporated almost completely, dropping kilometers below sea level and leaving buried salt over 2 km thick. Around 5.33 million years ago the Atlantic burst back through Gibraltar and refilled it in the Zanclean flood, one of the largest floods Earth has ever seen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messinian_salinity_crisis.

question: The Atlantic was not the first ocean to sit in its place. Geologist J. Tuzo Wilson showed that oceans open wide and then slam shut again in the same belts of the globe, over and over. Right where the Atlantic now lies, an EARLIER ocean had already opened and closed hundreds of millions of years before it. What is that vanished predecessor ocean called?
context: This open-and-shut rhythm is called the Wilson cycle, after J. Tuzo Wilson, who described it in 1966. It runs on a slow conveyor of rock: fresh crust is shoved out at mid-ocean ridges while old, cold, heavy crust is dragged back down at deep trenches. Because of it the map never stops rearranging -- roughly 250 million years from now the Atlantic is expected to close and today's continents to crowd into a brand-new supercontinent. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_cycle ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea_Proxima.

question: Deep under the streets of Paris, mile after mile of tunnel is lined with human bones. Skulls and thigh-bones are stacked into neat walls and archways. They are the remains of about six million people. What is this underground maze of bones called?
context: The bones were carted here in the 1780s from Paris's overflowing graveyards and later stacked into deliberate walls and archways; the famous count of about six million is only an estimate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs_of_Paris  (Legend.)

question: For hundreds of years Paris buried its dead in packed churchyards like the Cimetière des Innocents. The ground itself rose into a mound taller than a man. In the spring of 1780, the crowding finally caused a disaster that forced the city to act. What happened?
answer: Gas from the decaying dead burst through a cellar wall.
choices: The flooding Seine washed loose bones into the streets.
A fire tore through the cemetery's wooden crosses.
Gas from the decaying dead burst through a cellar wall.
Grave-robbers tunnelled into the burial vaults.
context: In spring 1780 the pressure of the rotting dead burst a wall into a neighbouring cellar. The city closed the Cimetière des Innocents and, from 1785, moved the bones by torchlight into the empty tunnels beneath the city — so the Catacombs' dead were relocated there, not buried where they now lie. Source: history.com/articles/paris-catacombs-origins

question: The tunnels that now hold Paris's bones were not dug as tombs at all. For hundreds of years, workers had hollowed out these passages beneath the city for a totally different reason. The ground was left honeycombed with tunnels. Why had the tunnels been dug at first?
answer: To quarry the stone that Paris was built from.
choices: To quarry the stone that Paris was built from.
To carry the city's sewage down to the river.
To move soldiers secretly during sieges.
To store and cool the city's wine.
context: Paris was largely built from limestone dug out from directly beneath itself, honeycombing the ground with tunnels. When the mines emptied, those same galleries later became the perfect place to store the dead. Source: history.com/articles/paris-catacombs-origins

question: The Louvre, the Arc de Triomphe, and the very bone-walls of the Catacombs were all cut from a single pale, creamy building stone — laid down on a warm, shallow sea about 45 million years ago and quarried from directly beneath the city. Geologists gave this famous 'Paris stone' its own name. What is it called?
context: It is Lutetian limestone, named after Lutetia — the Roman name for Paris — and about 48–40 million years old. The Louvre, Les Invalides, Place de la Concorde and the Arc de Triomphe are all built from it. Portland, Bath and Caen stone are all real building limestones too, but from England and Normandy, not Paris. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutetian_Limestone

question: Deep beneath the streets of Paris, France, runs a maze of old limestone quarries. In the 1780s, when the city's cemeteries began overflowing, workers hauled millions of bones down into these tunnels and stacked skulls and thighbones into endless neat walls — the Paris Catacombs. Over the doorway leading in, a stone slab carries a stark French warning to every visitor. What does the warning say?
answer: Stop! This is the empire of Death.
choices: Stop! This is the empire of Death.
Remember, traveller, that you too must die.
Abandon all hope, you who enter here.
Here sleep the forgotten children of Paris.
context: The carved warning reads 'Arrête! C'est ici l'empire de la Mort.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs_of_Paris

question: In August 2004, French police on a training run in the off-limits quarry tunnels under Paris found a strange hidden room. It was about 3,000 square feet, wired with stolen power, and had a bar, stone benches, and a recording of barking dogs set up to scare people off. What had the secret tunnel explorers built down there?
context: The builders were 'cataphiles' — illegal explorers of the tunnels. Police reportedly found a bar and benches carved from the rock, plus a recording of barking dogs to frighten off intruders. The full network of quarry galleries beneath Paris runs up to about 300 km, most of it off-limits. Source: faroutmagazine.co.uk/the-mysterious-cinema-discovered-in-the-tunnels-of-the-paris-catacombs  (Legend.)

question: In the heart of old Paris, a small royal chapel hides a stunning secret on its upper floor. That upper room has almost no solid wall. Fifteen stained-glass windows, each 15 meters tall, show over a thousand Bible scenes and make the room glow like the inside of a jewel. What is this chapel called?
context: The Sainte-Chapelle's fifteen windows hold 1,113 separate scenes across about 670 sq m of stained glass; it was consecrated on 26 April 1248. Nearly two-thirds of that glass is still the original 13th-century glass. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainte-Chapelle

question: King Louis IX did not build the dazzling Sainte-Chapelle as an ordinary church. He raised the whole glass-walled chapel in the 1240s as one gigantic, gilded reliquary — a container built to hold a single sacred treasure he had bought at enormous cost. What holy relic was the Sainte-Chapelle built to house?
context: King Louis IX (Saint Louis) built the Sainte-Chapelle in the 1240s to house the Crown of Thorns and other relics of Christ's Passion. The upper chapel, where the relics were kept, was reserved for the royal family; the lower chapel was for servants and soldiers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainte-Chapelle

question: King Louis IX spent about 40,000 livres to build the entire Sainte-Chapelle — glass walls, gilded spire and all. He also had to pay for the Crown of Thorns relic that the chapel was built to hold. How did the price of the relic compare with the cost of the whole building?
answer: The relic cost more than three times the whole chapel.
choices: The relic cost about the same as the chapel.
The relic cost more than three times the whole chapel.
The relic cost roughly a tenth of the chapel.
The relic was a gift and cost nothing at all.
context: Louis IX paid about 135,000 livres for the Crown of Thorns — more than three times the roughly 40,000 livres it cost to build the entire Sainte-Chapelle around it. The container cost far less than the treasure inside. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainte-Chapelle

question: When the Paris Metro opened in 1900, the architect Hector Guimard shaped its street entrances from green cast iron. They curl and branch like plant stems and hold up orange lamps like flower buds. These famous entrances became the symbol of which art movement?
context: Art Nouveau means 'new art.' Guimard painted his railings green to imitate weathered brass, and his style became known as the 'style Métro.' He built 141 entrances (the last in 1913), and about 86 survive today as protected historical monuments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Métro_entrances_by_Hector_Guimard

question: The Eiffel Tower is 300 metres of bare wrought iron, standing fully exposed to the weather. On a hot, sunny summer day, the sun beats hard on one side of the tower while the other side stays in shade. Because of the way metal responds to heat, what does the tower actually do?
answer: Its sunlit side lengthens, tipping the top away from the sun.
choices: Its sunlit side lengthens, tipping the top away from the sun.
Its shaded side lengthens, tipping the top toward the sun.
It sinks a few centimetres deeper into its foundations.
It slowly twists around on its four feet.
context: The sun-warmed iron on the lit side expands and lengthens, so the top can shift by up to about 15 cm, leaning away from the sun — on a hot day the tower even stands a little taller, like a giant thermometer in wrought iron. It is 300 m tall, built for the 1889 World's Fair. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower  (Legend.)

question: Gustave Eiffel's iron tower was only ever meant to be temporary — built for the 1889 World's Fair and licensed to stand for just 20 years before being torn down for scrap. Yet it still stands today. What surprising new use convinced the authorities to keep it?
answer: It made a superb radio and telegraph antenna.
choices: It became the world's tallest tourist restaurant.
It served as a giant lightning rod for the city.
It anchored the cables of a planned river bridge.
It made a superb radio and telegraph antenna.
context: Permitted for only 20 years, the tower was saved because its great height made a superb antenna for wireless telegraph and radio. It was assembled from 18,038 iron pieces held by 2.5 million rivets, designed by engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower

question: At Perito Moreno Glacier in Patagonia, crowds wait on the boardwalks with cameras ready. They are listening for a boom loud as a cannon. That is the moment a tower of ice breaks off the glacier's front wall and crashes into the lake. Scientists have one word for this event. Which is it?
context: Calving is the sudden breaking-away of ice from the front of a glacier. Perito Moreno's ice wall runs about 5 km wide and rises roughly 74 m (240 ft) — as tall as a 20-story building — straight out of Lago Argentino, and blocks tumble off it throughout the day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perito_Moreno_Glacier.

question: Boats on Lago Argentino float right up to the tall face of Perito Moreno Glacier. The ice has been packed so tight for so long that it soaks up almost every color of sunlight. It gives back just one color instead of white. What color does the old, packed ice glow?
context: The oldest, most tightly compressed glacier ice has had nearly all its air squeezed out, so it absorbs the longer red wavelengths of sunlight and reflects the blue — giving the exposed ice face its startling deep-blue glow. Sources: blogpatagonia.australis.com; quasarex.com/patagonia/perito-moreno-glacier.

question: Perito Moreno is a giant tongue of blue-white ice in southern Argentina's Patagonia, part of a huge icefield that fills the southern Andes. For about 80 years, from the mid-1940s to the 2010s, it drew scientists and tourists from around the world. Most glaciers on Earth were slowly melting back in those decades. Perito Moreno could claim something almost no other big glacier of that time could. What was it famous for in those years?
answer: staying in balance instead of shrinking
choices: staying in balance instead of shrinking
having the deepest crevasses in the Andes
being the tallest ice cliff ever measured
flowing faster than any glacier on Earth
context: As glaciers worldwide retreated, Perito Moreno crept forward about 2 m a day, its advance almost exactly replacing the ice that calved off its front — so it stayed in near-perfect balance, earning the nickname the 'balanced glacier.' Honest update: that era has ended. A 2025 study found its front thinning jumped more than sixteenfold (from 0.34 m/yr in 2000-2019 to about 5.5 m/yr in 2019-2024), and it has retreated over 800 m since 2019 as it detaches from a ridge that once anchored it. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perito_Moreno_Glacier; nature.com/articles/s43247-025-02515-7.

question: Every few years, Perito Moreno Glacier creeps forward until its ice wall touches the far shore of Lago Argentino. That dams off one arm of the lake, the Brazo Rico. The trapped meltwater has no outlet, so it climbs surprisingly high before pressure breaks a way through. How much higher than the main lake can the penned-in water rise before it bursts free?
context: Perito Moreno is one of the only places on Earth where you can watch a glacier dam a lake. Pressed against the Península de Magallanes, the ice seals the Brazo Rico so completely that the trapped water can rise as much as 30 m (about 100 ft) — a 10-story wall of extra water — above the level of the main lake. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perito_Moreno_Glacier; quasarex.com/blog/the-perito-moreno-rupture-phenomenon.

question: Behind Perito Moreno's ice dam, the trapped water rises higher and higher with no way out. The pressure slowly tunnels a channel through the base of the ice, hollowing out a soaring arch that thins until it can no longer bear the weight above. Crowds travel from around the world and wait, sometimes for days, to see the spectacular climax of this cycle. What is this famous event called?
context: When the ice arch finally falls, the pent-up water roars through in a torrent — the celebrated rupture of Perito Moreno. It happens on no fixed schedule: on average about every 4 to 5 years, but sometimes twice in a year and sometimes not for a decade. Recorded ruptures include 1917 (the first documented), 1940, 1988, 2004, 2006, 2008, 2012, 2013 (twice), 2016, 2018, and 2019. Sources: quasarex.com/blog/the-perito-moreno-rupture-phenomenon; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perito_Moreno_Glacier.

question: Perito Moreno is spectacular, but it is only one of about 48 glaciers spilling off the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, a plateau of ice stretching some 350 km along the southern Andes between Argentina and Chile. This ice field is commonly called the third-largest reserve of fresh water on Earth; only two frozen places hold more. Which two are they?
context: Honest nuance on the superlative: some sources call the Southern Patagonian Ice Field the world's third-largest freshwater reserve (after the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets), while others describe it more precisely as the second-largest continuous ice field outside the poles, after Alaska's. Either way it is immense — its glaciers include Pío XI (Brüggen), the largest glacier in the Southern Hemisphere outside Antarctica, plus Viedma and Upsala. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perito_Moreno_Glacier; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Patagonian_Ice_Field.  (Legend.)

question: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen for at least two years in a row. It locks up soil across northern Siberia, Canada, and Alaska. About how much of all the land in the Northern Hemisphere does it cover?
context: The U.S. National Snow and Ice Data Center estimates permafrost underlies about 23 million square kilometers - roughly a quarter of the exposed land in the Northern Hemisphere, spread across Siberia, Canada, and Alaska. Permafrost simply means ground that stays at or below freezing for at least two years running. Source: https://nsidc.org/learn/parts-cryosphere/frozen-ground-permafrost/quick-facts-frozen-ground

question: In 2007, a reindeer herder by Siberia's Yuribei River found the body of a baby woolly mammoth. She was later named Lyuba. She had lain there for over 40,000 years, yet her skin and organs were still whole, as if she had died only weeks before. What had kept an Ice Age baby's soft body so perfect?
choices: A thick coat of tree resin
context: Siberia's permafrost is a natural deep-freeze for the deep past. Lyuba, found near the Yuribei River in 2007, had been frozen for more than 40,000 years, yet the ground preserved her skin, her internal organs, even her last meal still inside her stomach. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/mammoths

question: In Russia's Sakha Republic, a huge tadpole-shaped scar has ripped open in the ground. It is nearly a kilometer long and up to 100 meters deep, and it eats more land every year as the frozen soil thaws. Awed locals gave this growing chasm - the Batagaika crater - what grim nickname?
context: The Batagaika crater in the Sakha Republic is the world's largest permafrost 'megaslump' - a retrogressive thaw slump, a kind of thermokarst. Its exposed walls reveal frozen layers up to about 650,000 years old, the oldest known ground-ice in Siberia, and it keeps growing as the permafrost thaws and collapses. Source: https://www.livescience.com/planet-earth/arctic/gateway-to-the-underworld-the-enormous-permafrost-megaslump-in-siberia-that-keeps-getting-bigger

question: Yakutsk, in Russia's Sakha Republic, may be the coldest city on Earth, and it stands on permafrost that runs hundreds of meters deep. Here a heated building is a hazard: its own warmth would thaw the frozen soil beneath it, and the ground would soften and give way. How do the apartment blocks of Yakutsk avoid melting the very ground that holds them up?
answer: They stand on stilts driven into the ground
choices: They stand on stilts driven into the ground
They float on thick rafts of gravel
They pump cold brine through their foundations
They are jacked back level every spring
context: Yakutsk and Norilsk are the only two large cities in the world built on continuous permafrost. Their buildings stand on stilts driven into the frozen ground, lifting the heated floors clear of the soil so the permafrost stays frozen and the foundations don't sink and buckle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permafrost

question: On Russia's remote Yamal Peninsula, herders keep stumbling on mysterious, near-perfect round craters - some 60 to 80 meters across - punched into the flat tundra and ringed by a rampart of soil and ice hurled outward. The first appeared in 2014 and stunned scientists. What kind of crater is a Yamal crater?
context: Yamal's craters are gas-blowout craters: as the permafrost thaws, methane builds up underground until the ground bursts, flinging out a rampart of soil and ice. Instruments have measured methane inside them up to 50,000 times normal levels. They are NOT meteorite impacts or collapse sinkholes. The first was spotted near the Bovanenkovo gas field in 2014. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamal_crater

question: Beside the Kolyma River in Siberia, Sergey and Nikita Zimov run 'Pleistocene Park,' driving horses, bison, and muskoxen across the winter tundra to trample the deep snow into a thin, packed crust. Picture the frozen ground lying under a thick, loose, fluffy layer of fresh snow through the long Arctic winter. What does that deep, fluffy snow do to the frozen soil beneath it?
answer: It traps the ground's heat like a blanket
choices: It traps the ground's heat like a blanket
It draws out heat and freezes it harder
It reflects sunlight and keeps the ground cool
It has no real effect on the ground
context: Fluffy, un-trampled snow works like a blanket, trapping the ground's warmth and letting the permafrost thaw. At Pleistocene Park on the Kolyma River (founded 1996, about 160 square km), Sergey and Nikita Zimov's grazing herds pack that snow down so the deep cold reaches the soil - trampling cut winter ground temperatures by about 7 C. Their larger goal is to rebuild the ice-age 'mammoth steppe.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistocene_Park

question: The great terrace of Persepolis is reached by a wide double staircase of 111 shallow steps, each riser only about as high as your hand is wide. Tradition says the builders made the steps so low and broad for one memorable reason. What could visitors do on them?
answer: ride their horses straight up onto the terrace
choices: ride their horses straight up onto the terrace
roll the tribute-carts up to the halls
march ten soldiers up side by side
carry the king's throne on their shoulders
context: The 111 steps are only about 10 cm high and the flights nearly 7 m wide. A popular tradition says they were kept so shallow that riders could trot their horses straight onto the terrace; modern scholars dispute this, arguing the low risers were meant for a slow, dignified ceremonial ascent on foot. Source: surfiran.com/mag/persepolis; madainproject.com/persepolis; Lonely Planet (Grand Stairway).  (Legend.)

question: The Apadana of Persepolis, the hall where the Persian King of Kings received the world, once held up its cedar roof on 72 columns. A Greek visitor, used to the sturdy pillars of the temples back home, would have stared. How were the Persian columns so different?
answer: they soared far taller and more slender
choices: they soared far taller and more slender
they were half-sunk into the walls
context: Each Apadana column rose about 20 m -- the height of a six-story building -- yet was far thinner than any Greek column, like a stone reed. Of the original 72, only about 14 still stand today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persepolis; WebSearch on the Apadana columns.

question: Persepolis was the grand ceremonial capital of the ancient Persian Empire, built in what is now southern Iran around 500 BC by King Darius the Great. Its main hall, the Apadana, was held up by dozens of enormous stone columns, each supporting a roof of imported cedar beams. Look up at the very top of any Apadana column. What shape did the Persian sculptors carve for the capital that meets the beams?
answer: the front halves of two beasts, set back-to-back
choices: the front halves of two beasts, set back-to-back
a ring of curling acanthus leaves
a pair of scroll-like spiral volutes
context: Each capital showed the front halves of two animals set back-to-back -- twin bulls, twin lions, or twin eagle-headed griffins -- kneeling so their backs cradled the roof-beams. The paired royal beasts stood for the king's power and cosmic order. Source: WebSearch on Persian column capitals; metmuseum.org Achaemenid bull's-head capital.

question: Persepolis was the grand ceremonial capital of the ancient Persian Empire, in what is now Iran. Darius the Great began building it around 515 BC. Its greatest carving runs the whole length of the huge Apadana staircase. That carving is a stone parade, once painted in bright colors, of figure after figure marching in line toward the Persian king on his throne. Who are these twenty-three groups?
answer: subject peoples bearing tribute, each in native dress
choices: subject peoples bearing tribute, each in native dress
the royal bodyguard regiment called the Immortals
a long march of gods and winged spirits
the noble families of Persia and of Media
context: Twenty-three delegations of subject nations advance toward the king, each led by the hand by a Persian or Median usher, each dressed in its own national fashion, each carrying the special goods of its homeland -- a frozen stone photograph of the whole empire. Source: WebSearch (cabinet.ox.ac.uk apadana-tribute-reliefs; smarthistory.org).

question: On the great ceremonial stairway at Persepolis — the Persian capital in what is now southern Iran — carved reliefs show 23 tribute delegations from across the empire climbing the steps to bring gifts to the King of Kings. Each delegation wears its own homeland's clothes and carries its finest offering. The delegation from hot lowland Elam, near the city of Susa, brings one of the most startling gifts of all. What is it?
answer: a lioness padding along with her two cubs
choices: a lioness padding along with her two cubs
a two-humped camel loaded with bundles
an elephant tusk and a bundle of ivory
a chest of gold dust and silver rings
context: On the Apadana reliefs the Susians (Elamites) bring a lioness with her two cubs; other delegations bring the two-humped Bactrian camel, an elephant tusk from Nubia, and gold from India -- each gift a clue to its land. Source: thecollector.com/fascinating-facts-from-the-bas-reliefs-of-persepolis.

question: Everyone entering Persepolis first passed through the Gate of All Nations, where two colossal stone guardians loomed on either side to ward off any evil that approached the king. These famous winged creatures were carved to overpower anyone who came before the King of Kings. What were they?
answer: winged bulls with the heads of bearded men
choices: winged bulls with the heads of bearded men
winged lions with the heads of eagles
winged lions with the heads of women
winged bulls with the heads of rams
context: These guardians are lamassu -- winged bulls with human heads, believed to ward off evil. Persepolis's lamassu were given their natural four legs, unlike the older Assyrian winged bulls, which were carved with five so they looked complete from both front and side. Source: worldhistory.org Gate of All Nations; royalacademy.org.uk lamassu from the Gate of Xerxes.

question: In 330 BC Alexander the Great captured Persepolis, and soon its cedar roofs and painted halls roared up in flame; the palace-city never rose again. But the ancient writers who described the fire could not agree on why Alexander did it, and historians still argue over it today. What are the two rival explanations they hand down?
answer: planned revenge for Persia's burning of Athens, or a drunken feast
choices: planned revenge for Persia's burning of Athens, or a drunken feast
an accidental cooking-fire, or a lightning strike in a storm
a signal to his troops, or an offering to the Greek gods
to deny it to rebels, or to smother a plague in the city
context: The historian Arrian says Alexander burned Persepolis in cold, deliberate revenge for the Persian king Xerxes' burning of Athens in 480 BC. Diodorus, Plutarch, and Curtius tell a wilder tale: at a drunken victory feast the Athenian courtesan Thais urged it on and, after the king himself, hurled the first blazing torch into the palace. The ancient sources never agreed, and neither can we. Source: livius.org/sources/content/diodorus; worldhistory.org; brewminate.com.  (Legend.)

question: Alexander's fire left the palace of Persepolis in ashes. Scattered through the ruined record-rooms lay tens of thousands of soft clay tablets covered in cuneiform -- the working paperwork of the empire, listing workers' wages, food rations, and travel passes. What did the flames do to the tablets?
answer: baked them rock-hard, so they survive to be read
choices: baked them rock-hard, so they survive to be read
melted them into shapeless, unreadable lumps
cracked them into worthless, powdery dust
burned the writing clean off their faces
context: The fire that destroyed Persepolis paradoxically saved its greatest treasure: it baked the soft clay tablets as hard as pottery. More than 30,000 survived -- the Persepolis Fortification Archive -- written mostly in Elamite and recording the everyday accounts of the empire. Chicago's Oriental Institute unearthed them in the 1930s, letting us read the empire's daily records 2,500 years later. Source: iranicaonline.org/articles/persepolis-elamite-tablets; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persepolis_Administrative_Archives.

question: A fine Persian carpet, woven in Iran, can pack more than 300 tiny knots into a single square inch of fabric. The famous Ardabil Carpet, made in the 1500s and now kept in a London museum, contains about 26 million knots in total. Here is the amazing part: how were all those millions of knots made?
answer: Each one tied by hand, one at a time
choices: Each one tied by hand, one at a time
Stamped out in rows by a knotting machine
Pressed into the wool with a heated iron
Glued to the backing with boiled tree resin
context: The Ardabil Carpet holds roughly 26 million knots - about 300 to 350 in every square inch - and every one was looped and trimmed by a weaver's own fingers. No machine tied a single knot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardabil_Carpet

question: Sink your fingers into a real Persian carpet, hand-woven in Iran. It feels soft as plush cloth against your palm — but under your fingertips it is really made of millions of tiny stubs standing straight up like a very short, dense lawn. Each stub is the trimmed-off top of one what?
context: A knotted carpet has no woven picture on top. Its whole soft surface, the 'pile,' is nothing but the trimmed ends of millions of tiny wool knots, each looped by hand around the stretched threads of the loom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_carpet

question: The Ardabil Carpet is a huge sixteenth-century Persian carpet, over ten meters long, woven in Iran for a shrine and now the pride of London's Victoria and Albert Museum. Almost every old carpet in the world is anonymous — it carries no name at all. The Ardabil is a rare exception. Worked small into one corner, among the flowers, is the name Maqsud of Kashan. Who was he?
answer: The weaver who made the carpet
choices: The weaver who made the carpet
The Shah who ordered the carpet
The poet whose verse it carries
The merchant who later sold it
context: Maqsud of Kashan signed the Ardabil Carpet as 'a servant of the court.' It was finished in 946 of the Islamic calendar (1539-40 CE) under Shah Tahmasp, and above his name he wove a couplet by the poet Hafez. It hangs today in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardabil_Carpet

question: Old Persian rugs from Iran often show a garden seen from above. They follow an ancient fourfold plan called the chahar bagh — Persian for 'four gardens'. The design pictures a walled garden split into four equal quarters, each filled with painted flowers and fruit trees. What runs between the four quarters and divides them?
context: This fourfold plan - chahar bagh, 'four gardens' - splits a walled garden into four beds with cross-shaped water channels, so a garden carpet is a whole paradise garden seen from directly above. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_carpet

question: There are two great ways to tie a carpet knot. Turkish weavers use a symmetric knot looped evenly over two threads; Persian weavers use an asymmetric knot wrapped around just one. That single difference lets a Persian rug show one kind of design a Turkish rug renders only clumsily. Which kind?
choices: Large blocks of a single color
context: The asymmetric 'Persian' or Senneh knot wraps a single warp thread, so a design can bend into fine spiraling flowers and vines. The symmetric 'Turkish' or Ghiordes knot, looped over two threads, makes blockier, more geometric shapes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_carpet

question: The Ardabil Carpet is a huge sixteenth-century Persian carpet, over ten meters long, woven in Iran for a shrine in the town of Ardabil. Today it is the pride of London's Victoria and Albert Museum and one of the most famous carpets on Earth. Yet it hides a secret about how it began — one that most visitors who stand before it never learn. What is the surprising truth about the Ardabil?
answer: It was woven as one of an identical pair
choices: It was woven as one of an identical pair
It was cut down from a far larger carpet
It was left unfinished by its weaver
It was stitched together from many small rugs
context: The Ardabil was woven as one of two matching carpets, a pair made for the shrine at Ardabil. The larger went to London's V&A in 1893 (the designer William Morris urged its purchase for GBP 2,000); the second, smaller carpet now lives at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardabil_Carpet

question: Persian garden carpets copy real walled gardens. In Old Persian, such a garden had its own name: pairidaeza, from pairi ('around') and daeza ('wall'). It literally meant 'a walled-around place.' The Greek soldier Xenophon carried the word home, and from there it moved through the Bible into English. What everyday English word grew from pairidaeza?
context: Xenophon, a Greek who served in Persia, wrote the word down as 'paradeisos' for the walled royal parks; it passed through Greek and the Bible into English as 'paradise.' pairi = 'around,' daeza = 'wall.' Source: etymonline.com/word/paradise

question: In the 500s CE the Persian king Khosrow I owned the most fabulous carpet ever made - the 'Spring of Khosrow' - an entire spring garden knotted across his palace floor, so he could stroll among blossoms even in deep winter. Its garden paths, streams, and flowers were not made of ordinary thread. What were they made of instead?
answer: Gold paths, silver streams, and jewelled flowers
choices: Gold paths, silver streams, and jewelled flowers
Silver paths, crystal streams, and pearl flowers
Bronze paths, glass streams, and coral flowers
Ivory paths, amber streams, and enamel flowers
context: The 'Spring of Khosrow' (Baharestan) carpet covered the palace floor at Ctesiphon around 550 CE, its garden knotted in silk with paths of gold, streams of silver, and flowers of real jewels, so King Khosrow I could 'walk in the garden' even in winter. We know it only from later descriptions. Source: britannica.com/topic/Spring-of-Khosrow-Carpet  (Legend.)

question: Persian rugs from Iran are famous for taking a master weaver years to knot by hand, one tiny loop of wool or silk at a time. You will often hear a charming story told about them: every hand-knotted Persian carpet hides one small mistake, woven in on purpose. In this old Islamic tradition, why would a master weaver ruin a perfect carpet with a flaw?
answer: Because only God is perfect, never human work
choices: Because only God is perfect, never human work
To leave a hidden mark only the weaver could find
To let bad luck escape the finished rug
To make each carpet unlike every other
context: This is folklore, not a rule of the craft. Weavers sometimes spoke of the idea, but myth-debunkers note there is no real evidence carpets were made with a deliberate flaw - it is a charming tradition, not an actual weaving practice. Source: historymyths.wordpress.com  (Legend.)

question: When Arab armies stormed the Persian capital Ctesiphon in 637 CE, they carried off Khosrow's priceless silk garden carpet as war-loot. The Caliph Umar himself decided the fate of the greatest carpet ever woven. What did he order done with it?
answer: Cut into pieces and shared out among the soldiers
choices: Cut into pieces and shared out among the soldiers
Burned in the square as a pagan idol
Sent whole to hang in the mosque at Mecca
Locked away in the treasury at Damascus
context: When Arab armies captured Ctesiphon in 637 CE, the Caliph Umar had the Spring of Khosrow cut into pieces and shared among the soldiers as loot. Not a single fragment survives; we know the carpet only from the historian al-Tabari's account. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baharestan_Carpet  (Legend.)

question: The world's oldest knotted carpet, the Pazyryk carpet, is about 2,500 years old - yet wool should crumble to dust in a few centuries. It lasted only because of a freak accident inside a Scythian chieftain's burial mound high in Siberia's Altai Mountains. What saved it for 2,500 years?
answer: Water seeped in and froze it solid in ice
choices: Water seeped in and froze it solid in ice
Dry desert air slowly mummified it
A deep peat bog sealed it from all air
Falling volcanic ash buried it hard
context: Water flooded the Scythian tomb in the Altai Mountains and froze, sealing the Pazyryk carpet in ice until it was dug out in 1949. About 2,500 years old (5th century BC), it shows a row of horsemen and grazing deer and now lives in the Hermitage in St Petersburg. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazyryk_carpet

question: In Iran's carpet trade a dealer can often name a rug's home city at a single glance. Rugs from one great weaving city are famous for the 'Mahi,' or 'fish,' design - a field of small curved leaves swimming around a central medallion. Which city is the home of the fish-pattern carpet?
context: Iran's weaving cities each have a signature look: Tabriz its bold medallions and the 'Mahi' fish pattern, Isfahan its flowing 'Shah Abbas' florals, Kashan its dense fine-wool flower fields, and Kerman its bright pictorial gardens. Source: catalinarug.com

question: Petra is an ancient city hidden in the red sandstone cliffs of southern Jordan, built by a desert trading people called the Nabataeans over two thousand years ago. Its most famous monument, Al-Khazneh — 'the Treasury' — rises nearly 40 meters up the cliff, its columns and figures glowing pink in the desert sun. How did Petra's builders make this huge front?
answer: They carved it downward straight out of the solid rock cliff.
choices: They stacked and mortared cut sandstone blocks.
They carved it downward straight out of the solid rock cliff.
They cast it from concrete over a timber frame.
They assembled marble columns shipped from Greece.
context: Al-Khazneh was sculpted from the top down straight into the living sandstone cliff -- carved out, not built up from blocks. Petra's people cut whole temples, tombs, and a theatre this way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khazneh

question: Petra is an ancient city in the desert of southern Jordan, with temples and tombs carved right into the cliff walls of a hidden valley. People call it 'the Rose City' because those cliffs glow in bands of pink, red, and orange. The colors are richest in the low sun of morning and evening. What gives Petra's sandstone its rose-red color?
answer: Iron in the sandstone stains it red and orange.
choices: The glow of low, slanting sunlight.
Red paint the Nabataeans brushed on.
Iron in the sandstone stains it red and orange.
A crust of windblown desert dust.
context: The pink, red, and orange bands are iron oxides in the sandstone itself, so Petra is rose-coloured all the way through -- which is why it is called 'the Rose City.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petra

question: Petra's temples, tombs, and open-air theater were all cut into the walls of a hidden desert valley in southern Jordan. This was a real, busy capital, not a natural wonder. Which people built Petra as their capital?
context: The Nabataeans were a wealthy Arab trading people who turned a dry gorge into a caravan city of tens of thousands -- master engineers and stone-carvers, not simple desert nomads. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petra

question: To reach Petra's Treasury you walk over a kilometre through the Siq, a shadowy slot barely 3 metres wide with cliffs 150 metres high on either side. Many visitors assume this narrow passage must have been chiselled out by hand. In truth, what created the Siq?
answer: A crack where the rock was split apart by the earth.
choices: A river that carved the slot over the ages.
Wind slowly scouring away the soft sandstone.
A crack where the rock was split apart by the earth.
A meteor that gouged the passage on impact.
context: The Siq is a natural fault -- a crack where earth movements split the rock apart, later smoothed by water running down from Wadi Musa. It was never carved by hand or by a river. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siq

question: Petra, the ancient rose-red city carved into cliffs in southern Jordan, has one grand facade that dwarfs all the rest. Everyone calls it 'the Treasury', or Al-Khazneh, and imagines chests of gold sealed behind its doors. But archaeologists who studied the rooms inside found no vault and no gold — only bare, carved chambers. What was Al-Khazneh actually built to be?
context: Al-Khazneh was almost certainly a mausoleum, most likely built for the Nabataean king Aretas IV. The 'Treasury' name came much later, from local legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khazneh

question: Al-Khazneh, 'the Treasury', is the most famous carved facade at Petra, an ancient city cut into cliffs in southern Jordan. High on its front sits a giant stone urn, and for generations it was chipped and pocked with old bullet marks. Local marksmen fired at that urn again and again over the years, sure they could break it open. What did they believe was inside it?
answer: Gold sealed inside by an ancient pharaoh.
choices: An evil spirit trapped long ago.
Gold sealed inside by an ancient pharaoh.
A sacred spring waiting to burst out.
The bones of a Nabataean king.
context: The urn is solid sandstone and never held anything. Bedouin tradition said a pharaoh had hidden gold inside, so marksmen shot at it hoping to crack it open -- which is how Al-Khazneh got its nickname 'the Treasury.' (Legend.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khazneh

question: For over a thousand years Petra lay forgotten by the outside world, hidden in its desert valley and guarded by local Bedouin who let no stranger near. In 1812 the Swiss explorer Johann Burckhardt finally slipped inside -- by a clever trick. What was his ruse?
answer: He posed as a pilgrim seeking to sacrifice at Aaron's tomb.
choices: He bribed a guide with a purse of silver coins.
He posed as a pilgrim seeking to sacrifice at Aaron's tomb.
He claimed to be a healer sent to a sick sheikh.
He traded a fine stallion for safe passage.
context: Burckhardt, disguised as a Muslim pilgrim, claimed he had vowed to sacrifice a goat at the tomb of Aaron above the valley -- a pretext that got a guide to lead him through the Siq. He was the first European to see Petra in centuries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petra

question: Petra produced almost nothing of its own, yet it grew fabulously rich. Its wealth came from taxing the long camel caravans that trekked up from southern Arabia, loaded with two precious substances worth their weight in gold. What did those caravans carry?
context: The Nabataeans controlled the incense road, taxing caravans of frankincense and myrrh -- fragrant resins burned in temples across the ancient world. A single caravan could stretch for miles with up to 2,500 camels. Source: https://calvin.edu/news-stories/who-were-nabataeans-3

question: Petra, the ancient rock-carved city in southern Jordan, sat in a bone-dry gorge that saw almost no rain and had no river running through it. Even so, the Nabataean traders who built Petra supported a busy city of some twenty thousand people there for centuries. How did the Nabataeans supply a desert city that big with fresh water all year long?
answer: They caught flash floods in dams and hidden cisterns.
choices: They dug deep wells down to a buried aquifer.
They caught flash floods in dams and hidden cisterns.
They hauled it in by camel from the distant coast.
They melted mountain snow piped across the desert.
context: The Nabataeans built dams, rock-cut channels, and hundreds of underground cisterns that captured every flash flood and stored the water out of the sun. They caught so much that they even sold the surplus. Source: https://nabataea.net/explore/petra/petra-water-works/

question: For centuries Petra thrived on its brilliant water system and caravan tolls, though its trade had begun to fade. Then, in AD 363, a single catastrophe shattered its buildings and broke the channels and cisterns the city relied on -- and Petra never truly recovered. What struck the city?
context: The earthquake of AD 363 wrecked much of Petra and crippled the water network that made desert life possible, hastening the city's long, slow abandonment. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petra

question: The Treasury may be Petra's most famous facade, but it is not its largest. Petra's biggest monument stands about 47 metres tall, carved even higher into the mountainside and reached by a climb of roughly 800 rock-cut steps above the valley floor. What is this giant facade called?
context: Ad-Deir, 'the Monastery,' is Petra's largest carved facade -- about 47 m tall and 48 m wide. It was originally a Nabataean monument; its name comes from Christian crosses cut inside during the Byzantine era. The 800-step climb keeps it far quieter than the Treasury. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed-Deir,_Petra

question: The Nabataeans piped spring water for miles into Petra through clay pipelines. They shaped each pipe section with one clever detail that controlled the water's speed and cut down turbulence -- a refinement modern engineers only rediscovered in the last couple of centuries. What was it?
choices: A lead lining sealing every joint.
A spiral groove cut inside each pipe.
Small valves that opened on their own.
context: Each clay pipe had tapered ends that slotted into the next to reduce turbulence and control the flow, with settling basins to clean the water -- plumbing centuries ahead of its time, feeding a city in the desert. Source: https://interestingengineering.com/culture/amazing-engineering-feats-lost-city-of-petra

question: In the Zambales Mountains on Luzon in the Philippines, a jungle-covered peak had slept for about 500 years. It was so quiet that few of the farmers on its slopes knew it was a volcano at all. In June 1991 it woke in one of the century's biggest eruptions. Which mountain is this?
context: Mount Pinatubo rises in the Zambales Mountains of Central Luzon. Before 1991 it had been dormant for roughly 500 years and was so overgrown with jungle that hardly anyone recognized it as a volcano. Source: Wikipedia, '1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo'; USGS Fact Sheet 113-97.

question: Mount Pinatubo is a volcano on the island of Luzon in the Philippines. When it blew up on 15 June 1991, it shot an ash column about 40 kilometers into the sky and cooled the whole planet by roughly half a degree. That blast ranks as the second-biggest volcanic eruption on Earth in the whole 20th century. Only one eruption that century was bigger. Which one beat it?
context: Only Novarupta, in Alaska, outdid Pinatubo — its 1912 eruption was the largest of the 20th century. Pinatubo itself rated VEI 6, a 'colossal' blast on the Volcanic Explosivity Index. Source: Wikipedia, '1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo'; USGS Fact Sheet 113-97.

question: Mount Pinatubo's 1991 eruption set a record no other eruption has matched in the age of science tools. It fired about 17 million tonnes of one gas high into the stratosphere - the largest amount of its kind ever measured. Which gas did the volcano send into the sky?
context: Pinatubo injected about 17-20 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere — the largest sulfur injection ever recorded by instruments. High above the weather, that gas would slowly turn into a haze of fine sulfate droplets. Source: USGS Fact Sheet 113-97; Wikipedia, '1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo'.

question: For about two years after Mount Pinatubo erupted, the whole Earth ran a slight fever in reverse: average global temperatures fell by roughly half a degree Celsius — one mountain chilling an entire planet. High in the stratosphere, the volcano's veil of tiny droplets spread right around the globe. How did that veil cool the world below?
answer: It reflected sunlight back into space before it reached the ground
choices: It reflected sunlight back into space before it reached the ground
It choked the sky with dark ash that shaded the ground for years
It tore a hole in the ozone layer that let the surface heat escape
It chilled the oceans by burying them under cold volcanic dust
context: The sulfate haze acted like a planet-sized mirror, bouncing part of the incoming sunlight back to space and dimming the light reaching the surface by around 10%. The global chill peaked about 18 months later, around December 1992. Source: USGS, 'Volcanoes Can Affect Climate'; USGS, Self et al., 'The Atmospheric Impact of the 1991 Mount Pinatubo Eruption'.

question: Most of history's great eruptions struck with little or no warning. Mount Pinatubo was different: scientists from the Philippines' own institute, PHIVOLCS, working with the U.S. Geological Survey, read the swarming earthquakes, the rising volcanic gas and a swelling lava dome, and forecast the climactic blast about two days ahead. What did that forecast let officials do in the little time they had?
answer: Evacuate tens of thousands of people from the slopes
choices: Evacuate tens of thousands of people from the slopes
Reinforce the roofs across the towns downwind
Clear the ash from the roads and airfields
Steer the coming mudflows away from the villages
context: The PHIVOLCS-USGS forecast set evacuations in motion roughly 48 hours before the 15 June climax; about 60,000 people left the danger zones (some 100,000 were relocated in all). USGS credits the warning with saving 5,000 to 20,000 lives and averting at least $250 million in losses. Source: USGS, 'Remembering Mount Pinatubo 25 Years Ago'; USGS Fact Sheet 113-97.

question: In the town of Bacolor near Mount Pinatubo stands the 16th-century San Guillermo Church. It is now sunk to half its 12-meter height in gray volcanic mud, and people step inside through what used to be its second-story windows. The town was buried in 1995, four years after the eruption, when monsoon rain stirred the mountain's loose ash into a fast river of mud. What is this kind of volcanic mudflow called?
context: For years after 1991, monsoon rains kept remobilizing Pinatubo's loose ash into lahars — churning rivers of volcanic mud (not lava) that buried whole towns downstream. On 3 September 1995 a lahar filled San Guillermo Church in Bacolor, Pampanga; parishioners still worship inside, entering near the old upper windows. Source: Wikipedia, '1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo' and 'San Guillermo Parish Church (Bacolor)'; VERA Files.

question: Step into the Shanxi town of Pingyao and it feels like the 1600s. Gray courtyard shops, narrow lanes, and 20,000 people still live inside a whole Ming-Qing town. Pingyao lasted because - alone among China's old cities - it never tore down one great thing. What did Pingyao keep?
context: Pingyao's wall was rebuilt in gray brick over rammed earth in 1370, the third year of the Ming Hongwu Emperor — about 6,163 m (6.2 km) around and roughly 12 m high. While nearly every other old Chinese city eventually tore its walls down, Pingyao kept its entire Ming wall intact. Today around 20,000 people still live inside, and you can walk the full unbroken loop atop it; UNESCO named the town a World Heritage Site in 1997. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pingyao

question: Look down on Pingyao from above and its Ming builders' secret plan appears. The south gate forms a head, two wells just outside it are two eyes, the north gate is a tail, and the four side gates stick out like four legs. The whole town was shaped to copy one long-lived creature, hoping Pingyao would live just as long. Which creature is Pingyao built to resemble?
context: Seen from above, Pingyao is laid out as a tortoise: the south gate is the head, two wells just outside it are the eyes, the north gate is the tail, the four east–west gates are the four legs, and the zigzag streets form the pattern of the shell. The tortoise, a Chinese symbol of long life, was chosen so the town would 'live' as long as a turtle. Source: https://www.china-tour.cn/Pingyao/Ancient-City-Walls-Gates.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pingyao

question: On Pingyao's West Street stands Rishengchang, a shop opened in 1823 and known as China's first bank. Its big idea saved traders from a deadly job - hauling chests of silver coins across the country, where road bandits waited. Now a trader could hand his silver to Rishengchang in one city, travel the roads with nothing worth stealing, and pick up the same sum from a branch a thousand kilometers away. What did the trader carry instead of coins?
context: Rishengchang ('Sunrise Prosperity') opened on West Street in 1823 and is widely regarded as China's first 'draft bank' (piaohao) — the first modern-style remittance bank, not literally the first exchange of value. A merchant deposited silver at one branch and drew it out with a paper note at a distant branch, avoiding bandits; the bank grew to 50-plus branches, reaching Russia, Mongolia and Japan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishengchang

question: Pingyao's Ming wall has watchtowers along its top and battlements notched all around it. By old tradition the builders did not pick the numbers at random. They matched them to the sage Confucius: one watchtower for each of his gifted disciples, and one battlement for each of his students. How many did they build?
context: Pingyao's wall carries 72 watchtowers and more than 3,000 battlements, a count traditionally said to honor Confucius's 72 wisest disciples and his 3,000 students. Four larger towers stand at the corners, and a moat about 4 m wide and 4 m deep runs outside. This honoring is traditional lore rather than documented fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pingyao ; https://www.ancient-origins.net/ancient-places-asia/pingyao-021363  (Legend.)

question: By the 1800s something amazing had happened in Pingyao, a small walled town in the Shanxi hills far from any big city or seaport. About 22 draft banks were packed inside its walls - more than half of all such banks in the country. Together they moved much of the Qing empire's silver across thirty-plus cities. What nickname did this small town earn?
answer: the Wall Street of old China
