choices: the Wall Street of old China
the Fort Knox of old China
context: Because its draft banks handled so much of the empire's money, Pingyao was called the 'Wall Street of old China.' At its peak the small town held around 22 piaohao — among them Rishengchang and Weitaihou — more than half of all such banks in the country, doing business in 30-plus cities. Rishengchang controlled nearly half of China's silver trade before going bankrupt around 1914 and closing in 1932. Source: http://www.goshanxi.com.cn/pingyao/2023-11/20/c_940390.htm ; https://www.travelchinaguide.com/attraction/shanxi/pingyao/street.htm

question: Pisa is a city in central Italy, and its most famous sight is the marble Leaning Tower — really the bell tower of the cathedral on the Piazza dei Miracoli. It started tilting when workers had built only about the third story, around 1178 — long before it was even finished. The lean was never a design choice. What made the tower start to tilt so early?
answer: The soft, waterlogged ground gave way unevenly
choices: The soft, waterlogged ground gave way unevenly
An earthquake jolted the foundation loose
The marble blocks were set off-level
Coastal winds pushed hard on one side
context: The tower rests on a shallow foundation only about 3 metres deep, sitting on weak, waterlogged subsoil — layers of clay, fine sand and silt studded with old marine shells. That soft ground compresses unevenly, so one side settled more and the whole tower tipped. It was a foundation problem from the very start, not a flaw in the design. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa

question: For nearly two centuries builders kept working on Pisa's leaning tower, and when they added the upper floors they made the columns on the sinking side taller, hoping to straighten the climb back toward vertical. The fix left the tower with a strange, subtle shape you can still see today. What shape is the Leaning Tower actually built in?
context: Work on the 8-story tower stretched from 1173 to about 1372 — nearly 200 years, with a century-long pause during Pisa's wars with Genoa, Lucca and Florence. When building resumed around 1272 under Giovanni di Simone, masons made the columns and floors on the sinking side taller to fight the tilt. Because each phase leaned a little differently, the tower ended up subtly curved — banana-shaped — rather than straight. Source: https://www.ice.org.uk/what-is-civil-engineering/infrastructure-projects/stabilising-the-leaning-tower-of-pisa

question: By 1990 Pisa's tower leaned a dangerous 5.5 degrees and was edging toward collapse, so engineers closed it and searched for a way to save it. Their solution was gloriously counter-intuitive: to ease the tower back toward upright, they slowly scooped small amounts of soil out from under its foundation. Where did they dig?
answer: Under the high side, which had sunk least
choices: Under the high side, which had sunk least
Under the low side, which had sunk most
Under the south side, by the cathedral
Evenly under all four sides at once
context: The rescue was led by an international committee including engineer John Burland, using a method called 'underexcavation.' By drilling in and removing small amounts of soil from beneath the high north side — the side that had sunk less — engineers let that side settle so the tower eased back toward vertical. It pulled the top back about 44 cm, easing the lean to roughly 3.97 degrees. The tower reopened on 15 December 2001 and should stay stable for another 200-300 years. Source: https://www.building.co.uk/focus/the-man-who-saved-the-leaning-tower-of-pisa/1455.article

question: Polynesian families sailed thousands of miles across the open Pacific. They had no compass and no map. They packed water, taro, and piglets to settle new islands. What kind of boat carried them across that huge ocean?
context: Polynesians settled the largest ocean on Earth in double-hulled voyaging canoes — two long hulls lashed side by side with a deck between for people, water and food — sailing thousands of miles with no compass, chart or instrument, navigating purely by 'wayfinding' (the stars, sun, swells and signs of nature). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation ; https://hokulea.com/polynesian-wayfinding/

question: Draw lines between three far-flung islands: Hawaii in the north, Easter Island in the southeast, and New Zealand in the southwest. You get a huge patch of the Pacific, wider than any country on Earth. What is this vast ocean region called?
context: The Polynesian Triangle spans more than 10 million square miles — about 5% of Earth's surface, wider than any nation on the planet — with Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa (New Zealand) and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) at its three corners. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_Triangle ; https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/what-is-the-polynesian-triangle.html

question: On a moonless night halfway from Hawaii to Tahiti, a Polynesian navigator holds his course by memory alone. As a boy he learned that the horizon was divided into 32 named 'houses,' and he knows exactly which house each guiding star climbs out of and drops back into. Navigators had one name for this whole ring of star-houses. What did they call it?
context: The star compass divided the horizon into 32 'houses' (each 11.25° of arc); a navigator memorised exactly which house each guiding star rose out of in the east (hikina) and set into in the west (komohana), holding course by that ring of star-houses all night. Some Pacific navigators carried bearings for as many as 150 stars. Source: https://worldwidevoyage.hokulea.com/education-at-sea/polynesian-navigation/the-star-compass/

question: Several canoes are working their way toward the low Tuamotu atolls, and each crew locks onto a different sign of sea and sky to chase, sure it points to a hidden island just past the horizon. Only one crew has truly read the ocean and is being carried toward land. Which crew steered right?
answer: the crew following white terns at dusk
choices: the crew following white terns at dusk
the crew following white terns at dawn
the crew steering into the running swell
the crew chasing a frigatebird overhead
context: Terns and noddies roost on land but fly far out to sea at dawn to hunt fish, returning at dusk — so a navigator sails against the flock in the morning and with it in the evening, and the birds lead him home to the island. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: A master navigator bound for the Tuamotus does something that looks like sleeping: he lies flat in the bottom of the canoe, eyes shut, letting the hull's every motion pass through his body. From this alone he knows an island lies ahead, still hours away and far below the horizon. What is he feeling?
answer: swells that wrap around the island and cross beneath him
choices: swells that wrap around the island and cross beneath him
a current that keeps dragging the canoe off course
a chop that steepens over a rising seabed
a wind that bends around the land and shifts
context: Long ocean swells run in steady straight lines, and their pattern bends and wraps around an island; a navigator lying in the hull can feel an unseen island over the horizon by the way the crossing swells make the canoe pitch and roll. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation ; https://hokulea.com/polynesian-wayfinding/

question: In 1769 a Raiatean navigator named Tupaia joined Captain Cook's ship, and he drew the crew a sailing chart of 2,000 miles of the Pacific that named 74 islands and gave their bearings and sailing times. That map covered nearly a quarter of the whole ocean. Where had every scrap of that map come from?
choices: old charts kept by Tahitian priests
a Spanish map traded years before
Cook's own running survey of the coast
context: In 1769 the Raʻiatean priest-navigator Tupaia drew Captain Cook a chart from memory naming 74 islands (he knew about 130), covering the ocean within roughly 2,000 miles of Raʻiatea — a single man carrying a map of a quarter of the Pacific in his head. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: Sailing from Tahiti toward the Tuamotu atolls, a navigator watches the sky, not the sea. The atolls are rings of coral so low that they stay hidden below the horizon until a canoe is almost upon them. The wide, shallow lagoon inside each hidden atoll leaves a telltale mark on the cloud piled above it. What does the lagoon cast up onto that cloud?
context: A lagoon's shallow water throws a faint green tint onto the underside of the cloud piled above it; navigators sailing from Tahiti toward the low Tuamotu atolls watched the clouds for that green glow to reveal a hidden atoll like Anaa long before its land showed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: Maori tradition tells of the long-tailed cuckoo, whose migration inspired a daring guess. Each spring the bird vanished from tropical islands like Rarotonga into the empty southwestern horizon, and each autumn it returned. From this yearly journey the ancestors drew their conclusion and launched their canoes into open ocean to follow it. What had the cuckoo's flight told them?
answer: undiscovered land lay to the southwest
choices: undiscovered land lay to the southwest
rich fishing grounds lay to the southwest
a warm ocean current ran to the southwest
a belt of storms guarded the southwest
context: The long-tailed cuckoo (koekoeā) breeds only in New Zealand yet winters scattered across the tropical Pacific, migrating each spring; settlers bound for Aotearoa are thought to have reasoned that land lay to the southwest and followed the cuckoo — a roughly 1,700-nautical-mile (3,000 km) run from Rarotonga to New Zealand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_long-tailed_cuckoo ; https://teara.govt.nz/en/canoe-navigation/page-3  (Legend.)

question: The island of Raiatea in the Society group is remembered across the whole Pacific as 'Hawaiki,' the ancestral homeland the voyagers set out from. On it stands the grandest temple in Polynesia. It is a vast open-air platform of stone where navigators gathered before a voyage and chiefs sailed in from far-off islands to worship. Now a World Heritage site, what is this great marae called?
context: Raʻiatea's ancient name was Havaiʻi — the 'Hawaiki' named in Māori, Tahitian, Sāmoan and Hawaiian memory as the ancestral homeland. Its temple, the marae of Taputapuātea, was the religious heart of Eastern Polynesia and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taputapuātea_marae ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiki

question: For years, skeptics had insisted that Polynesians never truly navigated at all — that they had merely drifted onto their islands by luck. In 1976 a newly built double-hulled canoe, Hōkūleʻa, set out to answer them, sailing roughly 2,500 miles from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti with no compass and no chart, steering only by stars, swells and birds. A month later she glided into Papeʻete harbour. What was waiting to meet her on the shore?
choices: three French gunboats ordering her away
a dozen officials and little else
an empty shore, her arrival unannounced
context: Hōkūleʻa left Maui on 1 May 1976 and reached Papeʻete on 4 June — about 2,500 miles guided only by traditional wayfinding, no instruments — where some 17,000 Tahitians crowded the shore to greet her, proving the ancient methods truly worked and answering the 'accidental drift' theory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hōkūleʻa ; https://www.robertshawaii.com/blog/hokulea-a-tradition-of-hawaiian-voyaging

question: By the 1970s the ancient art of instrument-free wayfinding had died out in Hawaiʻi — not one Hawaiian could still do it. To guide Hōkūleʻa across open ocean to Tahiti, the crew had to seek out the last living master of the craft, a man named Mau Piailug, and persuade him to teach the knowledge back to them. Where had this vanishing art survived?
answer: on Satawal, a tiny island in Micronesia
choices: on Satawal, a tiny island in Micronesia
on Rapa Nui, at the far southeast corner
on Tahiti, in the Society Islands
context: Mau Piailug (1932–2010) of Satawal in Micronesia was a 'palu' master navigator of the Weriyeng school who had kept the vanishing knowledge alive and agreed to teach it back to the Hawaiians who had lost it; he guided Hōkūleʻa in 1976 and in 2007 led the first pwo master-navigator initiation on Satawal in 56 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Piailug

question: In AD 79 the volcano Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii under meters of ash in one day. The town then vanished from memory. It stayed lost until diggers hit a stone carved with its name. About how long had Pompeii been lost and forgotten?
context: Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, burying Pompeii under about 4-6 meters (13-20 ft) of ash and pumice, then sealing it under scorching pyroclastic flows. The town lay lost for roughly 1,700 years until an inscription naming 'Pompeii' was uncovered in 1763. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeii

question: The entrance hall of Pompeii's House of the Tragic Poet still holds a floor mosaic and two blocky Latin words, preserved in tile since Vesuvius buried the town in AD 79. Countless visitors have grinned once they learned the message. What does the Latin cave canem warn?
context: The mosaic sits in the entrance of the House of the Tragic Poet, built from tiny stone tiles called tesserae, showing a dog above the words CAVE CANEM -- 'Beware of the Dog.' It is essentially a Roman 'Beware of Dog' sign, 2,000 years old. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_the_Tragic_Poet

question: Pompeii's ash hardened into rock around the eruption's victims. The bodies inside slowly rotted away. They left hollow, person-shaped holes in the stone. In 1863 the dig's director, Giuseppe Fiorelli, came up with a famous trick that used these holes. What was his method?
answer: Pour liquid plaster in to cast the victims
choices: Pour liquid plaster in to cast the victims
Fill them with cement to steady the ruins
Lower wax models in for the museum
Press paper inside to take rubbings
context: The bodies had decayed inside the hardened ash, leaving voids. Fiorelli poured in liquid plaster, let it set, then chipped away the rock -- casting each victim in their exact final pose. Modern teams now use clear resin. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeii

question: In 79 AD, Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the Roman city of Pompeii in Italy under meters of hot ash. Centuries later, archaeologists poured wet plaster into the empty pockets left by bodies in the hardened ash, casting each victim's final pose. At Pompeii's House of Orpheus, a guard dog had been chained by its collar when the eruption came. Its plaster cast became one of the most famous of all. How was the dog caught in its final moment?
answer: On its back with all four legs in the air
choices: On its back with all four legs in the air
Crouched flat beneath a stone bench
context: The dog was chained at the House of Orpheus and caught on its back, all four legs thrust up, frozen mid-writhe as the ash rose. Its plaster cast is among Pompeii's most haunting. Source: https://seepompeii.com/en/pompeii-casts-where-they-are-found-and-what-they-are/

question: Pompeii's walls still carry more than 1,500 painted campaign slogans from the town's last election. They are real Roman posters, and some are nasty attack ads. One so-called 'endorsement' was really an insult, claiming a candidate was backed by a certain shady crowd. Who supposedly supported him?
context: Among 1,500+ preserved election notices, some used negative campaigning: one 'endorsement' claims all the late drinkers back a candidate, and another that a rival is supported by petty thieves. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/pompeiis-graffiti-captures-every-joke-boast-and-argument-of-an-ancient-roman-city-frozen-in-time-180987831/

question: The searing heat at Herculaneum saved things that almost never survive from ancient times. One of them is a round loaf of bread dug up in 1930, blackened and rock-hard but completely whole. What everyday detail can you still see baked into this 2,000-year-old loaf?
answer: Deep cuts splitting it into eight wedges
choices: Deep cuts splitting it into eight wedges
A crust studded with poppy seeds
A market ribbon knotted around it
context: The Herculaneum loaf survived scored into 8 wedges (a panis quadratus) and stamped with its baker's mark, naming the maker as a slave of Quintus Granius Verus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculaneum_loaf

question: Vesuvius's ash preserved thousands of messages that Pompeians had scratched around their town -- love notes, election jabs, and jokes that read like ancient social media. Tour guides today quote one of them more than any other, because its joke still lands 2,000 years later. Which real Pompeii scrawl is that famous line?
answer: A wall marveling it hasn't collapsed under so many scribbles
choices: A wall marveling it hasn't collapsed under so many scribbles
Successus the weaver's boast that he loves the barmaid Iris
Severus's taunt that Iris does not love his lovesick rival
A campaign smear that only petty thieves back a candidate
context: The full graffito, found scratched on several Pompeii walls, reads: 'I am amazed, O wall, that you have not collapsed, having to carry the tedious scribblings of so many writers.' It is an ancient complaint about graffiti -- written as graffiti. The other three choices are real Pompeii scrawls too: the weaver Successus and his rival Severus dueled on the walls over a barmaid named Iris ('you love Iris, but she does not love you'), and election notices claimed a rival was backed by the town's petty thieves. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/pompeiis-graffiti-captures-every-joke-boast-and-argument-of-an-ancient-roman-city-frozen-in-time-180987831/

question: Herculaneum sat closer to Vesuvius than Pompeii, and it was buried about 20 meters deep under pyroclastic flows near 500 degrees Celsius. Astonishingly, this fierce heat did not smash the town's wooden roofs, beds, doors, and food. It blackened and hardened them, keeping them almost whole for 2,000 years. What is this heat-driven preservation process called?
context: Herculaneum's deeper burial and hotter flows (near 500C) carbonized it -- driving off nearly everything but carbon, turning wood, food, and papyrus to charcoal that survived intact rather than being crushed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculaneum

question: At Pompeii, most victims were buried under falling ash. But at Herculaneum, archaeologists discovered about 300 people crowded together in stone boat-house chambers down by the ancient shoreline, where they had fled hoping for rescue by sea. What killed this huddled crowd?
context: About 300 skeletons were found in Herculaneum's shoreline boat-house vaults, killed almost instantly by heat shock as they waited for rescue. One, the 'Ring Lady,' still wore rings on her finger bones and reached a 1984 National Geographic cover. Source: https://bomv.commons.gc.cuny.edu/the-ringed-lady/

question: One grand seaside mansion at Herculaneum is now called the Villa of the Papyri. It once belonged to the family of Julius Caesar's father-in-law. It held about 1,800 papyrus scrolls that Vesuvius charred black. Why do scholars prize this find above nearly every other Roman one?
answer: The only library to survive intact from antiquity
choices: The only library to survive intact from antiquity
The oldest scrolls ever unearthed anywhere on Earth
The largest scroll collection in any museum today
The only ancient scrolls written in gold ink
context: The Villa of the Papyri, linked to Lucius Calpurnius Piso (Julius Caesar's father-in-law), held about 1,800 carbonized scrolls -- the only library to survive intact from the entire ancient world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculaneum

question: The Villa of the Papyri's blackened scrolls crumble to dust the instant anyone tries to unroll them, so for 250 years no one could read a word. Beginning in 2023, the Vesuvius Challenge finally cracked the problem by studying the scrolls while they stayed rolled tightly shut. Which technology let the team see and read the hidden writing?
answer: High-energy X-ray scans read by AI
choices: High-energy X-ray scans read by AI
Infrared cameras aimed at the ink
Strong magnets pulling the ink out
context: The Vesuvius Challenge (launched March 2023 by Nat Friedman, Daniel Gross, and scientist Brent Seales) scanned the scrolls inside a particle accelerator at resolutions as fine as 4 micrometers, then trained AI to read them virtually -- never opening them. The carbon-based Roman ink was invisible on X-ray, so models learned to spot a faint 'crackle' texture it left, an idea sparked by contestant Casey Handmer. Source: https://scrollprize.org/grandprize

question: Herculaneum was a Roman seaside town near Naples, buried in AD 79 when Mount Vesuvius erupted. In the ruins, diggers found a library of hundreds of papyrus scrolls, all charred black and rolled tight — too fragile to unroll without crumbling to dust. In October 2023, a 21-year-old American computer-science student named Luke Farritor used a scanner and machine learning to read a single word sealed inside one of those unopened scrolls. What was that first recovered ancient word?
context: Farritor, also a SpaceX intern, won the $40,000 First Word prize for reading 'porphyras' (Greek for 'purple') inside an unopened scroll. In February 2024 he and teammates Youssef Nader and Julian Schilliger won the $700,000 Grand Prize for recovering about 5% of a scroll -- a lost treatise on pleasure by the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus. Source: https://scrollprize.org/firstletters

question: Around 1600, one of the biggest cities in the world sat high on the freezing Bolivian plateau. About 120,000 people crowded into the thin, icy air. A cone-shaped mountain rose over the rooftops. What miners hauled out of it was the only reason anyone lived up there. What did they dig from the mountain?
context: Silver. The mountain was Cerro Rico ('Rich Hill'), and its silver made Potosi improbably huge: around 1600 the city held roughly 120,000 native Andeans plus about 6,000 Spaniards and 5,000 Africans -- the second-largest city on Earth after London, and one of the highest cities anywhere at about 4,067 m (13,343 ft). Tradition credits a Quechua herder, Diego de Huallpa, with first finding the silver in 1545. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi.

question: Five hundred years after its silver rush, the name of one cold Bolivian city still lives in a common Spanish saying: 'vale un Potosi.' Cervantes even worked the phrase into Don Quixote. When a Spanish speaker says a thing 'vale un Potosi,' what do they mean?
choices: that it's not worth the bother
that it's worth the long wait
context: 'Worth a fortune.' So much silver poured out of Cerro Rico that Potosi's name became shorthand for staggering wealth across the Spanish-speaking world. In Don Quixote, Cervantes has a character say that even 'the mines of Potosi would be too little to pay you.' Source: historia.nationalgeographic.com.es (de donde viene la expresion 'valer un Potosi').

question: Potosi's mint, the Casa de la Moneda, struck coins that circled the entire globe. Spanish treasure fleets carried them east across the Atlantic to Europe, while Manila Galleons carried them west across the Pacific to Asia. They were the closest thing the 1600s had to one world money. What nickname do we still know these famous coins by?
context: 'Pieces of eight' -- the Spanish eight-real silver coin (real de a ocho), minted by the millions at Potosi and carried worldwide by the treasure fleets and the Manila Galleons until it was the era's global money. It survives as the famous cry of Long John Silver's parrot in Treasure Island. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi.

question: To dig the silver, Spain's colonial rulers forced Andean villages into a labor draft called the mita, and starting in 1574 each highland community had to send about one in seven of its grown men down into Cerro Rico. So many never came back up that the mountain earned a grim name. What did people call it?
choices: the mountain that buries the brave
the mountain that takes the young
context: 'The mountain that eats men' (el cerro que come hombres). After 1565 the ore was refined with mercury (the patio process), which slowly poisoned the workers underground. The colonial death toll was never recorded and is fiercely disputed -- estimates range from hundreds of thousands up to about 8 million, though that largest figure is sometimes applied to the whole Viceroyalty of Peru rather than Potosi alone. Sources: npr.org (Bolivia's Cerro Rico, 'the mountain that eats men'); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico.  (Legend.)

question: For four hundred years Cerro Rico rose above Potosi as a near-perfect sharp cone. But five centuries of tunneling have bored more than 100 km of passages through it, and engineers who resurvey the peak year after year report a startling change to its famous silhouette. What is happening to Cerro Rico itself?
answer: it is slowly losing height and wearing down
choices: it is slowly losing height and wearing down
it is tilting steadily toward one side
it is cracking apart into two peaks
it is spreading outward across its base
context: It is shrinking. So much rock has been pulled out that the summit keeps subsiding several centimeters a year, and estimates of total height lost run from about 250 m (leaving it near 4,753 m in 2025) to as much as 400 m -- one mining engineer predicts it may end up a flat-topped 'truncated cone.' The danger was formal enough that in 2014 UNESCO placed Potosi and Cerro Rico on its List of World Heritage in Danger. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico; news.mongabay.com (2025).

question: For two hundred years, one mountain on the Bolivian plateau -- Cerro Rico -- supplied most of the silver mined anywhere on Earth, all of it locked inside the rock. Geologists can read the mountain's own stone to reconstruct how that metal first gathered there. How did the silver come to be sealed inside Cerro Rico?
answer: hot fluids rose through the cracks, cooled, and left the metal behind
choices: hot fluids rose through the cracks, cooled, and left the metal behind
ancient rivers washed metal grains down and buried them deep
a shallow sea dried away and left the metal in flat beds
a great meteorite struck and scattered metal through the rock
context: Hot, mineral-rich fluids. Cerro Rico is a polymetallic deposit of volcanic origin: superheated, mineral-laden water -- geologists call it hydrothermal, meaning 'hot-water-driven' -- circulated through fractures in the rock and, as it cooled over millions of years, crystallized out the silver, tin, lead and zinc. Those metal-filled cracks are what miners chase as 'ore veins.' The whole mineralized mass rises straight off the high Altiplano plateau. Source: metalorix.com (geology of Cerro Rico, Potosi).

question: On Prague's Old Town Square, a crowd gathers each hour beneath the old Astronomical Clock. Two little doors swing open. A carved skeleton beside the dial rings a bell and tips his hourglass. Then a line of carved figures glides past the open windows, one by one. Who are the figures that parade past each hour?
context: The clockwork 'Walk of the Apostles' has drawn crowds on the hour for centuries. The skeleton is Death, who rings his bell and turns his hourglass to show time running out, while the two little windows reveal the Twelve Apostles gliding past two at a time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: On top of Prague's Astronomical Clock, above the windows where the hourly show plays out, sits a small gilded bird. It was added when the clock was fixed up in the 1860s. When the figures finish their hourly round, it flaps its wings and gives a cry to say the show is over. What golden bird crowns the Orloj?
context: The gilded cockerel was added in an 1860s restoration; its cry closes the 'Walk of the Apostles' each hour, after which the crowd drifts away. A rooster announcing the hour echoes the bird's ancient role as herald of the dawn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: Four carved figures stand beside the dial of Prague's Astronomical Clock. Each is a warning: Vanity with a mirror, a miser clutching his gold, a skeleton for Death, and a turbaned figure for earthly pleasure. Each hour the skeleton rings his bell. The other three answer with the same gesture, as if to say they are not yet ready to follow him. What do the three figures do?
context: The four are the Orloj's carved vices: Vanity with his mirror, Greed the miser with his gold, Death the skeleton, and a turbaned Turk standing for earthly pleasure. When Death rings his bell and turns his glass, the other three shake their heads, as if refusing to follow him for one more hour. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: Prague's Astronomical Clock on the Old Town Hall was first written about in 1410, over 600 years ago. Among the great astronomical clocks of Europe, this earns the Orloj one big claim to fame. What is it?
answer: the oldest astronomical clock still running today
choices: the oldest astronomical clock still running today
the first astronomical clock ever built
the largest astronomical clock in the world
the most accurate astronomical clock ever made
context: The Orloj was built in 1410 by the clockmaker Mikulas of Kadan with Jan Sindel, an astronomy professor at Charles University. Older astronomical clocks were built before it, but all of them have stopped -- making Prague's the third-oldest ever constructed, yet the oldest one still keeping time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: Tucked inside the walls of Prague Castle is a lane of tiny, candy-colored cottages, their doorways so low a grown-up must stoop. They were built into the arches of the castle wall in the late 1500s to house Emperor Rudolf II's guards. Later a group of craftsmen moved in and plied their delicate trade there, and it is their craft that gave the little lane its name. What were these craftsmen?
context: Golden Lane (Zlata ulicka) began as cramped quarters for Rudolf II's castle guards in the late 1500s; goldsmiths later took over the cottages and gave the street its name. Centuries afterward the writer Franz Kafka spent about a year writing in cottage No. 22. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Lane

question: Thirty blackened baroque statues of saints line Charles Bridge as it crosses the Vltava on sixteen stone arches. Tourists file past most of them but crowd around a single bronze plaque at the foot of one statue, rubbing it smooth. Local tradition promises everyone who touches that plaque one particular reward. What does the tradition promise?
answer: that they will return to Prague someday
choices: that they will find their true love
that they will return to Prague someday
that they will be safe from drowning
that they will never go hungry
context: The statue is St John of Nepomuk, and rubbing the bronze relief below it is said to ensure the visitor's return to Prague (some say it also grants a wish). His statue, placed in 1683, is the oldest of the thirty on Charles Bridge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Bridge  (Legend.)

question: When Charles Bridge was going up across the Vltava in the 1300s, a Prague legend claims the master builders hardened their mortar with a surprising kitchen item. Whole Bohemian villages sent cartloads of it to the building site. What does the legend say the builders mixed in?
context: The legend is rich with detail: the town of Velvary is said to have boiled its eggs so they wouldn't smash on the road, and one village reportedly sent a wagon of cheese by mistake. Is it true? A 2008 Czech chemistry-institute test of the old mortar found protein traces that fit the tale, but a 2010 Charles University study found no organic additive -- so the egg legend is one that lab evidence only partly backs. Source: https://prague-now.com/history/charles-bridge-built-with-a-curve-and-with-egg/

question: One of Prague's most famous legends tells of Master Hanus, the clockmaker said to have built the Old Town's Astronomical Clock. The story goes that the town councillors, terrified he might build an even finer clock for a rival city, made sure he never could. According to the legend, what did they do to Master Hanus? (Historians say it never really happened.)
choices: they threw him in the river
context: The blinding of Master Hanus is Prague's most beloved clock legend: the tale says the councillors blinded him so he could never repeat his masterpiece, and that the ruined clockmaker climbed the tower and thrust his hand into the gears to stop the clock forever. In truth the Orloj was built in 1410 by Mikulas of Kadan with the scholar Jan Sindel; Hanus was a real later clockmaker who came to no such harm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: In 1393, King Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia had the priest John of Nepomuk bound and hurled from Charles Bridge into the Vltava -- legend says because John refused to reveal what the queen had told him in confession. He drowned and was later made a saint, and today his is the most-touched statue on the bridge. In art, one distinctive halo sets St John of Nepomuk apart from every other saint. What does his halo contain?
context: The five stars recall the legend that five lights appeared on the Vltava where John of Nepomuk drowned in 1393, on the order of King Wenceslaus IV. His 1683 bronze is the oldest statue on Charles Bridge, and touching the plaque beneath it is the tradition said to bring you back to Prague. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Nepomuk

question: St Vitus Cathedral rises inside Prague Castle. It holds the tombs of the Bohemian kings, but it guards something even more closely: the ancient Crown Jewels of Bohemia, the golden crown of St Wenceslas among them. They are sealed in a chamber whose door was built so that no single official, not even a king acting alone, could ever open it. What secures the door to the Crown Jewels' chamber?
answer: seven locks, their seven keys split among seven guardians
choices: seven locks, their seven keys split among seven guardians
two locks, one key held by the king and one by the archbishop
three locks, opened only when the three chief lords of Bohemia agree
five locks, their keys shared among the cathedral's canons
context: The Crown Jewels of Bohemia -- including the crown of St Wenceslas, made in 1347 -- rest in a chamber inside St Vitus Cathedral behind a door with seven separate locks. Seven keys are held by seven different people (among them the president, the prime minister, and the Archbishop of Prague), and all seven must gather in person before the door can be opened. The cathedral, begun in 1344 under Charles IV and not consecrated until 1929, also glows with an Art Nouveau stained-glass window designed by the Czech painter Alfons Mucha. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Vitus_Cathedral

question: Prague Castle has been the seat of Bohemian kings, Holy Roman emperors, and -- to this day -- the Czech president, its palaces, gardens, and the towers of St Vitus Cathedral crowning the hill above the Vltava. Guinness World Records singles Prague Castle out with one worldwide superlative. What record does it hold?
answer: the largest ancient castle complex in the world
choices: the largest ancient castle complex in the world
the oldest stone castle in the world
the tallest castle towers in the world
the most-visited castle in the world
context: Prague Castle sprawls over roughly 70,000 square metres -- about 570 metres long and 130 wide -- which earns it a place in Guinness World Records as the largest ancient castle complex in the world. Founded around 880, it is still the official residence of the Czech president. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Castle

question: On 23 May 1618, a crowd of furious Bohemian Protestants stormed into Prague Castle, seized two Catholic royal officials and their secretary, and threw all three out of a high window -- a drop of some 21 metres to the ground below. To everyone's amazement, not one of the three men died. Catholics cried that angels had caught them in mid-air; the Protestants scoffed that something far humbler had broken their fall. What did the Protestants say saved the three men?
context: The 1618 Defenestration of Prague hurled two imperial regents -- Jaroslav Borita of Martinice and Vilem Slavata of Chlum -- and their secretary Philip Fabricius from a Prague Castle window; all three survived the ~21 m fall by landing in the refuse heaped in the moat below. The quarrel helped ignite the Thirty Years' War, and the lucky secretary was later ennobled as 'Baron von Hohenfall' -- Baron of Highfall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defenestrations_of_Prague  (Legend.)

question: On the same plain in Java, a few miles from the tall Hindu towers of Prambanan, stands its great neighbor. It is not a spire at all but a vast, low, terraced Buddhist mound topped with rows of bell-shaped stupas. It is one of the largest Buddhist monuments on Earth. What is this neighboring monument called?
context: The two masterpieces are near-contemporaries on the same plain: Borobudur, the broad Buddhist mandala, and Prambanan, whose central Hindu tower stabs 47 metres (about 154 ft) straight up -- the tallest Hindu temple in Indonesia. Prambanan is the largest Hindu temple site in the country and the second-largest in all Southeast Asia, after Angkor Wat in Cambodia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan

question: A Javanese legend explains why so many shrines cluster at Prambanan. The spirit-summoning prince Bandung Bondowoso could marry Princess Roro Jonggrang only if he raised a thousand temples in a single night. His ghost-workers had finished 999 when the unwilling princess tricked them into fleeing before dawn. Cheated of his final temple and his bride, the furious prince took his revenge. What did he do to her? (Legend.)
context: The tale of Roro Jonggrang ('slender virgin') is folklore, not history. In the legend, the prince Bandung Bondowoso -- having killed her father, King Boko -- was told he could marry the princess only by building a thousand temples in one night; with summoned spirits he raised 999, but Roro Jonggrang lit fires and had her maids pound rice in the east to counterfeit the dawn. The roosters crowed, the spirits fled, and the enraged prince cursed her into stone as the missing final statue. Tradition still points to the statue of Durga slaying the buffalo demon, in the Shiva temple's north chamber, and calls it Rara Jonggrang -- the very princess turned to stone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rara_Jonggrang

question: Prambanan's three tallest towers stand in a row, and the middle one is a 47-meter spire, higher than the two beside it. It is dedicated to the Hindu god of destruction and rebirth, the cosmic dancer whose steps whirl the universe into being and out again. Which god does that great middle tower belong to?
context: The three tall central temples honor the Hindu Trimurti: the 47-metre central tower belongs to Shiva the destroyer, flanked by shorter temples for Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver, each about 33 metres tall. The whole compound was raised around 850 CE by the Hindu Mataram (Sanjaya) dynasty, begun by Rakai Pikatan and dedicated to Shiva -- its original Sanskrit name was Shivagrha, 'House of Shiva,' recorded in the Shivagrha inscription of 856 CE. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan

question: Walk the inner walls of Prambanan's main temple, and the carved stone unfolds panel by panel into one of Hinduism's greatest stories: a virtuous prince whose bride is snatched away by a ten-headed demon-king. Then comes the long war to win her back, fought with the help of an army of monkeys and their leaping, flying general. Which tale is carved into these walls?
context: Panel after panel along the inner balustrades follows the Ramayana: Princess Sita, carried off by the demon-king Ravana, and her rescue by Prince Rama with the help of Hanuman and his monkey army. The epic still comes alive at Prambanan today -- performed as an open-air ballet on full-moon nights beneath the towers. Prambanan was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan

question: Quebec City still has huge old stone walls you can walk on. They stretch about 4.6 km around the old town, with big gates and the St. Lawrence River far below. No other town north of Mexico kept its walls. So what makes Quebec special?
answer: the only town still ringed by walls
choices: the only town still ringed by walls
the oldest walled town on the continent
the first town Europeans fortified here
the biggest town the French ever built
context: Old Quebec is the only intact fortified colonial town in North America north of Mexico — about 4.6 km of ramparts you can walk atop, pierced by old gates. Most walled cities elsewhere pulled their walls down for traffic; Quebec's survived, and in 1985 UNESCO named the old town a World Heritage Site. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ramparts of Quebec City' / 'Old Quebec.'

question: The name 'Quebec' comes straight from an Algonquin word, 'kebec.' Long before any fort stood there, the word already described this exact place on the great St. Lawrence River, where the French would later build atop the cliff. What does 'kebec' mean?
choices: where the cliff meets the water
context: 'Kebec' is Algonquin for 'where the river narrows.' Just below the city the wide St. Lawrence squeezes tight against the cliffs — so whoever held the high rock commanded the water gateway to the whole interior of the continent. Champlain planted his 1608 settlement on exactly that chokepoint. Source: Wikipedia, 'Quebec'; Musee de la civilisation, Trousse Premiers Peuples.

question: When the French explorer Jacques Cartier scrambled up the great cliff above the St. Lawrence, he spotted stones glittering in the rock and was sure he'd struck it rich. He named the height Cap Diamant — 'Cape Diamond' — and the name stuck. But when the glittering 'diamonds' were examined, what did they turn out to be?
context: Cartier's 'diamonds' were only quartz — the blunder gave French the old phrase 'faux comme un diamant du Canada' ('false as a Canadian diamond'). But the name held: Cap Diamant, the cliff rising about 100 m straight out of the St. Lawrence, still crowns Quebec City, a natural fortress that decided where the town would stand. Source: Britannica, 'Cape Diamond'; Wikipedia, 'Cap Diamant.'

question: Crowning the cliff above Quebec City sits the Citadelle, a 'star fort' — instead of plain straight walls, its ramparts zigzag out into sharp angled points called bastions. This shape was not for looks. What did those jutting, angled points let the defenders do to anyone attacking a wall?
answer: catch them in crossfire from two sides
choices: catch them in crossfire from two sides
pour boiling oil straight down on them
keep the cannon hidden from their view
flood the ditch below with river water
context: The Citadelle is the largest British-built fortress in North America — four bastions and three straight curtain walls set at angles so every stretch of wall could be swept by fire from the bastions on either side, leaving attackers no blind approach. It is still an active army base, home of the Royal 22e Regiment (the 'Van Doos') since 1920, and a cannon still booms from it every day at noon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Citadelle of Quebec.'

question: One building rears over Quebec City's old town like a medieval castle — turrets, steep copper roofs, perched on the cliff edge above the river. Yet the Chateau Frontenac has always been a hotel, opened to its first guests in 1893. Who built this fairy-tale castle?
context: The Chateau Frontenac was raised by the Canadian Pacific Railway, which opened it in 1893 to lure travelers onto its trains — a 'castle' built to sell railway tickets. It holds a Guinness World Record as the most photographed hotel on Earth, and takes its name from Louis de Buade, Count of Frontenac, the governor who defended New France against British and Iroquois attacks in the 1690s. Source: Britannica, 'Chateau Frontenac'; WorldAtlas.

question: By the 1870s the British soldiers had marched out of Quebec City, and many townsfolk wanted the old stone walls and gates gone — they choked the traffic and seemed a useless relic. The ramparts were nearly torn down for good. Why can you still walk them today?
answer: the Governor General intervened to save them
choices: the Governor General intervened to save them
a sudden war made the walls needed again
the demolition crews hit bedrock and gave up
the walls proved too costly to tear down
context: The walls standing today are the masonry ramparts an engineer, Gaspard-Joseph Chaussegros de Lery, raised in 1745. When the British garrison left in the 1870s, Quebec nearly demolished them for road traffic — until Governor General Lord Dufferin intervened around 1871, even having grand gates rebuilt, so the fortifications would survive. That rescue is why Old Quebec is a walled city at all. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ramparts of Quebec City.'

question: Wet winds from the Pacific dump rain on southern Chile. Then they hit the tall Andes. The far side of the mountains gets almost no rain. A dry desert sits there, even close to the sea. What is this South American desert called?
context: Argentine Patagonia is a COLD winter desert -- average temperatures near 3 C with frequent frost -- and the largest desert in Argentina (about 673,000 sq km, roughly the 8th-largest on Earth). The Andes block the westerly Pacific winds so completely that much of it stays arid within about 200 miles of the sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patagonian_Desert

question: Wet Pacific wind blows steadily east across Washington State, in the northwestern United States, until it slams into the tall Cascade Range. The air is forced up the west slope of the mountains, and by the time it spills down onto the land east of the peaks almost all its water is gone — that eastern side stays dry. What happens to nearly all the water in the wet air as it climbs the western slope?
answer: it cools as it rises, condenses, and falls as rain there
choices: it cools as it rises, condenses, and falls as rain there
the warm air sinking down the far side dries it back out
the peaks block the clouds and scrape them off the wind
the thin summit air simply lets the water escape upward
context: This is the heart of every rain shadow: moist air forced up the windward slope expands and cools, its vapour condenses, and it falls as rain on that side -- so the air clears the crest already 'wrung dry,' leaving desert behind the mountains. Western Washington soaks under Pacific rain on the Cascades' windward flank, while the Columbia Basin just east lies in their dry shadow. The common misconception is that the far side is dry because the sinking air warms; the real cause is that the rain already fell on the way up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow

question: Snow can dust the sand dunes and hard winter frost grips a vast COLD desert that sprawls across Mongolia and northern China. It stays bone-dry because it lies high and far inland, walled off from the ocean's moisture by great mountain ranges to its south. Which desert is this?
context: The Gobi covers about 1.3 million sq km (the 6th-largest desert) across Mongolia and northern China. Sitting high and deep in the continent's interior, cut off from the sea, it is a COLD desert -- frost and even snow can settle on its dunes -- with only about 194 mm of rain a year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gobi_Desert

question: In the American West, four mountain ranges stand in a row. Each one steals more rain from Pacific storms moving east. The first is the Sierra Nevada. Past all four is a scorched valley. It is the driest and lowest place in North America, with Badwater Basin 282 feet below sea level. Name this valley.
context: Four successive mountain ranges, beginning with the Sierra Nevada, strip Pacific storms of their moisture before they reach the valley floor. Badwater Basin lies 282 ft (86 m) below sea level, and Death Valley averages under 2 inches of rain a year -- it recorded ZERO rainfall in 1929, 1953 and 1989. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Death_Valley; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_Valley

question: Mount Waialeale on Kauai gets soaked by trade-wind rain almost every day. Its 11,000 mm a year make it one of the wettest spots on Earth. But just 15 miles away, on the dry side of the island, one sunny town gets only 20 inches a year. Name that town in the mountain's rain shadow.
context: Mount Waialeale's summit sees rain on about 289 days a year and averages roughly 11,430 mm (450 in) -- a record 666 inches fell in 1982. Yet leeward Waimea, only about 15 miles away on the same island, averages just ~20 inches. The wettest and driest places on Kauai almost touch. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Wai%CA%BBale%CA%BBale

question: Down the eastern, leeward slope of the Rocky Mountains, a warm dry 'foehn' wind sometimes comes roaring off the peaks and can shoot the temperature up 25 F (14 C) in a matter of hours -- bare ground can appear where deep snow lay that morning. Ranchers named this snow-devouring wind. What do they call it?
context: As the dry air sinks down the leeward side it is compressed and warms -- a 'foehn' wind, which can raise the temperature by as much as 14 C (25 F) in hours. East of the Rockies this warm downslope wind is the chinook; 'snow eater' is the folk nickname it earned for how fast it strips the snow, while the rapid warming itself is well-documented meteorology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foehn_wind

question: On the Himalaya's southern, windward slopes the summer monsoon unloads staggering rain -- the Indian village of Mawsynram catches over 11,000 mm a year, among the rainiest places anywhere on Earth. But the mountains wring that air dry, so the great highland just north of the crest gets under 200 mm and is itself a bleak, cold desert. Name this rain-starved highland.
context: The Himalaya cast the most dramatic rain shadow on Earth. On the windward south side, Mawsynram and neighbouring Cherrapunji take well over 11,000 mm of monsoon rain a year, while just across the crest the Tibetan Plateau gets under 200 mm -- one of the greatest wet-to-dry contrasts found anywhere. Source: earthdate.org/episodes/rain-shadow

question: On July 10, 1913, a weather station on the floor of Death Valley recorded 134 F (57 C). For a hundred years it stood as the hottest air ever measured on Earth, though scientists now doubt it was correct. The spot is still the valley's main visitor hub. What is it called?
context: The 134 F (57 C) logged at Furnace Creek on 10 July 1913 held the world heat record for a century, but scientists now dispute its accuracy; the highest reliable modern reading is 130 F (54.4 C) in 2020. Furnace Creek sits on the valley floor behind four moisture-stripping mountain ranges. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Death_Valley  (Legend.)

question: New Zealand's Southern Alps stand broadside to the roaring westerly winds off the Tasman Sea. On the West Coast the rain pours down -- up to 15 metres a year near the mountain spine, feeding dense temperate rainforest. But cross barely 30 km to the eastern, sheltered side of the crest and the yearly rain collapses about fifteen-fold to a single metre, leaving the country's driest, brownest land. Name this dry eastern region.
context: The Southern Alps meet the prevailing westerlies head-on. The West Coast drinks up to ~15,000 mm of rain a year near the Main Divide (coastal towns ~3,000 mm), but only about 30 km east of the crest rainfall collapses to roughly 1,000 mm -- a near fifteen-fold drop -- making Central Otago the driest land in New Zealand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Alps

question: The hills around Jerusalem are green in winter and catch about 600 mm of Mediterranean rain. But the city sits on a ridge, and its eastern flank is the dry lee: walk just a few miles east and downhill and the rain falls to barely 100 mm, the green vanishes, and the bare, folded land plunges toward the Dead Sea -- a full desert only miles from the green Mediterranean coast. Name this desert at Jerusalem's edge.
context: The Judaean Desert lies in the rain shadow of the hills of Jerusalem, immediately east of the city. Rainfall drops from about 600 mm on the western, Mediterranean-facing side to roughly 100 mm in the east, where the land falls steeply to the Dead Sea -- a full desert only a few miles from the green coast. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaean_Desert

question: In 1950s Jamaica, a DJ would haul big speaker stacks into a dirt yard. Then he threw an all-night street dance. By mid-decade the best of these drew bigger crowds than any live band. What did Jamaicans call the whole rig -- the speakers and the crew?
context: The Jamaican 'sound system' — a mobile DJ outfit of huge speaker stacks and a generator — was the engine of the island's whole music culture, and the men who ran the biggest ones became stars. The first great commercial system belonged to Chinese-Jamaican businessman Tom Wong ('Tom the Great Sebastian'); rivals like Duke Reid and Coxsone Dodd battled for the loudest bass and the rarest records. Every genre that followed — ska, rocksteady, reggae, dub — was built to be played on these speakers. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sound system (Jamaican).'

question: Around 1962, when Jamaica became free, Kingston bands took American R&B records and sped them up. They put the guitar's beat on the off-beat, a springy up-stroke. Guitarist Ernest Ranglin said American R&B goes 'chink-ka,' but the new Kingston sound goes 'ka-chink.' What was this bouncy new genre called?
context: Ska was Jamaica's first homegrown pop genre — jumpy and brass-driven, born of American R&B sped up and flipped onto the off-beat. Its greatest band, the Skatalites, cut hard instrumental hits like 'Guns of Navarone,' while independence-year anthems such as Derrick Morgan's 'Forward March' (1962) caught the mood of a nation just cutting free from Britain. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ska.'

question: In the summer of 1966, the city of Kingston, Jamaica sweltered under a heat wave. Ska — the island's fast, brassy dance music with a hopping offbeat — was suddenly too jumpy to bear. In cramped Kingston studios, Jamaican bands slowed the tempo way down into a cool, easy sway. At that lazy pace, the electric bass finally stepped out front and led the whole song. What did the local musicians and dancers call this brand-new, slower sound?
context: Rocksteady took its name from Alton Ellis's 1966 hit 'Rock Steady,' and bandleader Lynn Taitt summed it up: 'Rocksteady is really slow ska.' It lasted barely two years, but by slowing everything down it handed the spotlight to the bass — the deep, rolling foundation that reggae would soon build its entire sound upon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rocksteady.'

question: One poor Kingston neighborhood -- its houses built from scrap wood and rubble -- turned out a huge lineup of music stars in the 1960s. Bob Marley, Peter Tosh, and Bunny Wailer of the Wailers all came from there. From its cramped housing yards, reggae went out to the world. What is this Kingston district called?
context: Trench Town, a poor Kingston neighborhood built of timber-and-rubble 'knog' housing, was the cradle of reggae — home also to Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, and Toots. Bob Marley immortalized it in 'No Woman No Cry' (1974), singing of sitting 'in the government yard in Trenchtown,' the real public-housing yard on First Street where he grew up. In 2018, UNESCO honored the reggae music of Jamaica as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, praising its voice on 'injustice, resistance, love and humanity.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Trench Town'; UNESCO (2018).

question: Producer Clement Dodd -- 'Coxsone' to everyone in Kingston -- ran a hit factory on Brentford Road. Fans called it 'the Motown of Jamaica.' It launched Bob Marley and the Wailers, Toots and the Maytals, Burning Spear, and the Skatalites. What was Coxsone Dodd's music house called?
context: Studio One was the beating heart of Jamaican recording — its house band and back catalogue shaped ska, rocksteady, and reggae, and its old rhythms are still sampled around the world. Coxsone Dodd's chief rivals each had a legendary room of their own, among them Lee 'Scratch' Perry's backyard Black Ark studio, built in 1973. Source: Wikipedia, 'Studio One (record label).'

question: In his small Kingston studio, a radio fixer named Osbourne Ruddock -- known as King Tubby -- took finished reggae records and wiped the vocals off them. Then he rebuilt the bare bass and drums into a spacey, echo-soaked track. It was the far ancestor of every modern remix. What Jamaican style did King Tubby help invent?
context: Dub — Jamaica's gift to the age of the remix — reportedly began by accident in 1968, when engineer Byron Smith left the vocals off a pressing of the Paragons' 'On the Beach' and the dance crowd went wild for the bare instrumental. King Tubby made dub an art, 'playing' his 12-channel mixing desk like an instrument in his tiny Waterhouse studio, riding echo and faders live. He was shot dead outside his Kingston home in 1989. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dub music' and 'King Tubby.'  (Legend.)

question: By the late 1960s, Kingston singles carried an instrumental 'version' on the flip side, the vocals gone and only the riddim left. At the dance, sound-system DJs stopped just spinning discs, grabbed the microphone, and rode the beat with their voices — hyping the crowd and trading rhymes live over the bare track. Pioneers like Count Machuki and U-Roy made it an art many historians now call a direct ancestor of American rap. What was this Jamaican vocal style called?
context: Toasting — the Jamaican DJ chanting rhythmically over an instrumental 'version' — is widely seen as one ancestor of rap. Its pioneers, Count Machuki and U-Roy, grabbed the mic at sound-system dances and 'chatted' over the bare riddims, turning the DJ from a record-spinner into a star performer in his own right. Source: Wikipedia, 'Toasting (Jamaican music).'

question: In 1985, a Kingston teenager named Wayne Smith and keyboardist Noel Davey hit the 'rock' preset on a cheap Casio keyboard. Producer King Jammy polished it into a hit. Out came the first fully computer-made Jamaican beat, the 'Sleng Teng' riddim. It kicked off a new all-electronic era, and that one robotic bassline turned up on about 500 records. What is this era called?
context: Here is the twist: the 'Sleng Teng' bassline that reshaped Jamaican music wasn't written in Kingston at all. It was a factory preset built in 1980 by a young Casio engineer in Japan, Hiroko Okuda, who had studied reggae for her thesis. She only learned years later that her little demo tune had sparked a whole genre — and was amazed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sleng Teng.'

question: Reykjavik is the capital city of Iceland, a small island country tucked up in the far North Atlantic. It sits at about 64 degrees north latitude on the island's southwest coast, only a short hop south of the Arctic Circle. Ships sailing in still see snowy mountains just behind the harbor. Among the capitals of the world, what record does Reykjavik's far-north spot earn it?
answer: the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign country
choices: the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign country
the coldest capital of any country on Earth
the world's only capital inside the Arctic Circle
the world's northernmost city of any kind
context: Reykjavik sits at 64 degrees 08' north. Nuuk, the capital of Greenland, actually lies a touch farther north at 64 degrees 10' N -- but Greenland is a self-governing territory of Denmark, not a sovereign state, so Reykjavik keeps the title of northernmost capital of a fully independent country. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: Reykjavik is the capital of Iceland, a volcanic island in the North Atlantic that sits just below the Arctic Circle. Through Reykjavik's long, dark northern winters almost every home stays cozy and warm, yet the city burns virtually no oil or coal — and its winter air stays clean and clear. What heats the whole city instead?
answer: naturally hot water piped up from volcanic rock
choices: naturally hot water piped up from volcanic rock
rooftop solar panels across the city
heat pumps drawing warmth from the sea
context: Naturally hot water is pumped from volcanic rock and run through a district-heating network that warms nearly all of Reykjavik's buildings; about 90% of Iceland's homes are heated this way. Because the city burns almost no fuel for heat, greenhouse-gas emissions from space heating in the Reykjavik area fell from around 270,000 tonnes a year in 1960 to roughly 12,000 tonnes today. Iceland's first geothermal district-heating system opened in 1930, warming a school, a hospital, a pool and about 60 homes. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geothermal_power_in_Iceland ; https://web.mit.edu/nature/archive/student_projects/2009/bjorn627/TheGeothermalCity/Reykjavik.html

question: Around the year 874, the first Viking-age Norse settlers rowed their longship into a wide bay on Iceland's southwest coast. As they neared shore, they saw pale plumes rising from the ground — steam venting up from natural hot springs in the rock. Struck by the sight, they gave the new settlement a plain name built from two Norse words: one for the curling steam, one for the bay. Today that place is Iceland's capital. What does the name 'Reykjavik' mean?
context: In Old Norse, reykr means 'smoke' and vik means 'bay,' so Reykjavik is 'Smoky Bay.' The settlers took the steam drifting off the hot springs for smoke and named their new home for it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: In Iceland's capital city of Reykjavik stands a tall pale church called Hallgrimskirkja, towering above the low houses around it. The Icelandic architect Gudjon Samuelsson designed it in the 20th century, and he wanted its shape to echo one of Iceland's most famous natural rock forms -- a form born from the island's fiery volcanic past. Which volcanic form did he copy for his church?
choices: jagged fields of black volcanic ash
context: Basalt is the dark volcanic rock that covers much of Iceland; when a thick lava flow cools slowly it cracks into tall, many-sided (often hexagonal) columns, like those seen behind the Svartifoss waterfall. Gudjon Samuelsson drew Hallgrimskirkja's stepped, upward-sweeping shape from those columns. Designed in 1937 and built from 1945 to 1986, the church stands 74.5 m (244 ft) tall -- the tallest in Iceland. Source: https://guidetoiceland.is/travel-iceland/drive/hallgrimskirkja

question: Reykjavik is the capital of Iceland, sitting near the Arctic Circle at the top of the world. You might expect it to be frozen solid all winter. Yet its winters rarely drop below minus 15 C -- often milder than cities hundreds of miles farther south. Something in the natural world keeps this far-north capital surprisingly warm. What is it?
answer: the warm Atlantic Ocean current along its coast
choices: the warm Atlantic Ocean current along its coast
heat rising from Iceland's volcanoes and lava fields
tall mountains that block the cold Arctic winds
warm winds blowing up from mainland Europe
context: The warm water of the North Atlantic (an arm of the Gulf Stream system) washes Iceland's coast and keeps Reykjavik's winters mild -- rarely below minus 15 degrees C, sometimes milder than places far to its south. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: In Reykjavik's high summer the sun never fully sets -- people mow their lawns and play football late at night in plain daylight, the sky still glowing at 1 a.m. Around December, though, the city gets only four or five dim hours of light a day. What is this bright, near-endless summer daylight called?
context: Because Reykjavik lies so far north, from about May 20 to July 24 the sun never sinks more than 5 degrees below the horizon, so summer nights never go fully dark -- the 'midnight sun.' The flip side comes near midwinter (about Dec 2 to Jan 10), when the city gets fewer than five hours of daylight and the sun climbs only about 3 degrees above the horizon. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: The city of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil has a name that means 'River of January.' The story goes that a Portuguese sailing fleet reached its huge, wide bay on January 1, 1502, and named the place for that first day of the new year. Strangely, there is no real river there at all. By the old story, why did they call it a river?
answer: Explorers mistook the wide bay for a river mouth
choices: Explorers mistook the wide bay for a river mouth
Mapmakers copied a mislabelled older chart
Settlers named it for a river back in Portugal
context: By the traditional account, a Portuguese fleet -- usually credited to Gaspar de Lemos and Goncalo Coelho -- sailed into the huge bay on 1 January 1502 and took its narrow, cliff-flanked entrance for the mouth of a great river, naming the spot 'River of January' for the month. There is no river: Rio in fact curls around a bay, Guanabara Bay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro  (Legend.)

question: Arms flung open 28 metres wide, a 30-metre figure of pale soapstone has watched over Rio since 1931 from the 700-metre granite peak of Corcovado. In the worldwide 07/07/2007 vote it was chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Which monument is this?
context: Christ the Redeemer (Cristo Redentor) is 30 m tall with arms 28 m wide on an 8 m pedestal, built of reinforced concrete faced in pale soapstone atop the 700 m peak of Corcovado, and inaugurated on 12 October 1931 after nine years' work. On 7 July 2007 it was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_the_Redeemer_(statue)

question: Long ago, Portuguese traders boiled sugar down and sold it as hard blocks molded into one shape. Rio's Pao de Acucar, the bare granite peak by the bay, was nicknamed 'Sugarloaf' because it looked just like that block. What shape was the block of sugar?
context: Refined sugar in that era was boiled down and molded into a tall cone -- a 'sugarloaf' -- for storage and shipping. Portuguese traders thought the bare 396 m granite dome at the bay's mouth looked just like one, so they named it Pao de Acucar; in English, Sugarloaf Mountain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarloaf_Mountain

question: Christ the Redeemer stands on a granite peak the Portuguese named Corcovado. A little cog railway has climbed 3.8 km through the Tijuca Forest to reach it since 1884. The name is a blunt joke about the mountain's shape. What does 'Corcovado' mean in Portuguese?
context: 'Corcovado' is Portuguese for 'hunchback,' after the peak's bent, humped profile. Since 1884 the Corcovado Rack Railway, a cog train, has climbed 3.8 km up through the Tijuca Forest to the summit that Christ the Redeemer now crowns. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corcovado; britannica.com/place/Mount-Corcovado

question: Since 1912, a small cable car called the Bondinho has carried riders up Rio's Sugarloaf. It goes up in two stages. It stops at Morro da Urca, then climbs to the 396-metre top. Engineer Augusto Ferreira Ramos built it very early. It counts as only the ___ passenger cableway ever raised on Earth.
context: The Sugarloaf cable car -- the Bondinho -- opened in 1912, reportedly only the third cableway ever built anywhere in the world. Dreamed up by engineer Augusto Ferreira Ramos, it climbs in two stages, pausing at Morro da Urca (220 m) before rising to the 396 m summit. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarloaf_Cable_Car

question: Guanabara Bay, the inlet Rio wraps around, reaches 31 km inland, scatters more than 130 islands, yet pinches to a mouth just 1.5 km wide, guarded by Sugarloaf. It began as a river valley on dry land; when the last Ice Age's meltwater lifted the sea, saltwater climbed the valley and drowned it. What is the geographer's term for a coastal inlet drowned this way?
context: A drowned river valley like this is called a 'ria' -- an old river-carved valley flooded when seas rose after the last Ice Age (unlike a fjord, whose valley was carved by a glacier). Guanabara Bay runs about 31 km inland, up to 28 km wide, narrows to a ~1.5 km mouth guarded by Sugarloaf, and holds more than 130 islands. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanabara_Bay

question: Sugarloaf and Corcovado are Rio's bald granite giants -- toughened cores of ancient rock left towering after ages of weathering stripped away the softer rock that once buried them. Geologists have one word for a lone hard-rock mass exhumed and left rising this way. Which term names it?
context: Such isolated bald domes are called bornhardts -- a dome-shaped kind of 'inselberg' (German for 'island mountain'). Geologist Wilhelm Bornhardt coined the idea in 1900 for the rock-islands he saw rising from African plains: a core of especially resistant granite is left standing as the softer rock around it weathers away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inselberg; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarloaf_Mountain

question: The dark-green mountains rising inside Rio -- the Tijuca Forest, one of the largest forests inside any city on Earth -- look like untouched jungle. Yet in the 1800s coffee plantations had stripped these very slopes bare, and the springs feeding the city were drying up. From 1861, on the orders of Emperor Pedro II, the rainforest we see today was brought back. How was Rio's Tijuca Forest restored?
answer: it was replanted by hand, tree by tree
choices: it was replanted by hand, tree by tree
it grew back on its own once farming stopped
it was seeded from aircraft after a fire
it was transplanted whole from the Amazon
context: The Tijuca Forest (~3,958 hectares) is one of the world's largest urban forests -- and hand-made. After coffee plantations stripped the slopes and choked the streams supplying Rio, Emperor Pedro II placed the land under federal control in 1861 and ordered it replanted, overseen by Major Manuel Gomes Archer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tijuca_Forest

question: Rio gave the world samba, the swaying music-and-dance at the heart of its Carnival. It grew in the early 1900s among Afro-Brazilian families in the dockside district nicknamed 'Little Africa,' nurtured in the home of a revered Bahian host, Tia Ciata. In 1917 the very first samba ever recorded became the smash hit of Carnival. What was that landmark song called?
context: Samba was born in the early 1900s in the Afro-Brazilian neighbourhoods near Rio's port, an area nicknamed 'Little Africa,' and incubated in the home of the Bahian matriarch Tia Ciata. The first recorded samba, 'Pelo Telefone,' was registered by the musician Donga in 1916 and became the hit of the 1917 Carnival. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba

question: One of the world's largest urban rainforests, Rio's Tijuca Forest, was replanted entirely by hand between 1861 and 1887 -- well over 100,000 trees pressed one by one into slopes that coffee plantations had scraped down to bare dirt. You might imagine an army of foresters. In fact, records credit most of that quarter-century of planting to a startlingly small crew. How many workers did the bulk of that planting?
context: Records credit most of that quarter-century of planting to just six enslaved workers -- Eleuterio, Constantino, Manuel, Mateus, Leopoldo, and Maria -- who set out more than 100,000 trees between 1861 and 1887, growing back an entire forest tree by tree under Major Manuel Gomes Archer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tijuca_Forest

question: High on its exposed 700-metre peak, Christ the Redeemer takes a beating from Rio's fierce summer storms. In February 2008 the statue's head, eyebrows, and fingers were chipped; in 2014 a fingertip broke clean off. Which storm hazard keeps scarring the figure this way?
context: Because it crowns an exposed ~700 m peak with its arms flung wide, Christ the Redeemer is struck by lightning often. A February 2008 strike chipped the head, eyebrows, and fingers; a 2014 strike broke off a fingertip. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_the_Redeemer_(statue)

question: The steep granite that makes Rio beautiful also makes it deadly. Heavy summer rain soaks the thin soil of the hillside favelas until whole slopes give way. After disasters in 2010 and 2011 -- the 2011 landslides north of Rio killed more than 900 people -- the city rolled out a new safeguard across its most exposed favelas. What did Rio install to protect hillside residents?
context: In January 2011, extreme rain in the mountains north of Rio set off thousands of landslides that killed well over 900 people -- among the deadliest natural disasters in Brazil's history; an April 2010 downpour of 288 mm in 24 hours had already triggered some 300 slides. Rio responded by installing 'Sirenes Cariocas' -- sirens that sound in hillside favelas when rainfall reaches dangerous levels. Source: rioonwatch.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_2010_Rio_de_Janeiro_floods_and_mudslides

question: In ancient Egypt, the Nile River flows north across the desert. Right before it pours into the Mediterranean Sea, it stops being one river — it splits into many small branches that spread out into a wide green fan of new farmland. The ancient Greeks who visited noticed the shape and named this kind of landform after a triangular letter of their alphabet. Which letter is it?
context: Herodotus wrote in the 5th century BCE of 'the Delta, as it is called by the Ionians.' The Greek capital delta, the letter shaped like a triangle, matches the Nile's fan of land almost perfectly. For centuries 'the Delta' meant only the Nile's mouth; only later did 'delta' become the word for any river-mouth fan of new land. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_delta  (Legend.)

question: The Nile Delta was the breadbasket of ancient Egypt. Its rich dark soil fed the pharaohs for thousands of years. Even though it sits at the north end of Egypt on the map, the old Egyptians knew the whole area by what name?
context: It sounds backwards, but the Nile flows north, so the delta is DOWNstream — the 'lower' end of the river — even though it lies in the north. Its topsoil runs up to 21 m (70 ft) deep, and the fan stretches about 240 km along the coast. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile_Delta

question: Most big rivers spread into a smooth fan where they meet the sea. The Mississippi does the opposite. It dumps mud into the Gulf of Mexico faster than the waves can push it aside. So it builds narrow fingers of land straight out into open water. Seen from above, this delta's shape is nicknamed after what?
context: The narrow lobes are called 'passes,' and the whole shape is the classic 'bird's-foot' delta. It forms because the river's sediment power overwhelms the Gulf's weak waves and tides, so the river builds the coastline on its own terms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River_Delta  (Legend.)

question: In the age of the pharaohs, the Nile River finished its long journey by fanning out to the Mediterranean Sea through seven different mouths. Ancient Greek writers named them one by one — the Pelusiac branch in the east, the Canopic in the west, the Sebennytic in the middle, and four more. Over the last two thousand years, thick river silt and modern flood-control dams have sealed the small branches off. How many of those seven mouths still carry the Nile to the sea today?
context: Only two flowing branches survive: the Rosetta and the Damietta, which give the delta its two great arms. The others — the Pelusiac, the Canopic, the Sebennytic and more — silted up or were closed by flood management. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile_Delta

question: A river delta's shape is decided by a three-way tug-of-war. When the river's mud-power wins, it pokes out long fingers like the Mississippi's bird's-foot. When the sea's waves win, they smooth the mud into a curved fan like the Nile's. A third force, when it dominates, slices a delta into a branching maze of long sandbars and islands — the shape where the Ganges and Brahmaputra reach the sea. Which force is it?
context: Geographers sort deltas by which of three forces wins: river (fluvial), wave, or tidal. Tide-dominated deltas like the Ganges-Brahmaputra get combed into long, finger-like sandbars aligned with the rise and fall of the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_delta

question: The Ganges and the Brahmaputra are two of Asia's biggest rivers. They join and dump so much Himalayan mud and rock into the sea that they build the largest river delta on the planet. More than 250 million people live on this green lowland. What is this delta called?
context: The Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna together build the Bengal (or Ganges-Brahmaputra) delta — over 105,000 km² across Bangladesh and India's West Bengal, the largest and most populous delta on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganges_Delta  (Legend.)

question: Along the seaward edge of the huge Ganges-Brahmaputra delta, salt-tough trees stand rooted in brackish water. Their tangled roots thread through an endless maze of tidal channels. It is the largest tidal forest of its kind on Earth. What is this coastal wilderness called?
context: The Sundarbans covers about 20,400 km² of the delta's seaward fringe and takes its name from the sundri tree (Heritiera fomes) that dominates it. It is the world's largest tidal mangrove forest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganges_Delta  (Legend.)

question: In the far north of Russian Siberia, the Lena River completes a 2,700-mile journey from the mountains of the south by fanning out across the frozen tundra of Yakutia. Its many mouths build the greatest of all the Arctic's deltas — a low, marshy fan nearly 250 miles (400 km) wide, reaching out into the icy Laptev Sea. Winter and summer up there are two completely different worlds. What happens to this vast Arctic delta over the course of a single year?
answer: It lies frozen as hard tundra through the long winter, then thaws into a lush green wetland each summer.
choices: It lies frozen as hard tundra through the long winter, then thaws into a lush green wetland each summer.
It stays locked beneath solid ice all year, never thawing even at the height of summer.
Its channels dry to cracked mud through the rainless season, then refill when the snowmelt returns.
It vanishes under deep snowdrifts each winter, then reappears as bare gravel flats in the short summer.
context: The Lena builds the largest delta in the Arctic, fanning about 400 km (250 mi) wide into the Laptev Sea off Siberia's north coast. It lies frozen as tundra for roughly seven months a year, then bursts into a lush wetland for a few short summer months when the thaw floods across its islands. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lena_Delta
