question: The Okavango River tumbles out of the Angolan highlands but never makes it to any sea. Instead it fans across a huge sunken basin into a glittering maze of channels, islands and lagoons that swells to three times its size each flood — then simply sinks away and evaporates into the sand. Which great desert does the Okavango vanish into?
context: The Okavango spills into a tectonic trough in Botswana's Kalahari Desert, one of the world's great inland (endorheic) deltas — almost none of its water ever reaches an ocean. At flood it spreads up to 15,000 km²; in 2014 it became the 1,000th UNESCO World Heritage site. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okavango_Delta  (Legend.)

question: A delta only grows while its river keeps feeding it fresh mud. Upstream dams have cut the Mississippi's sediment load nearly in half, and levees wall the river off from its own marshes — so the starved delta is sinking and drowning, handing Louisiana back to the Gulf of Mexico. At its worst, that coast was vanishing at a rate people described as losing how much?
context: USGS measured coastal Louisiana shrinking by about 2,006 square miles (5,197 km²) between 1932 and 2016. At its worst that was a football field of wetland lost every 34 minutes; even at slower recent rates it is roughly one every 100 minutes. Source: https://www.usgs.gov/news/national-news-release/usgs-louisianas-rate-coastal-wetland-loss-continues-slow  (Legend.)

question: Step inside Rome's Pantheon. The only daylight comes from one round hole at the very top of the dome. It is about 9 metres wide and open straight to the sky. What is this opening at the top of the dome called?
context: The Pantheon's opening is the oculus (Latin for 'eye'), about 9.1 m across, and it is the building's only source of daylight. As the sun crosses the sky, its shaft of light sweeps around the marble interior like a moving spotlight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: The Pantheon is an ancient temple in the middle of Rome, built by the Roman emperors almost 2,000 years ago. Its huge concrete dome has a round hole cut through the very top, open straight to the sky. When a storm blows over Rome, rain pours right down through that hole and lands on the marble floor below. Yet the old temple never floods, even in the worst downpour. How is the rain water dealt with?
answer: small drain holes in the floor
choices: small drain holes in the floor
gutters along the base of the walls
a bed of sand beneath the paving
channels feeding a pool at the centre
context: The floor is very slightly domed (convex) and holds 22 nearly invisible drainage holes that carry the rainwater into an underground channel — a system that has kept the Pantheon dry for roughly 1,900 years. Source: https://thepantheonrome.com/pantheon-oculus/  (Legend.)

question: Rome's Colosseum held about 50,000 fans. They came in through 80 arched entrances around the outer wall. Above every arch, the Romans carved the same kind of marking. What did they carve above each one?
context: Each of the 80 entrances was carved with a number (I to LXXX); a spectator's ticket sent them to the right numbered arch and straight to their seat — crowd control that works exactly like a modern stadium. Capacity estimates range from about 50,000 to 80,000. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum

question: The Pantheon's dome is 43.3 metres across, and the Romans set its height — from the floor up to the opening at the crown — to that exact same 43.3 metres. Because the width and height match so perfectly, one ideal solid would fit precisely inside the great rotunda. What solid fits exactly inside the Pantheon?
context: Because the dome's height to its crown equals its 43.3 m width, a full sphere 43.3 m across fits exactly inside the rotunda. It remains the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome — built with no steel reinforcement — after about 1,900 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome  (Legend.)

question: The Pantheon's giant dome could crack under its own weight, so Roman builders got clever with the concrete mix. At the base they packed in heavy travertine stone, but higher up they switched to lighter and lighter stone as the dome curved toward the crown. Near the very top, what light volcanic stone did they pack into the mix?
context: Near the very top the Roman builders packed the concrete with pumice, a volcanic rock so full of air pockets it can float on water. The mix grades from heavy travertine near the base, to terracotta, then to light volcanic tufa and pumice near the top; the dome is also 6.4 m thick at its base but only 1.2 m thick around the crown. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: On hot afternoons a huge cloth roof called the velarium was pulled across the Colosseum crowd from 240 tall wooden poles. Rolling it out and back was skilled, dangerous, high-up work, so the Romans didn't use locals. Instead they marched in a trained crew from a military base about 200 kilometers away near Naples. What kind of base did the awning crew come from?
context: The awning crew were sailors from the imperial fleet's base at Misenum, on the Bay of Naples — men who already knew how to handle sail and rigging in the wind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velarium  (Legend.)

question: After Rome fell, most of its ancient buildings were slowly torn apart, their marble and stone hauled away to raise new palaces and towers. Yet the Pantheon still stands whole — the best-preserved building of ancient Rome. What spared it from being quarried for its stone?
answer: it was turned into a church
choices: it was turned into a church
it was made into a fortress
it was rebuilt by an emperor
it was buried by a flood
context: In AD 609 Pope Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres, so it was protected and maintained instead of stripped for building stone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: Begun in 312 BC by the official Appius Claudius Caecus, the Via Appia was the first of Rome's great paved highways, running dead straight out of the city on tightly-fitted blocks of volcanic stone you can still walk today. So prized was this road that the Romans gave it a grand royal nickname. What did they call the Via Appia?
context: Its Latin nickname was regina viarum, 'the queen of roads.' Its polygonal lava paving stones can still be walked about 2,300 years later. The road first ran ~212 km from Rome to Capua and was later extended to the port of Brundisium (modern Brindisi). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian_Way  (Legend.)

question: Roman harbours and sea walls have stood in salt water for 2,000 years, and modern scientists traced that strength to one special ingredient the Romans dug from the ground near Pozzuoli, on the Bay of Naples. Mixed with lime and water it forms a mineral glue so tough it even sets hard underwater. What was this key ingredient?
context: The ash is called pozzolana, after Pozzuoli near Naples; blended with lime it makes a hydraulic cement that hardens even underwater, which is why Roman marine concrete has lasted 2,000 years in the sea. Source: https://www.sciencealert.com/we-finally-know-why-ancient-roman-concrete-lasts-thousands-of-years

question: Modern concrete decays and weakens within decades, yet Roman concrete has stood for 2,000 years. In 2023 an MIT-led team traced its endurance to tiny white flecks of lime scattered through the ancient mix — flecks that give Roman concrete one remarkable ability modern concrete lacks. What can it do?
context: The lime flecks (lime clasts) form when the Romans 'hot-mixed' the concrete with reactive quicklime. When water seeps into a crack, the flecks dissolve and re-crystallize as calcium carbonate, gluing the crack shut before it can spread. In the MIT test (led by Prof. Admir Masic), cracked hot-mixed concrete sealed itself within two weeks, while concrete made without quicklime did not heal. Source: https://news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106  (Legend.)

question: Rome's aqueducts carried water for tens of miles into the city with no pumps — just a channel sloping gently downhill the whole way, so gently that too little tilt would leave the water stalled and stagnant. The Roman writer Vitruvius even set a rule for the least slope a channel could have. Over each kilometre of its long run, how far did a typical aqueduct actually drop?
context: The channels ran gently downhill the entire way, often dropping just a few centimetres over a whole kilometre. The Roman engineer Vitruvius advised a minimum tilt of about 1 in 4,800 (roughly 20 cm per kilometre). With no pumps anywhere on the route, that barely-there slope still moved water for tens of miles across arches and through tunnels into Rome. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Roman_aqueduct

question: Long before Rome had an empire, its early kings faced a swampy, flood-prone valley where the Forum would later stand. In the 6th century BC they built the Cloaca Maxima, the 'Greatest Sewer' — a huge stone drain to carry the water away to the Tiber. What is most astonishing about the Cloaca Maxima now?
answer: it is still in use today
choices: it is still in use today
it was rebuilt three times over
it now carries a subway line
context: Begun under the Etruscan king Tarquinius Priscus in the 6th century BC, the Cloaca Maxima still carries rainwater down to the Tiber roughly 2,500 years later — one of the world's oldest sewers still in use. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloaca_Maxima  (Legend.)

question: Easter Island is a tiny dot of land far out in the South Pacific — the loneliest inhabited island on Earth, with 2,000 miles of empty ocean in every direction. The Rapa Nui people who lived there carved the famous giant stone heads called moai. They also chiseled rows of tiny signs onto flat wooden tablets. Those signs are called rongorongo, and no one alive has fully cracked them. What is rongorongo's place in the whole story of writing?
answer: The only script ever invented anywhere in the Pacific
choices: The only script ever invented anywhere in the Pacific
The oldest writing system in the world
The largest writing system, with thousands of signs
The fastest writing ever to spread worldwide
context: Across the thousands of islands of Oceania, only Rapa Nui developed a glyph-script of its own -- which is why rongorongo is so often called the only writing ever invented anywhere in the Pacific. Scholars still debate whether it is true writing or a proto-writing 'memory aid' for chants, so its exact status is unsettled. Roughly 600 distinct signs are known: stylized people, plants, and seabirds like the frigatebird, most carved into Pacific rosewood. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo.  (Legend.)

question: Rongorongo, the tiny glyph-script of Easter Island, is read in a baffling style called 'reverse boustrophedon.' You begin at the bottom-left corner and read one line straight across. To read the very next line, what must you do with the whole wooden tablet?
answer: Flip the whole tablet upside down
choices: Flip the whole tablet upside down
Read the next line from right to left
Turn it over to read the back face
Rotate it a quarter-turn and read down
context: In reverse boustrophedon, every other line is carved upside down, so a reader flips the tablet a full 180 degrees at the end of each line and reads on. The glyphs stand only about a centimetre tall. The longest surviving text, the 'Santiago Staff,' carries roughly 2,920 of them; the Mamari tablet seems to hold a lunar calendar -- one of the very few passages scholars have even tentatively identified. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo.

question: Egyptian hieroglyphs and the Maya script both fell silent when their last native readers died, yet scholars later learned to read them again. Easter Island's rongorongo also lost its trained tablet-chanters in the 1862 Peruvian slave raids. Where does rongorongo stand today?
answer: It is one of the world's last completely undeciphered scripts
choices: It is one of the world's last completely undeciphered scripts
A bilingual tablet unlocked it, like the Rosetta Stone
It proved not to be real writing, just carved decoration
Computer analysis of its glyphs finally cracked the code
context: One islander later told Bishop Jaussen that 'there was nobody left on the island who knew how to read the characters, since the Peruvians had brought about the deaths of all the wise men.' Only about two dozen inscribed objects survive worldwide, and rongorongo remains completely undeciphered; scholars still argue over whether it was ever true writing at all. Egyptian hieroglyphs were also unreadable for centuries before the Rosetta Stone cracked them -- but rongorongo has no such key. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo; history.com/articles/easter-island-people-rapanui.

question: Rotorua, in New Zealand, carries a nickname no other city would want: 'Sulphur City.' A whiff of rotten eggs hangs over the whole town, because the hot rock deep underground constantly leaks one particular gas up through the soil. Which gas is it?
context: It is hydrogen sulphide (H2S) -- the very gas that gives rotten eggs their stink -- seeping up from Rotorua's geothermal ground. Locals wear the 'Sulphur City' nickname (and the joke name 'Rotten-rua') with a grin. Carbon dioxide and methane are odourless, and sulphur dioxide smells sharp and acrid rather than eggy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotorua

question: At Rotorua, on New Zealand's North Island, the ground itself steams and hisses. In the Whakarewarewa valley on the edge of town, one geyser puts on a bigger show than all the rest. Every hour or two — up to twenty times a day — it roars to life and blasts boiling water as high as 30 metres into the air. It is the biggest active geyser anywhere in the Southern Hemisphere, and the local Maori guides know it by a short name. What is this geyser called?
context: Pohutu -- Maori for 'big splash' -- is the largest active geyser in the Southern Hemisphere (not the whole world; the tallest active geyser is Yellowstone's Steamboat). Old Faithful also erupts in Yellowstone, Strokkur in Iceland, and Lady Knox is a real geyser at nearby Wai-O-Tapu. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pohutu_Geyser

question: On the North Island of New Zealand lies the town of Rotorua, where the ground itself steams and bubbles from underground heat. At Whakarewarewa village there, the local Te Arawa Maori families still cook the way their grandparents did -- using no fire and no stove at all. How do they cook a basket of corn, seafood, and greens?
answer: they lower it into a naturally boiling hot spring
choices: they lower it into a naturally boiling hot spring
they bake it on hot stones in an earth oven
they smoke it slowly over a driftwood fire
they dry it for days in the summer sun
context: The Te Arawa and Tuhourangi people lower flax baskets of food on cords into the boiling Parekohuru hot spring, and build wooden steam boxes over natural vents -- cooking corn, seafood and vegetables with the ground's own heat, no fire needed. (Hot stones in an earth oven is the hangi, the more familiar Maori method used where there is no geothermal spring.) Source: whakarewarewa.com / en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whakarewarewa

question: At the Whakarewarewa valley in Rotorua, one smaller geyser can be trusted to play first. It sprays up 7 to 9 meters a few minutes before the big geyser roars to life. Guides watch it as a natural signal that the great eruption is about to begin. What is this smaller signal geyser called?
answer: the Prince of Wales Feathers Geyser
choices: the Prince of Wales Feathers Geyser
context: The Prince of Wales Feathers Geyser got its name during a 1901 royal visit, because its triple plume resembled the three feathers of the Prince of Wales crest; it reliably plays just before Pohutu, so it earns the nickname 'the Indicator.' Kereru is another Whakarewarewa geyser, Lady Knox is at Wai-O-Tapu, and Waimangu was a famous New Zealand geyser (now dormant). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whakarewarewa

question: The Champagne Pool at Wai-O-Tapu, near Rotorua, is one of New Zealand's most photographed wonders. It's a steaming blue pool ringed by a bright orange shelf where minerals crust out of the scalding water. Which two elements paint that vivid orange rim?
context: The orange rim is a crust of arsenic and antimony minerals -- orpiment and stibnite -- settling out of water that also carries faint traces of gold and silver. The pool fizzes like a glass of champagne because carbon dioxide bubbles rise through it. It is about 65 m across and 62 m deep; its surface sits near 74 C, while the water feeding it from below reaches roughly 260 C. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne_Pool

question: Rotorua is not a lone hot spot. Its geysers, boiling mud and steaming ground are the northern end of a single vast volcanic system that runs down the middle of New Zealand's North Island, reaching south to the volcanoes of Tongariro. What is this whole volcanic belt called?
context: The Taupo Volcanic Zone stretches across the central North Island, where the crust is being slowly pulled apart and thinned, letting magma rise close to the surface and boil the groundwater. Rotorua sits at its northern end. The Auckland, Coromandel and Northland volcanic regions are all real, but they are separate systems. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taupo_Volcanic_Zone

question: The volcanic region that powers Rotorua holds a planetary record. Over the last 350,000 years it has erupted more than 3,900 cubic km of lava from over 300 separate eruptions -- more than anywhere else on Earth. It is the world's most productive source of which volcanic rock?
context: Rhyolite is a pale, silica-rich lava that tends to erupt explosively rather than flow quietly. The Taupo Volcanic Zone is the most productive rhyolitic volcanic region on Earth, which is why the whole area -- Rotorua's geysers included -- sits over such shallow, restless heat. Basalt, andesite and obsidian are other real volcanic rocks, but the zone's record is for rhyolite. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taupo_Volcanic_Zone

question: At the Ryoan-ji temple in Kyoto, monks carefully tend a famous dry rock garden made of almost nothing at all. Its ingredients are only a low earthen wall, a flat patch of raked white gravel, and fifteen plain stones. Only one green, living plant is allowed to grow among these stones. What is that plant?
context: The only green at Ryoan-ji is a thin skirt of moss ringing the base of each stone — everything else is gravel and rock. Karesansui means 'dry landscape': a garden of stone and sand with no pond, no stream, and almost no plant life, built to be looked at rather than lived in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryōan-ji.

question: Ryoan-ji is famous the world over for one thing: a bone-dry rectangle of gravel and stone, a garden with no water at all. Yet the temple grounds also cradle a large, peaceful pond older than the rock garden itself. For centuries people knew this pond by an affectionate name borrowed from the waterbirds that came to spend each winter on it. By what name was the pond long known?
context: Ryoan-ji is known everywhere for its waterless garden, yet the temple grounds hold a large old pond, Kyoyochi, dug long before the rock garden. People long called it the Oshidori-ike — the 'Mandarin Duck Pond' — for the mandarin ducks that came to winter there, a reminder that water and life surround the one bone-dry courtyard the temple is famous for. Source: discoverkyoto.com/places-go/ryoan-ji/.

question: Every morning at Ryoan-ji, a monk rakes the white gravel into long straight lines and curved sweeps around each of the fifteen stones. In a dry Zen garden like this, the raked gravel is meant to stand for one natural element. What does the raked gravel represent?
context: The classic reading of a karesansui: the raked gravel is water and the standing stones are islands or mountain peaks rising from it — an entire seascape conjured in a bone-dry courtyard. The furrows are recombed by hand every day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryōan-ji; studiomatrx.org/architecture-canon/ryoan-ji-rock-garden.

question: Ryoan-ji's garden holds fifteen stones set in five clusters, placed so cleverly that from anywhere on the wooden porch, at least one stone is always hidden behind another. A visitor sees fourteen at most, never all fifteen at once. An old temple story names one thing that lets a person finally see every one of the fifteen. What reveals all fifteen at once?
answer: reaching a state of inner enlightenment
choices: reaching a state of inner enlightenment
rowing a boat across the temple pond
waiting for the light of a full moon
climbing up to the abbot's private room
context: From every spot on Ryoan-ji's veranda at least one of the fifteen stones stays hidden behind another, so a visitor can only ever count fourteen. Temple tradition offers a single exception: it is said that only a person who has reached inner enlightenment could ever behold all fifteen at once. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryōan-ji; sacred-japan.net/guides/ryoanji/.  (Legend.)

question: Behind the fifteen stones runs a low wall, and part of Ryoan-ji's quiet beauty is the soft brown, cloud-like blotches that stain it. The monks did not paint those patterns, and no artist designed them. What slowly created the stains over the centuries?
answer: oil seeping out of the clay
choices: oil seeping out of the clay
rain washing rust from the tiles
context: When the wall was built, its clay was boiled together with rapeseed oil. Over the following centuries the oil slowly wept back out through the surface, leaving the soft brown, cloud-shaped stains prized today. The Japanese have a word for this kind of beauty found in age, weathering, and imperfection: wabi-sabi. Source: muza-chan.net/japan/index.php/blog/ryoanji-earthen-wall; najga.org/using-earthen-walls-for-japanese-gardens.

question: Near Ryoan-ji's stone garden in Kyoto sits a low stone water basin ringed by four Japanese characters. Read on their own, the four make no sense — each is only half a character. The empty center of the basin is itself meant to be read as a fifth character, one that all four share to become complete. Which character is the empty center?
context: The empty center reads as 口 (kuchi), the character for 'mouth' — a simple box shape that completes each of the four surrounding characters. Joined together they read 'ware tada taru wo shiru': 'I know only contentment,' a Zen teaching about needing no more than you already have. The basin is said to have been donated by Tokugawa Mitsukuni, a lord of the Tokugawa family. Source: traditionalkyoto.com/gardens/ryoan-ji/; discoverkyoto.com/places-go/ryoan-ji/.

question: High up in the Andes Mountains of Bolivia — on the huge treeless plateau called the Altiplano — there lies a blinding white plain nearly two miles above the sea. Stand in the middle and it stretches perfectly flat to the horizon in every direction, brighter than fresh snow. Nothing breaks it: no hill, no rock, not a single plant, not even a bird. What world geographic record does this Bolivian plain hold?
context: The Salar de Uyuni sprawls across 10,582 km2 of the Bolivian Altiplano -- roughly 100 times the size of the USA's Bonneville Salt Flats -- making it the largest salt flat on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: After a few centimeters of rain, the Salar de Uyuni turns into a thin sheet of still water. For a few weeks it stretches about 129 kilometers across before it dries. What title does this flooded plain earn?
context: After the rare rains, a thin sheet of dead-still water turns the Salar into a flawless reflector about 129 km (80 miles) across -- the world's largest natural mirror, where sky and salt blur into a single white void. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: The Salar de Uyuni is a treeless plain high in the Bolivian Andes, hundreds of kilometers from the nearest forest or quarry. With no wood or stone to build with, the small hotels there cut their walls, beds, and tables from the one thing the plain offers without limit. What is that material?
context: With no rock or timber for hundreds of kilometres, hotels here -- the Palacio de Sal, Luna Salada, and Playa Blanca -- are built almost entirely of cut salt blocks: walls, beds, tables, and floors. Source: https://www.forbes.com/sites/jimdobson/2018/01/05/escape-to-the-last-jedi-battleground-in-bolivia-and-stay-in-a-hotel-made-entirely-out-of-salt/

question: Across all 10,582 km2 of the Salar de Uyuni the ground rises and falls by less than a single metre -- it is the flattest large surface on Earth. Space agencies like NASA prize this glass-smooth, dazzling-bright plain for one particular job. What do they use it for?
choices: to track the planet's slow wobble
context: Because the Salar is so flat and bright, satellites are calibrated against it about 5 times better than against the ocean surface; NASA's ICESat used it to verify its altitude measurements to within about 2 cm. Source: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20050071074 ; https://icesat.gsfc.nasa.gov/icesat/publications/GRL/fricker-2.pdf

question: Under the dry salt crust of the Salar de Uyuni lies a hidden lake of buried brine, and dissolved in it sits roughly a fifth of the world's known supply of one soft, silvery metal. It is the metal at the heart of nearly every phone and electric-car battery. Which metal is trapped in the brine below?
context: The brine beneath the crust holds a huge share of the world's lithium RESOURCES -- Bolivia has roughly 22% of the known global total (about 23 of ~105 million tonnes). That figure is the store in the ground, not the amount actually mined. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: High in the Andes mountains of Bolivia, more than two miles above sea level, stretches the Salar de Uyuni -- a flat white plain of pure salt so vast it can be seen from space. It holds an estimated 10 billion tonnes of salt, sitting far from any ocean. Where did such a mountain of salt come from?
answer: the dried-up bed of an ancient Ice-Age lake
choices: the dried-up bed of an ancient Ice-Age lake
a cut-off ancient arm of the Pacific Ocean
mineral ash blasted out by nearby volcanoes
salt dust blown up from the Atacama Desert
context: The whole flat is the dried bed of Lake Tauca, an Ice-Age lake that filled the basin during the Pleistocene and then evaporated away roughly 12,000-13,000 years ago, leaving the salt behind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: Cross the blinding-white Salar de Uyuni toward its middle and a rocky hill suddenly breaks the emptiness -- Incahuasi, an 'island' marooned in a sea of salt. Its slopes bristle with thousands of a single strange plant, the tallest topping 12 metres and some over a thousand years old. What covers Incahuasi Island?
context: Incahuasi Island's giant cacti (Trichocereus/Echinopsis) reach up to 12 m and grow only about 1 cm a year, so the tallest are over a thousand years old. The 'island' itself is fossilized coral and stromatolites -- a petrified reef stranded at about 3,650 m, proof this white desert was once underwater. Source: https://www.machupicchu.org/isla-incahuasi-2026-the-cactus-island-in-the-uyuni-salt-flats.htm

question: Rivers run down off the Andes into the basin of the Salar de Uyuni, but the basin has no exit -- not one river carries its water on to any sea. A basin cut off like this can only lose its water to evaporation, so its salt stays behind and piles up instead of washing away. Geographers call such a sealed, outlet-less basin 'endorheic'. What other famous body of water is so salty for the very same reason?
context: A basin with no outlet to the sea is 'endorheic' (from the Greek for 'flowing within'): its water can only leave by evaporating, so dissolved salts and minerals stay trapped and concentrate over time -- which is why salt and lithium pile up at Uyuni. The Dead Sea lies in the same kind of sealed, endorheic basin, with no river carrying its water out to any ocean, so evaporation has left it famously, extraordinarily salty. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: At the heart of Samarkand in Uzbekistan, a huge stone square opens up. On three sides it is framed by tall Islamic colleges. Its Persian name simply means 'sandy place'. What is this famous plaza called?
context: The Registan ('sandy place' in Persian) was Samarkand's medieval marketplace and the ceremonial heart of Timur's empire, framed by three great madrasas: the Ulugh Beg (1417-1420), the Sher-Dor (1619-1636), and the Tilya-Kori (1646-1660). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registan

question: Islamic religious buildings almost never show living beings. Their walls are covered with patterns and holy writing instead. Yet the grand doorway of the Sher-Dor college on Samarkand's Registan famously breaks that rule with a startling scene of animals. What does the Sher-Dor doorway show?
answer: two tiger-lions chasing does under sun-faces
choices: two tiger-lions chasing does under sun-faces
a phoenix and a dragon around a flowering tree
peacocks flanking a cypress under a crescent moon
context: 'Sher-Dor' means 'Lion-Bearing.' Two striped tiger-lions chase white does across the portal while sun-discs with human faces rise from the cats' backs — an echo of pre-Islamic Zoroastrian sun-symbolism. Such figural images are rare in Islamic sacred art, which is what makes the 1619-1636 mosaic so startling. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher-Dor_Madrasa

question: In Samarkand stands the Gur-e-Amir, the tomb of the conqueror Timur (Tamerlane). Crowning it is a huge bright-blue dome, deeply ribbed and bulging outward in a rounded shape. It is fondly nicknamed for an everyday object it resembles. What is the Gur-e-Amir's dome most often compared to?
context: The melon-shaped, ribbed azure dome of the Gur-e-Amir (built 1403-1404) is about 15 metres across and 12.5 metres high, its bright-blue tiles set with deep rosettes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gur-e-Amir

question: Climbing a Samarkand hillside is the Shah-i-Zinda, a narrow lane lined with more than twenty blue-tiled tombs. Its name means 'The Living King', honoring Kusam ibn Abbas, a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad. Legend says enemies beheaded Kusam as he prayed, and then he did something amazing. What, in the legend, did Kusam then do?
answer: carries his severed head down a deep well
choices: carries his severed head down a deep well
rises into the sky on a shaft of light
sleeps in a cave until the last day
steps from his tomb each night to pray
context: The Shah-i-Zinda ('The Living King') is an avenue of more than twenty blue-tiled mausoleums, among the finest tilework in Central Asia. By legend Kusam ibn Abbas, beheaded at prayer, took up his own head and descended a well where he lives to this day — an oral tradition, not history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah-i-Zinda

question: Timur ordered the Bibi-Khanym mosque in Samarkand to be the biggest in all Islam. Its outer walls were longer than a football field, its main dome some 40 meters high. It was finished in 1404, but it had been thrown up at reckless speed. What happened to the great Bibi-Khanym soon after it was finished?
answer: bricks began falling from its great dome
choices: bricks began falling from its great dome
cracks split its huge entrance arch
its minarets leaned and had to be propped
its foundations sank into the soft ground
context: Raised in just 1399-1404 with the plunder of Timur's Indian campaign, the Bibi-Khanym mosque (outer walls 167x109 m, main dome ~40 m) was among the largest ever attempted — and so over-ambitious that masonry began dropping from its dome within a few years. Later earthquakes ruined it further; it was rebuilt in the 20th century. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibi-Khanym_Mosque

question: The Tilya-Kori college on Samarkand's Registan also served as the city's Friday mosque. Its prayer hall is one of the most dazzling rooms in Central Asia. Every surface, from the walls to the domed ceiling, is worked in a single precious material that also gives the building its name. What covers the inside of the Tilya-Kori?
context: 'Tilya-Kori' means 'Gilded.' Built 1646-1660, it served as both a madrasa and Samarkand's main Friday mosque; its prayer hall is lavishly covered in gold leaf worked over intricate patterns — the source of its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registan

question: The Sher-Dor Madrasa is one of three great Islamic colleges facing the Registan square in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Its 17th-century front is covered in tile mosaic — above the huge arch, two tigers with lion's manes carry the rising sun on their backs, a rare picture of living creatures on a Muslim building. When Uzbekistan won its independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, that beloved mosaic became a proud national symbol. Where does the Sher-Dor's tiger-and-sun design turn up in everyday Uzbek life?
context: The Sher-Dor's tiger-lion-and-sun mosaic, echoing ancient Zoroastrian sun-symbolism, became a symbol of Uzbek identity and is printed on the country's 200-som banknote. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher-Dor_Madrasa

question: The bulging blue dome over Timur's tomb, the Gur-e-Amir in Samarkand, dazzled the imperial line Timur founded. For two hundred years afterward, they built their great buildings with domes modeled on it. Which world-famous domed building is a direct descendant?
context: The Gur-e-Amir's ribbed, bulbous turquoise dome became the template for the dynasty Timur founded — the Mughals of India. Its shape returns at the Bagh-e-Babur in Kabul, Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, and, most famously, the Taj Mahal in Agra. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gur-e-Amir

question: The dark slab over Timur's grave in Samarkand's Gur-e-Amir is the largest single block of jade on Earth, brought to the city by his grandson Ulugh Beg. Before it ever reached Samarkand, the great green stone had already lived two lives far to the east. It was first a treasured object in a Chinese emperor's palace. Then, in the hands of a khan descended from Genghis Khan, the block was cut down to serve as what?
context: Over Timur lies the world's largest block of dark-green nephrite jade, brought from the east by Ulugh Beg. It had earlier been a worship-object in a Chinese emperor's palace and then the throne of a Chagatai khan — a descendant of Genghis Khan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gur-e-Amir

question: Timur's grandson Ulugh Beg ruled Samarkand more as a scientist than a king. Around 1428 he raised a great observatory there, whose main instrument was so vast it had to be partly sunk into a trench cut into the hillside. That instrument was a curved stone arc roughly 40 meters long, used to fix the positions of the sun and stars. What kind of astronomical instrument was this giant buried arc?
context: The Fakhri sextant was a stone meridian arc with a radius of about 40 metres, partly sunk in a hillside trench — the largest astronomical instrument in the world in its day. Ulugh Beg's observatory dated to about 1428. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulugh_Beg_Observatory

question: A famous legend clings to Samarkand's giant Bibi-Khanym mosque. It tells that the master builder fell in love with Timur's wife as he worked, and swore he would finish the great mosque only if she granted him one thing first. In the tale, what did the architect demand before he would complete Bibi-Khanym?
context: By this Samarkand legend the kiss burned a mark onto the queen's cheek, and the enraged Timur then decreed that women should veil their faces so as not to tempt other men — a folk origin-tale, not documented history. Source: https://www.advantour.com/uzbekistan/legends/bibi-khanym.htm

question: Ulugh Beg, the astronomer-king of Samarkand, calculated the exact length of the year in the 1430s using naked-eye instruments alone — no telescope, no accurate clock. Remarkably, his figure was closer to the truth than the one Copernicus would reach a full century later. How far off was Ulugh Beg's measurement of the year's length?
choices: by a quarter of an hour
context: Ulugh Beg measured the year as 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes, 15 seconds — wrong by under a minute, and more accurate than Copernicus a century later. His trigonometric tables were correct to eight decimal places. Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Ulugh_Beg/

question: In June 1941 the Soviet scientist Mikhail Gerasimov opened Timur's tomb in Samarkand to study the conqueror's bones. An inscription was later said to warn that whoever disturbed the grave would 'unleash an invader more terrible than I.' Barely two days after Gerasimov opened the tomb, a world-shaking event seemed to answer that warning. What happened on 22 June 1941?
answer: Germany stormed into the Soviet Union
choices: Germany stormed into the Soviet Union
the siege of Leningrad was lifted
context: This is a famous legend, and historians call it coincidence — people close to Gerasimov say the curse tale was invented. He opened the grave on 19-20 June 1941; on 22 June Hitler launched Operation Barbarossa, the invasion of the USSR. Timur was reburied with full Islamic rites in December 1942, weeks before the Soviet victory at Stalingrad. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_of_Timur

question: In the early 1900s, Rio de Janeiro had a district by the docks called 'Little Africa'. There Bahian migrant women threw house parties. At those parties, African drumming, dance, and the Candomble religion all blended into a brand-new city music. What was this Rio-born music called?
context: Tia Ciata's home in the Pequena África (Little Africa) district near the port was the legendary incubator: the Bahian 'tias baianas' (aunties) mixed Candomblé, cooking, and drumming into the new urban samba. Distractors are real genres born elsewhere — tango in Buenos Aires, rumba in Cuba, calypso in Trinidad. Source: Wikipedia 'Samba' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba).

question: For years Rio de Janeiro's Carnival parade wound through regular downtown streets. Then in 1984 the city opened a permanent parade arena, built for nothing but the parade. Oscar Niemeyer designed it, and its grandstands seat about 90,000. What is this stadium called?
context: The Sambódromo Marquês de Sapucaí opened in 1984; its roughly 700 m avenue ends at Niemeyer's giant tri-legged 'Apotheosis' arch. The distractors are all real Rio landmarks — the Maracanã football stadium, the Copacabana Palace hotel, and the Teatro Municipal opera house. Source: Wikipedia 'Sambadrome Marquês de Sapucaí' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sambadrome_Marqu%C3%AAs_de_Sapuca%C3%AD).

question: In 1920s Rio de Janeiro, police often bothered Black street drummers just for playing. So around 1929, the Estacio neighborhood formed the first organized Carnival group. They boldly named it 'Deixa Falar' ('Let Them Talk'). The idea spread across the city, and today rival groups parade for the Carnival crown. What are these Rio Carnival groups called?
context: 'Deixa Falar' (c. 1929, Estácio) pioneered the escola de samba model, and marching as one organized group also helped shield players from the police. The distractors are real Carnival groups from other places — New Orleans has krewes, Cuba and Argentina have comparsas, Uruguay has murgas. Source: Wikipedia 'Samba' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba).

question: In a Rio Carnival parade, drummers march together in a giant drum band called the bateria, and one drum sets the master tempo that every other drummer and dancer locks onto. Its deep, booming pulse has been nicknamed the 'heartbeat' of the whole ensemble. Which drum anchors the group?
context: The biggest, the surdo de primeira (up to about 26 inches across), pounds out the marcação beat that anchors the entire bateria. The distractors are its real bandmates — the tiny high cuíca, the small tamborim, and the two-toned agogô bell. Source: Go Samba 'The Mighty Surdo' (https://gosamba.net/blogs/news/the-mighty-surdo); Wikipedia 'Surdo' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surdo).

question: In the drum section of a Rio Carnival parade, one drum wails a high, laughing squeak that can slide up into a chattering, monkey-like cry. Brazilians named it after a screeching opossum famous for making the same eerie sound. Which drum makes this laughing sound?
context: The cuíca is a friction drum: a stick fixed inside the drumhead is rubbed with a wet cloth, and pressing a finger on the outside of the head slides the pitch up into a monkey-chatter or down into a moan. It is named after a screeching Brazilian opossum. Source: Wikipedia 'Cuíca' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cu%C3%ADca).

question: In the late 1950s in Rio, guitarist João Gilberto figured out how to fold an entire samba band's rhythm onto a single classical guitar. He sang over it in a soft, almost whispered voice — a cool, hushed break from the brassy Brazilian singers who came before him. What was this new style called?
context: Around 1957–59 in Rio's South Zone, João Gilberto's gentle 'batida' guitar and whispered voice became bossa nova — literally 'new trend' or 'new wave.' The 1959 record 'Chega de Saudade' is often called its birth. The distractors are real Brazilian styles: the ballad-like samba-canção, the older instrumental choro, and the later tropicália. Source: Wikipedia 'Bossa nova' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bossa_nova).

question: The song usually credited as the first samba ever put on record set Rio's 1917 Carnival ablaze. A musician known as Donga had registered it the year before. Scholars still argue whether a slightly earlier tune deserves the 'first' crown. What was this pioneering record called?
context: 'Pelo Telefone' means 'By Telephone' — a surprisingly modern title for 1917. Donga registered it in late 1916; it was released January 19, 1917. Scholars debate whether a slightly earlier tune was truly first, so the honor is contested. The distractors are other real Brazilian songs from later decades. Source: Wikipedia 'Samba' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba).  (Legend.)

question: In the winter of 1962, a 17-year-old girl named Heloísa strolled past the Veloso bar each day on her way to a Rio de Janeiro beach. Two regulars there — the composer Tom Jobim and the poet Vinícius de Moraes — were so struck that they wrote a soft bossa nova song about her, and it grew into one of the most-recorded pop songs in history. Which beachside neighborhood, which also gave the song its title, was she walking to?
context: The song is 'The Girl from Ipanema' (Garota de Ipanema, 1962), music by Tom Jobim and Portuguese lyrics by Vinícius de Moraes — often cited as the second-most-recorded pop song ever, behind only the Beatles' 'Yesterday.' The real 'girl,' Helô Pinheiro, walked past the Veloso bar, later renamed 'Garota de Ipanema' in the song's honor. The distractors are neighboring Rio beach districts. Source: Wikipedia 'The Girl from Ipanema' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Girl_from_Ipanema); The Rio Times.

question: The U.S. Navy wanted San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge painted in black-and-yellow stripes so passing ships could spot it in the fog. Consulting architect Irving Morrow overruled them, choosing a single bold color that stays visible in the mist yet suits the hills and sea around it. By what name is the bridge's signature color known?
context: Morrow liked the reddish primer the steel arrived coated in and fought to keep it; 'International Orange' became the bridge's identity and is repainted continuously to keep it glowing against the fog. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate_Bridge  (Legend.)

question: Everyone knows the Golden Gate Bridge -- but explorer John C. Fremont wrote the name 'Golden Gate' back in 1846, more than ninety years before the bridge opened. In his day the name marked a real feature you could see on the water itself. What did 'Golden Gate' first name?
answer: the ocean strait into the bay
choices: the ocean strait into the bay
the island in the middle of the bay
the long beach along the ocean shore
the calm harbor deep inside the bay
context: Fremont likened the strait to Byzantium's 'Golden Horn,' picturing a golden gateway to Pacific trade -- and he named it in 1846, roughly eighteen months before gold was even found at Sutter's Mill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate  (Legend.)

question: San Francisco still runs the last manually operated hill railway of its kind left on Earth. Its operator hauls back on a tall lever with his whole body to inch each little car up slopes far too steep for ordinary streetcars. What is that lever actually doing to move the car?
answer: clamping onto a moving cable that runs endlessly beneath the street
choices: clamping onto a moving cable that runs endlessly beneath the street
meshing a toothed wheel into a notched rail up the middle of the track
swinging a pole up to a live electric wire strung overhead
letting a sinking counterweight on a parallel track pull it up
context: Andrew Hallidie opened the first line, the Clay Street Hill Railroad, on September 1, 1873; a constantly moving underground cable does the pulling, and the operator's grip is the only link between car and cable. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_car_(railway)  (Legend.)

question: For nearly two centuries, Spanish ships sailed up and down the California coast. They slipped past the mile-wide gap of the Golden Gate without ever noticing the huge bay hidden behind it. When that great harbor was finally discovered in 1769, how did it happen?
answer: a party exploring overland spotted it from a high ridge
choices: a party exploring overland spotted it from a high ridge
a storm drove a Spanish galleon in through the narrow gap
a Russian fur-trading fleet charted it from the open sea
a native guide led coastal missionaries to it on foot
context: On November 4, 1769, Gaspar de Portola's overland expedition sighted San Francisco Bay from Sweeney Ridge, near today's Pacifica; the first ship to actually sail in through the Golden Gate, Juan de Ayala's San Carlos, did not arrive until 1775. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay  (Legend.)

question: On a summer afternoon, San Francisco can shiver under gray fog while valleys inland bake past 100 F, and that inland heat pulls in ocean air. As the sea air is cooled below its dew point, it turns into a low advection fog that then pours through the Golden Gate like a slow gray river. What chills the incoming ocean air enough to fog it up?
answer: the cold California Current running down the coast
choices: the cold California Current running down the coast
a cold undersea canyon lurking just off the coast
meltwater from the distant Sierra Nevada snowpack
icy air sliding down off the high inland desert
context: The California Current pulls cold, deep water up along the shore (upwelling), chilling the marine air into the low 50s F just offshore; dragged inland by the summer heat, that cold air is why San Francisco summers are famously foggy and cool. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_fog

question: Alcatraz Island held America's most feared federal prison from 1934 to 1963. It was a bare rock barely a mile from the crowded San Francisco waterfront. Wardens boasted that no one could break out and survive — not because of the cell walls, but because of what waited just beyond them. What made escape from 'the Rock' considered nearly impossible?
answer: the deadly cold and ripping currents of the surrounding bay
choices: the deadly cold and ripping currents of the surrounding bay
sheer sea-cliffs dropping straight down into deep water
a pack of guard dogs loosed across the island each night
a triple ring of electrified razor-wire fencing
context: The bay hovers near 50-55 F with currents strong enough to sweep a swimmer out the Golden Gate; the island sits about 1.25 miles from shore. In the famous June 1962 escape, Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers rafted off on prison-made floats and were never seen again. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcatraz_Island  (Legend.)

question: While building the Golden Gate Bridge, chief engineer Joseph Strauss hung a giant safety net beneath the deck -- the first ever used on a job that size. Over the months it caught nineteen workers who slipped and fell hundreds of feet toward the strait. Those men, snatched from death in mid-air, gave themselves a grimly cheerful nickname. What did they call their group?
answer: the Half Way to Hell Club
choices: the Half Way to Hell Club
the Bottom of the Bay Club
context: Strauss's movable net saved nineteen men, but the bridge still cost eleven lives -- ten of them on February 17, 1937, when a work platform tore loose and ripped through the net into the strait. The bridge opened three months later, on May 27, 1937. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate_Bridge  (Legend.)

question: At dawn on April 18, 1906, the San Andreas Fault ruptured just off San Francisco and the ground heaved violently. Yet when the ruin was finally tallied -- some 25,000 buildings gone across 490 blocks -- investigators found the shaking itself had not done the worst of it. What actually leveled most of the city after the ground stopped moving?
answer: fires that raged unchecked through the broken city
choices: fires that raged unchecked through the broken city
a towering tsunami surging in through the Golden Gate
a second, far larger aftershock the following night
floodwater pouring from the city's shattered reservoirs
context: The quake snapped both the gas mains that fed the fires and the water mains needed to fight them; an estimated 80-95% of the destruction came from three days of flame, and over 3,000 people died. The San Andreas marks where the Pacific and North American plates grind past each other. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906_San_Francisco_earthquake  (Legend.)

question: When the Loma Prieta earthquake struck during the 1989 World Series, most of San Francisco rode it out -- but the Marina District shook hardest, and its buildings sank and burned. There the ground briefly lost all firmness and flowed like a liquid, an effect geologists call 'liquefaction.' Why did the Marina turn to jelly while bedrock neighborhoods held firm?
answer: it stands on loose rubble and sand dumped in as landfill
choices: it stands on loose rubble and sand dumped in as landfill
it was built over a buried, still-flowing underground creek
it lay on thin sand spread straight over hard bedrock
it rested on deep clay dried and cracked by long drought
context: The Marina sits on rubble and bay mud dumped as fill for the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition; violently shaken, the water-logged fill lost its strength and behaved like a fluid, so buildings there tilted, sank, and caught fire while homes on bedrock nearby stood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Loma_Prieta_earthquake

question: San Francisco's Lombard Street runs down a hill so steep -- about a 27% grade, more than four times a steep highway -- that a car pointed straight down that one block would be nearly impossible to control. Rather than close it off, in 1922 the city rebuilt that single block into the famous spectacle tourists now creep down at 5 mph. What did engineers build into the block to tame the plunge?
answer: a set of tight switchbacks that zigzag cars down
choices: a set of tight switchbacks that zigzag cars down
a run of shallow terraced ramps stepping down
a single hairpin curve sweeping around the block
a rough cobbled surface to grip the tires
context: The natural block plunges at about a 27% grade -- roughly a 27-foot drop over 100 feet, more than four times a steep highway -- so in 1922 the city rebuilt that one block into eight tight switchbacks with a 5 mph limit, making a slope too steep to drive straight down into something cars can zigzag safely. (It is a 27% grade, not '27 degrees' -- a common mix-up between two very different steepnesses.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombard_Street_(San_Francisco)

question: Nearly all the rain and Sierra Nevada snowmelt from about 40% of California funnels toward the sea through a single narrow gap -- the Golden Gate. Two great rivers gather that runoff from the north and the south, meet in a wide inland delta, and let San Francisco Bay flush it out to the Pacific. Which two rivers drain California's heartland out through the Golden Gate?
answer: the Sacramento and the San Joaquin
choices: the Sacramento and the San Joaquin
context: The Sacramento (draining the north) and the San Joaquin (draining the south) join in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, then empty through San Francisco Bay and out the Golden Gate -- the single outlet for runoff from roughly 40% of the state. (It is a huge estuary, though the Salish Sea to the north is larger.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay

question: Santorini in the Aegean Sea is a crescent of cliffs about 300 m high, curving nearly all the way around a deep blue bay that ferries sail straight into. The island is the rim of one huge volcano whose middle collapsed and let the sea pour in. Geologists have a special name for this giant collapse-pit -- what is it?
context: That flooded pit is a caldera: Santorini's spans about 12 by 7 km, its water reaching 385 m deep, with the white towns of Fira and Oia perched on the rim. A crater is only the small vent at a volcano's mouth -- a caldera is the vast basin left when the emptied summit collapses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santorini_caldera

question: Right in the middle of Santorini's drowned volcanic bay sit two small islands of bare black lava. The younger one has slowly risen from the seabed since the great eruption and is still growing today, proof that the volcano is only sleeping and not dead. What is this young black lava island at the bay's center called?
context: Nea Kameni ('New Burnt Island') is a lava dome about 114 m high that has grown inside the flooded crater in eruptions since the ancient collapse; its older twin is Palea Kameni ('Old Burnt Island'). Thirasia and Aspronisi are surviving pieces of the original caldera rim across the bay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nea_Kameni

question: The buried Bronze Age town of Akrotiri on Santorini was found nearly stripped of anything precious. For years, excavators turned up only a single small gold object in the whole town. It was hidden inside a wooden box within a clay chest — a tiny hollow figurine of which animal?
context: The little gold ibex -- a wild mountain goat -- was found in 1999 and is one of only a handful of gold objects ever recovered at Akrotiri. Bulls, lions, and dolphins all appear in Aegean art of the age, but this figurine is a goat. The near-total absence of treasure hints the townsfolk carried their valuables away. Source: worldhistory.org/image/1358/gold-ibex-akrotiri/

question: Akrotiri on Santorini lies buried under volcanic ash exactly as Pompeii does, and just as completely. Three-story houses still stand, paved streets, painted walls, even clay pipes carrying water indoors. As archaeologists dug through this frozen Bronze Age town, one ordinary thing they fully expected to uncover turned up almost nowhere. What did they find almost none of?
context: Unlike Pompeii -- whose victims left body-shaped hollows now cast in plaster -- Akrotiri held almost no human remains. Warned by earthquakes, its people seem to have evacuated in an orderly way before the eruption, so the 'Minoan Pompeii' is a whole town with almost no one left in it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akrotiri_(prehistoric_city)  (Legend.)

question: Around 1600 BC, the volcano at Thera — today's Santorini — erupted in one of the mightiest explosions in human history. It shot a column of ash and pumice roughly 35 km (about 20 miles) straight up into the sky. Which layer of Earth's atmosphere did the ash punch into?
context: At about 35 km the plume drove well into the stratosphere (roughly 10-50 km up), where the ozone layer sits and airliners never fly. Ash and gas flung that high can dim sunlight around the world for years. The eruption blasted out an estimated 28-41 cubic km of rock. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_eruption

question: Spyridon Marinatos, the archaeologist who uncovered Akrotiri, argued that the memory of Thera's catastrophe echoed down the centuries into one of Plato's most famous stories about a lost realm. In the story, a brilliant Bronze Age world had been wrecked in a single disaster. Most scholars reject the link, since the dates and geography don't fit. Which legendary lost land did Marinatos tie to Santorini?
context: Marinatos (and later Angelos Galanopoulos) proposed Thera as the origin of Atlantis, the island Plato described in his dialogues Timaeus and Critias as vanishing 'in a single day and night... into the depths of the sea.' It is a popular idea but is not accepted by current scholarship. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_eruption  (Legend.)

question: In the heart of Seoul stands a walled royal palace where the kings of the Joseon dynasty once held court, founded in 1395 with a name that means roughly 'palace of shining blessings.' Twice a day, guards in bright silk robes still march out to change the watch beneath its painted gate. What is this palace called?
context: Gyeongbokgung was founded in 1395 by King Taejo, the founder of Joseon; its name was drawn from a line in the ancient Chinese Book of Odes wishing the new dynasty long, bright happiness. It stayed the dynasty's main palace, and the changing-of-the-royal-guard ceremony is re-enacted today at its main gate, Gwanghwamun ('gate of light and harmony'). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeongbokgung

question: Just uphill behind Seoul's royal palace, the Bukchon quarter has kept its rows of old homes. They have heavy gray tile roofs that curve up at the eaves. They wrap around walled courtyards, tucked between the glass office towers of modern Seoul. What are these traditional houses called?
context: A hanok is the traditional Korean house, built with a tiled or thatched roof and warm floors. Bukchon ('north village,' for its site north of the old Cheonggyecheon stream) was historically the residential quarter of the yangban -- Joseon's high officials and nobility. Machiya and minka are Japanese houses; a siheyuan is a Chinese courtyard house. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukchon_Hanok_Village

question: Inside a traditional Seoul home, the family sits, eats, and even sleeps directly on the floor. Heat and smoke from the kitchen firebox are drawn through stone tunnels laid beneath a thick masonry floor. That warms the whole room from underneath. The warmest spot, nearest the fire, is saved for elders and honored guests. What is this traditional heating system called?
context: Ondol heats a room from below: the agungi (firebox) in the kitchen sends heat through gudeul (stone flues) under the floor before smoke escapes up an outdoor chimney -- so Koreans traditionally live at floor level on the warm stone. A hypocaust is the Roman version, a kang is a Chinese heated sleeping platform, and an irori is a Japanese sunken hearth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ondol

question: About 50 km north of Seoul's palaces, the Korean peninsula is slashed clean across by a strip of land, roughly 250 km long and only 4 km wide. Fences, watchtowers, and mines have kept the two Koreas apart since the guns fell silent in 1953. What is this fortified dividing strip called?
context: The DMZ was created by the armistice signed on 27 July 1953, which halted the Korean War without a peace treaty. It runs about 4 km wide (2 km on each side of the central Military Demarcation Line) near the 38th parallel. Despite the name 'demilitarized,' it is one of the most heavily fortified borders on Earth. Sources: https://grokipedia.com/page/Korean_Demilitarized_Zone ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Demilitarized_Zone

question: Ringed by granite peaks and split by the broad Han River, Seoul is a huge city of some ten million people, yet a real wilderness of bare rock domes and forest trails rises at its northern edge, and in 1983 it was made a national park. Very few big cities on Earth hold a real mountain-hiking national park inside their own city limits. Which mountain is this?
context: Bukhansan means 'mountain north of the Han.' Made a national park in 1983 (Korea's 15th), its bare granite domes draw millions of hikers a year and are world-famous for rock climbing. Hallasan is the volcano on Jeju Island, Seoraksan lies on the east coast, and Namsan is the small hill in central Seoul crowned by N Seoul Tower. Sources: https://grokipedia.com/page/Bukhansan_National_Park ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukhansan

question: In 1592, Japanese armies invaded Korea and burned the great Gyeongbokgung palace to the ground. You might expect Joseon's kings to rebuild their chief royal palace within a few years. Instead, the blackened site at the center of the capital met a far stranger fate. What became of the ruined palace?
answer: it was left in ruins for nearly 270 years
choices: it was left in ruins for nearly 270 years
it was left in ruins for only about 20 years
it was rebuilt even grander within a decade
it was replaced by a brand-new capital city
context: The 1592 invasion is remembered as the Imjin War. Gyeongbokgung was not rebuilt until the 1860s, when the regent Heungseon Daewongun -- ruling for the boy-king Gojong -- finally raised it again after roughly 270 years of abandonment. So the palace tourists walk through today is largely a 19th-century reconstruction of the 1395 original. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeongbokgung

question: For nearly seventy years, no farmer has plowed and no bulldozer has broken ground inside the Korean Demilitarized Zone. It is the mine-laced no-man's-land between two armies that never signed a peace treaty. Sealed off from all human hands for so long, the deadliest border on Earth quietly became something no general ever planned. What did the abandoned strip turn into?
choices: a buried maze of secret tunnels
context: With people locked out since 1953, nature reclaimed the DMZ's abandoned rice paddies as wetlands and forest, making it one of the best-preserved strips of temperate habitat in the world. Endangered red-crowned cranes and vulnerable white-naped cranes now winter in the mined no-man's-land -- rare wild things thriving on the ground where thousands of soldiers once died. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/travel/wildlife-thrives-dmz-korea-risk-location-180967842/

question: The wild granite mountain Bukhansan at Seoul's edge and the Gyeongbokgung palace at the city's heart look like they belong to different worlds. Yet Joseon's founders treated them as one system: following pungsu (Korean geomancy), the court read the mountain's ridge to settle a single decision about the palace back in the 1390s. What did Bukhansan help decide?
choices: which way its throne would face
how high its main hall could rise
how many gates it would have
context: In Korean geomancy a 'guardian mountain' at one's back marks an auspicious site, and Bukhansan served as the guardian mountain to the north of the Joseon capital. Its granite ridge helped fix exactly where Gyeongbokgung was placed in the 1390s -- so the mountain at the city's edge and the palace at its heart are geographically linked. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Bukhansan_National_Park

question: In the Cherokee homeland of the southern mountains, a man named Sequoyah did something almost no one has ever done alone. He could not read a single word of any language, yet he still did it. What did Sequoyah create?
answer: a complete writing system for his people's language
choices: a complete writing system for his people's language
a spoken war code later used by the U.S. Army
a system of knotted cords for keeping records
a hand-sign language shared among many tribes
context: Sequoyah was born around 1770 in Tuskegee, in what is now Tennessee, deep in the Cherokee country of the southern Appalachians. He is one of the very few people in recorded history known to have invented a writing system from scratch -- and the only one known to have managed it while completely unable to read any language. Source: education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/sequoyah-and-creation-cherokee-syllabary/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoyah

question: Learning to read English can take a child years. But in Cherokee country, Sequoyah's new script gave each spoken syllable — sounds like 'ga,' 'no,' and 'hi' — its own single symbol, about 85 in all. Once those symbols were learned, how fast could a Cherokee speaker learn to read their own language?
answer: in a few days to a few weeks
choices: in a few days to a few weeks
in a single afternoon of practice
in a couple of months of lessons
in about a year of steady study
context: Because each symbol stands for a whole syllable rather than a single sound, Sequoyah's invention is a SYLLABARY, not an alphabet -- about 85 symbols (originally 86, later streamlined). The Cherokee National Council officially adopted it in 1825. The linguist Albert Gallatin marveled that a Cherokee could become literate almost the moment the symbols were learned. Source: education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/sequoyah-and-creation-cherokee-syllabary/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee_syllabary

question: In the early 1820s, in the Cherokee towns of the southern Appalachian mountains, Sequoyah spent years working out a written alphabet for the Cherokee language — one symbol for each syllable. When he showed off his paper marks, his own neighbors were afraid. They thought the strange scribbles must be witchcraft, and Sequoyah was put on trial as a sorcerer. To prove that the marks carried real speech and not magic, what test did Sequoyah use?
answer: he had his daughter read back words he wrote in a separate, closed room
choices: he had his daughter read back words he wrote in a separate, closed room
he wrote down a bystander's words and read the same page aloud himself
he matched his symbols one by one against the settlers' printed book
he had elders memorize a message and repeat it after seeing the marks
context: His daughter Ayoka was only about six. Father and daughter were shut in different rooms; each wrote down messages, the papers were carried between them, and Ayoka read aloud words her father had written and could not possibly have overheard -- proving the marks truly carried speech. Even Sequoyah's own wife had at first feared the writing as sorcery. Source: smithsonianmag.com/innovation/man-created-written-language-cherokee-did-efficiently-elegantly-peers-thought-magic-180988850/; education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/sequoyah-and-creation-cherokee-syllabary/

question: In 1828, from their capital at New Echota in Georgia, the Cherokee Nation began printing something no Native people had made before. It was a newspaper set in two columns, one in Sequoyah's script and one in English. What was this first Native American newspaper called?
context: The first issue of the Cherokee Phoenix appeared on February 21, 1828, printed in both the syllabary and English at New Echota, the Cherokee capital in Georgia. Its first editor was Elias Boudinot, whose Cherokee name was Galagina, 'Buck' Oowatie. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee_Phoenix

question: In the Cherokee country of the southern mountains, Sequoyah liked the look of the letters he saw in a settler's spelling book, so he borrowed some of their shapes for his own syllabary. A symbol shaped like the English letters D or R turns up in his script. But what did Sequoyah do about the sounds those borrowed shapes originally made?
answer: he gave the borrowed shapes entirely new Cherokee sounds
choices: he gave the borrowed shapes entirely new Cherokee sounds
he kept each shape's original English sound to help learners
he flipped every borrowed shape to signal a different sound
he placed the borrowed shapes in English alphabetical order
context: Some Cherokee symbols also resemble Latin, Greek, and Cyrillic letters, but not one of them shares the sound of the letter it looks like. Sequoyah, who could not read English, chose the shapes purely because he liked them, with no idea what sounds they carried -- so a Cherokee character shaped like 'D' or 'R' sounds nothing like ours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee_syllabary

question: The giant sequoia trees of California, the most massive living things on Earth, are popularly said to have been named in Sequoyah's honor. But the Austrian botanist Stephan Endlicher, who coined the genus name 'Sequoia' in 1847, never wrote down his reason. Some scholars doubt the tribute story entirely. What origin do these skeptics propose instead?
answer: the Latin sequi, 'to follow,' because its seed count fell in sequence after related trees
choices: the Latin sequi, 'to follow,' because its seed count fell in sequence after related trees
a Latin word meaning 'gigantic,' because the trees dwarf every other kind around them
a Sierra Nevada valley, because the earliest known specimen was measured there
an early surveyor's surname, because he was the first to map the great groves
context: This is the popular tribute, not a proven fact. The Austrian botanist Stephan Endlicher coined the genus name 'Sequoia' in 1847 but never recorded why; the story that it honors Sequoyah only spread in the 1850s and 1860s. Some scholars argue Endlicher drew the name from the Latin sequi, 'to follow,' because the number of seeds per cone fell in sequence after related trees. Either way, the giant sequoia and coast redwoods are among the largest and tallest living things on Earth. Source: landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu/discovery-and-naming-sequoiadendron-giganteum-sierra-redwood; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoiadendron_giganteum  (Legend.)

question: Sequoyah's syllabary never died out. It traveled west with the Cherokee people during the forced removal of 1838, the Trail of Tears, and today it fills daily life around the Cherokee Nation's capital at Tahlequah, Oklahoma — on street signs, in immersion-school classrooms, and even on people's phones. How does a script invented back in 1821 now appear on modern smartphones and laptops?
answer: it joined Unicode, the code behind all on-screen text
choices: it joined Unicode, the code behind all on-screen text
Apple and Google each ship their own Cherokee font
it borrows the Unicode block reserved for Latin letters
each device first needs a downloadable Cherokee keyboard app
context: The syllabary was added to the Unicode standard (blocks U+13A0-13FF and U+AB70-ABBF), so it types on any computer or phone; Cherokee immersion schools teach it with syllabary keyboards. Road and street signs carry it in Tahlequah, Oklahoma and in Cherokee, North Carolina, and the Cherokee Phoenix is still published from Tahlequah today -- the script having survived the Trail of Tears of 1838. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee_syllabary; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee_Phoenix; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoyah

question: Around 1800 BC, someone at the Serabit el-Khadim turquoise mine in Egypt's Sinai desert scratched a few dozen rough signs into the rock. Those signs became the parent of nearly every alphabet on Earth today. Greek, Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, and our own ABCs all trace back to them. Who took this first step toward writing?
context: The signs are called the Proto-Sinaitic script, from about 1900-1800 BCE, and they are the oldest known ancestor of the alphabet -- the line runs from these scratches to Phoenician, then Greek and Latin, and on to our own letters. The astonishing part is who made them: Semitic-speaking laborers from Southwest Asia and the Nile Delta who worked the turquoise mines, not scribes or royalty. Scholars still debate the exact century -- an early date around 1850 BCE (the alphabet born inside Egypt) versus a late date around 1550 BCE (developed later in Canaan). Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sinaitic_script; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serabit_el-Khadim; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_alphabet.

question: At Serabit el-Khadim, workers built their alphabet by borrowing Egyptian hieroglyphs. They used each picture for only the first sound of its name. So the picture of an eye stood for one sound, and the picture of a head for another. Our own letter B started the very same way, as a simple picture of one everyday object. What did that first B actually show?
context: The trick is called acrophony -- 'first-sound' writing. The miners took a handful of Egyptian hieroglyphs but used each picture only for the first sound of its Semitic name: the house, bayt, gave 'b' (our B); the ox-head, alp, gave the throat-catch that opens 'ox' (our A); the water-squiggle, mem, gave 'm' (our M). A whole alphabet grew from a few pictures used for their opening sounds. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_alphabet; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sinaitic_script.

question: For years, the scratches at Serabit el-Khadim looked like meaningless doodles, until 1916, when the Egyptologist Alan Gardiner noticed the same short group of signs repeating again and again. Reading each sign as its first sound, he found that they spelled out a real word he recognized, and that single word cracked the entire code. What did the repeated word turn out to be?
context: The repeating signs spelled l-b-'-l-t -- 'to Baalat', meaning 'to the Lady'. Baalat was the Canaanite miners' name for Hathor, the Egyptian goddess worshipped at Serabit as 'Mistress of Turquoise'. Because those few signs spelled a name by first-sounds, Alan Gardiner's 1916 reading proved the marks really were an alphabet -- and that ordinary desert miners, not a royal court, had taken the first step toward the ABCs. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serabit_el-Khadim_proto-Sinaitic_inscriptions; library.biblicalarchaeology.org (Gardiner 1916).

question: Seville's bell tower, the Giralda, rises about 96 metres. But its lower shaft is far older brick, raised by the Almohads between 1184 and 1198. A Renaissance bell room was stacked on top only centuries later. What was that original 12th-century tower built to be?
answer: the minaret of the city's great mosque
choices: the minaret of the city's great mosque
the watchtower over the river approach
the lighthouse for ships reaching port
the keep of the Almohad royal castle
context: The Giralda's lower ~50 m is the original Almohad minaret, begun in 1184 and finished in 1198. Rather than tear it down, Christian Seville stacked a Renaissance belfry on top in 1558-1568 — a Muslim prayer-tower reborn as a cathedral bell tower, minaret re-used, not erased. Source: Wikipedia (Giralda), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giralda; Grokipedia (Giralda) checked first.

question: The Giralda is the tall bell tower of Seville Cathedral in southern Spain, first built by Muslim rulers in the 1100s as the minaret of a great mosque. Step inside and you notice something odd: there is not a single stair. Instead, 35 broad, gently sloping brick ramps spiral all the way up around the tower's core. The builders made those ramps wide and easy on purpose. What could someone do all the way to the top of the Giralda?
answer: ride a horse all the way to the top
choices: ride a horse all the way to the top
roll the great bells up to hang them
wheel carts of building stone upward
carry pilgrims up in sedan chairs
context: The Giralda's 35 ramps let a rider climb to the summit on horseback — by tradition the muezzin rode up to call the faithful to prayer. The gentle grade replaces stairs entirely, spiralling around the tower's solid brick core. Source: Wikipedia (Giralda), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giralda.

question: Beside the Giralda, on the cleared footprint of Seville's demolished great mosque, Christian builders labored from 1401 to 1506 on an immense new church. It was so vast that even their own canons reportedly vowed onlookers would 'take us for mad.' What claim to fame does the finished Seville Cathedral hold?
answer: the largest Gothic church in the world
choices: the largest Gothic church in the world
the tallest cathedral in the world
the largest brick-built church in the world
the widest nave of any church in Europe
context: Seville Cathedral (built 1401-1506 on the demolished mosque's footprint) is about 126 m long and 76 m wide — the largest Gothic church on Earth. When finished it even took the 'largest cathedral' title from Constantinople's Hagia Sophia, which had held it for roughly a thousand years. The canons' reported vow: a church so grand 'those who see it finished will take us for mad.' Source: Wikipedia (Seville Cathedral), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral.

question: In the city of Seville in southern Spain stands a grand old bell tower called the Giralda. The name comes from the Spanish word 'girar,' meaning 'to turn.' The tower earned that name in 1568, when a striking new feature was added to its very top -- something that never stops moving. What is it?
answer: a bronze statue on top that pivots to face the wind
choices: a bronze statue on top that pivots to face the wind
a spiral ramp that turns as it climbs the tower
a ring of bells that swivel as they toll the hours
a beacon that once revolved to guide river ships
context: The turning feature is El Giraldillo — a ~4 m, ~1,500 kg bronze statue of Faith set on the summit in 1568 that swings to face the wind like a weathervane. The whole tower took its name, 'the Giralda' (from girar, 'to turn'), from this giant pivoting figure. Source: Wikipedia (Giralda), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giralda.

question: Inside the great cathedral of Seville in Spain lies the tomb of Christopher Columbus, the Genoese explorer who sailed for the Spanish crown to the New World in 1492. His grave breaks the usual rule for what a tomb should look like -- his coffin has never been lowered into the ground at all. How is it displayed instead?
answer: lifted aloft on the shoulders of four bronze bearers
choices: lifted aloft on the shoulders of four bronze bearers
suspended over the altar from four iron chains
raised high on a single tall porphyry column
set upright inside a huge bronze cathedral door
context: Four crowned bronze bearers — representing the medieval kingdoms of Castile, León, Aragón and Navarre — hold Columbus's coffin aloft, so he seems carried in endless procession rather than buried; sculptor Arturo Mélida installed it in 1899. Spain and the Dominican Republic long both claimed his real bones, until 2024 DNA testing led by José Antonio Lorente of the University of Granada confirmed the Seville remains are truly Columbus's. Source: Wikipedia (Tomb of Christopher Columbus), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Christopher_Columbus.

question: In the 1500s and 1600s, Spanish law required that every treasure fleet returning from the Americas -- hulls heavy with New World gold and silver -- sail to one single required port to be counted and taxed by the crown. That port was Seville in southern Spain. Yet Seville makes an odd choice for a great sea port, because of one strange fact about where it actually sits. What is that fact?
