answer: it lies far inland, reached only up a winding river
choices: it lies far inland, reached only up a winding river
it sits on an exposed island out in the Atlantic
it hides behind a long sandbar blocking the coast
it lies below sea level, ringed by earthen dikes
context: Seville sits about 90 km inland, up the winding Guadalquivir, which meets the Atlantic at Sanlúcar de Barrameda — yet from 1503 its Casa de Contratación (House of Trade) held a royal monopoly on all trade with the Americas: every ship to and from the Indies had to register in this river-city, until the monopoly moved to Cádiz in 1717. Sources: Wikipedia (Casa de Contratación) and Port of Seville, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_Contratación; Grokipedia (Casa de Contratación) checked first.

question: In Shanghai, a long row of grand European stone banks and hotels lines the west bank of the Huangpu River. Its old towers make it look like a slice of old London dropped into China. What is this famous waterfront called?
context: The Bund's roughly 52 historic buildings — Gothic, Baroque, Neoclassical, Art Deco and Beaux-Arts — went up after China's defeats opened the treaty ports; by the 1863 International Settlement, British, French, American and Japanese banks and trading houses stood shoulder to shoulder facing the river, staring across at what is now Pudong. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bund

question: Stand on Shanghai's Bund at night and look across the Huangpu River, and the far bank blazes with a wall of glass supertowers. Yet as recently as 1990 that same shore held rice paddies, farmland and warehouses. It was opened for building almost overnight. What is this space-age district called?
context: China opened Pudong for development on April 18, 1990 — the district's 'birthday.' In one generation its Lujiazui riverfront became the first place on Earth where three supertall skyscrapers rose within a few blocks, staring back across the Huangpu at the century-old Bund like the future facing the past. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pudong

question: Hidden in Shanghai's old town lies the Yu Garden, a Ming-dynasty jewel. Pavilions, ponds and rock piles fit into barely two hectares. The official Pan Yunduan spent nearly twenty years building it. He built it not for himself, but as a peaceful spot for whom?
context: Pan Yunduan built the Yu Garden between 1559 and 1577, folding pavilions, ponds and rockeries into barely two hectares; its name evokes peace and comfort in old age. Its prized Exquisite Jade Rock is a porous, 5-ton, 3.3-m boulder said to come from an emperor's collection. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu_Garden

question: Rising over Pudong's skyline, one supertower corkscrews as it climbs 632 metres, its glass skin spiraling a full 120 degrees from base to crown. The twist isn't mere style: it loosens the wind's grip, cutting the building's wind load by nearly a quarter. Which tower is it?
context: The Shanghai Tower reaches 632 m (2,073 ft) across 128 floors — China's tallest building, and the world's 2nd or 3rd tallest, not the tallest overall. Designed by the American firm Gensler, its spiral form uses about 25% less structural steel and saved roughly US$58 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Tower

question: The grand riverfront's name, the 'Bund,' isn't Chinese at all — the Chinese call it Waitan, 'the outer bank.' British traders who built the treaty-port waterfront borrowed the word 'bund,' meaning an embankment or dyke, from the language of one of Britain's other colonies. Which language gave us 'bund'?
context: 'Bund' entered English from Hindustani, meaning an embankment or dyke, and traveled the British trade routes to Shanghai; the Chinese name, Waitan, means 'outer bank.' Foreigners built the waterfront after China's defeat opened the treaty ports. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bund

question: A train with no wheels glides just above its guideway on magnets, then streaks along at 431 km/h (268 mph) — for seventeen years the fastest passenger train in regular service anywhere on Earth. This Shanghai maglev was built to whisk travellers to a single destination. Where does it race?
context: Opened in 2004, the Shanghai maglev was the world's first commercial high-speed maglev line, covering the ~30 km from Longyang Road to Pudong Airport in under 8 minutes and holding the regular-service speed record from 2004 to 2021. On a non-commercial test run on November 12, 2003, it hit 501 km/h (311 mph) — faster than many small planes cruise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_maglev_train

question: On the Bund stands the 1923 HSBC (Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation) Building, its doorway flanked by two bronze lions rubbed shiny by generations of passers-by. When it opened, its owners boasted it was 'the most luxurious building' anywhere between two far-flung landmarks. Which two did they name?
answer: the Suez Canal and the Bering Strait
choices: the Suez Canal and the Bering Strait
the Cape of Good Hope and Cape Horn
the Panama Canal and the Strait of Malacca
the Strait of Gibraltar and the Sea of Japan
context: The 1923 HSBC Building, guarded by two bronze lions, was boasted to be 'the most luxurious building between the Suez Canal and the Bering Strait' — a stretch spanning much of the globe. Next door, the 1927 Custom House carries a clock tower built to imitate London's Big Ben, nicknamed 'Big Ching.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bund

question: In Shanghai's old town, the Nine-Turn Bridge crosses a lotus pond toward the Huxinting Teahouse not in a straight line but in a series of sharp, deliberate zigzags. According to local folklore, why did the builders bend it into nine crooked turns?
answer: To block evil spirits, who move only in straight lines
choices: To block evil spirits, who move only in straight lines
To slow visitors so they savor the garden views
To keep the wooden walkway clear of the flood line
To trace the nine bends of a nearby sacred river
context: The spirit-blocking story is folklore: tradition holds that evil spirits can travel only in straight lines, so the crooked turns supposedly bar them. The zigzag bridge leads to the Huxinting Teahouse, built in 1784 in the middle of the pond — Shanghai's oldest surviving teahouse — and the nine turns also carry numerology, since nine, the highest single-digit odd number, symbolizes completeness and is linked to heaven and the emperor. Source: foresyteapp.com/yu-garden-nine-turn-bridge-shang (corroborated by trip.com and theculturetrip.com)  (Legend.)

question: In Yemen, about 500 tower houses stand jammed inside a single wall at Shibam. Some rise five to eleven stories high. The explorer Freya Stark reached it in the 1930s and called it 'the Manhattan of the desert.' What material are these tall desert houses actually built from?
context: Freya Stark, the British explorer who crossed the Hadhramaut in the 1930s, made 'the Manhattan of the desert' stick — but unlike Manhattan's steel and glass, every one of Shibam's roughly 500 towers is raised from sun-dried mud brick, packed inside a single defensive wall and rising five to eleven stories. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shibam; National Geographic, 'This Ancient Mud Skyscraper City is the Manhattan of the Desert.')

question: Shibam's mud towers rise eleven stories from nothing but sun-dried earth, and by rights the desert wind should batter them apart, yet they have ridden out the gales of the Wadi Hadhramaut for centuries. Hidden inside the thick walls is the reinforcement that lets each tower take the wind. What is it?
choices: a cage of woven palm ribs
context: Shibam's builders laced an internal matrix of wooden beams through the mud walls, tying each tower together so it can resist the lateral push of the wind — the hidden reinforcement that keeps an all-earth high-rise standing, with nothing on the outside to give it away. (Source: archup.net, 'Shibam / Hadramout,' on the internal timber matrix.)

question: Mud brick is soft and heavy — stack it into an eleven-story tower and it should slump and crack under its own weight. Yet Shibam's tallest towers, rising over 30 metres, have stood in the Yemeni desert for centuries. What is the builders' main trick for keeping them upright?
answer: the walls taper, thick at the base and thin at the top
choices: the walls taper, thick at the base and thin at the top
a deep stone foundation reaches down to bedrock
the towers lean inward and brace on one another
iron rods are threaded through every floor
context: Shibam's tower walls are about 1.2 m thick at the base and taper to roughly 0.4 m at the top, with smaller bricks laid on the upper floors. Widening the base and lightening the crown spreads the load so sun-dried mud brick can safely rise more than 30 m. (Sources: archup.net and clickpetroleoegas.com.br, 'Shibam / Hadramout.')

question: The Shwedagon Pagoda rises over Yangon. It is Myanmar's holiest shrine. Pilgrims show their faith by pressing something small against the base of the great stupa with their fingertips. What do they press onto it?
context: The Shwedagon is a literal mountain of gold: its bell-shaped stupa rises about 99 m (367 ft counting its crown) and is sheathed in over 20,000 solid gold plates - 8,688 on the lower stupa and 13,153 above. Ordinary pilgrims keep it alive by buying thin squares of gold leaf and pressing them onto the lower stupa by hand, so the shrine is re-gilded by the faithful themselves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shwedagon_Pagoda; sacred-destinations.com; factsanddetails.com.

question: Four covered stairways climb Singuttara Hill up to the Shwedagon's marble floor. At each gateway stand a pair of huge guardian statues, lion-dog beasts with white bodies and golden heads. In Myanmar, what are these temple guards called?
context: The four covered stairways climb the hill from the cardinal directions, each gate guarded by a pair of chinthe - Burmese leogryphs with white bodies and golden heads. The chinthe is so iconic that it appears on Myanmar's national currency. Source: sacred-destinations.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shwedagon_Pagoda (leogryph guardians at the four entrances).

question: At the very tip of the Shwedagon's stupa sits a small golden orb, studded with thousands of diamonds and crowned by a single large diamond. Stand on exactly the right spot at sunrise or sunset, and the top gem does something the ancient artisans planned. What does the gem appear to do?
answer: It flashes red, then green, then white
choices: It flashes red, then green, then white
It beams a single ray straight upward
It appears to float above the spire
It seems to slowly spin in place
context: The tip holds the 'sein bu,' a hollow golden orb set with 4,351 diamonds (about 1,800 carats), and resting on its point a single huge diamond of about 72 carats (sources say 72-76). Ancient artisans aimed the gem so that from the right spot on the terrace at dawn or dusk it flashes color - sources variously describe red, green, and white, or red, orange, and purple. Source: renown-travel.com; seasia.co; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shwedagon_Pagoda.

question: The Shwedagon is said to enshrine relics of the four Buddhas of this present age - among them a staff, a water filter, and a piece of robe. But the relic that makes the whole hill sacred, and the reason pilgrims circle the stupa clockwise and barefoot, belongs to the Buddha Gautama. What is it said to be?
context: By tradition the shrine enshrines relics of the four Buddhas of this age - the staff of Kakusandha, the water filter of Konagamana, a piece of Kassapa's robe, and eight hairs from the head of Gautama. Because the sacred hairs are believed to lie inside, worshippers circle the stupa clockwise and barefoot, removing their shoes at the very foot of the covered stairways. This is religious tradition, not a physical claim. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shwedagon_Pagoda.  (Legend.)

question: The 23-ton bronze Singu Min bell, cast in 1779, once hung at the Shwedagon. When British forces occupied Yangon, they hauled the huge bell off as war loot - but it slipped from their barge into the Yangon River and sank to the bottom, and their engineers gave up trying to raise it. How did the Burmese townspeople get their bell back?
answer: They floated it up on rafts of bamboo
choices: They floated it up on rafts of bamboo
They dragged it out with teams of elephants
They waited for the dry season and dug it free
They raised it with chains and pulleys
context: The recovered Singu Min (Maha Ganda) bell hangs in its pavilion to this day; the Burmese refloated the 23-ton bronze by lashing bamboo beneath it until it rose. Nearby hangs the even larger 42-ton Tharrawaddy Min bell of 1841. An earlier giant - the roughly 300-ton Great Bell of Dhammazedi (1485) - was carried off by the Portuguese mercenary Filipe de Brito in 1608 and lost in the Bago River, never recovered. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shwedagon_Pagoda; renown-travel.com.

question: Around the base of the Shwedagon stand eight planetary posts, one for each day of the Burmese week - which runs to eight days because Wednesday splits at 6 p.m., its evening half becoming the day of the shadow-planet Rahu. Each post carries its own animal emblem, and worshippers pour cups of water over the one for the day they were born. Which animal marks the post for that Rahu half of Wednesday?
context: The Burmese week runs to eight days because Wednesday splits: until 6 p.m. it is Wednesday, and from 6 p.m. to midnight it becomes the day of Rahu, the shadow-planet. Each of the eight posts carries an animal emblem - garuda for Sunday, tiger for Monday, lion for Tuesday, a tusked elephant for Wednesday morning, and a tuskless elephant for Rahu's evening half, then a mouse for Thursday, a guinea pig for Friday, and the naga (dragon-serpent) for Saturday. Worshippers find the post for the day they were born and pour cups of water over its Buddha image for luck. Source: myanmar2day.com; tourhq.com.

question: For centuries, pilgrims from across Buddhist Asia have donated gold to keep the Shwedagon gilded. The custom traces to a famous 15th-century queen of Bago, Shin Sawbu, who reportedly donated gold to cover the stupa. She set the pattern for every donor who followed her. What did she reportedly give?
choices: A solid gold statue of herself
A thousand bars of pure gold
A golden bell for each shrine
context: Queen Shin Sawbu, the 15th-century ruler of Bago, is said to have donated her own body weight in gold to gild the stupa, beginning the custom of pilgrims from across Buddhist Asia giving gold to maintain it ever since. This is tradition rather than documented fact. Source: renown-travel.com; sacred-destinations.com.  (Legend.)

question: A sheer column of granite juts about 180 metres straight up out of the flat jungle of central Sri Lanka. This natural rock tower is now called Sigiriya. In the 5th century a king turned it into his royal capital. Where on the rock did he build the palace itself?
choices: On an island in the moat
context: Sigiriya is an inselberg -- the hardened granite magma plug of a long-dead volcano -- rising about 180 m above the plain (349 m above sea level). King Kashyapa set his palace on the roughly flat summit, a royal court in the sky. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya.

question: The only path to Sigiriya's summit narrowed near the top. Every climber was forced up a staircase leading into the open mouth of a colossal brick beast crouching against the rock. Passing through its jaws was the last gate to the palace above. What animal was this great gatehouse built as?
context: The gate gave the rock its name: Sinhagiri, 'Lion Rock,' which wore down to 'Sigiriya.' You climbed a staircase set between the lion's enormous paws and into its mouth. The head collapsed centuries ago, so today only the two carved paws survive -- each about 3 m long -- flanking the roughly 1,200-step climb. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; nationalgeographic.com.

question: Halfway up the sheer face of Sigiriya, a shallow overhang has sheltered a row of life-sized figures from sun and monsoon rain for about 1,500 years. Around two dozen survive from a painted band that once ran 140 metres along the cliff. What do these figures show?
context: These are the famous 'cloud maidens' -- bare-shouldered celestial women (apsaras), among the oldest surviving frescoes in Sri Lanka (Anuradhapura period). Only about 21-22 remain of a band that may once have held some 500 ladies, 140 m long and 40 m high. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; nationalgeographic.com.

question: Just below Sigiriya's cliff frescoes runs a long wall of brick, coated by the ancient builders in a hard, pale lime plaster. Sinhalese tradition holds that King Kashyapa prized this wall for one startling reason as he walked beside it. What did tradition say he could do at its surface?
context: This is the Mirror Wall: the lime plaster was polished so glassy that, tradition says, King Kashyapa could see his own reflection as he passed. Brick masonry lies beneath the mirror-bright coating, which still shines in places today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; ccf.gov.lk.  (Legend.)

question: Long after King Kashyapa's time, ordinary travellers kept climbing Sigiriya to see its famous cliff paintings. Below the paintings ran a long plastered wall. Generation after generation added something to it. Over 1,500 survive from the 700s to the 900s, left by everyone from governors to housewives. What did these visitors leave behind?
context: The Mirror Wall is covered in over 1,500 short poems -- ancient graffiti admiring the painted maidens. One marvels at 'the rock that captivates the mind'; another, some 1,200 years old, reads: 'The caress of the gentle breeze was delicate upon their bodies, illuminated by the light of the moon's rays.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; nationalgeographic.com.

question: King Kashyapa raised the whole Sigiriya fortress partly out of fear: he had seized Sri Lanka's throne by murdering his own father, and he dreaded the vengeance of his half-brother Moggallana, who had fled overseas to raise an army. In 495 CE that army finally returned. Where did Kashyapa meet his end?
answer: On the battlefield below the rock
choices: On the battlefield below the rock
In his palace on the summit
context: As Moggallana advanced, Kashyapa's troops turned aside to skirt a swamp; believing himself abandoned, the king took his own life on the battlefield at the foot of his own rock. Afterward Sigiriya was given over to Buddhist monks. (The death is known from the Sinhalese chronicles.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; nationalgeographic.com.  (Legend.)

question: At the foot of Sigiriya spread symmetrical royal water gardens, fed through underground clay pipes and pressure chambers built by King Kashyapa's engineers around 1,500 years ago. Set flush into the garden paths are round fountains cut from limestone plates. What still surprises visitors about these ancient fountains?
answer: They still jet water when it rains
choices: They still jet water when it rains
They mark the four compass points
They doubled as the palace sundials
context: Fed by the monsoon, the limestone-plate fountains still spurt water after some 1,500 years -- among the oldest surviving landscaped, hydraulic gardens on Earth. The grounds stack three garden kinds up the slope: the symmetrical water gardens on the flat approach, wilder boulder gardens with carved stone seats, and terraced gardens climbing to the cliff. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; ccf.gov.lk.

question: For nearly two thousand years, long camel caravans hauled Chinese silk about 6,400 km westward across the Central Asian deserts to markets in Persia and Rome. In 1877 a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, drew a map of this old trade network and gave it the lasting name 'Silk Road.' Every westbound caravan set out from the same great Chinese imperial capital. Which city was that starting point?
context: Every Silk Road caravan bound for the Mediterranean began at Chang'an — today's Xi'an — the ancient imperial capital that anchored the road's eastern end. From there the 6,400-kilometre caravan network crossed the Central Asian deserts to the west. For two thousand years the traders never had one name for the route; the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen coined 'Seidenstrasse' — 'Silk Road' — only in 1877. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road

question: In Henan province, in central China, archaeologists digging out a Stone Age village of the Yangshao culture uncovered a scrap of woven silk. It dates to about 3630 BC, making it the oldest piece of silk cloth ever discovered on Earth. What had this most ancient silk been used for?
choices: binding a bundle of ritual millet
context: The woven silk from about 3630 BC — over five thousand years old — was found at a Yangshao site in Henan wrapped around the body of a child, a sign that silk was treasured as something precious and sacred from the very dawn of the craft. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_silk

question: Most countries have coastlines fixed by nature, but Singapore keeps getting bigger. Since the 1960s the crowded island has grown by about a quarter. It holds the world record as Earth's fastest-growing country. Which process gave it all this extra ground?
context: Land reclamation grew Singapore from about 582 km² in the 1960s to roughly 723 km² today — a ~24% gain and the fastest of any nation (a Guinness World Record). Volcanic eruptions, river sedimentation (delta-building), and coral reef growth all add land in nature, but only reclamation — piling imported sand into the shallow sea — builds Singapore's new coast on purpose. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reclamation_in_Singapore; guinnessworldrecords.com

question: The island nation of Singapore sits in Southeast Asia, only about 85 miles from a famous imaginary line drawn around the middle of the Earth. Singapore has no four seasons at all. Instead it gets steamy heat and heavy rain almost every day of the year. Which line does the island nearly straddle?
context: Lying just ~137 km (85 miles) north of the equator, where the sun stays nearly overhead all year, Singapore has no summer or winter — only warm, wet weather. The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn and the Prime Meridian all cross the globe elsewhere. Source: britannica.com/place/Singapore; distancefromequator.com

question: On Singapore's Marina waterfront, at Gardens by the Bay, stand 18 steel towers up to 50 metres tall. Each is wrapped in living ferns and vines. They collect rainwater, run on solar power, and glow every night in a light show. What are these giant plant-covered towers called?
context: Gardens by the Bay's 18 Supertrees, 25–50 m tall, are vertical gardens on steel frames; the tallest carry solar cells and rainwater collectors, and they light up nightly in the 'Garden Rhapsody' sound-and-light show. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardens_by_the_Bay

question: At Singapore's Jewel Changi Airport, rainwater collected on the huge glass roof pours down through a round opening in the dome. It is ringed by a terraced garden of ferns and palms. This spectacular indoor cascade is called the Rain Vortex. Which world record does it hold?
choices: the world's most powerful indoor waterfall
context: Jewel Changi Airport's Rain Vortex, opened in 2019, drops 40 m and can flow up to ~37,850 litres a minute. Its Guinness record is specifically for height — the world's tallest indoor waterfall — not for age, size, or power. By comparison, outdoor giants like Venezuela's Angel Falls (~980 m) tower far higher, but no indoor cascade falls farther than the Rain Vortex. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewel_Changi_Airport

question: In 1967 Singapore's first prime minister, Lee Kuan Yew, launched a plan to turn the young island nation into a lush, tree-filled city. For decades afterwards he planted a young tree himself almost every year, and government crews lined every road and public square with greenery. Singapore adopted a new nickname to match this bold new identity. What was it?
context: Lee Kuan Yew, nicknamed the nation's 'Chief Gardener,' made greenery state policy from 1967, and Singapore embraced the 'Garden City' name; today it has over 100 hectares of rooftop gardens and green walls. 'Lion City' (from Singapura) is its older name, 'Green City' is a generic label used for many eco-cities, and 'Pearl of the Orient' belongs to other Asian ports. Source: cnbc.com; nas.gov.sg/archivesonline/gardencity

question: With almost no room for natural rivers or lakes, Singapore made a bold move right downtown. In 2008 it completed the Marina Barrage, a dam sealing off Marina Bay from the sea. Rain slowly flushed the salt away, and today this bay in the city's heart mainly provides what?
context: Sealed from the tides and refreshed by rain, Marina Bay became Singapore's 15th reservoir — a freshwater drinking supply in the middle of downtown that also eases floods in low-lying Chinatown and hosts kayakers and dragonboats. The Marina Barrage opened 31 October 2008. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marina_Barrage

question: Beside the Supertrees at Gardens by the Bay rises the Flower Dome, a cool, dry hall of plants about 1.2 hectares in size, roofed by one great curve of steel and glass and filled with olive trees, baobabs, and desert succulents. In 2015 it set which Guinness World Record?
context: The Flower Dome, opened 2012, spans about 1.2 hectares under a column-free steel-and-glass shell — the world's largest columnless glasshouse (Guinness, 2015) — kept cool and dry to grow olive trees, baobabs, and desert succulents. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardens_by_the_Bay

question: Singapore was running low on sand for new land, since its neighbours had banned selling it, yet the crowded island still demanded more ground. In 2016 it borrowed a centuries-old technique from the Netherlands, the country that constructed much of its farmland below sea level. Rather than pile sand into the shallows, engineers enclose a patch of sea and pump it dry, using far less sand. What is a tract of land reclaimed this Dutch way called?
context: A polder is land reclaimed the Dutch way — ringed by a dike and pumped dry — and Singapore adopted the method in November 2016 to build new land using far less sand than piling it into the sea. A cofferdam also walls off water and pumps it dry, but only temporarily, to work in the dry on a bridge pier or dam foundation; a breakwater is an offshore wall that calms the waves; a caisson is a watertight box sunk to build underwater foundations. Singapore turned to polders because its neighbours had cut off its sand: Malaysia banned exports in 1997, Indonesia (once over 90% of the supply) in 2007, and Vietnam in 2009. Only about 10% of the country was reclaimed by 1991, and it plans to add roughly another 7–8% by 2030. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reclamation_in_Singapore

question: West of the city, Singapore fused seven small offshore islets into a single artificial island, completed in 2009 and covering over 3,500 hectares. Though the country pumps no crude oil of its own, this made-from-scratch island refines about 1.5 million barrels a day. What is it called?
context: Jurong Island, completed in 2009, was formed by reclaiming and merging seven islets (from ~991 to over 3,500 hectares). With no crude of its own, Singapore refines about 1.5 million barrels a day here, ranking among the world's top three refining centres. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurong_Island

question: Singapore grew up beside a narrow sea-gate between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, the shortest sea route between the Indian and Pacific oceans. At its tightest, near the city, this passage pinches to just 2.8 km wide. What is this waterway called?
context: The Strait of Malacca is the shortest sea route between the Indian and Pacific oceans; near Singapore, the Phillips Channel narrows to about 2.8 km. The Straits of Hormuz, Gibraltar, and Dover are famous sea-gates elsewhere — joining the Persian Gulf, the Mediterranean, and the North Sea to their neighbouring waters — but only Malacca threads its narrows past Singapore between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strait_of_Malacca

question: In the winter of 1850, a fierce storm battered the Orkney islands off the far northern tip of Scotland. It stripped the grass and sand from a low mound above the Bay of Skaill. When the storm dropped, it had revealed the stone walls of a village buried for about 5,000 years. What is this Stone Age village called?
context: A wild storm in the winter of 1850 tore the turf from a mound above the Bay of Skaill, exposing the stone houses. Excavation eventually revealed a complete Neolithic (Stone Age) village -- the best-preserved in all of Western Europe. Source: Historic Environment Scotland, historicenvironment.scot/visit-a-place/places/skara-brae/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.

question: The stone village of Skara Brae on Orkney was built and lived in around 3200 to 2500 BC. Then it was abandoned and left to lie hidden for thousands of years. People often picture Egypt's Great Pyramid of Giza as belonging to the very dawn of history. How does Skara Brae's age compare with that of the Great Pyramid?
answer: older than the Great Pyramid by centuries
choices: older than the Great Pyramid by centuries
the same age as the Great Pyramid
younger than the Great Pyramid by a thousand years
younger than the Great Pyramid by two thousand years
context: Skara Brae was a thriving village around 3200-2500 BC, lived in for roughly 600 years -- older than Stonehenge and older than the Egyptian pyramids. Historic Environment Scotland puts it plainly: 'Long before Stonehenge or even the Egyptian pyramids were built, Skara Brae was a thriving village.' (The Great Pyramid of Giza dates to about 2560 BC.) Source: historicenvironment.scot/visit-a-place/places/skara-brae/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.

question: Drifting sand buried Skara Brae so gently and so fully, with its beds, dressers and tools, that it sealed a normal day of Stone Age life just as the villagers had left it. The little Orkney village earned a nickname from a famous buried city in Italy. What nickname did Skara Brae earn?
context: The nickname is only a comparison about preservation -- no volcano was involved. Wind-blown sand, not volcanic ash, gradually buried Skara Brae and sealed its furniture and tools, freezing a moment of Stone Age daily life much as Vesuvius's ash froze Roman Pompeii in AD 79. Source: thearchaeologist.org (Neolithic Skara Brae: the Scottish Pompeii); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.

question: At most ancient sites, the furniture is long gone, because wooden beds and chests rot away in a few centuries. Yet step into a house at Skara Brae, and the beds, seats and dressers still stand after 5,000 years, as solid as new. Why did this one village's furniture last when almost all other prehistoric furniture has crumbled?
answer: the villagers built it from stone, not wood
choices: the villagers built it from stone, not wood
the cold peat bog tanned and preserved the wood
it lay sealed airtight inside a rock-cut tomb
it was carved from rot-proof bog-oak
context: Windswept Orkney had almost no trees for timber, so the villagers made their furniture from flat slabs of local stone -- stone beds, stone seats and stone dressers -- which is why it has survived 5,000 years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae; historicenvironment.scot/visit-a-place/places/skara-brae/.

question: Orkney's weather is fierce -- wind, rain and salt spray driving in off the North Atlantic. The builders of Skara Brae set their houses close together and connected them all, so the villagers could pass from one home to another without ever facing the storm. How were the houses of Skara Brae linked together?
answer: by low passages roofed over with stone slabs
choices: by low passages roofed over with stone slabs
by a single roofed hall all the doors opened onto
by tunnels bored down through the solid bedrock
by covered walkways around an enclosed courtyard
context: Skara Brae's houses were joined by low passages, roofed over with stone and only about a metre high, so people could move from home to home sheltered from the weather. The walls were further insulated by 'midden' -- composted ash, bone and shell -- packed between double stone skins. Source: orkneyology.com/skara-brae.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.

question: Skara Brae was astonishingly comfortable for a village 5,000 years old. Set into the thick wall of almost every home was a small stone cubicle, just large enough for a single person. Archaeologists think each cubicle served a very familiar everyday purpose. What do they believe these little wall-recesses were?
context: Skara Brae had a drainage system running in stone-lined channels beneath the houses, and each little wall-cubicle was plumbed into it -- one main reason archaeologists read the recess as a toilet. If so, it gave Skara Brae indoor sanitation that most later Orcadians would not have again until the 20th century. (The reading as a toilet is likely but not certain.) Source: orkneyology.com/skara-brae.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.  (Legend.)

question: Skara Brae was only one corner of a vast Neolithic ritual landscape on Orkney. Nearby rose the Ness of Brodgar, a great temple complex whose largest hall was deliberately shut down and abandoned around 2400 to 2200 BC. Rather than quietly walking away, the Stone Age community marked the closing with one enormous ceremony, and left unmistakable evidence heaped in the ruins. What did archaeologists find there, the remains of that great farewell?
answer: the shin-bones of some 400 slaughtered cattle
choices: the shin-bones of some 400 slaughtered cattle
the shards of thousands of smashed clay pots
a ring of carved stone balls set into the floor
the ashes of a huge timber roof burnt to the ground
context: The Ness of Brodgar, between the Ring of Brodgar and the Stones of Stenness, held 'Structure Ten,' one of the largest Neolithic buildings in northern Britain. Around 2400-2200 BC it was ceremonially closed with a vast feast: excavators found roughly 400 cattle tibias (shin-bones), the remains of hundreds of slaughtered animals. Skara Brae, Brodgar and Stenness together make up the UNESCO 'Heart of Neolithic Orkney.' (A closing feast is the leading interpretation of the bone deposit.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ness_of_Brodgar.  (Legend.)

question: For a few weeks around midsummer, St Petersburg never really goes dark. The sun barely dips below the horizon, and at midnight the sky still glows bright enough to walk the embankments or read outdoors. Crowds fill the bridges past 1 a.m. What are these luminous summer nights called?
context: Near the solstice St Petersburg gets about 18 hours 50 minutes of daylight, and even the rest of the night stays in bright twilight, light enough to read outdoors. This isn't the true 'midnight sun' (where the sun never sets at all): here it slips just below the horizon, so the sky glows rather than shines. The season fills the embankments and bridges with crowds past midnight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_sun; russiable.com/white-nights-st-petersburg/

question: Russia's second city, St Petersburg, is built across dozens of islands in the low, watery delta of the Neva River where it meets the Baltic Sea. More than 60 rivers and canals thread between the streets. Over 300 bridges tie the whole city together. This maze of water and islands earned it a nickname borrowed from a famous European water-city. What is it?
context: Land reclamation trimmed the delta's original ~101 islands to about 42, and the city is crossed by 342 bridges over its rivers and canals, with some tallies running past 500. All that water threading between the islands is why St Petersburg is called the Venice of the North. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bridges_in_Saint_Petersburg; introducingsaintpetersburg.com/bridges

question: In 1703 Peter the Great ordered a brand-new capital to be built on a cold, misty marsh at the mouth of the Neva. Forced peasants and Swedish war prisoners drove countless wooden piles into the swamp. Tens of thousands died in the mud. What grim folk nickname did St Petersburg earn as a result?
choices: the city of a thousand sorrows
context: The founding date, 27 May 1703, is still marked as the city's birthday. Peter the Great forced his capital onto ground everyone called unbuildable; conscripted peasants and Swedish prisoners of war drained the swamp and drove countless wooden piles, and tens of thousands of forced laborers died, the real human cost behind the grim folk name. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg

question: Deep in the cellars beneath St Petersburg's Hermitage art museum in Russia, a special staff has hunted rats and mice for nearly 300 years. Empress Elizabeth of Russia first brought them in during the 1740s to guard the imperial Winter Palace and its treasures from vermin. Every one of them still receives a name and a passport. What are these long-serving Hermitage guardians?
context: A resident population of cats has protected the Hermitage's cellars and courtyards from rats for centuries, a tradition dating back to imperial times: Empress Elizabeth first had cats brought in to guard the palace. They still work the basements today, though they are kept out of the galleries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitage_Museum

question: St Petersburg did not begin as grand palaces. It grew outward from the very first structure Peter the Great built here, on 27 May 1703, on tiny Hare Island in the Neva delta. That first fortification was the seed the whole imperial capital would spread out from. Which landmark was it?
context: The Peter and Paul Fortress was laid down on 27 May 1703 on tiny Zayachy (Hare) Island in the Neva delta. The citadel came first, and the imperial capital grew outward from it across the marsh; it is the founding kernel of the whole city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg

question: Behind the Winter Palace facade in St Petersburg, the Hermitage holds about three million works of art and artifacts. That enormous collection began when Catherine the Great bought a batch of paintings in 1764. Among the world's museums, where does that place the Hermitage?
context: The single largest is the Louvre in Paris; the Hermitage ranks second by the size of its collection. It grew from Catherine the Great's 1764 purchase of about 225 paintings from the Berlin merchant Johann Ernst Gotzkowsky, the batch that founded the imperial collection, now spread through the Winter Palace and its neighboring buildings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitage_Museum

question: On summer nights in St Petersburg, cross to the wrong side of the Neva after about 1 a.m. and you can be stranded until nearly dawn. For a few hours every night from spring to autumn, what do the Neva's great bridges do, cutting off all crossing until they close near sunrise?
answer: rise open to let ocean ships pass
choices: rise open to let ocean ships pass
lift to let spring ice floes through
close off for their nightly maintenance
swing shut against Gulf storm surges
context: St Petersburg is a working seaport, and ocean-going cargo ships can only move along the Neva when the bridges lift. In navigation season (roughly late April to November) the drawbridges open on a nightly schedule; the famous Palace Bridge splits open around 1:10 a.m. and lowers again near 4:55 a.m., so anyone caught on the wrong bank waits for dawn. Source: russiable.com/drawbridges-st-petersburg-schedules/; travelallrussia.com/blog/drawing-bridges

question: St Petersburg's Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood glitters inside with more than 7,500 square metres of mosaic, more than any other church on Earth. But its grim name comes from the very ground it covers: the exact spot where, in 1881, someone was killed. Who died there?
answer: a tsar, killed by a bomb blast
choices: a tsar, killed by a bomb blast
a grand duchess, lost in a fire
an army general, shot by an assassin
context: The victim was Tsar Alexander II, struck down by a bomb on this spot in 1881, the killing that gave the church its name, 'Savior on Spilled Blood.' Inside, over 7,500 square metres of mosaic cover the walls and vaults, more than in any other church in the world. Source: historyhit.com/locations/church-of-the-saviour-on-spilled-blood/

question: At Peter the Great's palace of Peterhof outside St Petersburg, more than 100 fountains have played every summer since 1721. The giant Grand Cascade shoots water skyward without using any machinery whatsoever. What lifts the water into those towering jets?
answer: gravity, from springs on higher ground
choices: gravity, from springs on higher ground
the daily rise and fall of Baltic tides
steady wind off the Gulf of Finland
context: The secret is elevation: water is gathered from natural springs in the Ropsha Heights about 22-24 km away and some 90 m higher, then channeled downhill. Arriving under its own weight, it has enough pressure to shoot skyward, no pumps needed. Engineered by Vasily Tuvolkov, the system has run this way since 1721, and the Grand Cascade alone feeds 64 fountains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peterhof_Palace; unesco.ru/en/news/55-peterhof/

question: The golden centerpiece of Peterhof, its tallest fountain, fires a single jet some 20 metres straight up and celebrates Russia's crushing victory over Sweden. At its heart, a gilded strongman is locked in combat with a great beast. Which hero and beast does the statue show?
answer: Samson tearing open a lion's jaws
choices: Samson tearing open a lion's jaws
context: The Samson Fountain marks Russia's victory over Sweden: a lion is Sweden's heraldic emblem, and Samson, standing for Russia, rips its jaws apart. Its single vertical jet reaches about 20 metres (66 ft), the tallest of all Peterhof's fountains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peterhof_Palace

question: St Petersburg's Bronze Horseman, a dramatic statue of Peter the Great rearing on horseback, stands on a single colossal slab of granite that once weighed about 1,500 tonnes, among the largest stones ever shifted by human hands. To move it, 400 men rolled it for months over a track of bronze balls. What is this famous rock called?
context: The Thunder Stone is a single granite boulder of roughly 1,500 tonnes (about 1,250 after carving), among the largest stones ever moved by people. Workers hauled it overland on a metal sled sliding over a track of bronze balls, 400 men over about nine months, with no animals or machines, then floated it the rest of the way by barge. The statue was sculpted by the Frenchman Etienne Maurice Falconet for Catherine the Great and unveiled in 1782; Alexander Pushkin's 1833 poem gave it the enduring name 'The Bronze Horseman.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Horseman

question: In St Petersburg the Neva River freezes solid for months every winter, yet around midsummer the sky never fully darkens and people linger outdoors at midnight. One single geographic fact about the city's position causes BOTH of these opposite extremes. Which fact?
choices: how low it sits above the sea
how far it lies inland from the sea
how mountainous the land around it is
context: At about 60 degrees north (59 degrees 57 minutes N), St Petersburg sits on the polar edge, far enough from the equator that the swing between summer and winter light is extreme. Near midsummer the sun barely dips below the horizon, giving the glowing White Nights; in deep winter it scarcely rises and the Neva locks in ice. Latitude alone sets the whole rhythm of the city's year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg; russiable.com/white-nights-st-petersburg/

question: Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, was built exactly where the freshwater Lake Malaren spills out into the salty Baltic Sea. Instead of hugging one bank of the water like most cities, Stockholm spreads itself right out over the harbor. How is the historic city laid out?
choices: A city raised on 14 wooden piers
A city split by 14 river channels
context: Stockholm sits on 14 islands at the outlet of Lake Mälaren into the Baltic, historically nicknamed 'the city between the bridges' (Staden mellan broarna) for the bridges stitching its islands together — Wikipedia counts about thirty bridges in the central city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Stockholm

question: In Gamla Stan — Stockholm's medieval old town, crowded onto one small island — the streets twist and narrow between tall ochre-gold houses. Tightest of them all is a stepped alley called Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, the narrowest street in the whole city. How wide is it where it pinches down the most?
answer: About 90 centimeters — barely a shoulder's width
choices: About 90 centimeters — barely a shoulder's width
About 3 meters — a single cart's width
About 6 meters — two carts side by side
context: Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, a stepped alley in Gamla Stan, is the narrowest street in Stockholm — about 90 cm at its tightest squeeze. Gamla Stan ('the Old Town'), crowded onto the island of Stadsholmen, dates to the 13th century and is one of the largest and best-preserved medieval city cores in Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_stan

question: Old Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, sits on 14 islands where a big lake called Malaren meets the Baltic Sea, but that is only the start. Sail east from the city and the coast breaks up into countless little islands, skerries and bare rocks stretching far out into the Baltic. About how many islands in all make up the Stockholm Archipelago?
context: The Stockholm Archipelago scatters some 30,000 islands, islets, and skerries into the Baltic — a skerry being a small rocky islet too barren to build on. The exact total is genuinely uncertain: counts range from about 24,000 to over 30,000 depending on the source, so 'roughly 30,000' is the honest figure. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_Archipelago  (Legend.)

question: Ride the subway in Stockholm and the stations look nothing like an ordinary subway. Most of the roughly 100 stops open into caverns of raw unfinished bedrock painted with color, and at T-Centralen huge blue vines climb straight up the bare stone. What nickname has the Stockholm Metro earned around the world?
context: The Stockholm Metro is called 'the world's longest art gallery': more than 90 of its ~100 stations are painted, sculpted, or blasted straight into the bare bedrock and decorated by over 150 artists along 105.7 km of track. At T-Centralen, the central hub, Per Olof Ultvedt painted cave-like blue vines and leaves across the raw rock. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_metro  (Legend.)

question: In August 1628, crowds packed Stockholm's harbor to cheer the pride of the Swedish navy, the Vasa. She was the tallest, most heavily armed warship the kingdom had ever built, glittering with hundreds of gilded carvings. For all that glory, the Vasa is remembered today for one humiliating fact. What is it?
answer: She capsized and sank in the harbor on her very first voyage
choices: She capsized and sank in the harbor on her very first voyage
She rotted at her moorings, never once putting to sea
She was captured by the Danish fleet within a year
She was lost with all hands in a storm off Poland
context: On 10 August 1628, the Vasa capsized and sank on her maiden voyage after sailing barely 1,300 m — going down only about 120 m from shore, as roughly 30 people drowned, in full view of the watching crowd. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasa_(ship)

question: To make the Vasa a terror at sea, her builders crowded two full decks of heavy bronze cannon high in her hull — but left too little ballast down in her belly to steady all that weight up top. On her first voyage, a light breeze pushed on her sails and she heeled far over to one side. That single lean sank her. Why?
answer: Her open lower gunports let the sea pour in
choices: Her open lower gunports let the sea pour in
Her tall masts snapped and dragged her under
Her powder store caught fire deep in the hull
Her loose cannon smashed out through the deck
context: The Vasa's center of gravity sat too high over two gundecks of cannon, with too little ballast below; a light gust heeled her, and water flooded in through the open lower gunports until she went down. She carried 64 guns, mostly 48 heavy 24-pounder bronze cannon — the very weight, mounted high, that doomed her. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasa_(ship)

question: A wooden warship left on the seabed for 333 years should be a shapeless smear of debris. Wood-boring shipworms devour oak hulls in most oceans within decades. But the Baltic is too cold and too fresh for them, so they never touched the sunken Vasa. When she was raised in Stockholm in 1961, how much of her original 17th-century oak was still intact?
context: Because the cold, brackish (low-salt) Baltic water excludes the wood-eating shipworm Teredo navalis, about 98% of the Vasa was still original oak when she was raised in 1961 after 333 years on the bottom. She is the only almost-fully-intact 17th-century ship ever salvaged, now displayed whole in the Vasa Museum (opened 1990). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasa_(ship)

question: The Stockholm Archipelago is not finished forming — it is still slowly emerging from the Baltic Sea, its islands standing a few millimeters higher above the water every year. Old shorelines creep inland, and new bare-rock skerries break the surface for the first time. All across Scandinavia the land is quietly climbing out of the sea. What keeps lifting these islands out of the water year after year?
choices: A slow fall in the sea level
Silt piling up from the rivers
context: As the kilometer-thick ice sheets of the last Ice Age melted, the enormous weight lifted off the crust, which is still slowly springing back — post-glacial (isostatic) rebound — raising the Stockholm region about 3 mm a year and lifting the archipelago's 'joint valley landscape' up out of the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_Archipelago

question: In Stone Town on Zanzibar, families traditionally built one part of the house before the walls went up. Hundreds still stand along the narrow alleys. Each is a heavy slab carved with symbols that showed the owner's trade, faith, and wealth. What is it?
context: Stone Town is famous for more than 500 hand-carved wooden doors. The door went up first when a house was built, and its carvings advertised the owner -- Qur'anic verses for the devout, a fish for a fisherman, lotus flowers and chains for prosperity. (Source: Wikipedia 'Stone Town'; TingaTinga Art 'The Zanzibar Door'; Preservation Journey 'The Doors of Zanzibar')

question: Stone Town gets its very name from its building material. While the surrounding coastal villages rose in mud and thatch, its merchants cut a local rock into blocks, bound them with lime mortar, and raised the tall multi-storey houses that still crowd the alleys today. Which of these is that local building stone?
context: The stone is coralline ragstone -- fossil coral quarried from the reef -- laced with mangrove-pole timber. Fusing Swahili, Arab, Indian and European styles, the old town became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. (Source: UNESCO WHC 'Stone Town of Zanzibar'; Wikipedia 'Stone Town')

question: The oldest doors of Stone Town bristle with rows of fat brass spikes jutting from the wood, but Zanzibar itself never faced a siege. The design came from India, where such heavy studs served one grim purpose: to blunt an attack that could otherwise batter a gate off its hinges. What were the studs first meant to stop?
context: Indian fort gates were studded to keep war elephants from battering them down. Zanzibar never fought such a war, so on the island the brass spikes became pure decoration -- a badge of a merchant's wealth during the spice-trade boom. (Source: TingaTinga Art 'The Zanzibar Door'; Atlas Obscura 'The Doors of Stone Town'; Preservation Journey 'The Doors of Zanzibar')  (Legend.)

question: Under its Omani sultans, farms spread across Zanzibar until the small island grew more of one aromatic spice than anywhere on Earth. Traders stopped bothering with its real name and just called it the 'Spice Island.' Which spice did Zanzibar grow more of than any other place?
context: The Omani ruler pushed clove plantations across the island, and by the mid-1800s Zanzibar dominated the world clove trade -- the source of the 'Spice Island' name. (Source: Britannica 'Said ibn Sultan'; Capable Africa Tours 'History of Zanzibar'; BlackPast 'Sultanate of Zanzibar')

question: One of the twentieth century's most famous rock singers began life in 1946 in an ordinary house in Stone Town's alleys -- born Farrokh Bulsara to Parsi parents, before his family left the island while he was still a boy. His birthplace is now a small museum on the visitor trail. Which rock star was born there?
context: He was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town in 1946; the family later moved to England, where he became Freddie Mercury, frontman of the band Queen. The house where he lived is now a small museum. (Source: Machu Picchu 'Stone Town Zanzibar Guide 2026'; Wikipedia 'Stone Town')

question: Around 1840, the Omani sultan Said bin Sultan did something startling: he moved his capital from Muscat in Arabia across the ocean to Stone Town, a small African island his family ruled. A ruler almost never leaves his ancestral seat. What made this little island worth more to him than Oman?
choices: its fort on a sea strait
context: The wealth pouring out of his East African clove and trade empire had grown larger than Oman's own revenue, so Said bin Sultan moved his capital from Muscat to Stone Town around 1840. (Source: Britannica 'Said ibn Sultan'; Gulf News 'Zanzibar: A slice of Oman'; BlackPast 'Seyyid Said')

question: Stone Town once held East Africa's largest slave market, the hub through which traders bought and sold captives carried from deep in the African interior. After Britain forced the trade to close, workers raised a Christian cathedral on that exact ground -- and set its altar on the precise spot where one grim fixture of that market had stood. What had stood where the altar now sits?
context: The Anglican Christ Church Cathedral was begun on Christmas Day 1873 and opened in 1879 on the old slave-market site; its altar stands where the market's whipping post once stood. Below, the cramped underground cells where captives were packed to await sale are still preserved. (Source: Wikipedia 'Christ Church, Zanzibar'; Pongwe 'Christ Church Cathedral & the Old Slave Market')

question: In 1883 Sultan Barghash bin Said built a vast ceremonial palace on the Stone Town seafront, its marble floors and tall pillared verandas rising over the coral-stone alleys. People named it Beit-al-Ajaib -- the 'House of Wonders' -- for the marvels it was the first building in all of East Africa to contain. What made the palace so wondrous?
answer: it had electric light and an elevator
choices: it had electric light and an elevator
it had a rooftop garden and a zoo
it had gold walls and an ivory throne
it had a moat and a working drawbridge
context: The House of Wonders (Beit-al-Ajaib), built by Sultan Barghash in 1883, was the first building in East Africa to have an elevator and the first in Zanzibar with electric light, running water and marble floors -- hence its name. A corner of it collapsed during a restoration in 2020, and Oman offered to help rebuild it. (Source: The National 'What is the House of Wonders?'; Wikipedia 'Stone Town'; Anadolu Agency)

question: On top of Stonehenge, flat stone slabs sit in a ring above the standing stones, and they do not just balance. To lock each slab in place, the builders carved a joint from woodworking into solid 25-ton stone about 4,500 years ago. What is this classic wood joint called?
context: A tenon -- a carved knob on top of each upright -- was dropped into a mortise, a hollow cut into the underside of the lintel, reproducing a woodworking joint in solid stone around 2500 BC. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge

question: Stand at the center of Stonehenge at dawn on one special morning each year. The rising sun climbs up above a single outer stone, the Heel Stone, and then pours straight down the monument's main line into the ring. This 5,000-year-old alignment is keyed to which sunrise?
context: At midsummer the sun rises over the Heel Stone and runs along Stonehenge's axis, so the monument works as a roughly 5,000-year-old solar calendar marking the year's turning points. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Solstice_at_Stonehenge

question: The stone slabs crowning Stonehenge do more than sit end to end. Each curved slab is locked to its neighbors with a second woodworking joint, so the whole capping circle ties into one continuous interlocking hoop. No other prehistoric stone monument does this. What joint links the slabs end to end?
context: A tongue carved on one lintel's end slotted into a groove in the next, so Stonehenge's sarsen lintels interlocked all the way around the ring like fitted timber -- unique among the world's ancient stone circles. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge

question: One of Stonehenge's stones carries a spooky old English legend. The story goes that the Devil, certain no one could ever count all the stones, caught a friar quietly tallying them and hurled a huge block to strike him down. According to the tale, what happened when the flung stone reached the friar?
answer: it bounced off the friar's heel
choices: it bounced off the friar's heel
it crushed him where he stood
it split in two as it fell
it sank deep into the soft ground
context: In the folk tale the stone struck the friar's heel so hard it dented the stone -- which is why the outlying block is nicknamed the 'Friar's Heel' or Heel Stone. This is legend, not history. Source: https://blog.stonehenge-stone-circle.co.uk/2011/03/16/stonehenge-folklore/

question: Stonehenge is built from two very different kinds of rock. The giant outer sarsens are local, but the smaller inner 'bluestones' -- just 2 to 4 tons each -- were dragged an astonishing 230 km (about 140 miles) to Salisbury Plain, one of the longest stone-hauls of the entire ancient world. Where did the bluestones come from?
context: The bluestones were quarried in the Preseli Hills of west Wales and moved roughly 230 km to Stonehenge -- among the longest-distance transports of monument stone known anywhere in the ancient world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge

question: Lying at the very centre of Stonehenge is a single long slab, five metres of pale stone, so easy to overlook that visitors once strolled right over it -- the 'Altar Stone.' It lies flat rather than standing upright, and much of it is hidden from view today. What keeps so much of the Altar Stone out of sight?
answer: a huge toppled sarsen lying across it
choices: a huge toppled sarsen lying across it
deep soil that drifted over and buried it
a thick mat of turf grown across it
a heap of chalk rubble piled over it
context: The Altar Stone (Stone 80) lies flat near Stonehenge's centre, partly pinned beneath a toppled sarsen, Stone 55, that fell across it -- which is why much of the slab stays hidden and it is so easily missed today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altar_Stone_(Stonehenge)

question: For centuries the source of Stonehenge's biggest stones -- the 25-ton sarsens of the outer ring -- was a complete mystery. Then in 2020, scientists read the chemical fingerprint locked in the stone and matched it to one particular place. Where did the great sarsens come from?
context: A 2020 study led by geographer David Nash traced 50 of the 52 surviving sarsens to West Woods near Marlborough, only about 25 km north of Stonehenge, using portable X-ray fluorescence. Source: https://theconversation.com/stonehenge-how-we-revealed-the-original-source-of-the-biggest-stones-143564

question: Archaeologists digging at the Welsh quarry that gave Stonehenge its bluestones turned up a puzzle. The stones were cut there around 3400 BC, but they were not standing at Stonehenge until roughly 2900 BC, which is centuries later. What do many archaeologists now suspect happened in between?
answer: the bluestones first stood in an older Welsh monument
choices: the bluestones first stood in an older Welsh monument
the Welsh quarry kept cutting stone for other circles
the quarry dates were measured wrongly
the stones lay abandoned at the quarry for ages
context: The centuries-long gap hints the Preseli bluestones may have been raised in a stone circle in Wales first, then dismantled and carried to Salisbury Plain -- though this remains a hypothesis. Source: https://phys.org/news/2019-02-quarrying-stonehenge-bluestones-dated-bc.html

question: The flat Altar Stone at Stonehenge's centre was long assumed to be just another of the Welsh bluestones. Then in 2024, fresh laboratory tests delivered a shock: this six-tonne slab had not come from Wales at all, but from a source hundreds of kilometres away that no one had suspected. Where did the Altar Stone actually come from?
context: In 2024 researchers traced the Altar Stone to the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland -- over 700 km away and the longest journey known for any stone in any Neolithic monument. Source: https://theconversation.com/stonehenges-giant-altar-stone-came-all-the-way-from-north-east-scotland-heres-how-we-worked-out-this-astonishing-new-finding-236630

question: Tracing Stonehenge's Altar Stone to a source hundreds of miles from Salisbury Plain was only half the shock. The other shock was how a six-ton slab likely made that journey, long before the wheel is thought to have reached Britain. How do researchers think the Altar Stone got to Stonehenge?
answer: shipped by sea along the coast
choices: shipped by sea along the coast
floated down a chain of rivers
context: Because a 700 km overland haul of a six-tonne slab would have been extraordinary long before the wheel reached Britain, researchers think the Altar Stone most likely reached Salisbury Plain by sea, carried along Britain's coasts from northeast Scotland. Source: https://theconversation.com/stonehenges-giant-altar-stone-came-all-the-way-from-north-east-scotland-heres-how-we-worked-out-this-astonishing-new-finding-236630

question: The 2020 fingerprinting study matched 50 of Stonehenge's 52 surviving sarsens to the very same source at West Woods. But two of the giant stones -- numbered 26 and 160 -- stubbornly refused to match the rest. What does this tell archaeologists about those two sarsens?
answer: they came from a different, still-unknown source
choices: they came from a different, still-unknown source
they are natural boulders, never quarried at all
they were added by Victorian restorers
they are the oldest stones on the whole site
context: Stones 26 and 160 did not share West Woods' chemical signature, meaning at least two of Stonehenge's giant sarsens were hauled from a second source that has still not been identified. Source: https://blogs.bournemouth.ac.uk/research/2020/07/30/conversation-article-stonehenge-how-we-revealed-the-original-source-of-the-biggest-stones/

question: Gangkhar Puensum is a 7,570-metre peak that rises on the border of the small Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan and Chinese Tibet. In Bhutan, the government honours its high peaks as the sacred homes of the gods. Among all the world's great mountains, Gangkhar Puensum holds one very unusual record all its own. Which record is it?
choices: The most remote of all great peaks
The last great peak to be mapped
context: Gangkhar Puensum (7,570 m / 24,836 ft) on the Bhutan-Tibet border is the highest mountain on Earth that has never been climbed; its Dzongkha name means 'White Peak of the Three Spiritual Brothers.' Four expeditions failed in 1985-86, Bhutan banned peaks over 6,000 m in 1994 and all mountaineering in 2003 out of respect for the peaks as homes of gods, and a 1998 Japanese permit was later revoked. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangkhar_Puensum

question: Machapuchare, whose name means 'Fish Tail' for its twin-forked summit, is a sacred peak in the Nepalese Himalayas. It has been climbed by exactly one expedition in all of history. In 1957 a British team led by the mountaineer Jimmy Roberts reached a point only about 50 metres below the very top -- and there they turned around and came down. Why did they stop so close to the summit?
answer: They had promised the king to leave the top untouched
choices: They had promised the king to leave the top untouched
A sudden storm drove them back down the ridge
Their food and oxygen supplies had run out
A wall of unstable ice blocked the final climb
context: Machapuchare ('Fish Tail,' 6,993 m / 22,943 ft) in Nepal's Annapurna region was attempted only once, in 1957, by a British team under Jimmy Roberts; Wilfrid Noyce and A.D.M. Cox reached about 50 m below the top and stopped because King Mahendra had granted permission on one condition: no one set foot on the summit. The team kept the promise, no permit has been issued since, and the peak is sacred to the Gurung people as a home of Shiva. A rumored 1980s ascent by Bill Denz is unconfirmed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machapuchare

question: Kangchenjunga, at 8,586 m the third-highest mountain on Earth, straddles the border of Nepal and Sikkim. When Joe Brown and George Band made its first ascent in 1955, they had promised Tashi Namgyal, the Chogyal (ruler) of Sikkim, to honor the mountain's sacredness. What did that promise lead them to do at the very end of the climb?
answer: Stop a few steps below the true summit
choices: Stop a few steps below the true summit
Bury an offering at the true summit
Climb the last stretch only by night
context: Kangchenjunga (8,586 m / 28,169 ft), the world's third-highest mountain on the Nepal-Sikkim border, saw its first ascent in 1955 by Joe Brown and George Band, who stopped a few steps below the true summit to keep a promise to Tashi Namgyal, the Chogyal of Sikkim, that the very top stay inviolate; Norman Hardie and Tony Streather did the same two days later, and many climbers still honor the custom. The name means 'the Five Treasures of the High Snow' - salt, gold, turquoise, sacred scriptures, and invincible armour - said to reveal themselves to the devout in times of peril. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangchenjunga

question: Kawagarbo is the tallest peak in China's Yunnan province, and it has never been climbed. The Tibetans below it believe standing on the summit would be a disaster for them all. In 2001 the local government made that reverence law and banned every climb. What do they believe would happen if someone reached the top?
answer: Their guardian warrior god would abandon them
choices: Their guardian warrior god would abandon them
The mountain's glaciers would flood the valleys
The winter snows would never melt again
The spirits of the dead would lose their way
context: Kawagarbo / Kawa Karpo (Meili Snow Mountain, 6,740 m / 22,113 ft), the highest peak in China's Yunnan province, has never been summited; Tibetans believe their guardian warrior god would abandon them if any human stood on top. On 3 January 1991 a nighttime avalanche killed all 17 members of a Sino-Japanese expedition, one of the deadliest mountaineering disasters in history, and in 2001 the local government permanently banned all climbing on religious grounds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawagarbo

question: Mount Kailash, a 6,638 m black pyramid rising alone above the western Tibetan plateau, is sacred at once to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and followers of Bon. Thousands of pilgrims walk the ancient path that circles its base. What is the mountaineering story of its summit?
answer: Its summit has never drawn a single expedition
choices: Its summit has never drawn a single expedition
Its summit turned back one team just short
Its summit ended one expedition in a deadly avalanche
Its summit draws pilgrims to a shrine each summer
context: Mount Kailash (6,638 m / 21,778 ft) in western Tibet has no recorded ascent at all - not stopped short like Kangchenjunga, but never attempted. It is sacred to four religions at once (Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Bon), pilgrims circle its base, and China prohibits all climbing; a 2001 Spanish permit request was refused. Reinhold Messner was reportedly offered a permit in the mid-1980s and declined, in a much-quoted but loosely worded remark suggesting climbers 'go and climb something a little harder' (treat as attributed legend). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash

question: Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain at 3,776 m, is an active volcano revered in Shinto belief as the home of the goddess Konohanasakuya-hime, with shrines built at its very summit. Every summer, from July to early September, Fuji observes a tradition tied to its sacred peak. What is that tradition?
answer: Pilgrims climb by the thousands to worship at the top
choices: Pilgrims climb by the thousands to worship at the top
Its summit shrines are sealed against all visitors
Only the mountain's priests may ascend above the clouds
Fires are lit around its base but never its peak
context: Mount Fuji (3,776 m / 12,389 ft), Japan's highest peak and an active volcano, is sacred in Shinto to the goddess Konohanasakuya-hime, with shrines at its summit. Rather than forbidding the top, it invites pilgrims up: an official season runs July to early September, and about 300,000 people climb each year as an act of devotion. Some sacred mountains you must not touch; others you climb to worship. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fuji

question: High on a frozen mountain in Arctic Norway, a lone door in the snow opens into a vault. Inside are backup copies of the world's food crops. They came from over 80 countries so farming could restart after a global disaster. What is this famous 'doomsday' backup called?
context: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, near Longyearbyen in Norway's high-Arctic Svalbard islands, opened in 2008 as a free backup for the world's roughly 1,700 other seed banks, holding duplicate samples from gene banks in over 80 countries — the Arctic World Archive, also on Svalbard, stores data rather than seeds. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Svalbard_Global_Seed_Vault

question: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault was drilled 130 meters into a mountainside whose rock has stayed frozen solid, year-round, for thousands of years. That is why engineers chose this remote Arctic spot. Even if the power failed, the mountain itself would keep the seeds cold for free. What is this kind of frozen Arctic ground called?
context: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen year-round for years on end. Deep in the mountain the permafrost would keep the seeds frozen even without power, while machines chill them further to −18°C; engineers estimate a total freezer failure would still take roughly 200 years to warm the chambers to 0°C. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svalbard_Global_Seed_Vault

question: Longyearbyen, the tiny town beside the Svalbard vault, sits at about 78° North — no settled town on Earth lies closer to the North Pole. Step past the last houses and you are in true Arctic wilderness, so by old local rule every resident is urged to carry one particular thing whenever they leave town. What is it?
context: By long-standing Svalbard practice, people carry a rifle outside the settlements because of polar bears. Longyearbyen, at about 78° N, is the world's northernmost town with a permanent population over 1,000; nearby Ny-Ålesund lies even further north but is a research station, not a town. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longyearbyen

question: Most people thought the Svalbard Seed Vault would stay sealed until some far-off global disaster. But in 2015 its doors were opened for the first withdrawal ever, and 128 crates of wheat, barley, lentil and chickpea seeds were shipped out to be regrown elsewhere. What disaster had wiped out the original collection and forced the vault to prove itself?
context: The seeds belonged to the ICARDA gene bank in Aleppo, Syria, whose researchers had to abandon the city during the civil war. The vault's first-ever withdrawal — about 38,000 samples in 128 crates — was regrown at safe stations in Lebanon and Morocco, then re-deposited. The 'doomsday' vault had done its job for real. Source: https://www.seedvault.no/2019/09/11/withdrawal-of-icarda-aleppo-seeds-accomplished/

question: In 2017, alarming news reports announced that Svalbard's 'doomsday' Seed Vault had flooded: a warm winter had thawed the frozen mountainside, and meltwater came seeping into the vault's entrance tunnel. Deep inside sat millions of irreplaceable seeds. What actually became of them?
answer: the water froze in the tunnel before reaching them
choices: the water froze in the tunnel before reaching them
about a third of the samples thawed and spoiled
a batch of the oldest wheat seeds was ruined
they were flown to the mainland as a precaution
context: The meltwater reached only about 15 m into the entrance tunnel and froze, touching some electrical gear but never getting near the seeds, which sit behind a second sealed door deeper in the mountain. No seeds were harmed. Norway later rebuilt the tunnel to be waterproof, at a cost of about $13 million. Source: https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/doomsday-seed-vault-flooded/

question: The Arctic town of Longyearbyen still has a small cemetery, but it stopped accepting new burials around 1950 — ever since, the dead have been flown south to mainland Norway instead. The reason lay underground: townsfolk had made an unsettling discovery about anyone laid to rest in the frozen soil there. What was it?
answer: the frozen ground had preserved the bodies, which never decayed
choices: the frozen ground had preserved the bodies, which never decayed
the shifting soil kept pushing the coffins back up to the surface
meltwater had flooded and collapsed the older graves
there was never soil soft enough to dig a proper grave
context: Burials stopped around 1950 after bodies of townsfolk who died in the 1918 flu pandemic were found still preserved in the permafrost, undecayed decades later — researchers later exhumed some hoping to study the 1918 virus. It isn't literally 'illegal to die' there; there are simply no burial options, so the dead are flown to mainland Norway. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longyearbyen

question: On Bennelong Point, a narrow spit of land jutting into the harbor of Sydney, Australia, stands a building whose roof rises in a cluster of great white curved shells. They lean together like sails swelling in the wind above the water. It opened in 1973 as one of the most famous concert halls in the world. Which building is this?
context: The Sydney Opera House opened in 1973 on Bennelong Point, its white 'shells' reading as sails over the water. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most recognized buildings on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House

question: Just across the harbor from the Sydney Opera House, a huge steel arch leaps clear over the water of Sydney Harbour in Australia. It opened in 1932 as one of the widest steel-arch bridges in the world. To Australians, its shape looked exactly like a common household object, and they gave the Sydney Harbour Bridge a nickname after it. Which object?
context: The Sydney Harbour Bridge, opened in 1932, is one of the world's widest long-span steel-arch bridges. Sydneysiders looked at its great curved silhouette and dubbed it 'the Coathanger,' and the name stuck. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge

question: For years engineers were stumped by the swooping white roof shells of the Sydney Opera House in Australia. Each shell seemed impossible to cast in concrete. Then in 1961 the Danish architect Jorn Utzon cracked the puzzle: every one of those shells could be cut from the surface of the same simple imaginary geometric form. Which form was it?
context: Utzon's 1961 'spherical solution' let every shell be cut from the surface of one imaginary sphere (about 75 m radius), so all shared a single curve and could be mass-cast from common moulds -- the breakthrough that finally made the roof buildable. Source: sydneyoperahouse.com/our-story/the-spherical-solution

question: The Sydney Opera House in Australia, designed by the Danish architect Jorn Utzon and finished in 1973, has a roof made of great curved shells. From across the harbor those shells gleam a smooth, even white. But up close they never look flat or plain -- in changing light they seem to shimmer and shift. What actually covers the giant shells?
answer: a million glazed tiles in two shades of white
choices: a million glazed tiles in two shades of white
thousands of polished white marble slabs
hundreds of enameled white steel panels
many coats of specially mixed white paint
context: The shells wear about 1,056,006 tiles made in Sweden by Hoganas, in two finishes -- glossy white and matte cream -- laid in a chevron pattern so the roof shimmers and never looks flat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House

question: The Sydney Opera House in Australia stands on a narrow tongue of land jutting out into Sydney Harbour. Before construction began in the 1960s, this same point had been home first to an old stone battery called Fort Macquarie, and later to a busy tram depot -- both were cleared away to make room for the new building. What is this famous point of land called?
context: Bennelong Point honors Bennelong, an Aboriginal man who lived alongside the first British governor, Arthur Phillip. A fort and then a tram depot (Fort Macquarie) stood there before both were demolished for the Opera House. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House

question: The Sydney Harbour Bridge in Australia is a single vast steel arch that springs high above the water of Sydney's harbor. Today, harnessed to a safety cable and dressed in grey jumpsuits, adventurous visitors can do something on this bridge that almost no other great bridge in the world allows tourists to do. What is it?
answer: climb the arch on foot to its very summit
choices: climb the arch on foot to its very summit
walk a glass floor hung beneath the road deck
ride a lift up a stone pylon to a lookout
abseil down a steel cable to the water below
context: On 'BridgeClimb,' visitors roped to a safety line ascend the steel arch to its summit -- 134 metres, more than 400 feet, above the harbor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge

question: Sailing into Sydney's great harbour, Port Jackson, you pass the rocky Heads at its mouth and the water fans out into a maze of deep coves branching inland for miles. It is sheltered and deep enough for the greatest ships to ride in safety. What do geographers call this kind of coastal feature?
context: A ria is a river valley drowned by rising seas -- here, Port Jackson's ancient valleys flooded as Ice Age ice melted, giving Sydney a shoreline that branches for miles and runs deep enough for the greatest ships. (A fjord, by contrast, is a drowned GLACIER-carved valley.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Jackson
