question: Governor Arthur Phillip steered the First Fleet into Sydney's harbor in 1788 and was stunned by its size and shelter. He wrote that here was 'the finest harbour in the world,' with room for a fleet so vast he fixed it in a single ringing phrase. What did he say could ride there in perfect safety?
answer: a thousand ships of the line
choices: a thousand ships of the line
a hundred ships of the line
every ship in the Southern seas
context: Arriving in Port Jackson in 1788, Phillip called it 'the finest Harbour in the World, in which a thousand Sail of the line may ride in the most perfect security.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Jackson

question: At the grand opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge in 1932, huge crowds waited for Premier Jack Lang to cut the ceremonial ribbon. Suddenly a man in military uniform, Francis de Groot, spurred his horse forward and -- before Lang could act -- did something that stole the moment and got him arrested. What did de Groot do?
answer: slashed the ribbon with his cavalry sword
choices: slashed the ribbon with his cavalry sword
seized the scissors and hurled them into the harbor
chained his horse across the empty roadway
tore down the official banner overhead
context: Before Premier Lang could cut the ribbon, de Groot galloped up and slashed it with his cavalry sword, declaring the bridge open 'in the name of the people.' He was arrested and the ribbon retied for the official ceremony. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge

question: Sydney's sea-cliffs, the rocky 'Heads' at its harbor mouth, and its grand old buildings all glow the same warm honey-gold, cut from the local stone the whole city rests on. Braided rivers laid down this sandstone grain by grain around 230 million years ago, back when the very first dinosaurs were appearing. In which geological period did that happen?
context: Sydney rests on Hawkesbury sandstone, laid down by braided rivers ~230-240 million years ago in the Triassic. Quarried for the city's cliffs, harbor 'Heads,' and grand old buildings, its warm color earned nicknames like 'yellowblock' and 'yellow gold.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkesbury_sandstone

question: Jorn Utzon, the Danish architect who dreamed up the Opera House's soaring shells, did not stay to complete them. In 1966, worn down by bitter fights over money and control, he resigned and left Australia, and a local team finished the building. Honored at last with architecture's Pritzker Prize in 2003, Utzon died in 2008 -- one quiet sorrow shadowing his triumph. What was it?
answer: he had never once returned to Australia to see it
choices: he had never once returned to Australia to see it
he had asked to have his name struck from it
he had spent his last years suing the government
he had never designed another major building
context: Utzon resigned in 1966 amid disputes over money and control; an Australian team finished the building. He won the Pritzker Prize in 2003 but died in 2008 having never returned to Australia to see his masterpiece complete. Source: classical-music.com (Sydney Opera House history)

question: In the early 1900s the French conservators of the Ecole francaise d'Extreme-Orient restored temple after temple across Angkor. At Ta Prohm -- where huge roots had poured over the walls and cracked the roofs apart -- they made a famous decision. What did they do with the temple?
answer: They braced it against collapse and left it wrapped in the jungle.
choices: They braced it against collapse and left it wrapped in the jungle.
They felled the trees and rebuilt the galleries stone by stone.
They dismantled the temple and moved it to safer ground.
They cleared the roots and laid a formal garden around it.
context: When the Ecole francaise d'Extreme-Orient restored Angkor in the early 1900s, they deliberately left Ta Prohm tangled in forest 'as a concession to the general taste for the picturesque.' The conservator Maurice Glaize said it was chosen because it had 'best merged with the jungle, but not yet to the point of becoming a part of it' -- wild enough to be spectacular, sound enough not to collapse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: Ta Prohm is now the most famous 'lost temple' in the world, and locals point tourists to it by a nickname borrowed from Hollywood. In 2001 an adventure blockbuster filmed its star sprinting through these root-choked galleries, and the temple has carried the movie's name ever since. Which film was it?
context: The 2001 film Lara Croft: Tomb Raider, starring Angelina Jolie, was shot among Ta Prohm's roots -- Lara picks a jasmine flower and falls through the earth into the ruins -- and the site has been the 'Tomb Raider temple' ever since, the world's most famous 'lost temple.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: Deep in the jungles of Cambodia stand the ruins of Ta Prohm, a Buddhist temple abandoned centuries ago in the great Angkor complex. Enormous pale roots pour over the temple's stone walls and pry the ancient carved blocks apart. Most of these roots belong to a single giant species of tree that towers high above the ruins. What tree is it that holds Ta Prohm in its grip?
context: The dominant giant is the silk-cotton tree (Tetrameles nudiflora, locally called 'spung'), joined by smaller strangler figs (Ficus gibbosa). The trees never grew up from the ground: birds dropped their seeds onto the temple's gallery roofs, the seedlings took hold high up, and their roots crept DOWN through the walls, splitting the stonework as they descended. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: Ta Prohm was not only a temple but also a working monastery. Its founding stone still stands at the site, and it brags about the workforce needed to run this complex: hundreds of dancers, dozens of high priests, thousands living inside the walls, and many more in villages that fed them. How many people did the inscription say served Ta Prohm?
context: The figure comes from Ta Prohm's foundation stele (inscription K.273), which records that nearly 80,000 people were needed to maintain and serve the monastery -- including 615 dancers, 18 high priests, and 12,640 people living inside the temple walls. Its real name was Rajavihara, the 'Royal Monastery,' built by the Khmer king Jayavarman VII and consecrated in 1186; scholars suspect the stele's numbers were inflated to glorify the king. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm  (Legend.)

question: Agra's Taj Mahal is famous as a monument to love, but it is truly a tomb. Emperor Shah Jahan raised this vast white marble hall over the grave of one person he lost in 1631, mourning so deeply that he gave up music and fine clothes for two years. For whom was it built?
context: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child. Shah Jahan's grief became a building project that ran for roughly two decades, turning a personal loss into the most beautiful tomb on earth. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: The Taj Mahal's tomb gleams white because its brick core is entirely sheathed in one prized stone, quarried more than 300 km from Agra and dragged there by oxen and elephants. Masons chose it for a whiteness no nearer rock could match. Which stone sheaths the Taj Mahal?
context: The white marble came from the Makrana quarries in Rajasthan, still worked today, while the red sandstone of the surrounding complex came from Fatehpur Sikri. The other choices are famous white marbles too -- Carrara from Italy, Pentelic from Greece, Proconnesian from Turkey. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: Visitors to the Taj Mahal swear the tomb wears a different color at every hour -- blush pink at dawn, dazzling white at midday, and soft gold beneath a full moon. Photographers return year after year to catch each fresh shade. Why does the tomb seem to change color through the day?
choices: the dome is sheathed in gold leaf
colored glass fills the arched windows
river mist tints the stone at dawn
context: Nothing is ever painted or coated. The fine Makrana marble is faintly translucent and simply reflects whatever light falls on it, so the tomb glows pink at sunrise, white at noon, and gold under the moon. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: Inside the Taj Mahal, two beautifully carved marble tombs sit at the center of the great domed hall, ringed by an inlaid screen, and thousands of visitors file past them each day believing they stand over the dead. But Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal are not there. Where do their bodies actually lie?
answer: in a plain vault one floor below
choices: in a plain vault one floor below
inside the hollow of the great dome
under the mosque beside the tomb
context: The ornate tombs on display are false cenotaphs. The real graves sit in a plain, undecorated lower chamber, laid north-south with the faces turned toward Mecca -- a Mughal convention that kept the actual resting place simple and hidden. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: The four slender minarets at the corners of the Taj Mahal's platform were not built standing straight up: each leans about two degrees outward, away from the great dome. Study of the tomb has shown this tilt was deliberate, worked in by its Mughal builders. What were they planning for?
context: The outward lean is an earthquake-safety trick centuries ahead of its time: if a quake ever toppled the towers, their built-in tilt would carry them falling away from the tomb rather than crashing down onto the dome. Source: tajwithguide.com (25 fascinating facts about the Taj Mahal).

question: The Taj Mahal's white marble is scattered with flowers, vines, and leaves so finely shaded that visitors take them for paintings. They are not paint at all: look closely at a single blossom and you find it built from as many as 64 separate pieces. What are the Taj's flowers actually made of?
answer: cut gemstones set into the marble
choices: cut gemstones set into the marble
colored enamel fired onto the surface
context: The craft is pietra dura, called parchin kari here: chips of agate, jasper, carnelian, and lapis cut and polished flush into the marble so a whole garden of flowers glows in stone. A single cenotaph blossom can hold 64 inlaid pieces. Source: tajwithguide.com (25 fascinating facts about the Taj Mahal).

question: A famous story says the grieving Shah Jahan meant to raise a second Taj Mahal in black marble on the far bank of the Yamuna -- a dark twin to hold his own tomb, joined to the white one by a bridge. Ruins of dark stone across the river seemed to prove it. When archaeologists excavated those ruins in the 1990s, what did they find?
answer: white marble blocks blackened by age
choices: white marble blocks blackened by age
the foundations of an unfinished black tomb
a buried cache of black marble slabs
a bridge footing pointing across the river
context: The 'Black Taj' is a legend. The 1990s excavation showed the dark ruins across the river were ordinary white marble stones darkened by centuries of weathering -- there was never a black twin. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: Tallinn's Old Town is the medieval heart of Estonia's capital. It is all narrow cobbled lanes, red-tiled roofs and church spires, ringed by a stone wall with towers. Most such old town centers are long gone, bombed flat or turned into museums. What is remarkable about Tallinn's?
answer: it is still a lived-in, working town
choices: it is still a lived-in, working town
it was rebuilt from rubble after the war
it is an open-air museum of moved houses
it is a modern replica built for tourists
context: Tallinn's Old Town is a rarity: a still-lived-in medieval city of cobbled lanes and red-tiled roofs, not a ruin or a museum but a working town. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 1997 for its 'exceptionally intact 13th-century city plan' -- one of Europe's best-preserved medieval towns. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tallinn Old Town' (UNESCO 1997).

question: Tallinn, the capital of Estonia on the Baltic coast, was ringed in the Middle Ages by a great stone town wall. When it was finished, the wall bristled with 46 defensive towers along a rampart up to 16 metres high. Most medieval town walls in Europe have long since crumbled away to nothing. How many of Tallinn's original towers still stand guard around the old town today?
answer: about half of them -- some two dozen towers
choices: about half of them -- some two dozen towers
all forty-six, every one still intact
just one lone surviving gate tower
none at all, only their foundations
context: In its 16th-century prime Tallinn's wall ran about 2.4 km, stood 14-16 m high and up to 3 m thick, and carried 46 towers -- one of the most fortified towns in northern Europe. About half survives today: nearly 2 km of wall and around two dozen towers still stand, one of the best-preserved medieval city walls in northern Europe. Source: inyourpocket.com 'Town Fortifications'; historyhit.com 'Tallinn City Walls'.

question: Tallinn is really two old towns stacked together: the merchants' lower town down below, and the ruler's upper town called Toompea sitting on a hilltop. Danes, German knights, Swedes, and Russians each held the upper town in turn. What building sits on top of Toompea today?
context: Toompea, the upper town on the hill, was held in turn by Danes, the Livonian Order, Swedes and Russians; Estonia's parliament, the Riigikogu, meets in Toompea Castle today. The merchants' lower town spread below, and the two stayed separate towns until they were administratively united in 1878. Source: Wikipedia, 'Toompea'.

question: Tallinn spent the Middle Ages as a rich merchant town on the Baltic, its harbour crowded with cargo ships and its guildhalls and spired churches raised on trading profits. Tallinn owed that wealth to membership in one great medieval alliance of northern European trading towns. Which league was it?
context: The Hanseatic League was the great medieval merchant network of the Baltic and North Seas. Tallinn's guildhalls and spired churches survive so nearly intact that UNESCO listed the whole Old Town in 1997 as a preserved town of 'medieval and Hanseatic origin'. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tallinn Old Town'.

question: Tallinn's St Olaf's Church has been rebuilt again and again: its towering spire has drawn lightning at least eight times and burned the whole church to the ground three times. Sailors far out in the Gulf of Finland still use it as a landmark. By old tradition, before the great fire of 1625 that spire had earned Tallinn one astonishing world record. What was it?
choices: the tallest lighthouse in the Baltic
the largest church in northern Europe
the northernmost cathedral in the world
context: By tradition St Olaf's spire soared to about 159 m and was the tallest building in the world from 1549 until lightning burned it in 1625 -- though historians reckon the true medieval height was more like 115-125 m, so the record is a claim, not a certainty. The steeple has been struck by lightning at least eight times and the church has burned down three times; it still stands about 124 m tall, a landmark visible far out at sea. Legend/claim flagged. Source: Wikipedia, 'St. Olaf's Church, Tallinn'; visitestonia.com.

question: Toompea's hill fooled attackers who took it for a man-made rampart -- but it is wholly natural. It is the tip of the Baltic Klint, a pale limestone cliff-line running for hundreds of kilometres along Estonia's coast, its 20-30-metre drop handing the upper town a ready-made wall of rock. What is the general geographic name for this kind of long, steep coastal cliff-line?
context: Toompea's hill is part of the North Estonian Klint, a subsection of the Baltic Klint -- a pale limestone escarpment that runs for hundreds of km along the coast. 'Klint' is the local name for this kind of long cliff-line; geographers call it an escarpment (a long steep face where higher ground drops to lower). Rising 20-30 m above the lower town, it gave the upper town a natural rampart before a single wall was built. Source: Wikipedia, 'Toompea'.

question: Mount Tambora erupted on an Indonesian island in April 1815. The blast was heard about 2,600 km away on the island of Sumatra. It sounded so much like heavy gunfire that troops there were sure a battle had begun nearby. What did the soldiers on Sumatra do?
answer: Marched out to defend a nearby post they believed was under attack
choices: Marched out to defend a nearby post they believed was under attack
Fired their own cannons in reply to the distant booming
Rushed to load ships and evacuate the governor to safety
Fled far inland, certain that warships were shelling the coast
context: The eyewitness detail comes from Sir Stamford Raffles's memoir, which records that the noise was 'almost universally attributed to distant cannon.' Tambora's 1815 blast was the largest eruption in recorded human history, and its roar carried roughly 2,600 km (1,600 mi) to Sumatra. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora  (Legend.)

question: Mount Tambora, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, erupted with terrific fury in April 1815 and killed about 71,000 people in all. Only around 11,000 of those died from the eruption itself -- the choking ash cloud, the fiery pyroclastic flows, and the tsunamis that swept the nearby coasts. What killed the far larger number in the weeks and months afterwards?
answer: Starvation, after the ashfall smothered the islands' crops
choices: Starvation, after the ashfall smothered the islands' crops
Floods, as rivers dammed by falling debris burst downstream
Wildfires that spread from the still-glowing ash
Fresh eruptions from the crater the following spring
context: About 71,000 people died in all -- some 10,000-12,000 in the eruption itself (ash, pyroclastic flows, and 4-metre tsunamis), and tens of thousands more from the starvation and disease that followed once the ash smothered the fields of Sumbawa and nearby islands. It remains the deadliest eruption in recorded history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora

question: Tambora's 1815 eruption threw so much dust and haze around the globe that the following year, 1816, brought freakish cold to lands half a world away. In New England, snow fell in June and killing frosts returned in July and August; across Europe and North America the grain harvests failed. By what haunting name did people come to remember 1816?
context: Snow lay about 46 cm (18 in) deep at Cabot, Vermont on June 8, 1816, and Americans nicknamed the disaster 'Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death.' The freakish cold was traced back to the dust and haze from Tambora's eruption the year before. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer  (Legend.)

question: Beside Lake Geneva in the cold, storm-dark summer of 1816 -- its skies dimmed by Tambora's distant haze -- a group of English writers were trapped indoors for days. To pass the time, Lord Byron challenged each of them to write a ghost story. Eighteen-year-old Mary Shelley took up the dare and began a novel that would become one of the most famous horror stories ever written. What did she start writing that gloomy summer?
context: The gathering was at Byron's rented Villa Diodati on Lake Geneva. The same ghost-story contest produced John Polidori's 'The Vampyre' (an ancestor of Dracula), and Byron wrote his apocalyptic poem 'Darkness,' imagining a world where the sun goes out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer  (Legend.)

question: The failed harvests of 1816 sent oat prices soaring, and across Europe horses grew too costly to feed. Looking for a way to travel without a horse, the German inventor Karl Drais built and rode a wooden 'running machine' that he showed off in 1817. That strange machine, born of a hungry year, is remembered as the direct ancestor of what everyday machine?
context: With oats scarce and expensive, Karl Drais's pedal-less 'running machine,' or draisine, of 1817 is widely remembered as the direct ancestor of the bicycle -- a chain running from a volcano in Indonesia to the machine kids ride today. The famine is the commonly cited spur for his invention. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer  (Legend.)

question: The deepest wonder of Tambora is how a mountain in Indonesia could cool the entire planet. The eruption flung millions of tonnes of sulfur gas high into the stratosphere. There it turned into a fine haze of sulfate droplets that circled the globe for over a year, dimming the sun and cooling the planet by more than half a degree. What did this haze physically do to the sunlight passing through it?
answer: Reflected much of it straight back out into space
choices: Reflected much of it straight back out into space
Absorbed it up high, warming the haze but not the ground
Bent it away from the equator and toward the poles
Scattered it into a red glow that carried no heat
context: Tambora lofted an estimated 60 megatons of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it formed sulfate aerosols that reflected sunlight and cooled the globe by roughly 0.4-0.7 C for over a year. The eruption column reached about 43 km (27 mi) up; the resulting 'dry fog' dimmed the sun enough that people could see sunspots with the naked eye, and it tinted the lurid skies in J.M.W. Turner's paintings. Sources: https://grokipedia.com/page/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora

question: Tambora did not only bury villages: it wiped out an entire small kingdom on Sumbawa, along with its people and their language, all gone in 1815. Nearly two centuries later, in 2004, archaeologists dug through 3 m of ash and found a house frozen in that moment. They uncovered bronze bowls, iron tools, and two of the kingdom's people right where the blast caught them. What nickname did Tambora's lost kingdom earn?
context: In a 2004 dig, volcanologist Haraldur Sigurdsson uncovered the buried house under about 3 m of ash. The Tambora people's language, thought to be related to the Mon-Khmer tongues of mainland Southeast Asia, was wiped out with them. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambora_culture ; https://today.uri.edu/news/uri-volcanologist-discovers-lost-kingdom-of-tambora/  (Legend.)

question: In the Scottish Highlands, a tartan's whole criss-cross design comes from one small block of colored stripes. The block repeats over and over across the cloth to make the pattern. Design that block, and you have designed the tartan. What do weavers call it?
context: The repeating block is the 'sett' — fix the sett and the whole tartan follows, since the same sequence of stripes just repeats across the cloth. Warp and weft are the lengthwise and crosswise threads; twill is the diagonal 2/2 weave tartan is woven in. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartan

question: On a cold night out on the open hills of the Scottish Highlands, a clansman needed no bedroll and no blanket at all. He simply unbelted the long tartan cloth he had worn wrapped around his body all day, rolled himself up in its heavy folds, and slept where he lay on the heather. Which iconic Highland garment was this?
context: The feileadh mor, or 'great kilt' (belted plaid), really was a single four-to-six-yard length of tartan belted at the waist with the top draped over the shoulder. The image of a Highlander unbelting it to sleep rolled up inside like a blanket is the traditional picture of how handy the one-piece garment was. The tailored knee-length 'small kilt' came later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_kilt  (Legend.)

question: The oldest piece of tartan-like cloth ever found in Scotland is called the Falkirk tartan. It was woven around the 3rd century AD. It survived because someone had jammed the scrap of checked wool into the mouth of a buried clay pot as a stopper. What was the little rag keeping sealed inside?
answer: a hoard of Roman silver coins
choices: a hoard of Roman silver coins
the ashes of a cremated chief
context: The 'Falkirk tartan,' from about the 3rd century AD, is the oldest tartan-like cloth found in Scotland. The checked scrap of undyed wool had been used to plug a pot holding almost 2,000 Roman coins — a humble rag stopping up a small fortune. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartan

question: After the 1745 Jacobite Rising was crushed at the battle of Culloden in April 1746, the British government in London turned its anger on the everyday clothing of the Scottish Highlands. Its Dress Act, passed that same year in 1746, took direct aim at the kilt and tartan cloth worn by Highland men. What did the law actually do to Highland dress?
choices: required a licence to wear it
context: The Dress Act of 1746, part of the Act of Proscription after the Jacobite defeat at Culloden, outlawed the plaid, the little kilt, and tartan for men and boys across the Highlands — one of the rare times a government has banned a pattern of cloth outright. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_Act_1746

question: Under Britain's Dress Act of 1746, which banned Highland dress after the Jacobite defeat at Culloden, a Scottish Highlander caught wearing the kilt or a tartan plaid for the first time was jailed for six months. A second offence brought a far harsher sentence -- the same one Scottish courts handed out to thieves, forgers and other serious criminals. What was done to a repeat offender?
choices: branded on the cheek with hot iron
context: A first offence under the Dress Act meant six months in prison; a second meant being 'transported to any of His Majesty's plantations beyond the seas' for seven years — exile for the crime of wearing your own clan's cloth. The ban ran 36 years before its repeal in 1782. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_Act_1746

question: Many Highland families treat their clan tartan as an ancient badge handed down for centuries. In fact, the neat rule that each clan owns one fixed pattern was cemented at a single big event. There the novelist Sir Walter Scott persuaded the chiefs to parade in matching setts. At which event did this 'invented tradition' take hold?
answer: King George IV's 1822 visit to Edinburgh
choices: King George IV's 1822 visit to Edinburgh
the Jacobite defeat at Culloden in 1746
the lifting of the tartan ban in 1782
Queen Victoria's move to Balmoral in the 1850s
context: When King George IV visited Edinburgh in 1822, Sir Walter Scott choreographed a tartan pageant so lavish it fixed the 'one clan, one tartan' image in the public mind — largely a romantic invention, not ancient law. The stout king even wore a Royal Stuart kilt cut so short he added pink tights to cover his knees. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visit_of_George_IV_to_Scotland

question: Many of Scotland's 'official' clan tartans trace back to the Vestiarium Scoticum, an 1842 book that claimed to copy a lost ancient manuscript listing each clan's true sett — but scholars proved it a fake. Its two authors, Welsh-born brothers named Allen, propped up the hoax with a bold lie about their own ancestry. What did they claim to be?
choices: heirs of the executed Lord Lovat
context: The Vestiarium Scoticum (1842) claimed to reproduce a lost ancient manuscript giving each clan's true sett, and many 'official' clan tartans still trace to it — but it was exposed as a forgery. Its authors, the Welsh-born Allen brothers, styled themselves the 'Sobieski Stuarts' and falsely claimed to be grandsons of Bonnie Prince Charlie, dressing fake ancient tartans in fake royal glamour. Rob Roy MacGregor, Simon Fraser (Lord Lovat, beheaded after Culloden), and Flora MacDonald were all real Jacobite-era Highlanders, but the brothers claimed no descent from them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestiarium_Scoticum

question: In Washington, the Hoh Rain Forest is soaked by about 140 inches of rain a year. Every trunk hangs heavy with moss and lichen. Yet it grows in a cool northern climate, not the steamy tropics. What do we call a rainforest like this, drenched and mossy but growing in the cool?
context: A cool, drenched, moss-hung forest like the Hoh is a TEMPERATE rainforest -- rainforest without the tropics. The North American rule of thumb: cool (mean temperature about 4-12 degC) and soaked with more than 140 cm (55 in) of rain a year, so a rainforest does not have to be hot. The Hoh's giants are Sitka spruce and western hemlock, draped in 'lettuce lichen.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoh_Rainforest and /wiki/Temperate_rainforest.

question: The tallest living thing on Earth is not an animal but a tree. It stands over 116 metres tall, higher than a 35-story building, in the cool, foggy forests of northern California near the coast. Two climbers found it in 2006 and named it Hyperion. What kind of tree is Hyperion?
context: Hyperion is a coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens), measured at 116.22 m (381.3 ft) -- the tallest known living tree on Earth. Chris Atkins and Michael Taylor found it in Redwood National Park on 25 August 2006. In 2022 the National Park Service closed the area (fines up to $5,000) after visitors trampled the ferns at its base, and its exact spot is kept secret. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperion_(tree).

question: In Washington's Hoh Rain Forest, walk beneath the mossy giants and you may notice a strange sight. A row of young hemlocks and spruces stands in a dead-straight line, evenly spaced, as if set out with a ruler along the ground. What lined the seedlings up in such a perfect row?
answer: they sprouted along a fallen tree trunk that has since rotted away
choices: they sprouted along a fallen tree trunk that has since rotted away
park rangers replanted that strip in rows after a wildfire
their seeds washed into a dead-straight crack in the bedrock
they followed the line of an old logging road through the grove
context: The rotting trunk was a 'nurse log' -- as it decays, moss, needles and soil fill it and seedlings take root along its length. When the log finally crumbles away, the young trees are left standing in a dead-straight 'colonnade' that traces exactly where the old giant fell. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nurse_log.

question: On the seaward side of Washington's Olympic Mountains, the forest drinks over 140 inches of rain a year. Yet a dry scrubland just 15 miles east of the peaks gets only about 8 inches. What makes one side of the same mountains a soaking rainforest and the other side almost a desert?
answer: moist ocean air is forced up the western slope, cools, and rains out before crossing the peaks
choices: moist ocean air is forced up the western slope, cools, and rains out before crossing the peaks
the cold ocean current offshore chills the eastern air until it can no longer hold rain
the eastern side sits under a belt of sinking dry air that rings the globe at that latitude
warm winds from the south drench the western slope and leave the eastern side dry
context: This is orographic rain: moist Pacific air is shoved up the windward slope, cools, and dumps its water before crossing the crest -- so the seaward side can get over 140 in a year while a rain-shadow desert 15 miles east gets about 8 in. The same recipe grows every temperate rainforest on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orographic_lift.

question: The Pacific Northwest has a mirror twin far to the south: on the coast of southern Chile, a cool, dripping forest is pinned on a narrow strip between the open Pacific and the wall of the Andes, drenched by up to 6,000 mm of rain a year. It is the second-largest temperate rainforest on Earth. What is this Chilean rainforest called?
context: It is the Valdivian rainforest, named for the Chilean city of Valdivia -- a cool, dripping forest getting 1,000 to over 6,000 mm of rain a year, the second-largest temperate rainforest on Earth after the Pacific Northwest. Its signature tree, the alerce (Fitzroya), is a cypress relative; one giant, the Gran Abuelo, was ring-counted at 3,622 years in 1993. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdivian_temperate_rainforest and /wiki/Fitzroya.

question: New Zealand's far southwest is one of the rainiest corners of the whole planet. Westerly gales tear in off the Tasman Sea, and Milford Sound is soaked by about 8,000 mm of rain on roughly 200 days a year, feeding a dense rainforest of southern beech. What is this drenched southwest region of New Zealand called?
context: It is Fiordland. Westerlies off the Tasman Sea are forced straight up over the mountains, so Milford Sound catches about 8,000 mm (310 in) of rain on some 200 days a year -- among the wettest inhabited places on Earth. The rainforest is southern beech, wrapped around the glacier-carved fiords that give the region its name. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiordland.

question: Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are the forests people name first as the planet's great carbon stores. Yet an Australian study weighed the carbon held in cool, wet temperate rainforests -- the mossy giants of places like Tasmania -- against tropical forest. Acre for acre, how does a temperate rainforest's carbon store compare?
answer: it locks away even more carbon than a tropical rainforest
choices: it locks away even more carbon than a tropical rainforest
it holds only a small fraction of a tropical rainforest's carbon
it holds almost exactly as much as a tropical rainforest
its stored carbon leaks back out faster than a tropical rainforest's
context: Acre for acre, temperate rainforest can out-store the tropics. An Australian National University study (Keith, Mackey & Lindenmayer, PNAS 2009) measured 377 tons of carbon per hectare above ground in temperate moist forest versus 171 tons in tropical rainforest; Australia's Mountain Ash forests reached up to 2,844 tons per hectare including roots. Being cool, they rot slowly, so the wood piles up -- among the densest carbon stores on land. Source: news.mongabay.com/2009/07/temperate-forests-store-more-carbon-than-tropical-forests-finds-study/.

question: In the 1300s, the Aztec people built their great capital city Tenochtitlan high in the mountains of central Mexico. They chose an island in the middle of a shallow lake, ringed by water on every side, with no farmland of its own. On which large lake did they raise their island city?
context: Tenochtitlan was founded on islands in shallow, salty Lake Texcoco, traditionally dated to about 1325. Lake Pátzcuaro and Lake Chapala are real lakes elsewhere in Mexico; Titicaca lies far to the south, high in the Andes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Aztec legend says their god Huitzilopochtli promised them a homeland. He told them to settle where they saw a certain sign, on a nopal cactus in the marsh. When they finally spotted it there, they founded Tenochtitlan. What did they see on the cactus?
context: The eagle-on-a-cactus omen is the Mexica founding legend — and that exact image sits at the centre of Mexico's flag and coat of arms today. (The modern flag adds a serpent in the eagle's beak; the oldest Aztec pictures show just the eagle on the cactus.) Source: Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan' and 'Coat of arms of Mexico'.

question: Tenochtitlan had no fields of its own, so the Aztecs staked out long beds in the shallow lakebed, piling up dredged mud and rotting plants and lashing them down with willow roots. These lake-garden plots were so rich they cropped up to seven times a year. What were they called?
context: Chinampas are often called 'floating gardens,' though they were rooted to the lakebed, not floating. Andenes are Inca terraces, waru waru are Andean raised fields, and a milpa is a maize-bean-squash plot. Source: Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Tenochtitlan was the great capital of the Aztec Empire, a city of some 200,000 people built on an island in a shallow Mexican lake. Its garden plots were split by a grid of canals, and people got around mostly by canoe, gliding between the houses on the water. When the Spanish conquistadors arrived in 1519 they were stunned, and nicknamed the canal city after which European water-city?
context: The Spanish called Tenochtitlan 'the Venice of the New World.' Amsterdam, Bruges, and Stockholm are all famously threaded with canals too. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinampa'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Three broad raised roads carried travelers across the water to island Tenochtitlan. One ran north to Tepeyac, one south to Iztapalapa, and one west to Tlacopan, each wide enough for ten horsemen abreast. The Aztecs gave these causeways a defense that could seal the city off from an attacking army. What was it?
context: The raised roads across the water are called causeways; gaps in them were spanned by wooden bridges the Mexica could pull up, cutting the island off. Cortés had to fight past exactly this defence in 1521. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Because Lake Texcoco was too salty to drink, the Aztecs piped fresh water into Tenochtitlan from the springs of Chapultepec, a wooded hill to the west. The stone aqueduct had two parallel channels running side by side. Why two channels instead of one?
answer: so one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
choices: so one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
so one carried water and the other carried off sewage
so the second doubled the flow in the dry season
so a cracked channel could be swapped for the spare
context: Aztec rulers began the twin aqueduct around 1418; one channel carried water while the other was scrubbed clean, so the city never ran dry. Moctezuma reportedly bathed every day thanks to the fresh Chapultepec water. Source: Grokipedia, 'Chapultepec aqueduct'; Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: The Aztec way of farming on lake-bed plots did not die with Tenochtitlan. In the canals of one district in southern Mexico City, people still pole flat boats between the surviving old garden plots today, drawing visitors from all over the world. What is this 'floating-garden' district called?
context: Xochimilco, in southern Mexico City, still keeps working chinampas and canals — a living remnant of Tenochtitlan's farming, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinampa'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: At the sacred heart of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, in what is today Mexico City, rose a great stepped pyramid crowned with two shrines standing side by side at its summit. One shrine was dedicated to Huitzilopochtli, the fierce Aztec god of war and the sun. The other honoured Tlaloc, the ancient god of rain and lightning. Priests climbed both stairways daily to offer sacrifice. By what name is this twin-shrined pyramid known today?
context: The Templo Mayor was the sacred centre of the Mexica world; its twin shrines honoured war and rain, the two forces the city lived by. The Pyramid of the Sun stands at Teotihuacan; El Castillo and the Caracol at Chichén Itzá. Source: Grokipedia, 'Templo Mayor'; Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Just north of Tenochtitlan lay a huge market. Cortes claimed sixty thousand people came to trade there every single day: gold, obsidian blades, turkeys, healing herbs, and cotton cloth, all under one roar of haggling voices. In which neighboring sister-city was this great market held?
context: The market of Tlatelolco, Tenochtitlan's twin city, astonished the Spanish; friar Sahagún and soldier Bernal Díaz put the daily crowd at 20,000–40,000, Cortés at 60,000. Texcoco and Tlacopan were Tenochtitlan's partners in the Triple Alliance; Azcapotzalco was an older rival city. Source: mexicolore.co.uk, 'The great market of Tlatelolco'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: After Spanish forces and their native allies razed Tenochtitlan in 1521, they built their colonial capital right on its ruins. The new city flooded again and again. So over the following centuries, engineers did something drastic to Lake Texcoco itself. What was it?
choices: they dammed it into a reservoir
they dredged it into a harbour
context: The fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521 was both a real razing — Cortés and his allies besieged the island for over 90 days, cutting its aqueduct — and a real epidemic collapse, as smallpox swept the city beforehand. To end the floods afterward, the Spanish drained Lake Texcoco almost completely; it shrank by more than 95%, leaving modern Mexico City on the dry old lakebed. Source: Grokipedia, 'Lake Texcoco'; Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: In 1978, workers digging a trench beneath the streets of downtown Mexico City struck the edge of a huge carved stone disc more than three metres across. The find led archaeologists straight to buried Tenochtitlan's holiest temple. Whose dismembered body was carved across the great disc?
context: The Coyolxauhqui Stone, over three metres wide, shows the Aztec moon goddess dismembered by her brother Huitzilopochtli in myth. Struck by chance on 21 February 1978, it triggered one of the largest urban digs in history, uncovering the Templo Mayor beneath modern Mexico City. Source: smarthistory.org, 'Templo Mayor: the Coyolxauhqui Stone'; Wikipedia, 'Coyolxauhqui Stone'.

question: Modern Mexico City stands on the soft clay bed of Lake Texcoco, the Aztec lake the Spanish drained long ago. As that old lakebed dries and squeezes together, parts of the city drop by as much as 50 centimetres a year, and the great Metropolitan Cathedral visibly leans. What is the geologist's single word for this slow sinking of the land?
context: Subsidence — the gradual sinking of ground — has lowered parts of Mexico City more than 10 metres in a century as the drained lakebed compacts. Erosion wears land away, liquefaction turns soil to slurry in an earthquake, and subduction is one tectonic plate sliding beneath another. (Tenochtitlan's peak population, an estimated 200,000–400,000, is a modern estimate, not a census.) Source: ScienceAlert, 'How fast Mexico City is sinking'; Grokipedia, 'Sinking cities'.

question: Straight as an arrow and about 40 m wide, a road runs for over 2 km through the ruined city of Teotihuacan, lined with flat platforms. Long after the city was empty, the Aztecs decided those platforms must be the tombs of old lords. They named the road to match. What did they call it?
context: The Aztecs came upon Teotihuacan centuries after its fall and, certain the platforms flanking the great road were royal tombs, named it Miccaotli -- the Avenue of the Dead. They were wrong: the platforms are temple bases, not graves. The road runs about 40 m wide and some 4 km long. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'  (Legend.)

question: Beside the great avenue at Teotihuacan, an ancient ruined city north of modern-day Mexico City, one flat-topped mountain of stone and rubble rises about 65 metres high. Its square base measures nearly 230 metres to a side, making it one of the largest pyramids anywhere in the world. Which of Teotihuacan's pyramids is this?
choices: the Temple of the Feathered Serpent
context: The Pyramid of the Sun stands about 65.5 m (215 ft) high on a base roughly 230 m square -- the largest building at Teotihuacan and one of the biggest in ancient Mesoamerica. Its name, like the city's, was given by the much later Aztecs. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pyramid of the Sun.'

question: Around 500 CE, Teotihuacan -- a vast city of stone pyramids and apartment compounds in the Valley of Mexico -- was among the very largest cities anywhere on Earth, with well over 100,000 people living inside its walls. For all the ruins archaeologists have unearthed and studied over the past century, one basic fact about these people no one has been able to recover. Which?
context: Teotihuacan's own people left no readable record of what they called themselves or their city; 'Teotihuacan' is a name the Aztecs coined centuries later, so scholars simply call them 'the Teotihuacanos.' Population estimates for its peak run from 100,000 to well above. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: Most families at Teotihuacan lived in wide one-story stone apartment blocks. The inner walls blazed with painted murals. The most famous one, at a block called Tepantitla, shows a great mountain pouring out streams of water. Dozens of tiny human figures are scattered across the land below. What kind of place do scholars think this mural shows?
answer: a watery paradise of the afterlife
choices: a watery paradise of the afterlife
a great flood that drowned the valley
a map of the city's canals
the mountain where its stone was quarried
context: The Tepantitla mural, often called the Paradise of Tlaloc (Tlalocan), is usually read as a blissful, watery afterlife tied to the rain god -- the mountain gushes water while people swim, sing and gather flowers below. Teotihuacan's apartment walls were covered in such vivid paintings. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan'; Tepantitla murals.

question: The name we use today, 'Teotihuacan,' did not belong to the people who built the city. It was coined much later by the Aztecs, who found ruins grander than anything they knew and gave them a Nahuatl name so lofty it is now the only name the city has. What does 'Teotihuacan' mean?
context: Awed by the abandoned city, the Aztecs named it Teotihuacan in their Nahuatl language -- usually glossed as 'birthplace of the gods' or 'the place where the gods were born.' It was to them a sacred site of creation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: Teotihuacan's workshops had a near-monopoly on a prized material dug from nearby hills. It was a fine volcanic glass called obsidian. Knapped razor-sharp, it was traded far across Mesoamerica. Everyone else used ordinary black obsidian, but Teotihuacan's had one trait that stood out. What made it easy to spot?
context: The Sierra de Pachuca yielded a rare golden-green obsidian found almost nowhere else in Mesoamerica. Teotihuacan controlled its supply, working it into blades, mirrors and ornaments that traveled hundreds of miles in trade -- a signature of the city's reach. Source: Ponomarenko 2004; Tulane University research on Pachuca green obsidian.

question: When Teotihuacan's Temple of the Feathered Serpent was built around 150-200 CE, its builders marked the dedication with a mass offering. Since then diggers have opened the pits beneath and around the pyramid. What did the builders bury there to consecrate the temple?
context: More than 200 people -- many with their hands bound, apparently war captives and soldiers -- were sacrificed and buried in pits beneath and around the Temple of the Feathered Serpent when it was dedicated about 150-200 CE, along with jade, obsidian and animal offerings. Source: Wikipedia, 'Temple of the Feathered Serpent, Teotihuacan.'

question: Teotihuacan was a huge city that drew people from all over Mesoamerica. In one neighborhood called Tlailotlacan, diggers found tombs, urns, and carvings in a foreign style. It was a whole quarter where people from far away kept the customs of their old homeland. Which people made this quarter their home?
context: Teotihuacan was a genuine melting pot. Its Tlailotlacan barrio housed Zapotec migrants from the Oaxaca Valley, who kept their homeland's tomb styles and hieroglyphs; other quarters held Gulf-coast and Maya traders. Bone-isotope tests confirm many residents grew up hundreds of miles away. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: In 2015, digger Sergio Gomez finished a tunnel under Teotihuacan's Temple of the Feathered Serpent. The passage had been sealed for 1,800 years. Inside he found jade statues, carved shells, and shiny pyrite spheres. His lamps also lit up pools of a strange liquid on the tunnel floor. What was this liquid?
context: Sergio Gomez of Mexico's INAH found pools of liquid mercury in the sealed chamber, along with jade statues, carved shells and pyrite spheres. He suspects the shimmering metal stood for an underworld river or lake -- and may mark the way to the first royal tomb ever found at Teotihuacan. Source: Archaeology Magazine, 27 April 2015.

question: At the north end of Teotihuacan's great avenue, the Pyramid of the Moon rises about 43 m, with the sacred mountain Cerro Gordo looming directly behind it. This was no accident: the builders deliberately tied the pyramid to the mountain at its back. In what way?
answer: its outline mirrors the mountain's silhouette
choices: its outline mirrors the mountain's silhouette
its stairway aims straight at the summit
it sits on the mountain's center line
its shadow reaches the peak at dawn
context: The 43 m Pyramid of the Moon was built to mimic the contours of Cerro Gordo, the mountain directly behind it, so that from the avenue the pyramid and peak read as one continuous silhouette -- binding the city's sacred architecture to the living landscape. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pyramid of the Moon.'

question: The entire city of Teotihuacan -- its long avenue, its pyramids, its thousands of buildings -- is deliberately rotated about 15.5 degrees off true north, all on one giant grid. Astronomers found the tilt is no mistake: it lines the whole city up with something in the sky. What did the builders orient their city to?
answer: sunrise and sunset on certain dates
choices: sunrise and sunset on certain dates
context: Teotihuacan's grid is turned about 15.5° east of north, and the Pyramid of the Sun's orientation records sunrise on 11 February and 29 October and sunset on 30 April and 13 August -- dates that likely anchored the ritual calendar. The whole city was squared to the sky, not the compass. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: For centuries Teotihuacan was the greatest power in Mesoamerica. Then around 550 CE, its main buildings were burned on purpose and the city fell. Diggers still argue about the cause. What is the leading answer today for what brought Teotihuacan down?
answer: a revolt from within the city
choices: a revolt from within the city
a war with a rival city
context: Because the burning around 550 CE targeted the elite civic buildings along the Avenue of the Dead rather than ordinary homes, most archaeologists now blame an internal uprising -- likely sharpened by drought and failed harvests -- instead of a foreign invasion. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: In the old Ethiopian city of Aksum in northern Africa -- once the capital of a powerful ancient kingdom -- a giant stone pillar called an obelisk stands 24 metres tall and weighs about 160 tonnes. Its sheer size is impressive, but the size is not the amazing part. What amazes builders and archaeologists is how this whole giant pillar was ___?
answer: carved from a single block of stone
choices: carved from a single block of stone
context: One solid piece of nepheline syenite, a hard granite-like rock, standing 24 m (79 ft) tall and weighing roughly 160 tonnes. Unlike Great Zimbabwe's mortarless dry-stacked walls or the stacked basalt logs of Nan Madol, the Obelisk of Axum is a single carved monolith. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: The Obelisk of Axum is carved to look like a tall Aksum tower-house. Fake window-frames climb all the way up its 24-metre height. At the bottom the carvers cut a fake doorway. Into that stone door they added one clever detail to make it look like a real home's entrance. What did they carve into the door?
context: The whole monolith imitates a nine-storey Aksumite tower-house laid out flat and stood upright, false windows and beams carved storey above storey. At the base its two false doors even carry carved false locks, as if the dead king's monument were a lived-in house. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/artifacts-other-artifacts/obelisk-axum-0011516

question: The top of the Obelisk of Axum is not a sharp point like an Egyptian obelisk. Instead it is carved into a smooth, rounded half-moon crown. Old fixings show the crown once wore a cover on top. That cover was stripped away long ago. What is thought to have capped the rounded top?
context: The moon-shaped crown was once fitted with metal frames or plates, thought to be bronze, so the grey stone skyscraper was capped in shining metal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: The ancient city of Aksum, capital of a powerful Ethiopian trading kingdom in East Africa, is famous for a field of huge carved standing stones called stelae at its edge. The tallest and most finely carved of these stones was each raised as a marker over something hidden in the ground below. What did the greatest stones of Aksum stand over?
answer: the tomb of a king or noble
choices: the tomb of a king or noble
a temple to the sun god
a spring feeding the city's wells
context: Rock-cut burial chambers and vaults run beneath the stelae field; the giant carved stones were grave-markers, the biggest and most decorated standing over the tombs of Aksum's kings and nobles. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksum

question: In 1937 the great Obelisk of Axum -- a 24-metre carved standing stone from the ancient Ethiopian city of Aksum -- was cut into three pieces by soldiers of an invading army. The pieces were hauled by truck to the coast and shipped overseas. Then the obelisk was raised again in the conqueror's own capital as a war prize. Which foreign power seized the obelisk, and in which city did they set it up?
context: Mussolini's Italy, having invaded Ethiopia, looted the obelisk in 1937, cut it into three sections, trucked it to the Red Sea port of Massawa, shipped it to Italy, and raised it in Rome near the Circus Maximus on 28 October 1937. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: After standing far from its homeland for 68 years, the looted Obelisk of Axum finally returned to Ethiopia in 2005. Its three colossal stone sections made the journey back to Aksum by the most dramatic means the modern age could manage. How did the obelisk travel home?
answer: flown aboard a giant cargo plane
choices: flown aboard a giant cargo plane
hauled home by a convoy of trucks
context: The pieces were flown home in April 2005 aboard an Antonov An-124, one of the world's largest cargo aircraft and among the heaviest airfreight loads ever carried. The operation cost Italy about $7.7 million; the obelisk was re-erected at Aksum and unveiled on 4 September 2008, home after 68 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: In 2002, while the looted obelisk still stood abroad, lightning struck its top and cracked the old stone. Builders blamed three steel bars driven through it in 1937. Those bars had turned the pillar into a huge lightning rod. When Ethiopia later rebuilt the obelisk, what strong modern material did they use to bind its pieces?
context: Italy's three steel bars had acted as a lightning rod, so when the obelisk was rebuilt at Aksum the steel was replaced with eight bars of Kevlar, the aramid fibre used in bulletproof vests, so it would no longer attract lightning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: In Aksum stands the Church of St Mary of Zion. Ethiopian Orthodox Christians hold that their church guards one of the most sacred relics in the whole Bible, said to have been carried to Ethiopia in ancient times and hidden ever since. According to this living tradition, which holy object rests inside the chapel at Aksum?
choices: a piece of the True Cross
context: Ethiopian Orthodox tradition holds that the Ark of the Covenant rests in the Church of St Mary of Zion, guarded by a single monk chosen for life who alone may see it and never leaves the chapel. The Kebra Nagast tells that Menelik I, son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba (Makeda), brought the Ark from Jerusalem. Presented here as a living sacred belief, held on its own terms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Our_Lady_Mary_of_Zion  (Legend.)

question: The Great Stele of Aksum lies broken into huge chunks across the field. It is about 33 metres long and weighs over 500 tonnes. It may be the largest single stone anyone ever cut to raise as a monument. How did this giant come to lie shattered on the ground?
answer: it fell while being raised and never once stood
choices: it fell while being raised and never once stood
an earthquake toppled it a thousand years later
invaders pulled it down and smashed it apart
its own weight cracked it after centuries upright
context: The Great Stele probably collapsed during the very attempt to stand it up and never successfully stood; as it toppled it crushed a stone chamber beneath it called Nefas Mawcha, and it lies where it fell to this day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksum

question: The stelae were quarried at Gobo Dura, a hill about four kilometres west of Aksum, then dragged all the way to the stelae field with no river and no wheels to help. Local Aksumite tradition still names a powerful helper that, it is said, hauled the giant blocks into place. According to that tradition, what moved the megaliths?
context: The quarry at Gobo Dura (Gobedra) and the roughly 4 km drag are established fact; the elephant-haulers are local tradition, presented as such. Unlike Egypt's obelisks, cut at distant Aswan and floated down the Nile, Aksum's stones were quarried close to home and moved by organized manpower. Source: https://www.africanhistoryextra.com/p/megalithic-landscapes-of-ethiopia  (Legend.)

question: The stelae were raised by no small town but by a Red Sea empire whose ships reached Rome and India. Around AD 270, under King Endubis, Aksum achieved something no other state south of the Sahara ever had, a true mark of a world power. What did Aksum become the first sub-Saharan state to do?
answer: mint its own gold and silver coins
choices: mint its own gold and silver coins
build a fleet of ocean-going warships
cut a great canal to the Red Sea
context: From about AD 270 under King Endubis, Aksum struck its own coinage in gold, silver and bronze, the first state in sub-Saharan Africa to do so. Later, under the Christian king Ezana, its coins swapped a pagan disc-and-crescent for the cross, among the first coins anywhere to bear a Christian cross. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksumite_currency

question: So mighty was the Red Sea empire that raised these stelae that in the 3rd century AD the Persian prophet Mani counted it among only four truly great kingdoms on all the Earth, writing that none surpassed them. Mani placed Aksum in that highest rank of world powers. Which three empires did he name alongside it?
context: In his Kephalaia, Mani listed four great kingdoms: Babylon and Persia, Rome, the kingdom of the Aksumites, and Silis (China), 'there is none that surpasses them.' Tiny Aksum was ranked beside Rome, Persia and China. Source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-137-11786-1_2

question: The Alps mountain range curves for about 1,200 km across the heart of Europe. Unlike most great mountain ranges, they belong to no single nation. Their snowy peaks stretch from the tiny principality of Monaco on the Mediterranean coast all the way east to Slovenia on the edge of the Balkans. How many separate countries does the Alpine range touch in all?
context: The Alps run in a crescent through eight nations — Monaco, France, Switzerland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Germany, Austria, and Slovenia — one great mountain wall shared across the center of Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps

question: High on the border where France, Italy, and Switzerland meet, in the great mountain range called the Alps, one white dome of ice and rock rises higher than any other peak around it. It reaches 4,808 metres tall -- the highest point in all of Western Europe. Which peak is this rooftop of the West?
context: Mont Blanc — French for 'White Mountain' — rises 4,808 m on the French-Italian border, the highest summit in the Alps and Western Europe. Monte Rosa (4,634 m), the Matterhorn (4,478 m), and the Eiger (3,967 m) all fall short. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps

question: On 8 August 1786, Dr. Michel-Gabriel Paccard and the crystal-hunter Jacques Balmat, both of Chamonix, clawed their way to the summit of Mont Blanc — the first humans ever to stand there. Their daring feat spread excitement across Europe and is remembered as the birth of a whole new sport. What is that sport called?
context: Dr. Michel-Gabriel Paccard and Jacques Balmat, both of Chamonix, made the first ascent of Mont Blanc on 8 August 1786 — a climb now seen as the birth of alpinism, the high-mountain sport that took its very name from the Alps. Bouldering (climbing low rocks), spelunking (cave exploring), and orienteering (cross-country navigation) are other outdoor pursuits. Source: 1786.travel

question: Climbers high on the Alps sometimes find fossil seashells in the rock beneath their boots — stone that once formed on an ocean floor, now lifted kilometers into the sky. The Alps rose when the African plate ground north into Europe and slammed shut the sea that had lain between them. What was that vanished ocean called?
context: As Africa drove into Eurasia, it closed the ancient Tethys Ocean and thrust its former sea floor skyward — which is why marine fossils and old seabed rock now sit atop Alpine peaks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_the_Alps

question: So much of Europe's fresh water starts high in the snowy Alps that geographers call the range Europe's 'water tower.' Snow and glaciers up there melt into rivers that flow off in every direction and reach four different seas -- the North Sea, the Mediterranean, the Adriatic, and the Black Sea. Which of these great European rivers is born high in the Alps?
context: The Rhine, the Rhône, the Po, and the Inn (a Danube tributary) all rise in the Alps, which supply up to about 90% of some lowland regions' water. The Rhine begins as Alpine meltwater in eastern Switzerland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps

question: Ötzi was an ancient hunter whose frozen body came out of an Alpine glacier. He was carrying a fine axe with a shiny metal blade. The metal it was made of rewrote history. It proved metalworking had reached the Alps far earlier than scholars had thought. What was the blade made of?
context: Ötzi's axe blade was nearly pure copper, showing metalworking had reached the Alps by about 3,300 BC — earlier than scholars thought — even though he still carried flint tools and a bow. Source: britannica.com/topic/Otzi

question: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure of Geneva had chased Mont Blanc for years. He had even posted a cash prize for the first person to reach its top. In 1787, the year after that prize was won, Saussure climbed the peak himself. He spent four days on the mountain while porters hauled a heavy load up the ice. What did Saussure haul to the summit?
choices: chests of gold and silver coins
a carved altar of white marble
context: Saussure reached the summit of Mont Blanc on 3 August 1787 with porters and instruments, spending days taking scientific measurements on top. Decades earlier, in 1760, he had funded the cash prize whose lure helped spur the first ascent in 1786. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace-Benedict_de_Saussure

question: In September 1991, hikers crossing a high pass on the Italian-Austrian border spotted a brown, shriveled body half-melted out of the ice and assumed a climber had died there not long before. Then scientists dated the corpse — soon nicknamed 'Ötzi' — and got a shock. Roughly how long ago had this man actually died?
context: Hikers Erika and Helmut Simon found the body in the Ötztal Alps; dating showed 'Ötzi' died about 5,300 years ago — the oldest known intact human mummy, preserved on ice since the Stone Age. He is now displayed in Bolzano, Italy. Source: iceman.it

question: The force of Africa driving into Europe was so immense that whole slabs of rock slid tens of kilometers, stacking older layers on top of younger ones across the Alps — the reverse of nature's usual order. Geologists have a special name for these displaced masses of rock. What are they called?
context: A 'nappe' (French for 'tablecloth') is a large sheet of rock folded over and thrust far from where it formed; the Alps are the classic example, with older rock shoved atop younger. Synclines are downward folds, while horsts and grabens are up- and down-dropped fault blocks — all real tectonic structures, but not the far-traveled thrust sheets that define Alpine geology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_the_Alps

question: In 1837, after years of work in the high Alps, Louis Agassiz stunned a room of Swiss scientists. He made a claim about Europe's deep past that most refused to believe. Yet time proved him right. What did Agassiz argue had once buried much of the continent?
context: Reading glacier tracks — moraines, out-of-place 'erratic' boulders, and polished bedrock — Agassiz told the Swiss Natural History Society at Neuchâtel on 24 October 1837 that ice sheets had once covered Europe: the birth of the Ice Age theory. Source: hgss.copernicus.org

question: Deep in the rainforests of South America, one enormous river carries about a fifth of all the fresh water that the world's rivers pour into the oceans each year. That is more water than the next seven biggest rivers on Earth put together, all rolled into one. Which river is it?
context: The Amazon's average discharge is about 215,000–230,000 cubic metres per second — enough to make it the largest river on Earth by volume, though not the longest. (The Congo is a distant second by discharge.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).

question: The Amazon River in South America pours out more water into the ocean than any other river on Earth -- more than the next seven biggest rivers put together. For that reason many people call the Amazon the greatest river of all. But it loses one important contest to a river on another continent. That contest is the race to be the longest river in the world. Which river is generally counted longer?
context: By water volume the Amazon is unmatched, but the Nile is usually reckoned the longer river. The title is genuinely disputed: the Amazon's recognized length is about 6,400 km (some surveys report 6,575–7,062 km and, by following a different southern source, call the Amazon the longest). Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).  (Legend.)

question: The Amazon rolls through the rainforests of South America — the biggest river on Earth by volume, snaking through Peru, Colombia, and Brazil. Two careful measurements of the same stretch of it disagree wildly. One team records the river as about 11 km wide. The other, standing on the same bank, cannot even see the far side. Neither team is wrong. What accounts for the huge difference?
answer: One was taken in the dry season, the other at the flood's peak.
choices: One was taken in the dry season, the other at the flood's peak.
One counted the river's mid-stream islands, the other left them out.
One measured the deep central channel, the other the full surface.
One was recorded at high tide, the other at low tide.
context: In the dry season a broad stretch of the Amazon runs about 11 km across; at the height of the annual flood the same stretch can swell to over 48 km (about 30 miles) wide — more than four times as far — so a boat in the middle is out of sight of either bank, and at its mouth the estuary spans hundreds of kilometres. It is a river that changes size with the seasons. Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).

question: The Amazon River runs for thousands of kilometres through the rainforests of Peru and Brazil in South America. In flood it swells over 20 km wide, drowning the trees along its banks. Boats going up and down the water pass big river cities like Iquitos and Manaus. Along that whole vast run through the jungle, from the Andes to the Atlantic, how many bridges cross the main river?
choices: a dozen or so, across Brazil
dozens, up and down its length
context: Not one bridge crosses the Amazon's main stem. The only bridge over any part of the system is the Ponte Rio Negro (2011), linking Manaus and Iranduba — and it spans the Rio Negro tributary, not the Amazon's main stem, so 'no bridge over the Amazon' still holds. Source: Live Science, 'Why are there no bridges over the Amazon River?' (https://www.livescience.com/why-no-bridges-over-amazon-river).

question: At the city of Manaus, deep in the Brazilian Amazon rainforest, two huge rivers meet. The pale, sandy-brown Rio Solimões rolls in from the west, and the coffee-black Rio Negro joins from the north. The Solimões looks milky because it carries fine sediment washed all the way down from the Andes mountains. But nothing muddy darkens the Rio Negro. So what stains its water almost black?
answer: tannins leached from rotting leaves and jungle plants
choices: tannins leached from rotting leaves and jungle plants
oils and resins washed from flooded rubber trees
a bloom of dark microscopic algae in the slow water
soot blown in from distant rainforest fires
context: The Rio Negro is a 'blackwater' river: almost sediment-free, its water is stained dark like strong tea by tannins from decaying leaves and plants draining off the forest. The Solimões is a sediment-rich 'whitewater' river carrying Andean silt. Where they meet at Manaus, the two run side by side as the Meeting of the Waters (Encontro das Águas). Source: Wikipedia, 'Meeting of Waters' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters).

question: Near the Brazilian city of Manaus, deep in the Amazon rainforest, two enormous rivers meet -- the dark-tinted Rio Negro and the pale, muddy Rio Solimoes. But instead of blending, the two rivers flow side by side in a single channel for about 6 km without mixing their colours at all. What keeps the two rivers apart for so long?
answer: they differ sharply in temperature and speed
choices: they differ sharply in temperature and speed
a submerged rock ridge runs between their channels
a strip of thick floating weeds divides them
the Solimões is far saltier than the Rio Negro
context: The Rio Negro is warm (about 28 °C) and slow (~2 km/h); the Solimões is cooler (about 22 °C) and fast (4–6 km/h). The mismatch in temperature, speed, and density keeps them from mixing for roughly 6 km before they finally merge into the lower Amazon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Meeting of Waters' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters).

question: In Brazil, where the mighty Amazon meets the Atlantic Ocean, something amazing happens twice a year. The rising Atlantic tide drives a wall of water back up the Amazon against the river's own current. The wave can be 4 m high — as tall as a house — and roars for hundreds of kilometres upriver. People living on the banks hear it long before they see it. What is this river-wave called?
context: This is the pororoca, a tidal bore: at the spring tides near the equinoxes (September and March) the Atlantic tide funnels into the shallow river mouth and rears up into a wave up to 4 m high that races as far as 800 km inland. The name comes from the indigenous Tupi language and is usually translated 'great roar.' (The mascaret, aegir, and benak are real tidal bores on other rivers.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Pororoca' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca).

question: An ocean surfer counts a good ride in seconds. But the Amazon's pororoca is a single wave that keeps rolling upriver for kilometre after kilometre, and in 2003 the surfer Picuruta Salazar caught one and rode it without stopping. How long did that one ride last?
context: Riding the pororoca upstream, Picuruta Salazar stayed on one wave for about 37 minutes and 12.5 km (7.8 miles) in 2003 — a record ride. An annual pororoca surfing championship has been held since 1999 at São Domingos do Capim. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pororoca' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca).

question: Modern engineers could span the Amazon River in South America if they had to — bridges cross wider water elsewhere in the world. Yet along the river's whole length through Peru and Brazil, not one bridge crosses its main stem. The biggest obstacle is not the width and not the strong current — it is the ground itself along the banks. What makes the banks so hard to build a bridge on?
answer: they are soft, waterlogged, and shift with every flood
choices: they are soft, waterlogged, and shift with every flood
they are steep rock gorges too narrow to anchor a pier
they are honeycombed with deep limestone sinkholes
they are packed with hard clay that cracks in the heat
context: The Amazon's banks are soft, waterlogged wetland that shifts as the river rises and falls up to 10 m a year, so a bridge would need very deep foundations and miles of approach viaducts across the floodplain. There is also little reason to build one: the river runs through sparsely populated rainforest with few roads, and it is cheaper to move Manaus's factory goods to São Paulo by boat than by road. Source: Live Science, 'Why are there no bridges over the Amazon River?' (https://www.livescience.com/why-no-bridges-over-amazon-river).

question: Each year the central Amazon in Brazil rises and falls about 10 m from low to high water — the height of a three-story house. The floodwater spills far out into the rainforest, drowning the trees. For months at a time it turns huge stretches of jungle into a vast underwater forest, where fish swim between the trunks. What is this seasonal flooded forest called?
context: This drowned floodplain forest is the várzea, flooded each year by sediment-rich whitewater. The annual 'flood pulse' of roughly 10 m (locally 9–14 m) shapes life along the whole river, and fish move among the tree trunks to feed while the forest is underwater. (The pantanal, cerrado, and caatinga are other Brazilian landscapes.) Source: seasonal flood-pulse research, PMC / US National Library of Medicine (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7612842/).

question: The mightiest river on Earth begins as a trickle of snowmelt high on the Peruvian peak Nevado Mismi. Astonishingly, its westernmost source lies only about 160 km from one ocean — yet the river runs the entire width of South America before reaching the sea. Which ocean does the Amazon's source lie so close to?
context: The Amazon rises on Nevado Mismi (about 5,597 m) in the Peruvian Andes. Its westernmost source is only about 160 km from the Pacific, yet the water turns east and crosses the whole continent — running downhill through the Apurímac, Ucayali, and Marañón headwaters before it becomes the Amazon — to empty into the Atlantic some 6,400 km away. Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).

question: Where the Amazon finally meets the sea, its outflow is so enormous that its effect reaches far past the shoreline. More than 100 km out into the open Atlantic, sailors and satellites find the water strangely changed. What has the river done to the ocean that far from land?
answer: freshened it into a vast low-salt plume
choices: freshened it into a vast low-salt plume
warmed it into a band of unusually hot water
dyed it bright green with drifting algae
stilled its waves into a glassy calm
context: The Amazon's freshwater plume spreads a brownish, low-salinity layer across the open Atlantic — reaching well beyond 100 km from shore and covering nearly a million square kilometres of ocean surface, enough fresh water to measurably lower the sea's saltiness far from any coast. Source: Amazon–Orinoco plume literature review, SALINITY-PIMEP case studies (https://www.salinity-pimep.org/case-studies/river-plumes/amazon_orinoco/literature_review.html).

question: Cross most mountain ranges and you are through them in an hour or two of driving. But head inland from the coast of Chile into the central Andes, and the far edge can lie up to 700 km away -- for a range of such colossal length, none on Earth is broader. What gives the Andes this tremendous breadth?
answer: several parallel mountain chains side by side
choices: several parallel mountain chains side by side
a single broad dome of uplifted crust
a wide plain of stacked lava flows
a thick belt of tightly folded rock
context: The Andes are the widest mountain range on Earth for their enormous length, swelling from about 200 km to as much as 700 km across and staying 200-300 km wide along most of their run. That breadth comes not from a single wall of rock but from several parallel cordilleras -- mountain chains marching side by side -- with high basins and plateaus trapped between them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes.

question: The Andes are the world's longest mountain chain, running about 7,000 km down the western spine of South America from Venezuela to the tip of Chile. More than fifty of their peaks push above 6,000 m into the thin, freezing air, and they are packed close together. Only one other mountain region on Earth has this many giant peaks crowded into one place. Which region is that?
choices: the Southern Alps of New Zealand
context: Outside the Himalaya-Karakoram belt of Asia -- home to every one of Earth's fourteen peaks above 8,000 m -- no place packs together as many 6,000 m summits as the Andes. The Alps top out near 4,800 m and the Rockies near 4,400 m, so neither comes close. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes; Guinness World Records ('Over fifty of the Andes peaks reach over 6,000 metres').

question: High on the Andean plateau at 3,810 m lies Lake Titicaca. It sits on the border between Bolivia and Peru. Its cold, deep-blue water has been held sacred by Andean people for thousands of years. Across all of South America, what record does Titicaca hold?
answer: the largest lake on the continent
choices: the largest lake on the continent
the deepest lake on the continent
the saltiest lake on the continent
the youngest lake on the continent
context: By surface area Titicaca is the biggest lake in South America, and it is also widely described as the highest large lake in the world that boats can still navigate, sitting some 3,810 m above the sea. Reed boats and even 19th-century steamships have crossed its waters. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano ('the largest lake in South America'); navigable-lake claim widely reported.

question: Between the eastern and western chains of the Andes mountains in South America lies a vast highland called the Altiplano. It is a bare, wind-scoured tableland about 3,750 m high — higher than most mountain summits elsewhere in the world. It spreads across parts of Bolivia, Peru, Chile, and Argentina. Only one plateau on Earth is both bigger and higher than the Altiplano. Which one?
choices: the Colorado Plateau of North America
context: The Altiplano is the most extensive high plateau on Earth outside Tibet, and the world's second-highest. Its wide, flat basins -- floored with salt pans, shallow lakes, and volcanic ash -- formed as crust piled up and downwarped between the two Andean mountain chains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano ('the most extensive high plateau on Earth outside Tibet').

question: On the lonely high border between Chile and Argentina in South America, the Andes mountains bristle with fire-born peaks. There the huge cone of Ojos del Salado rises above the desert — a volcano whose crater sits under snow year-round. Among all the volcanoes on our planet, what record does this Andean giant hold?
choices: the most active volcano on Earth
