Meltwater pouring off the Great Aletsch runs first into the little Massa and then into one of the continent's great rivers. Which river does it ultimately swell?
context: Meltwater from the Aletsch's snout forms the Massa (through the Gibidum reservoir), which joins the Rhone. Alpine glaciers act as Europe's 'water towers,' storing winter snow and releasing it through the dry summer; the Alps supply about 40% of Europe's fresh water and feed the Rhine, Rhone and Po. But the Aletsch is shrinking fast -- studies project it will keep only about a tenth of its 2018 ice by the year 2100. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aletsch_Glacier; smartwatermagazine.com)

question: Off the northeast coast of Australia, in the warm blue Coral Sea, stretches the largest living wonder on Earth — the Great Barrier Reef. It runs for over 2,300 km and is built entirely from the tiny stony skeletons of billions of coral animals called polyps. Of all the structures on Earth, what record does the Great Barrier Reef hold?
answer: the largest structure ever built by living things
choices: the largest structure ever built by living things
the oldest structure ever built by living things
the tallest structure ever built by living things
the fastest-growing structure ever built by living things
context: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest structure on Earth built by living creatures -- a coral colossus over 2,300 km long off Queensland, Australia. It is so vast that it can be picked out from low Earth orbit, and astronauts and satellites have photographed it from space (the old 'visible from the Moon with the naked eye' version, though, is a myth). Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Barrier_Reef ; https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/gbrlargeststructure.html ; https://www.esa.int/Applications/Observing_the_Earth/Earth_from_Space_World_s_largest_living_structure

question: Off Australia's northeast coast stretches the largest coral reef in the world, the Great Barrier Reef. Its coral covers about 344,400 sq km of sea. It is about the same size as which European country?
context: The reef sprawls across about 344,400 sq km of the Coral Sea -- roughly the area of the whole of Italy (~301,000 sq km), and larger than the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and the Netherlands combined. Sources: https://greatbarrierreef.org/about-the-reef/how-big-is-the-great-barrier-reef/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Barrier_Reef

question: Coral looks like bright rock or branching plants. But each bumpy patch is really a group of thousands of tiny animals. The whole 2,300 km Great Barrier Reef is built from their stacked stony bones. What is each of these tiny reef-building animals called?
context: Each coral is a colony of thousands of tiny animals called polyps, each smaller than a fingernail. A polyp pulls dissolved limestone (calcium carbonate) out of seawater and lays down a stony skeleton; over thousands of years those stacked skeletons built the whole reef. Sources: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/gbrlargeststructure.html ; https://www.barrierreef.org/news/explainers/what-is-coral

question: Off the northeast coast of Australia stretches the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral system in the world. From a boat it looks like an endless single wall of coral running along the Coral Sea. But when you fly high above it in a plane and look straight down, the surprising truth appears in the blue below. What is the reef actually made up of?
choices: about 15 giant reefs in a row
context: The Great Barrier Reef is not a single reef but a system of about 2,900 separate reefs and 900 islands scattered across the Coral Sea -- which helped earn it a place as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981 and as one of the Seven Natural Wonders of the World. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Barrier_Reef

question: In 1975, a helicopter pilot flying over Hardy Reef — a small reef in the Whitsunday Islands, off the northeast coast of Australia — spotted something amazing in the coral below. It was tiny, only about 17 m across, but its outline was unmistakable and perfectly formed by nature. Ever since, tourists have paid to fly out just to photograph it. What makes this little reef so popular in photos?
answer: it is naturally shaped like a perfect heart
choices: it is naturally shaped like a perfect heart
it forms a perfect ring around a blue lagoon
it is the oldest coral in the whole reef
it is the only reef you can walk across
context: The formation is Heart Reef, a small, naturally heart-shaped cluster of coral at Hardy Reef in the Whitsundays, only about 17 m across. An Air Whitsunday pilot spotted it from the air in 1975, and it has since become one of the most photographed sights on the reef. Sources: https://www.tourismwhitsundays.com.au/icons/heart-reef ; https://greatbarrierreeftours.com/great-barrier-reef-sites/whitsunday-reefs/heart-reef/

question: Coral has grown off Australia for many thousands of years. But the reef we visit today is young. It grew in just the last 6,000 to 9,000 years, right on top of far older reefs. What happened at the end of the last Ice Age that let a fresh reef grow on those old ones?
answer: rising seas flooded the shallows above the old reefs
choices: rising seas flooded the shallows above the old reefs
warming water crept back over the old reefs
clearer water let sunlight reach the old reefs
melting ice fed fresh nutrients to the old reefs
context: The living reef is young -- it grew over roughly the last 6,000 to 9,000 years on the drowned foundations of far older reefs (some hundreds of thousands of years old). As the last Ice Age ended, melting ice raised the sea about 120 m, flooding new sunlit shallows where coral could grow up on the old rock. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Barrier_Reef

question: A few nights after the November full moon, the Great Barrier Reef puts on one of nature's greatest shows. Across 2,300 km of coral, billions of tiny polyps all act in the very same moment, just once a year. What are they all doing together?
answer: releasing eggs and sperm in a mass spawning
choices: releasing eggs and sperm in a mass spawning
swimming off to spend winter in deep water
shedding their old skeletons to grow fresh ones
changing color to hide from hungry fish
context: Once a year, a few nights after the November full moon, nearly the whole reef spawns at the same instant -- billions of polyps release pink-and-orange egg-and-sperm bundles in a single synchronized event called mass coral spawning. Corals use moonlight, longer spring days, and water above about 26 degrees C to time it, and different species spawn on different nights so they don't cross-breed. Sources: https://www2.gbrmpa.gov.au/learn/coral-spawning-101 ; https://www.barrierreef.org/news/explainers/what-is-coral-spawning

question: On one special night a year, a diver hanging in the dark water over the Great Barrier Reef is engulfed by billions of tiny pink, orange, red, and white bundles filling the sea all around, until visibility fades to a colorful blur. Divers reach for one famous winter comparison to describe it. What do they call the scene?
context: Divers describe the mass spawn as a slow-motion 'upside-down snowstorm' -- instead of white flakes falling, billions of pink, orange, red, and white bundles drift gently upward toward the surface, filling the water in every direction. Sources: https://www.australiantraveller.com/qld/great-barrier-reef/coral-spawning-in-the-great-barrier-reef/ ; https://www.barrierreef.org/news/explainers/what-is-coral-spawning

question: The Great Barrier Reef's giant spawn never happens by day -- the polyps always release their eggs in the dead of night. This timing is no accident: it gives the drifting eggs a far better chance of surviving. Why does spawning after dark save so many more eggs?
answer: most plankton-eating fish are asleep then
choices: most plankton-eating fish are asleep then
the night water is far calmer then
moonlight guides the eggs upward then
the cooler night water preserves them
context: The mass spawn happens only at night, when most plankton-eating fish are asleep -- so far more of the drifting eggs survive long enough to be fertilized. Sources: https://greatbarrierreeftours.com/coral-spawning-on-the-great-barrier-reef/ ; https://www.barrierreef.org/news/explainers/what-is-coral-spawning

question: When the sea stays too warm for weeks, Great Barrier Reef corals suffer what scientists call bleaching -- a vivid, colorful coral turns ghostly bone-white in a matter of days. Where does that sudden white color actually come from?
answer: its own bare limestone skeleton showing through
choices: its own bare limestone skeleton showing through
a coat of pale algae spreading over it
a crust of salt left by the warm water
a chalky fungus creeping across it
context: This is coral bleaching. Corals get their color from the algae in their tissues; when the water stays too warm -- just about 1 degree C above the summer average for around four weeks is enough -- the stressed coral expels its algae. Because coral tissue is see-through, the bare white limestone skeleton then shows through. A bleached coral is still alive but starving, and it can die if the heat doesn't ease. Sources: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/coral_bleach.html ; https://www.barrierreef.org/the-reef/threats/coral-bleaching

question: From a plane above Belize, you see a strange sight. Pale blue reef stretches for miles. In the middle sits one dark round hole, about 318 m across. It drops far below the shallow water around it. What kind of feature is this round deep pit?
context: It's the Great Blue Hole, a near-perfectly round marine sinkhole about 318 m (1,043 ft) across and 124 m (407 ft) deep, sitting in the Lighthouse Reef atoll off Belize. A 'blue hole' like this is a drowned karst sinkhole in limestone -- not a volcanic or impact crater. Source: geologyscience.com 'Great Blue Hole'; Wikipedia 'Great Blue Hole.'

question: You can't see the Great Blue Hole from Belize's beaches. To get there, you take a boat 70 km out to sea. A small ring of coral holds the famous dark hole in its lagoon. What is this ring of coral called?
context: The Great Blue Hole lies near the center of Lighthouse Reef, a small atoll about 70 km (43 miles) off the Belize mainland and Belize City, out in the open Caribbean. Source: geologyscience.com 'Great Blue Hole'; Wikipedia 'Great Blue Hole.'

question: Rewind to the last Ice Age, when so much water was frozen into glaciers that the sea stood about 120 m lower than today. The dry ground where the Great Blue Hole now sinks into the Caribbean held a feature you could have explored on foot -- one that the rising sea would later flood as the ice melted. What was there on that Ice-Age land?
context: During the last Ice Age this spot was a dry limestone cave on land, with the sea some 120 m lower. When the ice melted and the ocean rose, the cave's roof collapsed and seawater poured in and flooded it -- creating the Blue Hole. Source: geologyscience.com 'Great Blue Hole'; Forbes (Shukla, 2019).

question: Deep inside the flooded Great Blue Hole, divers noticed something odd about the giant stalactites hanging from the overhangs: not one hangs straight down. Every one leans about 5 degrees off-vertical, all in the same direction. Geologists puzzled over what could make so many stalactites lean the same way. What single cause explains it?
answer: the whole slab of limestone tilted after the stalactites had grown
choices: the whole slab of limestone tilted after the stalactites had grown
steady one-way sea currents pushed the growing tips aside
the stalactites grew slanted, reaching toward the light above
the flooding sea bent them as the water level climbed
context: The giant stalactites lean about 5 degrees off-vertical, all pointing the same way. Because a stalactite always grows straight down as water drips from its tip, geologists read this uniform lean as evidence that the whole limestone plateau tilted AFTER the stalactites had formed in the dry cave -- a sign the land itself shifted, not just the sea rising to flood it. Source: Wikipedia 'Great Blue Hole.'  (Legend.)

question: Descend past about 90 m inside the Great Blue Hole and you cross an invisible boundary into a layer of pure poison: no oxygen at all, no light, and nothing alive. Below this line the water lies black and dead-still, all the way to the 124 m floor. This deep dead zone is poisoned by high levels of one dissolved gas. Which one?
context: Below about 90 m the water holds no oxygen and hydrogen sulfide builds up -- the same gas that gives rotten eggs their stench, and the deepest water reeks of it. Nothing can breathe there, so the deep stays dark, still, and lifeless down to the 124 m floor; a 2018 submarine expedition mapped the layer with sonar. Source: Wikipedia 'Great Blue Hole'; Forbes (Shukla, 2019).

question: Explorers who reached the floor of the Great Blue Hole passed through a dead poison layer at 90 m. Below that, they found the dark seabed strangely covered. The same object was scattered everywhere, undisturbed for ages. What blankets the bottom of the Blue Hole?
choices: a layer of black volcanic sand
a tangle of old ship timbers
context: Divers nicknamed the bottom the 'conch graveyard.' Anything that falls or crawls into the hole sinks through the oxygen-less layer, suffocates, and cannot climb back out; with no currents to sweep them away, the empty shells simply stay put for ages. Source: Forbes (Shukla, 2019).  (Legend.)

question: The Great Blue Hole is only one jewel of the Belize Barrier Reef, a wall of living coral so magnificent that Charles Darwin, writing in 1842, called it 'the most remarkable reef in the West Indies.' Of all the barrier reefs on Earth, only a single one outranks Belize's for sheer size. Which reef is the world's largest, beating even Belize's?
context: The Belize Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef in the Northern and Western Hemispheres, second in the world only to Australia's Great Barrier Reef. Charles Darwin praised it in 1842 as 'the most remarkable reef in the West Indies,' and the whole reserve system became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996. Source: New World Encyclopedia 'Belize Barrier Reef'; everything-everywhere.com.

question: Deep under the green rolling hills of central Kentucky lies Mammoth Cave, a vast maze of stone passages winding through soft limestone. Cavers have been exploring and mapping its tunnels since the early 1800s, and they still keep finding new sections every year — over 685 km of passages so far. Of all the caves in the world, what record does Mammoth Cave hold?
context: Mammoth Cave National Park protects over 686 km (426 mi) of mapped passages — more than 1.5 times the length of the next-longest cave on Earth — all dissolved out of ancient limestone by water seeping underground, and still growing as cavers push new connections. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammoth_Cave_National_Park

question: Deep in the jungle of Vietnam, Son Doong holds the largest cave passage on Earth — a tunnel over 200 m (660 ft) high and 150 m (490 ft) wide. Explorers love to say one particular airliner could fly straight through it, wings clear of the walls. Which jet?
context: Son Doong's main passage is over 5 km long, 200 m high and 150 m wide — big enough that a Boeing 747 could pass through without its wings touching, or an entire New York City block of skyscrapers could stand inside. It was found by farmer Ho Khanh in 1990 and first surveyed by the British Cave Research Association in 2009. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C6%A1n_%C4%90o%C3%B2ng_Cave

question: In two spots the ceiling of Vietnam's Son Doong cave collapsed long ago, tearing open enormous skylights (called dolines) that let daylight pour onto the cave floor far below. Where that light lands, a startling sight has appeared deep underground. What?
context: So much sunlight floods through the second doline that a genuine jungle of trees and plants grows on the floor of Son Doong — a rainforest hidden inside a mountain. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C6%A1n_%C4%90o%C3%B2ng_Cave

question: Deep in the jungles of central Vietnam lies Son Doong, the largest cave passage in the world — a chamber so huge that whole city blocks could fit inside. The main hall runs over 5 km long, 200 m tall, and 150 m wide, big enough to hold a 40-story skyscraper. During the hot summer months, the space is so enormous it actually generates its own weather. What forms in the air of its huge chambers?
context: Warm, moist air off Son Doong's underground river meets the cooler cave air and condenses into drifting fog and clouds inside the chambers, mainly from June to August. Outside it can top 37C while the cave holds around 22-25C. Source: https://www.accuweather.com/en/weather-news/son-doong-cave-in-vietnam-worlds-largest-cave-is-so-big-it-has-its-own-weather/779176

question: In 1898, a teenage cowboy named Jim White spotted a dark hole in the New Mexico desert. He climbed down and became the first to explore Carlsbad Caverns. What did White use to lower himself into that first black pit?
context: Carlsbad Caverns was first explored in 1898 by Jim White, a teenage cowboy who climbed down on a homemade wire ladder into the black depths and named its grand chambers — among them the Big Room, which at nearly 1,220 m (4,000 ft) long is the largest cave chamber in North America. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlsbad_Caverns_National_Park

question: In Slovenia rises a rugged limestone plateau. It is so famous that geographers named a whole class of landscapes after it. On every continent, land of this kind carries the same name. Which landscape word did geographers borrow from this one Slovenian plateau?
context: The plateau is called Kras (German: Karst), in the Dinaric Alps of Slovenia reaching toward Italy's Adriatic coast. Because scientists first described its caves, sinkholes and disappearing streams here, geographers worldwide adopted 'karst' for every landscape of soluble rock that dissolves this way — so the whole global class of terrain is named after this one Slovenian plateau. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karst

question: Mammoth Cave grew where slightly acidic water could dissolve a thick bed of 330-million-year-old limestone. Its huge passages have survived so long because a hard, erosion-resistant rock layer caps the limestone like a protective roof. What is this caprock?
context: Mammoth's passages formed in Mississippian limestone about 330 million years old, capped by a hard sandstone layer. Rainwater turning mildly acidic dissolves the limestone below the sandstone, where the big walkable passages form; the resistant caprock keeps them from collapsing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammoth_Cave_National_Park

question: One cave in New Mexico was carved the 'wrong' way — not by rainwater soaking down from above, but by sulfuric acid rising UP from oil deposits deep below, eating the limestone from the bottom. The result is a maze hung with glittering 6-metre gypsum 'chandeliers' found almost nowhere else on Earth, now sealed to protect it. Which cave?
context: Lechuguilla Cave formed by 'hypogene' action — hydrogen sulfide seeping up from oil deposits turned to sulfuric acid and dissolved the limestone from below, hanging the cave with gypsum chandeliers up to 6.1 m (20 ft) long. Long thought a dead-end pit, it was broken into on 25 May 1986 after cavers followed wind roaring up through its floor; it is now sealed to all but approved scientists. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lechuguilla_Cave

question: The only two caves on Earth ever found to plunge more than 2 km straight down — Veryovkina and Krubera — descend into the very same mountain block in the Caucasus. Reaching the bottom takes expedition teams weeks. What is this deep-cave massif called?
context: Both Krubera (Voronya) at about 2,224 m and Veryovkina at about 2,209 m plunge into the Arabika Massif of the Western Caucasus in Abkhazia — the only two caves known to pass 2,000 m deep, with the depth record swapping between them on re-survey. A 2012 Krubera expedition sent 59 cavers from nine countries underground for 27 days. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veryovkina_Cave

question: High in the Caucasus mountains of Abkhazia, cavers plunge into Krubera, one of the two deepest caves on Earth — a shaft that drops more than 2 kilometres straight down into the dark. Russian-speaking explorers gave it a haunting nickname, Voronya, after the black birds that nest in its gaping entrance pit. Translated into English, what does Voronya mean?
context: Krubera Cave is nicknamed Voronya, Russian for 'Crow's Cave,' after the crows nesting in its entrance pit. In 2004 it became the first cave known to pass 2,000 m deep; diver Gennady Samokhin pushed its depth record further in 2007 and 2012. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krubera_Cave

question: Almost every great cave is dissolved from the top down: rainwater soaks through the soil, turns mildly acidic, and eats limestone from above — that is how Mammoth and most caves form. Lechuguilla broke the rule: its acid rose from oil deposits far below and dissolved the rock from the bottom up. Geologists have a special name for this rare, upside-down way of making a cave. What is it?
context: Top-down cave-making is called 'epigene': rainwater absorbs CO2 to form weak carbonic acid (H2O + CO2 -> H2CO3) that dissolves limestone from above. Lechuguilla instead formed by 'hypogene' action — sulfuric acid rising from oil deposits below — which is why its gypsum crystals are so bizarre. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karst

question: The five Great Lakes — Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario — spread across the border of the United States and Canada. Together they hold more than a fifth of all the fresh surface water on Earth. They sit in a chain of giant basins sunk deep into the land, all lined up in the same general direction. How were those huge basins gouged out?
answer: gouged out by the tongues of an ice sheet
choices: gouged out by the tongues of an ice sheet
blasted out by a giant meteorite
torn open along a crack in the crust
context: The tongues of the Laurentide Ice Sheet scooped out these hollows; when the ice retreated about 14,000 years ago, meltwater filled them to make Lakes Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario. Together they hold more than a fifth of the world's surface fresh water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes

question: The five Great Lakes — Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario — hold about 22,700 cubic km of fresh water between them. If you poured all that water out flat over the whole lower 48 states of the United States, the entire country would end up under a shallow flood. About how deep would that flood stand?
context: The Great Lakes hold about 5,472 cubic miles (22,810 km3) of water — enough to bury all 48 contiguous states roughly 9.5 feet deep — and their combined surface area is about the size of the United Kingdom. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes

question: Walk into New York City's Central Park and you can climb up onto Umpire Rock, a huge bare hump of stone in the middle of the meadow. Look closely and you'll see the rock is scratched and polished smooth. During the last Ice Age, about 20,000 years ago, a giant glacier ground right across Manhattan and rasped this rock flat. At the ice sheet's biggest, about how deep was the ice above Manhattan?
context: The polished bedrock is scored with long parallel scratches called glacial striations; the Central Park set runs north-to-south, recording the ice grinding south over New York. At the ice age's peak the sheet stood roughly 1,000 ft (300 m) thick over the city. Best seen at Umpire Rock. Source: https://www.nycgovparks.org/about/history/geology

question: During the last great chapter of Earth's climate history, huge ice sheets pushed south again and again across North America. That same ice scored the bedrock of Central Park in New York and gouged out the Great Lakes. Over some 2.6 million years, the ice came and went dozens of times — not one freeze but many. What do geologists name this whole epoch of repeated ice ages?
context: The Pleistocene ran from about 2.58 million years ago to 11,700 years ago — dozens of glacial advances and retreats, not a single freeze. Each cycle carved lakes, dropped the seas, and opened land bridges before the ice pulled back again. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Maximum

question: At the peak of the last ice age, so much water was locked in ice that the seas fell about 120 metres. The floor of the North Sea rose into daylight as real land, with grass, rivers, and wandering hunters. It joined Britain to Europe before the seas came back. What do scientists call this lost land?
context: Doggerland once joined Britain to France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, and Denmark. As the ice melted, seas rose between about 10,000 and 7,000 years ago, finally severing Britain from the mainland around 6500 BCE. At the Last Glacial Maximum sea level stood about 120 m lower than today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doggerland

question: The drowned floor of the North Sea still gives up its secrets: trawler nets scraping the seabed haul up the bones of ice-age animals and, now and then, objects shaped by human hands. In 1931 one net dredged up a finely worked tool, thousands of years old, from land that lay dry when hunters walked it. What was that tool?
context: The 1931 find was a 220 mm barbed antler point — a harpoon or fish spear — trawled from the North Sea and dated between roughly 10,000 and 4,000 BCE. Nets still bring up mammoth and lion bones alongside prehistoric tools from the drowned country of Doggerland. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doggerland

question: Greenland's ice sheet is no leftover winter snow — it is a surviving splinter of the ice-age world, in places about 3.4 km thick, still burying most of the island. Where scientists drill cores down to its very base, they reach ice that first fell as snow and froze roughly how long ago?
context: The Greenland Ice Sheet still buries about 80% of the island, up to ~3.4 km thick. Its oldest ice is roughly a million years old, and a single ice sheet has covered Greenland since about 2.6 million years ago — a genuine relic of the ice ages. A full melt would raise seas about 7.4 m. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_ice_sheet

question: Antarctica's ice sheet weighs so much that it has pressed the bedrock of the whole continent hundreds of meters downward, like a heavy person sinking into a soft mattress. Geologists say that if all that ice ever melted, the crushed continent would slowly rise back up over thousands of years — the same way the mattress puffs back into shape once you climb off. What do they call this slow bounce-back of the land?
context: The Antarctic Ice Sheet holds about 61% of all the fresh water on Earth (and roughly 90% of the world's total ice — a separate figure). At the pole, the ice age simply never left. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_ice_sheet

question: Antarctica's ice is not just vast but crushingly deep, plunging to nearly 4.8 km at its thickest — deep enough to bury whole mountain ranges out of sight. Imagine that entire ice sheet melting away into the sea. By roughly how much would it lift the world's oceans?
context: Antarctic ice reaches a maximum near 4.8-4.9 km (deepest at the Astrolabe Subglacial Basin) and averages over 2 km. A total melt would raise global sea level by about 53 m (175 ft), redrawing every coastline on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_ice_sheet

question: High on the frozen plateau at Dome C, Antarctica, researchers at Concordia Station drilled a single ice core more than 3 km straight down, almost to the bedrock. Every layer holds one year's snowfall and tiny sealed bubbles of the actual ancient air. How far back in time does the Dome C core's climate record reach?
context: The EPICA core at Dome C (Concordia Station, 75S) was drilled about 3,270 m down to within a few metres of bedrock. Its layers and trapped air bubbles preserve a climate diary reaching back roughly 800,000 years — the oldest samples of ancient atmosphere ever recovered. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Project_for_Ice_Coring_in_Antarctica

question: Read downward through the Dome C ice, the great freezes return in an eerily steady rhythm — a deep ice age roughly every 100,000 years. This beat is no accident: it keeps time with slow, clockwork changes in the shape of Earth's orbit and the tilt and wobble of its spinning axis. What is this family of orbital rhythms that paces the ice ages called?
context: The Milankovitch cycles were worked out in the 1920s by the Serbian scientist Milutin Milankovic: a ~100,000-yr change in orbital shape (eccentricity), a ~41,000-yr nod of the axial tilt, and a ~23,000-yr wobble of the spin axis (precession). The EPICA ice shows about 8 glacial cycles marching to that ~100,000-yr beat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milankovitch_cycles

question: Here is the honest puzzle at the frontier of ice-age science. For the past million years — read from the Antarctic ice and deep-sea mud — the great freezes have pulsed almost perfectly in step with a slow ~100,000-year change in the shape of Earth's orbit, the tightest match in the whole theory. Yet scientists still argue over WHY this cycle, of them all, sets the master beat. What is strange about the ~100,000-year orbital cycle driving the ice ages?
answer: it barely changes how much sunlight Earth receives
choices: it barely changes how much sunlight Earth receives
it warms the poles but never the tropics
it is driven by the Moon rather than the Sun
it only affects the Southern Hemisphere
context: This is the '100,000-year problem.' The freezes track the ~100,000-year eccentricity cycle almost perfectly, yet that cycle barely alters the total sunlight Earth receives — so why it dominates is still debated (proposed answers include feedbacks, frequency modulation, and stochastic resonance). The match is fact; the mechanism is not settled. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milankovitch_cycles  (Legend.)

question: In the town of Djenné, in the West African country of Mali, a giant building rises above the market square. It is the Great Mosque of Djenné, as tall and wide as a European cathedral and one of the most famous sights in all of Africa. Every wall, tower, and spiky beam sticking out of its skin is built from the same simple stuff. What is the Great Mosque made of?
context: The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick (adobe) building on Earth — cathedral-sized, yet built from nothing but sun-dried earth, on a platform about 75 m by 75 m raised 3 m above the market square. The structure standing today is a 1907 rebuild in the traditional Sudano-Sahelian style, on a sacred site where the first mosque was raised in the 13th century; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Djenn%C3%A9

question: Three tall towers (minarets) rise from the earthen walls of the Great Mosque of Djenné, each about 16 metres high. Balanced at the very tip of each minaret sits one surprising object that visitors often photograph. What tops each of the mosque's minarets?
context: The three minarets each stand roughly 16 m tall, and the ostrich egg crowning each one is said to stand for fertility and purity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Djenn%C3%A9

question: Hundreds of palm-wood beams called toron jut straight out of the walls of the Great Mosque of Djenné, poking out all over like the quills of a porcupine. Visitors assume they are just decoration, but the toron do a hidden practical job. What are the toron for?
choices: they anchor the heavy roof beams
they act as spouts to drain rainwater
context: The toron are bundles of Rodier palm wood that project about 60 cm from the walls. Far from decoration, they are permanent built-in scaffolding: they are climbed each year to re-plaster the mosque, without which the earthen walls would erode away in the rains. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Djenn%C3%A9

question: Djenné's Great Mosque is built of sun-dried earth, so the heavy seasonal rains would slowly melt it away if it were left alone. To save it, the mosque's entire surface is re-coated with fresh mud once every year, before the rains arrive. Who carries out this yearly re-plastering of the Great Mosque?
context: The festival is called the crépissage. Guided by the guild of master masons (the barey ton), men climb the toron scaffolding to smear on fresh mud while women carry water — the whole giant building is re-skinned by hand in essentially a single day. Neighborhood teams even race to finish their section first, cheered on by drummers and griot storytellers, with the winning team taking a cash prize. Source: https://religionunplugged.com/news/2023/1/29/the-worlds-largest-mud-brick-building-is-a-mosque-rebuilt-every-year

question: Outside the Great Mosque of Djenné, the Sahel sun bakes the town in ferocious daytime heat. Yet step inside the vast prayer hall and the air stays remarkably cool — with no air conditioning, no fans, and no machinery of any kind. What keeps the inside of the mosque so cool?
answer: the thick earthen walls soak up the heat
choices: the thick earthen walls soak up the heat
small windows keep the sunlight out
a natural spring flows beneath it
cool winds blow in off the desert
context: The walls are about 16-24 inches thick, and their huge thermal mass acts like a natural battery — soaking up the fierce daytime heat and releasing it slowly after dark, so the vast prayer hall stays cool with no machinery at all. Small ceramic-capped vents in the roof let the hottest air escape. Source: https://www.studiomatrx.org/architecture-canon/great-mosque-of-djenne

question: Just 3 km from modern Djenné lies Djenné-Djenno. Founded around 250 BC, it is one of the oldest known cities in sub-Saharan Africa. Iron-workers, goldsmiths, and merchants lived there for over 1,500 years before the city was left empty. When archaeologists dug into its earthen mound, one kind of buried object made the site world-famous. What did the diggers pull from the mound?
context: Founded around 250 BC and abandoned around 1400 AD, Djenné-Djenno is one of the oldest known cities in sub-Saharan Africa. Its decades-long excavation, led by archaeologists Susan and Roderick McIntosh, unearthed striking terracotta figurines up to 50 cm tall — often bearded horsemen, and some figures shown covered in the symptoms of tropical disease or with a snake coiled in attack. At its peak (about the 6th-9th centuries AD) the city held around 20,000 iron-workers, goldsmiths, and merchants, and its pottery traveled some 750 km — proof of a thriving African city deep in the interior, long before outsiders imagined such places existed. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Djenne-Djenno/

question: About 2,200 years ago, ancient Greek travelers named seven great Wonders of the World — huge structures worth crossing the sea to see. The list included the Lighthouse of Alexandria, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, and the Colossus of Rhodes. Among all seven, the Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt holds one striking distinction that sets it apart from the rest. What is it?
answer: It is the only one still standing today.
choices: It is the only one still standing today.
It is the only one ever built of stone.
It is the only one that stood in Egypt.
It is the only one built for a king.
context: Every other ancient wonder -- the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the Colossus of Rhodes, the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the rest -- has been toppled by fire, war or earthquake. The Great Pyramid alone survives, roughly 4,500 years after it was built. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza  (Legend.)

question: About 4,500 years ago on the Giza plateau in Egypt, tens of thousands of workers spent decades cutting and hauling huge limestone blocks. Block by block, they raised the Great Pyramid — a mountain of stone as tall as a 45-story building. It was the tallest human-built structure anywhere on Earth for over 3,800 years. What did the ancient Egyptians build it to be?
choices: a temple to the sun god
context: It was raised as the burial place of the pharaoh Khufu (Greek: Cheops) around 2600-2560 BC, in Egypt's Fourth Dynasty; the architect is thought to have been Khufu's relative Hemiunu. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza

question: Around 2560 BC, in the desert at Giza in Egypt, workers finished the last polished capstone on the Great Pyramid. At 147 meters (481 ft) tall, it was the tallest thing any human being had ever built. And no taller building would rise anywhere on Earth for a very long time after. About how long did the Great Pyramid hold that world-height record?
context: At its original height of 146.6 m (481 ft), the Great Pyramid held the tallest-structure record for more than 3,800 years -- longer than any other building has ever held it -- until a medieval cathedral spire in England finally rose higher around AD 1311. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_world's_tallest_buildings  (Legend.)

question: The Great Pyramid was raised not by slaves but by teams of paid Egyptian workers, who split into proud work-gangs and scrawled their gang-names across the great stone blocks. One boastful crew-name still survives on the pyramid. What did that gang call itself?
context: The pyramid was built not by slaves but by paid, well-fed Egyptian crews who lived in a town beside Giza and were buried in tombs of honour close to their king. They organized into gangs and left their names on the stones -- one crew proudly called itself 'The Friends of Khufu Gang'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza  (Legend.)

question: The Great Pyramid held the record as the tallest structure on Earth for thousands of years. The record finally fell around AD 1311, when builders in England topped it with a soaring cathedral spire only a few metres higher. Which cathedral stole the crown?
context: Lincoln Cathedral's central spire reached roughly 160 m, beating the pyramid by only a few metres -- then the spire blew down in a storm in 1549 and was never rebuilt, handing the pyramid back a share of its glory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Cathedral  (Legend.)

question: The Great Pyramid at Giza in Egypt was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC. Its four huge sides are laid out so exactly that they are off by only a tenth of a degree — straighter than many modern skyscrapers. Khufu's workers had no compass, no laser, and no satellite to help. What did they line this monster monument up with?
choices: the midsummer sunrise over the desert
the course of the Nile past Giza
the yearly rising of the star Sirius
context: Each side faces one of the cardinal directions with an average error of just 3 minutes and 38 seconds of arc -- about 0.06 of a degree. How Khufu's builders achieved this without a magnetic compass is still debated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza  (Legend.)

question: In 1954, on the sunny south side of the Great Pyramid at Giza in Egypt, an archaeologist named Kamal el-Mallakh pried open a sealed rock pit that had been shut for 4,500 years. Inside were 1,224 pieces of cedar wood, laid in careful order like a giant flat-pack. When they were fitted back together, what had the Egyptians buried in the sand beside their dead pharaoh Khufu?
choices: a life-sized statue of the king
a heavy sledge for the coffin
a fleet of small model boats
context: The 'Khufu ship' is a 43-metre cedar vessel, dismantled and sealed in its pit for 4,500 years -- one of the oldest and best-preserved boats to survive from antiquity, probably meant to carry the king's spirit across the sky. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza

question: Deep inside the Great Pyramid, the King's Chamber is roofed not with limestone but with enormous dark granite beams -- the largest weighing about 80 tonnes, as much as a dozen elephants. The Egyptians floated that granite some 800 km down the Nile from a single southern quarry-city. Which city?
context: The hard granite came from quarries at Aswan, roughly 800-900 km up the Nile to the south. Moving 80-tonne beams that far by river and levering them into place high inside the pyramid remains one of the great feats of ancient engineering. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza  (Legend.)

question: Today the Great Pyramid looks like a rough brown staircase of bare blocks, but for thousands of years it gleamed brilliant white, sheathed in polished limestone that flashed in the sun. After a great earthquake shook those casing-stones loose in 1303, where did most of them end up?
answer: built into the mosques of nearby Cairo
choices: built into the mosques of nearby Cairo
context: Cairo's rulers carted the polished white Tura-limestone casing away to build mosques and fortresses. Stripped bare, the pyramid shrank from its original 146.6 m to about 138.5 m today, and its golden capstone was lost in antiquity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza  (Legend.)

question: In 2013, diggers at the Red Sea harbour of Wadi al-Jarf in Egypt found the oldest written papyrus ever seen on Earth. It is a workman's logbook kept about 4,500 years ago, in the reign of pharaoh Khufu, by a shipping inspector named Merer. Day by day, in his own words, what does Merer's diary say his crew of sailors was busy doing?
answer: ferrying boatloads of limestone up to Giza
choices: ferrying boatloads of limestone up to Giza
handing out copper chisels to the stone-cutters
rationing grain and beer to the work-gang
launching a funeral barge for the dead king
context: In the 'Diary of Merer', a Fourth-Dynasty inspector logs his crew ferrying white Tura limestone by boat up the Nile to Giza in Khufu's 26th regnal year -- the oldest inscribed papyrus ever found, and a real worker's-eye account of the Great Pyramid going up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary_of_Merer  (Legend.)

question: Directly above the King's Chamber the builders left five low, empty rooms, stacked one on top of another and roofed with massive granite slabs -- chambers nobody was ever meant to enter. Why did the Egyptians hide this strange stack of empty rooms in the heart of the pyramid?
answer: to spread the weight of the stone piled above
choices: to spread the weight of the stone piled above
to hide the pharaoh's treasure from robbers
to let the dead king's soul fly to the stars
to trap grave-robbers in false chambers
context: These five stacked 'relieving chambers' distribute the immense weight of stone overhead so the King's Chamber ceiling would not be crushed -- careful structural engineering. When they were opened in 1837, painted gang-names left by the work-crews were found on the hidden blocks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza

question: Narrow shafts, far too cramped to crawl through, angle upward from the Great Pyramid's inner chambers toward the sky. According to a famous -- and hotly disputed -- theory, around 2500 BC the southern shaft aimed almost exactly at one bright constellation. Which star-pattern was it?
answer: the three stars of Orion's Belt
choices: the three stars of Orion's Belt
the seven stars of the Big Dipper
context: The 'star-shaft' theory notes the southern shaft pointed near Orion's Belt -- which the Egyptians linked to the god Osiris -- while the northern shaft pointed near Thuban, the pole star of that era. But it is heavily contested: the shafts are blocked by stone and could never have been used to see the sky, and Thuban sat about 2 degrees off the true pole in 2500 BC, so most archaeologists treat the Orion idea as fringe. Source: https://earthsky.org/brightest-stars/thuban-past-north-star/  (Legend.)

question: At Giza in Egypt stand the Great Pyramids, raised from millions of cut limestone blocks that gangs of workers hauled up ramps and stacked into place over decades. Right at the pyramids' feet crouches the Great Sphinx — a stone lion with a human king's face, 20 m tall and 73 m long. How did Egyptian workers make this giant stone beast?
answer: By carving downward into a single ridge of natural rock
choices: By carving downward into a single ridge of natural rock
By stacking hundreds of cut limestone blocks
By shaping a core of sun-dried mud-brick
By heaping rubble and coating it in white plaster
context: The Sphinx was not built up like the pyramids beside it -- it was cut in place, straight down and inward, out of one natural rise of limestone bedrock. That makes it the largest monolith, or single-stone, statue to survive from the ancient world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Sphinx_of_Giza; worldkings.org.

question: Today the Great Sphinx at Giza in Egypt is bare tan stone, blending into the sandy desert around it. But archaeologists have found tiny flakes still clinging in the cracks of its face and body. Those flakes prove the huge lion did not always look this way when the pharaohs were alive 4,500 years ago. What do the traces show the Sphinx once was?
context: Flecks of red pigment survive on the face, with traces of yellow and blue on the body -- the Sphinx was once vividly painted. It also wore a braided royal beard; a fallen fragment of that beard is now in the British Museum in London, recovered when Giovanni Caviglia excavated Giza in 1817. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Sphinx_of_Giza; ancientegyptonline.co.uk.

question: Stand in front of the Great Sphinx at Giza in Egypt and something looks strange. The huge human head, carved 4,500 years ago, still has sharp cheekbones and a firm jaw. But the enormous lion body below it is lumpy and deeply worn away, as if a bath sponge had rotted around a marble bust. Why did the head last so much better than the body?
answer: The head was carved from harder, tougher limestone
choices: The head was carved from harder, tougher limestone
The head was buried in protective sand for longer
The head was repaired again and again by priests
The head faced away from the sandy desert winds
context: The Giza bedrock is layered. The upper layer, where the head was carved, is hard and durable, so the pharaoh's face has kept its detail. The lower layers that form the lion body are much softer, and thousands of years of wind and salt have eaten them into deep hollows. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Sphinx_of_Giza; studiomatrx.org.

question: There is a famous story that in 1798, when the French general Napoleon Bonaparte led an army into Egypt, his soldiers blasted the Great Sphinx's nose off with a cannon for target practice. It is a great tale. But historians insist it cannot possibly be true. What one clear piece of evidence proves the Napoleon nose-story wrong?
answer: Travelers sketched the noseless Sphinx decades before Napoleon was born
choices: Travelers sketched the noseless Sphinx decades before Napoleon was born
Napoleon's soldiers never actually marched as far as Giza
Cannon fire of that day could never chip such hard stone
Egyptian records blame a lightning strike for the damage
context: A drawing by the Danish traveler Frederic Norden, made in 1737 -- decades before Napoleon was even born in 1769 -- already shows the Sphinx with no nose. The 15th-century historian al-Maqrizi recorded that the nose had been deliberately smashed off around 1378 by Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr, who was angry that local people were leaving offerings to the statue for a good harvest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Sphinx_of_Giza; historyhit.com/who-broke-the-giant-sphinxs-nose.  (Legend.)

question: Standing upright between the Great Sphinx's colossal stone paws is a slab of granite carved about 3,400 years ago. It tells how a young prince, resting in the Sphinx's shadow while the statue lay buried to its shoulders in sand, heard it speak to him in a dream. According to the legend on the slab, what did the Sphinx promise the prince?
answer: That he would become pharaoh of Egypt
choices: That he would become pharaoh of Egypt
That he would live forever after death
That he would find a hidden treasure
That he would win a great desert battle
context: The prince was Thutmose IV. The granite slab, called the Dream Stela, records that he cleared the sand away as the Sphinx asked -- and he went on to rule Egypt around 1400 BC. The Dream Stela still stands between the Sphinx's paws today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Stele; pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/sphinx-stela.  (Legend.)

question: The rock walls of the pit that was quarried out around the Great Sphinx are cut with deep, rounded vertical grooves. Geologist Robert Schoch argued these grooves were worn by heavy rainfall, which would make the Sphinx thousands of years older than its usual date of 2500 BC. Mainstream geologists and Egyptologists strongly reject his idea. How do they explain the grooves instead?
answer: Salt crystallizing inside the stone flaked its surface away
choices: Salt crystallizing inside the stone flaked its surface away
Rising groundwater slowly dissolved the stone from below
Ancient quarry workers cut the grooves there on purpose
Blowing sandstorms scoured the walls into smooth flutes
context: Robert Schoch's 'water-erosion hypothesis' claims the grooves imply a date of roughly 7000 to 5000 BC, but mainstream geologists and Egyptologists reject it as pseudoarchaeology. They explain the weathering by salt crystallization -- salt soaked into the porous limestone repeatedly crystallizes and expands, flaking off the surface -- and they point to the archaeological evidence that dates the Sphinx to about 2500 BC. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphinx_water_erosion_hypothesis.

question: The Great Wall of China is not one single line marching across the map. It is a huge web of main walls, side walls, watchtowers, and rebuilt stretches, patched up by dynasty after dynasty over 2,000 years. In 2012, after six years of survey work, China finished measuring every single piece for the first time. Added together, about how far do all the walls of the Great Wall run?
context: The 2012 survey put the whole system at 21,196.18 km (13,171 miles) -- more than half the length of the equator (~40,075 km). The 9,000-km option is a real trap: the Ming wall alone runs about 8,850 km. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China (2012 National Cultural Heritage Administration survey).

question: The stretch of Great Wall on a thousand postcards is a restored section in the mountains just northwest of Beijing. It gets so mobbed -- nearly 10 million visitors in one year -- that officials now cap it at 65,000 people a day. Which section is this?
context: Badaling, the most visited and most heavily restored stretch, drew nearly 10 million visitors in 2018; the 65,000-per-day cap came in 2019. Mutianyu, Jinshanling and Simatai are other well-known sections near Beijing, far quieter. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China (Badaling visitor figures and cap).

question: Countless textbooks claimed the Great Wall is the one human structure you could pick out from the Moon with your bare eyes. It's false, and here is the scale of why: from the Moon, about 384,000 km away, the wall's width would show as a single faint line at an impossible distance. About how thin does it appear?
answer: like a human hair seen from 3 km away
choices: like a human hair seen from 3 km away
like a human hair seen from 1 km away
like a human hair seen from 10 km away
like a human hair seen from 30 km away
context: You cannot see the Great Wall from the Moon with the naked eye, and it is not reliably visible from low Earth orbit without magnification either. China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, returning in 2003, said: 'the scenery was very beautiful, but I didn't see the Great Wall.' Neil Armstrong said it was 'definitely not visible from the Moon.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China (Visibility from space); scientificamerican.com.  (Legend.)

question: For over 2,000 years, China's northern frontier was the empire's great weak point — an open plain that the fast horse warriors of the Mongolian steppe could sweep across at will. To hold that border, one dynasty after another piled up walls of packed earth, and later of stone and brick, sometimes linking older stretches, sometimes rebuilding from ruins. Which of these best tells how the Great Wall we know today truly came to be?
answer: walls begun before Qin, linked under Qin, rebuilt by Han and Ming
choices: walls begun before Qin, linked under Qin, rebuilt by Han and Ming
walls begun under Qin, extended by Han, rebuilt by Tang and Ming
walls begun by Han, linked under Sui, rebuilt by Song and Ming
walls begun before Qin, abandoned by Han, rebuilt by Yuan and Ming
context: The earliest border walls date to the 7th century BC; the First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang, linked existing walls around 221 BC; the Han, the Northern dynasties and the Ming each built their own. The 2012 survey counted 10,051 separate wall sections, 1,764 ramparts or trenches, 29,510 buildings and 2,211 fortifications and passes -- a network, not a line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China (History; 2012 survey breakdown).

question: The grand grey wall you see on China travel posters — cut stone battlements and watchtowers marching over the green mountain ridges outside Beijing — is mostly the work of one single dynasty. About 8,850 km of it was built between the years 1368 and 1644, to guard the Chinese heartland from Mongol raiders on the northern grasslands. Which Chinese dynasty raised this famous version of the Great Wall?
context: The Ming (1368-1644) wall runs about 8,851.8 km (5,500 miles): 6,259 km of built wall, 359 km of trenches and 2,232 km of natural barriers like ridges and rivers. Earlier dynasties built in rammed earth; the Ming upgraded to fired brick and cut stone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China (2009 Ming survey).

question: In the Gobi and the Gansu desert, the oldest surviving stretches of wall were built from whatever the empty land could give. Han-dynasty crews, two thousand years ago, tamped their ramparts from local materials that have lasted near Dunhuang ever since. What were these desert walls built from?
answer: reed and willow layers packed with sand and gravel
choices: reed and willow layers packed with sand and gravel
sun-dried mud bricks stacked in courses
packed loess earth faced with plaster
context: Some sections show about seven willow layers (~0.2 m thick) alternating with reed layers (~0.1 m thick), the plant matter binding the sand like rebar. After two thousand years of sandstorms, stretches near Dunhuang are still standing. Source: chinadiscovery.com Han Great Wall; travelchinaguide.com construction/material; ancient-origins.net reed study.

question: At its far eastern end the Great Wall does something it does nowhere else: it marches straight off the land and into the ocean. In 1579 the Ming pushed a stone spur about 20 m out into the Bohai Sea -- the one place the wall meets open water. By what name is this ocean-plunging landmark known?
context: Laolongtou -- 'Old Dragon's Head' -- near Shanhai Pass is the only place the Great Wall meets the sea; the spur looks like a dragon dipping its head to drink. It was built in 1579. The Nine-Eye Tower, the Wangjing (Beijing-viewing) Tower at Simatai and the marble Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass are other celebrated Great Wall landmarks -- but every one of them stands well inland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China; travelchinaguide.com Laolongtou.

question: Two thousand kilometres to the west, the Great Wall ends not in the sea but in the desert -- a lone fortress guarding the narrow Hexi Corridor, throat of the old Silk Road. A stone tablet there boasts it is 'the First and Greatest Pass Under Heaven.' Name this western stronghold.
context: Jiayuguan, the Jiayu Pass, begun in 1372 in Gansu, guarded the Silk Road's Hexi Corridor at the wall's western limit; its walls run 733 m and stand about 11 m high. The eastern Shanhai Pass, by contrast, anchors the wall at the sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiayu_Pass; chinahighlights.com Jiayuguan.

question: Legend says the dead who built the Great Wall were sealed inside it -- the tale of Meng Jiangnu holds that her weeping for her lost husband toppled a stretch of wall to bare the bones beneath. Yet archaeologists find no bodies in the wall at all. What they did find is the mortar the Ming used: slaked lime blended with one unexpected ingredient, a recipe so tough that weeds still struggle to root in it. What did the Ming mix into their mortar?
context: No human remains have been found built into the wall. The Ming bound their brick and stone with a mortar of glutinous 'sticky-rice' soup and slaked lime -- the rice starch making it so strong that weeds still struggle to root in it centuries later. The Meng Jiangnu tale -- her grief supposedly toppling a 400-km stretch to reveal the bones beneath -- has been retold for over 2,000 years as a protest against the wall's brutal conscript labour. And that labour was real: over the centuries, forced work on the walls cost an enormous, undeniable human toll. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China (sticky-rice mortar); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Meng_Jiang; topchinatravel.com Meng Jiangnu.  (Legend.)

question: One of the most repeated boasts about the Great Wall of China is that it is the only human-made thing you can pick out from outer space. Almost everyone assumes the idea was born in the 1960s, when the first astronauts orbited Earth and looked down. But the boast is much older than that. When was the 'visible from space' claim first written down?
answer: in the 1700s, from an English antiquarian
choices: in the 1700s, from an English antiquarian
in the 1960s, from the first astronauts in orbit
in the 1800s, from European Silk Road explorers
in Ming times, from China's own mapmakers
context: The claim traces to a 1754 letter by the English antiquarian William Stukeley and was popularised by a 1932 Ripley's Believe It or Not! cartoon -- both decades before any human left the ground (the first human spaceflight came in 1961). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China (Visibility from space); thevintagenews.com.  (Legend.)

question: Greenland, buried under a huge ice sheet nearly 2 km thick, is called the world's largest island — about 2.17 million square km of land. But Australia is much bigger, at about 7.7 million square km, and geographers leave Australia off the island list on one strict rule. What rule keeps Australia out?
answer: It is counted as a continent.
choices: It is counted as a continent.
It lies south of the equator.
context: Australia is bigger than Greenland but is classed as a continent, so Greenland keeps the 'largest island' crown — about 1.71 million km2, roughly 80% of it buried under one continuous ice sheet. Source: Wikipedia, 'Greenland ice sheet.'

question: Greenland is the world's largest island, sitting mostly inside the Arctic Circle, and almost all of it is buried under one enormous ice sheet. Imagine drilling straight down through the middle of that ice. You would grind through an astonishing depth of solid ice before your drill bit ever tapped the rock beneath. At its very thickest point, how deep is the Greenland ice?
context: At its deepest the ice reaches about 3,488 m (11,444 ft) — over 3 km — and averages roughly 1,673 m, close to a full mile of solid ice from top to bedrock. Source: Wikipedia, 'Greenland ice sheet.'

question: The Greenland ice sheet ranks as the second-largest sheet of ice on Earth — but 'second' hides how badly it is outmatched. All of Greenland's ice adds up to only about an eighth of the ice piled on the planet's true ice giant. Which land holds that colossal load?
context: Greenland's ice sheet holds about 2.9 million km3 of ice — yet that is only around 12% of the ice locked in the far larger Antarctic ice sheet. Source: Wikipedia, 'Greenland ice sheet.'

question: On 22 December 1991, an automatic weather station high on the Greenland ice sheet logged a truly shocking reading — the temperature fell to about minus 69.6 C (about minus 93 F), cold enough to freeze exposed skin in seconds. Scientists reviewed and confirmed the measurement decades later, and that brutal number still stands as a record. A record for what?
answer: the coldest ever recorded in the Northern Hemisphere
choices: the coldest ever recorded in the Northern Hemisphere
the coldest ever recorded anywhere on Earth
the coldest ever recorded at any inhabited research station
the coldest ever recorded on any ice sheet
context: The minus 69.6 C reading is the coldest in the whole Northern Hemisphere. Antarctica is colder still (near minus 89 C at Vostok), which is why this stands as a hemisphere record, not a global one. Source: Wikipedia, 'Greenland ice sheet.'

question: The Greenland ice sheet is a frozen freshwater reservoir on a scale that dwarfs imagination. If every last bit of it were to melt into the sea, the world's oceans would rise enough to redraw coastlines across the globe. By roughly how much would global sea level climb?
context: Melting all of Greenland's ice would raise global sea level about 7.4 m (24 ft) — enough to redraw coastlines worldwide. It is the second-largest ice mass on Earth after Antarctica. Source: Wikipedia, 'Greenland ice sheet.'

question: Picture the Greenland ice sheet lifted clean off the island for a moment. Its staggering mass of ice has loaded the land for hundreds of thousands of years, and geologists were stunned by what that endless burden has done to the bedrock at the island's center. What has become of central Greenland's bedrock?
answer: It has been pressed into a below-sea-level bowl.
choices: It has been pressed into a below-sea-level bowl.
It has been pushed up into a high plateau.
It has been split by a deep rift valley.
It has been scoured into a flat lowland plain.
context: The ice is so heavy it has pressed central Greenland's bedrock to roughly 300 m below sea level; about a fifth of the island's bedrock now sits below today's sea level. Strip the ice away and the interior would be a below-sea-level basin ringed by coastal mountains. Source: EarthDate, 'Under Greenland's Ice Sheet.'

question: In 2013, aircraft flying over Greenland with ice-piercing radar mapped a huge canyon hidden far beneath the ice sheet. The buried canyon runs more than 750 km long — longer than any open canyon anywhere on Earth's surface, longer even than the Grand Canyon in the United States. What most likely carved this hidden mega-canyon under the Greenland ice?
context: Found in 2013 with ice-penetrating radar from NASA's Operation IceBridge, this buried canyon runs more than 750 km (466 mi), up to 800 m deep, snaking north toward the Petermann Glacier fjord. Its V-shaped walls and flat floor mark it as the work of an ancient river that flowed before the ice came. Source: Wikipedia, 'Greenland's Grand Canyon'; NASA SVS, 'Greenland's Mega-Canyon.'

question: Scientists drill long cylinders of ice — called ice cores — from deep in the Greenland ice sheet, then read their thousands of stacked yearly layers like a frozen diary of the climate. Sealed inside the oldest ice is one ancient sample so perfectly preserved that scientists can measure it directly instead of estimating it from other clues. What is this trapped sample?
context: The famous GISP2 core, over 3 km long, records about 110,000 years of climate in its annual layers. The trapped bubbles are real samples of ancient atmosphere that scientists can measure directly. Source: NASA Earth Observatory, 'The Ice Core Record.'

question: Each summer the surface of the Greenland ice sheet blooms with dazzling pools and rushing rivers of electric-blue meltwater. Here and there, a whole river suddenly vanishes — plunging down a near-vertical shaft that bores clean through the ice to the bedrock far below, greasing the glacier's slide toward the sea. What are these roaring ice-shafts called?
context: A moulin is a near-vertical shaft carved by meltwater plunging through the ice. Reaching the bed, the water can lubricate the whole glacier's slide toward the sea. Source: Science/AAAS, 'The great Greenland meltdown.'

question: Beneath the edge of the Greenland ice sheet, at Hiawatha Glacier, radar in 2018 revealed a hidden circular basin about 31 km wide. It ranks as one of the largest features of its kind ever discovered on Earth. What most likely formed this buried ring-shaped structure?
context: The 31-km crater under Hiawatha Glacier was likely blasted by an iron asteroid about 1.5 km across. DISPUTED: early guesses tied it to the Younger Dryas (~13,000 years ago), but 2022 dating of melt-rock crystals put the impact at about 58 million years ago — the current best estimate. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hiawatha Glacier'; Science.org.  (Legend.)

question: Sermeq Kujalleq — the Jakobshavn Glacier on Greenland's west coast — is no sluggish trickle of ice. At its peak, this glacier was clocked racing toward the ocean faster than nearly any other glacier on Earth. Glaciers are proverbially slow, so brace yourself: how fast did Jakobshavn move at its fastest?
context: At its peak Sermeq Kujalleq raced over 45 m (150 ft) per DAY and is Greenland's biggest iceberg factory — about 35 billion tonnes of ice a year. Its Ilulissat Icefjord became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. Source: Wikipedia, 'Jakobshavn Glacier'; Smithsonian Ocean.

question: On the night of April 14th, 1912, the huge ocean liner Titanic struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic and sank on her first voyage, drowning over 1,500 people. That iceberg was not born in the open sea. About three years earlier, it had broken off a great glacier and drifted slowly south on the ocean currents. Which icy homeland did the Titanic iceberg most likely come from?
context: The Titanic's iceberg most likely calved from a Greenland glacier around 1909, then rode the West Greenland current up into Baffin Bay and south past Newfoundland before the April 1912 collision — a years-long journey. (Origin is a best estimate.) Source: titanicfacts.net, 'Titanic Iceberg.'  (Legend.)

question: For years, nearly everyone blamed warm air for melting Greenland's glaciers. Then scientists probing the deep fjords uncovered a second, long-overlooked culprit — one that gnaws at the glaciers from a direction almost no one was watching, causing giant tongues of ice to snap off. What is this hidden culprit?
context: Warm, salty Atlantic water sneaks into the fjords and melts the underwater ice fronts, undercutting glaciers so the ice above snaps off. In one survey of 226 glaciers, the 74 sitting in deep fjords caused nearly half of Greenland's ice loss from 1992 to 2017 — this is 'ocean-driven melt.' Source: Science Advances, 'Ocean forcing drives glacier retreat in Greenland.'

question: There is one warm ocean current so powerful that it moves more water than every river on Earth put together. It rises out of the warm tropics near Florida, races north along the east coast of the United States, and then peels off across the Atlantic Ocean toward Europe. It is one big reason London has such mild winters. What is this famous Atlantic current called?
context: Through the narrow Straits of Florida the Gulf Stream pushes about 30 million cubic metres of water every second (oceanographers call this 30 'sverdrups'), and swells to roughly 150 sverdrups south of Newfoundland - while ALL the rivers emptying into the Atlantic together add up to only about 0.6. Born in the Gulf of Mexico, it carries tropical warmth far up the US coast and out into the North Atlantic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream

question: London and Dublin sit as far north as Canada's Labrador coast, where harbours freeze solid all winter. Yet these cities almost never suffer a hard freeze. A branch of the Gulf Stream carries tropical warmth across the ocean to Britain and Ireland. What is that European-bound branch called?
context: The far, Europe-bound arm of the Gulf Stream is the North Atlantic Drift (also called the North Atlantic Current). London sits at about 51.5 degrees N and Dublin at 53.3 degrees N - the same band as Labrador's frozen Canadian coast - yet the Drift's warmth spares them the hard winters those latitudes 'should' bring. Sources: americanscientist.org/article/the-source-of-europes-mild-climate ; weatheronline.co.uk (North Atlantic Drift)

question: The Gulf Stream races north pressed close against the American shore, a warm ribbon hugging one beach after another. Then, off a long low cape jutting far into the Atlantic, it suddenly peels away from the land. From there it strikes across the open sea toward Europe. At which cape does the current abandon the coast?
context: The Gulf Stream clings to the US coast until roughly Cape Hatteras, North Carolina (near 35-36 degrees N), where it separates from the shore and heads out across the open Atlantic toward Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream

question: Long before anyone had mapped it, Nantucket whalers could find the Gulf Stream's invisible edge far out at sea, with no instruments at all. They read it three ways: by how the whales behaved, by the temperature of the water - and by one clue they could spot with their own eyes from the deck. What was that visible sign?
context: Nantucket whalers could read the Gulf Stream's invisible edge by three signs - the behaviour of the whales, the temperature of the water, and its colour - knowledge no instrument of the day could match. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream

question: The Gulf Stream's warm branch keeps flowing north the whole length of Norway's coast, holding the harbours open through winter deep inside the Arctic Circle. One such never-freezing port, Tromso, became famous as the launching place for what kind of daring voyages?
choices: the hunt for the Northwest Passage
trade voyages down to the Baltic
context: The warm current climbs the whole Norwegian coast, keeping ports ice-free through winter far above the Arctic Circle - including Tromso, long a gateway for polar expeditions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream

question: The Gulf Stream is a genuine river in the sea, a warm ribbon roughly 100 km wide with edges so sharp a ship can cross a sudden temperature change within minutes. But this ocean river is not merely a thin surface skin. Measured from top to bottom, how deep does it actually reach?
context: The Gulf Stream is a genuine 'river in the sea': about 100 km (62 miles) wide, 800-1,200 metres deep, with a top surface speed near 2.5 m/s (about 5.6 mph). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream

question: On Scotland's storm-lashed north-west coast, at the same latitude as Moscow and the shores of Hudson Bay, Inverewe Garden hides behind a ring of hills right in the path of the Gulf Stream's warmth. There, plants from far hotter lands grow outdoors the year round. Which tropical-looking trees most astonish visitors by thriving this far north?
context: At Inverewe Garden on Loch Ewe, north-west Scotland (about 57.8 degrees N - as far north as Moscow and Hudson Bay), palm trees, eucalyptus and other subtropical plants flourish, warmed by the Gulf Stream's drift and sheltered by a ring of mountains. Source: nts.org.uk/visit/places/inverewe

question: The Gulf Stream never runs in a straight line; instead it wanders through great sweeping loops. Every so often a whole loop pinches off and drifts away as a self-contained warm whirlpool up to 300 km across, wider than a small country. Cut loose from the parent current, how long can one of these runaway warm eddies keep spinning?
context: As the Gulf Stream meanders it pinches off spinning 'warm-core rings' - loops of warm water roughly 100-300 km across that break free, drift south-west, and can survive for months, sometimes up to a year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warm_core_ring

question: The Gulf Stream is not one of a kind. Every ocean has a fast, warm current sprinting up its WESTERN edge, hauling tropical heat toward the poles. In the Pacific this twin of the Gulf Stream sweeps north-east past Taiwan and Japan, its water so deep-blue it looks almost black. What is the Pacific's version called?
context: Every ocean basin has a fast, warm 'western boundary current' on its western edge; the Gulf Stream's Pacific twin is the Kuroshio, or 'Black Current' (Japanese kuro, 'black' + shio, 'tide'), named for its deep blue-black water. It carries about 50 million tons of seawater per second past Japan - by volume even more than the Gulf Stream, a flow likened to some 6,000 rivers the size of the Danube or Volga. Sources: earthdata.nasa.gov ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuroshio_Current

question: In 1768 Benjamin Franklin, working in London as a deputy postmaster, could not fathom why the King's mail packets took so much longer to cross the Atlantic than ordinary merchant ships. The reason was a powerful warm current - the Gulf Stream - that the packets fought head-on while the merchant skippers knew to skirt it. The man who explained the riddle to Franklin, and drew the current from memory to make the first chart of it ever produced, was his own cousin Timothy Folger. What was Folger's trade?
context: Puzzled that mail packets crossed slower than merchant ships, Franklin learned from his cousin, Nantucket whaling captain Timothy Folger, that the packets were fighting a warm current the whalers knew well. Folger sketched it from memory, and the chart was engraved and printed in London by 1769 - the first chart of the Gulf Stream. Folger added that the whalers had warned the British captains to steer clear, 'but they were too wise to be counselled by simple American fishermen.' Source: smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/benjamin-franklin-was-first-chart-gulf-stream-180963066/

question: On the Tongan island of Tongatapu stands a giant stone gateway. Two upright pillars support a single massive lintel across the top. The structure rises 5.2 metres tall and dates back about 800 years, earning it the nickname the Stonehenge of the Pacific. What do Tongans call this monument?
context: The Haʻamonga ʻa Maui is a trilithon — two standing stones capped by a lintel — about 5.2 m tall, standing near the village of Niutoua in the old royal district of Heketā at the north end of Tongatapu. Its likeness to England's prehistoric monument earned it the nickname 'Stonehenge of the Pacific,' and its grounds were made a national park in 1972. The distractors are all real Pacific stone wonders: Nan Madol is a ruined basalt city in Micronesia, the Latte Stones are carved pillars in the Mariana Islands, and the moai are the giant statues of Rapa Nui (Easter Island). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haʻamonga_ʻa_Maui.

question: The Ha'amonga 'a Maui has stood on Tongatapu for about 800 years, with each of its two pillars weighing 30 to 40 tonnes. A massive stone lintel bridges the tops of the pillars. The Tongans quarried and raised the whole gateway by hand, without any metal tools or cranes. What kind of stone did they use?
context: For a monument built without metal tools, cranes, or wheels, the material is the marvel: coral limestone, quarried from Tongatapu's own reef platform — a low coral island's one abundant building stone, essentially the pressed skeletons of ancient reef. The uprights hold up a lintel of roughly 15 tonnes, cut to drop into carved grooves so it locks in place by its own weight. Basalt built Micronesia's Nan Madol, granite the great works of Egypt, and sandstone much of England's Stonehenge — but Tonga's giants are made of reef. Sources: thearchaeologist.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haʻamonga_ʻa_Maui.

question: A short walk from the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui on Tongatapu stands a second monument, the ʻEsi Maka Faʻakinanga — a great stone tied to Tuʻitatui, the very king who raised the trilithon. His name itself means 'strike the knee.' Tongan tradition explains exactly why he had this stone set where it stands. What reason does the tradition give?
answer: he leaned against it, safe from any attacker behind him
choices: he leaned against it, safe from any attacker behind him
he sharpened his war-clubs against its rough face
he stood upon it to be seen above his people
he moored his royal war-canoe to it at high tide
context: Tongan tradition calls the stone the ʻEsi Maka Faʻakinanga, Tuʻitatui's throne or backrest: he leaned against it while holding court so that, with solid rock behind him, no assassin could creep up from behind. It fits his fearsome name — Tuʻitatui, 'strike the knee' — said to warn anyone who came too close as he sat. Source: worldhistorycommons.org/haamonga-maui-tonga.

question: The great trilithon on Tongatapu is called the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui — 'the Burden of Maui.' Tongan legend says the demigod Maui himself carried its colossal stones across nearly 1,000 km of open ocean on a giant canoe, certain the blocks were far too heavy for any mortal to move. From which distant island does the legend say Maui brought the stones?
context: Legend says Maui hauled the stones from ʻUvea (Wallis Island), nearly 1,000 km away, slung on his haʻamonga — a carrying-pole balanced across the shoulders with a load hung at each end, which is why the monument's name means 'the Burden of Maui.' In truth the coral limestone matches quarries on Tongatapu itself, so no ocean voyage was ever needed. ʻUvea, Samoa, Fiji, and Rotuma are all real islands of the central Pacific. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haʻamonga_ʻa_Maui.

question: About 12 km from the Ha'amonga 'a Maui, at the old royal capital of Mu'a on Tongatapu, rise the tombs of the Tu'i Tonga kings. There are about 28 flat-topped step-pyramids, built from massive stone slabs fitted together without any mortar. What are these terraced royal tombs called?
context: The Langi are the terraced tombs of the Tuʻi Tonga kings at Muʻa (Lapaha), the capital Tuʻitatui founded around 1200 AD when he moved the royal seat south from Heketā. Around 28 of these flat-topped step-pyramids survive; the grandest, the Paepae ʻo Teleʻa, is a three-tiered platform of huge slabs — some about 2.4 m wide — fitted together without mortar for a 16th-century king. (A marae is a Polynesian sacred courtyard, an ahu is an Easter Island statue platform, and the moai are the statues themselves.) Sources: book.tongapocketguide.com; whc.unesco.org tentative list, 'Ancient Capitals of the Kingdom of Tonga'.

question: In 1967 the Tongan king Taufaʻahau Tupou IV studied a small V-shaped notch cut into the top of the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui's lintel and argued it was no accident. With the historian Tevita Fale, he proposed that the trilithon was more than a royal gateway — that the notch was a deliberate sighting line to the sky. What did they claim the great stones secretly worked as?
answer: a stone calendar marking the solstices
choices: a stone calendar marking the solstices
a sundial telling the daily hours
a marker of the moon's monthly phases
a star map for ocean navigators
