context: King Taufaʻahau Tupou IV proposed in 1967 that the V-shaped notch lined up with sunrise at the summer and winter solstices, making the trilithon a giant stone calendar; the historian Tevita Fale identified the mark. It remains a THEORY — the astronomer C.F. Velt argued the notch is too small to be a reliable sighting device. What is certain is that Tuʻitatui, the 11th Tuʻi Tonga king, raised the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui around 1200 AD as a ceremonial gateway into his royal compound at Heketā. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haʻamonga_ʻa_Maui.

question: On the equator, over the Amazon and Congo, the sun beats down almost straight above. Most afternoons the sky fills with towering storm clouds and pours rain. That is why huge rainforests grow along the equator. In this steamy weather, what is the hot air doing?
context: This is the rising, upward branch of the great tropical loop. The blazing equatorial sun heats the surface air until it billows up into towering thunderclouds and dumps rain almost daily -- which is exactly why the Amazon and Congo rainforests sit in a band right on the equator. Source: Wikipedia, 'Intertropical Convergence Zone' (intense solar heating forces air upward in vigorous thunderstorms). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertropical_Convergence_Zone

question: Look at a globe and something jumps out: the Sahara, the Arabian Desert, the Kalahari, and the Outback all sit near 30 degrees north latitude. A matching desert belt runs along 30 degrees south too. This is no coincidence, and a single force parches them all. What is the air above these deserts doing?
choices: rising up off the baking sand
sweeping in cold from the poles
context: This is the sinking, descending branch of the loop. Air that rose at the equator drifts poleward high up, cools, and comes back down near 30 degrees -- and sinking air can't form rain, so the ground below bakes under clear skies. That one descending branch lines up the Sahara, Arabian, Kalahari, and Australian deserts at the same latitude in both hemispheres. (The Gobi and the Atacama are dry for a DIFFERENT reason -- blocking mountains and a cold ocean current -- not this sinking air.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Hadley cell.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadley_cell

question: One giant loop ties the whole tropical atmosphere together: air rising at the equator, drifting poleward high up, sinking near 30 degrees, and streaming back along the surface as the trade winds. An English lawyer and amateur weather-watcher first worked it out in 1735, to explain why the trade winds blow from the northeast rather than straight out of the east. This loop now carries his name. What is it called?
context: The man was George Hadley (1685-1768), an English lawyer who preferred physics to law and spent about seven years keeping the weather records for the Royal Society; this circulation loop is his one famous idea. The Ferrel and Polar cells are the real overturning loops of the mid-latitudes and the poles; the Walker cell runs east-west along the equatorial Pacific. Source: Wikipedia, 'George Hadley'; Britannica, 'George Hadley' (1735 paper, 'Concerning the Cause of the General Trade Winds'). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Hadley

question: For a sailing ship, the ocean belt right on the equator was a genuine nightmare. The winds there fall dead and stagnant, and a becalmed vessel could sit trapped for days or weeks with no way home, which proved deadly back when the wind was your only engine. What did sailors call this dreaded equatorial belt?
context: The doldrums sit under the loop's rising branch, right where the air is going straight up instead of blowing sideways -- so there is almost no surface wind. The 'calms of Capricorn' are a separate becalmed belt near 30 degrees south; the roaring forties are the fierce westerlies near 40 degrees south; the trade winds are the steady breezes that blow toward the equator. Source: Wikipedia, 'Intertropical Convergence Zone' (18th-century sailors called it the doldrums; ships becalmed for days or weeks). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertropical_Convergence_Zone

question: Right along the equator runs a rising, rain-making seam where the great tropical loop lifts skyward. It does not hold still, but slides north and south each year, chasing the sun's most direct rays. Where it drifts inland, it becomes the monsoon trough that pours seasonal rain over India and West Africa. What do meteorologists call this migrating rain-seam?
context: The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is where the northeast and southeast trade winds meet and lift -- the rising branch of the Hadley cell. It follows the 'thermal equator,' the band of most direct sunshine, marching north in the northern summer and south in the southern summer, which is what switches the monsoon on and off across India and the African Sahel. The Walker circulation is a separate east-west loop along the equatorial Pacific; the Madden-Julian Oscillation is a pulse of storminess that travels eastward around the tropics; the tropical easterly jet is a high-altitude wind, not a rain seam. Source: Wikipedia, 'Intertropical Convergence Zone.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertropical_Convergence_Zone

question: Near 30 degrees latitude, right under the loop's sinking, drying air, the ocean winds fall dead calm and the sky stays cloudless -- and sail-ships could lie stranded here for weeks on end. Sailors gave this becalmed 30-degree belt a grim, oddly memorable name. What is this calm belt called?
context: The horse latitudes sit near 30 degrees north and south, under the Hadley cell's sinking air, where calm, clear, high-pressure weather starves ships of wind. LEGEND says Spanish ships hauling horses to the Americas got becalmed here, ran short of water, and threw the dying horses overboard -- but Wikipedia treats that story as folk etymology. Better-documented explanations are a sailors' 'dead horse' ritual (marking the end of an already-spent pay advance) and the old word 'horsed' for being carried along by currents. The doldrums are the separate calm belt on the equator. Source: Wikipedia, 'Horse latitudes.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_latitudes

question: When equatorial air rises over the Amazon and Congo, it does not stop low. It keeps climbing 12 to 15 kilometres, about the cruising altitude of a passenger jet, until it slams into the ceiling of the weather layer. Then it fans out toward the poles. What is that ceiling of the weather layer called?
context: The rising branch tops out at the tropopause -- the ceiling of the troposphere, the layer where weather happens, about 12 to 15 kilometers up in the tropics (roughly a jet airliner's cruising altitude). Above it lies the calmer stratosphere. The stratopause, mesopause, and thermopause are the boundaries capping the higher atmospheric layers. Only after reaching this lid does the air turn and flow poleward toward the sinking 30-degree branch. Source: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Hadley cell' (tropical air rises to about 12-15 km at the tropopause). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadley_cell

question: Out over the ocean near 30 degrees, sinking air builds a vast dome of calm, cloudless, heavy air that barely moves all summer. It bakes the Sahara, gives the Mediterranean its dry summers, and flicks African storm-seeds west toward the Caribbean. What is this near-permanent subtropical high called?
context: The Azores High (also called the Bermuda High) is a subtropical high -- one of the semi-permanent domes of sinking air that the descending Hadley branch parks over the oceans. Its clockwise flow steers North Atlantic summer weather: the sinking air dries the Sahara and the Mediterranean, while its southern flank nudges African tropical waves toward the Caribbean, where some become hurricanes. The Hawaiian High is the matching dome over the North Pacific, and the St. Helena and Mascarene Highs are its counterparts over the South Atlantic and the South Indian Ocean. Source: Wikipedia, 'Azores High.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores_High

question: North of the equator, the trade winds crossing the North Atlantic toward the Caribbean slant in from the northeast; south of it, over the South Pacific, they veer the opposite way. Hadley guessed the spinning Earth must bend them, but his physics was slightly off. In 1835 a French scientist nailed the exact rule: on the turning planet, freely moving winds, ocean currents, even a long-range shell swing to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. The deflection now carries his name. What is it called?
context: The Coriolis effect is why the trade winds don't blow straight toward the equator but slant -- from the northeast in the Northern Hemisphere, the southeast in the Southern -- and why hurricanes spin. Hadley had the right instinct (Earth's rotation bends the winds) but used conservation of velocity instead of angular momentum; Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis supplied the correct mathematics in 1835. Source: Wikipedia, 'George Hadley' / 'Coriolis force.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Hadley

question: Satellite and weather records from the past 40 years show the great tropical loop is shifting as the planet warms: its dry, sinking 30-degree edge is creeping slowly poleward, a fraction of a degree of latitude each decade. Scientists find this is pushing the parched subtropical belt into regions that used to be wetter. Which of these regions is being pushed toward a drier future by that poleward creep?
context: As the planet warms, the Hadley cell is WIDENING -- its descending dry edge has shifted poleward by roughly 0.1 to 0.5 degrees of latitude per decade over the last ~40 years -- dragging the subtropical dry zone toward the Mediterranean, California, the American Southwest, southern Australia, and southern Africa, and threatening to make these already-marginal regions significantly drier. The equatorial Congo sits under the wet RISING branch, while Norway's coast and Arctic Canada lie well poleward of the expanding dry belt. Source: Climate Signals, 'Hadley Cell Expansion,' drawing on CMIP5/CMIP6 model studies. https://www.climatesignals.org/climate-signals/hadley-cell-expansion

question: On a summer midnight far in the north — high above places like Alaska or Scandinavia — long after the sun has set and the ground has gone dark, thin electric-blue and silvery wisps still shimmer high, high up in the twilight sky. They only appear near summer, and only close to the polar circle. What are these rare glowing high-altitude clouds called?
context: Noctilucent is Latin for 'night-shining.' The German scientist Otto Jesse coined the name and first photographed them in 1887; the first confirmed sightings had come in 1885, just two years after the great Krakatoa eruption. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noctilucent_cloud; researchgate.net 'Otto Jesse and the Investigation of Noctilucent Clouds.'

question: Over the summer twilight skies of Scandinavia, ordinary weather clouds and cruising jets stay near 10 km up. Noctilucent clouds float far higher, about 80 km up, near the edge of space. They live in a bitterly cold band that almost no other cloud can reach. What is that layer called?
context: At 76–85 km up they are by far the highest clouds on Earth — even high cirrus tops out near 12 km. They are best seen from the far-northern and far-southern belts, about 50 to 70 degrees latitude, in summer twilight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noctilucent_cloud.

question: Long after sunset over Scotland, every lower cloud has already turned black against the night sky. But noctilucent clouds keep glowing with a pale silvery-blue light for hours. Why can these clouds still shine when the sun has already set for the ground below?
answer: They still catch sunlight from below the horizon
choices: They still catch sunlight from below the horizon
They shine with a faint light of their own
They reflect the city lights far below them
They are set aglow by the northern aurora
context: You can catch them only in deep twilight, when the Sun sits 6 to 16 degrees below the horizon: the ground and low air are already in Earth's shadow, but the clouds 80 km up still catch sunlight from below the horizon. Their electric-blue tint comes from ozone, which soaks up the redder light as the low sunbeams skim through it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noctilucent_cloud.

question: In the summer twilight skies over northern Canada, noctilucent clouds are made from the tiniest ice crystals anywhere in the atmosphere, and up at 80 km each crystal still needs a solid speck to freeze around. A NASA satellite has found that about 3% of every crystal is a strange seed material. What do the ice crystals freeze onto?
context: As meteors burn up at the edge of space they leave nanometer-sized 'meteor smoke,' and the clouds' ice freezes onto it — but only where the air drops below about −120°C. Strangely, that coldest spot on Earth sits over the SUMMER pole, which is why summer is the season for these clouds. AIM (launched 2007) also found them growing brighter and creeping toward lower latitudes, perhaps as extra methane becomes water vapor high up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noctilucent_cloud; nasa.gov 'Meteor Smoke Makes Strange Clouds'; nasa.gov AIM highlights.

question: Behind the Himalayan wall spreads a highland so vast and high — averaging about 4,500 m and covering some 2.5 million square km — that it shows up clearly in photographs taken from space. People call it the 'Roof of the World.' What is this immense plateau?
context: The Tibetan Plateau is the highest and largest plateau on Earth — averaging around 4,500 m (14,800 ft) and sprawling across roughly 2.5 million square km, so vast it is easily picked out from orbit, which earned it the nickname 'Roof of the World.' Source: worldatlas.com/plateaus/tibetan-plateau.html; esa.int (Earth from Space: Roof of the world).

question: The Himalayas sweep across South Asia in one unbroken arc some 2,400 km long. They wall the Indian subcontinent off from the icy highlands of Tibet, and they hold Mount Everest, the tallest peak on Earth. Long ago, travellers who spoke Sanskrit — an ancient language of India — gave the whole range a simple two-word name. What does the name Himalaya mean?
context: 'Himalaya' is Sanskrit — hima ('snow' or 'frost') plus alaya ('dwelling' or 'abode') — literally the 'abode of snow.' The range runs as a continuous ~2,400 km (1,500 mile) arc dividing the Indian subcontinent from the Tibetan Plateau. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas.

question: Mount Everest, the tallest mountain on Earth at 8,849 m, sits at the top of the Himalaya range on the border of Nepal and Tibet. And it is not finished growing. Careful satellite measurements show its summit creeps about 4 mm higher every single year — that's about 40 cm each century. Something deep beneath the Himalaya keeps shoving the peak upward. What is doing the pushing?
choices: an ocean plate sliding under another
a plume of hot magma rising up
a long line of volcanoes erupting
context: The Himalayas keep rising because the Indian plate is ramming straight into the Eurasian plate — a continent-against-continent collision, not the ocean-plate subduction that builds volcanic ranges like the Andes. Everest gains roughly 4 mm a year (about 40 cm per century). Source: ucl.ac.uk (Mount Everest growing, 2024); nationalgeographic.com (why Mount Everest can grow and shrink).

question: Climbers speak with awe of the '8,000ers' — Earth's fourteen mountains whose summits pierce above 8,000 m into the thin-aired 'death zone.' Everest and K2 top the list. You might expect these giants to be scattered across the world's great ranges. Instead, how many of the fourteen crowd into the single mountain belt strung along the northern edge of the Indian subcontinent?
context: Every one of Earth's fourteen 8,000-metre peaks stands in the belt where India collides with Asia — 10 in the Himalaya proper (Everest, 8,849 m) and 4 in the adjoining Karakoram (K2, 8,611 m). No other mountain-building zone on the planet comes close. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Eight-thousander; grokipedia.com/page/Karakoram; cross-checked en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander.

question: India has not always been joined to Asia. Long ago the ancient Indian landmass ripped free from Gondwana — the giant southern supercontinent that once held today's Africa, Australia, South America, Antarctica, and India together in one piece. For the tens of millions of years before India ever crashed into Asia and shoved up the Himalayas, what was India?
choices: a chain of small volcanic islands
a shelf sunk beneath a shallow sea
a frozen land locked to the far south
context: India broke off Gondwana and spent millions of years as a separate island continent, drifting north across the Tethys Ocean before colliding with Asia about 50 million years ago — and it is still pushing northward a few centimetres a year. Source: earthsky.org (India's rapid continental drift); nationalgeographic.com (how India became the fastest continent).

question: Stand on the very summit of Mount Everest, 8,849 m up, and the grey rock beneath your boots is limestone. Yet limestone does not form in mountains at all — it takes shape somewhere else entirely, and this batch was only later lifted into the sky. Where did the rock now capping the highest point on Earth first form?
answer: on the floor of an ancient sea
choices: on the floor of an ancient sea
in the throat of a volcano
deep in the Earth's hot mantle
context: Everest's summit cap is grey Ordovician limestone that formed on the floor of the Tethys Ocean some 450-500 million years ago; India's collision with Asia scraped that old seabed thousands of metres into the sky. Just ~6 m below the summit, geologists have collected fossils of trilobites, crinoids (sea lilies) and other sea-floor creatures. Source: geologyin.com; montana.edu/everest (summit limestone); iugs-geoheritage.org (Ordovician rocks of Everest).

question: The Himalayan wall casts a giant rain shadow: moist monsoon air climbs the southern slopes and dumps its rain, then crosses the crest wrung dry, leaving the Tibetan side a cold desert under 200 mm a year. That soaked southern slope holds one of the rainiest inhabited places on Earth, drenched by over 11,000 mm a year. Which place is it?
context: On the Himalayas' southern slope, Cherrapunji (Meghalaya, India) is drenched by over 11,000 mm of rain a year, among the wettest inhabited places on Earth. Moist monsoon air is forced up the slopes, cools and dumps its rain, then crosses the crest wrung dry, leaving a 'rain shadow' desert on the Tibetan side (under 200 mm a year). Source: worldatlas.com (rain shadow effect); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas.

question: The Himalaya mountain range, arcing across Asia from Pakistan to Bhutan, cradles roughly 15,000 glaciers on its peaks and high ridges. Together they hold a greater mass of frozen water than any other mountain range on Earth — more ice than any place outside the Arctic and Antarctica themselves. Geographers gave this huge frozen reserve a memorable nickname. What do they call it?
context: With roughly 15,000 glaciers, the Himalaya holds more ice than anywhere on Earth outside the Arctic and Antarctic, which is why the range is nicknamed the 'Third Pole.' ('Roof of the World' belongs to the neighbouring Tibetan Plateau; 'Water Tower of Asia' names its role as a river source.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas.

question: About ten of Asia's greatest rivers — among them the Ganges, the Indus and the Brahmaputra — are born from the ice and snowmelt of the Himalaya and the neighbouring Hindu Kush. So many people farm and drink along these rivers that this single mountain system waters a staggering share of the human race. Roughly what share of all the people alive on Earth is that?
context: Around ten of Asia's major rivers — the Ganges, Indus, Brahmaputra and others — rise in the Himalaya-Hindu Kush ice and snow, and their water reaches roughly two billion people: close to a quarter of everyone alive. That reach is why the range is also called the 'water tower of Asia.' Source: education.nationalgeographic.org (water towers); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas.

question: Most tectonic plates creep along about as fast as your fingernails grow, only a couple of centimetres per year. Around 80 million years ago, the Indian continent tore north toward Asia at a startling speed. Compared with the fastest plate on Earth today, how fast was India moving?
context: Around 80 million years ago India sped north at roughly 15 cm — some estimates up to 20 cm — a year: about twice the top speed of any tectonic plate moving today, and the fastest continental drift yet known. That breakneck dash set up its slow-motion collision with Asia about 50 million years ago. Source: nationalgeographic.com (how India became the fastest continent); livescience.com (India-Eurasia fast collision).

question: The Tibetan Plateau rides about 4,500 m above sea level, and where India slams into Eurasia the crust beneath it has been stacked to some 70 km thick — roughly double the ordinary ~35 km. Counter-intuitively, it is largely BECAUSE the crust there is so thick that the plateau stands so high. How does thickening the crust lift the land?
answer: the deep root floats higher on the mantle
choices: the deep root floats higher on the mantle
hot magma inflates it from beneath
trapped gases push the surface upward
the planet's spin flings it outward
context: Thick crust behaves like a floating raft: the more you pile up, the deeper its 'root' sinks into the dense mantle — and the higher its top rides, exactly as a taller iceberg shows more above the water. The India-Eurasia collision doubled the crust beneath southern Tibet to about 70 km, giving the plateau a deep, buoyant root that holds it aloft. Source: sciencedirect.com (crustal structure, NW Himalaya & Indo-Gangetic Plain); search consensus (~35 km plain to ~70 km Tibet).

question: The Himalayas are so colossally heavy that they press down on the very plate carrying India, bending it downward like a plank weighted at one end. In front of the mountains that sag becomes a long, deep trough that fills with sediment washed off the peaks. Which vast, famously flat landform is this weighed-down trough?
context: The sheer weight of the Himalayas flexes the Indian plate downward into a 'foreland basin' — a trough that fills with sediment eroded off the range. That basin is the flat, fertile Indo-Gangetic (Ganges) Plain: the mountains, by their own weight, built the lowland at their feet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayan_foreland_basin.

question: The Matterhorn rises above the Swiss village of Zermatt, in the Alps of Europe, as an almost perfect stone pyramid. Four steep triangular faces climb to one sharp summit 4,478 m up. It is the most famous mountain outline in all of Europe, printed on Toblerone chocolate bars. What natural force carved a whole mountain into such a sharp pyramid?
choices: a volcano piling it up from below
a river cutting down its face
context: Over about a million years, four glaciers each ground a bowl-shaped hollow into a different side of the Matterhorn and ate inward until only this spire was left, 4,478 m above Zermatt (Switzerland) and Breuil-Cervinia (Italy). Its four faces even look roughly toward the four points of the compass. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matterhorn

question: High up in England's Lake District, hill-walkers can visit about 197 small, still, dark pools tucked into the fells. Each one sits in a rocky mountain hollow that an Ice Age glacier gouged out with its icy teeth, and then abandoned as the ice slowly melted away thousands of years ago. What is one of these little ice-born mountain lakes called?
context: 'Tarn' comes from the Old Norse 'tjorn,' a small mountain lake fed by no streams. Many are trapped behind a low dam of moraine — the rubble a glacier bulldozed along and dropped as it melted. The Lake District alone holds around 197 of them, among the best loved the Red Tarn beneath Helvellyn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarn_(lake)

question: In Snowdonia, Wales, a huge semicircular rock amphitheatre called Cwm Idwal curves around a dark lake on its floor — in 2005 voted the seventh greatest natural wonder in Britain. The Welsh call such an ice-scooped mountain bowl a 'cwm,' the Scots a 'corrie.' What is the general geographers' term for it?
context: 'Cirque' is French for a natural amphitheatre; 'cwm' (Welsh) and 'corrie' (from the Gaelic coire, a cauldron) name the same ice-scooped bowl — steep on three sides, open downhill. Cwm Idwal cradles the lake Llyn Idwal on its floor, and Britons once ranked it the seventh greatest natural wonder in the country. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cwm_Idwal

question: On Snowdon in Wales runs Crib Goch — 'the red ridge' — a crest so narrow that scramblers cross it astride, a cliff falling away on either hand; it is also one of the wettest spots in Britain, soaked by some 4,473 mm of rain a year. Geographers borrow the French word for a 'fish bone' to name a sharp mountain ridge like this, honed on both sides by ice. What is it called?
context: 'Arete' is French for a fish bone — an edge sharp on both sides. One forms where two glacier bowls gnaw toward each other from opposite sides until only a thin wall of rock survives between them. Crib Goch (923 m) is one of Snowdon's knife-edge crests; on Helvellyn, the aretes Striding Edge and Swirral Edge frame the Red Tarn between them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crib_Goch

question: The Matterhorn's four great faces are not equal, and its western wall alone rises about 1,400 m of near-vertical rock. All four sweep up to meet 4,478 m above Zermatt in one soaring spire, gnawed to that sharp point by four separate glaciers biting inward from every side. What do mountaineers call a peak carved to such a sharp point?
context: A peak carved to a point this way is a 'horn,' and the Matterhorn is its textbook example. Its four faces are of unequal size — the western the tallest at roughly 1,400 m — and four glaciers gnawed inward on every side until only the spire was left. The rule of thumb: wherever three or more cirques meet, the rock between them is worn down to a horn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matterhorn

question: On Helvellyn, in England's Lake District, the summit cliffs plunge in a steep semicircular headwall, the back wall of a cirque that ice once scooped from the mountainside. When a glacier still filled that hollow, a deep crevasse gaped where the moving ice tore away from rock frozen to the headwall. Meltwater trickled into the exposed cracks, froze hard, and pried blocks loose, quarrying the wall ever steeper. What is this gaping crevasse at a glacier's head called?
context: The gaping crevasse at a glacier's head is the 'bergschrund' (German for 'mountain cleft'). It opens where the moving ice tears away from ice frozen fast to the headwall; the meltwater that seeps in, freezes, and plucks blocks loose is the freeze-and-pry 'quarrying' that keeps a cirque's back wall so steep — the very wall that now rises above Red Tarn on Helvellyn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirque

question: In 1831 the young Charles Darwin scrambled through the Welsh valley of Cwm Idwal and walked straight past its story. Returning in 1842, after a bold new theory had taught naturalists how to read certain scratches, mounds, and stranded boulders, he was thunderstruck — writing that 'a house burnt down by fire did not tell its story more plainly than did this valley.' What had Darwin finally learned to see written in Cwm Idwal's rocks?
answer: that glaciers had once carved the valley
choices: that glaciers had once carved the valley
that floods had once drowned the valley
that seas had once covered the valley
that earthquakes had once shattered the valley
context: By 1842 a bold new idea — that great sheets of ice had once buried much of Britain — had taught naturalists to recognise the scratches, mounds, and out-of-place boulders that glaciers leave behind. Reading them at last in Cwm Idwal, Charles Darwin wrote that 'a house burnt down by fire did not tell its story more plainly than did this valley' — perhaps the clearest description ever written of reading a glacier's fingerprint in the land. Source: https://www.geolsoc.org.uk/science-and-policy/100-great-geosites/fire-and-ice/cwm-idwal-darwins-boulders/  (Legend.)

question: On Peru's Pacific coast, near the equator, you wade into the sea expecting warm tropical water. Instead you gasp. The Humboldt Current sweeps cold water up from Antarctica along South America's western shore, chilling the surf right through the tropics. How cold can Peru's tropical sea water actually drop?
context: That chill comes from the Humboldt Current, which drags cold sub-Antarctic water thousands of kilometres north along the shores of Chile and Peru — so a coast that sits deep in the tropics feels almost temperate. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current)

question: Along the coast of Peru and northern Chile in South America flows the cold Humboldt Current, sweeping icy water up from the direction of Antarctica. Cold water evaporates very little, so almost no rain-bearing clouds ever form and almost no rain reaches the shore. Which great desert stretches for hundreds of miles along this rainless Pacific coast — one of the driest places on Earth?
context: The Atacama is the driest place on Earth outside the poles — some spots may have gone centuries without measurable rain. The cold current cools the coastal air so it cannot rise and build rain-clouds. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current)

question: Off Peru, coastal winds push the warm surface water out to sea, and cold water rich in food rises up from below to take its place. That grows huge amounts of plankton, and Peru's fishery became the richest on Earth. In 1970 alone, it landed over 12 million tonnes. About what share of the entire world's fish catch was that?
context: One nation's tiny anchovies, off one cold coast, made up a fifth of everything humans pulled from the sea. Just a handful of upwelling zones — a sliver of the ocean — supply about a quarter of the world's fish. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current)

question: For thousands of years vast flocks of seabirds nested on three small islands off Peru, in a climate so rainless that their droppings never washed away. Layer by layer the droppings hardened into cliffs up to 60 m (200 ft) thick, and in the 1800s miners hacked out this 'guano' by the shipload. Which islands were these?
context: On the Chincha Islands the guano lay deeper than a twenty-story building is tall — preserved only because rain almost never falls there. The word 'guano' comes from the Quechua 'wanu.' (Source: audubon.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guano)

question: Every few years the sea off Peru turns unusually warm, the great anchovy shoals vanish, and the fishermen's boats come home empty. Peruvian fishermen named this dreaded warm spell El Niño — 'the little boy' — after the time of year it reliably peaks. Which 'boy' did the name honor?
choices: The first baby born each new year
A young saint of the fishermen
context: The warming peaks around December 25, so the fishermen named a recurring disaster after the newborn Christ. Scientists kept 'El Niño' for the whole Pacific-wide warming; its cool opposite is called La Niña. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Niño)

question: By the 1840s Peru had found that its greatest export was not gold or silver but the hardened seabird droppings mined off its coast. Ships crossed whole oceans to buy it, it became the nation's biggest source of money, and rival powers even fought over the deposits. What made this 'white gold' so priceless?
answer: It was the world's finest fertilizer
choices: It was the world's finest fertilizer
It burned as a clean lamp fuel
It was pressed into cheap bricks
It was ground into a rare medicine
context: Guano's nitrogen and phosphorus revived exhausted European and American farm soil. The craze ran so hot the U.S. passed the 1856 Guano Islands Act, letting citizens claim any unclaimed guano island — and Spain's seizure of Peru's richest guano islands sparked the Chincha Islands War of 1864–66. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guano)

question: Here is the hidden engine of Peru's upwelling. The coastal wind blows roughly parallel to the shore, yet it drags the surface water at a right angle away from the coast, and deeper water must rise up from below to replace it. What bends the moving water about 90 degrees away from the wind that drives it?
answer: The Coriolis force of Earth's spin
choices: The Coriolis force of Earth's spin
The gravitational pull of the Moon
The drag of the deep seafloor
context: This right-angle twist of wind-driven water is called Ekman transport. Because Earth's rotation deflects the moving surface layer, the wind ends up shoving it offshore — and cold, food-rich water wells up to fill the gap. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upwelling)

question: In 1972 the Peruvian anchoveta catch — the largest fishery on Earth — collapsed and never truly recovered. Years of overfishing had strained it, but the killing blow was a powerful El Niño flooding the coast with warm water. How did that warm water actually destroy the fishery?
answer: It sealed a warm lid over the upwelling
choices: It sealed a warm lid over the upwelling
It boiled the shallows too hot for fish
It turned the seawater acidic and toxic
It churned up mud that buried the shoals
context: The U.N. later called the anchoveta 'the most heavily exploited fish in world history.' El Niño's warm layer floats on top of the cold water and blocks it from rising, so the plankton starve — and the anchovies with them. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Peruvian_anchoveta_crisis)

question: El Niño's warm pool does not stay off Peru. As it drowns the South American coast in flooding rain, its influence ripples clear across the Pacific and rearranges the weather on the far side of the ocean. What does that same El Niño bring to Australia and Indonesia?
choices: Dead calm with no wind for weeks
context: Meteorologists call this long-distance linkage a 'teleconnection.' A strong El Niño can parch eastern Australia into drought and fire while Peru's coastal deserts bloom under freak rain — one warm pool, opposite disasters an ocean apart. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Niño)

question: The Humboldt has cousins scattered around the globe — cold, fish-rich currents that chill the coasts they hug. The single most intense upwelling on Earth churns off the desert coast of Namibia, near the town of Lüderitz, feeding another vast fishery. Name this African cousin of the Humboldt.
context: The Benguela's upwelling cell off Lüderitz is the most powerful on the planet. Like the Humboldt, it turns a cold current and a barren desert shore into one of the world's great fishing grounds. (Source: namibian.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upwelling)

question: Plot the four great cold-current fisheries on a world map, and a striking pattern appears at once: every single one hugs the same kind of coastline, which is exactly why the powerful upwelling that feeds them happens where it does. The four fisheries sit off Peru, off Namibia, off California, and off Morocco. Where do all four of these fishery giants sit?
answer: Along the western coasts of continents
choices: Along the western coasts of continents
Along the eastern coasts of continents
context: On the western edges of continents the prevailing winds blow toward the equator and, bent by the Coriolis force, shove the surface water offshore — so cold, food-rich water wells up all along these shores. That is why the world's biggest fisheries cluster on cold, west-facing coasts. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upwelling)

question: In northern Spain there is a cave called Altamira. Its ceiling is packed with painted bison so lifelike they seem to swell right out of the rock. People gave the ceiling a nickname taken from a famous Italian ceiling. What is Altamira's painted ceiling called?
answer: the Sistine Chapel of prehistoric art
choices: the Sistine Chapel of prehistoric art
the Mona Lisa of prehistoric Spain
the Last Supper of the Ice Age
the School of Athens of the Stone Age
context: Altamira's low ceiling writhes with a whole herd of bison; the Ice-Age painters used the natural bulges of the rock as the animals' humped shoulders and bellies, so the bison seem to stand out in three dimensions. Its beauty earned the nickname 'the Sistine Chapel of Paleolithic art.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_Altamira

question: In September 1940, four French teenagers went down a wooded hillside near Montignac. An animal had darted into a hole left by a fallen tree. They squeezed inside and dropped into Lascaux cave, its walls blazing with Ice-Age paintings. What animal led them to the cave?
context: The dog was named Robot, and his owner Marcel Ravidat came back with three friends -- Jacques Marsal, Georges Agnel, and Simon Coencas -- and slid down the shaft on 12 September 1940 because they hoped it was a secret tunnel to a nearby manor. Instead they had found Lascaux. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascaux  (Legend.)

question: Lascaux cave in France opened to tourists in 1948. But the warm damp breath from the crowds soon bred mold across paintings that had survived 17,000 years, and France sealed the real cave shut in 1963. So what do the many thousands who visit Lascaux today actually walk through?
answer: an exact, full-size replica of the cave
choices: an exact, full-size replica of the cave
a glass tunnel built over the paintings
context: Up to 1,200 visitors a day breathed out carbon dioxide and moisture, feeding the mold, algae, and lichen, so France closed the real cave in 1963. Today tourists walk through exact copies -- Lascaux II (opened 1983) and the full-scale Lascaux IV (opened 2016) -- not the original. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascaux

question: When France's Chauvet Cave was discovered in 1994, its horses and lions were painted so skillfully and lifelike that experts assumed the art had to be fairly recent. Then radiocarbon testing delivered a shock. Chauvet's paintings are among the oldest ever found anywhere on Earth. About how old are they?
context: Radiocarbon dating put Chauvet's horses, lions, and woolly rhinos at roughly 36,000 years old (about 37,000-33,500 years ago) -- among the oldest known cave paintings anywhere. Discovered on 18 December 1994, Chauvet was sealed from the start so it would not be ruined like Lascaux, and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chauvet_Cave

question: Deep inside France's Chauvet Cave, past the painted lions and rhinos, explorers came upon a strange, deliberate arrangement. A single object had been set squarely on top of a flat, fallen block of stone, like an offering placed on an altar. What had Ice-Age people set there?
context: More cave-bear skulls lay scattered on the floor around the block. Many scholars read this careful arrangement as a sign that Chauvet was a sacred, ritual place, not merely an art gallery -- one of the eeriest hints of Ice-Age belief. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/Chauvet_Cave/ ; https://archive.archaeology.org/1103/features/werner_herzog_chauvet_cave_primer.html

question: In 1879, eight-year-old Maria de Sautuola wandered into Altamira cave in Spain, looked up, and -- as the story is told -- cried 'Look, Papa -- oxen!', having spotted the great bison herd painted across the ceiling. When her father presented the discovery to Europe's leading scholars, how did they treat his find?
answer: They dismissed the paintings as a forgery.
choices: They dismissed the paintings as a forgery.
They hailed him as Spain's greatest scholar.
They rushed to dig for more caves.
They shipped the ceiling off to a museum.
context: Europe's experts insisted that Ice-Age people could not possibly have painted so beautifully, and Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola died in 1888 still branded a fraud. Only after more painted caves turned up in France did the leading skeptic, Emile Cartailhac, publicly apologize in his 1902 article 'Mea culpa d'un sceptique' ('the apology of a skeptic'). Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_Altamira ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcelino_Sanz_de_Sautuola  (Legend.)

question: In caves across Ice-Age Europe, from Lascaux to Altamira, prehistoric people left what scientists call some of the oldest signatures on Earth. A person would press part of their own body flat against the cave wall and blow powdered pigment all around it. Lifting the body away left a pale stencil that has lasted 30,000 years. Which body part did they stencil this way, over and over, across Europe?
context: An artist pressed a hand flat to the wall and blew a mouthful of powdered pigment all around it -- sometimes through a hollow bone tube -- then lifted the hand away, leaving a pale outline. Found in caves across Europe, these handprints are among the oldest 'signatures' humans have left anywhere. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascaux ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Chauvet_Cave/

question: Europe's painted caves -- Chauvet, Lascaux, and Altamira -- are the most famous Ice-Age art on Earth, yet they are NOT the oldest. In 2021, archaeologists dated a life-size painting of a wild pig to at least 45,500 years ago -- older than any European cave -- deep in a limestone cave on a tropical island far from Europe. On which island did they find the world's oldest known animal painting?
context: The painting, in the Leang Tedongnge cave, shows a Sulawesi warty pig and is dated to at least 45,500 years old -- far older than France's Chauvet Cave. It is a reminder that Europe's caves are the most famous Ice-Age art, but not the first. Sources: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/45500-year-old-pig-painting-worlds-oldest-animal-art ; https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.abd4648

question: On a bitter, clear morning over the frozen plains of North Dakota, the low Sun can appear flanked by two smaller bright suns — one burning to its left, one to its right, at the very same height. Farmers and old sailors had a homely name for this pair of false suns. What did they call them?
context: 'Parhelion' comes from Greek — para + helios, 'beside the sun.' The homely folk name 'sun dog' comes from the way the two false suns seem to follow the real Sun across the sky, the way a dog trails its master. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_dog; sciencenotes.org/what-is-a-sun-dog)

question: High over the Canadian prairies in deep winter, a faint luminous ring can encircle the Sun, with the two sun dogs sitting right on it. This ring always stands exactly 22 degrees out from the Sun — a width you can check against the sky using nothing but your own body. How wide across does the ring look?
answer: the span of your outstretched hand at arm's length
choices: the width of one finger held up at arm's length
the span of your outstretched hand at arm's length
the spread of both arms flung out to the sides
the width of the full Moon's bright round disk
context: This is the 22-degree halo, the most common of all ice-crystal halos. A hand held out at arm's length spans roughly 20 degrees — almost exactly the halo's radius, so the ring seems to just fit inside your outstretched fingers. Inside the ring the sky looks darker, because ice prisms bend no sunlight to angles smaller than 22 degrees. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/22-degree_halo)

question: Miles above the Rocky Mountains, in the highest, thinnest cirrus clouds, sunlight can bend into a pale 22-degree halo that shimmers with a faint hint of color, almost like a washed-out rainbow. Far overhead, millions of tiny prisms are bending that sunlight to make the ring. What are those prisms made of?
context: A rainbow is made by round droplets of liquid water; a halo is made by six-sided (hexagonal) ICE crystals high in cold cirrus — the same sunlight, split by different sky-stuff. The magic 22 degrees is simply the smallest angle a hexagonal ice prism can bend light: about 21.84 degrees. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/22-degree_halo; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_dog)

question: Around Fairbanks, Alaska, sun dogs and halos sometimes appear on a day with no clouds anywhere in the sky. On the coldest mornings, the freezing air right at street level fills with countless tiny drifting ice crystals. That is enough to bend the sunlight and paint a halo without a single cloud. What do northerners call this ground-level ice haze?
context: Diamond dust is a ground-level haze of tiny ice crystals that forms in very cold, moist air — proof you don't need high cirrus to get sun dogs and halos. It's famous around Fairbanks and across the far north, where halos can hang right down at street level. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_dog; carpenternaturecenter.org/sun-dogs-halos-and-diamond-dust)

question: On a still, bitterly cold night over the streets of Montreal, a glowing shaft of light rises straight up above a bright streetlamp. This is a light pillar, built by column-shaped ice crystals hovering with their flat faces held level in the freezing air. What does a light pillar look like?
answer: a single glow the same color as the lamp
choices: a single glow the same color as the lamp
a soft silver-white glow, whatever the lamp's color
a glow that flickers between light and dark
a full spread of rainbow colors, like a halo's
context: Unlike a 22-degree halo or a sun dog, which split sunlight into a faint rainbow, a light pillar is made by REFLECTION — light bouncing off the level faces of column-shaped ice crystals like millions of tiny mirrors — not by refraction (prism-splitting). Because reflection doesn't separate colors, a pillar simply glows in the color of whatever light it reflects: orange above a sodium street lamp, white above a low winter Sun. Pillars can even stretch below the light as well as above it. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_pillar)

question: Over the winter skies of Finland, the loveliest of all the ice-optics sometimes appears when the Sun sits low: the circumzenithal arc, a short bright band curving like a smile — an 'upside-down rainbow' whose colors glow even purer than a true rainbow's. Scientists insist it isn't rare at all, yet hardly anyone ever spots one. Why is it so easily missed?
answer: it hangs directly overhead, where almost nobody thinks to look up
choices: it hangs directly overhead, where almost nobody thinks to look up
it needs the Sun sitting almost exactly 22 degrees high, a narrow window
it forms only in a small patch low near the horizon
it lasts only a few seconds before the crystals drift apart
context: The circumzenithal arc forms when horizontal plate crystals let sunlight enter through their flat TOP face and leave by a SIDE face — the reverse of the path that makes a halo. Its colors are purer than a rainbow's because they overlap far less: blue-violet on top, red toward the Sun. It appears only when the Sun is below 32.2 degrees and glows brightest when the Sun is 22 degrees up — yet it's missed so often simply because it rides high overhead, where almost nobody thinks to look. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumzenithal_arc)

question: Over Stockholm on the morning of 20 April 1535, the sky filled for two hours with sun dogs and glowing rings of light. The uneasy city had the whole spectacle painted, and that picture — the Vadersolstavlan, or 'Sun Dog Painting' — still hangs in Stockholm's cathedral today. Besides being the oldest known image of sun dogs, the painting holds a second 'oldest' record as well. Which one is it?
answer: the oldest color view of Stockholm
choices: the oldest color view of Stockholm
the oldest royal portrait in Stockholm
the oldest color map of Stockholm
the oldest church mural in Stockholm
context: The Vadersolstavlan ('weather-sun painting') is the oldest surviving color depiction of Stockholm as well as the oldest known image of sun dogs. The reformer Olaus Petri read the eerie sky as a warning from God against King Gustav Vasa; the king took it as a jab at his rule and dismissed it. The version that hangs today in Storkyrkan cathedral is a 1636 copy by Jacob Heinrich Elbfas. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vadersolstavlan)  (Legend.)

question: In the 1400s, from Cusco high in the Peruvian Andes, the Inca ran a mountain empire of about ten million people. They built royal roads running thousands of miles, filled storehouses, tax rolls, and even a full census. But they never wrote a single word. How did Inca officials keep track of the empire's accounts?
context: The Inca called these knotted-string records quipu (also spelled khipu). From Cusco they governed millions across the Andes with cords instead of writing -- the accounting of a whole empire hung on colored strings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: The Inca of the Peruvian Andes had no writing, so they kept the empire's numbers on knotted strings called quipu. On one of these cords, a single knot can stand for a single unit or for a full hundred. Yet the two knots may be tied exactly alike. So what actually decides whether a knot counts as one, ten, or a hundred?
answer: how high up the cord it is tied
choices: how high up the cord it is tied
what color the cord was dyed
how tightly the knot was pulled
which way the cord was twisted
context: The quipu is a base-10 place-value machine: knots low on a hanging cord count ones, higher up tens, higher still hundreds and thousands. You read the number by a knot's position -- with your fingers as much as your eyes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: An Inca knot-keeper in the Andes must record 308 -- three hundreds, no tens, eight ones -- as clusters of knots along a single cord. The hundreds and the ones each get their knots, but the tens place is a zero. Reading the cord with your fingers, how does the quipu show that the tens row holds zero?
answer: that spot is left bare, with no knot at all
choices: that spot is left bare, with no knot at all
a special 'nothing' knot is tied there
that stretch of cord is dyed solid black
the cord is cut short just below there
context: Most striking of all: a bare gap with no knot is the Inca zero. They kept a place-holder for zero centuries before the idea reached much of Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: A trained Inca knot-keeper held an entire province's accounts in his cords and in his memory. He tracked the tribute owed, the llama herds, and the grain stored in every Andean storehouse. The Sapa Inca demanded these figures be flawless. By some colonial accounts, what could happen to a knot-keeper who got the imperial accounts wrong?
answer: he could be put to death
choices: he could be put to death
he could be fined a herd of llamas
he could be sent to the fields
he could be made to retie it
context: The role of khipukamayuq was hereditary and demanded a prodigious memory -- a single error in a knot's color, shape, or position could change the record. The death penalty comes from colonial-era testimony, so it is reported as claim, not certainty. Sources: worldhistory.org/Quipu; machutravelperu.com/blog/quipu  (Legend.)

question: Hand a modern scholar an Inca quipu from the Andes and the numbers come through clearly -- herd counts, tribute totals, and storehouse tallies all readable. But the same cords carry colors, cord-orders, and knot-patterns that may hide names, words, even whole stories. Where do we stand with that non-number content today?
choices: only a few cords have been read
context: We can fully read the quipu's numbers, but its possible 'language' -- part ledger, part story -- is still unread. In 2005 Gary Urton and Carrie Brezine argued that three figure-eight knots on one cord spell the place-name Puruchuco, perhaps the first word ever read off a quipu. Sources: theconversation.com; artsandculture.google.com (the Puruchuco khipus)

question: After Spain conquered Peru, church officials decided the Inca knot-records were dangerous -- 'idols of the devil,' one called them, obstacles to converting the Andean people to Christianity. In 1583 the Third Council of Lima ordered the quipu destroyed. What became of thousands of them?
context: Thousands of quipu were burned as idolatrous, and only about 1,400 pre-Columbian quipu survive today, mostly in museums -- the conquered people's own records largely erased by the men who conquered them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: Long ago, the Indus city of Mohenjo-daro sat in what is now Pakistan. It was laid out on a neat brick grid, complete with covered drains, as planned as any modern town. Its people also pressed a script of small signs onto stone seals. What is still true of that Indus script today?
answer: It cannot be read by anyone alive.
choices: It cannot be read by anyone alive.
It is still used to write Sindhi today.
It gave rise to the Arabic alphabet.
It was fully deciphered a century ago.
context: First unearthed at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, the Indus Valley script has resisted every reader since: no scholar can say what a single seal says. Its people mastered covered drains and grid streets, yet left us a writing we still cannot open. (grokipedia.com/page/Indus_script; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro)

question: Most of what survives of the Mohenjo-daro script is carved on tiny stamp seals, polished stones about the size of a coin. Each seal shows one animal above a line of signs. Among all these creatures, one appears far more often than the rest. Which animal turns up most on the Indus seals?
context: Scholars nickname it the 'unicorn,' but it is almost certainly a bull drawn side-on, the near horn simply hiding the far one. This one-horned figure stands above the signs on more Indus seals than any other creature. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_script)  (Legend.)

question: The ancient Indus Valley civilization built brick cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa about 4,500 years ago, in what is now Pakistan and northwest India. They left behind thousands of tiny inscriptions on seals and pottery — a mysterious writing that scholars still cannot read. Other ancient peoples wrote long inscriptions on temple walls and clay tablets. What is the longest text ever found in the whole Indus script, carved on a copper plate from Mohenjo-daro?
context: The record-holder carries just 26 signs, on a copper plate from Mohenjo-daro. There is no long text anywhere in the Indus world — no story, no law, no letter — leaving codebreakers with no paragraph to get a grip on. (grokipedia.com/page/Indus_script)

question: Around 2500 BCE the great Indus Valley civilisation built brick cities like Mohenjo-daro along the rivers of what is now Pakistan. Its people pressed tiny picture-signs onto small clay seals. In 1977 the linguist Iravatham Mahadevan cataloged 417 different Indus signs. Half a century later, scholars still cannot agree on one basic point about them. What have they never settled about the Indus signs?
answer: Whether its marks are truly writing at all
choices: Whether its marks are truly writing at all
Whether kings or traders carved the seals
Whether Harappa or Mohenjo-daro invented it
Whether it shaped later Indian scripts
context: Mahadevan's 1977 concordance counted 417 signs — too many for a 20-to-30-letter alphabet, yet far too few for a one-sign-per-word system that would need thousands. That maddening in-between has fueled a real scholarly fight over whether the Indus marks are true writing at all, or symbols that never recorded language. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_script)

question: Indus seals turn up far from home — in the Mesopotamian city of Ur, where merchants knew the distant Indus land as 'Meluhha.' On one Mesopotamian cylinder seal, a man named Shu-ilishu is labeled by his trade — a haunting reminder of how tightly Ur and the Indus cities were once bound by sea. What trade did Shu-ilishu practice?
choices: Scribe in the temple of Ur
context: The Akkadian cylinder seal names him 'Shu-ilishu, interpreter of the Meluhhan language' — proof that people once spoke and translated the Indus tongue. Yet even a named ancient interpreter cannot help us: the seals stay silent. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus-Mesopotamia_relations)

question: Egyptian hieroglyphs fell to the Rosetta Stone, and Greek's lost Linear B was eventually cracked too. Scholars fear the Indus script of Mohenjo-daro may never join them, defeated by one wall those other scripts never had to face. What is the deepest reason the Indus script still resists every codebreaker?
choices: Its clay tablets have all crumbled away
Its signs were deliberately kept secret
Too few seals have ever been dug up
context: Egyptian hieroglyphs were cracked with the Rosetta Stone, and Greek's Linear B was eventually read too, because scholars could tie the signs to a language they already knew. The Indus script has no such bilingual key, and no one knows what language its people spoke — so it may stay silent forever. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_script)

question: Seven miles up over the North Atlantic, a narrow band of wind screams from west to east. A jet from New York to London rides it and lands more than an hour early, while the flight home against it drags. What is this fast, high-altitude river of wind?
context: The jet stream flows near the tropopause, about 30,000 feet up, always west to east. The classic mix-up is the Gulf Stream — that is a warm WATER current in the ocean, not a wind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_stream

question: In the 1920s a Japanese weather scientist named Wasaburo Oishi ran a lab near Mount Fuji. From 1923 to 1925 he logged 1,288 upper-air readings. They proved a fierce, permanent wind blew high over Japan, the first record of the jet stream. What tool did he use to measure winds seven miles up?
context: Oishi released small hydrogen 'pilot balloons' and followed them with a theodolite — a surveying telescope — reading the wind's speed and direction at each height as the balloon rose. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasaburo_Oishi

question: Wasaburo Oishi had proved the jet stream existed over Japan in the 1920s. Yet the world's scientists ignored his breakthrough for decades. The reason was odd. An idealist, he wrote all 19 of his observatory reports in a made-up international language that almost no scientist could read. Which language was it?
context: Oishi was a devoted Esperantist. His 1926 report and 18 more through 1944 were all in Esperanto, so his jet-stream discovery sat unread until the West rediscovered the winds during World War II. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasaburo_Oishi

question: In World War II, Japan built about 9,300 balloon bombs called 'fu-go'. They were sent into the winter jet stream to drift 6,000 miles across the Pacific. Their target was North America, the very first intercontinental weapon. What were these balloon envelopes made of?
context: Each fu-go was many sheets of washi (mulberry paper) glued with konnyaku, a paste made from konjac potato. About 300 reached North America in 30 to 100 hours. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fu-Go_balloon_bomb

question: The jet stream that drives the winter storms of Europe and North America is not equally strong all year. It howls in winter and slackens in summer. It rides along a sloping boundary in the atmosphere, and the sharper the temperature difference across that boundary, the faster the jet stream blows. What is that boundary called?
context: The jet forms and speeds up along the polar front, the sloping boundary between cold polar and warm subtropical air. Winter's sharper cold-versus-warm contrast is why the jet stream is strongest then. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_stream

question: The jet stream almost never runs straight. Instead it wanders in enormous north-and-south loops that snake around the whole hemisphere, and when one plunges far south it drags a lobe of frigid Arctic air down into places like Texas or Georgia — a sudden cold snap. What are these giant meanders in the jet called?
context: These planetary meanders, called Rossby waves, ripple along the jet. A deep southward dip pulls Arctic air far below its usual range; a northward bulge lets warm air push up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_stream

question: In late June 2021 the jet stream buckled and locked in place over western North America, trapping a dome of scorching air that could not move on. Lytton, British Columbia hit 49.6°C — smashing Canada's heat record by almost 5 degrees — and over a thousand people died. Forecasters call this stuck, storm-stalling jet pattern a 'block,' and name its most common shape for a Greek letter. Which letter?
context: A ridge of high pressure that halts the eastward flow of weather is a 'blocking high'; the classic shape is the omega block, its loop mimicking Ω. The 2021 heat dome was one of the deadliest in North American history. Source: https://www.livescience.com/a-dangerous-omega-block-is-trapping-scorching-hot-air-over-the-us-and-canada

question: In February 2020 an unusually strong jet stream turbocharged flights across the Atlantic. A British Airways Boeing 747 crossed from New York to London in just 4 hours 56 minutes, reaching a ground speed of 825 mph — faster than the speed of sound at sea level. Yet no sonic boom ever thundered down. How can a plane race across the ground faster than sound without a sonic boom?
answer: Its airspeed stayed subsonic while the racing air carried it
choices: Its airspeed stayed subsonic while the racing air carried it
Its swept wings broke up the shock wave before it could form
The thin air seven miles up muffled the boom before it fell to earth
The tailwind blew the shock wave forward, far out of earshot
context: The plane's speed through the air stayed below the sound barrier — the whole river of air was racing east at hundreds of miles per hour and simply carried the jet along, setting a subsonic transatlantic record of 825 mph. A sonic boom depends on speed through the air, not speed over the ground. Source: https://www.flightradar24.com/blog/flight-tracking-news/special-event/british-airways-sets-new-transatlantic-speed-record/

question: High over the Arctic spins a vast ring of fast, jet-stream-like wind that normally bottles up the planet's coldest air, penning it near the pole. But when this ring weakens and wobbles, it can split apart, the jet stream buckles, and that trapped Arctic cold spills far south — as in the brutal February 2021 freeze that knocked out power across Texas. By what name do forecasters know this Arctic wind system?
context: When the stratospheric polar vortex is strong, it locks cold in the Arctic; a 'sudden stratospheric warming' can weaken and split it, sending the jet stream and Arctic air plunging south into North America and Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_vortex

question: The Kalahari is a vast semi-desert stretching across Botswana and Namibia in southern Africa. Its sand is about 90% quartz, a mineral that is naturally clear and colourless. Yet the Kalahari's dunes and plains glow a deep burnt red. Something very thin, wrapped around every grain of sand, gives it that colour. What coats the pale grains red?
answer: a thin coat of iron oxide
choices: a thin coat of iron oxide
a fine dust of windblown clay
a living crust of desert algae
a residue of dried mineral salts
context: Each grain of Kalahari sand is nearly pure quartz — colourless on its own — but wears a microscopically thin stain of iron oxide (the mineral hematite): iron that weathered out of the rock, was carried in by groundwater, and dried onto the grains. It is the same chemistry that turns iron rusty red. Source: USGS 'Iron oxide coatings give sand a red hue'; sandatlas.org/hematite; madsci.org 'Why is the sand of the Kalahari Desert red?'.

question: In southern Africa the Tswana people named this immense sweep of red sand across Botswana and Namibia after their own word Kgala. Travellers who cross its 900,000 km² of dunes learn very quickly why the name fits. What does the name Kalahari mean?
context: 'Kalahari' comes from the Tswana word Kgala, 'the great thirst' (or Kgalagadi, 'a waterless place'), for a vast land of sand with no permanent surface water, spreading about 900,000 km² across Botswana, Namibia and South Africa. Yet despite the name it is not a true desert but a semi-arid 'thirstland' that catches 110 to over 500 mm of rain a year — enough for grasses and camelthorn trees. Source: Wikipedia 'Kalahari Desert'.

question: The Okavango is one of Africa's great rivers, yet it never reaches the sea. It flows down into the Kalahari and fans out into a huge green wetland, where every drop is lost. The whole delta is a dead end for water. So by what route does almost all of the Okavango's water leave?
answer: it rises into the sky as evaporation and thirsty plants
choices: it rises into the sky as evaporation and thirsty plants
it sinks away to refill hidden underground lakes
it hardens into vast sheets of white surface salt
it is drunk and carried off by huge animal herds
context: The Okavango flows in from the Angolan highlands and dies in the sand: an estimated 96–98% of its water vanishes as evaporation and plant transpiration or soaks away, and almost none escapes. Because it drains inward and never reaches the sea, the Okavango forms a rare inland delta in an 'endorheic' (closed) basin; in the June–August flood it swells to about three times its permanent size, drawing animals from kilometres around. In 2014 it became the 1000th site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Source: Wikipedia 'Okavango Delta'.

question: The blinding-white Makgadikgadi salt pans — about 16,000 km² of dead-flat crust, among the largest salt flats on Earth — are the dried bed of a vast ancient lake that vanished around 10,000 years ago. When geologists traced how far its old shoreline once reached, the size of this long-gone Kalahari lake astonished them. How big was it?
choices: as large as the whole Sahara Desert
as vast as the Mediterranean Sea
context: The Makgadikgadi pans are the ghost of Lake Makgadikgadi, an ancient inland sea that covered roughly 80,000–275,000 km² — bigger than Switzerland, rivaling the United Kingdom or New Zealand — with an average depth around 30 m. Fed by the Okavango, Upper Zambezi and Cuando rivers, it existed from about 2 million until roughly 10,000 years ago. Source: Wikipedia 'Lake Makgadikgadi', 'Makgadikgadi Pan'.

question: About 20,000 years ago the great Kalahari lake, Lake Makgadikgadi, brimmed so full that it overflowed. Its waters spilled away to the northeast. Geologists believe that flood of lake water helped carve out one of Africa's mightiest waterfalls. Which waterfall did the vanished lake help create?
context: Around 20,000 years ago the brimming lake overflowed to the northeast, and that outflow helped cut the gorge of Victoria Falls on the Zambezi. A drying climate plus the Gumare fault lowering the land then let the Okavango spread out and starve the lake, and by about 10,000 years ago it was gone. Source: Wikipedia 'Lake Makgadikgadi'.

question: Out on the blinding-white Makgadikgadi salt pan, a lone crescent of granite called Kubu Island rises barely ten meters above the flatness. Marooned there, miles from the nearest water, grows a grove of gnarled, ancient trees, some more than 2,000 years old, that once shaded the shore of the vanished lake. What kind of ancient tree crowns Kubu Island?
context: Kubu Island (Lekhubu) is a crescent of granite over two billion years old, about a kilometre long and 10 m high, crowned with baobabs some estimated at over 2,000 years old that once stood on the vanished lake's shore. A national monument and sacred site — 'Kubu' means hippopotamus in Setswana — it holds stone-age relics including a curving dry-stone wall about 1.25 m high and 344 circular stone cairns left by people who lived at the water's edge. Source: Wikipedia 'Kubu Island'; amusingplanet.com 'Kubu Island: A Desert Island of Baobabs'.

question: The San people have lived in the central Kalahari for tens of thousands of years and can find water where a stranger would die of thirst. In a dry riverbed they scrape down to damp sand, sink a long hollow grass stem, and patiently suck the moisture up through it. To carry that hard-won water, they blow it through a second straw into a container, then cork it and bury it in the sand as a hidden canteen. What is that buried canteen?
context: The San carry the water home in ostrich eggshells, corked and buried as hidden canteens; in the driest months a buried wild tsama melon (a wild watermelon, its seeds about 35% protein) can be the only water for people and animals alike. The central Kalahari is the San's ancestral land, and DNA studies suggest their ancestors began diverging from all other humans roughly 200,000 years ago — among Earth's oldest continuous cultures. Source: Wikipedia 'San people'.

question: The Karakoram has some of the world's deadliest 8,000-meter peaks. Yet its name is far older than any climber's map. Turkic traders first used the word for the high Karakoram Pass, for what they saw at their feet. Later, Europeans used it for the whole range. What does 'Karakoram' mean?
context: 'Kara' means black and 'korum' (koram) means gravel or rubble in Turkic. The name first belonged only to the Karakoram Pass, whose high route is floored with dark, broken scree; European surveyors later stretched it over the entire range of giants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram

question: Only fourteen mountains on Earth rise above 8,000 meters. Most crowd the Himalaya. But one small tangle of Karakoram valleys, on the Pakistan-China border, packs four of these giants closer than anywhere else on the planet. Which four crown the Karakoram?
answer: K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum I, Gasherbrum II
choices: K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum I, Gasherbrum II
context: The Karakoram packs four of Earth's fourteen 8,000-metre peaks -- K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum I, and Gasherbrum II -- into one small knot of valleys, more giants per square mile than anywhere else. The Everest region and the rest of the Himalaya hold the other ten. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram

question: Hike for days up a wide highway of ice to a frozen crossroads called Concordia, high in the Karakoram mountains. Four of the world's mightiest peaks stand ringed around you at once. In 1975 an American photographer named Galen Rowell stood there in wonder and gave the amphitheatre a name that stuck. What did he call it?
answer: the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods
choices: the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods
the Rooftop Hall of the Snow Kings
the Cathedral of the Frozen Giants
the Great Court of the Sky Gods
context: Galen Rowell coined 'the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods' during the 1975 American K2 expedition and made it the title of his 1977 book. From Concordia (~4,600 m), where the Baltoro and Godwin-Austen glaciers meet, all four of the range's 8,000-metre peaks can be seen at once. Source: Galen Rowell, In the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods (1977); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltoro_Glacier  (Legend.)

question: Outside the Arctic and Antarctic, no place on Earth wears more ice than the Karakoram -- nearly a third of the whole range lies frozen. Down its heart grinds a single river of ice about 63 km long, spilling from the flanks of K2 to feed the Braldu River and, in time, the mighty Indus. What is the name of this great glacier?
context: The Baltoro Glacier runs about 63 km, one of the longest glaciers outside the polar regions, and its meltwater joins the Braldu and then the Indus. Outside the Arctic and Antarctic the Karakoram is the most heavily glaciated place on Earth -- roughly a third under ice, versus about 8-12% of the Himalaya and 2% of the Alps. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltoro_Glacier; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram

question: As the climate warms, nearly every mountain glacier on Earth is shrinking back — but the Karakoram range refuses to follow the pattern. In the early 2000s, geographer Kenneth Hewitt surveyed its ice and found dozens of glaciers behaving strangely. Scientists named the puzzle the Karakoram anomaly. What are these unusual glaciers doing?
context: Geographer Kenneth Hewitt named the 'Karakoram anomaly' in a 2005 paper: between 1997 and 2002, 13 glaciers (10-20 km long) advanced and 9 larger ones thickened by 5-15 m, some rebuilding moraines that had been ice-free for over half a century -- while glaciers almost everywhere else retreated. Source: Kenneth Hewitt, Mountain Research and Development 25 (2005)

question: Everywhere else, hot summers melt mountain ice -- so why is the Karakoram's growing? The leading explanation is a rare local weather pattern: each summer a pool of cold, high-altitude air settles over the range, wrapping it in cloud and snow and keeping its summers cool while the Himalaya to the south bakes -- so the ice is fed, not starved. Newcastle University scientists named this the Karakoram ___. What is the missing word?
context: The leading explanation is the 'Karakoram vortex,' a swirl of cold air that in summer contracts to sit over the range, keeping its summers cool and snowy while the rest of the Himalaya warms -- so the ice is fed, not starved. Proposed by a Newcastle University team (Nathan Forsythe, Hayley Fowler), it remains an active area of study, not settled fact. Source: sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/08/170807112835.htm; nature.com/articles/s41561-019-0513-5  (Legend.)

question: High in the Himalayas of Nepal, three ancient royal cities — Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur — sit close together in the green Kathmandu Valley. At the heart of each city is a wide plaza wrapped around the old king's palace, packed with tiered wooden temples. What is this palace plaza called?
context: Each of the three old capitals — Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur — kept its own royal court, so the valley has three Durbar ('palace') Squares, not one. Around each king's palace, generations of Newar craftsmen raised clusters of tiered, many-roofed temples, making the squares open-air museums of Nepali woodcarving. All three belong to the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site (WHC #121). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathmandu_Valley

question: On a hill above the city of Kathmandu in Nepal stands an ancient Buddhist shrine called Swayambhunath. Bold animals roam its long stone stairway in gangs and snatch snacks straight from pilgrims' hands. Because of these noisy locals, English-speaking visitors gave the hilltop shrine a nickname. What is that nickname?
context: Troops of rhesus macaques really do rule Swayambhunath's hill and its 365-step eastern stairway, so travelers have long called it the 'Monkey Temple.' A Buddhist legend explains them: the bodhisattva Manjushri, tending the hill, let his hair grow long, and the lice in it are said to have turned into the monkeys. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swayambhunath

question: On a green hill above the Kathmandu Valley rises Swayambhunath, a white, dome-shaped Buddhist shrine capped by a golden spire. On each of the spire's four sides is painted the same huge image, one of the most famous sights in all of Nepal. What is painted there?
context: The great painted 'all-seeing eyes' of the Buddha look out from all four sides of Swayambhunath's spire, symbolizing a wisdom that watches every direction at once. Between them curls a squiggle that looks like a nose; it is really the Nepali numeral 1, standing for unity and the single path to enlightenment. A stupa is a dome-shaped Buddhist monument, often holding relics. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swayambhunath

question: In Kathmandu, a richly carved wooden palace faces the main plaza. Its resident is a little girl chosen after a careful search; then she is kept apart, her feet never touching the open street. She appears at a lattice window so crowds below can bow and be blessed. What is this special child believed to be?
context: She is the Kumari — a young girl worshipped as the living embodiment of the goddess Durga (locally Taleju). Chosen as a small child and revered until adolescence, she lives in the Kumari Ghar in Kathmandu's Durbar Square and appears at its window on festival days; once, even the king came to receive her blessing. The tradition is centuries old and still observed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathmandu_Durbar_Square

question: On the valley floor just east of Kathmandu rises a vast whitewashed dome, one of the largest Buddhist stupas anywhere on Earth. Its base is circled all day by a slow river of pilgrims walking clockwise and spinning long rows of prayer wheels. Which great stupa is this?
context: This is Boudhanath, rising about 36 m (118 ft) — among the biggest stupas in the world. Walking clockwise around it while spinning prayer wheels inscribed 'Om mani padme hum' is called doing kora. After the 1959 Tibetan uprising, thousands of Tibetan refugees settled around it and built more than 50 monasteries, making Boudhanath a great living center of Tibetan Buddhism on the old Tibet-to-India trade route. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boudhanath

question: The Nepalese capital of Kathmandu takes its name from one old building in its main Durbar Square: a wide wooden pavilion called Kasthamandap that once sheltered travellers on the trade road. Local legend claims the whole huge pavilion came from one amazing source. From what was it said to be built?
answer: the timber of a single tree
choices: the timber of a single tree
the bones of a great serpent
context: The pavilion is Kasthamandap ('kastha' = wood, 'mandap' = pavilion), and the city of Kathmandu takes its very name from it. Tradition holds the whole rest-house was raised from the timber of a single great sal tree. Kasthamandap stood for centuries until it collapsed entirely in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake; it has since been rebuilt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathmandu_Durbar_Square  (Legend.)

question: The Buddhist Swayambhu Purana says the Kathmandu Valley was once a single vast lake, with a lotus of light blazing at its center. To reach that light and open the land for cities, the bodhisattva Manjushri came to the valley's rim and struck it a single blow, splitting the rock into the deep Chobar gorge, through which the whole lake drained away. What did Manjushri strike the rim with?
context: In the legend Manjushri cleaves the gorge with his flaming sword of wisdom, and the self-arisen ('Swayambhu') lotus of light comes to rest on the hill where Swayambhunath now stands. Remarkably, geologists agree the valley really was a lake for much of its deep past, slowly drained through the Chobar gorge — so the legend preserves a memory of the land's true history. Source: https://sacredsites.com/asia/nepal/swayambhunath_stupa.html

question: In the 1270s, a young architect from the Kathmandu Valley named Araniko led eighty Nepali craftsmen over the Himalayas to serve Kublai Khan. In the Mongol emperor's Chinese capital, they raised a great white temple-tower. Historians say Araniko's Newar tradition helped shape the temple form now seen as the very symbol of East Asia. Which building form is that?
