context: The architect was Araniko (Arniko, 1245–1306). When his king hesitated to send so young a man abroad, the boy answered, 'My body is indeed young, but my mind is not.' In Kublai Khan's capital Dadu (modern Beijing) he built the White Stupa of the Miaoying Temple, over 50 m tall, around 1279–1288, and the Khan made him Duke of Liang and Director of All Artisan Classes. The Kathmandu Valley's tradition of stacked temple roofs thus helped shape the pagoda across China and Japan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Araniko

question: Around 1500 BCE a vanished seafaring people called the Lapita set out from near New Guinea in wooden canoes and became the first humans to reach island after island across the western Pacific, from New Guinea eastward to Fiji. They left no writing behind. Yet archaeologists can pinpoint where the Lapita first landed on each island, because one calling card of theirs turns up on beach after beach. What is that clue?
context: That signature is called Lapita ware: reddish-brown clay stamped before firing with rows of tiny toothed ('dentate') geometric patterns, pressed in with a comb-like tool. Wherever a matching shard turns up, the first seafarers had reached that spot -- which is how we know who sailed into the empty Pacific first. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: The whole Lapita culture takes its name from one dig site on the island of New Caledonia. In 1952 an archaeologist there asked a local man what the spot was called and wrote it down as 'Lapita.' But the Haveke word he half-heard actually meant something else. What did it really mean?
context: The Haveke word was 'xapeta'a', meaning something like 'to dig a hole' -- so an entire ancient civilization ended up named, through an archaeologist's mishearing, after a word for digging (fittingly, exactly what archaeologists do). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: About 3,000 years ago, the Lapita people sailed out across the western Pacific in outrigger canoes, carrying with them a distinctive pottery decorated with fine dotted stamped patterns. Their pots show up island by island, from near New Guinea east to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa — an unbroken trail more than 4,000 kilometres long across open ocean. To archaeologists, what does this Lapita pottery trail record?
answer: the greatest ocean migration in prehistory
choices: the greatest ocean migration in prehistory
the widest trade network of the ancient world
the first empire to rule the open Pacific
the oldest island religion ever found
context: That trail maps the peopling of Remote Oceania -- the first humans ever to reach these far-flung islands, crossing thousands of kilometres of empty sea. It is counted as the greatest ocean-going migration in all of prehistory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: The Lapita were the leading edge of a huge seafaring expansion whose ancient roots lay far to the northwest. DNA from 3,000-year-old graves on Vanuatu links these first voyagers to native peoples of Taiwan and the northern Philippines. Which people did these Pacific voyagers become the direct ancestors of?
context: These first voyagers were the direct ancestors of the Polynesians -- the eastern leading edge of the great Austronesian expansion that began near Taiwan and the northern Philippines. Ancient DNA from the Teouma graves carries the classic 'Polynesian motif' (haplogroup B4a1a1a) and clusters the earliest settlers with indigenous Taiwanese and Philippine peoples rather than with the nearby Papuans. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: Around 1500 BCE the Lapita people set out from the Bismarck Archipelago near New Guinea in great double-hulled ocean-going canoes. They hopped from island to island, ever deeper into a Pacific that no human had ever sailed before. To settle each new island, what living cargo did they carry aboard these canoes across the open sea?
context: Their canoes were floating farms: pigs, dogs and chickens plus taro, yam, coconut and breadfruit, all carried to seed each new island with food. It was a provisioned, planned colonisation of empty islands -- powerful evidence the Lapita were skilled voyagers who sailed out on purpose, not castaways drifting on the current. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: At the 3,000-year-old Teouma cemetery on Efate island, Vanuatu -- the oldest burial ground ever found in the Pacific -- many Lapita skeletons lay in the ground with no skulls at all. Once a body's flesh had rotted away, the living Lapita carefully lifted out its skull. Where did archaeologists find some of these missing skulls?
context: On one old man's chest lay three skulls set side by side, with three more placed between another person's legs; a seventh was tucked inside a decorated Lapita pot -- part of over 100 vessels found at Teouma, the largest single haul of Lapita pottery anywhere. The site was found by chance in 2003 when a bulldozer clearing land for a shrimp farm turned up red pottery shards. Source: https://humanities.org.au/power-of-the-humanities/lapita-cemetery-in-vanutu-thelps-solve-ancient-mystery/

question: On a clear evening over the Pacific off Hawaii, beachgoers watch the Sun's last rim as it slips into the sea. In the one second before it vanishes, watchers sometimes catch it doing something startling. Sailors have told tales about it for hundreds of years. What can the Sun's final rim do?
context: The classic 'green flash.' It's best seen over a clean, unobstructed ocean horizon on a clear, still evening — off Hawaii, the California coast, or Key West — and it's over in a blink, about one to two seconds. The Sun doesn't really turn green; only a thin rim of green light shows at its very top edge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_flash.

question: As the Sun's disk touches the sea off California, the thick air near the water bends and fans its light like a weak prism, tinting the very top rim. At that edge, the Sun is really giving off both blue and green light — yet beachgoers only ever see a green rim, never a blue one. On its long slanting path through the air, what happens to the blue light?
answer: the air scatters it out of the beam
choices: the air scatters it out of the beam
water vapor absorbs it near the sea
it bends down below the horizon first
the red light overpowers and hides it
context: It's the same reason the daytime sky is blue: air molecules scatter short-wavelength blue light out of the beam (Rayleigh scattering). The low air over the horizon also bends and separates the Sun's colors like a weak prism (refraction and dispersion); with the blue scattered away and the red already set, a rim of green is the last light left at the Sun's edge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_flash.

question: An ordinary green flash is a one-second blink, gone before you can point. But in October 1929, at Admiral Byrd's Antarctic base of Little America near the Bay of Whales, the Sun barely sank at all — it crawled sideways along the ice horizon. Byrd's men watched a brilliant green spot flash on and off, on and off, at the edge of the world. How long did that green flash keep flickering?
context: Byrd's own account: 'a tiny but brilliant green spot... no sooner disappeared than it flashed forth again... it remained on the horizon with short interruptions for thirty-five minutes.' Near the poles the Sun moves almost parallel to the horizon, so instead of a one-second blink the flash can wink on and off for many minutes; optics researchers reconstructed the 16 October 1929 event in a 2015 study. (Little America sat near the Bay of Whales at about 78 degrees S — not the geographic South Pole.) Sources: aaas.org/membership/scientia/catching-elusive-green-flash; opg.optica.org/ao/abstract.cfm?uri=ao-54-4-B54.

question: In the coldest winters of the Little Ice Age, from about 1300 to 1850, the River Thames in London froze hard enough to walk on. The name sounds huge, as if mile-high ice sheets had crushed the continents. In Europe and North America, how much colder than winters today were the coldest Little Ice Age winters?
context: Despite the fearsome name, the Little Ice Age (c.1300-1850) was a modest, patchy REGIONAL cooling — European and North American winters ran up to about 2°C colder than today's — not a true planet-wide glacial ice age with continental ice sheets. You read it not in mile-high ice but in frozen rivers, advancing glaciers, and the winter art people painted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Ice_Age.

question: In the coldest winters of the Little Ice Age, the River Thames in London froze so hard that people held fairs on it. These were the famous frost fairs, with rows of tents, shops and taverns. At the very last one, in 1814, they led a single big animal onto the ice below Blackfriars Bridge to show how thick it was. What animal walked across the frozen Thames?
context: Londoners called these ice carnivals 'frost fairs' (the term dates to the fair of 1608), pitching tents, shops, taverns, and even printing presses on the frozen Thames. The February 1814 fair was the last great one, and the elephant led across the ice below Blackfriars Bridge is its most famous — and most often-retold — image. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames_frost_fairs.  (Legend.)

question: Londoners blamed the cold of the Little Ice Age for freezing the Thames, but the river's own shape did half the work. Before the 1800s, the Thames ran broad, shallow, and slow, and one crowded medieval bridge spanning it on nineteen fat stone piers pinched the current into narrow arches. At low tide, drifting ice jammed against it, held back the water like a dam, and the river froze solid. Which Thames bridge choked the river into a near-dam?
context: Old London Bridge's nineteen piers wore bulky timber 'starling' casings that squeezed the tide into narrow arches, damming the sluggish, shallow river until it froze. It was demolished in 1831 and replaced with wider arches, and through the 1800s the banks were walled with embankments — so the Thames ran narrower, deeper, and faster, and it has never frozen solid in London since. The frost fairs ended partly because the RIVER changed, not only because the climate warmed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames_frost_fairs.

question: In the Alps above Chamonix, France, the Little Ice Age drove the Mont Blanc glaciers forward. The ice ground downhill and buried whole hamlets, until by 1616 one village had only six houses left standing at the ice front. Around 1645 the frightened villagers summoned the Bishop of Geneva, who climbed to the glacier's snout and performed a solemn church rite there on the ice. What rite did the bishop carry out?
context: The advancing ice between about 1600 and 1610 destroyed the hamlets of Le Chatelard (settled since the 1200s), La Bonnenuit, and La Bonneville. The exorcism didn't work — only the end of the Little Ice Age, two centuries later, finally halted the glaciers. Recorded tradition. Sources: chamonix.net history of Chamonix glaciers; academic.emporia.edu Late Holocene climate.  (Legend.)

question: As the Little Ice Age froze the canals of the Netherlands each winter, a Dutch painter named Hendrick Avercamp turned the frozen waterways into art. Deaf and unable to speak, he was nicknamed 'the mute of Kampen.' His crowded 1608 canvases show entire towns swarming out onto the ice. What winter pastime, painted again and again by Avercamp and still a Dutch passion today, fills those frozen-canal scenes?
context: Avercamp's 'Winter Landscape with Ice Skaters' (1608) helped pioneer the Dutch winter-landscape genre — a whole art form born from the Little Ice Age's frozen canals, and a near-photographic record of those winters. Skating on the frozen waterways became a lasting Dutch passion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendrick_Avercamp.

question: Around 985 Erik the Red led Norse settlers to Greenland, and through the milder centuries that followed they built a thriving farming colony — a few thousand people on some 500 farms, raising cattle and sheep at the edge of the habitable world. Then the Little Ice Age crept in, and by the late 1400s the colony had dwindled and vanished. Historians still debate the causes, but the central climate blow was straightforward. What did the deepening cold do that doomed the Greenland farms?
answer: left summers too short to grow winter hay
choices: left summers too short to grow winter hay
buried the farms under advancing glaciers
froze the soil into permanent permafrost
locked the fjords in ice all year round
context: The Western Settlement emptied around 1350 and the Eastern by the late 1400s. Cooling shortened the growing season and disrupted the seal hunt — but the colony had also funded itself by exporting walrus ivory to Europe, and that trade collapsed when African elephant ivory undercut it and the walrus were over-hunted. So climate was one thread among several, not the whole story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_colonization_of_North_America.

question: The Dasht-e Lut, a desert in southeastern Iran, is the hottest place on the whole planet's surface. It is so remote and so scorching that its record heat was clocked not by a thermometer on the ground but by satellite from orbit. Out on the bare sand, you truly could fry an egg. What temperature did the satellites record?
context: That 80.8 C (177 F) reading, captured by NASA's MODIS satellite instrument in 2018, is the hottest land-SURFACE temperature ever recorded anywhere on Earth -- an earlier 2005 pass had already clocked 70.7 C. One thing worth remembering: this is the temperature of the GROUND, seen from space, not of the air. The world's hottest reliably-recorded AIR temperature is much lower -- 56.7 C (134 F), set at Furnace Creek in California's Death Valley on 10 July 1913. Sources: NASA Science, 'Iran's Lut Desert'; Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (MODIS surface-temperature study); WMO Death Valley air-temperature record.

question: The Dasht-e Lut roasts hotter at ground level than any other desert on Earth -- hotter even than deserts that get more blazing sun. The secret lies in what the desert floor is made of, and its colour. Why does the Lut's ground heat up so ferociously?
answer: Ancient lava blackened it, so it drinks sunlight like a black iron pan
choices: Ancient lava blackened it, so it drinks sunlight like a black iron pan
Dark obsidian gravel sheets it, baking like a tray of broken glass
A red iron crust bakes it, hoarding the day's heat long past sundown
Fine volcanic ash blankets it, dark and soft as fireplace soot
context: More than half the Lut's surface is covered by dark volcanic rock, blackened by ancient lava -- and dark ground drinks in sunlight instead of bouncing it away, exactly like a black cast-iron pan left in the sun. A ring of mountains around the basin then traps that heat, with almost no wind to carry it off, so the surface bakes far past what the sunshine alone could explain. Sources: NASA Science, 'Iran's Lut Desert'; Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (over half the surface covered by volcanic rock).

question: The Lut Desert in eastern Iran is one of the hottest places ever measured from space — its bare ground has been clocked at over 70°C. The single hottest patch of the whole Lut is a scorched black plateau the locals call Gandom Beryan, Persian for 'Toasted Wheat.' A local legend explains that curious name. According to the tale, how did the plateau earn it?
answer: A load of wheat left out on it was scorched black by the ground within days
choices: A load of wheat left out on it was scorched black by the ground within days
Traders roasted their wheat there by burying the sacks in the scalding sand
Bread left on the rock came out toasted golden by the heat of the ground alone
A caravan hauling wheat vanished on it, leaving only spilled, blackened grain
context: Gandom Beryan ('Toasted Wheat') is a dark plateau in the northern Lut, long reputed to be the desert's single hottest ground. The story that a stash of wheat, simply left on the surface, blackened within days is folk legend rather than measured fact -- but it fits a place whose bare ground is the hottest ever measured on the planet. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (Gandom Beryan); Adventure Iran, 'Gandom Beryan Lut Desert'.

question: For ages, fierce winds roaring in from the northwest have hurled sand against the Lut's bedrock, grinding it into long parallel ridges called 'kaluts.' Geologists call these ridges yardangs, and they run for tens of kilometres across the desert. Seen from high above, what do the ridges look like?
answer: the streets and towers of an abandoned ghost city
choices: the streets and towers of an abandoned ghost city
a single giant fingerprint pressed into the sand
the curved ribs of some enormous buried beast
a frozen sea of rolling, wind-worn stone waves
context: These corrugated ridges are yardangs -- rock and hard sediment carved by relentless, sand-laden wind. In the Lut, the winds sweep in from the northwest between June and October, sculpting yardangs up to 75 m tall that run for over 150 km. From high above, the endless ranks of ridges and hollows look so much like a ruined metropolis that the region is nicknamed the 'abandoned city of ghosts' -- and the Lut holds some of the finest yardangs found anywhere on Earth. Sources: NASA Science, 'Iran's Lut Desert'; UNESCO World Heritage Convention; Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (yardangs to 75 m, over 150 km).

question: When UNESCO — the United Nations culture and science agency — inscribed the Lut Desert on its list in 2016, Iranians hailed it as a first. For decades, every one of Iran's World Heritage Sites had been palaces, mosques, and ancient cities like Persepolis and Pasargadae. The Lut was an altogether new type of site. What type of site was it?
answer: a natural site -- the raw land honoured for its own sake
choices: a natural site -- the raw land honoured for its own sake
an endangered site -- a treasure judged already at risk
a transboundary site -- one wonder split across two nations
a mixed site -- wild desert wrapped around ancient ruins
context: On 17 July 2016, at UNESCO's 40th session in Istanbul, the Lut Desert (World Heritage list no. 1505) became the first NATURAL site anywhere in Iran to earn World Heritage status, inscribed for its yardangs and vast sand seas under criteria vii and viii. Every Iranian site listed before it had honoured human culture; the Lut was the first chosen to protect the land itself. Sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, list no. 1505; IFP News, 'Lut Desert inscribed... Iran's first natural site'.

question: The Maldives is a chain of about 1,200 tiny coral islands scattered across the Indian Ocean southwest of India. The land barely rises above the sea. Its average height is only about 1.5 metres above the water, and even its very tallest spot rises only a few metres more. What world record does the Maldives hold?
context: No nation has a lower high point. The Maldives averages about 1.5 m (4.9 ft) above sea level, and even its natural summit on Addu Atoll is only about 2.4 m (7 ft 10 in). A resort on Villingili markets a 5.1 m landscaped mound as the 'highest peak in the Maldives,' but that is an artificial dune, not natural ground. Source: Wikipedia, 'Geography of the Maldives'; earthsky.org.

question: A ring of coral reef enclosing a shallow blue lagoon is called an atoll. The Maldives, a nation of about 1,200 tiny islands in the Indian Ocean southwest of India, is built almost entirely from these ring reefs. The English word 'atoll' was borrowed straight from the language the Maldivian people themselves speak. What is that language called?
context: English 'atoll' comes from the Dhivehi word 'atholhu.' Dhivehi is the language of the Maldives; Sinhala (Sri Lanka), Tamil, and Malayalam are neighboring South Asian languages, but the word 'atoll' came only from Dhivehi. Source: Wiktionary, 'atoll'; Wordnik.

question: Charles Darwin puzzled over atolls like those of the Maldives. Each is a ring of living coral standing alone in the open ocean, with just a lagoon in the middle and no island at all. In 1842 he gave a bold answer. A volcanic island had once risen there, and its coral reef grew around the shore. Then something happened to that island. In Darwin's theory, what became of the volcanic island?
answer: it slowly sank beneath the sea
choices: it slowly sank beneath the sea
it slowly eroded away in storms
it was buried under drifting sand
it split off on the moving seafloor
context: Darwin's 'subsidence theory,' published in 1842 in his first book, The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs: the volcano slowly sank while the reef-building coral kept growing upward toward the sunlight it needs, so when the island finally vanished under the sea, a ring of living coral marked where it had stood. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs'; Britannica, 'Darwinian subsidence theory.'

question: Standing on the Keeling atoll in the Indian Ocean in 1836, Charles Darwin was struck that this whole vast reef had been built by tiny, soft coral animals, one grain at a time. In The Voyage of the Beagle he wrote that these 'mountains of stone' made humanity's grandest ancient ruins seem small. He named the single most famous of them. Which monument did Darwin say the coral dwarfed?
context: Darwin wrote: 'We feel surprise when travellers tell us of the vast dimensions of the Pyramids and other great ruins, but how utterly insignificant are the greatest of these, when compared to these mountains of stone accumulated by the agency of various minute and tender animals!' Source: Darwin, The Voyage of the Beagle, ch. 20; standardebooks.org.

question: Astonishingly, Charles Darwin worked out how atolls form before he had ever seen one. Sailing on HMS Beagle in November 1835, he studied the coral reef ringing one lush Pacific island and sketched his entire sinking-island theory on the spot. Only months later did the Beagle reach a true atoll, the Keeling Islands, to test it. At which Pacific island did Darwin first dream up his theory?
context: Darwin first sketched the subsidence idea after visiting Tahiti in November 1835, then tested it against a real ring-reef when the Beagle surveyed the Keeling (Cocos) Islands in April 1836 -- six months before the voyage came home. He had the theory before he had the proof. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs'; darwinproject.ac.uk.

question: For over a century, Charles Darwin's atoll theory stayed unproven. No drill could bore through the towering pile of coral to reach whatever lay at its base. Then in 1952, engineers on Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific drilled straight down through more than four thousand feet of coral. Finally the bit reached the floor beneath. What did the drillers find waiting at the very bottom?
context: At Enewetak in 1952, drills bored through roughly 4,200-4,600 ft (about 1,300-1,400 m) of coral and struck volcanic basalt -- the drowned volcano Darwin had predicted in 1842, confirmed more than a century later. Earlier holes fell short: Funafuti in the 1890s reached about 1,114 ft and Bikini in 1947 about 2,556 ft, both still in coral. Source: royalsociety.org; Britannica, 'atoll.'

question: The Maldives is so low that it lives on the front line of rising seas: a coral atoll is alive and can grow taller as the ocean climbs, but only so fast. In 2009, the country's president, Mohamed Nasheed, staged a dramatic first for any government to force the world's climate summit to pay attention. What did Nasheed do to sound the alarm?
choices: marched his ministers to the North Pole
chained himself to the summit gates
shut every airport in the country
context: In October 2009, President Mohamed Nasheed and his ministers, in scuba gear, held a cabinet meeting about 5 m (16 ft) underwater and signed a document to hand to the Copenhagen climate summit. Nasheed even floated buying higher land abroad (naming Sri Lanka, India, and Australia) as a possible new home for the population; his successor later dropped the idea. The UN's IPCC has warned the low atolls could become uninhabitable this century if seas rise faster than the coral can build. Source: CBC News; commondreams.org.

question: The Challenger Deep is the deepest spot on Earth. It sits at the bottom of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, almost 11 km down. Now picture dropping Mount Everest, the tallest mountain, into it. How far under the sea would the peak still be?
context: Challenger Deep bottoms out around 10,935 m (about 6.8 miles) down — more than 2 km deeper than Everest is tall (8,849 m), so the whole mountain would vanish beneath the surface. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench (2021 depth study; 'more than 2 km farther from sea level than the peak of Mount Everest').

question: The Challenger Deep in the western Pacific Ocean is the deepest known point on Earth's surface — the seafloor plunges nearly 11 km straight down, deeper than Mount Everest is tall. It sits at the very bottom of the Mariana Trench, and the nearest big island is only a few hundred km away. Which island is it?
context: Guam, the largest of the Mariana Islands, is the nearest sizeable inhabited land to the Challenger Deep, which lies roughly 300 km to the southwest in the western Pacific. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('about 200 km east of the Mariana Islands near Guam').

question: In 1872 a British Royal Navy ship was refitted as a floating scientific laboratory and sent on a four-year voyage around the world to sound the deep oceans. In 1875, over a trench in the western Pacific, its crew dropped a weighted rope nearly 8,000 metres down to the seafloor. That was the deepest sounding of the whole trip. Which ship took it?
context: HMS Challenger sounded 4,475 fathoms (about 8,184 m) here on 23 March 1875 during its 1872-76 round-the-world science voyage — the deepest reading of the whole trip — and the deepest point on Earth, the Challenger Deep, was later named for the ship. NASA named a space shuttle after the very same vessel. Sources: geology.com/records/bathyscaphe-trieste.shtml; ocean.si.edu (HMS Challenger expedition); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger.

question: The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific Ocean is the deepest gash on the whole planet's seafloor — its lowest point, the Challenger Deep, plunges nearly 11 km straight down. It stretches about 2,550 km from end to end near the island of Guam, but it is never more than about 70 km wide. If you looked straight down on the trench from a satellite map, what shape would you see it curve into?
context: The Mariana Trench is a crescent-shaped gash about 2,550 km long but only 69 km wide, curving across the western Pacific seafloor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('crescent-shaped... about 2,550 km in length and 69 km in width').

question: For 85 years after it was discovered, no one had touched the bottom of the Challenger Deep. Then, on 23 January 1960, a tiny steel sphere slung beneath a fuel-filled float sank for nearly five hours into the black, and two men became the first ever to stand at the deepest point on Earth. Who were they?
context: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh rode the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom on 23 January 1960 after a descent of nearly five hours — the first humans ever to reach the deepest point on Earth, and for 52 years the only ones. Sources: geology.com/records/bathyscaphe-trieste.shtml; earthmagazine.org (Benchmarks: 23 January 1960).

question: Deep into the Trieste's 1960 descent toward the Challenger Deep floor, the two-man crew suddenly heard a startling bang echo through the cabin. Something on the craft had cracked under the monstrous pressure — yet they chose to keep sinking. What had cracked?
context: On the way down, the Trieste's outer Plexiglas viewport cracked under about 16,000 psi of pressure with a loud crack; Piccard and Walsh kept descending anyway, but the crack and stirred-up silt limited them to about 20 minutes on the bottom. Source: geology.com/records/bathyscaphe-trieste.shtml.

question: In March 2012, at the bottom of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, a lone pilot rode the tiny sub Deepsea Challenger down almost 11 kilometres to the seafloor of the Challenger Deep. It was the deepest solo dive ever attempted. The strange part: the man crammed inside the sub was famous for directing hit Hollywood movies. Who made the dive?
context: James Cameron, director of Titanic and Avatar, dived solo to about 10,908 m in the Deepsea Challenger on 26 March 2012 — the deepest solo dive ever. His descent took 2 hours 37 minutes and he spent about three hours on the bottom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepsea_Challenger.

question: The Challenger Deep is the deepest known spot in the world's oceans, at the bottom of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific. Down there almost 11 km of seawater press on everything at over a thousand times the pressure you feel at sea level. Concentrated onto a spot the size of your thumbnail, that force is like balancing which of these on it?
context: At the bottom the water presses at about 1,086 bar (15,750 psi) — roughly 1,072 times sea-level pressure, or about 8 tons on every square inch, like balancing an elephant on your thumbnail. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('1,086 bar... approximately 1,071.8 times... eight tons per square inch').

question: No ray of sunlight ever reaches the floor of the Challenger Deep, so nothing there can grow by photosynthesis. Instead, the animals of the deep live on a constant, faint fall of dead plankton and scraps sinking from the sunlit ocean far above. Scientists gave this endless food supply a poetic name — what is it called?
context: No sunlight reaches the pitch-black trench floor, so life there depends on 'marine snow' — a steady drift of dead plankton and organic scraps sinking from the sunlit ocean far above. Sources: csmonitor.com (What James Cameron saw 6.8 miles deep); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench.

question: The Challenger Deep is not a simple crack in the seafloor. It marks the line where the old, cold Pacific Plate bends downward and slides beneath the smaller Mariana Plate, dragging ocean crust back down into Earth's hot mantle. Geologists call this plate-swallowing process by what name?
context: The Challenger Deep is a subduction zone: the old, cold Pacific Plate bends and dives beneath the smaller Mariana Plate, recycling ocean crust down into the mantle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('the Pacific plate is subducted beneath the smaller Mariana plate').

question: Along the edge of the Mariana Trench, at least 19 enormous mounds rise from the seafloor — among the biggest 'volcanoes' of their kind anywhere on Earth. Fluids wrung from the Pacific Plate as it dives beneath the Mariana Plate are forced up through cracks in the crust, building these giants. Surprisingly, what do they erupt?
context: At least 19 serpentinite 'mud volcanoes' rise along the Mariana forearc: fluids squeezed from the subducting Pacific Plate turn mantle rock into serpentine mud that oozes up through faults and feeds sunless chemosynthetic microbes at the edge of life. Sources: pnas.org/content/109/8/2831; publications.iodp.org (IODP Expedition 366).

question: In the Swiss Alps, the Matterhorn rises 4,478 metres above the mountain village of Zermatt. It looks like a giant rock pyramid — exactly the shape a Toblerone chocolate bar copies. Climbers long ago noticed a neat trick about the mountain's four steep faces. What does each face point toward?
context: The four faces point almost exactly north, east, south, and west — three sit on the Swiss side, the south face on the Italian side. The lonely 4,478 m (14,692 ft) pyramid is so iconic it inspired the Toblerone chocolate logo. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Matterhorn; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matterhorn.

question: The Matterhorn, the pyramid-shaped peak on the Swiss-Italian border in the Alps, looks like a stone spike shoved straight up out of the earth. Geologists say the truth is the opposite: the peak is only the hard rocky core left standing after everything around it was slowly stripped away over millions of years. What did the stripping?
choices: a river carving a canyon through it
context: Four glaciers gnawed bowl-shaped hollows (cirques) into four sides of the same peak at once, grinding the rock between them into knife-edge ridges that meet at a point. A summit carved to a spike this way is called a glacial 'horn' — and a four-faced one is textbook enough that geologists call it the 'Matterhorn type.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramidal_peak; britannica.com/science/horn-glacial-landform.

question: Stand on the very summit of the Matterhorn, in Switzerland, and the rock beneath your boots is not European at all. The mountain's top slice is a slab of crust that was shoved up and over Europe when another whole continent slammed into it and squeezed an ancient ocean shut. Which continent's rock forms that summit?
context: Only the top ~1,000 m is African: it is gneiss of the Dent Blanche nappe, a slice of the African (Adriatic) plate thrust up and over Europe when the two continents collided and closed the ancient Tethys Ocean. The rest of the mountain sits on European bedrock — so the very summit of a Swiss peak is a piece of Africa. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dent_Blanche_nappe; earthlymission.com.

question: On 14 July 1865 Edward Whymper's team of seven became the first people ever to stand on the Matterhorn's summit — on Whymper's ninth attempt. Starting down, the least experienced climber, Douglas Hadow, slipped and pulled three companions off the ridge. The rope tying those four falling men to the three above them snapped, and all four plunged nearly 4,000 feet. What was damning about that particular rope?
answer: it was the oldest, weakest one, kept only as a spare
choices: it was the oldest, weakest one, kept only as a spare
it had frayed on the sharp rocks during the climb
it was the thinnest, lightest cord they carried
it had been nicked by a falling rock earlier
context: The snapped rope was the oldest and weakest the party carried, brought only as a reserve; the four fell about 4,000 ft down the north face. Whymper and the two Taugwalder guides survived. In 'Scrambles Amongst the Alps' (1871) Whymper wrote that he watched them slide 'downwards on their backs... endeavouring to save themselves,' and warned that courage and strength count for nothing without prudence. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Whymper; smithsonianmag.com.

question: High on the Matterhorn's Hörnli ridge in 2003, a block of rock the size of four houses suddenly broke loose without warning, and helicopters had to lift about 90 climbers off the peak to safety. Investigators discovered that the mountain's cracks had, for thousands of years, been held firmly shut by a hidden binder — until it finally gave way. What was that binder?
choices: natural mineral cement between the grains
compacted rubble wedged in its cracks
context: That ice is permafrost — frozen groundwater cementing the rock's cracks. In the 2003 heatwave it thawed and about 1,500 m3 of rock (roughly four houses' worth) broke off the Hörnli ridge, forcing helicopters to evacuate around 90 climbers. The scare launched the PermaSense project, which now monitors the crumbling ice inside the mountain. Source: news.uzh.ch (Matterhorn-Permasense); futurity.org.

question: Sensors bolted onto the Matterhorn reveal that its rocky summit is never truly still — it quivers up to 14 times more than its base. Some of that faint sway comes from distant earthquakes, but researchers were amazed to find the peak is also rocked, tremor by tiny tremor, by something hundreds of miles away with no quake involved. What keeps nudging it?
answer: the pounding of far-off ocean waves
choices: the pounding of far-off ocean waves
the roar of faraway mountain winds
the churn of a great distant river
context: The summit resonates like a slow tuning fork, swaying up to ~14 times more than its base. Much of it is 'microseism' — faint, ceaseless ground vibration made when ocean waves pound far-off coastlines and ripple through the Earth to the peak; nearby seismic tremors add more. A landlocked Alpine giant, gently rocked by the sea. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Matterhorn.

question: The lower Mississippi is the great river winding through the American South down to the Gulf of Mexico. Along its slow flat course, water races on the outside of every bend and eats the bank away. On the inside of the bend, it slows down and drops sand. Bend by bend, over centuries, this turns a straight river into big lazy curves across the whole valley. What are these grand bends called?
context: The fast outer bank becomes a steep 'cut bank' (or river cliff); the sheltered inside builds a gentle 'point bar' of sand — erode on the outside, deposit on the inside, and the whole train of bends slowly crawls downstream. The word 'meander' itself comes from the Buyuk Menderes (ancient Maiandros) River in Turkey, whose bends were so famous that, so the story goes, the Greeks copied them into the repeating 'Greek key' fret carved on the Parthenon. Source: Grokipedia, 'Meander,' corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Meander.'

question: A Mississippi bend can loop so tight that only a thin strip of land splits the two arms of the river. Then a big flood cuts straight across that neck. The river takes the shortcut. The old bend is left behind as a still lake. What is this kind of lake called?
context: An oxbow lake is named for the oxbow, the U-shaped wooden collar that curved around an ox's neck in a plow yoke — the very shape of the abandoned loop. Australians call it a 'billabong,' Texans a 'resaca.' The Mississippi valley is freckled with them: Arkansas's Lake Chicot is the largest oxbow lake in North America, and Tennessee's Reelfoot Lake was born when the great 1811-12 New Madrid earthquakes reshaped the ground. Source: Grokipedia, 'Oxbow lake,' corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Oxbow lake.'

question: When a Mississippi bend gets cut off, the still pond slowly fills in. First it turns to swamp, thick with mud and reeds. Then it dries out for good. All that is left is a faint curved line on the valley floor. You can spot it from a plane. What is this dry ghost of a lost bend called?
context: Geographers call this dry, curved trace a 'meander scar' — the fossil footprint of a bend that no longer exists. The full sequence runs oxbow lake to marshy swamp to dry scar, sometimes over centuries. From the air the old scars stack in curved stripes, mapping every path the river once took across its floodplain. Source: Grokipedia, 'Oxbow lake,' corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Oxbow lake.'

question: In Utah, the San Juan River winds in tight loops 300 m below the desert. It flows over 6 miles to move just 1.5 miles ahead. Unlike the Mississippi, which loops through soft mud, the San Juan is trapped in sheer stone walls. It cut them straight down as the land slowly rose. What do geologists call bends sunk deep in solid rock?
context: These are 'entrenched' (or 'incised') meanders — bends sawn straight down into bedrock. Long ago the San Juan wandered near sea level; then the Monument Upwarp slowly lifted the whole region, and the trapped river cut downward to keep pace, engraving its old loops 300 m into stone. The Goosenecks are the finest example of entrenched meanders on Earth. Sources: Visit Utah, 'Rafting the San Juan River'; Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Goosenecks State Park.'

question: At Horseshoe Bend near Page, Arizona, the emerald Colorado River sweeps almost a full circle around a lone butte of Navajo Sandstone, running 300 m (1,000 ft) below the overlook rim just downstream of Glen Canyon Dam. The loop is nearly closed — only a thin neck of rock still separates the incoming river from the outgoing river. Ages from now the Colorado will saw clean through that neck and desert the loop. What will it leave standing where the neck once stood?
context: Horseshoe Bend is a single incised meander. About 5-6 million years ago regional uplift trapped the Colorado in its bed and forced it to cut straight down instead of sideways, wrapping it around the butte you see today. When the river finally saws through the narrow neck, it will bypass the great loop and leave a natural rock bridge spanning the gap — the same neck-cutting shortcut that strands an oxbow lake on a lowland river, here performed in solid stone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Horseshoe Bend (Arizona).'

question: On the Colorado in Utah, beside what is now Lake Powell, a river once abandoned an entire bend. A few thousand years ago the water cut straight across its own neck, shortened its course by 6 miles, and walked away for good. Left behind is a dry, rock-walled ring wrapped around a central mesa 600-750 ft tall — a fossil oxbow carved in stone that looks like a donut from the Space Station. In the desert Southwest, geologists have their own word for such a stranded, dried-up incised loop. What is it?
context: Geologists literally call an abandoned, incised cutoff meander a 'rincon,' after this very place — The Rincon on the Colorado. When the river took its 6-mile shortcut a few thousand years ago, it stranded the old loop high and dry around its central mesa; from orbit the ring looks like a tire or donut dropped in the desert. It is a fossil oxbow lake, except carved in rock instead of mud — the whole story of this ladder frozen in stone. Sources: NASA Earth Observatory, 'Lake Powell and the Rincon, Utah'; Wikipedia, 'Incised meander.'

question: In the heart of Cambodia in Southeast Asia, one strange river connects a huge inland lake to the mighty Mekong River. For half the year, in the dry season, it flows south into the Mekong as expected. But when the summer monsoon swells the Mekong to bursting, this smaller river actually reverses course and runs backward, filling the lake. Which river is this?
context: The Tonlé Sap River links the great Tonlé Sap lake to the Mekong. For half the year it drains the lake southeast into the Mekong; then the monsoon flood reverses it. It is one of the only rivers on Earth to switch direction twice every year. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tonlé Sap.'

question: The Mekong is Southeast Asia's mightiest river, flowing about 4,900 km from the Tibetan Plateau down through China, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam. By the time it reaches southern Vietnam it fans out into a vast delta, splitting into a spread of arms that pour to the sea. Vietnamese people named the whole river after a mighty creature they pictured in those winding arms. Which creature?
context: In Vietnamese the delta is Sông Cửu Long — the 'Nine Dragons River' — named for the great arms it splits into on its way to the sea. The same river carries other names upstream: in China it is the Lancang, 'turbulent green river,' and in Thailand and Laos it is Mae Nam Khong, 'Mother of Water.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Mekong.'

question: The Tonlé Sap normally drains its lake gently down into the Mekong. But each year the Mekong swells so high that its level climbs above the smaller river's mouth and shoves the whole flow backward, up into the lake. What makes the Mekong rise that high?
choices: Tides pushing up from the sea
A reversal of the trade winds
context: The reversal is driven by the monsoon flood pulse — not by tides. From about June the monsoon soaks the whole Mekong basin, the big river swells until its level tops the Tonlé Sap's mouth, and water pressure alone forces the smaller river to run backward until the rains ease around October. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tonlé Sap.'

question: In central Cambodia lies Tonlé Sap, a huge shallow lake connected to the Mekong River by a short river of the same name. In the dry season the lake is barely a metre deep — you could almost wade across it — and covers about 2,700 km². Then the monsoon comes. The flooding Mekong swells so high that it shoves its own tributary backwards, pouring flood water into the lake for months. At its peak, how much bigger has Tonlé Sap grown?
choices: About one and a half times
context: The flood swells Tonlé Sap lake from roughly 2,700 km² to about 16,000 km² — nearly six times — and lifts its depth from about 1 m to 9–14 m, drowning the ring of forest around its shore. The reverse-flow up the river peaks near late August at about 10,000 m³/s. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tonlé Sap.'

question: In southern Laos, near the border with Cambodia, the mighty Mekong River spreads out to about 14 km across — its widest point along its entire 4,300 km journey from Tibet to the sea. Here the river breaks into a huge maze of channels winding around thousands of small forested islands. Local Lao people have a name for this island maze. What do they call it?
choices: Ha Long, the Bay of Sea-Stacks
context: Si Phan Don means 'the 4,000 Islands.' Here the Mekong spreads to about 14 km — its widest anywhere along its 4,350 km course — braiding around thousands of sandy islands and rocky islets in the lowland channels of southern Laos. Source: Wikipedia, 'Si Phan Don.'

question: In southern Laos, Southeast Asia, the mighty Mekong River hits a giant cluster of rocky islets and thunders through them as the Khone Phapheng falls. It is not a tall waterfall at all — barely 20 metres, no dizzying plunge, nothing tourists travel far for. Yet among all the waterfalls on Earth, Khone Phapheng holds one genuine world record. Which one?
choices: The most powerful waterfall on Earth
The most remote waterfall on Earth
context: Khone Phapheng is the widest waterfall in the world — measured about 10.8 km (10,783 m) from one edge of its many channels to the other, though it is not tall. Its 9.7 km barrier of rapids is the reason the Mekong can never be sailed all the way up into China. Source: Wikipedia, 'Khone Phapheng Falls.'

question: In the 1890s, French steamboat crews tried again and again to force their vessels up the Mekong past Khone Phapheng Falls in southern Laos — and the wall of rapids beat them back every time. To move boats and cargo around the impassable falls, what did the French build across the islands of Don Det and Don Khon?
answer: A railway to carry the boats
choices: A railway to carry the boats
A canal cut around the rapids
context: Unable to steam past the falls, the French laid a portage railway across the islands of Don Det and Don Khon — running 1893–1940, the first railway in Laos. Boats were hauled from the water, carried by rail around the barrier, and refloated above it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Si Phan Don.'

question: The longest mountain range on Earth is a single chain about 65,000 km long that wraps almost all the way around the planet, and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is just one stretch of it. Yet almost no explorer has ever laid eyes on it. Where does nearly this entire range lie?
choices: Buried beneath the Antarctic ice cap
Sunk under the sands of the Sahara
Covered by the Amazon rainforest canopy
context: Earth's true longest mountain range is the global mid-ocean-ridge system, a single volcanic seam roughly 65,000 km (40,400 mi) long that winds around the whole planet almost entirely beneath the seas; the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the stretch running down the middle of the Atlantic. Source: Wikipedia, Mid-ocean ridge (Grokipedia checked first, fetch blocked).

question: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge stays hidden 2.5 km under the Atlantic. Almost nobody sees it. But one volcanic island sits right on top of it. Its own eruptions stacked so much rock that the plate boundary runs across dry land. You can hike its canyons and steaming cracks. Which island is it?
context: Iceland sits directly on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, so the plate boundary crosses the island on dry land. At Thingvellir the rift opens into walkable cliffs and fissures, including the great gorge Almannagja ('everyman's gorge'). Note: the boundary is really a broad zone of many fissures, not one tidy crack. Source: Wikipedia, Thingvellir.

question: Down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean runs a huge underwater mountain range called the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Molten rock rises up from below and pushes the two tectonic plates on either side slowly apart, so the whole Atlantic Ocean is quietly getting wider every year. The spreading rate is surprisingly close to the speed of one everyday thing you can watch on your own body. What is it?
context: The ridge spreads about 2.5 cm (1 inch) a year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow, so the Atlantic widens at that same crawl, year after year. Source: Wikipedia, Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

question: Running down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean from Iceland almost to Antarctica is a great underwater mountain range called the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. There two of Earth's tectonic plates slowly pull apart, and hot magma from the mantle wells up into the gap and freezes into brand-new ocean floor. This constant manufacturing of fresh crust along the ridge has a two-word name. What is it?
context: At a spreading center two plates separate and mantle magma rises to fill the gap, freezing into fresh ocean crust; this endless crust-making is called seafloor spreading, and it is why the Atlantic keeps growing. Source: Wikipedia, Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

question: In Iceland's Thingvellir lake, a flooded crack called Silfra holds water so clear that divers seem to float in midair. Silfra has a boast almost nowhere else can match. Divers glide right through the gap where two great plates pull apart. Which two plates are they?
answer: The North American and Eurasian plates
choices: The North American and Eurasian plates
The Pacific and North American plates
The Nazca and South American plates
context: At Silfra, divers glide through a flooded fissure in the rift between the North American and Eurasian plates, in water so clear that the 'Cathedral' section stays visible almost its full ~100 m length. The 'swim between two continents' is the beloved, slightly simplified version: the boundary is a wide rift zone, and Silfra is one crack within it. Source: Wikipedia, Silfra.  (Legend.)

question: Just after 7 a.m. on November 14, 1963, the cook aboard the trawler Isleifur II, fishing off Iceland's south coast, saw a dark column of smoke rising from the open sea where the charts showed only water. It was no burning ship: the sea kept erupting for days from a volcanic vent 130 m down. What was forming before the crew's eyes?
answer: A brand-new island rising from the sea
choices: A brand-new island rising from the sea
A rogue wave building over deep water
A whirlpool spinning above a wreck
A raft of pumice drifting on the tide
context: The smoke the cook saw was the birth of Surtsey, a brand-new island erupting from a seafloor 130 m (430 ft) down off Iceland's south coast on November 14, 1963. Source: Wikipedia, Surtsey.

question: At Thingvellir, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge splits Iceland into cliffs and gorges. In this natural bowl, Icelanders started a body in the year 930. It kept meeting at the rift almost every year until 1798. It is one of the oldest of its kind still alive on Earth. What was it?
answer: One of the world's oldest parliaments
choices: One of the world's oldest parliaments
One of the world's oldest high courts
One of the world's oldest royal councils
One of the world's oldest church synods
context: The Thingvellir rift, where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge splits Iceland, hosted Iceland's Althing, founded in 930 AD; it met there almost every year until 1798, making it one of the world's oldest surviving parliaments. Source: Wikipedia, Thingvellir.

question: Silfra's water is famous for being almost unbelievably clear, clean enough to drink straight from the fissure. The secret is its long journey: glacial meltwater from the Langjokull ice cap does not flow to Silfra overland. Instead it sinks underground and creeps through porous lava rock that filters it perfectly clean before it wells up into the crack. Divers are often startled to learn how long the water spends hidden underground on that journey. About how long?
context: Silfra's water is glacial meltwater from Langjokull, Iceland's second-largest glacier about 50 km away; it percolates underground through porous lava for 30 to 100 years, emerging at a frigid 2-4 degrees C, filtered clear and clean enough to drink. Source: Wikipedia, Silfra.

question: Since it cooled in 1965, the new island of Surtsey has been sealed off. Only a small handful of scientists may ever set foot on it. All other visitors are banned. Iceland guards it so tightly for one big science reason. By keeping human boots off the raw rock, what can researchers do on Surtsey that they cannot do almost anywhere else?
answer: Watch life colonize bare new land from scratch
choices: Watch life colonize bare new land from scratch
Track a colony of a nearly extinct seabird
Mine a volcanic mineral found nowhere else
Measure the ridge spreading faster than anywhere
context: Sealed since 1965, Surtsey is a natural laboratory where scientists watch life colonize bare volcanic rock from scratch; the first plant, sea rocket (Cakile arctica), sprouted in 1965, and Surtsey became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008. Source: Wikipedia, Surtsey.

question: In the 1950s, American geologist Marie Tharp spent years mapping the Atlantic seafloor by hand. She turned ship depth readings into the first real map of the ocean bottom. Along the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge she traced one long feature no one had expected. The find helped overturn how scientists thought Earth worked. What did Tharp spot running down the ridge's spine?
answer: A deep rift valley down the crest
choices: A deep rift valley down the crest
A trench of crushed old crust
context: Mapping the Atlantic floor in the 1950s, Marie Tharp and Bruce Heezen found a deep rift valley running down the ridge's spine, a key clue that the plates were pulling apart and a cornerstone in proving plate tectonics. Source: Wikipedia, Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

question: Almost the entire Mid-Atlantic Ridge stays about 2.5 km underwater, so why does Iceland alone rise so high above it that a whole country stands in the daylight? The reason is a rare double dose of magma: Iceland does not just sit on the spreading ridge, it also sits directly over one more deep source of heat at the same time. What is that second magma source beneath Iceland?
context: Iceland rises above the waves because it sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge AND over a deep mantle hotspot at once; the double magma supply piles the ridge into a plateau instead of hiding it ~2.5 km underwater like the rest of the ridge. The plume's exact depth is still studied, but the hotspot itself is well established. Source: Wikipedia, Iceland hotspot.

question: This small island rides the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. It is one of the most restless places on Earth. A fresh eruption pops up in Iceland every few years. Of all the basalt lava that has erupted worldwide in written history, Iceland alone poured out a huge share. About how much?
answer: Roughly a third of it all
choices: Roughly a third of it all
Roughly a tenth of it all
Roughly a hundredth of it all
context: Iceland erupts on average about every 3-4 years and has produced roughly a third of all the basaltic lava erupted anywhere on Earth in recorded history, a staggering output for one small island. Source: Wikipedia, Iceland hotspot.

question: The lower Mississippi is the great river that winds through the American South down to the Gulf of Mexico. It never takes the short way to the sea. It loops and coils in big lazy S-bends, wandering sideways for miles across the flat valley before turning back toward the Gulf. What are these big sweeping bends called?
context: Those looping curves are meanders, named after the winding Menderes River in Turkey. On its flat lower floodplain the Mississippi wanders so freely it can travel miles sideways for every mile it gains toward the sea. Source: NPS 'Mississippi River Facts' (nps.gov/miss/riverfacts.htm); Mississippi Valley Traveler, 'Geology of the Mississippi River.'

question: The Mississippi runs 2,350 miles to the Gulf. But at its start, you can wade across it in your pants. It is only 20 to 30 feet wide, its narrowest spot. It trickles out of one small lake in the north woods of Minnesota. Which lake is the river's humble source?
context: Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota is the river's conventionally accepted source. Explorer Henry Schoolcraft coined the name in 1832 by splicing the Latin ver-ITAS ('truth') and CA-put ('head') to spell out 'true head.' From this ankle-deep stream the Mississippi runs 2,350 miles to the sea. Source: NPS 'Mississippi River Facts' (nps.gov/miss/riverfacts.htm); Britannica 'Lake Itasca.'

question: Drift down the lower Mississippi River as it winds in big lazy S-curves through the flat lowlands of Louisiana and Arkansas. All along the way, you pass one quiet, curved lake after another sitting just off the main channel — each one shaped like a bent bow or a horseshoe. They are what's left when the river cuts a new straighter path in a flood and abandons a big meander loop. What are these curved leftover lakes called?
context: It's an oxbow lake — a loop the river pinched off and left behind, curving beside the main channel with still water and no current. Louisiana and Arkansas are dotted with them. Source: Geography Realm, 'How Oxbow Lakes Form' (geographyrealm.com/how-oxbow-lakes-form/); Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Lake Chicot.'

question: The Mississippi River winds across the flat American Midwest in long looping curves called meanders. A meander never sits still. As the water sweeps around a bend, it slams hard into one side and drops fresh sand on the other, so the whole loop slowly crawls sideways across the plain year after year. Where does the water strike hardest and eat its bank the fastest?
answer: The outer bank of the bend
choices: The outer bank of the bend
The inner bank of the bend
The straight stretch above the bend
The shallow bed below the bend
context: The current runs fastest on the outer bank, so that is where it cuts hardest, while sand piles up on the slow inner bank. That steady lopsided erosion is why every meander migrates across the floodplain. Source: Geography Realm, 'How Oxbow Lakes Form' (geographyrealm.com/how-oxbow-lakes-form/).

question: Where the Mississippi at last reaches the Gulf of Mexico, it doesn't stop at a single mouth. At a place called Head of Passes it forks into three long channels — Southwest Pass, South Pass, and Pass a Loutre — that carry its muddy water far out into the open sea on their own thin ribbons of land. This sprawling delta is known worldwide by the name of the shape it makes. Which shape?
context: It's a bird's-foot delta. At Head of Passes the river splits into Southwest Pass, South Pass, and Pass a Loutre, each riding its own finger of mud into the Gulf. Most deltas fan out in a triangle; the Mississippi's is one of the few splayed like a bird's foot. Source: Wikipedia 'Head of Passes'; USACE Mississippi Valley Division, 'Bird's Foot.'

question: The Mississippi has left many cut-off oxbow lakes down its valley. The grandest sits in southeast Arkansas. It is a 22-mile ribbon of water, a mile wide, bent like a huge letter C. It traces a path the river ran about 600 years ago before it took a shortcut. Which lake is this, the largest oxbow in North America?
context: It's Lake Chicot in southeast Arkansas — about 22 miles long and the largest oxbow lake in North America, cut off roughly 600 years ago when the Mississippi carved itself a shorter path. Source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Lake Chicot'; Wikipedia 'Lake Chicot, Arkansas.'

question: The Mississippi and its tributaries gather rain from all or part of 31 states and two Canadian provinces — from the Rockies in the west to the Appalachians in the east — draining about 40% of the continental United States, some 1.2 million square miles. That vast basin is the third-largest of any river on Earth, and only two rivers in the world drain a bigger one. Which two rivers outrank the Mississippi?
context: The Amazon and the Congo. The Mississippi drains about 1.2 million square miles — all or part of 31 states and two Canadian provinces, roughly 40% of the continental United States — making its basin the third-largest on Earth, out-drained only by the Amazon in South America and the Congo in Africa. Source: NPS 'Mississippi River Facts'; US EPA 'The Mississippi/Atchafalaya River Basin.'

question: In the winter of 1811–12, a series of violent earthquakes tore through the Mississippi Valley near New Madrid, Missouri. In one spot the shaking dropped whole tracts of forest into a hollow below the water line, and the Mississippi rushed in to fill the sunken ground, creating a brand-new lake across the line in northwestern Tennessee. Two centuries on, the bare stumps of the drowned trees still stand right up out of the water. What is this earthquake-made lake called?
context: It's Reelfoot Lake in northwestern Tennessee. The 1811–12 New Madrid quakes sank the land and the Mississippi flooded in; the drowned bald-cypress stumps still rise from the shallow water today. Source: USGS 'Summary of the 1811–1812 New Madrid Earthquakes Sequence.'

question: The New Madrid quakes of 1811-12 hit with three huge shocks, each about magnitude 7. They rang church bells hundreds of miles away. Boatmen on the Mississippi swore they watched the river do something impossible for hours before the water calmed. What did the scared rivermen say the Mississippi did that night?
context: They reported it running backward. The quakes uplifted the riverbed and set off giant sloshing 'seiche' waves that briefly shoved the current upstream for a few hours — a real but temporary, local illusion, not a permanent reversal. Source: USGS '1811–1812 New Madrid Earthquakes'; UCSB Geography, 'When the Mississippi Flowed Backwards.'  (Legend.)

question: The restless Mississippi keeps leaping into new channels, and every so often it redraws the map itself. In an 1881 flood the river jumped its banks, abandoned its old bed, and cut a brand-new channel right past Kaskaskia — the very first capital of Illinois — leaving the little town marooned by the shifted river. What strange situation does that leave Kaskaskia in today?
answer: An Illinois town reached by road only through Missouri
choices: An Illinois town reached by road only through Missouri
An Illinois town reached only by boat across the river
A town that switched from Illinois to Missouri
A town split in two by the Illinois–Missouri line
context: Kaskaskia is now an exclave of Illinois sitting on the west bank, reachable by road only from Missouri. The 1881 flood shifted the Mississippi into a new channel and cut the old capital off from its own state. Source: FOX2 'The Illinois village located in Missouri'; Wikipedia 'Kaskaskia, Illinois.'

question: High in the Khasi Hills of northeast India, near the border with Bangladesh, warm monsoon winds crash into steep slopes and dump their moisture as endless rain. One small village up there gets almost 39 feet of rain a year — enough to submerge a two-story house. It is the wettest inhabited place on Earth. What is this village called?
context: Mawsynram, home to about 1,300 Khasi people, catches around 11,872 mm (467 in) of rain a year and has held the Guinness record for wettest inhabited place since 1985 — narrowly beating its neighbour Cherrapunji. The crown is contested, though: the Colombian rainforest towns of Lloró and López de Micay report even higher long-term averages. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Mawsynram ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mawsynram  (Legend.)

question: In the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, in northeast India, some of the heaviest rain on Earth pours off the high plateau. Fed by that endless rain, a single column of water drops straight down 340 metres — over 1,100 feet — into a deep green pool below. It is the tallest plunge waterfall in all of India. What is it called?
context: Nohkalikai Falls, near Cherrapunji, drops 340 m (1,115 ft) in a single unbroken column into a turquoise plunge pool — India's tallest plunge waterfall. Its flow roars in the monsoon and thins to a ribbon in the dry season. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nohkalikai_Falls ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Cherrapunji

question: High on the plateau of Meghalaya in northeast India sits a small town that catches the full brunt of the monsoon storms rolling in from the Bay of Bengal. From August 1860 to July 1861 this one town was drenched by about 26,470 millimetres of rain — roughly 86 feet of water in a single year, the greatest yearly rainfall ever measured anywhere on Earth. Which town set this record?
context: Cherrapunji (Khasi name Sohra) recorded 26,470 mm from August 1860 to July 1861 — about 86 feet of rain in twelve months, a single-year record still cited by Guinness. During that same deluge, July 1861 alone brought roughly 9,300 mm, the greatest one-month rainfall ever measured on Earth. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Cherrapunji ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherrapunji  (Legend.)

question: Every summer over India, a wet wind sweeps in off the warm Indian Ocean and drenches the whole subcontinent with rain for months. Then, as winter comes, the wind reverses direction, dries out, and dies away. Farmers call this seasonal wind cycle the monsoon, and their whole growing season depends on it. What flips the winds around each year to launch the monsoon?
answer: In summer the land heats up faster than the ocean.
choices: In summer the land heats up faster than the ocean.
In summer the ocean heats up faster than the land.
The Himalayas melt and chill the summer air.
The Indian Ocean's currents reverse each summer.
context: In summer the Indian landmass heats faster than the surrounding ocean; hot air rises over the continent, leaving low pressure, and moisture-laden sea air sweeps in to replace it — the summer (southwest) monsoon. In winter the pattern reverses and dry air flows back out to sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoon_of_South_Asia

question: For over a thousand years, sailors and traders from the Middle East rode the seasonal winds across the Indian Ocean, sailing east in summer toward India and back west in winter. The very word 'monsoon' came from these traders' own word 'mawsim,' meaning 'season.' Which language of the Middle Eastern merchant world gave us the word 'monsoon'?
context: 'Monsoon' comes from the Arabic 'mawsim,' meaning 'season.' Arab sailors named the winds that flipped direction with the time of year, riding them out across the Indian Ocean and home again; European traders later carried the word into English. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoon_of_South_Asia

question: Why is Meghalaya, in particular, drenched while much of India stays parched? The Khasi Hills stand as an east-west wall directly in the monsoon's path; moist sea air funnels up, is shoved higher over the hills, cools, and pours out as rain. Which body of water feeds that soaking air?
context: Meghalaya's Khasi Hills form an east-west wall that intercepts the Bay of Bengal branch of the monsoon. Moist air funnelling up off the bay is forced upward over the hills, cools, and dumps its water — a process geographers call orographic (relief) rainfall. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Mawsynram ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mawsynram

question: The town the British wrote down as 'Cherrapunji' never called itself that — the name was a garbling of its true Khasi name, which colonial officials couldn't pronounce. In 2007 Meghalaya officially restored the original. What is the town's real name?
context: The Khasi name is Sohra (soh-ra); British officials heard it as 'Cherra,' and Bengali plainsfolk added 'punji' (a cluster of villages), giving 'Cherrapunji.' Meghalaya officially restored the name Sohra in 2007. Some accounts trace 'Sohra' to a word for 'land of oranges.' Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Cherrapunji ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherrapunji

question: Across India a billion farmers watch the sky each spring for the monsoon's dramatic arrival — the 'burst,' when the skies finally open. The rains sweep ashore first around June 1, then roll north to blanket the whole land by mid-July. In which state does the monsoon make landfall first?
context: The monsoon's onset — the 'burst' — normally reaches Kerala, at India's southern tip, around June 1, then advances north to cover the whole country by mid-July. With over half of India's cropland rain-fed, the timing of the burst is watched like a heartbeat; a Reserve Bank of India governor once called the monsoon 'the real finance minister of India.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoon_of_South_Asia

question: In Meghalaya, the Khasi people don't build their footbridges. They grow them. They train living tree roots across flooded rivers for years, until the roots knit into a span. It can carry dozens of people, and it grows stronger for generations. The dangling roots they weave come from which tree?
context: The Khasi weave the living aerial roots of the rubber fig (Ficus elastica) across rivers, guiding them for decades until they interlock. Unlike a wooden bridge, a living root bridge keeps growing — getting stronger over centuries and, by some accounts, lasting several hundred years and carrying fifty people at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_root_bridge ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Mawsynram  (Legend.)

question: Cherrapunji, high in the hills of Meghalaya in northeast India, is drenched every summer by some of the heaviest monsoon rain on the planet — and yet its people run short of drinking water every dry season and must trek far downhill to fetch it. That is the cruel paradox: one of the wettest towns on Earth goes thirsty. What turned it thirsty?
answer: Cleared forests let the rain sheet off the bare slopes.
choices: Cleared forests let the rain sheet off the bare slopes.
The winter monsoon dumps all its rain far out at sea.
The limestone hills swallow every river underground.
The town sits far above its nearest valley river.
context: Despite record rainfall, Cherrapunji faces dry-season water shortages: deforestation has stripped the slopes, so the rain sheets straight off and washes the topsoil away instead of soaking in, and residents must trek far for drinking water in winter. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherrapunji ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Cherrapunji

question: In the drenched hills of Meghalaya in northeast India, the Khasi people grow bridges instead of building them: they patiently train the long living roots of rubber-fig trees across a stream until the roots knit into a walkway strong enough to carry a person. Below the village of Nongriat spans the most celebrated of all these living root bridges, the Umshiang — roughly two centuries old and built like no other root bridge on Earth. What makes the Umshiang unlike all the rest?
answer: It carries two root walkways stacked one above the other.
choices: It carries two root walkways stacked one above the other.
It is roofed over against the endless monsoon rain.
It stretches over a kilometre across the gorge.
It grows from a single tree rooted midstream.
context: The Umshiang Double-Decker Root Bridge below Nongriat has two stacked levels of living roots, spans about 30 m, and is roughly 180-200 years old. Builders trained the roots along hollowed-out betel-nut (areca) palm trunks used as scaffolding, then grew a second bridge directly above the first. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umshiang_Double-Decker_Root_Bridge ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Umshiang_Double-Decker_Root_Bridge  (Legend.)

question: To the Khasi, weaving a living root bridge is no mere feat of engineering but a sacred inheritance. Their bridges echo an old Khasi legend of the 'jingkieng ksiar,' a shining golden ladder that, in the world's first days, joined two realms together. Which two realms did it link?
context: In Khasi tradition the root bridges echo the 'jingkieng ksiar,' a golden roots-ladder said to have once connected heaven and earth. The Khasi treat their living architecture as a sacred inheritance rather than a mere footpath — sophisticated engineering that is grown, not built. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_root_bridge  (Legend.)

question: Even an old eruption no one saw leaves a trace. A big volcano blasts gas high into the sky. Winds spread it around the globe. It settles into layered polar snow. Deep in Greenland's ice, scientists spot the eruption as a sharp chemical spike in one year's layer. Which volcano gas makes the tell-tale spike?
context: Volcanic sulfur (as sulfur dioxide) rises into the stratosphere, turns to sulfate, and rains onto the ice sheets, so each year's frozen snow locks in a record of past eruptions. The giant spike near 1257 is the largest in the Greenland and Antarctic ice for about 7,000 years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1257_Samalas_eruption

question: High on the Indonesian island of Lombok, hikers climb for days to a crater lake called Segara Anak. It is 200 metres deep, cradled in a huge bowl. The bowl was left when an older mountain blew itself apart in 1257. On the rim today stands Lombok's tallest peak, Indonesia's second-tallest volcano. What is it called?
context: The 1257 eruption blew an older volcano apart and left the Segara Anak caldera, a crater lake about 200 m deep. Mount Rinjani, Indonesia's second-highest volcano, stands beside it and is still active today, towering over the blue lake. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Samalas ; https://volcano.si.edu/volcano.cfm?vn=264030

question: For 750 years the polar ice held a puzzle. A huge eruption around 1257 spiked sulfur levels in ice at both poles, yet nobody could identify the volcano responsible. In 2013 a team led by geographer Franck Lavigne finally cracked the case. They matched tiny glass shards frozen in the ice to one volcano that had blown itself apart. Which volcano did they identify?
context: Lavigne's team published the match in 2013, ending a 750-year search: the glass ash chemistry pinned the 1257 eruption on Mount Samalas, a VEI-7 blast whose column shot roughly 43 km into the sky before the mountain collapsed into the Segara Anak caldera. https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1307520110 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Samalas

question: Long before scientists tracked down the 1257 eruption, the people of Lombok already knew. A Javanese chronicle written on palm leaves, the Babad Lombok, tells how Mount Samalas collapsed and its flows buried a royal capital. That city then vanished from history and its ruins have never been located. What was this lost capital of the Lombok kingdom called?
context: The Babad Lombok says Samalas's flows destroyed Pamatan; this local memory, kept for centuries, matched what scientists later found in the ice -- a rare case where an oral-written tradition and ice-core chemistry told the same story. Samalas's fallout even reached medieval Europe, feeding the great famine of 1258. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1257_Samalas_eruption  (Legend.)

question: In AD 536, a strange haze dimmed the sun across Europe and Asia for about 18 months. The Byzantine writer Procopius recorded that the sun 'gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon,' and summer snow and famine followed. For centuries the cause stayed a mystery; scientists now blame one kind of disaster, though they still cannot agree which struck or where. What dimmed the sun in 536?
context: Ice cores confirm a massive eruption around 536, but its source is genuinely disputed: a high-latitude northern volcano (Iceland has been proposed) is a leading suspect, and Ilopango in Central America was long blamed too. 536 is often called 'the worst year to be alive' -- Chinese records note summer snow, famine spread, and the Plague of Justinian struck from 541. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_winter_of_536 ; https://www.science.org/content/article/why-536-was-worst-year-be-alive  (Legend.)

question: About 74,000 years ago, Lake Toba on Sumatra produced the largest volcanic eruption in nearly 2 million years. Ash buried much of the planet. Some scientists, led by Stanley Ambrose, put forward a startling but heavily debated idea about what this catastrophe did to early humans. What does this disputed hypothesis claim Toba nearly did to our ancestors?
answer: crashed their numbers to just a few thousand
choices: crashed their numbers to just a few thousand
drove them out of Africa for the first time
wiped out their use of stone tools
split them into two separate species
context: Ambrose's 'Toba bottleneck' idea holds the eruption crashed the human population to a few thousand -- but it is genuinely debated: stone tools at Jwalapuram in India look nearly unchanged above and below Toba's ash, hinting people there survived. Lake Toba is today the world's largest volcanic crater lake, with Samosir Island sitting inside it. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toba_catastrophe_theory  (Legend.)

question: In Provence, in southern France, a cold dry wind roars down the Rhone valley to the Mediterranean. It bends the tops of the cypress trees, flattens the grass, and blows every cloud from the sky. What is this famous Provencal wind called?
context: The mistral averages about 50 km/h with gusts to 100 km/h down the Rhône valley, and it is one of Europe's most persistent regional winds, blowing 100 to 150 days a year. Its name comes from the Provençal/Occitan word for 'masterly' -- the master wind. Provençal folklore even claims it blows in multiples of three days: 3, 6, or 9. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistral_(wind)

question: Vincent van Gogh painted outdoors at Arles in 1888, right in the teeth of the mistral, which kept trying to snatch his canvas and easel away across the fields. Before he could paint each day, he had to do one thing to fight the wind so it could not carry his work off. What did van Gogh do to keep painting through the mistral?
answer: staked the easel to the ground with iron pegs and ropes
choices: staked the easel to the ground with iron pegs and ropes
weighted the canvas down with a ring of heavy stones
propped the easel against an old olive tree for shelter
built a low screen of cut cypress branches around himself
context: Van Gogh drove iron pegs into the ground and lashed his easel legs to them so the mistral could not carry the canvas away. He prized the pure, clear light the wind left behind once it had scoured every cloud from the sky. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistral_(wind)

question: A hot dusty wind blows off the Sahara, picks up moisture as it crosses the Mediterranean, then dumps red desert dust as rain on southern Italy. This 'blood rain' can even stain the snow of the Alps a rusty orange color. Which named wind carries it north across the sea from Africa?
context: The sirocco wears a different name on every coast: scirocco in Italy, jugo in Croatia, xlokk in Malta. The same Saharan dust that reddens its rain can tint Alpine snow orange, and in Venice the sirocco helps pile up the acqua alta floods. Speeds reach about 100 km/h, peaking in spring and autumn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirocco

question: In West Africa, from late November to March, a dry north-easterly wind blows Saharan dust south all the way to the Gulf of Guinea.
