It hazes the sky so thickly that airliners are sometimes grounded. But after the sticky tropical heat, its bone-dry air feels so refreshing that people across the region fondly nickname it 'the Doctor.' What is the real name of this wind?
context: The harmattan's relative humidity can fall below 15% -- toward 5% in places -- cracking lips and causing spontaneous nosebleeds, while temperatures swing from about 9°C at dawn to as high as 35°C by afternoon. Its dust haze grounds flights and costs airlines millions, yet the dry relief from tropical mugginess earns it the fond name 'the Doctor.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmattan

question: In Egypt each spring, a scorching, sand-laden wind roars up out of the south, able to raise the temperature 20°C in two hours and bury Cairo's streets under blowing dust. Its name is simply the Arabic word for 'fifty' -- for the roughly fifty days across March, April and May over which it keeps returning. What is this Egyptian wind called?
context: 'Khamsin' is Arabic for fifty. The wind can gust to about 140 km/h and has stopped armies: during Napoleon's 1798 Egyptian campaign his soldiers choked and fainted in walls of dust, and in the WWII North African campaign blowing sand blinded troops while static electricity rendered their compasses useless. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khamsin

question: On the north-eastern shore of the Adriatic, around Trieste and Croatia's Dalmatian coast, cold air piles up over the mountains until it spills across the peaks and avalanches down onto the warm sea. In 1998 a violent gust reached 248 km/h at the Maslenica Bridge. What is this fierce Adriatic wind called?
context: The bora is a katabatic wind -- cold, dense air draining downhill under its own weight -- and its name comes from Boreas, the Greek god of the north wind. Gusts reach about 220 km/h at the town of Senj, and the December 1998 record of 248 km/h was clocked on the Maslenica Bridge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bora_(wind)

question: Across a dried-out lakebed in the southern Sahara -- the fossil floor of a vast vanished inland sea, Mega-Lake Chad -- lie the powdery skeletons of countless long-dead microorganisms. Winds funnel across this basin and lift more than 700,000 tons of the pale dust into the sky in a single day, more than anywhere else on the planet. What is this dustiest place on Earth called?
context: The Bodélé Depression is the fossil bed of ancient Mega-Lake Chad; its surface is diatomite, made of the silica skeletons of long-dead microorganisms. Winds funneled between the Tibesti and Ennedi mountains lift over 700,000 tons of dust a day, with dust storms on roughly 100 days a year -- the single largest dust source on the planet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bod%C3%A9l%C3%A9_Depression

question: The Amazon grows on surprisingly poor soil. Its rivers wash one vital nutrient away faster than rotting leaves can replace it, so the forest should slowly starve. Instead, Saharan dust blown across the Atlantic each year settles on the Amazon and replaces almost exactly the missing nutrient. Which nutrient does the desert dust carry to feed the rainforest?
context: NASA satellites (CALIPSO; Yu et al. 2015) measured about 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust settling on the Amazon each year, carrying roughly 22,000 tons of phosphorus -- close to what the forest loses to its rivers annually. Amazon soils are famously phosphorus-poor, so the desert's dust helps keep the world's greatest forest fed. (Iron in Saharan dust likewise fertilizes ocean plankton, which is why it is a tempting wrong answer.) Source: https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/goddard/nasa-satellite-reveals-how-much-saharan-dust-feeds-amazons-plants/

question: The Namib stretches nearly 2,000 km down Namibia's Atlantic coast. The cold Benguela current offshore has kept it bone-dry for at least 55 million years, since long before humans walked the Earth. This makes the Namib the world's what?
context: The Namib is widely called the oldest desert on Earth, having stayed arid for at least 55 million years (some estimates reach 55-80 Myr). The cold Benguela current chills the Atlantic air offshore, wringing out its moisture before it ever reaches land. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namib; nationalgeographic.com.  (Legend.)

question: Along the Atlantic coast of southern Africa stretches the Namib, one of the oldest deserts on Earth. The Nama people have herded goats along its dry edges for many centuries, and they gave it its name in their own click language, Khoekhoegowab. The single Nama word they used — which the whole desert still carries today — means what in English?
context: 'Namib' comes from the Nama language (Khoekhoegowab) and means roughly 'vast place' — also rendered as 'an area where there is nothing.' The name fits a desert running about 2,000 km down the coast. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namib; britannica.com/place/Namib.

question: At Sossusvlei, star-shaped dunes climb more than 300 metres above the desert floor. They are so steep that climbers sink to their ankles in the soft sand with every single step of the way up. The tallest of them all, standing at roughly 325 metres, goes by what nickname?
context: At Sossusvlei the star-shaped dunes top 300 m, and 'Big Daddy' reaches about 325 m — among the tallest dunes anywhere on Earth. Climbers sink to their ankles in soft sand the whole way up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sossusvlei; sossusvlei.org.

question: In the heart of Namibia's Namib desert lies Sossusvlei, a sea of towering dunes that burn deep orange-red every sunrise. The oldest dunes blaze reddest of all: Dune 45, the postcard-famous ridge near the road, is heaped from sand about 5 million years old. What coats each grain of that ancient sand and gives it such a fiery colour?
context: The sand is coated in iron oxide — rust — which deepens as it ages, so the oldest dunes are the reddest. Dune 45, a famous roadside dune about 45 km from the Sesriem gate, is roughly 80 m tall and built of sand around 5 million years old. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sossusvlei.

question: Real rain almost never falls on the western Namib — barely 5 to 10 millimetres in a whole year. Yet the desert teems with life, because the cold Benguela current offshore breeds a thick grey blanket that sweeps in from the Atlantic on more than 180 days a year, and every living thing here drinks it in. What is this dependable source of water?
context: Real rain is almost nil on the western Namib (~5-10 mm a year, versus ~85 mm at the eastern edge). The cold Benguela current spins up thick sea fog that rolls inland on 180+ days a year, and the whole ecosystem drinks it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namib.

question: Deep in Namibia's Namib desert lies Deadvlei, a blinding-white clay pan ringed by towering orange dunes. On the flat pan stands a grove of coal-black camelthorn trees, scorched dark and twisted, that died roughly 900 years ago when the shifting dunes cut the pan off from its water. How has their wood lasted nine centuries out here without crumbling to dust?
answer: the desert air is far too dry for it to rot
choices: the desert air is far too dry for it to rot
the sun slowly baked the wood into solid stone
seeping minerals replaced the wood with rock
a thick crust of salt sealed it from decay
context: The camelthorn (Vachellia erioloba) trees died roughly 600-900 years ago (about 1340-1430). They are NOT petrified or fossilized — the wood is simply desiccated: scorched black by the sun and far too dry to rot. Many tourist guides wrongly call them 'petrified,' but no minerals have turned them to stone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadvlei.  (Legend.)

question: Kolmanskop sprang up in 1908 after a railway worker discovered a diamond in the sand, sparking a frenzied rush. German settlers raised a lavish little town in the dunes, complete with a grand ballroom and even a tram. Its diamond riches also bought one astonishing first for the entire southern hemisphere. What was it?
context: In 1908 railway worker Zacharias Lewala found a diamond and showed inspector August Stauch, sparking a rush. The Germans built a lavish town with a ballroom, tram, and the first X-ray station in the southern hemisphere. The diamonds ran out and Kolmanskop was abandoned by 1956; today the dunes pour through its doorways. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmanskop.

question: The Namib's northern shore is strewn with the bleached bones of whales and seals and the rusting ribs of wrecked ships, where cold sea fog and hidden reefs have doomed sailors for centuries. The San people who knew this dreaded coast gave it what haunting name?
answer: The Land God Made in Anger
choices: The Land God Made in Anger
context: The San people called this bone-strewn shore 'The Land God Made in Anger'; Portuguese sailors called it 'The Gates of Hell.' Cold Benguela fog and offshore rocks wreck ships, and the great dunes run straight into the pounding Atlantic surf. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeleton_Coast.  (Legend.)

question: In September 1909 the German cargo steamer Eduard Bohlen struck the shore in thick fog on the Skeleton Coast of Namibia, the wreck-strewn edge of the Namib desert. For over a century since, the blowing sand and the constantly shifting shoreline have been at work on her rusting hull. What strange sight does the wreck of the Eduard Bohlen present today?
answer: it lies stranded far inland among the dunes
choices: it lies stranded far inland among the dunes
only its funnel still breaks the offshore waves
the tides long ago dragged it back out to sea
it lies smashed along the surf at the shoreline
context: The Eduard Bohlen ran aground in thick fog on 5 September 1909. Today its rusting hull sits about 400 m inland: blowing sand buried it as the shoreline crept seaward, marooning a ship in a sea of sand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eduard_Bohlen; atlasobscura.com.

question: The Welwitschia, a gnarled plant found only in the Namib and able to live 2,000 years, sprawls across the gravel plains as a tangle of torn, leathery straps. The wind has split and frayed those straps for centuries — yet they all grow from the very same leaves the plant first sprouted, and it never grows a single new one. How many leaves does a Welwitschia grow in its entire life?
context: The Welwitschia can live 1,000-2,000 years and grows only two strap-shaped leaves for its whole life. Those same two leaves keep growing (up to ~4 m long) and get shredded into ribbons by the wind. It survives largely on fog moisture. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welwitschia.

question: Across the Namib's grasslands lie thousands of 'fairy circles' — bare reddish rings several metres wide, each fringed by a ring of taller grass, that appear and fade over 30 to 60 years. Two teams of scientists have battled for over a decade over what makes them: one blames sand termites gnawing the roots, the other says the grasses organise themselves to share scarce water. So where does the science stand today?
answer: no one has proven either side yet
choices: no one has proven either side yet
the termite side has clearly won
the water side has clearly won
both sides were shown to be wrong
context: Fairy circles live out a 30-60 year cycle. Two real hypotheses compete: sand termites (Psammotermes allocerus) engineering the rings (Norbert Juergens, 2013) versus grasses self-organising to share scarce water (Stephan Getzin, Walter Tschinkel). A 2025 review leaned toward the plant-water side, but the question remains famously contested — so it is honestly taught as an open one, with no verdict. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy_circle_(Africa).  (Legend.)

question: Egypt is almost all desert. Yet one thin ribbon of green farmland runs its whole length, following the one river that crosses the sand. The Greek historian Herodotus said the whole country existed only because of that river. He gave Egypt a lasting nickname. What did he call Egypt?
context: Herodotus (c. 450 BCE) wrote that Egypt was 'the gift of the river' -- often rendered 'the gift of the Nile' -- because the entire civilization depended on the river's water and silt; without it, Egypt would be nothing but Sahara. (The 'bride of the Nile' was a separate later legend about offerings thrown to the flood.) Source: Carnegie Museum of Natural History, carnegiemnh.org/egypt-and-the-nile/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile.

question: In Egypt, 'Upper Egypt' is the SOUTHERN part of the country while 'Lower Egypt' is the NORTHERN part -- the opposite of what a map suggests. The names follow the river, not the compass, because the Nile does something few great rivers do. Which way does the Nile flow?
choices: South, into the heart of Africa
context: The Nile runs from highlands in the south down to the Mediterranean in the north -- one of the few major rivers that flows northward. Egyptians named the land by the river's flow, so the upstream south is 'Upper Egypt' and the downstream north is 'Lower Egypt.' Source: Carnegie Museum, carnegiemnh.org/egypt-and-the-nile/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile.

question: Before modern dams, each summer's Nile flood spread a fresh coat of rich mud across Egypt's fields. That mud was the secret behind the country's famous harvests. The Egyptians were so defined by this precious soil that they named their homeland after its color. What did they call their country?
context: Egyptians called their fertile valley Kemet, 'the Black Land,' after the dark silt the flood left behind, and the lifeless desert beyond it Deshret, 'the Red Land.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile (kmt = 'black,' the color of the flood sediment).

question: Egyptians have always thought of the Nile as their own river, but the water flowing past them fell as rain astonishingly far away, deep in the heart of the continent. The steady year-round flow of the White Nile pours out of a single vast lake thousands of kilometres to the south. Out of which great lake does the White Nile flow?
context: The White Nile flows out of Lake Victoria at Jinja, in Uganda, and runs steadily all year -- keeping the Nile alive between the summer floods. Its water reaches Egypt from thousands of kilometers away; the Nile's whole drainage basin spreads across eleven African countries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile; Britannica, britannica.com/place/Blue-Nile-River.

question: The ancient Egyptians ignored spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Their entire calendar had just THREE seasons, each named for what the Nile was doing to the land. The first and most important season of their year was the one that buried the fields under water and fresh silt. What was this season called?
context: Egyptians split the year into three river-seasons: Akhet, the flood (mid-June to mid-October), Peret, the growing season, and Shemu, the harvest; the flood began in July and peaked in August. (Sopdet was the star Sirius, whose dawn rising heralded the coming flood.) Source: Study.com, study.com/academy/lesson/egypts-three-predictable-seasons.html.

question: Each summer the Nile rose, but never by the same amount twice -- a strong flood one year, a feeble one the next. To read the exact height of each flood, Egyptian priests built the 'nilometer': a marked stairway, a column, or a deep well cut down to the water and ruled off in cubits. Reading it early each year gave the priests the power to forecast something months in advance. What did the nilometer let them predict?
answer: the size of the coming harvest
choices: the size of the coming harvest
the height of the next year's flood
the coming of the desert winds
the safest sites for new temples
context: A nilometer was a marked column, a stairway down to the water, or a deep well, calibrated in cubits; a good flood could raise the river about 7 meters (23 feet). Reading the flood height early let the priests forecast the size of the coming harvest -- whether the year would bring plenty or famine. Source: WorldAtlas, worldatlas.com/articles/ancient-egyptians-used-the-nilometer-to-predict-floods.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilometer.

question: Boats heading up the Nile south of Aswan ran into trouble: six rough stretches where the river tumbles over hard rock into shallow, boulder-choked rapids -- too wild to sail through. These barriers blocked river traffic and marked the ancient frontier between Egypt and Nubia. What are these six rocky rapids called?
context: Six cataracts break the Nile between Aswan and Khartoum -- whitewater over hard rock rather than sheer falls. They blocked boats and marked the ancient frontier with Nubia; the second cataract now lies drowned under Lake Nasser. Source: Egypt United Tours, egyptunitedtours.com/nile-river-delta/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile.

question: The Nile begins as two very different rivers. The White Nile flows out of the great lakes of central Africa, running steady all year round. The Blue Nile roars down from monsoon-soaked highlands far to the south, carrying the summer floodwaters. At one bustling capital these two branches finally join into the single Nile that crosses the desert to Egypt. Which capital sits where the Blue and White Nile meet?
context: At Khartoum, capital of Sudan, the clear-running White Nile from Lake Victoria meets the flood-bearing Blue Nile from the Ethiopian highlands to form the single Nile. The muddy Blue Nile and paler White Nile can be seen flowing side by side, unmixed, for a stretch below the city. Source: Britannica, britannica.com/place/Blue-Nile-River; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile.

question: For thousands of years, Egypt's astonishing farmland was renewed each summer by the fertile silt the Nile left behind -- the very soil that fed the pharaohs. Yet that mud was not Egyptian at all. The Blue Nile and the Atbara tear it loose from the mountains of one country far upstream and carry it thousands of kilometers north. Egypt's legendary fertility is really the washed-away soil of which land?
context: The Blue Nile and the Atbara supply most of the flood's water and about 97-98% of its sediment, stripping it from the Ethiopian highlands and carrying it north -- so the legendary fertility of Egypt is really Ethiopian mud. Source: Britannica; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile ('97% of transported sediment from the Atbarah and Blue Nile').

question: As the Nile nears the Mediterranean, its single channel splits into a spreading web of smaller waterways and marsh, laying down a broad triangle of new land at the river's mouth. The ancient Greeks thought this triangle looked just like a capital letter of their alphabet and named the feature after it. Ever since, every river mouth built this way, anywhere on Earth, has borne that same name. What is such a river mouth called?
context: The Greeks named the Nile's triangular mouth after their letter delta (the triangular capital), and Herodotus is thought to be the first writer to describe it that way -- so every 'river delta' on Earth is ultimately named after the Nile's. The Nile Delta fans across about 22,000 km2 of coastline. Source: The Historian's Hut, thehistorianshut.com/2020/08/25/the-origin-of-the-geographical-term-delta/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile_Delta.

question: For more than two thousand years the Nile wore the crown of the longest river on Earth, and record books still often list it that way, at roughly 6,650 kilometers. But scientists who remeasured a rival river argued that it runs longer -- depending on which faraway headwater you count as the true source. So the Nile's ancient title is now genuinely disputed. Which river contests the Nile's claim to be the longest?
context: Guinness and Britannica traditionally crown the Nile the world's longest river at about 6,650 km, but a 2014 Brazilian study measured the Amazon at roughly 6,992 km, longer -- depending on which headwater counts as the source. The Nile is far smaller by water, though: its flow is only about 1% of the Amazon's, because the Amazon drains a rainforest while the Nile crosses a desert. Source: Britannica; phys.org; nationalgeographic.com/science/article/amazon-longer-than-nile-river.

question: Since the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970, the Nile's yearly flood no longer reaches Egypt -- the dam holds back almost all the river's silt in the reservoir behind it, so farmers must now buy fertilizer to replace the free mud they lost. But cutting off that silt has changed the coastline itself, where the delta meets the sea. What is happening to the Nile Delta now?
answer: It is eroding and sinking into the sea
choices: It is eroding and sinking into the sea
Salt water is creeping inland across it
It is drying into a barren salt flat
It is splitting into many new channels
context: The Aswan High Dam (1970) traps about 98% of the Nile's silt -- roughly 100 million tons a year -- in Lake Nasser. Starved of new mud, the delta is now shrinking: Mediterranean currents erode the coast faster than the river can rebuild it, while the old clay soils compact (subside) and the sea rises. Source: SERC Carleton, serc.carleton.edu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile ('the delta has begun to shrink because of erosion').

question: About 10 km from the town of Bodo in northern Norway, the strait called Saltstraumen erupts four times a day. The turning tide rams a whole fjord's worth of seawater through a gap only about 150 m wide, racing up to 40 km/h. What world record does this violent flow hold?
context: Saltstraumen, about 10 km southeast of Bodø, is measured as the world's strongest tidal current -- commonly cited up to roughly 40 km/h (about 20-22 knots) as the tide turns four times a day. (Wikipedia 'Saltstraumen'; VisitNorway / Visit Bodø.)

question: Four times every day, the ocean tide roars through a narrow strait called the Saltstraumen, near the town of Bodo on Norway's Arctic coast. As the tide turns, the racing water coils into enormous spinning whirlpools that Norwegian sailors have feared for centuries — swirls that utterly dwarf the little vortex above a draining bathtub. How large do the Saltstraumen's whirlpools actually grow?
answer: up to 10 m across and 5 m deep
choices: up to 10 m across and 5 m deep
up to 2 m across and 1 m deep
up to 25 m across and 12 m deep
up to 60 m across and 30 m deep
context: At Saltstraumen the whirlpools reach up to 10 m across and 5 m deep -- strong enough to capsize or swallow a small boat, so local boaters cross only at slack water when the current briefly rests. (Wikipedia 'Saltstraumen.')

question: The deadly whirlpools off the Norwegian coast gave English a word for any scene of violent sucking chaos: 'maelstrom.' Norse and Dutch sailors coined it long ago. Before it ever meant chaos in general, the word painted a plain vivid picture of the water. What does 'maelstrom' really mean?
context: 'Maelstrom' comes from Dutch/Norse malen ('to grind') and strøm/straum ('stream') -- literally a 'grinding stream.' The word entered English through 19th-century sea tales set at the Norwegian whirlpools. (Wikipedia 'Moskstraumen.')

question: Four times a day the tide reverses at Saltstraumen, forcing the sea through a strait only about 150 m wide. It looks like a modest Norwegian narrows, but the volume of water on the move is staggering. About how much seawater pours through Saltstraumen between one slack tide and the next?
context: Up to 400 million cubic metres of seawater force through the roughly 150 m strait every six hours -- about 3,000 m³ every second at the entrance. Because the same volume must cross a far narrower opening in the same span of time, the water has to speed up, which is exactly what turns an ordinary tide into Saltstraumen's ferocious flow, racing up to 40 km/h. (Wikipedia 'Saltstraumen'; nordnorge.com.)

question: Off the tip of Norway's Lofoten Islands churns the Moskstraumen -- a whirlpool that terrified Arctic sailors for centuries and gave rise to dark legends. In 1841 a famous writer turned it into fiction: a fisherman is dragged down into its spinning funnel and barely escapes to tell the tale. Which writer's tale was it?
context: The Moskstraumen, off Moskenesøya in the Lofoten Islands, inspired Edgar Allan Poe's 1841 'A Descent into the Maelström' -- the tale that carried the word 'maelstrom' into English. It surfaces again in Jules Verne's 'Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas' (1870) and in Herman Melville's 'Moby-Dick' (1851), where Captain Ahab invokes it. (Wikipedia 'Moskstraumen'; 'A Descent into the Maelström.')  (Legend.)

question: The Moskstraumen — the great tidal maelstrom that Edgar Allan Poe and Jules Verne both wrote about — churns off the southern tip of Norway's Lofoten Islands, near the small island of Mosken. For centuries Arctic sailors dreaded rounding this stretch of coast, and its whirlpools helped give the world the very word 'maelstrom'. Where exactly does the Moskstraumen form?
answer: in open sea between two islands
choices: in open sea between two islands
at the mouth of a broad fjord
in a channel between two skerries
context: Unlike most great whirlpools, the Moskstraumen forms in the open sea between Mosken and Moskenesøya in the Lofoten Islands -- which helped make it so baffling to sailors. Modern surveys put its current near 3-5 m/s, strongest in July and August; older accounts wildly exaggerated its power. (Wikipedia 'Moskstraumen.')

question: Everyone pictures Egypt when they hear the word 'pyramid.' Yet Egypt does not hold the record. About 255 ancient pyramids, more than twice Egypt's number, still crowd the deserts of a single country, built long ago by a kingdom of its own. Which country has the most pyramids on Earth?
context: It's Sudan, not Egypt. About 255 ancient pyramids stand along the Nile in modern Sudan — more than double the roughly 120 in Egypt — raised at three great royal fields: El-Kurru, Nuri, and Meroe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubian_pyramids

question: Far up the Nile in what is now Sudan, south of Egypt, stand the hundreds of steep little pyramids of Meroe. They were not built by Egyptians at all. They rose from a mighty African kingdom that rivaled Egypt for centuries — one so strong that around 750 BC its own kings marched north and ruled Egypt itself as pharaohs. What was this kingdom?
context: The builders were the Kingdom of Kush (also called Nubia), a full civilization in its own right, not a lesser copy of Egypt. Earlier Kushite kings from Napata even ruled all of Egypt as the 25th Dynasty, the 'Black Pharaohs,' beginning with King Piye around 727 BCE. Meroe became Kush's greatest royal necropolis after the capital shifted there around 590 BCE. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubian_pyramids

question: At Meroe, on the Nile in what is now Sudan, the kings and queens of the ancient Kingdom of Kush raised their royal pyramids by the dozen. Their pyramids look nothing like Egypt's famous giants at Giza — they gave the Sudanese desert a skyline unlike any other in the ancient world. What distinctive shape does a Nubian pyramid cut against the sky?
answer: tall and narrow, rising in steep spikes
choices: tall and narrow, rising in steep spikes
low and broad, spreading like wide cones
climbing in giant steps, like a staircase
flat on top, like a raised platform
context: Nubian pyramids are inclined near 70 degrees, far steeper than the roughly 40-to-50-degree Egyptian ones, and rise from footprints about five times smaller for the same height — only 6 to 30 metres tall. That sharp, crowded, needle-like silhouette is what gives Meroe its unmistakable skyline. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramids_of_Mero%C3%AB

question: Deep inside Egypt's Great Pyramid, the pharaoh's burial chamber is sealed within the stone itself. A Kushite king at Meroe was laid to rest quite differently: his tomb was a suite of rooms cut down into solid bedrock. So where did his builders put the pyramid?
answer: right on the surface above it
choices: right on the surface above it
on a cliff across the river
hidden far out in the desert
context: A Nubian pyramid was raised directly on top of a rock-cut burial chamber, reached by a stairway — so the pyramid was a marker standing over the tomb rather than a container holding it, the opposite of the Egyptian design. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubian_pyramids

question: At the ancient royal city of Meroe, on the Nile in what is now Sudan, many of the grandest pyramids covered the tombs of women. Early in the 1st century CE, one such woman — Amanishakheto — was laid to rest beneath the steep pyramid known as N6, buried with a hoard of gold jewelry. She was one of several powerful women of the Kingdom of Kush honored this way. What was Amanishakheto to the Kingdom of Kush?
answer: a queen ruling in her own right
choices: a queen ruling in her own right
the queen mother of a boy king
a great king's most favored wife
the chief priestess of the temple
context: Amanishakheto (early 1st century CE) was one of several powerful women who ruled Kush in their own right — not as a king's wife or as regent for a young son — and she was laid to rest in her own royal pyramid, N6, at Meroe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanishakheto

question: King Piye, the Kushite pharaoh who once conquered Egypt, was so devoted to one thing that when he died he was buried standing upright beside four of them at El-Kurru. This was the very first burial of its kind seen in the Nile valley in over 500 years. Beside four of what was Piye laid to rest?
context: It was his horses. Piye loved them so dearly that he was buried standing beside four of his favorites at El-Kurru — the first royal horse burial in the Nile valley in more than 500 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piye

question: The Bible's book of Acts tells how the apostle Philip baptized the treasurer of 'Candace, queen of the Ethiopians' (Acts 8:27). That Greek name 'Candace' came straight from 'kandake,' a Kushite word carved on the monuments of Meroe. In Kush, what was a 'kandake'?
context: 'Kandake' was simply the Kushite word for their royal queen — a title borne by many women across the centuries, not one person's name. Greek and Roman writers borrowed it as though it were a personal name, which is why the Bible speaks of 'Candace, queen of the Ethiopians' (Acts 8:27), whose treasurer Philip baptized — a phrase that nearly reads 'Queen, queen of the Ethiopians.' To them, 'the Ethiopians' meant the people of Kush. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kandake

question: Visit Meroe today and dozens of its pyramids stand oddly flat on top, their peaks gone — and weather is not to blame. In 1834 an Italian named Giuseppe Ferlini took explosives to about forty of them, dismantling each one from the summit downward. What was he after?
context: Ferlini was after gold — and his gamble paid off at the pyramid of Queen Amanishakheto, where he found a royal hoard reported as 10 bracelets, 9 shield-rings, 67 signet rings, and many amulets, now split between museums in Berlin and Munich. His top-down demolition of about forty pyramids is why so many at Meroe stand flat-topped today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramids_of_Mero%C3%AB

question: In 1910 archaeologists at Meroe unearthed a bronze head of the emperor Augustus, hacked from a Roman statue and buried by Kushite raiders beneath a temple's threshold to be walked over. Nearly 2,000 years underground, one thing about the head still startles visitors. What?
answer: its inlaid eyes still stare out lifelike
choices: its inlaid eyes still stare out lifelike
its skin is still bright with paint
its surface is still gilded in gold
its crown is still set with jewels
context: Its eyes: inlaid glass pupils set in irises of calcite (stone) survived intact, giving the buried emperor a startlingly lifelike gaze. The 'Meroe Head' came from a statue that Kushite forces under Queen Amanirenas carried off when they raided Roman Aswan (Syene) around 25 BCE; buried under the temple step so worshippers would trample Rome underfoot, it is now in the British Museum. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mero%C3%AB_Head

question: At the ancient Kushite city of Naqa, in the desert of what is now Sudan, the kings of the Kingdom of Kush raised a Lion Temple to their own fierce war-god. On its stone walls he prowls with a lion's head — and in one striking carving he bears three heads and four arms. What was the name of this fearsome Kushite lion-god?
context: He was Apedemak, a lion-headed war-god with no counterpart in Egypt — proof that Kushite religion was its own, not a borrowing from the north. His temples stand at Naqa and at Musawwarat es-Sufra, where the earliest was built by King Arnekhamani in the late 3rd century BCE. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apedemak

question: The ruined city of Meroe still lies ringed by great black mounds — the piled-up slag of centuries of iron smelting, for Meroe was one of the ancient world's mightiest ironworking centers. Awed by those heaps, the scholar A. H. Sayce nicknamed Meroe after one of the great smoke-and-furnace cities of industrial England. What nickname did he give it?
context: Meroe was one of ancient Africa's great iron-smelting centers, and centuries of furnaces left the huge black slag heaps that still ring the site. Struck by their scale, the scholar A. H. Sayce nicknamed Meroe 'the Birmingham of Africa,' after the English industrial city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mero%C3%AB

question: Kush wrote in its own Meroitic script, a set of about two dozen signs first used in the 3rd century BCE. Here is the strange part: scholars still cannot fully understand what most Meroitic texts actually mean, because writings that pair the language with a known tongue are so scarce. And yet, thanks to Francis Llewellyn Griffith around 1909, a scholar today can do one particular thing with any Meroitic inscription. What is it?
choices: trace where its signs came from
know which way it should be read
context: The answer is pronunciation. Around 1909 Francis Llewellyn Griffith worked out the sound of every Meroitic sign, so its roughly 23 characters can be read aloud, letter by letter — yet because texts pairing Meroitic with a known language are so scarce, the language itself is still only partly understood. It is a rare case of a deciphered script whose language remains largely unread. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mero%C3%AB

question: One ocean is so enormous that, all by itself, it is larger than every continent and island on Earth put together. All the world's dry land could sink into it and there would still be room to spare. Which ocean is this?
context: The Pacific spans about 165 million sq km, while every continent and island combined covers only about 149 million sq km -- so all of Earth's land really would fit inside the Pacific basin with room left over. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pacific Ocean'; NOAA Ocean Exploration, 'How big is the Pacific Ocean?'

question: The Pacific holds tens of thousands of islands. They range from coral rings to volcanic peaks, from the Aleutians all the way to New Zealand. How does its tally of islands compare with the world's other oceans?
answer: more than all the others combined
choices: more than all the others combined
about the same as the Atlantic alone
fewer than the Indian Ocean holds
roughly a tenth of the world's total
context: The Pacific holds more than 25,000 islands -- more than all the world's other oceans put together -- yet its average depth is still about 4,000 meters (13,000 ft). Source: Wikipedia, 'Pacific Ocean'.

question: The Pacific carries a strangely gentle name for such a huge storm-swept ocean: 'the peaceful sea.' The explorer who named it in 1520 did so only after fighting his battered fleet through fierce storms at the tip of South America. Then he sailed out at last onto flat calm water. Which explorer gave it that name?
context: Magellan named it 'Mar Pacifico' -- Spanish and Portuguese for 'peaceful sea' -- during the first voyage ever to sail around the world. The calm was partly luck: his route happened to slip past the Pacific's storms. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pacific Ocean'.

question: Far out in the vast, empty South Pacific lies the single spot on Earth that sits farthest from any land at all -- what geographers call the 'oceanic pole of inaccessibility.' From this lonely point, the nearest shore of any kind is almost 1,700 miles away in every direction. What is this spot called?
context: Point Nemo's three nearest scraps of land are all tiny and hundreds of miles off: Ducie Island in the Pitcairn group to the north, Motu Nui islet by Easter Island to the northeast, and Maher Island off Antarctica to the south. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pole of inaccessibility'; Britannica, 'oceanic pole of inaccessibility'.

question: Point Nemo lies so unimaginably far from any coast that roughly 1,670 miles of open water stretch away in every direction. Ships and aircraft almost never pass near it. This creates a startling situation. Much of the time, the humans physically closest to Point Nemo are somewhere almost no one would guess. Who are they?
context: The International Space Station orbits only about 250 miles up, while the nearest people on the surface can be more than 1,600 miles away -- so when the ISS passes overhead, its crew becomes the closest humans to the loneliest spot on Earth. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pole of inaccessibility'.

question: The loneliest place in the oceans is Point Nemo, adrift in the empty South Pacific. It takes its name from a fictional sea captain in Jules Verne's novel 'Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas.' The captain chose that name because in Latin it named exactly what he had chosen to be. What does 'Nemo' mean in Latin?
context: 'Nemo' is Latin for 'nobody' -- a fitting name for the most cut-off spot on Earth. The point itself was pinpointed by computer in 1992 by the Croatian survey engineer Hrvoje Lukatela. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pole of inaccessibility'.

question: The water around Point Nemo lies farther from people than anywhere else on Earth, so space agencies have turned it into a deliberate crash zone. Since 1971 they have steered close to 300 worn-out satellites, cargo freighters, and even entire space stations down to burn up and splash into this one empty patch of sea, keeping the falling wreckage far from any town or ship. Spaceflight engineers gave this lonely target a fittingly grim nickname. What do they call it?
context: Close to 300 satellites, cargo ships, and space stations have been guided down into this stretch of ocean, which has earned the grim nickname 'the spacecraft cemetery.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Spacecraft cemetery'.

question: In March 2001 the sky over the remote South Pacific blazed as a 130-ton space station, one of the largest outposts ever built in orbit, was deliberately steered into a fiery re-entry. It broke apart in a fireball before its pieces splashed into the sea near Point Nemo. Which station made this final plunge?
context: Mir, Russia's 130-ton station, was guided down to burn up over the 'spacecraft cemetery' near Point Nemo in March 2001. China's Tiangong-1 later fell in 2018, and America's Skylab came down over Western Australia back in 1979. Source: Wikipedia, 'Spacecraft cemetery'.

question: The Pacific is encircled by a colossal loop, some 25,000 miles long, where slabs of the ocean floor plunge beneath the surrounding continents, building long chains of volcanoes and setting off most of the planet's earthquakes. Geographers gave this loop a vivid name. What is it called?
context: The Ring of Fire holds roughly three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes, and about 90% of all earthquakes strike along it -- all because the Pacific's plates keep diving beneath the continents around them. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ring of Fire'.

question: The Pacific hides the deepest place in all of Earth's oceans -- a narrow gash in the seafloor within the Mariana Trench where the water plunges nearly seven miles straight down. It is so deep that if Mount Everest were set on the bottom, its summit would still lie more than a mile beneath the waves. What is this deepest point named?
context: The Challenger Deep bottoms out at about 10,911 meters (35,797 ft) -- deeper than Mount Everest (8,849 m) is tall. It is named for HMS Challenger, the British ship whose crew first sounded these depths in the 1870s. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pacific Ocean'.

question: The world's most famous straw hat has been called the 'Panama' for over a century. Yet not a single one was ever woven in Panama. For about four hundred years, these light hats have been made by hand in the coastal towns of another country. Where are 'Panama' hats really made?
context: It's one of geography's great mislabels: the 'Panama' hat is Ecuadorian through and through, hand-woven on Ecuador's coast — especially in Montecristi and Cuenca — from 'toquilla straw,' the fiber of the toquilla plant (Carludovica palmata), a palm-like plant native to that coast. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_hat

question: Ecuador's coastal weavers make the hat. Yet the whole world knows it by a different country's name: Panama. People have spun many stories about how that mix-up happened. What really fastened Panama's name onto Ecuador's hat?
answer: Traders shipped the hats to the world through Panama's busy ports.
choices: Traders shipped the hats to the world through Panama's busy ports.
The hats first went on sale in a big open-air Panama City market.
Panama's government registered the hat style under its own name.
A Panama City newspaper coined the catchy name to sell more hats.
context: Panama was a booming trade crossroads in the 1800s, and Ecuador's hats were funneled through it to reach buyers everywhere — so the world credited the busy port, not the true source. The name spread when California Gold Rush prospectors crossing the Isthmus of Panama bought the hats for sun protection and, back home, said they'd gotten them 'in Panama.' It was cemented in 1906, when President Theodore Roosevelt was photographed wearing one at the Panama Canal construction site — an image that made the hat an international fashion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_hat

question: In the coastal town of Montecristi in Ecuador, a master weaver spends months hand-weaving a single hat from finely split toquilla-palm fibre — the 'superfino', the finest grade of Panama hat ever made. The weave is so unbelievably fine that collectors prove a real one with a single showstopping test. What can a true Montecristi superfino hat do?
answer: roll up small enough to slip through a wedding ring
choices: roll up small enough to slip through a wedding ring
fold flat enough to mail inside an envelope
stretch to twice its width and spring back
keep its shape after a year pressed flat
context: The other traditional test: a true superfino is woven tightly enough to hold water without leaking. The rarest have up to 3,000 weaves per square inch and can take a master weaver eight months to finish; in 2014 Ecuadorian weaver Simon Espinal set a record at 4,000 weaves per square inch. UNESCO added the traditional weaving of the toquilla-straw hat to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list on December 5, 2012. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_hat  (Legend.)

question: Roman workers finished the Pantheon in Rome almost 1,900 years ago, and its dome still holds a building record no one has ever broken. Not even modern cranes or new materials have topped it. What record does the Pantheon's dome still hold?
context: Nearly 1,900 years on, no one has topped it: the Pantheon still carries the largest UNREINFORCED (steel-free, 'plain') concrete dome ever built. Modern domes only go bigger by hiding steel bars inside the concrete. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: The Pantheon in Rome is a vast circular hall, and unlike most temples it has no rows of windows down its walls. Even so, from dawn to dusk a bright patch of sunlight lights up its marble interior. Where does all that daylight get in?
answer: through a round opening at the crown of the dome
choices: through a round opening at the crown of the dome
through the great bronze doors at the entrance
through narrow gaps between the roof tiles
through slots among the sunken ceiling coffers
context: That round opening at the crown of the dome is the oculus — Latin for 'eye,' about 9 meters across — and it is the Pantheon's single source of daylight; there are no side windows at all. It stares straight up at the open sky. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: The oculus — the round hole at the top of the Pantheon's dome in Rome — has no glass or cover, so when storms roll over Rome, rain falls straight down inside the temple. Yet the marble floor never floods. Why not?
answer: the floor is gently sloped to hidden drains
choices: the floor is gently sloped to hidden drains
a bronze lid slides across the hole in storms
rising warm air turns the rain to mist
temple servants once bailed it out by hand
context: The marble floor is domed just enough to slope about 30 cm down to small drainage holes — and that 2nd-century Roman drainage system still carries the rain away today. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome ; https://www.archeoroma.org/sites/pantheon/

question: Architects love a hidden secret of the Pantheon in Rome: the height from the floor up to the crown of the dome is exactly equal to the width of the round hall — 43.3 meters each way. Because those two measurements match perfectly, one simple shape would fit exactly inside, touching the floor and the top of the dome at once. What shape is it?
context: Floor-to-crown height and floor width are both 43.3 m, so a 43.3-meter sphere fits precisely inside, kissing the floor and the very top of the dome — the interior comes out very nearly a perfect half-sphere. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: The Pantheon's porch in Rome rests on 16 grey and pink granite columns, each nearly 12 meters tall. The Romans quarried them in the deserts of Egypt and floated them down the Nile and across the sea to Rome. What is astonishing about how each column was made?
answer: each is a single solid block of stone
choices: each is a single solid block of stone
each is built from stacked stone drums
each is hollow to save on weight
each hides a brick core beneath the granite
context: Each shaft is one monolithic piece weighing 50-60 tonnes. The grey columns came from the Mons Claudianus quarry in Egypt's eastern desert, the pink ones from Aswan — floated down the Nile and shipped across the Mediterranean. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mons_Claudianus ; https://journal.eahn.org/article/id/7477/

question: Look up inside the Pantheon's dome in Rome and you see 140 sunken square panels, called coffers, set in five rings that shrink toward the center. Besides decorating the ceiling, what vital job do these coffers do?
answer: they lighten the dome so it weighs less
choices: they lighten the dome so it weighs less
they let rainwater drain off the roof
they hide iron beams inside the dome
they trap warm air to heat the hall
context: The 140 coffers (five rings of 28) scoop material out of the ceiling, so the dome weighs far less than a solid one would — beauty and engineering in one carving. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome ; https://www.pantheonroma.com/en/2026/02/11/the-pantheon-dome-a-marvel-of-ancient-roman-architecture/

question: In the Pantheon's dome in Rome, the Romans graded the concrete as it rose: heavy stone chips low down, then lighter and lighter material higher up, so the dome would not crush itself under its own weight. Near the crown they used the lightest volcanic rock of all. Which rock did they choose?
context: The recipe ran from heavy travertine chips at the base, through lighter terracotta and volcanic tufa, to porous pumice near the oculus. Engineers estimate a solid heavy-concrete dome would have carried about 80% greater stresses — likely too much to stand. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome ; https://www.pantheonrome.org/en/rome-pantheon/architecture/pantheon-architecture-dome-engineering

question: In the city of Rome, ancient marble temples once stood on nearly every hill. As the Roman Empire fell, popes and princes tore them apart, carting off the columns and stone to raise new churches and palaces. Almost every temple vanished — but one great round temple, the Pantheon, still stands nearly whole today. What happened in AD 609 that saved the Pantheon from being pulled down?
answer: it was turned into a Christian church
choices: it was turned into a Christian church
an emperor made it his private palace
it was buried in river mud for ages
a law forbade anyone to touch it
context: In AD 609 Pope Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres ('St Mary and the Martyrs') — which is why it was maintained instead of quarried, and survives nearly intact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: The Pantheon's concrete dome in Rome weighs as much as hundreds of elephants, yet for nearly 1,900 years it has stood with no steel inside it and no column beneath its center. All that crushing weight has to go somewhere. Where does the dome pour its load?
answer: into its own colossally thick walls
choices: into its own colossally thick walls
into the granite columns of the porch
into a hidden inner shell of brick
into stone buttresses ringing the outside
context: The dome has no steel, no keystone, and no central support — where a keystone would sit, there is only the open oculus. Its half-sphere geometry channels the load straight down into the rotunda's walls, which swell to as much as 6.4 m thick to carry it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: For centuries the Pantheon in Rome kept its ancient bronze, until the 1600s, when Pope Urban VIII of the Barberini family stripped the bronze from its porch — so much that Romans jeered, 'What the barbarians didn't do, the Barberini did.' Most of that bronze was melted down and recast. What is the most famous thing the Pantheon's bronze became?
answer: a bronze canopy over St Peter's altar
choices: a bronze canopy over St Peter's altar
the temple's own tall bronze doors
a giant statue of the pope himself
a ring of bells for St Peter's tower
context: The stripped bronze was recast into cannons for Castel Sant'Angelo and, most famously, Bernini's towering baldachin — the great bronze canopy over the high altar of St Peter's Basilica. The Roman quip puns 'Barberini' on 'barbari' (barbarians). Sources: https://www.pantheonrome.org/en/history ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter%27s_Baldachin

question: High in the French Alps above the village of Chamonix, the huge white peak of Mont Blanc towers over the valleys. As the sun drops behind the mountain, the villages below fall into cold blue shadow. Yet the topmost snowfields on the summit suddenly blush pink and orange, as if lit by a lamp from nowhere. Climbers have one word for this rosy light that clings only to the highest peaks. What is it called?
context: German climbers call it Alpengluehen. Because only the very highest summits catch the color while the valleys stay dark, the peaks look like they float, lit from nowhere. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpenglow)

question: Stand on a ridge in the Alps at dusk and turn your back on the fiery sunset. Look at the sky opposite the Sun and you'll catch a soft pink band glowing there, about 10 to 20 degrees above the far horizon. What is this pink arch in the anti-sunset sky called?
context: It is named for the cestus, the girdle or breast-band of the Greek goddess Aphrodite, whom the Romans equated with Venus. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belt_of_Venus)

question: From a summit in the Alps at dusk, look below the pink Belt of Venus and you will see a darker blue-grey band hugging the horizon. As dusk deepens, this dark band slowly climbs higher into the sky, lifting the pink arch ahead of it. That rising dark band is a shadow, but a shadow cast by what?
context: Astronomers call it the 'twilight wedge' or Earth's shadow. As the Sun sinks farther below the horizon, the planet's own shadow rises through the atmosphere, and the pink Belt of Venus rides up on top of it. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belt_of_Venus)

question: In the Dolomites the dusk glow has its own Ladin name, enrosadira, 'the turning-rosy,' as the pale limestone crags burn red, then purple, then fade to night. A Ladin legend gives the fire a magical cause: the peaks are the enchanted rose garden of King Laurin, a dwarf-king who was captured and cursed his own garden so no human eye should ever glimpse its roses again. Yet the roses still blaze red for a moment at dawn and dusk. Why did Laurin's own curse fail to hide them then?
answer: his curse forgot the twilight, neither day nor night
choices: his curse forgot the twilight, neither day nor night
the stolen princess frees his garden each dusk
his magic belt sets the flowers alight at night
the roses had already turned to stone by then
context: Germans still call these peaks the Rosengarten ('rose garden'), Italians the Catinaccio. In the tale, Laurin, captured after kidnapping a princess, swore no one should see his roses 'neither by day nor by night', but overlooked the twilight in between, so they still glow for that instant. (Ladin folk legend; suedtirol.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Laurin)

question: Lake Hillier, a bubblegum-pink pool on Middle Island off Western Australia, lies just a sandbar away from the deep-blue Southern Ocean. Scoop up a glassful and it stays every bit as pink -- the color travels with the water, so it is no reflection of the sky. What actually tints the whole lake pink?
context: Lake Hillier stays pink even in a glass because the color is life, not a mineral or a sky-trick: a community of salt-loving microbes -- the green alga Dunaliella salina plus pink halophilic bacteria and archaea -- tints the whole 600-metre pool, which sits just beyond a thin rim of sand from the blue Southern Ocean. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Hillier

question: Lake Hillier gets its pink color from a tiny alga called Dunaliella salina. Battered by water eight times saltier than the sea, the alga defends itself by flooding its cells with one protective pigment. It packs the pigment so densely that this alga is the richest natural source on Earth. Which pigment is it?
context: The pigment is beta-carotene -- the very same orange pigment that colors carrots. Stressed by extreme salt and sun, Dunaliella salina packs it to about 14% of its dry weight, making the alga Earth's best natural source of beta-carotene, so the pink lake and the orange carrot share one chemical. A 2022 metagenomic study showed pink bacteria such as Salinibacter ruber add even more pigment alongside the alga. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9768965/

question: Senegal's rose-pink Lake Retba, or Lac Rose, holds a brine up to ten times saltier than the sea in water only three metres deep. Each day up to three thousand workers wade into this stinging pink water for six or seven hours to hand-harvest its salt -- and before they go in, they coat their skin all over with a local tree fat so the ferocious brine cannot burn them. What do they rub on their skin?
context: The protectant is shea butter, pressed from the nuts of the West African shea tree; its fat shields the harvesters' skin from the searing 40%-salt brine as up to 3,000 workers pull roughly 38,000 tonnes of salt from Lake Retba each year. The rose color comes from the same Dunaliella salina algae as Lake Hillier -- proof the hue is living, not mineral: when heavy flooding once diluted the salt in 2022, Retba briefly turned green. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Retba

question: A shimmering green curtain ripples across the sky over Tromso, in Arctic Norway, on a clear, dark winter night. What lights up this glowing sky?
answer: charged particles streaming from the Sun
choices: charged particles streaming from the Sun
the deep cold of the Arctic air
the glow of the city lights
context: Earth's magnetic field funnels the solar wind - a stream of charged particles blown off the Sun - down toward the poles, where the particles crash into atoms high in the air and make them glow. The lights need no reflection, no cold and no moon at all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: Tromso in Norway, Fairbanks in Alaska, and Yellowknife in Canada sit in different countries, thousands of kilometers apart. Yet all three catch the northern lights on most clear nights. Each lies beneath the same ring of sky where the aurora concentrates. What is this zone called?
context: The aurora is not scattered at random: it rides a ring about 6 degrees wide in latitude, centered roughly 67 degrees from the geomagnetic pole. Those three towns all sit almost exactly under this auroral oval - which is why they are the world's great aurora-watching towns. Standing right at the pole, you would be inside the ring and see less. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: On winter nights in Fairbanks, Alaska, the northern lights ripple across the sky like huge curtains of colored fire. The most common color of that aurora is a soft glowing green, shining about 100 kilometers above the ground. That green light pours from one particular gas in our atmosphere, kicked into glowing when charged particles blasted off the Sun crash into it. Which gas glows green?
context: The green comes from atomic oxygen glowing at a wavelength of 557.7 nanometres - the single most frequent auroral color. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: Fairbanks, in the interior of Alaska, sits almost directly under the auroral oval — the ring around the magnetic north pole where the northern lights glow most nights of the year. Scientists there log over 200 possible aurora nights every year, which sounds like a huge number. But on a truly clear, dark night during aurora season, how often do the lights actually appear overhead?
answer: about four nights out of five
choices: about four nights out of five
on very nearly every clear night
about one night out of five
context: Fairbanks sits almost directly beneath the auroral oval, so on a clear, dark night the lights appear roughly four times out of five - one of the most reliable aurora shows on Earth. Source: explorefairbanks.com/explore-the-area/aurora-season/

question: The people of Finland have watched the northern lights ripple over the frozen fells for as long as anyone remembers. They call the auroras 'revontulet,' a magical old name from a Finnish folk tale. In the story, a swift animal races across the snowy hills, and its bushy tail flicks bright sparks up into the winter sky. What does 'revontulet' mean in English?
context: The name comes from a legend that an Arctic fox raced across the fells and struck sparks from the snow with its tail. There is even a grain of truth: in the bone-dry Arctic air, a fox's fur really can throw off tiny static-electric sparks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revontulet

question: Yellowknife sits in Canada's far north, on the shore of Great Slave Lake, right under the auroral belt. On most nights the northern lights over the city shine that familiar soft green. But during an unusually violent solar storm, a rare blue-purple skirt appears along the very bottom edge of the aurora, glowing beneath the usual green ribbon. Which gas in our atmosphere produces that blue-purple fringe when solar particles hit it?
context: The blue and purple light comes from molecular nitrogen glowing lower down, and it shows up mainly during intense solar activity - a different gas from the oxygen that makes the green and red above it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: On a truly powerful night over Tromso, a rare deep-red crown glows at the very top of the aurora, high above the green - up beyond 200 km, where the air is almost pure emptiness. Up there a single glowing atom is left so undisturbed that it is strangely slow to release its light. How long can that take?
choices: a few billionths of a second
context: That red crown is also oxygen, but far higher - above 150 to 200 km. The air is so thin an oxygen atom can glow undisturbed, taking anywhere from under a second to nearly two minutes to shed its energy as 630-nm red light. Where the air is denser, collisions snuff the glow before it can appear. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: For hours the aurora over Yellowknife, Canada hangs as a calm, quiet green arc. Then, around local midnight, it suddenly erupts - the whole sky writhing and dancing with twisting curtains that flare and fade over the next hour or two. Space scientists have a name for this overnight eruption. What is it called?
context: This sudden flare-up near midnight is an auroral substorm: after energy from a solar storm builds up in Earth's magnetic tail, it dumps into the upper air all at once, and the quiet arc explodes into motion for about one to three hours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: Abisko is a tiny village high in Swedish Lapland in the far north of Sweden, tucked in a valley beside the long Lake Torneträsk. Aurora hunters love it for a strange gift: even when thick cloud smothers the whole surrounding region, a patch of clear sky often opens right over Abisko. Locals call this patch the 'blue hole.' What natural trick keeps that piece of sky clear?
answer: dry air sinking down the sheltered side of the mountains
choices: dry air sinking down the sheltered side of the mountains
warm water breathing heat up off the long lake
the aurora's own glow gently burning the cloud away
sea winds sweeping the clouds off to the east
context: Abisko sits in the rain-shadow of surrounding mountains and the 75-km-long Lake Tornetrask: air rising over the peaks drops its moisture on the way up, then sinks dry on the far side, tearing a roughly 10-20 sq km hole in the clouds. Abisko averages about 65-70% clear winter nights, versus 40-45% for Tromso 250 km west. Source: lightsoverlapland.com

question: During a colossal solar storm in September 1859, the aurora blazed so far south and so brilliantly that in Boston people could read ordinary newspaper print outdoors near 1 a.m. Telegraph operators disconnected their batteries - and still kept sending messages for two hours. What was carrying the current down their wires?
choices: leftover charge stored in the wires
static from the cold, dry air
current leaking up from the ground
context: This was the Carrington Event, the most powerful geomagnetic storm on record. The same charged particles that lit the sky induced electric currents in the long telegraph lines - enough that some operators worked for about two hours with their batteries switched off, running on auroral current alone, while sparks leapt from the equipment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: When the northern lights blaze over Norway, a matching curtain called the aurora australis can glow over Tasmania at the very same moment. Sometimes the swirls are identical, like a reflection in a mirror. Why do the far north and far south match so exactly, at the very same instant?
answer: both sit at the two ends of one magnetic field line
choices: both sit at the two ends of one magnetic field line
both reflect off the same layer of high cloud
the Sun fires a single beam straight through the planet
both are lit by the same passing comet
context: These are conjugate auroras. Earth's magnetic field lines arc from the far south to the far north; the same burst of particles slides down both ends of one line at once, painting near-identical displays in both hemispheres. The match is sharpest near the equinoxes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: Around 2016, aurora chasers in Alberta, Canada kept photographing a strange mauve ribbon arcing clear across the sky, riding above a green 'picket fence' of vertical bars. They nicknamed it STEVE (Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement). When scientists studied it, they got a shock: STEVE is not truly an aurora at all. What is it really?
answer: a river of superheated gas flowing across the sky
choices: a river of superheated gas flowing across the sky
moonlight bouncing off a sheet of high ice cloud
a night-time rainbow lit by faint starlight
smoke from far-off wildfires glowing pink
context: The Alberta Aurora Chasers named it after the animated film Over the Hedge; scientists later back-formed STEVE into 'Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement.' A 2018 NASA-led study found STEVE is not made by particles raining down like an aurora - it is a ribbon of gas only about 25 km wide but hundreds of km long, near 3,000 C, streaming west-to-east at about 6 km per second. The green 'picket fence' beside it, though, IS aurora-like. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STEVE

question: The Red Sea, between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, is not sitting still. Two huge tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart along its middle, and every year the sea grows about a centimeter wider. Given millions more years, it will grow into a whole new ocean. That slow spreading speed matches one everyday thing you can watch on your own body. What is it?
context: Africa and Arabia are splitting apart along the Red Sea Rift at roughly 1 cm a year (rising toward about 1.5-1.6 cm/yr in the south) -- about the speed a fingernail grows. Slow as it seems, over millions of years that is enough to build a whole ocean. Source: Wikipedia, 'Red Sea Rift' (spreading rate ~1 cm/year); Eos/ScienceDirect corroboration.

question: The Red Sea is a long, narrow arm of ocean lying between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, joined to the Indian Ocean through a slim southern strait. Sailors have known for centuries that its water is noticeably saltier than the open ocean it connects to. The whole sea lies in a belt of hot, nearly rainless desert. What makes the water of the Red Sea so much saltier than ordinary seawater?
answer: the sun evaporates it fast while no rivers refill it
choices: the sun evaporates it fast while no rivers refill it
salt domes on the seabed slowly dissolve into it
desert sandstorms keep dumping salt onto it
a narrow strait bottles up ocean salt inside it
context: With average salinity near 40 parts per thousand (up to 41 by the Gulf of Suez) versus about 35 for normal seawater, the Red Sea is one of the saltiest and warmest seas on Earth. Fierce evaporation under a desert sun, plus almost no river inflow to replace the lost water, concentrates the salt. Source: Wikipedia, 'Red Sea' (high evaporation, low precipitation, no significant rivers).

question: The Red Sea began less than 45 million years ago, and new sea floor is still being paved down its middle as Africa and Arabia drift apart. Given tens of millions more years, it could open into a full ocean. One of today's great oceans was born this same way when the supercontinent Pangaea broke apart. Which ocean?
context: Geologists nickname the Red Sea a 'baby ocean' -- a young ocean basin that began forming less than about 45 million years ago, one of the few places you can watch continental rifting turn into ocean floor today. Its slow spreading could eventually widen it into a full ocean, the way the Atlantic opened when Pangaea split apart. Source: ScienceDirect, 'Structure and morphology of the Red Sea'; Eos; Wikipedia, 'Red Sea Rift'.

question: The Red Sea's water is usually a bright turquoise, so its name is a puzzle. The leading guess blames a tiny living thing. Every so often, huge numbers of them drift through the water, and as they die they tint the surface a rusty red-brown. What are these color-changing organisms thought to be?
context: This is a leading but unsettled explanation: blooms of a reddish cyanobacterium, Trichodesmium erythraeum, can cloud the usually turquoise water and turn the surface reddish-brown as the bloom dies off. An alternative scholarly theory holds that 'red' simply meant the direction 'south' in some ancient color-for-direction naming. Source: Wikipedia, 'Red Sea'; LiveScience, 'Is the Red Sea Really Red?'.  (Legend.)

question: At the Afar Depression in Ethiopia, the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the East African Rift all converge at a blistering triple junction. There the African plate is doing something no other continent's plate is doing today. It is slowly cracking into two separate plates that creep apart. What are these two new plates called?
context: At the Afar Depression the Red Sea rift meets the Gulf of Aden and the East African Rift at the Afar triple junction, where the African plate is splitting into the Nubian and Somali plates as the Arabian plate pulls away -- three plates parting at once. The same rift runs more than 6,000 km south through Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania: Africa slowly tearing itself apart. Source: Wikipedia, 'Red Sea Rift'; Eos, 'Are We Seeing a New Ocean Starting to Form in Africa?'.

question: Two kilometers down in the Red Sea, a submersible's lights sweep across a real beach with lapping waves at the very bottom of the sea. Beyond it stretches a still, mirror-smooth lake whose water is so heavy that it never blends into the surrounding ocean, and any fish that blunders in is killed within seconds. What are these deadly seabed features called?
context: Deep-sea brine pools are lakes of water 3 to 8 times saltier and denser than the sea above; the brine sinks into hollows and lies unmixed, with its own surface, shoreline and slow waves in the dark. The toxic, oxygen-free water kills animals that stray in, so the floors are littered with dead fish and crabs -- yet mussels, microbial mats and tube worms crowd the rim. They are known in only three seas on Earth (the Gulf of Mexico, the Mediterranean, and the Red Sea), with about 25 described in the Red Sea alone. Source: LiveScience, 'New brine pools found in Red Sea'; OceanX.

question: Two kilometers down in the Red Sea lies the Atlantis II Deep. Its water is about 68 C, and it is so salt-choked that nothing can live in it. Yet mining companies dream about it, because the mud there holds the richest known hoard of dissolved metals anywhere on the ocean floor, packed about a thousand times denser than in seawater. Which three valuable metals is it richest in?
context: The Atlantis II Deep, about 2,000 m down, is roughly 68 C, salt-saturated (~250 parts per thousand) and airless -- and it holds the largest known metal-ore deposit on any seabed, with copper, cobalt and zinc concentrated about 1,000 times more than in ordinary seawater. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atlantis II Deep'.

question: As the oceans warm, coral reefs around the world are bleaching and dying when the water rises just a degree or two above their summer peak. But one reef is a startling exception: its corals shrug off water 5 to 7 C hotter than their summer maximum and came through recent record-breaking heatwaves without bleaching at all. Which reef is this heat-proof survivor?
answer: the Gulf of Aqaba reef, at the Red Sea's northern tip
choices: the Gulf of Aqaba reef, at the Red Sea's northern tip
the Great Barrier Reef, off eastern Australia
the Belize Barrier Reef, in the Caribbean
the Maldives reefs, in the Indian Ocean
context: The reefs at the Gulf of Aqaba, the Red Sea's northern tip, tolerate water about 5-7 C above their summer maximum -- heat that would bleach and kill reefs elsewhere -- and rode out recent record marine heatwaves without mass bleaching. Scientists think they inherited this because their ancestors re-colonized the sea from the Arabian Sea through the hot southern Red Sea, a natural filter that let only heat-tolerant corals survive, so the ones now living in the cooler north carry built-in heat resistance. Source: ScienceDirect (Gulf of Aqaba thermal refuge); Earth.org; NCBI/PMC coral studies.

question: Ringing the Pacific Ocean is a giant horseshoe-shaped belt of volcanoes stretching about 40,000 kilometers around the coasts. The belt climbs the Andes Mountains of South America, sweeps up along North America's Pacific coast through the Cascades and Alaska, and curls down through Japan, the Philippines, and out to New Zealand. What do geographers call this fiery volcanic belt around the Pacific?
context: The Ring of Fire traces the rim of the Pacific for roughly 40,000 km (25,000 mi), from the tip of South America up through North America, across the Bering Strait, and down past Japan to New Zealand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire ; https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/plate-tectonics-ring-fire/

question: More than 450 volcanoes ring the Pacific in one big horseshoe. They run through the Andes, the Cascades, Japan, and Indonesia. Of all the active volcanoes on Earth, about how many sit along this belt?
context: National Geographic counts about 452 volcanoes along the belt — roughly three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes — all riding above ocean plates that dive into deep trenches around the Pacific. Source: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/plate-tectonics-ring-fire/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire

question: About 90 percent of the world's earthquakes strike along a single arc — the Ring of Fire, a giant horseshoe of fault lines and volcanoes wrapping the Pacific Ocean through the Andes of South America, up the U.S. and Alaskan coast, and down through Japan and the Aleutian Islands. Most of the biggest quakes ever recorded happened inside this belt too. Why does this one Pacific rim shake so much harder than the rest of the planet?
answer: ocean plates diving beneath the land
choices: ocean plates diving beneath the land
mantle plumes rising up under the rim
the deepest ocean basin pressing down
the planet's thinnest crust cracking open
context: About 90% of the world's earthquakes, including most of the largest ever recorded, strike along the Ring of Fire, because so many ocean plates are grinding down beneath the land there. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire

question: Japan is a nation of volcanic islands. Near Tokyo, on the main island of Honshu, the Pacific Plate slides beneath Japan and slowly pushes up a nearly perfect snow-capped cone. It rises 3,776 metres, the highest mountain in the country. It last erupted in 1707 and has been quiet ever since. Japanese pilgrims and painters treat it as their most sacred peak. What is this famous volcano called?
context: Mount Fuji stands 3,776 m near a junction of the Eurasian, North American, and Philippine Sea plates, close to where the Pacific Plate subducts. Its last eruption was the Hoei eruption of 1707-08. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fuji

question: Along the border between Chile and Argentina in South America, the Nazca Plate slides beneath the continent. That slow crash of plates lifts up the Andes, the world's longest mountain chain. On this high border stands a huge snow-streaked cone of a volcano called Ojos del Salado. What record does this mountain hold?
choices: the most active volcano on Earth
context: Ojos del Salado reaches 6,893 m (22,615 ft), lifted by the Nazca Plate diving beneath South America. Aconcagua is a touch higher at about 6,960 m, but it isn't a volcano — so Ojos del Salado is the tallest volcano anywhere on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojos_del_Salado

question: High on the border of Chile and Argentina stands Ojos del Salado, a great snow-streaked volcano built by the slow crash of tectonic plates in the Andes. Near its summit, tucked inside one of its craters, sits a small pool of water fed by melting snow — a crater lake. Of all the lakes on Earth, which record does this crater lake hold?
answer: the highest lake in the world
choices: the highest lake in the world
the highest lake where fish live
context: Near the summit of Ojos del Salado, at roughly 6,480-6,500 m, a small crater lake fed by permafrost and snowmelt is the highest lake in the world — higher even than the highest navigable lake, Lake Titicaca. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojos_del_Salado

question: In the U.S. Pacific Northwest, the Cascade Range holds a line of snow-capped volcanoes — Mount Rainier, Mount Hood, and Mount St. Helens among them. All of these mountains burn because a small ocean plate lying just off the Washington and Oregon coast is slowly diving beneath the North American continent, melting into fresh magma deep below. Which plate's dive under North America feeds this line of Cascade volcanoes?
context: The small Juan de Fuca Plate slides under North America along the Cascadia subduction zone, feeding the Cascade arc — Mount St. Helens, Mount Rainier, and Mount Hood among them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: On the morning of May 18, 1980, a magnitude-5.1 earthquake shook Mount St. Helens, a Cascade volcano in Washington State. Seconds later the whole bulging north face of the mountain broke loose and slid away, and the volcano tore itself apart in a sideways blast that flattened forests for miles. That 1980 eruption set a world record that still stands today. What record did Mount St. Helens set?
answer: the largest landslide in recorded history
choices: the largest landslide in recorded history
the deadliest eruption of the 20th century
the tallest ash plume ever measured
context: The magnitude-5.1 quake shook the whole north face of Mount St. Helens loose, unleashing the largest landslide (debris avalanche) in recorded history and a sideways blast that flattened forest across a fan 19 miles long. The summit dropped 401 m, from 2,950 m to 2,549 m. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: Mount Tambora sits on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa. In April 1815 it unleashed the most powerful eruption in recorded history. Its explosions were heard 2,600 kilometers away. When the roar finally died, what had the blast done to the mountain itself?
answer: blasted away about a third of the whole mountain
choices: blasted away about a third of the whole mountain
raised a brand-new cone inside the old crater
split the island of Sumbawa clean in two
sank its entire summit beneath the sea
context: Tambora's April 1815 eruption reached VEI 7 — the most powerful in recorded history — blasting out some 37-45 cubic km of rock and ash and dropping the mountain from about 4,300 m to 2,851 m, leaving a caldera 6-7 km wide. The blasts were heard at least 2,600 km (1,600 mi) away. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora

question: Mount Tambora hurled so much ash and sulfur high into the atmosphere in 1815 that it veiled the sun and cooled the whole planet by about half a degree. Across the Northern Hemisphere the following year, frost and snow ruined the growing season. What did people come to call 1816?
context: So much ash and sulfur dimmed the sky that global temperatures fell about 0.5°C, giving 1816 its nickname the 'Year Without a Summer,' with snow and frost striking the Northern Hemisphere in mid-summer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora

question: Along the deep Pacific trenches of the Ring of Fire — where an ocean plate bends downward and sinks beneath a continent, feeding volcanoes like Japan's Mount Fuji — the diving plate carries wet seawater and hydrated minerals down with it.
