question: The thousands of warriors in Pit 1 are not arranged as a random crowd. They stand in tight battle ranks, and every single row faces the exact same direction, gazing outward toward the horizon. The First Emperor lined them up this way on purpose. Which way does his whole army look?
context: The pits sit about 1.5 km east of the tomb mound, and the warriors face east -- toward the rival warring states the First Emperor had conquered and the direction his old enemies had once come from -- set as an eternal vanguard. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army

question: In 1920, in Soviet Russia, a young scientist named Lev Termen showed off a strange new electronic instrument. You played it without touching it — waving your hands between two metal antennas — and it made a spooky, wavering wail. That ghostly voice later filled old horror and flying-saucer films. What was Termen's invention called?
context: Lev Termen — known in the West as Leon Theremin — invented it in Russia in October 1920, the first musical instrument you play without ever touching it. One critic described its voice as 'a cello lost in a dense fog, crying because it does not know how to get home.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin

question: At Iceland's Thingvellir, a footpath drops into a deep canyon. On one side rises a cliff of the North American plate, and the Eurasian plate forms the far wall. Nowhere else on land can you walk between two continents in the open air. What type of plate boundary runs through here?
context: At Thingvellir the two plates spread apart about 2 cm a year; over the 10,000 years since the lava flowed there, the ground has widened roughly 70 m and dropped some 40 m. This is a DIVERGENT boundary -- the one place on land where you can walk inside the seam between two continents. (thingvellir.is/en/education/nature/tectonic-movements)

question: At Silfra in Iceland, divers drop into a flooded crack in the earth. The crack is filled with glacier melt so clear they can see almost 100 metres, the length of a football pitch. Floating down the narrow gorge, they reach out and do something that is possible in almost no other spot on Earth. What can they do?
answer: touch two tectonic plates at once
choices: touch two tectonic plates at once
swim through a flooded lava tube
float in water too salty to sink
glide beneath the edge of a glacier
context: The Silfra fissure runs right through the rift between the North American and Eurasian plates -- stretch out your arms and a hand rests on each side. Its water is glacial melt filtered through porous lava for decades, giving visibility of around 100 m. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silfra)

question: Off the Pacific coast of South America, a deep ocean trench plunges just offshore, dropping thousands of metres straight down. Rising up behind it stand the Andes mountains, with tall snow-capped volcanoes running down their spine. Two tectonic plates meet here, and one is slowly sliding down beneath the other. What type of plate boundary makes a coast like this?
context: Where the Nazca plate dives under the South American plate at the Peru-Chile Trench, melting rock feeds the Andes' volcanoes and lifts its great peaks. One plate diving beneath another is a CONVERGENT (subduction) boundary. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes)

question: Earth's ten tallest mountains all rise in Asia, in the Himalaya and Karakoram ranges. But far away in South America, along the long spine of the Andes on the border of Argentina and Chile, stands the highest peak found anywhere outside Asia. It reaches 6,961 metres above the sea. Name this South American mountain.
context: Aconcagua, in Argentina's Andes, reaches 6,961 m -- the highest summit outside Asia, and the tallest in both the Americas and the Southern Hemisphere. The Andes themselves run about 8,900 km, the longest continental mountain range on Earth. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes)

question: In California, the San Andreas Fault runs some 750 miles up the state. Where it crosses fences, roads, and dry creek beds, it has jogged them sideways out of line, and every so often the ground lurches free in a sudden earthquake. What type of plate boundary is the San Andreas?
context: Along a TRANSFORM boundary the plates neither build new crust nor swallow old -- they just grind sideways. The San Andreas runs about 750 miles through California; a slip on its northern reach caused the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault)

question: The Pacific plate is slowly hauling the western sliver of California toward the northwest along the San Andreas Fault. Los Angeles rides that moving plate; San Francisco, up the coast, sits mostly on the plate next door. Millions of years from now, what becomes of the two cities?
answer: Los Angeles will drift north to sit beside San Francisco
choices: Los Angeles will drift north to sit beside San Francisco
Los Angeles will sink beneath the deep Pacific Ocean
Los Angeles will crumple upward into new mountains
Los Angeles will stay locked in place, unmoving, forever
context: Because the Pacific plate creeps northwest, Los Angeles inches toward San Francisco by a few centimetres a year. In several million years the two cities are expected to end up side-by-side neighbours -- still separated by the grinding fault. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault)  (Legend.)

question: Earth's entire rocky shell -- every continent and all the ocean floors -- is cracked into only about seven or eight major slabs. One of them dwarfs the others, spanning some 103 million square kilometres, larger than any continent. Which is Earth's largest tectonic plate?
context: The Pacific plate covers about 103 million km2, flooring most of the Pacific Ocean -- the biggest of the roughly 7-8 major plates (plus about 15 minor ones) that tile the planet. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Plate)

question: At Iceland's Thingvellir, the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates gradually creep apart only about two centimetres each year, steady and unstoppable. That is roughly the same speed at which one particular part of your own body actually grows. Which part is it?
context: Plates typically move a few centimetres a year -- about as fast as your fingernails grow (your hair actually grows several times faster). At Thingvellir the North American and Eurasian plates part at roughly 2 cm a year. (usgs.gov/faqs/how-fast-do-tectonic-plates-move)

question: Tectonic plates usually creep along just a few centimetres a year. But in 2005, at the Dabbahu volcano in Ethiopia's Afar desert, the ground split open along a gash 60 kilometres long and up to 8 metres wide. How long did geologists say this huge rip took to tear open?
context: The 2005 Dabbahu event opened a 60-km fissure in about two weeks, releasing an estimated 400 years of built-up crustal stress almost overnight. Afar is a rare triple junction, where the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and East African rifts all meet and pull apart. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afar_Triangle)

question: Along the East African Rift, a great crack that runs down the eastern side of Africa from Ethiopia south through Kenya and Tanzania toward Mozambique, the ground is slowly splitting apart. Geologists expect that in roughly 10 million years a long strip of the continent will finish tearing away from the rest of Africa. As the two pieces pull apart, what will be born in the widening gap between them?
context: As the East African Rift widens, the sea is expected to flood in, splitting off a slab of Africa and creating a brand-new ocean basin in about 10 million years -- the same process that long ago opened the Red Sea. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afar_Triangle)  (Legend.)

question: Stand on a beach in California and watch the sea for a whole day. Twice each day the Pacific Ocean slowly climbs high up the sand, then quietly slides all the way back out again — like the sea taking two long breaths. These daily rises and falls of the ocean are called tides. What in the sky does most of the pulling that lifts these tides?
context: The Moon's gravity is the true master of the sea — its tide-raising pull is more than twice the Sun's (the Sun adds only about 46% as much). Twice a day the whole ocean answers the Moon and rises. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: Along one funnel-shaped coast, the sea climbs the height of a five-story building, about 16 metres, then falls again, twice each single day. These are officially the highest tides found anywhere on Earth. Which coast is it?
context: This is the Bay of Fundy, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in eastern Canada — a world-record tidal range near 16 m. Ungava Bay in northern Quebec runs so close that some call the record a tie. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Fundy.

question: The Bay of Fundy is a long funnel-shaped inlet between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick on the east coast of Canada. It has the highest tides on Earth. Every time the tide floods in, about 100 billion tonnes of seawater pour up into the bay — then pour out again hours later. That single half-day surge outmatches one astonishing benchmark. Which?
answer: more water than every river on Earth combined
choices: more water than every river on Earth combined
more water than a whole year of rain on Canada
more water than all five Great Lakes hold
more water than the Amazon moves in a month
context: Each half-tide moves roughly 100 billion tonnes of water in or out of the Bay of Fundy — about twice the combined flow of every river on Earth over the same time. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Fundy.

question: Far out in the open ocean the Moon lifts the sea only about half a metre — a swell so gentle a passing ship never feels it. Yet the same tide rears up 16 metres, the height of a five-story building, twice each day inside the Bay of Fundy on Canada's east coast. What turns that gentle ocean swell into such a coastal giant?
answer: the funnel shape of the bay, stacking the water higher
choices: the funnel shape of the bay, stacking the water higher
the Moon pulling harder directly over Canada
cold northern seawater piling up denser and taller
the great depth of the bay multiplying the pull
context: Tides are born tiny in the open sea — the Moon lifts it only about 54 cm — and grow into giants only where the shape of the coastline funnels and stacks them. Fundy's tapering funnel is the world champion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: At Mont-Saint-Michel, the island abbey off the coast of Normandy in France, the tide can sweep across the flat sands very fast. An old warning, often credited to Victor Hugo, matches its speed to one alarming thing. What is it?
context: The saying — often credited to Victor Hugo — is that the sea comes in 'as swiftly as a galloping horse.' Treat it as vivid lore, not a measured speed; the real danger at Mont-Saint-Michel (tidal range about 14 m) is fast-rising water and quicksand that can strand walkers on the flats. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mont-Saint-Michel; thegoodlifefrance.com.  (Legend.)

question: On the Bay of Fundy in eastern Canada, as on most coasts around the world, the sea rises to a high tide not once but twice each day, about twelve hours apart. The Moon's pull on our oceans creates that rhythm — but it does so in a way that raises the water in two places at once, not one. What does the Moon actually raise on Earth to give two daily highs instead of one?
answer: a bulge of water on both the near and far sides at once
choices: a bulge of water on both the near and far sides at once
a single bulge the spinning Earth sweeps past twice
a bulge that sloshes back and forth across the ocean
a ring of raised water circling the whole equator
context: The Moon pulls hardest on the ocean facing it, raising a near-side bulge, and least on the far-side water, which is 'left behind' as a second bulge. Earth turns through both each day, so most coasts get two high tides. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: Twice each month, at the new Moon and again at the full Moon, the Sun and Moon line up directly in a row and together heave the seas together, lifting the tides to their very highest. Tide-watchers on the Bay of Fundy know these enormous tides especially well. What are these highest twice-monthly tides called?
context: 'Spring' here means 'springing up' or bursting forth — the tide leaping to its peak — not the season. These highest tides come when the Sun and Moon pull in a straight line, at the new and full Moon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: The Bay of Fundy's everyday tides already top out near 16 metres. Yet in October 1869 the water at Burntcoat Head, Nova Scotia, surged to a staggering 21.6 metres — a world record never beaten since. What extra force heaped those final metres onto an already-towering tide?
answer: a violent windstorm driving a surge ashore
choices: a violent windstorm driving a surge ashore
a sudden snowmelt flood pouring down the rivers
the wave from an offshore undersea earthquake
a heavy, days-long downpour swelling the bay
context: The record came during the Saxby Gale of October 1869: fierce winds and abnormally low pressure drove a storm surge on top of a tide already running unusually high. Burntcoat Head's routine maximum is about 17 m — the 21.6 m mark was a storm-amplified one-off, not the everyday tide. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burntcoat_Head,_Nova_Scotia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1869_Saxby_Gale.

question: On the estuary of the Rance river, in Brittany on the northwest coast of France, engineers opened a landmark power station in 1966. President Charles de Gaulle himself came to inaugurate it. For the next 45 years no rival of its kind grew any larger anywhere in the world. What was this station the first in the world to do?
answer: turn the ocean's tides into electricity
choices: turn the ocean's tides into electricity
turn the ocean's waves into electricity
turn the ocean's heat into electricity
turn the ocean's currents into electricity
context: It was the Rance Tidal Power Station — the world's first tidal power plant, using 24 bulb turbines to harness the estuary's roughly 8 m (up to 13.5 m) tide. It stayed the largest tidal station on Earth for 45 years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rance_Tidal_Power_Station.

question: The Sun and Moon are not always allies. About a week after the spring tides, at the quarter (half) Moon, they pull crossways to one another and partly cancel — so even the mighty Bay of Fundy runs slack, the sea barely rising and falling. What are these weakest tides called?
context: 'Neap' is an old Anglo-Saxon word meaning roughly 'without the power.' At the quarter Moon the Sun's pull works crossways to the Moon's, so the two partly cancel and the tides run slack. (In line, at new and full Moon, they give the towering spring tides.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: Between the Canadian provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, the Bay of Fundy is shaped like a long narrow funnel. Many bays around the world have a funnel shape too, and yet the Bay of Fundy alone grows the highest tides on the planet — up to 16 metres, taller than a house. What lucky coincidence makes the Bay of Fundy the champion, and not just another funnel-shaped bay?
answer: its natural sloshing rhythm matches the tide's own beat
choices: its natural sloshing rhythm matches the tide's own beat
it faces straight into the Atlantic's fastest current
its rivers pour in more fresh water than any other bay
it lies at the one latitude where the tides peak
context: This lucky match is called tidal resonance: Fundy's water naturally sloshes back and forth on nearly the same ~12.5-hour rhythm as the tides, so each tide pushes at just the right moment — like timing shoves on a swing — building the water ever higher. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Fundy.

question: At Saint John, New Brunswick, the Saint John River tumbles over a hidden rock ledge as a churning rapid on its way to the sea. Twice a day, when the giant Bay of Fundy tide floods in, something almost unbelievable happens to that rapid. What?
answer: the whole rapid flips and the river runs backward, uphill
choices: the whole rapid flips and the river runs backward, uphill
the rapid swells and doubles into a roaring waterfall
the rapid drowns beneath the flood into a deep whirlpool
the rapid falls calm, smoothing into a glassy stillwater
context: This is the Reversing Falls (Reversing Rapids) at Saint John: at high tide the Fundy flood overpowers the Saint John River and forces the rapid to run upstream, against its own current, over an underwater rock ledge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reversing_Falls.

question: As the Bay of Fundy tide charges up the Petitcodiac River near Moncton, it rears into a tidal bore — a moving wall of water rolling upstream against the current. In July 2013 two California surfers caught that wall and set a North American record. For what feat?
choices: the fastest surf ride ever clocked
the most surfers on one wave
the tallest bore wave ever ridden
context: Surfers Mark Whitbread and Colin Wessels rode the Petitcodiac bore about 29 km (18 miles) over two and a half hours — a North American record for the longest wave ever surfed. A tidal bore forms when a big incoming tide funnels into a narrowing river. Source: cbc.ca (Moncton tidal bore, July 2013).

question: For five centuries a ship leaving Europe rode one steady wind across the tropical Atlantic. It was a broad belt of warm wind blowing out of the northeast, day after day. It pushed sail after sail west to the Americas, and never once turned against them. What are these winds called?
context: In the Northern Hemisphere the trade winds blow from the northeast; in the Southern, from the southeast, both curving toward the equator. This same reliable highway of wind carried immense wealth and the great Columbian exchange of crops, animals, and ideas between continents, and it also carried European colonization of the Americas and the ships of the transatlantic slave trade. The wind was neutral; what sailed on it was not. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trade winds' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds).

question: These winds carried England's merchant ships across the tropical Atlantic for centuries, so everyone assumes 'trade winds' comes from commerce and cargo. But the word 'trade' here is much older than that money meaning. Sailors used it long before, in the salty phrase 'the wind blows trade.' What did 'trade' actually mean back then?
context: 'Trade' here comes from a 14th-century sense meaning a track, course, or direction, from the nautical phrase 'to blow trade' (to blow steadily one way). Only later, because these winds were so vital to England's merchant fleet crossing the Atlantic, did the money-meaning of 'trade' attach itself and stick. An etymology twist: the name is older than the commerce it came to serve. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trade winds' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds); Wiktionary, 'trade wind' (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/trade_wind).

question: In 1492 Columbus let the steady northeast wind push him due west from the Canary Islands to the Americas. But the same wind at his back made going home impossible, because it would only shove him further west. So for the trip back, he climbed north into cooler middle latitudes to catch a different belt of wind, higher up, that blows back toward Europe. What are these homeward winds called?
context: Columbus began his return on 16 January 1493, looping north to ride the westerlies home. The outbound trades and the homebound westerlies together form a great clockwise wheel of wind across the North Atlantic, the gyre that made round-trip sailing possible. Source: Wikipedia, 'Voyages of Christopher Columbus' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus).

question: Right at the equator, the trade winds of the two hemispheres meet head-on, cancel each other out, and rise straight upward instead of blowing across the sea. What they leave behind is a belt of dead, breathless calm. A sailing ship, with wind as its only engine, could sit motionless there for weeks under a broiling tropical sun. What is this equatorial calm belt called?
context: Scientists call this belt the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ); 18th-century sailors named it the 'doldrums' for its stagnant, spirit-sapping calm. Do not confuse it with the horse latitudes, the separate calm belts near 30 degrees where ships were also becalmed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Intertropical Convergence Zone' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertropical_Convergence_Zone).

question: For 250 years, from 1565 to 1815, great Spanish treasure ships hauled Asian silk, porcelain, and Mexican silver back and forth across the entire Pacific twice each year. They rode the trade winds outward and the warm Kuroshio current home, linking a Spanish port in the Philippines to Acapulco on Mexico's coast. It was one of the longest-lasting sea routes in all of recorded history. What is this great Pacific crossing called?
context: The Manila galleons ran for 250 years (1565-1815), an early engine of globalization pouring American silver into Asia and Asian silk into the Americas and Europe. It was also a lifeline of Spanish colonial trade, and it ended as Mexico moved toward independence. Source: Wikipedia, 'Manila galleon' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_galleon).

question: A Portuguese caravel beating back up the west coast of Africa faced a maddening trap. The coastal winds and currents ran steadily against it, so a straight dash home to Portugal was hopeless. The captains' escape was to sail the wrong way first, striking hundreds of miles out into the open ocean toward Brazil, away from home. Only far out there could they swing around and finally catch the westerlies back to Europe. What did the Portuguese call this looping detour?
context: 'Volta do mar' means 'turn of the sea.' Its Pacific cousin, the tornaviaje, was cracked by the friar Andres de Urdaneta in 1565. Historians hold that Europe's sea empires could not have arisen without this wind-gyre trick; a 13th-century Genoese expedition, the Vivaldi brothers, sailed south past the Canaries and likely perished, unable to beat back upwind for want of it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Volta do mar' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_do_mar).

question: Here is the puzzle hidden inside the trade winds. Air is pulled toward the band of low pressure lying along the equator, so you would expect it to blow straight south in the north and straight north in the south. Instead, in BOTH hemispheres the wind arrives leaning firmly westward, the very slant that let sailing ships ride it clear across an ocean. What phenomenon, arising from the Earth's rotation, bends the equator-bound wind into that westward slant?
context: The Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern, giving equator-bound wind its westward push. If the Earth ever stopped spinning, the slant would vanish and the winds would blow straight toward the equator. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coriolis force' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriolis_force); 'Trade winds' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds).

question: The Lombok Strait is barely 35 km wide. From Bali you can see across the water to the island of Lombok. Yet step ashore, and the wild animals have changed completely, as if you had crossed to another continent. What is this sharp wildlife border called?
context: Cross the Lombok Strait and Asia's tigers and monkeys give way to Australia's marsupials and cockatoos. The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace mapped this frontier in 1859; Thomas Henry Huxley named it 'Wallace's Line' in 1868, and it is also called the Wallace Line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Line; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombok_Strait

question: During the ice ages, the seas fell about 120 metres. Dry land linked island to island across the region. But the animals of Bali and Lombok never mixed, even across a narrow strait. Why did that one gap never close into dry land?
answer: its channel is far deeper than the seas ever fell
choices: its channel is far deeper than the seas ever fell
the seas there never dropped as far as elsewhere
a swift current kept sweeping the sand away
its seabed kept sinking as fast as the seas fell
context: The Lombok Strait plunges to at least 250 metres — more than twice the ice-age sea drop — so its floor never surfaced as land. Everywhere else the falling seas welded islands into two giant landmasses; only across deep gaps like this one did the divide hold. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Line; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombok_Strait

question: West of the line, Bali, Java, Sumatra and Borneo sit in shallow sea, rarely deeper than 50 metres. They all rest on one wide underwater shelf. When ice-age seas fell, that shelf became dry land and joined the islands into one big peninsula. Which shelf do these western islands sit on?
context: This is the Sunda Shelf, welded to the Asian mainland. At ice-age low sea it formed 'Sundaland,' a peninsula of Asia spanning roughly 1.85 million square kilometres, where water rarely exceeds 50 metres deep. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunda_Shelf

question: During the last ice age, the seas fell about 120 metres. East of the Wallace Line — the deep-water gap that keeps Asia's animals from mixing with Australia's — that drop uncovered a wide shallow seabed south of the equator. A person could once walk right across it from Australia to New Guinea on dry ground. Which shallow shelf joined Australia and New Guinea into one landmass back then?
context: This is the Sahul Shelf, the Australian continental shelf. At low sea it formed the landmass 'Sahul,' joined to New Guinea across the Arafura Shelf; ancient drowned shorelines here now lie 100-140 metres below today's sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahul_Shelf

question: Between the two great shelves lies a scatter of islands — Sulawesi, Lombok, Flores, Timor — that deep water kept apart from BOTH sides, so they were never joined to Asia or to Australia. Their wildlife is a strange half-and-half mix of the two. What do naturalists call this in-between zone?
context: This is Wallacea — about 347,000 square kilometres of islands, Sulawesi the largest — ringed by deep-water straits on every side, so its life is a blend of Asian and Australian types found nowhere else. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallacea

question: Where Asian and Australian wildlife blend together across the islands between the shelves, a single boundary was not enough, so mapmakers added others. One of them runs along the eastern rim of that blend zone, pressed tight against the Australian shelf, and was drawn in 1896. What is this eastern line called?
context: Richard Lydekker drew this line in 1896 along the edge of the Sahul Shelf, marking the eastern rim of Wallacea. Between it and Wallace's Line runs Weber's Line, the balance point where Asian and Australian life meet in equal measure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydekker%27s_Line; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weber%27s_Line

question: Far north of Bali, a second great gap along the Wallace Line splits the huge islands of Borneo and Sulawesi. This one is vast — 130 to 370 km across, ten times wider than the narrow strait at Bali — yet it divides Asian and Australian wildlife just as sharply, and for the very same reason: it plunges to about 2,500 m deep. What is this wide, deep gap called?
context: This is the Makassar Strait, between Borneo and Sulawesi — 130 to 370 km across, far wider than the 35 km Lombok Strait, yet plunging to about 2,500 m in its northern basin. That proves the Wallace Line's real barrier is deep water, not mere distance. Source: britannica.com/place/Makassar-Strait

question: In the early 1800s, a swirling couple-dance called the waltz swept into the grand ballrooms of Vienna, the capital of Austria. Newspapers of the time called it a shocking foreign dance and printed page after page of angry complaints. Of all the things critics fussed about, what did they call the real scandal?
answer: The man held the woman close, face-to-face, his hand at her waist
choices: The man held the woman close, face-to-face, his hand at her waist
Unmarried couples danced together with no chaperone between them
The women bared their arms and shoulders in daring ball gowns
Couples broke off to dance as pairs instead of in group sets
context: Earlier ballroom dances kept couples apart in group formations; the waltz's closed hold - man and woman face-to-face, his hand at her waist, turning together - was the shocking part. In July 1816 The Times of London denounced it as an 'indecent foreign dance,' warning of 'the voluptuous intertwining of the limbs.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz

question: The elegant Viennese waltz did not begin in grand ballrooms. It grew out of a rough, stomping folk dance in the same lilting three-beat time, danced by peasants in the villages of Austria and Bavaria and then cleaned up for the city. What was this peasant dance called?
context: The Ländler was a stomping Austrian and Bavarian peasant dance in 3/4 time; sped up and refined, it became the ballroom waltz. (Modern scholars increasingly treat the two as parallel 'sibling' dances rather than strict ancestor and descendant.) Source: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/stories/11-facts-viennese-waltz/

question: The word 'waltz' comes from the German verb 'walzen' - to roll or turn - a nod to the dance's whirling spin. As the dance spread through Austria and southern Germany, the earliest known appearance of the word in print, in 1748, turned up in a single official document. What sort of document gave 'waltz' its written debut?
context: 'Waltz' comes from the German 'walzen,' to roll, turn, or revolve - for the dance's rolling rotation. The word first appears in print in 1748, in the text of a dance ban. Source: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/stories/11-facts-viennese-waltz/

question: In 1863 in Vienna, the Habsburg emperor Franz Joseph placed the famous waltz composer Johann Strauss the Younger — writer of 'The Blue Danube' — on the imperial payroll with an official salaried post inside the Austrian royal court. What court title did Strauss hold?
answer: Music Director of the Royal Court Balls
choices: Music Director of the Royal Court Balls
Music Director of the Imperial Court Opera
Music Director of the Court Chapel Choir
Music Director of the Emperor's Chamber
context: Johann Strauss II (1825-1899) wrote over 500 dance pieces, hundreds of them waltzes, and in 1863 was named KK Hofballmusikdirektor - Music Director of the Royal Court Balls. His father, Johann Strauss I, had forbidden a musical career, wanting the boy to become a banker. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Strauss_II

question: Johann Strauss the Younger's 1866 waltz 'By the Beautiful Blue ___' became Vienna's unofficial anthem, the tune the city reaches for whenever it wants to feel most itself. He named it for the broad river that curls through the heart of Vienna. Which river fills the blank?
context: 'By the Beautiful Blue Danube' (An der schönen blauen Donau), composed 1866 and premiered in 1867, became Vienna's unofficial anthem. It began as a choral piece with satirical lyrics and only a mild success; the orchestral version at the 1867 Paris World's Fair made it a triumph. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blue_Danube

question: In 1814-15, the monarchs and diplomats of Europe gathered at the Congress of Vienna to redraw the continent's map after Napoleon's fall. Yet months passed with little settled, and Prince Charles-Joseph de Ligne mocked that the Congress 'does not advance.' What had swallowed up the delegates' time and energy in the host city?
answer: an endless whirl of balls and dancing
choices: an endless whirl of balls and dancing
secret treaties argued in back rooms
long state banquets and royal hunts
context: At the Congress of Vienna (Sept 1814 - June 1815), the balls so filled the diplomacy that Prince Charles-Joseph de Ligne quipped 'Le congrès danse beaucoup, mais il ne marche pas' - 'the Congress dances a lot, but does not advance.' Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Congress_of_Vienna

question: Egypt sits in the middle of the Sahara Desert in northeast Africa. Across it flows one great river that runs the 'wrong' way — south to north — into the Mediterranean Sea. Long ago, each summer, this river's floods spread a layer of rich black mud on the dry desert soil. That yearly gift of mud fed the farms of ancient Egypt for thousands of years. Which river is this?
context: The Nile flows about 6,650 km from the highlands of central Africa north to the Mediterranean — long enough to rival the Amazon for the title of the world's longest river. Its yearly summer flood laid down fresh black silt (the Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'the black land'), letting farms flourish in a desert. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile

question: Deep in the rainforests of South America, one great river pours out about a fifth of all the fresh water that all the world's rivers together deliver to the oceans. By itself, this single river dumps more water into the sea than the next seven biggest rivers on Earth put together. Which river is this?
context: The Amazon discharges roughly 215,000–230,000 cubic metres of water every second — about a fifth of all the fresh water Earth's rivers pour into the oceans, and more than the next seven largest rivers combined. Even where it first enters Brazil it already out-discharges every other river on the planet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River

question: Asia's longest river runs about 6,300 km from end to end. It tumbles down from high on the Tibetan Plateau in western China, then slices a chain of dramatic gorges through steep cliffs on its long journey east across China to the Pacific Ocean. Which river is this?
context: The Yangtze runs about 6,300 km entirely within China — Asia's longest river and the third-longest on Earth. Where it carves the Three Gorges through Mount Wushan, engineers built the Three Gorges Dam, the largest hydro-electric power station in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangtze

question: North America's biggest river starts as a small stream from Lake Itasca in Minnesota. It then gathers the water of nearly half the United States on its long run south to the Gulf of Mexico. Which river is this?
context: The Mississippi rises at Lake Itasca and drains all or part of 32 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces — a basin of about 3.2 million sq km, roughly 40% of the continental United States. Joined with the Missouri, it forms the fourth-longest river system on Earth (about 5,970 km), behind only the Nile, Amazon, and Yangtze. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River

question: One European river flows through or borders more countries than any other river on Earth — ten of them — winding from Germany's Black Forest all the way to the shores of the Black Sea. Which river is this?
context: The Danube touches ten countries — Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova, and Ukraine — more than any other river on Earth. Europe's second-longest river (about 2,850 km, after the Volga), it is also the only river to flow past four national capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube

question: Each summer the Nile suddenly swells into a great flood. About 70% of that flood water comes down one branch, the Blue Nile. It roars off one highland after heavy summer rains. From which highland does the Blue Nile's flood come?
context: The Blue Nile pours out of Lake Tana on the Ethiopian Highlands. When the summer rains soak those highlands, the Blue Nile delivers about 70% of the flood racing down the main Nile (and roughly 54% of its flow across the whole year) — the surge that once flooded Egypt's fields on schedule. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile

question: The White Nile carries less water than the Blue Nile. But it is the branch that makes the Nile so long. Its farthest streams trickle from the hills around one huge lake in East Africa. Around which lake do the White Nile's farthest sources lie?
context: The White Nile's remotest headwaters gather around Lake Victoria in East Africa. Though it carries less water than the Blue Nile, this is the branch that gives the Nile its enormous length. The two branches then race north toward their meeting deep in the desert. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile

question: At one great city, two rivers flow together and become the single Nile: the pale, sediment-milky White Nile and the darker, clay-stained Blue Nile, their waters meeting with a visible colour line. At which city do the Blue Nile and White Nile join?
context: Khartoum, the capital of Sudan, sits exactly where the two Niles join. The pale White Nile (milky with quartz and feldspar sediment) and the darker Blue Nile (stained with Ethiopian clay) meet with a visible boundary before merging into the single Nile that flows on to Egypt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile

question: One African river cuts canyons so deep that its bed plunges about 220 m straight down into cold, pitch-black water — deeper than any other river anywhere on Earth. Which river runs the deepest in the world?
context: The Congo plunges to about 220 m (720 ft) in its dark canyons — the deepest river on Earth. It ranks only third by the volume of water it carries (behind the Amazon and the Ganges–Brahmaputra), but no river runs deeper. In its lightless depths a blind, colourless fish, Lamprologus lethops, evolved cut off from the world above. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River

question: The Congo winds in an enormous arc through the rainforests of central Africa, and somewhere along that curving course it pulls off a feat no other great river in the world can match. What is the Congo's one-of-a-kind feat?
choices: it empties into an inland sea
it reverses its flow each rainy season
context: The Congo is the only major river on Earth to cross the equator twice — its huge curving course dips south of the equator and swings back north again. Near its mouth it hurls itself toward the Atlantic through Livingstone Falls, a staircase of enormous rapids. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River

question: Near the Brazilian river-city of Manaus, two Amazon tributaries famously meet but refuse to blend, running side by side for about 6 km: the coffee-black Rio Negro and its pale partner. What is the pale partner river called?
context: The Rio Solimões is the name Brazilians give the pale, sediment-heavy upper Amazon — cool (~22°C), fast (4–6 km/h), and milky with silt washed down from the Andes. Beside it runs the coffee-black Rio Negro, warm and slow and stained dark by decayed leaves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters

question: Near Manaus in Brazil, two big Amazon tributaries meet at the famous 'Meeting of the Waters': the coffee-black Rio Negro and the pale, sandy-brown Rio Solimões. Instead of blending, they run side by side for about 6 km with a sharp line straight down the middle of the river. What keeps the two waters from mixing for so long?
answer: they differ in temperature, speed, and density
choices: they differ in temperature, speed, and density
a submerged rock ridge divides the channel
the Rio Negro's water is too oily to blend
opposing tides from the sea hold them apart
context: At the Meeting of the Waters (Encontro das Águas) by Manaus, the two rivers refuse to blend because they differ in temperature, speed, and density: the Rio Negro is warmer (~28°C), slow (~2 km/h), and nearly sediment-free, while the Rio Solimões is cooler (~22°C), fast (4–6 km/h), and heavy with Andean silt. They flow side by side for about 6 km before finally mixing into the Amazon. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters

question: On the great Yangtze River in central China, boats sail east from the old walled town of Baidicheng. For nearly 200 miles the river squeezes between towering cliff walls hundreds of metres tall. Then it finally opens out again at the city of Yichang. What is this famous run of three canyons called?
context: The Three Gorges — Qutang, Wu, and Xiling — run about 193 miles (311 km) down the Yangtze from Baidicheng in Chongqing to Yichang in Hubei. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges

question: Along the Yangtze River in central China, three canyons together are known as the Three Gorges. Of these three, one is loved above the rest for its beauty: a 45-km stretch of steep cliffs and twelve famous peaks, crowned by a legendary spire called Fairy Peak. Which of the Three Gorges is this most beautiful one?
context: Of the three gorges, Qutang is the shortest (just 8 km) and Xiling the longest (66 km), but Wu Gorge (45 km) is the most celebrated, famed for its Fairy Peak and its row of twelve peaks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges

question: Near the city of Yichang in central China, a colossal wall of concrete blocks the Yangtze River. It stands 185 metres tall and stretches more than 2 km wide. Its 32 huge turbines generate more electric power than any other single power station on Earth. What is this record-breaking dam called?
context: Built at Sandouping near Yichang and completed in 2012, the Three Gorges Dam is the largest hydroelectric power station on the planet — 22,500 MW from 32 main 700-MW generators, making over 100 terawatt-hours of electricity a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges_Dam

question: The Three Gorges Dam holds back a lake 600 km long. That is 40 billion tonnes of water lifted above the old riverbed. In 2005, NASA said this had a tiny but real effect on the whole planet. What did the raised water do to Earth?
answer: slowed its spin, lengthening the day
choices: slowed its spin, lengthening the day
sped up its spin, shortening the day
context: In 2005, NASA geophysicist Benjamin Fong Chao and colleague Richard Gross calculated that raising about 40 billion cubic metres of water so high shifts enough of Earth's mass to lengthen the day by roughly 0.06 microseconds — 60 billionths of a second, far too small to feel. Source: https://www.sciencefocus.com/news/human-structures-slowing-earths-spin

question: When the Three Gorges Dam sealed the Yangtze, the rising reservoir drowned whole towns and farmland up and down the valley, ancestral homes lost for good beneath the water. Clearing the flood zone in time meant not moving a village or two but resettling a major city's worth of people all at once. Roughly how many were forced from their homes?
context: Filling the reservoir forced about 1.3 million people from their homes to clear the valley before the water rose. Planning documents projected that 13 cities, 140 towns, and 1,350 villages would be partly or wholly flooded. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges_Dam

question: In 2005 NASA reported that China's giant Three Gorges Dam had lifted 40 billion tonnes of water up into its long reservoir above the old Yangtze bed, and that this had ever so slightly slowed Earth's spin. Scientists explain the trick with a spinning figure-skater, who can change her speed just by moving her arms. To slow her spin, the way that raised water slows the planet, what does the skater do with her arms?
context: It is the moment of inertia: moving mass farther from the spin axis makes a turning body rotate slower, so the raised reservoir slows Earth just as a skater slows by spreading her arms. For scale, the natural 2004 magnitude-9.0 Indian Ocean earthquake shortened the day about 2.68 microseconds — dozens of times more than the dam. Source: https://www.sciencefocus.com/news/human-structures-slowing-earths-spin

question: For 1,500 years the Yangtze's gorges were China's most poetic landscape, their cliffs carved with verse by passing travelers. The Tang master Li Bai caught them in one immortal line, written as his small boat shot downstream between the canyon walls: a sound followed him, echoing endlessly from both sides of the river even as ten thousand mountains flew past. In Li Bai's line, what was making that sound?
context: Li Bai wrote, 'While monkeys keep howling at both sides of the river, the boat has swiftly passed thousands of mountains.' Poets had carved verse into these cliffs since the Northern Wei dynasty, over 1,500 years ago — much of it now drowned beneath the reservoir. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges

question: Asia's longest river empties into the sea beside Shanghai, yet 6,000 km inland its very first trickle is glacier-melt seeping from the ice atop 6,621-metre Geladaindong Peak in the Tanggula Mountains. On which vast highland is the Yangtze born?
context: The Yangtze is born from glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau, the 'roof of the world.' Its traditional source is the ice atop 6,621-metre Geladaindong Peak, which feeds the Tuotuo headwater stream at the start of the river's 6,236-km journey east to the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geladaindong_Peak

question: Across northern China flows a mighty river 5,464 km long whose water runs a strange yellow-brown colour all the way from the mountains to the sea. That very colour is where the river got its name — the Yellow River. What actually turns the water yellow-brown as it flows?
answer: fine mud it carries in the water
choices: fine mud it carries in the water
golden algae blooming on the surface
context: The color comes from fine sediment: as the river cuts through soft, pale highland soil it picks up enormous amounts of suspended silt, and that mud tints the water yellow-brown for nearly its whole length. (Wikipedia, 'Yellow River')

question: Through its middle course the Yellow River saws down through a vast upland of soft, pale earth piled over 90 m (300 ft) deep — soil so loose that summer rains wash it into the water by the ton. What upland is this?
context: That wind-blown dust is called loess — fine grit that winds carried off deserts like the Gobi and piled over roughly 2.6 million years into the Loess Plateau, 50–80 m thick on average and over 90 m in places. More than 90% of the river's silt is stripped from this one region as it slices through. (Britannica, 'Loess Plateau')

question: The Yellow River flows right past the old capital of Kaifeng in Henan, where families have farmed and traded along its banks for 2,000 years. Yet a visitor who climbs the city wall and looks toward the water gets a shock. Why?
answer: the river flows higher than the city's rooftops
choices: the river flows higher than the city's rooftops
the river plunges over a waterfall taller than the wall
the river splits into dozens of braided channels here
the river disappears into a canyon below the city
context: Two thousand years of silt piling up in the channel forced people to wall the Yellow River in with levees built ever higher, until at Kaifeng its bed climbed about 10 m (33 ft) above the streets — some surveys say 13–14 m — held in only by those man-made banks. Geographers call such a channel a 'suspended,' 'above-ground,' or 'hanging' river: it literally flows overhead behind its levees. (Wikipedia, 'Yellow River'; MDPI Sustainability 2019)

question: Along the middle Yellow River in northern China stretches a huge region called the Loess Plateau. It is blanketed in a soft, pale, wind-blown soil called loess that lies tens of metres deep and is very easy to dig into. For many hundreds of years, farming families across the Loess Plateau built their homes in a very unusual way. How did they typically make their homes?
answer: by carving cave-rooms straight into the cliffs
choices: by carving cave-rooms straight into the cliffs
by weaving domed huts from reeds and mud
by raising timber houses up on tall stilts
by stacking bricks baked from river clay
context: These carved dwellings are called yaodong — homes dug straight into the soft loess cliffs, made from the very soil the river is busy washing away downstream. (National Geographic Education, 'Loess')

question: Because its silt-raised bed leaves it forever ready to burst free, the Yellow River has broken its banks and drowned the northern plains again and again — its 1931 flood is often ranked the deadliest in recorded history. For this, the Chinese gave the river a grim two-word name. Which is it?
context: Between about 595 BC and 1946 the Yellow River flooded some 1,500 times and changed its main course 26 times; the 1931 flood's death toll is estimated at 1–4 million and the 1887 flood's at 900,000–2 million — among the worst disasters ever recorded. For its floods the river is called 'China's Sorrow'; for the civilization it fed, it is also called 'China's Pride.' (Wikipedia, 'Yellow River')

question: Deadly floods were only half the Yellow River's story. Its silt also spread a soft, mineral-rich yellow soil across the floodplain — loose enough to till with the simplest tools and generous with grain year after year. Chinese tradition honors this yellow-earth valley with one famous title. Which is it?
choices: the granary of the northern plains
the heartland of the Bronze Age
the birthplace of the Silk Road
context: The soft, fertile loess soil was easy to farm, so China's earliest villages clustered along the Yellow River thousands of years ago; the Loess Plateau and this floodplain are together remembered as 'the cradle of Chinese civilization.' (Britannica, 'Loess Plateau')

question: The Yucatan is a flat slab of soft limestone. Rain soaks straight down through the rock. So there are hardly any rivers on top. Instead, round water-filled pits open in the jungle. The old Maya drank from them. What are these natural wells called?
context: The name comes from the Yucatec Maya word ts'ono'ot (dzonot), meaning a well or place of reachable groundwater, and is often glossed 'sacred well.' An estimated 6,000 to 10,000 cenotes pockmark the peninsula. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: Divers who slip into a Yucatan cenote float in water so glass-clear they seem to hang in midair, the cavern walls sharp far below them. Cenotes are famous the world over for this glassy clarity. Why is the water so clear?
answer: rain seeps down so slowly that its sediment settles out
choices: rain seeps down so slowly that its sediment settles out
sunlight kills the algae that would cloud the water
cold water keeps silt frozen at the bottom
ocean tides flush the sinkhole clean each day
context: Cenote water is rainwater that has filtered for years down through porous limestone, leaving its particles behind, so the pools glow a deep, transparent blue. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: Map the cenotes across northwest Yucatan and something strange shows up. The thickest ones line up in one huge curve across the flat jungle. Geologists were stunned to see what lies buried under this Ring of Cenotes. What does the ring trace?
answer: the rim of a giant asteroid-impact crater
choices: the rim of a giant asteroid-impact crater
the fault line of an ancient earthquake zone
the shoreline of a long-vanished inland sea
the channel of a collapsed underground river
context: The ring is a belt only about 5 km wide with a radius near 90 km -- roughly 180 km across -- curving from Celestun on the west coast past Homun and Tekit and back north to Dzilam. It marks the buried rim of the Chicxulub crater; the sinkholes are the surface fingerprint of the impact that ended the age of the dinosaurs 66 million years ago. Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5784/

question: Off the Yucatan's Caribbean shore, a living wall of coral runs more than 1,000 km. It goes past Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, and Honduras. This is the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef. Among all the barrier reefs on Earth, how does it rank?
answer: second-largest, behind only Australia's Great Barrier Reef
choices: second-largest, behind only Australia's Great Barrier Reef
the largest of all, ahead of Australia's Great Barrier Reef
second-largest, behind only New Caledonia's reef
second-largest, behind only the Red Sea's reef
context: The Mesoamerican Barrier Reef is the second-largest barrier reef on Earth, outstretched only by Australia's Great Barrier Reef. It runs more than 1,000 km along Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, and Honduras -- where the Yucatan's underground rivers finally reach the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_Barrier_Reef_System

question: The crater buried beneath the Ring of Cenotes has a name: Chicxulub. About 66 million years ago an asteroid roughly 10 km wide -- the size of a small mountain -- slammed into this exact spot, blasting a crater 180 km across and throwing up enough rock and soot to darken the whole sky. What did this single impact bring to an end?
context: The Chicxulub impactor hit near the present town of Chicxulub Puerto with force millions of times greater than a nuclear bomb. The debris and darkness triggered the mass extinction that wiped out the non-bird dinosaurs and about three-quarters of all species -- the leading scientific explanation for the end of the Cretaceous. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Chicxulub

question: A cenote is not dug. It is dissolved. A little acid in rainwater seeps into the soft rock. Drop by drop, over thousands of years, it eats the rock hollow. A cave forms, then a roof caves in and opens a round pit to the water below. What is this kind of landscape called?
context: Karst is landscape shaped where water slowly dissolves soluble rock like limestone, riddling it with caves, sinkholes, and underground rivers. The Yucatan is one of the largest karst platforms on Earth, which is why its cenotes number in the thousands. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: On the flat Yucatan peninsula of Mexico, rain sinks straight down through the soft limestone, so almost no rivers run on top — the only water pools open in round sinkholes called cenotes. To the old Maya, cenotes were more than wells: they were holy doors into the spirit world. The Maya knelt at their edges and prayed to the one god who could send rain from the sky. Which Maya god were the cenotes for?
context: The Maya believed cenotes were gateways to Xibalba, the underworld -- and above all they belonged to Chaac, the hook-nosed god of rain and lightning. In a land whose only water hid underground, the god who filled the wells mattered more than any other. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_Cenote  (Legend.)

question: Dive into one Yucatan cenote and, with the right training, you could swim through drowned stone passages to reach cenotes far across the jungle -- beneath the surface they nearly all connect into one flooded maze. This hidden, water-filled network holds a world record. What record do the Yucatan's flooded caves hold?
answer: the longest underwater cave systems on Earth
choices: the longest underwater cave systems on Earth
the deepest underwater cave systems on Earth
the widest underwater cave systems on Earth
the clearest underwater cave systems on Earth
context: Sistema Sac Actun ('White Cave' in Maya) maps about 378 km of submerged passage; in 2018 divers found a channel linking it to the Dos Ojos ('Two Eyes') system. Nearby, Sistema Ox Bel Ha ('Three Paths of Water') has over 435 km mapped -- the two are rival claimants for the longest underwater cave on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistema_Sac_Actun

question: At Chichen Itza, one giant cenote stood apart, joined to the temples by a raised stone road. This was the Sacred Cenote. From 1904 to 1910, Edward Thompson dredged its floor and dove in a diving helmet. He hauled up thousands of Maya offerings: gold, jade, incense, copper bells. Mixed in with the treasure, what else did he bring up?
context: Edward Herbert Thompson recovered thousands of offerings along with human remains -- evidence of sacrifices to the rain god Chaac. The Sacred Cenote is about 60 m across, its water surface 27 m below the rim, and a 300 m raised stone road, a sacbe, once linked it to Chichen Itza's temples. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_Cenote  (Legend.)

question: In 2007, cave divers dropped into a pitch-black flooded chamber deep beneath the Yucatan, a pit they named Hoyo Negro -- the 'Black Hole.' On a ledge far below the surface, scattered among the bones of Ice Age sabre-toothed cats and giant ground sloths, lay the nearly complete skeleton of a teenage girl. Why did this skeleton, later nicknamed 'Naia,' stun scientists?
answer: she is one of the oldest Americans ever found
choices: she is one of the oldest Americans ever found
she had been buried with a hoard of gold
she stood well over seven feet tall
she was a wholly unknown human species
context: Naia was a 15-to-16-year-old girl who fell into the then-dry cave around 12,000 to 13,000 years ago, near the end of the last Ice Age; rising seas later flooded the chamber. She is among the oldest and most complete humans ever found in the Americas, helping trace how the first people reached the continent. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/140515-skeleton-ice-age-mexico-cave-hoyo-negro-archaeology

question: On the open grasslands of Tuva, in Siberia, a lone herder opens his mouth. One voice sounds two notes at once. A low steady drone hums, and a bright pitch floats above it. What is this steppe singing called?
context: Across Tuva and neighboring Mongolia the art is called khöömei, a Turkic word meaning 'throat' or 'larynx.' A single herder, standing alone on the steppe, can sound like two singers at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing

question: Out on the vast grasslands of central Asia — the Mongolian steppe, in the countries of Mongolia and the Russian region of Tuva — herders sing a strange low-humming song called throat-singing, in which a single singer can produce two notes at once. Ask a Tuvan or Mongolian throat-singer where their sounds come from. They all give the same answer: the sounds are not made up, they are borrowed. Borrowed from what?
answer: the wild sounds of the steppe itself
choices: the wild sounds of the steppe itself
the melodies of old Mongol war songs
the cries of their own herds and dogs
context: Singers liken the deep growl to the howling winds of winter, and the rolling trill called borbangnadyr to a bubbling brook — so one person's song becomes a map of the homeland: wind, water, and open sky. The whole art grows from an animist belief that a place's spirits live in its sound as much as its shape. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing  (Legend.)

question: On the grassy steppe of Tuva in southern Siberia, a herder can push a single voice into two notes at once — a low humming drone with a bright whistle floating above it. This art is called throat-singing, and each style has its own name. The highest style is a piercing, flute-like whistle that seems to hover far above the drone, like a thin wind slicing across the steppe. What is that whistling style called?
context: Sygyt, the high whistle, is one of three main styles, alongside the deep growling kargyraa and khöömei used as its own style, said to sound like 'wind swirling among rocks.' Singers point the tongue against the gums to force the piercing tone out clear and bright. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing

question: On the steppe of Tuva in southern Siberia, herders practise throat-singing — pushing one voice into a low drone and a bright whistle at the same time. A throat-singer often plays alongside a two-string fiddle whose neck rises into a carved horse's head above the pegs. Its low bowing sounds like horses trotting across the grasslands. What is this Tuvan fiddle called?
context: The igil is Tuva's horsehead fiddle; Mongolia bows a larger cousin, the morin khuur. Played low and steady beneath the voice, its rhythm falls like hoofbeats under the singer's drone. Both fiddles are carved with a horse's head — fitting, for music made by a people who live on horseback. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igil

question: Tuva has a throat-singing style built on a steady rocking pulse, flicked out by the soft palate opening and closing as the singer drones. Riders recognize the motion at once: the style's name, ezengileer, is taken straight from a piece of a horseman's kit, and the song sways in time with it. Which piece gave the style its name?
context: Ezengileer takes its name from ezengi, the Tuvan word for a stirrup, and its bouncing pulse imitates the sway of a rider posting at a trot. It joins a whole gallery of styles — each one, singers say, a different piece of the moving steppe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing

question: A Tuvan singer's second, whistling pitch sounds like sorcery, but it is pure physics. He holds one low droning note, slowly reshapes his mouth and throat, and a bright separate pitch rings out above the drone — yet it is not a second voice. What is that high pitch, really?
answer: a faint overtone already inside the drone, amplified loud
choices: a faint overtone already inside the drone, amplified loud
an echo of the drone bouncing off the hard palate
the drone itself sliding rapidly up to a high note
air forced into a thin whistle between the teeth
context: Acousticians call this biphonation from filtering: one sound source split into two pitches. The singer's mouth focuses a narrow band of overtones — roughly the 6th to 12th harmonics of the drone — into a single sharp peak while hushing the neighbors, so one faint harmonic rings out as a separate note. UNESCO calls it 'a melody of harmonics' riding a continuous drone. Sources: https://elifesciences.org/articles/50476 ; https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/mongolian-traditional-art-of-khoomei-00396

question: Twice a day on England's River Severn, the tide rushes in. It rears up into a wall of water about 2 m tall. The wall races up the river, the wrong way. Surfers paddle out to ride it. What is this upstream wave called?
context: On the Severn the bore rides one of the greatest tidal ranges on Earth — about 13 m between high and low water — which is why surfers can chase a single wave miles inland. A tidal bore forms only where a big flood tide is funneled into a shallow, narrowing river mouth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severn_bore

question: On the Amazon, the tidal bore arrives as a distant rumble heard long before it is seen — a wall of water up to 4 m high that surges as far as 800 km upstream, tearing at the banks as it goes. Its name in the local Tupi language means 'great roar.' What is the Amazon's tidal bore called?
context: 'Pororoca' may come from a Tupi word meaning 'great roar' — the wave is heard as a rumble before the wall of water appears. It can rush up to 800 km inland, ripping trees off the banks; surfers and kayakers chase it for miles. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca  (Legend.)

question: An ocean surfer is lucky to ride one wave for twenty seconds before it collapses. But a tidal bore is a single wave that never breaks — it just keeps rolling upstream for miles. In 2003, Brazilian surfer Picuruta Salazar caught the Amazon's pororoca and rode it 12.5 km up the river without once falling off. For how long did he stay on that one wave?
context: Because a bore is one wave that keeps reforming as it climbs the river, a rider can stay on it far longer than any ocean wave allows. Salazar's 12.5 km, 37-minute ride on the Guama River in 2003 is remembered as one of the longest in surfing history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca  (Legend.)

question: The pororoca doesn't only rush inland — its pounding erosion reshapes the coast, tearing whole trees from the banks. Near the Amazon's mouth lies low, flat Caviana Island. Between 1845 and 1850, the relentless bore did to Caviana something few waves ever do to solid land. What happened to Caviana Island?
context: Between 1845 and 1850 the pororoca's erosion split Caviana Island, near the Amazon's mouth, into two parts — a wave rearranging the map. The same bore constantly tears trees and mud from the banks as it charges inland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca

question: China's Qiantang River, near Hangzhou, has the biggest tidal bore on Earth — a roaring wall of water up to 9 m tall that charges upstream at 40 km/h, three times the height of England's Severn bore. Crowds have lined its banks each autumn to watch for over a thousand years. What is this giant bore nicknamed?
context: The Qiantang bore, nicknamed the 'Silver Dragon,' is the world's largest. Tide-watching here is over a thousand years old: the Southern Song court set a Tide Watching Festival on the 18th day of the 8th lunar month, and the world's oldest known tide table (AD 1056) was made for this river. In 2013 Typhoon Trami doubled the bore's height and it broke over the barrier into the crowd. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiantang_River  (Legend.)

question: For centuries, boats on France's Seine had to reckon with the mascaret — a tidal bore the locals called 'la barre' that surged up from the sea. Then, by the 1960s, it simply vanished, and today the lower Seine has no bore at all. What made the Seine's mascaret disappear?
choices: the sea's tidal range slowly shrank
the river's course was rerouted inland
context: A tidal bore needs a shallow, narrowing, funneling estuary; deepening the Seine's channel for shipping erased that geometry and 'la barre' was gone — proof a bore can be engineered out of existence. The reverse can happen too: Canada's Petitcodiac bore, choked by a 1968 causeway, came back after the gates were reopened in 2010. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascaret

question: At Tikal in Guatemala, Temple IV rises about 70 metres. It is the tallest pyramid in the city. A climber at the top pops out into open sky. She has risen above the one thing that hides every other ruin for miles. What has the climber risen above?
context: Temple IV rises about 70 m (roughly 64.6 m from its own platform to the top of the roof-comb) — high enough to look out over an unbroken sea of treetops. Accuracy note: it is NOT the tallest pre-Columbian structure. It is roughly the second-tallest still standing, after the Great Pyramid of Tonina, and Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun may once have topped it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_IV

question: Two great stone pyramids stand face to face across Tikal's Great Plaza. The Maya named the taller, eastern one — a steep royal tomb-pyramid — for a fierce predator of the Peten jungle. Which animal gives Temple I its name, the 'Temple of the Great ___'?
context: Temple I is the 'Temple of the Great Jaguar,' named for a carved lintel showing a king seated on a jaguar throne. Facing it across the plaza is its shorter twin, Temple II, the 'Temple of the Masks.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: A film crew once hauled cameras up Temple IV at Tikal. They shot the view over the endless jungle. In the movie, this became the surface of an alien world in one of the most famous sci-fi sagas ever made. Which film borrowed Tikal as its alien planet?
context: In Star Wars: A New Hope (1977), the view from Temple IV's summit stands in for the rebel base on the forest moon Yavin 4. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_IV

question: Around 900 CE, the people of Tikal walked away from their great city. The rainforest swallowed the plazas and temples for nearly a thousand years. Across the whole Maya lowlands, what do most researchers now blame for this collapse?
context: The leading explanation is decades of severe drought, worsened by the Maya's own deforestation and soil erosion, though the exact trigger is still debated. After the collapse, the jungle reclaimed Tikal for roughly a thousand years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: Temple I at Tikal climbs to its summit shrine in a staircase of nine great stepped terraces. The Maya architects chose the number nine on purpose, to echo a sacred nine that stood at the heart of their view of the world. What did the nine terraces stand for?
answer: The nine layers of the underworld
choices: The nine layers of the underworld
The nine tiers of the heavens
context: Temple I's nine stepped terraces are widely thought to represent the nine levels of the Maya underworld. Its roof-comb is built as two parallel stone walls with a hollow vault between them, cutting the weight while giving a huge surface to carve the king's image. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_I  (Legend.)

question: In the rainforests of northern Guatemala rise the towering limestone pyramids of a ruined Maya city. When its kings ruled it, over a thousand years ago, they probably called it Yax Mutal. Centuries after the jungle swallowed the temples, later Yucatec Maya speakers gave the abandoned place a new, plainer name — Tikal. What does 'Tikal' roughly mean?
context: 'Tikal' is a later Yucatec Maya name meaning roughly 'at the waterhole' — a fitting name for a city with no rivers or lakes that lived and died by its rain-fed reservoirs. Its Classic-era name was likely 'Yax Mutal.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: For centuries Tikal shared the Maya world with rival superpowers. Its fiercest enemy rose in the forest lowlands to the north — a city whose kings called their dynasty the 'Snake Kingdom' and stamped a snake-head glyph on every monument. Which city was Tikal's great northern rival?
context: Calakmul, in modern Campeche, Mexico, about 35 km north of the Guatemala border, was the seat of the Kaan ('Snake') dynasty — Tikal's great rival across the Classic Maya lowlands. Its emblem glyph was a snake head reading 'Kaan.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calakmul

question: In 1962, archaeologists tunneled deep into Temple I at Tikal and broke into the sealed tomb of King Jasaw Chan K'awiil I. On the burial bench, still resting on the royal skeleton, lay the richest treasure ever found at the city. What jewel-work adorned the dead king?
answer: A necklace of heavy jade beads
choices: A necklace of heavy jade beads
context: The necklace held 114 carved jade beads and weighed 3.9 kg (8.6 lb). Burial 116 also held a jade mosaic vessel carved with the king's own portrait, 37 inscribed human bones, jaguar pelts, spondylus shells, and pearls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_I

question: Tikal drank only rainwater, caught off its wide plazas and held in huge lined reservoirs — water that, in a hot jungle, should have turned foul within weeks. A 2020 study showed the Corriental reservoir somehow stayed clean for centuries, making it the oldest known water-purification site in the Americas. How did the Maya keep it drinkable?
context: The Maya filtered the water through imported zeolite and coarse quartz sand — a natural molecular sieve that stripped out microbes and even toxins like mercury. It is the oldest known water-filtration system in the Western Hemisphere, about 2,000 years old, and the minerals were hauled roughly 30 km (18 miles) from ridges near the Bajo de Azucar. Sources: nature.com/articles/s41598-020-75023-7; uc.edu/news/articles/2020/10

question: In the rainforest of what is now Guatemala, the ancient Maya city of Tikal survived only because its people caught and stored rainwater in enormous stone reservoirs. But those same reservoirs may, in the end, have turned against the city. Sediment laid down in Tikal's largest reservoirs as it declined is laced with a poison that had leached in from the brilliant red pigment the Maya painted across their walls and tombs. Which toxic metal fouled Tikal's water?
context: Sediment studies of Tikal's largest reservoirs found them fouled with mercury, leached from cinnabar — the red pigment the Maya prized — along with blooms of toxic blue-green algae (cyanobacteria). Together they would have made the water undrinkable as the city declined. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: For hundreds of years, English speakers said 'from here to ___' to mean the farthest place on earth. The blank was a real, dusty city in what is now Mali. Which city's name became this saying for the middle of nowhere?
context: 'As far as Timbuktu' and 'from here to Timbuktu' became English shorthand for the ends of the earth — yet Timbuktu is a real, reachable city of about 85,000 people in modern Mali. In the 1800s Europeans imagined it as a place of mythical riches at the world's edge. Source: NPR/WLRN, 'From Here to Timbuktu'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.  (Legend.)

question: Timbuktu grew rich at a crossing point. Camel trains staggered out of the Sahara. They loaded their cargo onto boats on a great river 20 km to the south. Which river carried Timbuktu's trade into West Africa?
context: Timbuktu sits on the southern edge of the Sahara about 20 km north of the Niger River — the exact point where desert camel caravans met the river boats. That meeting of sand and water is what made it a great trading city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.

question: The lands south of Timbuktu had lots of gold. But they badly needed one thing from the desert. Traders said the two were swapped at nearly equal weight. Camels hauled this cargo south out of the deep Sahara, from Taghaza and Taoudenni. What was it?
context: Slabs of salt cut at the Saharan mines of Taghaza and Taoudenni were hauled south by camel; salt was so scarce in the gold-rich south that it was famously said to trade toward its weight in gold — an exaggeration, but salt worth pennies in the desert could sell for gold at the Sahara's edge. The 'azalai' caravans ran several thousand camels at a time, each carrying four or five 30 kg slabs on the roughly three-week trip from Taoudenni, about 660 km north. Sources: worldhistory.org, 'The Salt Trade of Ancient West Africa'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azalai.  (Legend.)

question: All through Timbuktu stand the domed shrines of Sufi holy men, the marabouts. The town honors them as guardians watching over the city. Many of these saints lie buried inside its walls. What nickname does this give Timbuktu?
choices: the City of a Thousand Saints
context: Timbuktu is nicknamed the 'City of 333 Saints' for the 333 Sufi marabouts buried in shrines across the town, whose tombs the people venerated as protectors of the city. In 2012 militants smashed several of these tombs; local masons later rebuilt them with UNESCO support. Timbuktu has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988. Sources: newageislam.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.

question: Timbuktu is a desert trading town, but its people also saved up to 700,000 old hand-written books in home libraries. Some cover medicine, law, and poetry. Which two subjects are the books most famous for?
context: European colonizers spread a myth that Africa kept no written records — yet Timbuktu's families had guarded, for centuries, up to an estimated ~700,000 hand-written manuscripts covering astronomy, mathematics, medicine, law and poetry. The city's astronomy manuscripts, with their star charts and planetary tables, are among the most celebrated: hard proof that pre-colonial West Africa had literate, scientific scholarship centuries before European colonies, directly against the false 'Africa had no written history' trope. (The count is an estimate — hence 'up to ~700,000.') Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu_Manuscripts.  (Legend.)

question: In the West African country of Mali, on the southern edge of the Sahara Desert, sits the old trading city of Timbuktu. Long ago, camel caravans crossed the sands to reach it carrying gold, salt, and books. In the middle of the flat sunbaked town rise three great mosques -- Djingareyber, Sankore, and Sidi Yahya -- each about 700 years old. Their thick tapered towers bristle with wooden beams sticking straight out from the walls. What material are these mosques built from?
context: All three mosques are built of mud and adobe, not stone. Djinguereber, the oldest, was built in 1327 on the order of the emperor Mansa Musa and designed by the Andalusian architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili; Sidi Yahya was founded around 1400 and completed about 1440. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; grokipedia.com/page/Djinguereber_Mosque.

question: Around 1510 the traveler Leo Africanus wandered Timbuktu's crowded markets and marveled at its trade. Of everything sold there, he wrote, one good brought its sellers 'more profit than all other merchandise' — worth more even than gold. What was it?
context: Leo Africanus wrote of Timbuktu that 'there is more profit made from this commerce than from all other merchandise' — hand-written books were the single most valuable trade good, worth more than a slave, and owning them was how the wealthy showed off their standing. Source: brians.wsu.edu, Leo Africanus, 'Description of Africa' (1526).  (Legend.)

question: Timbuktu's greatest scholar, Ahmed Baba, wrote more than forty books of his own and filled his home with a personal library of over 1,600 volumes — a treasure in a city where books were the most precious goods of all. Then in 1591 a Moroccan army stormed Timbuktu. What did the conquerors do to Ahmed Baba?
choices: held him for a heavy ransom
put him to death in the square
burned his house to the ground
context: Ahmed Baba (1556–1627) was Timbuktu's greatest scholar and a chancellor of the Sankoré madrasa — the heart of what is remembered as the University of Timbuktu, one of the world's oldest centers of higher learning, said to have taught as many as ~25,000 students at its height (a historical estimate). He wrote more than 40 books and kept a personal library of over 1,600 volumes, which he lost when Moroccan invaders exiled him from the city in 1591. Timbuktu's modern manuscript-research institute is named the Ahmed Baba Institute in his honor. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; muslimheritage.com, 'The University of Sankore, Timbuktu'; face2faceafrica.com.

question: For years European explorers died trying to reach Timbuktu, dreaming of a fabled city roofed in gold. When the Frenchman René Caillié finally walked in and out alive in 1828 to claim a 10,000-franc prize, what did he actually find there?
context: René Caillié (1828) was the first European to reach Timbuktu and return alive, collecting a 10,000-franc prize from the Geographical Society of Paris. Expecting gold, he found only 'a mass of ill-looking houses built of earth.' The Briton Alexander Gordon Laing had reached the city first, in August 1826, but was murdered by his escorts just after leaving. Leo Africanus's earlier tale of a single 970-pound gold ingot in the ruler's treasury had helped feed the golden-city legend. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/René_Caillié; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gordon_Laing; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.

question: Rows of palm-wood beams called toron jut straight out from the mud walls of Timbuktu's great mosques. They are no decoration: the builders left them as permanent scaffolding, so that once a year the whole town can carry out one essential task together. What is that yearly task?
context: The toron — projecting Rodier-palm beams — are permanent built-in scaffolding: the mud skin must be re-plastered by the whole town every year in a communal festival, the crépissage, or the seasonal rains would slowly dissolve the building.
