Sources: reviewofreligions.org, 'Places of Worship: Timbuktu Mosque'; grokipedia.com/page/Sudano-Sahelian_architecture.  (Legend.)

question: In 2012, armed fighters seized Timbuktu and began destroying anything they judged un-Islamic. The city's ancient manuscripts were in serious danger. A quiet local librarian named Abdel Kader Haidara ran a secret rescue that saved about 350,000 of them. How did he and his helpers get them out?
answer: floating them downriver in metal trunks
choices: floating them downriver in metal trunks
burying them in jars under the desert
sealing them inside the mosque walls
context: Librarian Abdel Kader Haidara and a network of helpers secretly smuggled roughly 350,000 manuscripts out in metal trunks and footlockers, spirited past checkpoints and floated down the Niger River by boat to safety in Bamako. It was a race against real destruction: on 25 January 2013 the retreating militants swept about 4,200 manuscripts off the tables of the Ahmed Baba Institute and set them on fire — only a fraction, because most had already been smuggled out. Sources: nationalgeographic.com, 'The Badass Librarians of Timbuktu'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.  (Legend.)

question: High in the Andes of Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca, lie the massive stone ruins of Tiwanaku — carved gateways, sunken courtyards, and giant statues. The city was already old and abandoned when the Inca first came upon it. Where does Tiwanaku fit on a timeline of the great American civilizations?
choices: At the same time as the Aztec
context: Tiwanaku flourished roughly AD 500-1000 and had collapsed by about AD 1000 -- centuries before the Inca empire arose in the 1400s. The two are a common mix-up because both centered on the Andes near Lake Titicaca. Source: Grokipedia: Pumapunku; Wikipedia: Tiwanaku.

question: The ruined Andean city of Tiwanaku sits on an enormous flat highland by Lake Titicaca, over two miles above the sea. This plateau stretches across Bolivia and Peru and rises higher than most peaks in the Alps. Spanish-speaking geographers gave it a plain descriptive name that just means 'high plain.' What Spanish name do they use for this Andean plateau?
context: The altiplano is the widest high plateau on Earth outside Tibet. Tiwanaku sits on it at about 3,850 m (12,630 ft) above sea level, near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca -- a plain so lofty it rises above most European peaks. Source: Grokipedia: Pumapunku; Wikipedia: Pumapunku.

question: At the ruined Andean city of Tiwanaku in Bolivia, one carved doorway stands apart from all the rest. It was cut from a single 10-ton block of andesite stone. Above the opening a carved figure — probably an Andean creator god — stands with a staff raised in each hand and a halo of rays around his head. What do we call this famous gateway?
context: The Gateway of the Sun is cut from a single 10-ton block. The commanding figure on its lintel -- holding a staff in each hand, its head ringed by rays -- is usually identified as the creator god Viracocha, though some scholars suggest the Aymara weather god Thunupa. Source: Wikipedia: Gateway of the Sun.

question: High in the Bolivian Andes near Lake Titicaca sit the ruins of Tiwanaku, a pre-Inca city that flourished more than a thousand years ago. Beside it stands the temple of Pumapunku, whose stone blocks are so matched and sharp-edged they look machine-made. Every block was cut to the exact same letter shape. What shape were the Pumapunku blocks?
context: Pumapunku's H-blocks lock together like precise puzzle pieces, forming blind miniature gateways. Their machine-like precision has made the site a magnet for 'ancient aliens' claims -- but archaeologists credit skilled Tiwanaku masons. Alexei Vranich points to well-preserved earlier stonework at nearby Pukara and Chiripa as proof the skill grew among the Titicaca-basin peoples themselves, and Franco Rossi has criticized alien theorists for dismissing the Aymara as incapable builders. Source: Grokipedia: Pumapunku; Wikipedia: Pumapunku.

question: At Pumapunku, a temple beside the ruined pre-Inca city of Tiwanaku high in the Bolivian Andes, the builders used no mortar at all. Yet the stones fit so tightly a knife won't slip between the joints. Every block was locked to the next by a trick that still amazes engineers today. What held the giant stones together?
answer: molten metal cast into I-shaped cramps
choices: molten metal cast into I-shaped cramps
iron staples hammered across the joints
reed ropes lashed around the blocks
wooden pegs driven into the seams
context: In carved notches at the joints, Tiwanaku metalworkers poured molten metal that hardened in place into I-shaped cramps of a distinctive copper-arsenic-nickel bronze alloy -- casting the clamps directly at the stone to bind block to block without mortar. Source: Wikipedia: Pumapunku.

question: Pumapunku's builders had no wheels, no strong pack animals, and no iron. Yet they quarried their hardest blocks on a peninsula about 90 km away, then transported them across Lake Titicaca. The largest stone at the site, a red-sandstone slab, ranks among the heaviest worked stones in the ancient Americas. Roughly how much does that single slab weigh?
context: The red-sandstone slab weighs an estimated 131 tonnes -- a calculated estimate, not a measurement -- and came from a quarry about 10 km off. Pumapunku's harder andesite blocks travelled far farther still: quarried on the Copacabana Peninsula about 90 km away, they had to be moved across (or around) Lake Titicaca itself. Source: Wikipedia: Pumapunku; Grokipedia: Pumapunku.

question: Nights on the high plain around Tiwanaku freeze hard, which should have killed the crops. Instead the Tiwanaku fed a city of many thousands by building long raised planting beds separated by water-filled channels. The water absorbed the daytime sun and released warmth after dark, while the cold air settled into the ditches instead of onto the plants. What is this frost-beating raised-field system called?
context: These raised beds -- called waru waru (also suka kollus) -- were typically 4-10 m wide and up to 100 m long, raised about a meter high. By trapping the day's heat in the channel water they kept the soil roughly 1 degree C warmer at night, out-yielding ordinary fields and helping feed a Tiwanaku of an estimated 10,000-20,000 people around AD 800. The system faltered when a long drought gripped the altiplano around AD 1000, coinciding with the city's decline. Source: Wikipedia: Waru Waru; Wikipedia: Tiwanaku.

question: At one busy Tokyo crossing, every light turns red at the same time. Then up to 3,000 people rush across from every side at once, cutting straight through the middle. Which Tokyo district has this 'scramble crossing,' the busiest on Earth?
context: This is the famous Shibuya Scramble (Shibuya Crossing), which opened in 1973. When the lights change, pedestrians surge across from all sides at once -- up to about 3,000 people per green light. Surveys estimate around 260,000 people cross on a weekday and up to 500,000 on the busiest days, making it the most famous pedestrian crossing on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shibuya_Crossing  (Legend.)

question: Greater Tokyo has about 37 million people packed into one huge sprawl of streets and buildings. That is nearly as many people as the whole state of California. Where does that rank Tokyo among all the cities ever built?
choices: the second most populous on Earth
context: Greater Tokyo (the Tokyo-Yokohama agglomeration) is home to roughly 37 million people -- the largest single urban area in human history, about the population of the whole state of California or the country of Poland. Rankings depend on where you draw the boundary: a narrower UN definition counts about 33 million, and fast-growing Delhi is projected to overtake Tokyo within about a decade. Source: Statista 2025 urban agglomerations; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Tokyo_Area  (Legend.)

question: Tokyo has not always gone by that name. For over 250 years it was the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns. Then in 1868, the young Emperor Meiji moved his court there from Kyoto and gave it the name Tokyo. What was it called before?
context: For over 250 years the city was called Edo, capital of the Tokugawa shoguns. When the shogunate fell in 1868, the young Emperor Meiji moved his residence there from Kyoto and renamed it Tokyo (東京), meaning 'Eastern Capital' -- the capital to the east of the old one, Kyoto. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo; britannica.com/place/Tokyo

question: In 2012, Japan finished a slim white broadcasting spire on the eastern edge of Tokyo. It climbs 634 meters into the sky — a number chosen because in old Japanese it can be read 'Musashi,' the ancient name for the surrounding region. When it opened, it was the tallest tower on Earth. Which of these Japanese towers holds that record?
context: The Tokyo Skytree rises 634 m (2,080 ft) and opened on May 22, 2012 as a broadcasting tower -- the tallest tower in the world, beating China's Canton Tower (600 m). Some buildings are taller (Dubai's Burj Khalifa is 828 m, Kuala Lumpur's Merdeka 118 is 679 m), but a 'tower' has less than half its height as usable floor space, so the Skytree still holds the tower record. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree

question: One of Tokyo's busiest trains has no last stop. It runs in a big ring around the middle of the city. It links Shibuya, Shinjuku, and Ikebukuro, then comes back to where it started. Which line is this?
context: The Yamanote Line is Tokyo's famous loop line, circling the city center in a continuous ring that connects its biggest hubs -- Tokyo, Shinjuku, Shibuya, Ikebukuro and more. One full loop takes about an hour. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamanote_Line

question: About 3.5 million passengers pour through a single Tokyo railway station every day -- nearly six times as many as its closest rival, Paris's Gare du Nord -- making it the Guinness-record holder for the busiest station on Earth. Which station is it?
context: Shinjuku Station holds the Guinness World Record as the busiest railway station on Earth -- about 3.5 million passengers a day before the pandemic, and still 2.7 million in 2022. Its nearest rival, Paris's Gare du Nord, handles only around 600,000. It has well over 200 exits. Source: guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/busiest-station; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinjuku_Station

question: At the exact center of the world's biggest city, a wide moat and high stone ramparts wall off a vast island of forest and gardens -- the grounds of the old Edo Castle. What fills this green, guarded heart of Tokyo?
context: The Imperial Palace (Kokyo), residence of the Emperor of Japan, sits on the grounds of the former Edo Castle, ringed by wide moats and forest at the exact center of Tokyo -- so a great island of trees and water fills the heart of the world's biggest city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Imperial_Palace

question: Out in Tokyo Bay lies Odaiba, a district of shopping malls, a giant Ferris wheel, and a life-sized Gundam robot. It began in 1853 as a ring of cannon batteries built to fend off Commodore Perry's American warships. What kind of ground is this whole waterfront district built on?
context: Odaiba is built on reclaimed land -- one of many artificial islands in Tokyo Bay, where about 249 km2 of ground has been created from the sea. It began in 1853 as a ring of gun batteries ('daiba' means 'battery') to defend Edo against Commodore Perry's 'Black Ships,' and was rebuilt into a futuristic waterfront in the 1990s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odaiba; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Bay

question: Before any emperor lived at the heart of Tokyo, that walled ground was Edo Castle. It served as the fortress capital of the Tokugawa shoguns for two and a half centuries. Among the fortresses of its age, what record did Edo Castle once hold?
answer: the largest castle in the world
choices: the largest castle in the world
the tallest castle in the world
the oldest castle in the world
the strongest castle in the world
context: In its heyday Edo Castle was the largest castle in the world: its outer defenses ran about 16 km (10 miles) around and covered roughly 230 hectares -- more than double Osaka Castle's 106. Today's Imperial Palace grounds are only about a third of the original castle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo_Castle; worldhistory.org/Edo_Castle  (Legend.)

question: Tokyo has been shaken to rubble and rebuilt more than once, because the Kanto plain sits in one of the most geologically violent settings on Earth. What is the underground reason the city is so dangerously earthquake-prone?
answer: three tectonic plates collide beneath it
choices: three tectonic plates collide beneath it
a single deep fault line splits it
a volcanic hotspot rises beneath it
its soft soil amplifies far-off quakes
context: The Kanto region sits on a rare triple plate boundary: the continental (North American/Okhotsk) plate is being pushed under by BOTH the Philippine Sea plate and the Pacific plate, which dive beneath it. (Older texts call the continental plate 'Eurasian.') This double subduction makes Tokyo one of the most seismically active cities on the planet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Great_Kanto_earthquake; agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com (dual subduction under Tokyo)

question: At 11:58 on the morning of September 1, 1923, a magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck Tokyo and Yokohama. About 105,000 people died -- yet remarkably few were killed by the shaking or by falling debris. What caused the overwhelming majority of the deaths in the Great Kanto earthquake?
answer: a firestorm that swept the city
choices: a firestorm that swept the city
context: The Great Kanto earthquake struck at 11:58 a.m. -- lunchtime, when thousands of charcoal cooking fires were burning across a city of wooden houses. Whipped by winds from a passing typhoon, the fires merged into firestorms (one 'fire tornado' at a former clothing depot killed tens of thousands alone), causing about 90% of the roughly 105,000 deaths. The quake was driven by the Philippine Sea plate slipping beneath the continental plate along the Sagami Trough. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Great_Kanto_earthquake

question: The Tokyo Skytree stands exactly 634 meters tall, and that oddly precise number was no accident -- it was chosen as a hidden pun. Read as digits in an old style of Japanese counting, 6-3-4 sounds out a single Japanese word. What does '634' spell?
context: 634 metres was chosen as a pun: in an old style of Japanese counting, 6-3-4 reads 'mu-sa-shi' -- Musashi, the ancient name of the province and plain that Tokyo was built on. This kind of number-wordplay is called goroawase. The Skytree opened in 2012 as the world's tallest tower. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree; britannica.com/topic/Tokyo-Sky-Tree

question: On spring afternoons, the sky over Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, and Nebraska can turn green-black. Those plains spawn more twisters than anywhere on Earth. What nickname do weather experts give this strip of land?
context: Tornado Alley isn't an official line on any map but a nickname for the central Great Plains, where cold, dry air off the Rocky Mountains collides with warm Gulf moisture to breed more twisters than anywhere on Earth. The Dust Bowl was the 1930s drought that scoured these same plains; Hail Alley is the High Plains belt battered by the nation's worst hail; Hoosier Alley is a smaller tornado zone around Indiana and the Ohio Valley. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tornado_Alley

question: Tornado Alley — the great stretch of the United States plains reaching from Texas up through Oklahoma, Kansas, and Nebraska — spins up more twisters than anywhere on Earth. Every spring, from April through June, two very different air masses come racing at each other over these flatlands and slam together. Which clash of air feeds Tornado Alley's storms?
answer: dry air off the Rocky Mountains riding over moist air from the Gulf of Mexico
choices: dry air off the Rocky Mountains riding over moist air from the Gulf of Mexico
cool marine air off the Pacific sliding under hot air from the Mojave Desert
monsoon moisture from the Gulf of California damming against the Sierra Madre
frigid Arctic air from Canada pouring down onto the humid Atlantic Seaboard
context: The setup is a layer cake of instability: dry, cool air spilling east off the Rockies rides up and over warm, wet air streaming north from the Gulf of Mexico. The trapped moist layer bursts upward into towering, rotating thunderstorms called supercells - the parent storms of most violent tornadoes. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tornado_Alley

question: Each spring over the Texas Panhandle, a hidden line splits hot dry desert air from wet Gulf air. Cross it and the air can drop tens of degrees within a mile. Storm chasers wait on it because huge rotating storms often fire right along it. What do forecasters call this line?
context: A dryline marks where hot, dry desert air meets Gulf moisture, often draped over the Texas Panhandle and western Plains in spring. Counterintuitively, the dry air is denser and wedges underneath the moist air, helping shove it upward into storms. Cross a dryline and the humidity - not the temperature - drops off a cliff. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dryline

question: On the evening of May 31, 2013, a colossal tornado dropped from a supercell thunderstorm and tore across the flat farmland near El Reno, Oklahoma. Storm chasers driving portable Doppler radar dishes clocked winds inside it past 300 miles per hour, and at one point the twister spread over 2.6 miles from edge to edge. Which world record does the El Reno tornado hold?
context: El Reno's tornado spread 2.6 miles (4.2 km) from edge to edge - the widest ever measured on Earth. Its winds screamed past 300 mph on mobile radar, yet surveyors rated it only EF3: tornado ratings read the damage left on the ground, not the wind itself, and this giant churned mostly over open country. Its record is width, not strength. Eight people died, including veteran storm researcher Tim Samaras, his son Paul, and Carl Young of the TWISTEX team - the first professional tornado researchers ever killed while chasing. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/2013_El_Reno_tornado

question: In Tornado Alley, forecasters rank each twister on one damage scale. A 0 snaps branches and peels shingles. A 5 rips asphalt off the road and lifts a well-built house right off its base. What is this scale called?
context: Ted Fujita of the University of Chicago introduced his F scale in 1971; the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale replaced it in the United States on February 1, 2007. An original F5 meant winds of roughly 261 to 318 mph - 'incredible damage.' Because the scale reads the wreckage on the ground rather than the wind directly, a ferociously fast tornado can still earn a middling rating if it stays over open country. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_scale

question: The Great Plains see the most tornadoes, but a belt across the Deep South - Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Georgia - kills far more people per storm. Meteorologists nicknamed it 'Dixie Alley.' What makes Dixie Alley's tornadoes so much deadlier than the ones out on the Plains?
answer: they strike after dark, when families are asleep and cannot see them
choices: they strike after dark, when families are asleep and cannot see them
they pack far stronger winds than any tornado the Plains can muster
they linger on the ground for hours, not the usual few minutes
they hurl grapefruit-sized hail ahead of the funnel
context: Dixie Alley's twisters strike disproportionately at night - about 29% after dark versus 19% on the Plains - and they hide in rain and dense forest, so people never spot the funnel. Night tornadoes kill roughly 2.5 times as many people, catching families asleep. The meteorologist Allen Pearson coined the name 'Dixie Alley' in 1971. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tornado_Alley

question: In southern China, along the Li River near Guilin, hundreds of steep gray hills rise from flat green rice fields. They look like a crowd of stone thumbs, shaped by water over ages. What is this kind of land called?
context: This is 'tower karst' — solid limestone slowly dissolved away by rainwater over millions of years, not pushed up by any volcano or earthquake. The word 'karst' itself comes from the Kras Plateau in Slovenia, the barren limestone country where these dissolving-rock features were first studied. Karst is no rare oddity: it covers roughly a fifth of the continental United States, and karst springs and aquifers supply about a quarter of the world's drinking water. Sources: Grokipedia 'Guilin' and 'Karst'; Wikipedia 'Tower karst' and 'Karst'.

question: In southern China, the Li River winds through Guangxi province past hundreds of tall, thumb-shaped limestone peaks. The back of China's 20-yuan banknote shows the single most famous view along the river. On it, a lone fisherman poles a slim bamboo raft past sharp peaks perfectly doubled in glassy still water. Which real bend of the Li River is this?
context: The spot is Yellow Cloth Shoal (Huangbu), just downstream of Xingping. It is named for a big flat beige slab of rock lying on the clear riverbed that looks like a sheet of yellow cloth spread out underwater; seven karst hills of different sizes stand around it, and it is famed for the finest peak-reflections on the whole Li River. Sources: lirivercruises.com (Li River 20-yuan note); topchinatravel.com (Li River).

question: In southern China's Guangxi province, the city of Guilin stands at the head of the Li River, ringed by the strange limestone thumb-hills that the Song-dynasty poet Fan Chengda (a 12th-century travel writer) once judged the finest scenery under heaven. The city's ancient name comes from a fragrant flowering tree that grew thick around it. What does the name 'Guilin' mean?
context: Guilin means 'forest of sweet osmanthus' — it was named for the fragrant osmanthus (cassia) trees that perfume the city each autumn. Its karst scenery was so admired that the Song-dynasty poet Fan Chengda praised it as the finest under heaven. Sources: Grokipedia 'Guilin'; Wikipedia 'Guilin' (Fan Chengda).

question: Along the Li River, Chinese geographers sort the stone towers two ways — fenglin, 'peak forests' of separate spires standing on a plain, and fengcong, 'peak clusters' of cones sharing one base. Both took millions of years to form. How did these towers come to stand so high above the flat land?
answer: rain slowly dissolved away the land around them
choices: rain slowly dissolved away the land around them
an ancient volcano pushed them up as plugs
an earthquake fault thrust them up from below
an ice-age glacier carved them from the plain
context: Both fenglin ('peak forest' of separate towers) and fengcong ('peak cluster' of cones on a shared base) are carved DOWN by dissolving water, never pushed UP by any earthquake or volcano — the towers are simply the hard rock left standing after the softer surrounding limestone dissolved away over millions of years. Sources: Waltham, 'Fengcong, fenglin, cone karst and tower karst'; corroborated ScienceDirect (S0169555X13003826).

question: Slovenia's rocky Kras Plateau is the land that gave 'karst' its name. On its bare limestone, rainwater soaks up a gas from the air and turns into a weak acid. That acid drips for ages and hollows out caves and sinkholes below. Which acid is it?
context: The acid is carbonic acid: rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil to form it, and this weak acid slowly dissolves the calcium carbonate that limestone is made of — the single reaction behind every cave, sinkhole, spring and stone tower on Earth. Slovenia's Kras Plateau, where these dissolving-rock features were first studied, is the barren limestone country that gave 'karst' its name. Sources: Grokipedia 'Karst'; Wikipedia 'Karst'.

question: In Vietnam's Gulf of Tonkin, roughly 1,600 islands crowd out of the emerald sea in a maze of quiet channels — a place so strange that its name means 'descending dragon.' Ha Long Bay is the world's grandest example of what?
context: Ha Long Bay is drowned tower karst — the very same limestone towers as Guilin, but here the sea rose after the last ice age and flooded the valleys between them, leaving about 1,600 islands in the Gulf of Tonkin. 'Ha Long' means 'descending dragon': legend says the gods sent a mother dragon and her young to defend Vietnam, and the jewels and jade they spat out turned into this wall of stone islands blocking invaders. Thailand has a smaller cousin — the lone limestone tower in Phang Nga Bay nicknamed 'James Bond Island' after the film The Man with the Golden Gun. Sources: Grokipedia 'Hạ Long Bay'; Wikipedia 'Ha Long Bay' and 'Tower karst'.

question: In Yunnan's Stone Forest (Shilin), rain dissolved the rock from the top down into a maze of tall grey blades and pinnacles — some 50 meters high — that you can wander between on foot. Stranger still is where all that stone began: more than 270 million years ago, long before the pinnacles existed, this ground lay somewhere very different. Where did it lie?
context: Shilin's limestone is over 270 million years old: it began as shell-and-seafloor mud when the region lay beneath an ancient sea, then hardened into limestone and was later dissolved from the surface down into these 50-meter blades — karst at ground level instead of towering river hills. The local Sani (Yi) people tell of Ashima, a girl forbidden to marry the man she loved, who turned to stone in the forest and gave it her name. With Guilin and dozens of other sites, Shilin is protected as the 'South China Karst' UNESCO World Heritage Site, one of Earth's largest karst regions at roughly 500,000 square kilometers. Sources: Grokipedia 'Stone Forest'; Wikipedia 'Stone Forest' (Ashima legend; 270-million-year age; Yi/Sani).

question: In Hunan province, Zhangjiajie's forest of thousands of sheer sky-pillars — the floating peaks that inspired the Hallelujah Mountains in the film Avatar — looks exactly like a field of giant tower karst. But no acid ever dissolved them, and they are not karst at all. What rock are these pillars actually made of?
context: Zhangjiajie's pillars are quartz sandstone, shaped by freeze-thaw ice and running water — not limestone dissolved by acid — so despite looking like giant tower karst, they are not karst at all. Their floating-peak silhouette inspired the Hallelujah Mountains of James Cameron's Avatar. It is the classic trap: not every stone tower is karst — the real test is whether acid slowly dissolving limestone made it. Source: Wikipedia 'Zhangjiajie National Forest Park' (quartz sandstone; 'not the product of chemical dissolution'; Avatar Hallelujah Mountain).

question: Most plate boundaries either crash and build mountains, or pull apart and leak lava. But one runs 1,200 km up California. There, the Pacific plate slides slowly past the North American plate, without crashing or splitting. Which famous fault is this?
context: The San Andreas Fault is the flagship transform boundary, running roughly 1,200 km (750 miles) up California. Unlike a subduction zone, where one plate dives beneath another, or a spreading ridge, where plates pull apart and new crust wells up, a transform boundary makes no new crust and destroys none — the two plates simply grind sideways past each other. The Alpine (New Zealand), Denali (Alaska), and North Anatolian (Turkey) faults are other real transform faults. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault; USGS.

question: On California's dry Carrizo Plain, a stream called Wallace Creek runs toward the San Andreas Fault. Its lower half is found again 130 m to the northwest, dragged along by the plates. Most of that shift crept up over ages, but 23 feet of it jumped at once in a great 1857 quake. Which quake gave Wallace Creek that jolt?
context: Wallace Creek is a textbook 'offset stream': the San Andreas has sliced its channel and dragged the downstream half about 130 m (425 ft) northwest over thousands of years — but roughly 23 ft of that jump happened in a single instant during the 1857 Fort Tejon earthquake, the great quake that ruptured this southern stretch of the fault. On the treeless Carrizo Plain — under 9 inches of rain a year, so nothing overgrows the ground — you can still walk the dog-legged bend today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrizo_Plain.

question: In the great 1906 San Francisco earthquake, the San Andreas Fault didn't crack at a single point — in one violent instant it split open along a continuous seam, leaving roads and fences that crossed it jogged out of line. The whole San Andreas runs about 750 miles. How much of that entire fault tore open in this one rupture?
answer: more than a third of it
choices: more than a third of it
context: The 1906 rupture tore along roughly 477 km (296 mi) of the San Andreas at about magnitude 7.9 — more than a third of the fault's entire 750-mile length ripped open in a single instant. Along the way the two sides slid up to about 6 m (20 ft) past each other horizontally, leaving fences and roads with a clean 20-foot jog that became textbook evidence of how the fault moves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906_San_Francisco_earthquake.

question: California's San Andreas Fault is a giant crack in Earth's crust where two tectonic plates grind past each other. Everything west of the fault sits on the Pacific plate and drifts slowly northwest. So Los Angeles creeps away from the rest of California at a few inches a year, while San Francisco stays put on the other plate. Fast-forward that motion 20 million years. Where does it put Los Angeles?
context: Los Angeles rides the Pacific plate; San Francisco sits on the North American plate; the two creep past each other at 1-2 inches a year. Project that steady slide forward about 20 million years and Los Angeles — today some 350 miles south — would draw right up alongside San Francisco. Not a collision, just two cities that end up neighbours. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault; USGS.

question: The tiny town of Parkfield sits squarely astride the San Andreas Fault, and it has logged a magnitude-6 earthquake at almost clockwork intervals — in 1857, 1881, 1901, 1922, 1934, 1966, and 2004, roughly one every 22 years. So reliably do its quakes arrive that Parkfield has given itself a nickname. What does the town call itself?
answer: the Earthquake Capital of the World
choices: the Earthquake Capital of the World
the Earthquake Capital of the West Coast
context: Parkfield, home to only a few dozen people, straddles the San Andreas and has produced a magnitude-6 quake about every 22 years since 1857 — so predictably that the USGS made it the site of a long-running earthquake-prediction experiment, wiring the ground with instruments. Its proud self-given title: 'the Earthquake Capital of the World.' Source: https://www.earthquaketracker.org/faults/san-andreas; USGS Parkfield experiment.

question: Turkey's North Anatolian Fault is a near twin of the San Andreas Fault, and its great earthquakes have come in an orderly chain since a devastating quake struck Erzincan in 1939. Each rupture piles stress onto the next section, so the fault tears open piece by piece, like a zipper. Toward which great city has that chain of quakes been steadily working its way?
context: The 1939 Erzincan quake (magnitude ~7.9, over 32,000 dead) began a westward-marching sequence: each rupture transferred stress to the neighbouring segment, more than 1,000 km of the fault breaking over the century. The 1999 Izmit quake (magnitude 7.6, over 18,000 killed) struck less than 100 km east of Istanbul, loading the last unbroken 'Marmara gap' right beneath the city — the segment seismologists now watch most closely. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Anatolian_Fault.

question: A great strike-slip fault runs down the Jordan Rift Valley through the Levant, where the Arabian plate has ground about 105 km north past the African plate. Like the San Andreas, it mostly just slides sideways — but wherever its line steps to one side, the crust caught between the steps has pulled apart and dropped into a deep pit. Strung out along this one sliding fault, those dropped basins have filled with water to make a famous chain. Which three bodies of water sit in the pits this fault opened?
answer: the Dead Sea, the Sea of Galilee, and the Gulf of Aqaba
choices: the Dead Sea, the Sea of Galilee, and the Gulf of Aqaba
the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, and Lake Nasser
the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, and the Sea of Azov
the Persian Gulf, the Tigris, and the Euphrates
context: Where a strike-slip fault steps sideways, the crust in between stretches and drops, opening what geologists call a 'pull-apart basin.' The Dead Sea Transform's left-stepping bends dropped the pits now filled by the Sea of Galilee, the Dead Sea, and the Gulf of Aqaba. The Dead Sea's shore, about 430 m below sea level, is the lowest dry land on Earth — a record that exists only because two plates are sliding past each other. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea_Transform.

question: In northwestern Turkey near the Aegean coast, a grassy mound called Hisarlik looks at first like one weathered ruin. But when archaeologists began digging in the 1800s, they found city built on top of city — Homer's legendary Troy among them — layered again and again over about 3,000 years. How many cities are stacked inside the mound?
context: Labelled Troy I to Troy IX from bottom to top, the nine cities span roughly 3000 BC to 500 AD -- each one raised on the levelled rubble of the last, piling ~15 metres of ruins into a single hill. (worldhistory.org, Discovery of Troy; UNESCO WHS 849)

question: At Hisarlik the stone ramparts and gateway of Troy still stand -- solid, real, and climbable today. Yet the single most famous object from the whole tale of Troy's fall was never once found in the ground, and belongs entirely to legend. Which fabled object was it?
context: Homer's Iliad set the Trojan War at this mound, and the stone walls are genuine -- but no horse was ever excavated. Oddly, the wooden horse isn't even in the Iliad: it turns up only later, in the Odyssey. (Wikipedia: Trojan Horse)  (Legend.)

question: Hisarlik rises about 15 metres above a flat plain in northwest Turkey, yet the hill is not natural. For three thousand years, mud-brick towns rose and fell on the very same spot, each collapse lifting the ground a little higher until a whole hill had formed. Archaeologists across the Near East have one short, specific name for an ancient mound built up like this. What is it?
context: A tell is a mound raised from the layered remains of successive settlements; Hisarlik, Jericho, and Megiddo are famous examples. A barrow and a kurgan are burial mounds, and a midden is an ancient rubbish heap. (worldhistory.org; UNESCO WHS 849)

question: Troy sat on the hill of Hisarlik. Most of the nine Troys were built from mud brick, so their walls melted into a soft hill. But Troy VI had huge walls cut from a much harder rock quarried nearby. That is why they still stand today. What stone are Troy's mighty walls built from?
context: Troy VI's citadel walls -- mortarless cut blocks sloping inward -- still rise 9-10 m in places and stand up to 5 m thick, much of the horseshoe circuit and its gates surviving at Hisarlik today. The humbler mud-brick cities simply crumbled into the mound. (Wikipedia: Troy)

question: The showpieces of the gold hoard Heinrich Schliemann dug from Hisarlik were its glittering golden crowns, fit for royalty. Caught up in Homer's tale, Schliemann gave them a romantic nickname that has clung to them ever since. What did he call the gold diadems of 'Priam's Treasure'?
context: 'Priam's Treasure' held gold diadems nicknamed the 'Jewels of Helen,' along with about 8,750 tiny gold rings, gold goblets, silver vases, and copper weapons. Schliemann tied the crowns to Helen of Troy, the runaway queen of Homer's tale whose flight launched the war. The Mask of Agamemnon and the Cup of Nestor came from Mycenae, and the Ring of Minos from Crete. (Wikipedia: Priam's Treasure)

question: Slicing north-south through the Hisarlik mound is a colossal man-made gash, about 40 metres wide and dug clear down to bedrock. It was torn out in the 1870s by a treasure-hunting excavator in his impatient rush to reach Homer's Troy, wrecking priceless layers on the way down. Visitors still call this great scar by its digger's name -- which is it?
context: Heinrich Schliemann's Trench -- about 40 m wide and cut to bedrock -- sliced straight through the Late Bronze Age citadel, the very layer now thought to be Homer's Troy, destroying much of what he was hunting for. Blegen, Korfmann, and Dorpfeld were later, more careful excavators of the mound. (Wikipedia: Schliemann's Trench; worldhistory.org)

question: The ancient Greek poet Homer told of the Trojan War in his epic poem The Iliad — a ten-year Greek siege of the walled city of Troy. For centuries no one knew if Troy had been real. Then diggers at the mound of Hisarlik in Turkey found not one Troy but a stack of ruined cities built on top of each other across thousands of years. Archaeologists number the layers Troy I through Troy IX. Homer's Trojan War is most often matched to which layer?
context: As of 2013 only about 2-3% of Troy's lower city had been excavated, and roughly 2 m of the mound's surface has eroded away over the centuries, carrying buried evidence with it. Most of Troy still lies underground, waiting. (Wikipedia: Troy)

question: The gold hoard from Hisarlik became world-famous as 'Priam's Treasure,' named for the Trojan king of Homer's war. The gold is real -- but when archaeologists finally dated the layer it lay in, the royal label collapsed. Set against the true war-era Troy of King Priam, how far off is this treasure's age?
context: The hoard came from the Troy II layer, roughly 2400-2200 BC, while Priam's war-era city is Troy VI/VIIa, around 1250 BC -- so the gold predates any King Priam by about a thousand years. The treasure is real; the 'Priam' label is wrong. (Wikipedia: Priam's Treasure; worldhistory.org)

question: For a hundred years, people pictured Troy as just the small stone fort on top of the mound at Hisarlik. Then in the late 1980s, Manfred Korfmann's team found a whole lower town around it. A wide ditch cut into the bedrock ringed the town. Once that lower town is counted, how much bigger is the real Troy than the fort everyone thought?
context: Korfmann's lower town covered about 30 hectares, ringed by a defensive ditch cut into the bedrock -- proof that Troy was over sixteen times the size of the citadel-only ruin everyone had pictured. (Wikipedia: Troy)

question: The Troy VIIa houses at Hisarlik were crammed with stores for hard times: sunk deep into their clay floors stood colossal jars, some taller than a grown man, for hoarding grain, oil, and water. Greek archaeology has a specific name for storage jars of this giant, floor-sunk kind. What are they called?
context: Pithoi are giant storage jars; sunk into the Troy VIIa floors alongside rooms subdivided into cramped quarters, they read like a town packing in people and hoarding food -- bracing for a siege. Amphorae carried wine and oil, kraters mixed wine, and kylikes were drinking cups. (Wikipedia: Troy)

question: One layer in the Hisarlik stack reads like a 3,000-year-old crime scene: sealed beneath a black burn line, its lanes strewn with sling-stones and Greek-style bronze arrowheads, its dead left lying unburied where they fell. Fire, weapons, and slaughter -- this is the storming and sack that best fits Homer's tale of a city put to the torch. Which of Troy's nine stacked cities is this, the layer archaeologists call the closest match to Homer's sacked Troy?
context: Fire, embedded weapons, and unburied dead mark a violent sack rather than a natural disaster or slow decline, making Troy VIIa (~1300-1180 BC) the best archaeological match for the sacked Troy of Homer's tale. Carl Blegen led its excavation. Troy II was Schliemann's early treasure layer, the grander Troy VI just below fell instead to a natural disaster, and Troy IX was the late Roman-era city. (worldhistory.org; Wikipedia: Troy)

question: When an undersea earthquake jolts the seafloor, it flings up a huge wave that races across the ocean. People used to call this a tidal wave. Scientists say that name is wrong — the Moon's tides have nothing to do with it. The right word is the Japanese word 'tsunami.' What does 'tsunami' really mean?
context: 'Tsunami' (津波) joins tsu, 'harbour,' and nami, 'wave' — named because the swell that seemed slight far out at sea reared up to wreck Japan's harbours. Calling it a 'tidal wave' is wrong: tides are the gentle Moon-and-Sun pull on the whole ocean, while a tsunami is the water column shoved upward when a quake heaves the seafloor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: A tsunami is a giant wave born when an undersea earthquake jolts the seafloor. Out on the deep Pacific, that wave is just a small bump on the surface — a ship right over it would hardly feel it. But below the surface, the whole ocean is racing at more than 800 km/h. That is about as fast as which of these?
context: A tsunami is not a wind-blown surface wave — an undersea quake sets the entire depth of the ocean moving at once, so it carries immense energy while barely rising above the swell. In deep water it can race at over 800 km/h (about 500 mph), roughly a jet's cruising speed, crossing an entire ocean in hours; a passing ship feels almost nothing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: On 26 December 2004 a magnitude ~9.1 quake ruptured the seafloor off Sumatra and sent tsunamis sweeping across the whole Indian Ocean, killing about 228,000 people in 14 countries — the deadliest tsunami ever recorded. Afterward, one stark reason the toll ran so high stood out above the rest. What was it?
answer: the region had no tsunami warning system
choices: the region had no tsunami warning system
the tremor felt too small to fear
the waves struck in the dead of night
the earthquake had cut every phone line
context: In 2004 the Indian Ocean had no tsunami buoys and no alert network at all, unlike the Pacific — so the coasts got no warning whatsoever. The waves were still noticed ~8,500 km away at Struisbaai, South Africa. Worst hit were Aceh in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Tamil Nadu in India, and Khao Lak in Thailand. The disaster spurred the world to build an Indian Ocean warning system. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake_and_tsunami.

question: The giant quakes that make tsunamis happen in the same places again and again. Alaska, Japan, Chile, and the Cascadia coast are all strung along one great belt around the Pacific. That is why the world's oldest tsunami warning center keeps watch from Hawaii at the ocean's heart. What is this quake belt called?
context: The 'Ring of Fire' is the horseshoe of subduction-zone trenches and volcanoes rimming the Pacific, where oceanic plates dive beneath others and unleash the megaquakes that shove up tsunamis — off Alaska, Japan, Chile, and Cascadia. The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center, the world's oldest, was set up in Hawaii to watch it; the Indian Ocean had no such guard in 2004. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: On All Saints' morning in 1755, a huge quake shook Lisbon for minutes. Then the harbor sea drained away. Ships lay on the bare mud and crowds walked out to gawk. Forty minutes later, a tsunami rolled back over them. Why does the sea sometimes pull back like that before a tsunami hits?
answer: the wave's trough reaches shore before its crest
choices: the wave's trough reaches shore before its crest
the quake drops the seabed and drains the bay
the wave draws the water up into its crest
the falling tide happens to meet the wave
context: The Lisbon quake (~M7.7+) shook for up to six minutes on All Saints' Day; the sea then drew back, luring the curious onto the mud before the tsunami engulfed the harbour ~40 minutes after the shock; a firestorm then burned for days, and ~40,000–50,000 died. The sea withdraws only when the wave's trough leads its crest — so it happens often, not always. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake.

question: Racing across deep water, the 2004 tsunami stood only about a meter tall. But when it swept into the shallows at Banda Aceh in Sumatra, the front slowed down. Water behind piled into it, and it reared up 15 to 30 meters high. What is this piling-up of a wave in shallow water called?
context: In deep water a tsunami's crests can be 200 km apart yet only ~1 m tall; nearing shore, 'shoaling' slams on the brakes — speed falls from ~800 to under 80 km/h and the wavelength shrinks, so the trailing water piles the wave up into a towering wall. At Banda Aceh in 2004 it rose 15–30 m, with a maximum around 51 m. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: On Maikhao Beach in Phuket, Thailand, on 26 December 2004, ten-year-old Tilly Smith watched the sea froth and pull far back. Curious adults wandered out onto the wet sand. But Tilly screamed for everyone to run. She had seen the warning signs before. Where had she learned them just two weeks earlier?
choices: from a survivor of an earlier wave
context: Tilly Smith's teacher, Andrew Kearney at Danes Hill School, had shown the class the warning signs just two weeks earlier — the sea pulling back, the water frothing, waves that go out but don't return — using footage of the 1946 Aleutian Islands tsunami. Recognizing all three at Maikhao, she got the beach and hotel evacuated, and about 100 people were saved. A geography lesson literally saved lives. Source: International Tsunami Information Center (itic.ioc-unesco.org).

question: When the volcano Krakatoa blew itself apart in the Sunda Strait in 1883, the blast was one of the loudest sounds ever heard. People caught it thousands of kilometers away. Yet of the roughly 36,000 people it killed, the blast itself claimed only a small share. What killed most of them?
context: Of the roughly 36,000 people killed by Krakatoa's 1883 eruption in the Sunda Strait, more than 34,000 died not from the explosion but from the tsunamis it raised — waves some 30–37 m high that crashed onto the coasts of Java and Sumatra. The blast itself was heard about 4,500 km away in Perth, Australia, one of the loudest sounds ever recorded. Volcanoes, not only earthquakes, can raise killer waves. Source: ncei.noaa.gov, 'On This Day: Historic Krakatau Eruption of 1883.'

question: High above the hamlet of Aneyoshi in Miyako, Japan, a stone slab carved by ancestors generations ago bears a stark command: 'Do not build any homes below this point. Remember the calamity of the great tsunamis.' Then, in 2011, the greatest tsunami in living memory surged up the valley toward the village. What became of every household that had obeyed the ancient stone and built above its line?
context: The Aneyoshi stone reads in full: 'High dwellings are the peace and harmony of our descendants. Remember the calamity of the great tsunamis. Do not build any homes below this point.' In 2011 the wave climbed the valley and halted about 100 m below the stone — and every household that had stayed above it survived. Japan has hundreds of such tsunami stones, some over 600 years old, many placed after an 1896 tsunami killed ~22,000 — ancestral knowledge carved to outlast living memory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami_stone; nbcnews.com.

question: On 9 July 1958 an earthquake dropped 30 million cubic metres of rock off a cliff into the narrow inlet of Lituya Bay, in Alaska. The splash surged 524 metres up the far mountainside — higher than the Empire State Building — and tore away the whole forest. This was the tallest wave ever recorded on Earth, yet how many people did it kill?
context: This was a landslide megatsunami, not an ocean-crossing tsunami: the rockfall's splash surged 524 m (1,719 ft) up the far slope — taller than the Empire State Building — the tallest wave ever recorded. Because Lituya Bay is a remote Alaskan inlet, only about five people died, on fishing boats caught in the bay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1958_Lituya_Bay_earthquake_and_megatsunami.

question: On 11 March 2011 a magnitude ~9.0 quake struck off Japan's Oshika Peninsula; the tsunami ran up to 40 metres high, pushed 10 km inland at Sendai, and overwhelmed one coastal site whose failure turned a natural disaster into a nuclear one. Which site did the wave overwhelm?
context: The magnitude ~9.0 quake struck 72 km off the Oshika Peninsula; the tsunami killed about 19,759 people, ran up to 40.5 m at Miyako, and pushed 10 km inland at Sendai, where people had only 8–10 minutes' warning. It flooded the Fukushima Daiichi plant and caused three reactor meltdowns — a natural disaster that became a nuclear one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Tōhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami.

question: Almost every great Maya city was hidden deep inland under thick jungle. But one was built right on the edge of a low cliff, its stone temples looking straight out over open water. Tulum, on the Yucatan coast of Mexico, is the only major Maya city set on the sea. Which sea meets the cliffs below it?
context: Tulum stands on a cliff about 12 metres (39 ft) high on the east coast of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula -- the only major Maya city built on the coast, while almost all the others hide inland in the jungle. Below its temples the Caribbean glows famously turquoise. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tulum'.

question: The Maya called their clifftop city Zama long before anyone renamed it Tulum. Its temples stand on a low cliff on the Yucatan coast, looking straight out across the open Caribbean. What does that older Maya name, 'Zama', mean?
context: Zama means 'dawn' or 'sunrise' -- fitting, because the cliff faces due east, so the temples catch the very first light coming up over the Caribbean each morning. The name we use today, 'Tulum', is different and much newer: it comes from the Yucatec Maya word for 'wall', pointing to the great rampart that ringed the city. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tulum'; Ancient Origins.

question: El Castillo, the tallest temple crowning Tulum's clifftop, looks out over the Caribbean cove where the city's traders once beached canoes loaded with obsidian, jade and salt. Archaeologists think this seaside temple quietly did a second job beyond worship. What do they think it doubled as?
context: This beacon role is an interpretation, not a proven fact. Because El Castillo lines up with the one natural break in the offshore reef, researchers think lights placed in its windows could have been lined up to guide trading canoes safely through that channel into the sheltered cove. Tulum was a busy Postclassic port trading obsidian, jade and salt. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tulum'.  (Legend.)

question: Cross far to the north — Siberia, Alaska, northern Canada — and the trees run out on the treeless plain called tundra. Under a thin summer layer of moss and grass, the deeper soil never thaws. Winter freezes it right through, and summer never reaches down to warm it. It stays frozen solid all year, every year. What is this always-frozen ground called?
context: 'Permafrost' means ground that stays at or below 0 C (32 F) for at least two years straight. Only a thin top 'active layer' — averaging about 1.5 m — thaws each summer; below that the freeze runs deep, reaching roughly 1,493 m down in Siberia's Lena and Yana river basins. About 15% of the Northern Hemisphere's land sits on permafrost. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permafrost

question: In the Siberian village of Oymyakon, drivers keep their engines running around the clock so the fuel won't freeze solid, and school carries on until the air sinks past -55 C. Only about 500 people endure winters like this, year after year. What record does Oymyakon hold?
answer: the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth
choices: the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth
the coldest air temperature ever recorded on Earth
the northernmost inhabited village on Earth
the snowiest inhabited town on Earth
context: Oymyakon, in Sakha (Yakutia), hit an official -67.7 C (-89.9 F) on 6 February 1933 — the coldest reading ever at a permanently inhabited place. (Antarctica's Vostok station is colder still, but no one lives there year-round.) The nearby town of Verkhoyansk is its twin 'Pole of Cold.' Oymyakon's yearly swing is astonishing: from that -67.7 C low up to +34.6 C one summer, over 100 C apart. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oymyakon

question: Yakutsk, in eastern Siberia, is the biggest city on Earth built on permafrost. That is soil frozen solid far below the streets. A warm apartment block set right on that soil would melt the ice and slowly sink and crack. How do Yakutsk's builders hold up a big apartment block so its heat cannot melt the ground below?
answer: a grid of concrete piles sunk deep into the ground
choices: a grid of concrete piles sunk deep into the ground
an insulated gravel pad spread over the frozen soil
a ventilated crawl space kept open to the cold air
a refrigerated slab chilled by buried cooling pipes
context: Yakutsk (about 355,000 people) is the largest city on Earth built on continuous permafrost. Its concrete piles are driven deep into the frozen ground, holding buildings up on an air gap so their warmth can't reach and melt the ice below — otherwise the foundations would sink and split. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakutsk

question: Across the Arctic lowlands of Siberia and Alaska, ice-rich permafrost sometimes thaws. The ice that once held the soil grains together melts away. The land sags into a messy jumble of pits and hollows, and meltwater pools in the low spots. Geologists have a name for this pockmarked land born of melting ground. What is it called?
context: Thermokarst is named after 'karst' — the pitted, sinkhole-riddled landscape that limestone makes as it dissolves — because thawing permafrost leaves the same lumpy, sunken look. Water pooling in the hollows forms thermokarst lakes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermokarst

question: Across the shallow lakes of Siberia's tundra, as the frozen mud warms, a gas from ancient decay bubbles up through the water. When winter locks the lake surface in ice, the rising bubbles freeze in place, stacking into eerie pale discs trapped in the clear ice. Which gas, seeping from the thawing permafrost, forms these frozen bubbles?
context: As Arctic lake beds thaw, ancient organic mud releases methane — a potent greenhouse gas — that bubbles upward; when the surface freezes, the bubbles stack into pale white discs locked in the ice. Studies of Siberian thaw lakes found methane escaping far faster than scientists once thought. Source: nature.com/articles/nature05040

question: Deep in Siberia's Sakha Republic, the ground itself is coming apart. After loggers cleared a hillside in the 1960s, the bared permafrost began to thaw and cave in, ripping open the Batagaika crater — a gash now a kilometre long and up to 100 metres deep, its raw walls crumbling wider by more than 10 metres every year. The awe and dread it stirs earned it a grim local nickname. What do people call it?
context: The Batagaika crater in Sakha is the world's largest permafrost megaslump, still growing as its headwall retreats over 10 m a year. Its collapsing walls slice open an estimated 200,000 to 650,000 years of frozen record, exposing buried ancient forests and the bones of woolly mammoth, musk ox, and Ice-Age Lena horses. 'Gateway to the Underworld' is a local nickname. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batagaika_crater

question: In 2007, reindeer herders by the Yuribei River in Siberia stumbled on 'Lyuba,' a baby woolly mammoth — and she was no heap of old bones. Her skin, her organs, even the last meal in her stomach were still intact after roughly 42,000 years in the ground. What had kept her whole body preserved for all those millennia?
answer: the frozen ground had kept her like ice
choices: the frozen ground had kept her like ice
a tar pit had sealed her airtight
peat-bog acids had tanned her hide
dry desert air had mummified her
context: Permafrost is a natural deep-freezer. Baby mammoth 'Lyuba,' found in 2007 near the Yuribei River, spent roughly 42,000 years frozen with her skin, organs, and last meal preserved — which is why Siberia's frozen ground, not tar pits or bogs, is where whole Ice-Age mammoths keep turning up. Source: mymodernmet.com/lyuba-baby-woolly-mammoth/

question: Tundra isn't only a polar thing. Climb high enough up a tropical mountain — Ecuador's Andean volcanoes right on the equator, or Kilimanjaro over tropical East Africa — and the forest thins, then quits at the treeline, giving way to bare rock, cushion plants, and low mosses: alpine tundra, treeless for the very same reasons as the far north (too cold, too short a season for trees). Now follow that mountain treeline as you travel from the tropics toward the poles. What happens to its height?
answer: it sinks lower and lower until it reaches the sea
choices: it sinks lower and lower until it reaches the sea
it climbs higher and higher until it caps the summit
it stays at one fixed height at every latitude
it drops away all at once at the Arctic Circle
context: Alpine tundra sits above the treeline on tall mountains anywhere on Earth — the Andes, the Himalayas, even peaks in the tropics — while ARCTIC tundra lies at high latitude near the poles; both are treeless for the same reason (too cold, too short a growing season). As you move from the equator toward the poles, the alpine treeline drops lower and lower, until near the poles it reaches sea level and the mountain's alpine tundra merges with the polar tundra at the coast. (Chimborazo in Ecuador sits almost on the equator; Kilimanjaro lies about 3 degrees south, in the tropics.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_tundra

question: At the mouth of Yosemite Valley in California stands one huge wall of pale granite. It is about 100 million years old. Its face rises some 3,000 feet from bottom to top with no break in it. Climbers need days to reach the top. What is this giant rock called?
context: El Capitan is often called the largest exposed granite monolith on Earth. Glaciers didn't gouge Yosemite Valley out of nothing — they widened, deepened, and polished a river-cut gorge, leaving sheer walls like El Capitan towering over the flat green floor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Capitan

question: In California's Sierra Nevada mountains lies Yosemite Valley, a granite-walled canyon inside Yosemite National Park. As you enter the valley, the first waterfall you meet is a slim ribbon of water that drops 620 feet straight down a sheer cliff. Unlike many Sierra falls, it flows every month of the year. What is this welcoming waterfall called?
context: Bridalveil Fall drops 620 ft (188 m) and flows year-round. To the Ahwahneechee people it was 'Pohono,' the Spirit of the Puffing Wind — gusts funnel up the cliff and blow the thin ribbon sideways, sometimes sweeping it away before it reaches the ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridalveil_Fall

question: Bridalveil Fall doesn't tumble down a slope into Yosemite Valley — it leaps clear off the cliff and free-falls the whole way. It pours from what geologists call a 'hanging valley': a side valley left stranded high on the main valley's wall. Why did that side valley end up stranded so far above the floor?
answer: its smaller side-glacier couldn't grind as deep as the main glacier
choices: its smaller side-glacier couldn't grind as deep as the main glacier
the tributary river later cut its bed far below the side valley
a rockslide buried the lower end of the side valley long ago
an earthquake dropped the main valley floor much lower
context: The main glacier gouged Yosemite's deep U-trough while the tributary's smaller glacier could only scratch a shallow groove — so when the ice melted the side valley was left dangling, and its stream now free-falls off the lip. Bridalveil is the classic American hanging-valley waterfall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging_valley

question: In 1911 a young J.R.R. Tolkien hiked Switzerland's Lauterbrunnen Valley — a deep glacial cleft barely a kilometer wide, walled by limestone cliffs nearly 1,000 m high and laced with dozens of free-falling waterfalls. That valley of walls and waterfalls became his picture of which place in Middle-earth?
context: Lauterbrunnen's cliffs and cascades became Tolkien's mental picture of Rivendell, the elven refuge. The valley is a 'true cleft' whose roughly 1,000 m walls hold a local count of some 72 waterfalls. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauterbrunnen

question: Pure ice is far too soft to scratch hard granite. Yet at Yosemite's Lembert and Pothole Domes, the bedrock is buffed to a glassy shine so slick that hikers slip on it. All of it was the work of a glacier long since gone. If soft ice cannot grind granite, what actually did the polishing?
answer: grit and boulders frozen into the base of the ice
choices: grit and boulders frozen into the base of the ice
the sheer crushing weight of the overlying ice
meltwater streams rushing beneath the glacier
rain and wind wearing the rock after the ice left
context: Grit and rock frozen into a glacier's underside turn the moving ice into a sheet of sandpaper that abrades and polishes the bedrock. You can still see — and slip on — this glacial polish at Yosemite's Pothole and Lembert Domes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_striation

question: The lakes of Glacier National Park, Montana, glow an unreal turquoise — and it isn't from any dissolved mineral. The melting ice keeps pouring in rock particles that simply never settle out; they hang suspended and scatter the sunlight into that glowing blue-green. Geologists have a name for this glacier-made sediment. What is it?
context: Glacial flour is rock ground so fine by the ice that it never settles, staying suspended and scattering light into that turquoise glow. The park's namesake ice is fading fast — from about 150 glaciers in 1850 to roughly 25 by 2010. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier_National_Park_(U.S.)

question: Staubbach Falls leaps 297 m off a sheer cliff in Switzerland's Lauterbrunnen Valley — the highest free-falling waterfall in the country — dropping so far that the wind tears the water into drifting spray long before it reaches the ground. The Swiss named it 'Staubbach' for what that airborne water resembles. What does the 'Staub' in that name mean?
context: Staubbach Falls plunges 297 m (974 ft) — Switzerland's highest free-falling waterfall — and pours, like Bridalveil, from a hanging valley. It falls so far that the wind scatters the water into drifting spray, so the Swiss named it 'Staubbach,' the 'dust brook.' Its ghostly mist has drawn writers for centuries — Goethe visited in 1779 and wrote 'Gesang der Geister über den Wassern' ('Song of the Spirits over the Waters'). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staubbach_Falls

question: As a glacier grinds its way through a mountain valley, it drags along stones and grit frozen into the bottom of the ice. In California's Yosemite Valley, that grit both polished the exposed granite bedrock smooth and gouged it, cutting long, straight grooves called striations. Geologists hunt for these scratches because they reveal one specific thing about a glacier that vanished ages ago. What?
answer: the direction the ice once flowed
choices: the direction the ice once flowed
the thickness the ice once reached
the speed at which the ice moved
the year the ice finally melted
context: Because striations run the way the ice moved, geologists read them like arrows to reconstruct the path a vanished glacier took across the land — long after the ice itself is gone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_striation

question: Norway's Sognefjord snakes more than 200 km inland between towering rock walls, its water some 1,300 m deep, yet a shallow bar of bedrock still guards its mouth where it meets the open sea. A fjord like this is really just one familiar landform that the sea has flooded. Which?
context: A fjord is simply a glacial U-trough the sea has drowned — the same shape, flooded. The shallow bedrock 'sill' at Sognefjord's mouth is the ridge the glacier left behind; even its side valleys still 'hang,' meeting the main channel far above the deep floor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fjord

question: Yosemite Valley's cross-section gives its history away: not the sharp, narrow V of a river-cut canyon, but a smooth, rounded U-trough. A river and a glacier erode in fundamentally different ways, and that shape is the fingerprint. What does a glacier do to the rock that leaves a valley rounded into a U rather than notched into a V?
answer: it grinds along its whole width and base at once
choices: it grinds along its whole width and base at once
it presses down so hard it flattens only the floor
it plucks blocks from the highest walls alone
it dissolves the granite chemically with its meltwater
context: A river erodes at a single point, leaving a sharp V; a glacier plucks and grinds along its entire width and base, shaving the walls into a smooth parabolic U. That U-versus-V is the fingerprint that tells geologists ice, not water, shaped a valley — a transformation that can take 10,000 to 100,000 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U-shaped_valley

question: In the flat desert heart of Australia, the great rock Uluru rises 348 m straight up from a flat plain. Geologists took a German word for such a lone desert peak. They call Uluru an inselberg. What does that German word mean?
context: Uluru rises 348 m above the plain — taller than the Eiffel Tower — yet that is only its exposed part; measured from sea level, the summit stands 863 m up. A lone resistant mass rising abruptly from a flat plain like this is an inselberg, German for 'island mountain.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru

question: In the red desert heart of Australia stands the great rock Uluru. About 25 km west of Uluru rises a second formation of dozens of huge red domes, one the local Aṇangu people call Kata Tjuta. English maps once labeled it 'the Olgas,' but the Aṇangu name captures the sight far better. What does 'Kata Tjuta' mean in the Aṇangu language?
context: Kata Tjuta means 'many heads' in Pitjantjatjara, and it is a perfect name: the formation is a cluster of 36 separate rounded domes, 25 km west of Uluru. Europeans long called it 'the Olgas' after its tallest dome, Mount Olga. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kata_Tjuta

question: Uluru is a giant lone rock rising from the flat red desert of central Australia. At dawn and dusk, its whole surface seems to catch fire — the rock blazes deep red and orange, then fades to purple and grey. Break a piece open, though, and it is plain grey inside. So why does Uluru's outer surface glow red?
answer: iron in the rock has rusted
choices: iron in the rock has rusted
red desert dust has settled on it
a skin of red clay covers it
red rock lichen has spread over it
context: Uluru is made of arkose, a sandstone rich in the pink mineral feldspar. Iron in its outer skin has oxidized — literally rusted — so the surface reflects red and orange light and the whole rock seems to glow at sunrise and sunset, even though fresh, unweathered Uluru stone is grey. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru

question: People call Australia's Uluru 'a single rock,' which makes it sound like something you could stroll around in a minute. But this great lone stone rises 348 metres out of the flat red desert and runs on and on at the base. A marked walking trail loops the entire rock. About how far is one full lap around Uluru?
context: The base walk around Uluru runs 9.4 km — nearly six miles just to circle one rock. Walking it gives a real sense of the monolith's bulk: what you see above ground is one continuous, unbroken hump of stone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru

question: Uluru looks like an enormous boulder set on top of the flat desert plain. Its rock layers, though, are tilted almost straight up on end — nearly vertical, like the pages of a book stood on its spine. Studying that tilt, geologists made a startling discovery about the rock. What did they find?
answer: most of it is buried, like an iceberg
choices: most of it is buried, like an iceberg
it is hollow, riddled with caves
it was once the core of a volcano
it is slowly sinking into the sand
context: Uluru's layers were folded until they tilted almost vertical (about 85°), and they plunge kilometres straight down into the earth — the exposed rock is estimated to be at least 2,400 m thick, most of it hidden underground like the bulk of an iceberg. The giant we see is only the tip. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru

question: Uluru gets nearly all the postcards, but 25 km west stands its neighbor Kata Tjuta. The tallest of Kata Tjuta's 36 domes, Mount Olga, hides a surprise when you compare its height with Uluru's. Measured from the desert plain, how tall is Mount Olga next to the famous Uluru?
choices: almost exactly as tall as Uluru
about half as tall as Uluru
context: Mount Olga, the tallest of Kata Tjuta's domes, reaches 1,066 m above sea level — about 546 m above the plain, roughly 200 m higher than Uluru's 348 m rise. So the less-famous formation is actually the taller one. The explorer Ernest Giles named the peak in 1872 for Queen Olga of Württemberg. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kata_Tjuta

question: Tucked against the base of Uluru in central Australia's red desert is a sacred site called Mutitjulu. Here the Aṇangu people tell an ancient story about Kuniya the python and Liru the deadly snake, and how their fight scarred the rock face itself. What natural feature sits at Mutitjulu, right at the foot of Uluru?
context: The Mutitjulu waterhole is a permanent water source at Uluru's base — precious in the desert — and a sacred Aṇangu site tied to the ancestral story of Kuniya the python and Liru the venomous snake. Parks Australia asks that the full story be learned at the place itself rather than casually retold. Source: https://uluru.gov.au/discover/culture/stories/kuniya-liru-stories/  (Legend.)

question: The Aṇangu are the traditional owners of Uluru, and to them the rock is deeply sacred. In 2019, acting on a decision the Aṇangu themselves made about how their sacred site should be treated, Parks Australia carried out their wishes. What did the Aṇangu decide?
answer: climbing the rock would end for good
choices: climbing the rock would end for good
photographing the rock would be banned
the whole park would close to visitors
visitors would need a permit to enter
context: Ownership of Uluru was formally returned to the Aṇangu on 26 October 1985. Exactly 34 years later, on 26 October 2019, the summit climb was permanently closed — at the Aṇangu's request, as their decision, out of respect for the sacred rock. Uluru and Kata Tjuta were jointly listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 for both their natural and their Aboriginal cultural value. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru

question: The sandstone that makes up Australia's great rock Uluru is staggeringly old — it formed around 550 million years ago, when Earth's continents were arranged in ways no map today would recognise. To grasp how ancient that is: when Uluru's rock was forming, which of these was only just appearing on Earth?
context: Uluru's arkose sandstone is roughly 550 to 530 million years old, from the Neoproterozoic into the early Cambrian — older than the dinosaurs by some 300 million years, and older than nearly every animal that ever walked the Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru

question: Uluru and Kata Tjuta rise from the same desert, just 25 km apart. Yet they weathered into very different shapes. Uluru is one smooth block. Kata Tjuta is 36 towering domes. Uluru is solid sandstone. What is Kata Tjuta made of, that split it into 36 heads instead?
context: Kata Tjuta is conglomerate — cobbles and boulders of many rock types cemented in a sandstone paste, like natural concrete. That coarse, uneven rock weathered into 36 separate rounded heads, while Uluru's finer, more uniform arkose sandstone eroded into one smooth block. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kata_Tjuta

question: In the flat red heart of Australia, one huge rock rises 348 meters straight up from a dead-flat desert. It is 9.4 km around at its base. Open plain runs to the horizon in every direction. What do geographers call a lone rock mountain like Uluru that stands over a flat plain?
context: Uluru is the world's most famous inselberg (German for 'island mountain') — a mass of tough rock left standing when the softer land around it slowly wore away. It rises 348 m above the plain, measures 9.4 km around its base, and its summit reaches 863 m above sea level. Source: Wikipedia, 'Uluru'.

question: The Anangu are the Aboriginal keepers of Uluru. Their sacred Tjukurpa stories (the Dreaming) are more than legend. The stories have been told for tens of thousands of years. They help people stay alive in the harsh desert. They also map onto Uluru's caves and gullies. What life-or-death knowledge do they also hold?
answer: where and when to find water and food
choices: where and when to find water and food
how to forecast the coming year's weather
which stars mark each season's turning
how to heal sickness with desert plants
context: Tjukurpa is the foundation of Aņangu culture — not written down but memorised and passed to the right people across tens of thousands of years. Its stories map ancestral events onto real places, but they also record how to travel and where and when to find water and food — practical survival knowledge woven into sacred law. Source: Parks Australia, uluru.gov.au (Tjukurpa).

question: The 348-metre red dome of Uluru that rises above the desert is only the tip. Geologists have traced its rock continuing straight down beneath the sand, so that — like an iceberg — most of Uluru's mass is hidden underground. Roughly how far down does the rock reach below the surface?
context: What shows above ground is only the tip of Uluru: its arkose sandstone keeps going straight down, with exposed rock strata at least about 2.4–2.5 km thick — so most of the rock's bulk is hidden underground, like an iceberg. Source: Wikipedia, 'Uluru' + Australian Govt DCCEEW.

question: At dawn and dusk, Uluru seems to catch fire — its whole face glows a deep, burning red across the desert. Yet step into the caves at its base and the very same rock is plain grey, so the colour is only skin-deep. What has turned the outer surface of this grey rock red?
answer: iron in the rock has rusted
choices: iron in the rock has rusted
red desert sand has stained it
red algae has spread across it
the sun's heat has scorched it
context: Uluru glows red because iron in its outer rock has literally rusted — the red skin is oxidised iron. The fresh arkose underneath is actually grey, and you can still see that original grey colour inside Uluru's caves. Source: Australian Govt DCCEEW + uluru.gov.au (Geology).

question: At the base of Uluru lies Mutitjulu, the one waterhole that holds water the whole year. For countless generations it has been the most trusted Anangu campsite in a harsh desert. In Anangu Tjukurpa, a powerful ancestor watches over Mutitjulu and all that happens there. What kind of creature is this guardian?
context: In Tjukurpa, Mutiṭjulu is the home of Wanampi, an ancestral water snake believed to guard the pool. Mutiṭjulu is the only permanent (year-round) waterhole at Uluru and was for centuries a key Aņangu campsite. Source: Parks Australia, uluru.gov.au (Water) + Australian Govt DCCEEW.  (Legend.)

question: The Anangu closed the Uluru climb for good in October 2019. To outsiders, the reason seemed clear: the rock is sacred. But the sign the Anangu left at the base gave a different main reason. It surprised many visitors. It came from how they see their duty under Tjukurpa. What worried the Anangu most?
answer: the safety of the visitors themselves
choices: the safety of the visitors themselves
litter left behind on the steep trail
disturbance to the local desert wildlife
context: The Aņangu base sign read: 'This is our home. As custodians, we are responsible for your safety and behaviour. We worry about you and we worry about your family.' The climb closed on 26 October 2019 — the 34th anniversary of 'Handback', the 1985 return of the land to its traditional owners. Board chairman Sammy Wilson called it not a loss but a celebration: 'The land has law and Culture... Closing the climb is not something to feel upset about but a celebration.' Source: Parks Australia, uluru.gov.au (climb closure).

question: Uluru's rock began as flat layers of sand laid down more than 500 million years ago. Long afterward, a vast mountain-building event called the Alice Springs Orogeny squeezed and buckled this whole region of Australia for tens of millions of years. Read the bands on Uluru today and you can see what that squeezing did to its once-flat layers. How do those layers lie now?
choices: left as a gently sloping ramp
context: Uluru's arkose is about 550–530 million years old. The Alice Springs Orogeny (~400–300 million years ago) tilted its once-horizontal layers to a dip of about 85° — almost straight up and down. Source: Wikipedia, 'Uluru'.

question: About 30 kilometres west of Uluru rises Kata Tjuṭa, a cluster of 36 steep-sided red domes whose Pitjantjatjara name means 'many heads.' Uluru itself stands 348 metres above the plain. How does the height of Kata Tjuṭa's tallest dome, Mount Olga, compare with Uluru?
answer: taller than Uluru, by roughly 200 metres
choices: taller than Uluru, by roughly 200 metres
shorter than Uluru, by roughly 200 metres
almost exactly as tall as Uluru
barely a third of Uluru's height
context: Kata Tjuṭa's tallest dome, Mount Olga, rises about 546 m above the plain (1,066 m above sea level) — roughly 198 m higher than Uluru's 348 m. Kata Tjuṭa is made of conglomerate — cobbles and boulders of granite and basalt cemented together — a completely different rock from Uluru's arkose sandstone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kata Tjuta'.

question: Ushuaia sits on the island of Tierra del Fuego, facing the Beagle Channel. Its motto reads 'fin del mundo, principio de todo' -- 'end of the world, beginning of everything.' Cruise ships bound for Antarctica pick up their passengers at its docks. What is Ushuaia billed as among the world's cities?
context: Ushuaia (~82,000+ residents) is billed as the world's southernmost CITY and the last big port before Antarctica -- one of only five 'Antarctic gateway' cities, the closest to the Antarctic Peninsula (~1,000 km), and it handles over 90% of all tourists who visit Antarctica. Honest caveat: a smaller Chilean town, Puerto Williams, sits a little farther south across the Beagle Channel, so Ushuaia is really the southernmost city of substantial SIZE. Its own name comes from the native Yamana word for a 'bay penetrating westward.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ushuaia; mercopress.com; earthobservatory.nasa.gov)
